1935-01-26.text: 'VANCOUVER. Jan. 26 (AP).-—Fifteen dead and four missing persons were counted today in storm-wracked British Columbia. An undetermined number were injured. Thousands of workers were summoned to restore wire and rail communications to storm-bound communities. Snow slides from the Rockies claimed nine of the 15 lives. The storm struck last Sunday, bringing unprecedented snow and flood conditions. A huge slide from Sumas mountain carried away 10 homes.

MOSCOW, Jan. 26. UP)—Valerian Kuibesheff, vice president of the council of people's commissars and member of the all-powerful political bureau of the communist party, died Friday of arteriosclerosis. The communist leader, who ranked with Joseph Stalin as one of the nine most powerful men in the Soviet, had suffered heart trouble for some time.

(Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) NEW YORK, Jan. 25—At least 34 persons were known to have perished and 12 others were feared lost tonight as boards of inquiry assembled to fix the blame for the sinking of the Ward liner Mohawk off the New Jersey coast last night. Eight of the victims were known passengers. Four women were among the unidentified dead. All except one of the bodies were recovered from the frigid Atlantic by searching vessels. Airplanes and the U. S. Navy Blimp K-1 directed operations from overhead. The 33 virtually frozen bodies were transferred from other craft to the coast guard patrol boat Icarus and sent to Bellevue Morgue in New York. The 34th victim, Kari R. Bart, of Philadelphia and Westmount, N. MARKS, Miss., Jan. 25--Red Cross workers cut lanes through ice tonight to reach marooned and suffering victims of an unprecedented North Mississippi Delta flood, while residents in at least a dozen towns south of here prepared to meet raging torrents of the Coldwater River. At least 25 lives already have been claimed by the waters and approximately 18,000 other persons were isolated and homeless. Baton Rouge, La., Jan. 26. (P)— Senator Huey P. Long arrived here today after an auto dash from New Orleans announcing that mob violence must stop and that he would make an inquiry into the plot. Reaching the capital last night where 100 men had threatened his dictatorship, he seized the parish courthouse, Long established command of the militia and other state men and ordered a 9 o'clock investigation of what he said was a murder plot involving four sheriffs and the district attorney.

(Associated Press Staff Writer) BATON ROUGE, La., Jan. 25— (AP)—Armed resistance to Huey Long’s dictatorship flared tonight as a group of more than 100 inflamed anti-Long citizens with shotguns, pistols and rifles seized East Baton Rouge courthouse. The movement was executed so quietly that the armed forces were in full possession of the parish seat of government before news of the coup spread. The invaders met with no opposition. Determined men shouldering sundry weapons guarded the entrances to the building and admitted only persons presenting proper identifications. The source of the movement remained clothed in mystery. The guards refused to identify themselves. Questions were met with smiles and grim responses that “you won't find out.” Wild rumors filled the town. Chicago, Jan. 25.—(/P)—Enraged at being stricken from relief rolls, a crippled youth and his mother today shot to death a case worker in their home and then stormed a relief agency where they fatally wounded the supervisor and shot down two other employees before turning their guns on themselves. They died instantly. Miss Caroling Watlare, supervisor of the agency, was the second of the targets of the mad attack to die. 1935-01-21.text: GENEVA. Jan. 19, (AP) - Great Britain has tried the system of public works as a remedy for unemployment and found it wanting. The experience is set forth in a 300-page volume, "National Public Works", published by the League of Nations on the basis of replies from 29 nations, including the United States. Britain’s reply was that "the experiment of large public works as a method of dealing with unemployment has been tried and has failed, and it is not intended to repeat it." It said the British view was that the ultimate test of each work must be its social or economic value.

NEW YORK (UP) — Two British warships raced to the aid of the British tank ship Valverda, afire in mid-Atlantic today while the stricken vessel’s crew fought to keep the flames from spreading to the oil cargo. “We can’t hold out much longer,” the radio operator of the Valverda tapped out to a startled seaboard. A few hours later he reported flames had eaten through the decks from the engine room and were spreading toward great storage tanks loaded with crude oil. Once the tanks are reached, all will be over for the Valverda. The operator coolly tapped out his signals despite the raging holocaust. “Flames on deck,” he reported. “Keeping into wind to keep fire from cargo. Burning fast. Urgently need assistance.” Engine rooms of tank ships are in the extreme stern. Seamen ashore reconstructing the scene from the operator's fragmentary reports, surmised that the entire stern of the ship was a

Florence, Italy, Jan. 21.—(P)— Former Queen Helen of Rumania Sunday denied the truth of rumors published in London that she was engaged to marry a prince of the house of Colonna. To the Associated Press correspondent who apprised her of the London dispatch she said the news was absolutely without foundation. She said she knew the Colonna family only through meeting them in ordinary society circles.

LONDON, Jan. 21.--(INS)--A fire aboard the Oil Tanker Valverde in mid-ocean which sent half a dozen vessels rushing to her aid was brought under control today, according to a wireless message received by her owners here. *The engine room was gutted by the fire,” the message read. The vessel is believed out of danger. The crew was unharmed.

New York, Jan. 20. (#)—Sir Malcolm Campbell, the British automobile speed merchant and present holder of the world’s mile record, will attempt to set up a new standard for the distance at Daytona Beach, Fla. between February 12 and 25 in his rebuilt Blue Bird. William F. Strum of Indianapolis, the Briton’s American representative, disclosed today that Campbell, Lady Campbell, six mechanics and a party of the speedster’s friends would reach New York Jan. 29 on the Aquitania and entrain immediately for Florida. Campbell's friends will include Major Goldie-Gardiner and Robin Grosvenor, heir to the Duke of Westminster. The famous racing machine will be on the same boat and Campbell expects to unpack it in Daytona by February 3.

BRUSSELS, Jan. 21.--(».-The Belgian government acted forcibly today to stamp out agitation in the Cantons of Eupen and Malmedy for a return to Germany. Additional troops marched into the area and a number of agitators for a union with the Reich, inspired by the recent Saar plebiscite, were jailed.

VIENNA, Jan. 21—(AP)—King Zog of Albania, the world’s only bachelor sovereign, is eager to wed—and he prefers an American girl, friends disclosed today. Beauty alone will not be a key to the throne. The lonely 39-year-old ruler has stipulated that his bride also must have ability and charm—and an income of one million dollars a year! The dying wish of Zog’s mother, Queen Mother Sadije, a few weeks ago, was that her son marry so he might provide an heir to the throne. Not only is Zog a bachelor, but he has four unmarried sisters on whom, at his request, parliament conferred the titles of “princess.”

1935-01-22.text: By Associated Press, Glasgow, Scotland, Jan. 22-5 A message to owners of the British tanker Valverda reported today the vessel is in “no immediate danger” but one member of the crew is dead. Relayed by the British Motor Liner Rangitiki, the message said: “The fire is now confined to the refrigerator. The vessel is in no immediate danger, Taylor, third engineer, succumbed to injuries. All others safe.” “Taylor” was 28, a resident of Port Glasgow. Gow, Harrison and Company own the Valverda, whose oil cargo was threatened when flames broke out in the engine room Sunday. The ship is about 1,000 miles off the coast of Florida. The Valverda said the Frobisher probably would tow her to Bermuda, approximately 800 miles away. Fire broke out in the Valverda’s engine room Sunday night and raged unchecked yesterday while the vessel sent out frantic calls for help. Last night the ship's master, Capt.

| Glasgow, Jan. 22.—Third Engineer S. Taylor, twenty-eight, of the Tanker Valverda, died of injuries received in a fire which threatened to destroy the ship in mid-Atlantic, Capt. T. C. Thomas, the ship's master, wirelessly reported today. | Thomas’ message said: “Fire now confined to refrigerator. Vessel in no immediate danger. Taylor, third engineer, succumbed to injuries. All others safe.” The time the message was dispatched was not given. An earlier message said that the fire had “subsided.” Taylor was from Glasgow. It was expected that the light cruiser Frobisher, cadet training ship bound for Trinidad, would try to take the Valverda in tow for Bermuda today.

New York, Jan. 21.—(#)—Fire in the British tanker Valverda, disabled in the Atlantic 1,200 miles east of the Bahamas, was conquered tonight, according to a message reported to have been sent to its owners, and the French ship Petit Terre was standing by. “Engine room completely gutted. Flames now subsided,” read the message reported to have been sent to Glasgow by Captain T. C. Thomas.

Ordered into Somaliland to Put Down Tribal War. Paris, Jan. 22 (©)—French forces including camel troops and airplanes were ordered to the southwest frontier of French Somaliland today to put down a tribal war which already has cost the lives of 97 members of the French colonial administration. The French action followed a battle January 18, just reported to the French capital, in which M. Bernard, French chief of the Gobad region, 16 native soldiers, and 80 natives were slain in the Lake Abbe region. Bernard and his men had gone to investigate a battle reported raging between the rival Aiss Amaras and the Issa tribes of nomads in that region. French authorities described it as "a purely local fight between tribes" not involving the Ethiopians, on whose border the action took place. The Ethiopian government, however, will be asked to help pursue and capture the battling tribesmen. Bernard

LONGUEUIL, Que., Jan. 22, (AP). Five children burned to death early today when washing hung on a clothesline over the kitchen stove to dry caught fire. A roomer and six other members of the family of Emile Gadbois, four of them children, were taken to a hospital suffering from burns. The dead were all children of Gadbois, their ages ranging from 11 years downward.

MONTREAL, Jan. 22.—(UP)—Five children, the oldest of whom was 10, lost their lives today, and seven other persons were injured by fire at the home of Emile Gadbois at Longueuil. The children, four girls and a boy, were found huddled together in an upstairs bedroom when firemen arrived. Three other children were badly burned and are in a hospital in critical condition. The parents, Mr. and Mrs. Emile Gadbois, were burned about the face and hands as they tried to take the children from the burning house.

TOKYO, Jan. 22.—(#)—Sinkiang, a huge northwestern territory nominally belonging to China, was indicated by statements in high official quarters today as the future scene of a contest between the expansionist ambitions of two great Asiatic powers, Japan and Soviet Russia. A spokesman for the Japanese government said the Soviet’s alleged economic and political penetration of Sinkiang ‘menaces’ the peace and stability of Eastern Asia, which it is Japan’s mission ‘to maintain.’ This development was mentioned by Koki Hirota, foreign minister, in a formal address to the diet. VIENNA, Jan. 21 (AP)—Bachelor King Zog of Albania—39 years old and not bad-looking—is casting around for a $1,000,000-a-year American bride with enough intelligence and courage to help him reform his backward and sometimes violent little mountain kingdom. The million-dollar part of it is not a joke, and so far has been the principal objection to all well-meant suggestions. American brides with seven-figure annual incomes and other necessary qualifications (1, advanced thought; 2, ability; 3, personal attractiveness) admittedly are not plentiful. On several occasions King Zog has confided to friends that he would like an American girl as a bride, being more western in his ideas than inclined toward a Mohammedan marriage. 1935-06-13.text: Sandringham, England, June 13, U.P)—King George was reported improved today while he remained under close medical supervision, suffering from bronchial catarrh which caused fear for him. Physicians assured Queen Mary that the king's illness was not serious and said that he needed only

LONDON. (AP) A five year building program for Reichsführer Hitler's proposed new German fleet will be drawn up, naval circles indicated, when Anglo-German naval talks resume here Friday. Joaquim von Ribbentrop, Hitler's ambassador extraordinary for the conversations, will return to London from Berlin Thursday. It was believed Gen. Von Ribbentrop, who has been in consultation with Hitler at the latter's Bavarian mountain retreat, was returning with authority to negotiate an agreement to be submitted to other naval powers, including the United States. It is now understood the British have given up hope of paring down Hitler's demand for tonnage to 35 percent of Great Britain's, but are demanding that this percentage be applied separately to each of the various categories of warships.

BERLIN, June 13—Several hundred persons were reported killed today in a blast at the explosives factory at Reinsdorf near Wittenberg. All the factory's workshops were destroyed. Many houses in the vicinity were demolished and window panes for a radius of several miles were smashed. Between noon and 6:40 p.m. ambulances were carrying the smashed bodies of dead and dying workmen from the debris of the factory to hastily-constructed sheds near the scene. Physicians, surgeons, and Red Cross workers from throughout the district were summoned to Reinsdorf.

AWRY FER TE, S000, VOC Press) ROME, June 13 (UP).—Italy is seeking to establish a protectorate over Abyssinia, retaining the present dynasty of Emperor Haile Selassie, it was said authoritatively today. Abyssinia, it was said, was ready to cede to Italy the province of Ogaden, to be joined to Italian Somaliland, It was said in Abyssinian circles here that Haile Selassie was ready to make concessions to Italy by offering the disputed zone of Ogaden. Diplomatic exchanges are proceeding with Great Britain and France, it was learned, to find a way to harmonize the contemplated Italian relations with the existing treaty.

- BERLIN, June 13—(#)—Unconfirmed and unofficial estimates place the number of dead in the explosion of the Westphalian Anhalt explosives factory today as high as one thousand but the ministry of propaganda in Berlin said that the toll would be less than 100. The factory employs 13,000 workers. The explosion was called one of the worst catastrophes in German industrial history. It occurred while the factory was working at full shift and there were hundreds of workers in the different shops which collapsed following the blast. Windows in houses several miles away were smashed and debris, stones and metal were projected in the air for long distances. All ambulances in Wittenberg were requisitioned and every physician in the district was ordered to hurry to the scene, strong forces of the army, storm troopers and labor corps, were put to digging in the debris for the dead.

PARIS, June 13.—(#)—Philippe Marcombes, minister of education, fell dead today in the Elysee Palace as he entered the council chamber for the first council of ministers since the cabinet of Premier Pierre Laval was granted extraordinary powers. Marcombes had just entered the large room where President Albert Lebrun was to preside at an important meeting. He suffered an apoplectic stroke.

ATHENS.—(#)— A religious revolt stirred Greece Wednesday with the arrest of three archbishops of the Greek church as a precaution, authorities said, against possible violence. The archbishops had severed their connection with the church and urged the clergy to follow them, accusing Archbishop Chry-sostomos of betraying the church's interests by accepting the Gregorian calendar. A statement by the three described the Gregorian calendar as “a sacrilegious western invention” and also accused the archbishop of tolerating Roman Catholic, Protestant and Communist propaganda. They will be placed on trial Friday.

Berlin—A terrific explosion with scores killed, occurred today in an explosives factory at Reinsdorf, near Wittenberg, in Prussian Saxony. Although the explosion occurred at 3 p.m. the ministry said the main factory was still burning tonight and workers were imprisoned within. The telephone operator at Wittenberg told the United Press it was impossible to get near the scene and that all hospitals were crowded with injured.

1935-07-24.text: (Copyright 1935, by the Associated Press) LONDON, July 24—Great Britain intends to make a firm move at Geneva next week to solve the Italo-Ethiopian impasse, it was learned today. It will press for a full airing of the issues in a final effort to avert an open break, but is taking no chances with its own security. Communication lines to East Africa are jammed with instructions for strengthening the empire's political and military position about Ethiopia. The government will base its actions at Geneva on full support of the League of Nations covenant, an authoritative source said, but does not intend to become a lone policeman to enforce the covenant provisions if the league council should fumble the dispute.

LONDON, England (UP) — A hint of possible collaboration between Great Britain and the United States to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia was given in the House of Commons today by Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary. Sir Samuel, replying to a question of Brigadier General Edward L. Spears on whether Britain was trying to achieve a joint policy with the United States, revealed that he already had expressed to Ambassador Robert W. Bingham, Britain’s “satisfaction with the recent utterances of Secretary Hull about the obligations taken by all signatories of the Kellogg pact.” Sir Samuel assured the House that the government “is always ready to cooperate with the United States government to preserve peace.” The foreign secretary refused to commit Britain in advance on what action she would take if hostilities break out. Wimbledon, Eng., July 24 (AP)—A straight set victory by Wilmer Allison of Austin, Texas, over Sheiner Henkel, of Germany, enabled the United States to eliminate Germany today from the Davis Cup tennis competition and qualified America to meet Great Britain in the challenge round starting Saturday. The veteran Texan, who lost nine pounds in participating in a grueling uphill doubles victory over the Germans yesterday, accounted for the young German by the scores of 6-1, 7-5, 11-9 and clinched the interzone final series by a score of 3-1. Germany's downfall was started last Saturday by young Don Budge of Oakland, Cal., with a four-set victory over Henzel. WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 24 (UP) America’s Davis Cup team today earned the right to challenge England for the historic tennis trophy when Wilmer Allison of Austin, Tex., defeated Heinrich Henkel, 6-1, 7-5, 11-9, in the deciding match of the European zone finals with Germany. Allison's victory comprised the necessary third win in the five match series with Germany. In the fifth match, which was reduced to an exhibition status, Donald Budge, of Oakland, Cal. defeated Baron Gottfried von Cramm, 0-6, 9-7, 8-6, 6-3.

Sir Samuel Hoare, Great Britain's foreign secretary, lauded the United States government in an address to the House of Commons because of its attitude on the dispute between Italy and Ethiopia. He promised: “His Majesty’s government will always be ready to cooperate with the United States government in seeking to preserve peace.” Authoritative British sources said Great Britain would do its utmost at Geneva to prevent action or non-action by the League of Nations council which would “legalize” the threatened war. 1935-07-27.text: Santa Monica, Cal, July 25, — Here is how getting into wars starts. Italy warned England that they were not to sell arms to Abyssinia. That's verging on fighting talk. Guess we will be able to keep out of it for we don't seem to have anything anybody wants (of course only on credit). Went down last night to a world’s championship wrestling match. Us movie actors are advised to go there by our producers so we can learn how to act. It was a fine show. Everybody enjoyed it. But wrestling managements are overlooking an extra big revenue, for folks would pay even more to see them rehearse with each other before the match. Copyright McNaught Syndicate.

London, July 27.—Europe’s diplomats last night pushed eleventh hour efforts to get Premier Benito Mussolini to accept economic concessions instead of military victory in Ethiopia, but indications were Il Duce would accept nothing less than a protectorate. That, Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia has said repeatedly, is unthinkable. Great Britain awaited an official statement of Italy’s claims and charges against the African nation, but it learned unofficially Il Duce would insist upon the protectorate. The extraordinary session of the League of Nations Council to consider plans for peace has been called for July 31 or August 1. Supporting the view that war—despite all Britain’s and the League’s efforts for peace—was imminent were these developments yesterday: 1. Ethiopia was reported unwilling to revive the Italo-Ethiopian commission which broke up at Scheveningen, the Netherlands, over

LONDON, July 27. (P).--Closing of the Suez Canal to Italian warships as a means of averting war between Italy and Ethiopia was urged upon Great Britain today. Such a step was advanced by the reputable London "Law Times" as a measure of disciplinary action to be sanctioned by the League of Nations. The proposed closing of the canal would be in line with Britain’s temporary ban on arms shipments to both Italy and Ethiopia. The "Law Times" urged that Great Britain close the canal as a "protecting power." The Suez Canal is the key factor in Premier Mussolini’s heralded campaign against Ethiopia since its closing would force Italy’s warships to detour thousands of miles. It would necessitate their going clear around Africa to reach Eritrea or Italian Somalia.

(Bunny) Austin gave Great Britain a clean sweep today of the two opening singles matches against the United States in the Davis Cup challenge round. Austin defeated Wilmer Allison in five sets, 6-2, 2-6, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5 and Perry cut down young Don Budge, 6-0, 6-8, 6-3, 6-4. Their victories sent England away to a flying start in defense of the coveted trophy won from France in 1933 and defended successfully against the United States last year. Barring something on the order of a complete debacle of form, Perry will be a top-heavy favorite to defeat Allison Tuesday when the order of today’s singles lineup is reversed for the last two matches of the five-match series. LONDON, July 26. (UP) — New British proposals for settling the Italo-Ethiopian conflict were rejected by Premier Benito Mussolini tonight. For the second time Il Duce turned his back on proffers of British good offices to avert war in East Africa when he rejected suggestions that he restrict his claims on Ethiopia to economic and commercial demands. Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Rome, also told Il Duce Britain would exert her good offices in Addis Ababa to arrange direct Italo-Ethiopian discussions of economic concessions to Italy. He emphasized Britain would support any reasonable economic claims in Ethiopia. But Mussolini refused to renounce his objective — political annexation. Britain now is seeking assurances from Mussolini that Italy will not open hostilities against Ethiopia as long as Anglo-Franco-Italian diplomatic negotiations continue. Meanwhile, she hopes for defin

ee 6 Se OO COMPO EET London, July 27—Hopes of achieving an Italo-Abyssinian compromise at Geneva decreased with alarming suddenness today with Premier Mussolini’s announcement he will participate only if discussions are limited to conciliation. His note to the League of Nations, throwing entire responsibility for Italian attendance upon Ethiopia, demanding a pledge that "unrelated" topics will not be brought into the agenda, came as a surprise. Plans for the council meeting went forward as scheduled, but Britain is placing more faith in discussions proceeding in Rome. There is some feeling a basis might be found for a tri-partite parley to reach an adjustment of the dispute outside of Geneva. LONDON, July 26.—The Evening Standard claimed today that the Foreign Office and War Office jointly are considering sending troops to Addis Ababa to protect the British legation in the Ethiopian capital. The paper quoted the War Office as saying, “the matter has been under consideration for some time but there has been no decision yet.”

MALVERN, England, July 26. (7)—George Bernard Shaw, he of the white beard and twinkling eyes, couldn't find time to rest even today—his 79th birthday. For the last week, he has been a familiar figure striding over the Malvern hills when not occupied in rehearsals of his new play for next week's drama festival.

But are the facts of Italy’s needs and the complaints made against the Ethiopian government sufficient cause for plunging into war?” Pledging Britain’s continued efforts for peace,

GENEVA, Sept. 11 (4)—The powerful voice of Great Britain demanded peace today and pledged its support of the League of Nations’ covenant “in its entirety.” A growing tenseness between Italy and Britain was apparent after Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, outlined London's policy. His speech was interpreted as a friendly warning to Mussolini to go slow, an indication Britain would not shun sanctions if she felt them necessary and a warning that if a settlement is not reached the “main bridge” binding England to the European continent will have collapsed. The impression was growing in League circles that the real tension is not between Italy and Ethiopia nor between Italy and the League, but between Italy and Britain. This view was strengthened when an Italian spokesman warned that Ethiopia’s plea must not be regarded as having any practical bearing upon the real problem before the leag

BY A. & OV se (Associated Press Foreign Staff) ROME, Sept. 11 (4).--The newspaper La Tribuna today designated the speech of Sir Samuel Hoare, British Foreign Secretary, before the League of Nations’ Assembly at Geneva as a veiled threat both to the League and to France. “The orator evidently wished to indicate that when the League of Nations’ Assembly becomes incapable of solving the Italian-Ethiopian problem according to the British viewpoint, the government in London might vote to leave the League,” said the newspaper.

A group of smaller nations, led by The Netherlands and Belgium supported Great Britain Thursday in opposition to the Italian military conquest of Ethiopia. Representatives told the League of Nations they decried an arms invasion, and wanted maintenance of non-aggression principles. Favorable reports were noticeable but were lacking on negotiations to swerve Italy from her course. Military preparations continued in the Mediterranean area. Britain ordered three more battalions of soldiers to Malta. Italy sent 5,900 troops from Naples with sailing orders to East Africa. Emperor Selassie expressed gratitude for the British stand backing the league covenant, and opposing aggression.

(By The Associated Press) Bath, Maine, Sept. 11—A man reputedly resembling Alvin Karpis, No. 1 public enemy, who was brought to police headquarters here after an automobile accident today, was later identified as another man, state highway officer, Harry L. Thompson, announced.

ROME (#) — The Italian press renewed its bitter attack on Great Britain today in the face of its proposals for the Anglo-Franco-Italian conferences to consider the broad aspects of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Premier Mussolini’s newspaper, Il Popolo Romano, condemned Sir Samuel Hoare in an editorial commenting on Sir Samuel’s remark to the British House of Commons that the Italo-Ethiopian trouble provided the world with a grave crisis. The paper said “this course is tantamount to logic and justice.” “After Hoare’s discourse,” Il Messaggero, “Italy will pursue its course without frustration, appealing again to justice in its civilizing mission.”

LONDON, Sept. 11.—(AP)— The nucleus of the British imperial defense council met with Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin today for the third time in less than a month while Sir Samuel Hoare, the foreign secretary, at Geneva, was making a definite demand for League of Nations integrity. No disclosure was made of the subjects discussed at 10 Downing street, but the two-and-a-half hour conference was interpreted as a precursor to further steps to prepare Britain for action in view of the present grave threat of a war which might involve the British Colonies. Hoare’s address, on which Baldwin collaborated, contained the declaration that it would be “dangerously misleading to hold and encourage illusions” that British fidelity to the League could not be relied on. Baldwin, who came from his country place for the meeting, was joined at 10 Downing street by Ramsay MacDonald, Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell

LONDON, Sept. 12.—Three battalions of infantry will leave soon for Malta, Britain’s naval base in the Mediterranean off the Italian coast, it was announced today. It was reported on reliable authority today that three warships, each bearing troops, left Portsmouth for Malta unannounced last weekend.

1935-07-18.text: LONDON, England. (UP) — A diplomatic deal to justify an Italian drive against Ethiopia and give Emperor Haile Selassie the choice of war or unconditional surrender to the powers’ terms was indicated today, as the cabinet met to discuss the crisis. Council to Meet The League of Nations council will meet at Geneva between July 25 and August 2, to consider the Italian-Ethiopian situation. But meantime, Great Britain is urging a pre-council meeting of the three allied nations: Britain, France and Italy, to work out a plan which would avert the possibility that some unsporting small nation represented in the council might defend the Ethiopian cause. Britain is urging also that Italy itself raise the Ethiopian crisis in the council, and outline its complaint and its demands. Must Decide Technically, the council is supposed to meet July 25 to name a neutral chairman with a deciding vote for a j

Bournemouth, England, July 18. —(AP)—The world of letters mourned today the passing of George William Russell—AE—Irish journalist, poet and painter. Already ill on his return from a trip to the United States a few months ago, Russell suffered a setback during the summer’s first heat wave and died last night at a home. He was 68 years old. The funeral will be Saturday in Dublin. The British press published many tributes to Russell today, pointing out that he was both a poet and an economist—a dreamer and a practical businessman. Newspapers recalled that he hit on his pen name, AE, accidentally. He used the signature “AEON” in one of his earliest works. When the printer could decipher only the first two letters, Russell decided to adopt the shortest known pseudonym. (Continued on Page Seven)

LONDON (A.P.) - A poignant story of a struggle to remake the shattered lives of 80,500 people torn from their homes in Nazi Germany was revealed today in a report by an American expert to a League of Nations commission. It represented the result of nearly two years of work by James G. McDonald of New York, drafted by the League of Nations in an effort - fought by the German government - to place those who fled Nazi Germany. Between the lines of the factual, statistical report was visible the picture of the thousands of families of Jews and others wandering over the globe seeking means of self-respecting sustenance. It was disclosed that the United States has absorbed 6,000 of the refugees. Palestine has absorbed most - 27,000 - and France is caring for 10,000. In terms almost cold in their objectivity, McDonald, high commissioner for German refugees, told the facts of his work and his id

BOURNEMOUTH, England, July 17 (P) — George William Russell, Irish journalist, writer and painter, known to poetry lovers by the cryptic pen name “AE,” died tonight. He was 68 years old. Although primarily noted as a poet, AE was an energetic Jack of many trades—a painter, businessman, organizer, editor and co-founder of the famous Abbey Theater in Dublin. Already ailing when he returned from the United States a few months ago, he suffered a setback in London during the first heat wave of summer.

LONDON, July 18—(#)— The Reuters correspondent at Hankow reported today that a missionary from the hills of the Han valley stated cholera had broken out among the 300,000 refugees who had fled there from the

LONDON, July 18. (WP)—Lord Marley, whip of the Labor party in the House of Lords, today made an attack on the quality of American munitions supplied to the allies in the World War during his testimony before the Arms Traffic Commission. Lord Marley, who won a distinguished service cross in the Navy during the war and then was transferred to France in command of a trench mortar and anti-aircraft unit, said American shells “always were bursting in the muzzle of the gun instead of among the enemy.” The former artilleryman, appearing as a witness on behalf of the Union of Democratic Control, urged greater publicity for arms manufacture to assist in the prevention of corruption and advocated national ownership to avoid the temptation of warmongering and the temptation of the profit from sales of munitions.

Rome. (AP)-- Mario Stoppani reported that he bettered the world's distance record for seaplanes when he landed today at Berbera, British Somaliland, after a flight of 4,996 kilometers (3,103 miles) from Trieste. Standing record of 4,300 kilometers was held by France. Stoppani, an Italian aviator, took off with a navigating officer and radio operator at 4:21 a.m. yesterday from Trieste for the straight line flight to Berbera. They remained in the air a little less than twenty-five hours.

SOUTHAMPTON, England, July 18.--(UP)--Douglas Fairbanks and Lady Sylvia Ashley arrived here today on the Empress of Britain, completing a tour of the world started several months ago. The veteran screen star and his companion motored to a secret destination in the country for a house party of big guests aboard the yacht Caroline during the first stages of the trip. Fairbanks declined to comment on reports that he would be marrying shortly Lady Ashley.

1935-07-05.text: | WIMBLEDON, Eng, July 5 (AP) — Fred Perry, dashing British star of the courts, captured the All-England tennis championship for the second successive year today, defeating Baron Gottfried von Cramm of Germany in the final round. Although von Cramm battled the Briton every inch of the way, he never had a chance against the black-haired champion. At every vital point, Perry had the shots he needed to win and von Cramm consistently was caught flat-footed by the Briton's smashing drives. Perry, a heavy favorite from the start, lived up to his reputation as the world’s greatest amateur. He dominated the match throughout and never looked like anything but a certain winner.

LONDON, (UP)—Great Britain, rebuffed in continental Europe, may eventually seek support of the United States and Japan in its efforts to prevent an Italian war on Abyssinia, unofficial sources reported Friday. What action can be taken, officials hesitate to discuss. But there is increasing talk of an effort to impose economic penalties on Italy if Benito Mussolini insists on his war. It is reported here that the government has decided it cannot act alone to invoke or execute any measures stronger than persuasive ones against Italy. Hope Remains Hope still is held that collective action may be agreed on among League of Nations members. If a policy were agreed upon, it was said, the United States and Japan would be asked to support it. Any appeal made to the United States would be independent of that made to the United States from Abyssinia direct, and would be in the nature of one to aid

Rumors of an impending restoration of the monarchy in Austria today brought into Europe's spotlight two young people—the Archduke Otto, 22 years old, and his 20-year-old fiancée, Princess Maria. Otto is pretender to the non-existing Austrian throne by virtue of the fact that he is the son of the late emperor Karl, the last king to occupy that throne. Princess Maria is the youngest daughter of King Victor Emmanuel and Queen Elena of Italy. Otto was only six years old when the Austrian revolution at the end of World War I overthrew his father. Most of the time since then he has lived in exile in Belgium where he is known officially as the Duc De Bar. Throughout his brief life he has been carefully trained for kingship. His numerous tutors and servants have paid him the homage ordinarily accorded a reigning monarch. He is handsome, dignified, and scholarly. Princess Maria made her debut int

London, July 8.—George Washington Hill, president of the American Tobacco Co., and Miss Mary Barnes, his 39-year-old secretary, gave notice today to the London register office of their forthcoming marriage. Hill, who is 51 years old and a widower, was accompanied to London by his daughter, Gertrude. The tobacco magnate was listed in 1931 as one of America’s “million-dollar-a-year executives.” He succeeded his father as president of the American Tobacco Co. ten years ago and has been with the company 31 years. He also is a director of the Cuban Tobacco Co. and the Henry Clay and Bock Co. He is a member of a number of smart clubs in New York City and of the Congressional club in Washington. Several years ago fire which started in a Christmas tree destroyed his 40-room country home at White Plains.

Follonica, Italy, July 5 -- Former King Alfonso of Spain was slightly injured today when the automobile he was driving turned over while en route from Rome to Leghorn. His injuries were confined to bruises on the forehead. His aide-de-camp suffered a fractured collarbone. Their injuries were dressed on the spot with the assistance of passing motorists.

Berlin, July 6. (4)--A pilot and five mechanics were killed Friday when a trial plane crashed through the door of a house at Britz, a Berlin suburb near Tempelhof airdrome. The cause of the crash was not determined.

ADDIS ABABA, Abyssinia (UP) — Abyssinia, faced with the threat of war on a major scale by Fascist Italy awaited today reply from the United States government to its latest appeal for world aid—invocation of the Paris peace pact. The pact—the Briand-Kellogg pact—is one that pledges 59 world nations to renounce war as an instrument of national policy and to seek solution of disputes by pacific means. Guaranteed in theory against attacks from Italy by reason of its membership in the League of Nations, the government sought support of the United States, a non-member of the league, through the only remaining instrument. As part of its preparation for war, the government intends to adhere to the Geneva Red Cross convention of 1929, and an Abyssinian Red Cross society is being formed. Royal princesses are going into training as nurses.

BERLIN, July 5.—A technical experimental plane crashed into a dwelling house in the Berlin suburb of Britz today, killing its six occupants and two occupants of the house. Several other persons were injured. The house was set afire.

1935-07-19.text: Adis Ababa - Haile Selassie, calling his people to resist Italian invasion, abandons hopes of avoiding war. London - Diplomats take emperor’s speech as tantamount to mobilization order; British speed up peace efforts. Rome - Duce tells nations military preparations in Eritrea are in good shape; East Africa command reports water supply plentiful. Naples - S. S. Ganges sails with more than 1,000 soldiers; seven other steamers being loaded. Geneva - League expects small states to demand protection of Ethiopia's integrity; Ethiopia adheres to International Red Cross convention.

Lewes, Del., July 19 (INS)—Rewarding weeks of painstaking efforts, a group of New England treasure hunters have located the British sloop of war, Debraak, it was reported here today. The sloop sank 140 years ago in a squall and is believed to have carried to a watery grave $10,000,000 in Spanish gold. The salvagers, who have left for Providence, R. I., to obtain equipment for raising the ship, reported bringing to the surface a length of the ship’s railing which tallies with the known construction of the sloop. They said the treasure ship lies sunk in mud near Cape Henlopen. Harry Morgan, the diver with the party, said the wreck agrees with the description of the Debraak.

LONDON, July 15.—The British cabinet today was reported to have virtually abandoned hope of averting war between Italy and Abyssinia. Although for obvious reasons such a position could not be divulged officially at this time, there was strong belief the cabinet reached the conclusion that there are two insurmountable obstacles to peace in Africa. These were: 1. Premier Benito Mussolini’s refusal to accept merely economic concessions as a basis for recall of his troops and peace with Ethiopia, and 2. Emperor Haile Selassie's rejection of any peace proposal involving in any way Ethiopia's political independence. Although diplomatic talks in the hope that some form of conciliation might be reached were continued in London, Paris, and Rome, British ministers faced the realization there was little hope left of averting hostilities. For this reason it was understood Britain was extremely unlik

LONDON, July 19. (4)--Great Britain's drive for peace between Italy and Ethiopia took on added impetus today from Emperor Haile Selassie’s appearance for defense of his empire. After a prolonged cabinet discussion yesterday of the crisis, the ministers were expected to hold further meetings within the next few days in an attempt to reach a definite decision on Britain's policy. Various peace organizations and advocates pressed for decisive action, based on the League of Nations covenant. Discussions were continued at Rome and Paris in search of means to avert an open conflict in East Africa. Some quarters expressed belief that the attitude to be taken by England before a special session of the League of Nations council would not be settled finally until the eleventh hour, anticipating that the situation might undergo rapid changes before the meeting probably about July 25. Suggestions th

(By United Press.) LONDON, July 19.--A plan to convoke an immediate French-British-Italian meeting at Paris in hope of averting war between Italy and Ethiopia was understood to have been abandoned today because no basis for agreement could be found.

Belfast—(INS)—The Protestant-Catholic disturbances in Belfast, a week old today, took a grave turn this morning when Protestants forced many Catholic families to evacuate their homes under threat of burning them down. The evicted Catholic families took shelter in wooden huts in the parks, where they were guarded by combined police and military forces who all week long have been unable to check daily shooting and rioting affrays in which eight have been killed. The eighth fatality, Hugh Falloon, died today from wounds received previously. Churchmen and businessmen united to form a citizen’s committee to halt the riots between Protestants and Catholics, the latter a minority in the north of Ireland, which began last Friday night. Further serious trouble is looked for on Monday, when shipyard employees will return from their vacations. It was feared members of the rival faiths would refuse

Cairo, Egypt, July 18--(#)—The English flier, H. L. Brook, who is attempting a new flight record from England to Cape Town, crashed today at Mersa Matruh and was reported injured. The reports received here did not make known the extent of his injuries nor the amount of damage done to his plane. He took off from Lympe aerodrome shortly after midnight today in an effort to beat Mrs. Amy Mollison’s record of four days and six hours for the flight.

(At Addis Ababa, official circles said increasing indications Italy intended to use force against her had led Ethiopia to begin extensive preparations “to meet an emergency.” (At London, Britain's peace-seeking diplomats waited the outcome of explorations at Rome and Paris to decide how war might perhaps be averted.) Rome newspapers published long front-page editorials emphasizing in vigorous language what they described as the “inevitability” of war with Ethiopia. The Giornale d'Italia, often officially inspired, attacked the efficacy of diplomatic efforts to halt hostilities. Such formulae, the newspaper said, “are capable only of alte

1935-07-16.text: London, July 16.--(—Two persons were killed today in the blazing wreckage of an airplane which crashed at the edge of Heston Airdrome after a take-off for Spithead for the silver jubilee review of the British fleet. The plane crashed as it lost altitude after taking off with seven passengers and burst into flames. The dead were two passengers, Major J. H. Hobbs and H. Newhouse. The pilot and the five other passengers, including one woman, Margaret Vickers, were rushed to a hospital suffering from burns and injuries.

PORTSMOUTH, England, July 16. UP)—King George today reviewed the long gray lines of warships of Great Britain’s grand fleet. Aboard the royal yacht Victoria and Albert he steamed slowly through the eight impressive files representing his empire’s might on the seas. The combined fleet roared out the royal salute of 21 guns as the Victoria and Albert—named in honor of England's great queen of the 19th century and her consort, approached the battleships. His majesty was accompanied by three of his sons—the Prince of Wales, the Duke of York and the Duke of Kent, all in naval uniform. Ashore and afloat, a quarter million cheering subjects watched the royal yacht, its brass funnels glinting, get under way from Portsmouth at 2 p.m., for the two-hour sail to the review anchorage at Spithead off this harbor.

LONDON, July 15 (#)—A final decision rejecting Lloyd George's “new deal” program for Great Britain, modelled after that in Washington, was taken tonight by the cabinet. A detailed statement of reasons for the action will be published next Monday.

LONDON, July 16.—UPI—Two passengers of unknown nationality were killed today when an airplane crashed as it took off from Heston airport here for Spithead, where King George will review a gigantic naval fleet this afternoon. Five passengers and the pilot, flying officer Stanley Fine, were saved. All were injured. Nationalities of those killed were not known. It was reported there were Americans on the plane, but the agents who chartered it for the review party said there were none. The airplane appeared to lose height as it took off from the airdrome, a principal London airport. It crashed into a country lane just outside the port, and caught fire. Prompt work by the airport fire brigade and ambulance crew prevented a bigger death list, but two bodies remained in the blazing plane.

While the government has held up permission of arms firms to ship munitions to Addis Ababa, it is unable to prevent citizens from enlisting in the emperor’s army. A rush of applicants have sent their names to the Ethiopian legation here. These offers are “much appreciated,” the minister said, but pending further instructions from Emperor Haile Selassie he is not taking active steps to enlist volunteers. PORTSMOUTH, Eng., July 16.—The Duke of Kent lost his shirt today playing golf against his elder brother, the Prince of Wales. The two princes met on the links at Hayling Island before the jubilee naval review. Wales was in good form and Kent was losing. The latter peeled off his shirt and the game went on. They quit two holes short with Kent far down and with little time left to get to the review. Then Kent went back after his shirt. It was gone.

ROME, July 15. (---Italian authorities opened an investigation today of the strange deaths in a bathing resort of an American art teacher and her male British friend. Mrs. May Katherine Thompson, 40, of Brooklyn, N. Y., and H. N. Scott, British subject who was director of the American Express company in Italy, were found dead yesterday in the sulphur baths at Acque Albule, a popular bathing resort near Rome.

London, July 16 (4)—A dispatch to the Reuters (British) news agency from Cairo, Egypt, said it was understood today that the government has banned export of Egyptian camels to the Italian colony of Eritrea. The dispatch said this action followed reports of increased activity by Italian agents.

1935-07-04.text: WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 4.—(/)— For the third time since 1929, Helen Jacobs and Mrs. Helen Wills Moody today battled their way into the final round of the all-England tennis championships. Miss Jacobs played some of the finest tennis of her career to eliminate the 3 to 1 favorite, Hilda Krahwinkel Sperling of Germany, 6-3, 6-0, while Mrs. Moody, six-times winner of the Wimbledon crown, swept aside Joan Hartigan, top-ranking Australian, 6-3, 6-3. Mrs. Moody, playing in her first major tournament since a back injury forced her to default to Miss Jacobs in the third set of the American championship finals of 1933, thus gained the Wimbledon final round for the seventh time in her career. She was beaten for the title by Kitty McKane of Great Britain in 1924, then defeated Senorita Elia de Alvarez of Spain in 1927 and 1928; Miss Jacobs in 1929 and 1932; Elizabeth Ryan in 1930 and Dorothy Round i

LONDON, July 4—Great Britain, determined to curb Italian ambitions in Africa, is prepared to take the lead in eventual blockade of Italy by other powers if hostilities break out in Abyssinia, it was indicated today. Such a course was hinted when authoritative sources, commenting on Rome reports that the British cabinet is laying plans for an economic blockade of Italy to restrain the latter’s East African venture, said “such a measure is miles ahead of the present stage.” It was considered significant that there was no denial of the reports, such as would almost certainly have been forthcoming in view of their prevalence were they without foundation. Meanwhile, to win French support of the British stand in the Abyssinian crisis, the government was embarked on a program of reconciliation with France, whose feelings were ruffled by the recently signed Anglo-German naval accord. The cabinet

Ethiopia has appealed to the United States to find a way to keep peace in East Africa under the Kellogg-Briand pact, by which Italy renounced war as an instrument of national policy. Emperor Haile Selassie himself, in a statement to The Associated Press, asserted that Ethiopia will collaborate with any nation for peace, as long as her independence and integrity are not threatened. United States State Department officials declined to comment in Washington pending receipt of the Ethiopian note. A spokesman for the Italian government asserted in Rome that Italy’s attitude toward the appeal would not change in her border controversy with Ethiopia. The London Daily Express reported that Italy has concluded a military agreement with France, providing for joint frontier defense which would leave Italy free to concentrate in Africa, but the News Chronicle expressed an opinion that Premier Benito

VIENNA, (AP) — The ancient Hapsburg monarchy took a long stride on the comeback trail Thursday after the Austrian cabinet voted to restore properties of the old royal family. Monarchists were jubilant and set afoot numerous schemes to further the move for assumption of the throne by the youthful "Kaiser Otto I." Several royalist leaders hastened for Steenockerzeel castle in Belgium, where the 22-year-old Archduke Otto of Hapsburg, pretender to the Austrian throne, is living with his family. There was note of caution, however, in the exultation of the legitimists. Having waited 17 years for an opportunity to revive the monarchy which fell with Emperor Carl in 1918, they do not wish to fail now. The deepest concern felt by the sponsors for a restoration was over the reaction abroad to the movement. An impression prevailed that the attitude of the Little Entente nations was more favorable t

Brussels. (P) - A royalist close to young Archduke Otto of Hapsburg, pretender to the Austrian throne, predicted today early restoration of the monarchy. While negotiations for an enthronement of "Kaiser Otto I" in Vienna swung to his seat of exile here, the royalist said all obstacles to prompt restoration have been cleared but one — the opposition of Prince Ernst von Starhemberg. The 22-year-old pretender himself said, "I do not deny that negotiations are in progress, but I regret that I cannot now discuss the matter." The archduke conceded, however, that he had been "pleased to shake hands" with Baron Karl Karwinsky, undersecretary of the Austrian department of justice. The royalist, whose identity was withheld, but who said he was in close touch with Otto, asserted: "We count on his return to Austria within a few weeks after the anti-Hapsburg laws are abolished. BERLIN. Two more Ger- mans too eager to learn or too willing to divulge Germany's precious military secrets died under the ax of the headsman, bringing to seventeen the number of persons executed or sentenced for espionage during recent months. Heads to roll were those of Egon Bresz, 28, convicted of trying to procure armaments secrets, and Bruno Hindemann, 63, convicted of betraying military information. Wilhelm Battesch, 48, who was tried with them in the dread people's court, was sentenced to life imprisonment for revealing military information. Semiofficial quarters disclosed several more persons are awaiting trial, and little hope is held that mercy will be shown them in view of the Reich's determination to keep its rearmament secrets.

NAPLES, July 4.—(#)—Old Mount Vesuvius displayed exceptional volcanic efforts today for residents of Naples and Fourth of July visitors to resorts around the famous blue bay. Scientists at the national observatory on the mountain, however, asserted that the volcano was merely giving vent to eruptions now considered

VIENNA, July 28—(AP)—The way to wealth and power stretched smoother before handsome young Archduke Otto of Hapsburg tonight after the Austrian cabinet voted to restore Hapsburg properties seized when the Dynasty was ousted in 1919. If the federal diet meeting July 9 approves the cabinet’s action—had it almost invariably does—the 22-year-old pretender to the Austrian throne will be the better off by some dozen castles, valuable business property, vast forests and rich farms. Jubilant at what they termed another long step toward early restoration of the monarchy, several Royalist leaders left tonight for Steenockerzeel castle in Belgium where Otto is living with his mother, former Empress Zita and his brothers and sisters. The impression obtained in some quarters that Otto would be advised not to let the prospect of sudden wealth lead him to any unwise move toward getting the throne back,

1935-07-23.text: BY ALDEN W. WILSON. Copyright, 1935, By The Associated Press. London, July 23.—Coincident with the concentration of Italian troops in East Africa, Great Britain is massing what naval experts rate as the strongest, fastest fleet ever assembled in the Mediterranean. Terse official announcement disclosed today that the capital ship strength in the Mediterranean is being increased at least 80,000 tons and that the fastest ships soon are to be centered at Malta, a base which commands the Italian routes to the Red Sea. British experts said that although many more capital ships were sent into the Mediterranean (Continued on Page Seven)

LONDON, — Great Britain’s lawmakers were informed by their government on Monday that the British are definitely abandoning the principle of naval ratios reached in conjunction with the United States, Japan, France, and Italy at Washington in 1922. Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, First Lord of the Admiralty, said it was being done to keep from wounding the national pride of some nations who did not wish to accept permanent inferiority. New System He revealed that the start in the direction of throwing the ratios overboard had been made in the Anglo-German naval agreement, which he explained as another means sought to accomplish the same result as ratios for naval limitation. Sir Bolton said the new system would be based on a series of naval programs which by agreement would accommodate the various naval strengths in such a way as to provide adequate navies.

LONDON, July 23. (UP)—Great Britain today completed arrangements to evacuate its subjects from Ethiopia in event of an emergency. Coincidentally it warned missionary societies here that their missionaries, scattered in remote districts of the country, should be concentrated around Addis Ababa, the capital. It advised also that the missionaries should leave the country now with their wives and children. Will Urge League Action PARIS, July 23. (UP)—Great Britain will urge a strong League of Nations attitude to prevent war between Italy and Ethiopia and an accompanying breakdown of the League covenant at a meeting of the League council late this month, it was said on reliable authority today.

(Copyright, 1935, International News Services) GENEVA, July 23.--Fearing general uprising of all African blacks in a “holy war” against white superiority, Great Britain is determined to force League of Nations procedure to prevent a conflict even if it means Italian withdrawal from Geneva. This was the statement made to International News Service by a high league official today as the council prepared to meet within a few days in a final effort to find a common ground for solution of the Italo-Abyssinian crisis. Britain will have the support of France in her determined effort to uphold the “white men's burden” because of her own extensive colonial interests in Africa, this spokesman said. His remarks were interpreted as an explanation of Britain’s apparent willingness to drop negotiations for tripartite conversations among Britain, France and Italy in favor of routine league procedure, d

WASHINGTON, July 22.--An attempt to achieve a compromise agreement putting a limit on the world’s big navies is foreseen by many observers studying disclosures made at London yesterday. The British admiralty announced yesterday that it was abandoning naval ratios, such as the famous 5-5-3 formula limiting the fighting fleets of Great Britain, the United States and Japan. It was indicated that Britain would seek other means of avoiding the costly naval race which so many students of the subject fear. While American officials declined any comment on the British announcement, observers saw in it material to build the framework for a new limitation conference. The Washington treaty, which set up the 5-5-3 ratio in 1922, provides that a conference shall be held in 1935 to discuss continuance of curbs on sea power. PARIS, July 23.—Great Britain will urge a strong League of Nations attitude to prevent war between Italy and Ethiopia, and an accompanying breakdown of the League covenant, at a meeting of the League council late this month, it was said on reliable authority today.

Plymouth, royal air force flying boat, carrying a crew of six, took off at 5:34 a.m. today in an attempt to blaze an all-empire trail from England to Singapore. The first leg of the flight was scheduled to end at Gibraltar.

Berlin, July 23 (4)—The organization of Catholic war veterans was dissolved in Prussia today by governmental decree and officials of the steel helmets—the German organization corresponding to the American Legion in the United States—said they feared their own body, throughout Germany, would be the next to be smashed. The dissolution of the Catholic veterans was ordered by Premier Hermann Wilhelm Goering of Prussia, who is also German minister of aviation, as a further step in the Nazi campaign to purge Germany of “political Catholicism.” It was said that Goering’s action undoubtedly would be paralleled by the governments of the other German states. The decree gave as its grounds that the unity of the German people was disturbed by the existence of separate veterans’ organizations. Meanwhile the Nazi fight against Jews was carried on with unabated violence. Some 500 Jewish children betwee

1935-08-22.text: London, Aug. 22. (UM)—the British cabinet, called into extraordinary session by the impending African crisis, is of “very clear mind as to what should be done.” That was the description of the four and three-quarters hours conference made by Ramsay MacDonald, lord president of the council, as he left 10 Downing street. The former premier seemed in happy spirits as he and his son, Malcolm, the colonial secretary, started for their homes. The 22 members of the cabinet fully discussed and outlined the plans the British will follow when the council of the League of Nations goes into action next month. Mainly, it was understood, they debated the question of sanctions—the punishment of nations which violate treaty or other international obligations. The sanctions which Britain might advocate before the league could include a joint closure of the Suez canal.

Associated Press Foreign Total. Paris, Aug. 22—(AP)—The worries of Premier Laval over the possible wrecking of the League of Nations were increased today. Fear was prevalent in France that hasty action by the British government would make Italy doubly determined to conquer the Ethiopian empire. The British cabinet would permit diplomatic activity to continue with Il Duce in a receptive mood. Although Mussolini has refused to brook interference with his campaign in East Africa, Laval has been negotiating with him with a view to limiting war, if he cannot prevent it entirely. French officials expressed belief it would be impossible for Great Britain to close the Suez Canal to Italian troopships, in enforcement of sanctions, without running the danger of Il Duce considering it a hostile act. They said there was no precedent for such an act. Since the 1886 treaty which neutralized the waterw

(By The Associated Press) Leaders of the British government laid the groundwork Wednesday to demand economic pressure against Italy in the event Benito Mussolini wages war on Ethiopia. The day’s developments in the rapidly-growing crisis: LONDON—Seven key members of the cabinet tentatively adopted plans to ask the full cabinet Thursday to press at Geneva for adoption of economic sanctions against Italy by league members in the event of war. WASHINGTON—The Senate speedily adopted a 7-point program designed to keep America neutral in the event of a foreign war. ADDIS ABABA—Emperor Haile Selassie, tears in his eyes, warned in an interview war between Italy and Ethiopia might eventually involve the whole world. ROME—The capital bustled with warlike preparations as troops were sent through preparatory to embarkation. Uniforms were everywhere in evidence. VIENNA—The official government newspap

ROME, Aug. 22. (7)—The Italian government today, for the first time, allowed a pleading note to creep into the officially inspired press which has been engaged in a polemic against Great Britain. The plea was summed up by Virgilio Gayda, political writer for the Giornale d'Italia, under the headline, "no conflict but collaboration." The most rampant of recent critics regarding Britain’s "obstructionism" to Mussolini's designs in Ethiopia, Gayda wrote today: "It is above all things certain that no general hostility toward England and all its vast empire exists in Italy." Pointing out the great distance between sectors of English opinion regarding Mussolini's aims in Ethiopia, Gayda pleaded for understanding of Italy's designs. "Those designs," he wrote, "signify a development of productive civil territory - a ban on three British possessions and an augmentation of the reciprocal economic

LONDON (#) — Great Britain’s crusade against war hung in the balance today as a score of solemn men met in the cabinet room at 10 Downing Street. There the decision to enter the World War was made 21 years ago, and there the cabinet today deliberated the new crisis which has arisen out of the Italo-Ethiopian conflict since parliament recessed August 2. When parliament adjourned, it was stated definitely that Britain was ready to abide by its obligations under the League of Nations Covenant, but would not play the role of “lone policeman” in maintaining peace. Now a new element has crept in—a growing fear that Mussolini has aspirations beyond mere conquest of Ethiopia which are a threat to British colonial possessions. With the United States firmly attached to the path of neutrality and France pleading for the need of the most extreme caution, the cabinet considered the hazardous question

LONDON, Aug. 22. (UP)—The Daily Mail’s Addis Ababa correspondent reported today that the Ethiopian government had decided at last to order general mobilization. The decision, the correspondent said, was taken yesterday at a meeting of ministers and tribal chieftains and other advisors to Haile Selassie at the royal palace.

LONDON, Aug. 22.—(INS)—Determined to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia if possible, Great Britain will maintain her arms embargo against both nations, it was officially announced tonight. The announcement followed the special emergency meeting of the cabinet, which decided what measures must be taken to maintain peace. It was stated, however, the arms decision is subject to change at any time.

Addis Ababa, Aug. 22.—(AP)— Baron Muzzi Falconi, an Italian consul, accidentally shot himself with a revolver last Tuesday, it was learned today when the wounded man was brought to the Italian hospital here. Accompanied by his wife (whom London reported to be the daughter of the British minister to Ethiopia), the consul is on his way by caravan to his post at Debre Marcos in Godjam province. The accident occurred in Suralto forest. One of the two bullets fired grazed the baron’s lungs. When the shots were fired, he was examining a revolver. Although two days have elapsed since the shooting and the baron had lost a great deal of blood, doctors said they were hopeful of his recovery. The accident caused excitement in Addis Ababa in view of the strained situation between Italy and Ethiopia.

1935-08-17.text: RIS, Aug. 17.—(UP)—French, British and Italian delegates expected today a statement of minimum claims on Ethiopia by Benito Mussolini which will give a positive basis for negotiations and may foretell whether war between Italy and Ethiopia is inevitable. Pending receipt of Mussolini's statement the three-power conference was at a standstill and delegates were nervous. It was decided to name no time for a meeting until Mussolini was heard from. Baron Pompeo Aloisi, chief Italian delegate, talked at length to Mussolini last night on the telephone. He outlined the situation as it appeared after the opening statement of British limits of concession and his own statement of Italy’s demands, In the name of Premier Pierre Laval and of Anthony Eden, chief British delegate, Aloisi asked Mussolini for a specific statement of his claims. It was apparent from the delay that Mussolini, as well as the

Paris, Aug. 16 — Announcements offered Italy economic concessions tonight but Premier Mussolini’s unwillingness to tell France and England exactly what he wants balked efforts to avert a war. In a message from Ethiopia to the tri-power conference, Emperor Haile Selassie emphasized that he would not accept a military occupation. His offer climaxed long deliberations by Premier Pierre Laval of France, Anthony Eden of Great Britain, and Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy as the talks formally were opened. A British spokesman said Aloisi was pressed for a “frank statement” of what Mussolini wants. He declined to give it but instead quit the meeting and telephoned Duce, “into whose lap the whole thing has now been dumped,” the spokesman asserted. Through his minister to Paris, Haile Selassie laid the following proposal before the three powers: 1. A guarantee of the security of the Italian colonies

Paris, Aug. 17.—(#)—Premier Mussolini, of Italy, held up the three power conference seeking a way out of his dispute with Ethiopia, while he pondered a Franco-British demand for a showdown today. A forenoon meeting of the Italian, French and British conferees was postponed while the lean-faced Baron Pompeo Aloisi waited beside the telephone for Il Duce’s answer. War or peace remained as much of a problem as ever since the British and French said they were not certain just what Italy wants.

LONDON, Aug. 16 U.A— Italy intends to attack Ethiopia on two fronts during the first week in October, and will be prepared for a four-year campaign, according to expert military opinion. Italy will have the finest military equipment ever used in war. Ethiopia will have in its favor its formidable mountain barriers and its wild, steaming, disease-ridden lowlands. Information in the hands of the British military intelligence is that Italian military leaders themselves believe it will take four years to conquer the country completely. That it can be conquered, there seems no doubt — but at a great cost in blood and money. Wait For Season Whatever the outcome of war, British experts are now convinced that the Italians will launch their big scale military offensive during the first week of October. The estimate of the time is reached by the experts on the conviction that the Italians will wai

London, Aug. 16. (4) — Reuters (British) News agency today reported from Peiping the murder of Gareth Jones, British newspaper correspondent, by a band of Chinese. (Unconfirmed private report received in Peiping from Calgon, Inner Mongolia, that Jones’ body was found a few miles outside Phaoang to where the Chinese were carrying it.) Jones was making a first-hand investigation of conditions in China and was taken on July 29. Captured also at the time was Herbert Meuller, correspondent for a German news bureau. Meuller was released Aug. 1, after rough handling and permitted to go to Peiping with the demand that $40,000 should be paid for Jones.

SIMLA, India, Aug. 17—(?)—British troops and planes were dispatched from here today in an effort to disperse two thousand tribesmen reported to be concentrated in a threatening manner on the Gandat road in the northwest frontier province. Further details of the concentration were not available here.

London, Aug, 18—Great Britain called a preliminary naval conference today for October, but diplomatic circles were dubious over the prospect of holding it. These circles felt the trend of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute and the general naval situation made it uncertain that the five powers could get together. If they do, they will seek a limitation treaty replacing those expiring at the end of 1936. Those invited are the proposed signatories of a new Washington naval treaty—the United States, Japan, France and Italy.

London, Aug. 17. —A Reuters dispatch from Rome today reported 100 killed in a battle between Abyssinian and Assaimara tribesmen in East Africa. The report which Reuters said was contained in a semi-official statement in Rome said the battle occurred “near Adagalle in French Somaliland” but it was pointed out maps do not show an Adagalle but do locate Adagalla which is in Abyssinia, a full 50 miles from the French Somaliland frontier.

1935-03-31.text: MIAMI, Fla., Mar. 30, (P)—President Roosevelt today cruised in the neighborhood of Great Inagua Island of the British Bahamas trying his luck angling for barracuda and bonefish. Aboard the Astor yacht Normal, Mr. Roosevelt was reported enjoying perfect weather under a blazing tropical sun. Fishing luck was good.

LONDON, March 30. -- (7) — The Duke of Manchester was committed for trial today at London's Old Bailey on charges of obtaining £650 ($3,250) under false pretenses with intent to defraud. Specifically the charges were that the fifty-eight-year-old Duke pawned two pieces of jewelry belonging to his late American-born mother, Consuelo, Duchess of Manchester. He was released under £250 bail pending trial after pleading not guilty through counsel.

yy ASSOCIATED PRESS Anglo-Russian conversations at Moscow ended Saturday. Great Britain's probable stand in any European lineup against Germany’s rearmament still undisclosed. The Russian press, often officially inspired, bid for United States aid in helping keep European peace, the government's organ for heavy industry. America “can never isolate from Europe.” Adolf Hitler pushed ahead with plans to rearm the Reich, his cabinet authorizing the army to begin land for barracks, drill grounds, fortifications and the like, while France, watching crack reserve troops maneuver along the Eastern frontier, played host to Nickolas Titulescu, little entente spokesman, and sought to bind her Southern European Allies more tightly together. LONDON, March 30— (7) — Tall, taciturn Neville Chamberlain, Britain's chancellor of the exchequer, has placed England far in the black again, winding up the financial year with an actual surplus of 7,561,879 pounds or approximately $36,300,000. He figured the year's totals with a sharper budget pencil than necessary. His own modest estimated surplus was 7,960,000 pounds. This year’s figure was less than a quarter of last year's 31,147,860 surplus, but stood out as a bright mark in comparison to the deficit of nearly 236,000,000 pounds two years ago. Chamberlain, who is given more to silent work over his figures than to loquacious debate in the House of Commons, achieved the 1935 surplus despite the doting of 19,250,000 pounds in supplementary issues and the allocations of more than 12,000,000 pounds to the debt sinking fund. The surplus automatically goes towards reduction of the nationa

Moscow, Mar. 30. (4)—Capt, Anthony Eden of Great Britain late today finished his conversations with Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov over European security under “highly satisfactory” conditions, while the Soviet press, in what many believe to be a bid for American cooperation, said the United States “could not avoid becoming involved in a European war.” Results of the conversations were described here as “practical,” and Eden will depart tomorrow night for Warsaw after a joint communique is issued summing up the results of the talks. English and Russian sources both said nothing in the way of final agreements was reached.

LONDON, March 30 (UP)-- The government protested to Berlin today and received an apology for a statement by the German embassy here, denying that Reichsfuehrer Hitler had told Sir John Simon the German air force was equal to Britain's. Simon’s report impressed the cabinet, which had believed the British force 40 per cent superior. The German embassy statement: “It is not true that the fuehrer intimated to Sir John Simon that the present strength of the German air force is equal if not superior to the British.” Simon was indignant and telephoned to Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador to Berlin. Phipps protested, On instruction of Dr. Konstantin von Neurath, foreign minister, Prince von Bismarck, counsellor of the German embassy in London, apologized. Any formal agreements had been worked out, Capt. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, who has spent two days here talking with Maxim Litvi

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia—A)—Direct negotiations with Italy over the colonial boundary disputes were suddenly broken off today and a note sent to the League of Nations. Special measures were taken to protect foreigners in case of an outbreak of hostilities. These steps included the appointment of a new, energetic police chief for the Ethiopian capital. This new chief, named Diredaoua, was reorganizing the police force to make it effective for any eventuality.

Rome—(#)—Possession of gas masks by employees in Italy’s strategic industries was made obligatory today by the cabinet at a meeting presided over by Premier Mussolini. The cabinet also instituted an air command for East Africa, uniting the air forces of Eritrea and Somaliland. The body approved an elaborate law establishing an association for the distribution of gas masks, placing every facility possible in the way of purchase of them by the general public, which is urged to learn their use. The official gazette published a law under which men now in military service and about to complete their terms are kept under arms “until a day determined by the minister of war.”

1935-09-07.text: Rome, Sept. 6. ()—A hint that Italy might demand England's exclusion from Egypt if she continues to regard Italy as a threat to her in Africa was given today by the semi-official journal Azione Coloniale (Colonial Action). If Italy is a danger to the British Empire, the publication said, England is also a danger to the Italian Empire. “England affirms that Italian action in East Africa is injurious to her interests and her imperial security,” the article asserted. “The route to India, the territorial continuity between Cairo and Cape Town, the base at Aden, such are the principal British interests which would seem to be menaced by Italy.” “We want to speak rather of another imperial security—our own,” the journal continued.
