Copyright 1950 by United Press Geneva, Sept. 6—(UP)—For the first time in three days of diplomatic fencing, Italy tonight showed signs of weakening under the force of international pressure. Premier Benito Mussolini's representatives surprisingly withdrew objections to allowing Britain and France to sit on a five-man committee to study the Italo-Ethiopian question while the League council proceeds to other matters on its agenda. Still more surprisingly, the Italians announced they would recede from their previous refusal to sit at the council table if the Ethiopian representatives were present. They said they were willing to participate so long as the Ethiopians refrained.

BLACKPOOL, England. Sept. 7 — Three persons were killed when an airplane crashed in flames in the center of the city today and set fire to a house. Two of the victims were the pilot and a woman passenger. The third fatality was caused when the plane struck a woman pedestrian. The accident was caused by a mid-air collision with another plane while five ships belonging to Sir Alan Cobham's Aerial Circus were flying in formation.

| CHICAGO, Sept. 6 (AP)—A plea for peace, voiced by a dozen women leaders, rang ‘round the war-menaced world Friday. They sounded their supplications at Chicago, New York, London and Geneva—then launched a campaign to enroll 60,000,000 persons of all races in a crusade for concord. Dr. Mary E. Woolley, president of Mt. Holyoke College and member of the American delegation to the Disarmament Conference, addressed an audience in Chicago's Grant Park. The meeting and an International broadcast were sponsored by the Women's International League for Peace. The program honored the memory of the late Jane Addams, founder of the organization, on the 77th anniversary of her birth.

GENEVA, Sept. 7—(A)—The five-power committee of the League of Nations council, dealing with the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, today in effect asked the disputants not to resort to force pending efforts to solve their differences peacefully. The letter repeated the words of an official communiqué issued after today’s committee session which said that the committee “relies upon the governments concerned to refrain from any act that might hinder or compromise its efforts.” The members of the five-power committee were presented as recognizing fully that the problem turns on the possibility of satisfying Italy’s military ambitions in Ethiopia. Geneva, Sept. 6 (AP)—A last minute concession by Premier Mussolini made it possible for the League of Nations to put into operation its machinery tonight for a final desperate effort to prevent war between Italy and Ethiopia. In the darkest hour of the crisis, a sub-committee of five nations was named by the League Council to deal with the dispute. Great Britain, France, Spain, Poland and Turkey compose the membership. Mussolini Telephones Mussolini, making one of his rare concessions, telephoned his spokesman, Baron Pompeo Aloisi, he would no longer insist that Italy be on the committee if France and Britain were to be members. Previously, Il Duce had insisted that Italy be represented on the group if the great powers were. This demand from Mussolini was found impossible because if the Council put Italy on the committee it would also have to appoint Ethiopia. The virtual effect of the a

Berlin, Sept. 7.—()—The propaganda minister disclosed today that Dr. Hans Lather, German ambassador at Washington, has been instructed to protest the dismissal at New York yesterday of charges of unlawful assembly against five men arrested in the recent steamship Bremen incident. The protest was decided upon after a full report of Magistrate Louis Brodsky’s action had reached the foreign office. New York dispatches relating the release of the five men superseded other news in afternoon newspapers but Magistrate Brodsky's remarks in giving his decision were not published.

Berlin, Germany, Sept. 7.—(U.P.) —Germany will make a diplomatic protest to the United States against the action of Magistrate Louis B. Brodsky of New York in dismissing charges against men arraigned before him for participation in a riot, in which the Swastika flag was torn from the liner Bremen, it was learned today. The protest will be directed both to Washington and New York, it was said, and will be directed especially against the magistrate’s motives in dismissing charges against the five men. Brodsky compared the Swastika flag, Nazi banner, to the “black flag of piracy.” Its display in an American harbor, he said, was sufficient provocation for demonstrations of protest. Afternoon newspapers in Berlin indignantly attacked the New York court action, which grew out of arrests made at the time of an anti-Nazi demonstration on July 26 as the German liner was preparing to sail from the

1935-01-18.text: Halifax, N. S., Jan. 18.—(AP)—Capt. Duncan Milne, last man left aboard the stranded British freighter Kenkerry as she broke up on Black Rock Point, was drowned today as he climbed into the breeches buoy that had carried 28 of his crew to safety. The freighter, with 27 of her crew rescued but with her captain and chief engineer still aboard had split in half on the rocks of Black Point at Portuguese Cove earlier today. Watchers on shore waited in vain by the breeches buoy for the captain and his chief engineer, J. Dove, to leave the ship. Jarred by every smash of the breakers, the freighter split in half and waves carried the stern away. But the line was still attached to the foremast. Chief Engineer Dove got ashore while Captain Milne, true to the traditions of the sea, remained to the last—just a little too long. Watchers on the shore, peering through a raging snowstorm, saw Captain Mil

PORTUGUESE, N. S., Jan. 18 (AP)—Duncan Milne, master of the British freighter Kenkerry, which crashed on a reef in a blinding snow storm last night, was dashed to death in mountainous seas today when he attempted to reach shore by a breeches buoy. True to traditions of the seas, Capt. Milne remained with his battered ship until the crew of 28 was ashore. With the vessel falling apart beneath him, the captain fastened himself in the breeches buoy and was being hauled ashore when the floundering ship split, breaking the breeches buoy line and hurling the master into the sea. The 3290 ton freighter was bound for Halifax to load grain when she struck a blinding blizzard and was driven on the reef, only 200 yards off shore. Chief Engineer J. Dove who remained aboard until the last member of the crew was safe, barely escaped with his life. He was near the end of the breeches buoy line and Capt

HALIFAX, Jan. 17. (4—The British freighter Kenkerry, stranded on the dangerous Sambro ledges, was in danger of breaking up tonight off the Nova Scotia coast. Shortly before midnight the ship asked for lifeboats from Duncan Cove and began lowering her own in the stormy seas. Radio marine said a gale was blowing in the region where the ship went aground and that the Atlantic was extremely rough. There were fears for the safety of the crew of 27 as the 3,930 ton vessel reported her engine room flooded and her lighting system out of commission.

AMARILLO, Jan. 16.-(A)—Late old W. English, 32, Amarillo flyer, was killed instantly early today when the automobile he was driving crashed into the rear end of a truck three miles east of Amarillo. English was driving toward Amarillo at the time of the accident. He was believed to have been blinded by the headlights of an east-bound automobile. His chest was crushed and he suffered internal injuries. Robert Campbell was driver of the truck, which was loaded with farm machinery. English was manager and secretary-treasurer of English Field which he established in 1929 and which was named for him. At the time of his death, English was associated with Thornton Oxnard, president of the Amarillo Airport Corporation, in the drilling of a deep oil test near here.

GENEVA, Jan. 17—()-—-A successful 15-year experiment in international government virtually ended today as the League of Nations Council voted unanimously to return the Saar to Germany. While Pierre Laval, French Foreign Minister, solemnly urged rapprochement between France and Germany as “one of the essential conditions of effective guarantee of Europe's peace,” the League Council put the formal stamp of its approval on the will of Saarlanders expressed in last Sunday's plebiscite.

GENEVA (U.P) — Revival of the bitter dispute between Jugoslavia and Hungary, which recently caused a European crisis, was threatened Friday when Hungary disclaimed all responsibility for the assassination of King Alexander at Marseilles. In a memorandum to the League of Nations, Hungary declared exhaustive investigation proved it was in no wise made morally responsible for the assassination because it sheltered Croatian terrorists. The memorandum, the result of Jugoslavia’s demand that Hungary be held morally responsible for the assassination, was not expected to satisfy Jugoslavia. It was admitted that certain minor police officers “did not control Croat emigrants with the desired diligence” and that as a result a captain of gendarmes was dismissed and three policemen were sentenced to 30 days’ imprisonment. Hungary, the memorandum said, had decided in future to exert stricter control o

GENEVA, Jan. 18. — The Hungarian government officially washed its hands Friday of any responsibility in the assassination of King Alexander of Yugoslavia at Marseille last October. Reporting to the League of Nations the result of investigations suggested by the latter in connection with Yugoslav charges of Hungarian complicity, Budapest declared: “The minutest inquiry shows it is impossible to link, direct or indirect, Hungarian

'By The Associated Press. | GENEVA, Jan. 17.—The League of Nations council today unanimously voted for the annexation of the Saar basin territory to Germany. The council's action came as a result of last Sunday’s plebiscite in which 90 per cent of the voting inhabitants of the Saar registered their desire to be reunited with the nation from which their territory was cut off by the treaty of Versailles ending the world war. The council vote was made in a chamber packed with league representatives and spectators. Pierre Laval, foreign minister of France, made a solemn appeal for a rapprochement between France and Germany, declaring: “It is one of the essential conditions of an effective guarantee of the peace of Europe.”

GENEVA, July 31—Great Britain and France were believed tonight to have reached a common basis for action on League of Nations council procedure to soothe the tense Italo-Ethiopian dispute. At midnight, after a second conference with Anthony Eden, Great Britain’s chief envoy, Premier Laval of France was understood to have finally approved important modifications in a formula draft insisted upon by Eden. “It's finished for the moment,” Eden told the Associated Press as the conference ended a day of fatiguing “behind the scenes” maneuvers, forced by a flat Italian demand at today's opening council session that discussion of the crisis be limited to arbitration and British insistence on an ultimate thrashing out of the whole quarrel. (Copyright, 1935, by United Press) ADDIS ABABA, July 31.—(U.P)— Ethiopians, prepared to defend their ancient empire to the death if need be, looked to Great Britain today as the chief hope of averting a war with Italy. They believe that unless Britain acts war is certain, and they say they will accept none but an honorable peace. To rumors that Ethiopia would accept a form of international mandate—perhaps under the League of Nations—officials said stoutly that it was out of the question. They will accept no overlordship, they will agree to no political concessions to Italy, they said. But they are willing to give economic concessions, as Emperor Haile Selassie I said in a statement yesterday. Fear a Postponement. Addis Ababa — Emperor Haile Selassie ends council with tribal chieftains; mass recruiting begins; women demand right to fight, start raising funds. Rome — Italy maintains silence on Geneva efforts, sends more troops to East Africa; government raises interest rate on bonds to increase cash reserves. London — Commons hears liberal leader say war between blacks and whites may be perilous for British empire; Hoare welcomes U. S. disapproval of war; London Herald foresees revolt against Duce. LONDON, July 31.—(AP)—The British government took steps today to create a new All-India Federation, the great experiment in Indian self-government. Parliament gave final approval to the “New Deal” for India yesterday, completing its action on the India bill with House of Commons agreement to more than 500 more amendments made by the House of Lords. Arrangements were made for elections and creation of new state legislatures as early as possible in 1936 in what are at present the British Indian provinces. At the same time officials began work on the assignment given them by the new law of bringing the Indian states, now nominally under their own rulers, into the Federation. ROME— Mussolini’s newspaper insists “total solution” necessary; war monopoly of coal, coke, copper, minerals decreed. ADEN, Arabia— Reuters (British) news agency reports Ethiopia seeking Yemeni recruits. PARIS— French place hope for peace in Premier Laval’s mediation at Geneva. GENEVA, Aug. 1.-(INS)--Premier Benito Mussolini today flatly rejected a British demand for a four-power conference to settle peacefully the Italo-Abyssinian controversy. Also, by failing to approve a Franco-British formula for procedure of the League of Nations council's debate on the crisis, Il Duce forced postponement until tomorrow evening of a council session which had been scheduled for tonight. Abyssinia readily accepted the procedure proposal, but Italy delayed her answer, and League diplomats were compelled to scurry to hotel rooms and lobbies in attempts to find a way for the council to tackle the question of the threatened war.

1935-01-23.text: TOKYO. (UP). A new danger spot appeared on the vast, trouble-splotched map of Asia as Russia and Japan, two great powers equally confident of their destiny in the east, found their expansionist aims clashing in Sinkiang, huge northwestern territory nominally under Chinese rule. With threatened conflict in Manchuria apparently staved off by virtual agreement for Russia's sale of the Chinese Eastern railway, an official Japanese spokesman said the Soviet’s alleged penetration of Sinkiang “menaces the peace and stability of eastern Asia.” The maintenance of that peace and stability, the spokesman asserted, is Japan's mission. Earlier Koki Hirota, Japan's foreign minister, told the diet that the westward movement of Chinese communists, “coupled with the reported Sovietization of Sinkiang,” oblige the Japanese government to “watch with concern activities of the communist party and its armies

Rome, Jan. 2 (AP) - Heuator William Gibbs McAdoo, en route from the Far East back home, said today he was pleased that Japan had denounced the Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 "because this will enable the United States to build the navy of which she has a need." McAdoo said he had not been in favor of the Washington Naval Treaty for some years because of the bonds it placed on the United States. "America," he said, "should build the strongest navy possible so as to protect herself from all aggression." The California senator said he had formed this opinion on the basis of first-hand information collected on his trip into the Far East. "If the United States constructs her navy without regard to other powers," said McAdoo, "she can carry on her program of development without fear of complications."

(By The Associated Press) 18, Jan. 22. — A story of heroism in the face of certain death was told in dispatches from French Somaliland tonight as camel troops, prison sharpshooters and who slew 87 French colonial employees. The reports contained the first details of the death of Albert, after receiving appeals for help from the Issa tribe which had been attacked by rival tribesmen, the Ats Amuraés. After marching all day in an effort to cut off the raiders, the Frenchman and his force encamped near Marheito. At dawn he attacked. For two hours the little band fought desperately against an enemy numbering 800, armed with 1874 model rifles and short, sharp cutlasses. At last their ammunition gave out. Tribesmen, who fight to the heat of tom-toms, closed to Bernard.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 23 (AP)—Unconfirmed dispatches said today that Japanese military airplanes had bombed Tuhsikou and Tung-chetze, naming them as "places within Eastern Chahar Province" of China. These dispatches said that Japanese artillery had "shelled points within Chahar." The reports said that eight Japanese airplanes had participated in the alleged bombing expedition.

Shanghai. —(AP)— Chinese dispatches from Kalgan, received here today, said 2,000 Japanese and Manchukuoan soldiers had attacked three towns in eastern Chahar province. The report said Tuhsikou, a town near the Chahar-Jehol border, had been bombed from the air and shelled by artillery. Other attacks, the advices said, were launched against Kuyuan and Tungehetze, described as “places within Chahar province.”

ATHENS, Jan. 23—(P)—Greek newspapers said today many persons were killed and injured when a revolt of Greek inhabitants of the Italian-owned island of Kalymnos was quelled by aviators and marine detachments. The press gave as a basis of its reports stories allegedly told by those who fled to territory owned by Greece. Earlier reports from the same sources said Italian warships were en route to Kalymnos, one of the Dodecanese island group in the Aegean Sea.

BERLIN, Jan. 23—(4%—Germany mapped a huge farming program today in its fight against high prices and unemployment. “Farming on a big scale is intended,” said Carl Goerdeler, Nazi commissioner of prices. “The people will have an opportunity to offset a loss in wages by a short time to work on their own farm products. In addition, the Hitler government plans a heavy cut in corporation dividends to force down the German price level.

(By The Associated Press) FALL RIVER, MASS. JAN. 23—FOUR BANDITS HELD UP A UNITED STATES MAIL TRUCK TODAY, BOUND ITS DRIVER AND ESCAPED WITH REGISTERED MAIL WHICH POLICE SAID CONTAINED APPROXIMATELY $129,000 IN BANK NOTES AND SILVER. THE SHIPMENT WAS BEING TAKEN TO A FALL RIVER BANK FROM A TRAIN WHICH PREVIOUSLY HAD ARRIVED FROM BOSTON.

1935-03-15.text: MOSCOW, March 14.—()—A “peaceful, friendly solution” of far eastern problems was officially advocated here today simultaneously with semi-official warnings that the Soviet will increase “defensive measures” if the British diplomacy yields too much to Germany, Maxim Litvinoff, commissar for foreign affairs, suggested that nations interested in the far eastern situation start discussing withdrawal of armed forces from the vicinity of the Manchoukuo-Siberian border, This withdrawal, he said in an interview, would be “quite natural” if “the tension” in the far east continues to decrease, Published In Organ The assertion that the Soviet will build up its defenses if Great Britain, in forthcoming security negotiations, makes too great concessions to the Reich was made in an article signed by Karl Radek, one of the government's chief mouthpieces, which was published in Izvestia, the government

LONDON, March 15 (4P).—The British House of Commons today voted its approval, 158 to 48, of naval estimates for 1935 amounting to £60,050,000 (about $286,000,000), an increase of £3,500,000 over last year. The vote came after Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, First Lord of the Admiralty, assured the legislators that Great Britain still is willing to enter into negotiations for abolition of submarines and reduction in size of warships and cruisers. Japan's denunciation of the 1922 Washington Naval Treaty, he said, should not be regarded “too tragically.”

LONDON (WP) — The Saudi-Arabian legation announced Friday that an unsuccessful attempt was made Friday in Mecca to assassinate King Ibn Saud. The Saudi-Arabian kingdom is the dominant state in Arabia. Ibn Saud was proclaimed king in 1926. Three assassins armed with daggers tried to stab Ibn Saud and the crown prince while they were walking around the “holy stone” of the sacred city. Royal bodyguards shot the assassins down.

By The Associated Press A flurry of talk about armaments foamed up yesterday even as British statesmen completed plans to visit three European capitals in the cause of peace. London—Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, first lord of the admiralty, said Japan's denunciation of the 1922 Washington naval pact disappointed Britain. It was announced Joseph Stalin himself would confer with Capt. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, when the latter goes to Moscow after visiting Berlin with Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon. Eden also will visit Warsaw. Berlin—The Diplomatische Politische Korrespondenz, government mouthpiece, again warned Simon that forthcoming security conferences must be in the spirit of 'unlimited confidence, placing general European interests above special wishes.' While France— Paris — Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin, spurred by the 'new German air menace,' made ready to ask parliamen

MOSCOW, March 15 — It was officially announced today that Joseph Stalin, general secretary of the political bureau, will personally receive Capt. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, when the latter comes to Moscow this month to discuss ‘European peace. The communist leader is not expected to participate in the formal negotiations, but when Stalin and Capt. Eden meet they are expected to talk over the situation fully between themselves. It is a rare procedure for Stalin to receive foreign visitors personally. Among the few foreigners who have met him informally in the past are Ambassador Witham C. Bullitt of the United States, George Bernard Shaw and H.G. Wells.

London, Mar. 13 (INS)—The Canadian government may want to make the five baby Dionnes wards of King George V, but so far as the monarch’s own closest subjects are concerned, they’d rather have the famed quintuplets under the care of their own parents. This became clear today as London newspapers, prominently displaying news of the project, sounded out representative public opinion and learned that the motherhood of England is definitely in sympathy with the parents. Britain is watching the dispute between the Dionnes and the Canadian government with as much amusement as interest, however, as the term, “wards of the king” is a rather peculiar one. Actually, the British government itself has nothing to do with the affair, as it never interferes in Canadian local legislation and King George himself could hardly be expected to increase his own family cares by taking over the upbringing of the

LONDON, March 15.—(#)—Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani disclosed today that her personal philanthropies total $50,000 a year, every cent of which goes to charities in the United States. Furthermore, she served notice with a toss of her auburn locks that although she has been “giving to charities anonymously for years,” hereafter she will let the world know about her donations.

PARIS, March 15 (4,.--Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gordon Switz, of East Orange, N.J., and New York, were indicted with 30 other persons today as members of an alleged international spy ring. Magistrate Michel Benon, the examiner, sent the cases to the correctional court for trial, expected to begin early in April. The prosecution is expected to order a secret trial for Mr. and Mrs. Switz who have been held in prison for 15 months of questioning. The ring was purportedly headed by Madame Lydia Stahl, a Russian who was educated in New York.

1935-05-10.text: (Copyright. 1935, Associated Press) London, May 6.—King George V of England knelt today with the reverence of an humble pilgrim in ancient St. Paul's Cathedral to give thanks to God for completion of 25 years on the throne, while all his vast empire celebrated his jubilee with mingled prayers and merry-making. So tempestuous was the shouted acclaim that rolled along with him as his state procession proceeded from Buckingham Palace to the cathedral and back that the king was obviously stirred deeply. Queen Mary was as deeply affected by the thunderous ovations. Observers along the route thought they detected tears in her eyes. Most Touching Moment The day's most touching moment came in the cathedral when the king-emperor, his right hand over his brow, knelt while the Archbishop of Canterbury pronounced his blessing and at its conclusion, oblivious to the others rising about him, remained

Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, May 9.—Authoritative quarters said today the Union of South Africa is ready and willing to have Southwest Africa, formerly Germany’s, returned to the Reich. That revelation came as representatives of the dominions and colonies resumed their conversations with members of the British cabinet on questions of Britain’s foreign policy. Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, already has given the empire statesmen full accounts of his recent visit to Berlin during which Adolf Hitler, among other things, insisted that Germany’s right to colonies must be recognized. It was confidently expected the views of J. B. M. Hertzog, prime minister of the Union of South Africa, would be sought in the matter of giving back to Germany some of the territory she lost in the World War, because the Reich’s greatest losses were in Africa. Hertzog, it was understood, was prepared

LONDON, May 10.—(UP)—Abyssinia and Italy seemed preparing for big scale war today in the ancient country between the Italian east African colonies and the mountain capital of Abyssinia, Addis Ababa. Emperor Haile Selassie of Abyssinia, in an interview with the Addis Ababa correspondent of the London Daily Telegraph, announced that he would order general mobilization if Italy continued its war preparations. “Ethiopia (Abyssinia) will never accept a state of unofficial war such as prevailed when Japan carried out its operations in Manchukuo. We will immediately resist. “I still hope that the League of Nations council at its meeting May 20 will move definitely toward a peaceful solution of our frontier dispute with Italy. But if not, and if Italy carries its military preparations, we will mobilize.” A united press dispatch from Addis Ababa said that the government protested strongly to the

LONDON, May 10.—(P)—The Duke of Manchester today was found guilty in the Old Bailey of obtaining money under false pretenses and sentenced to nine months imprisonment. The 59-year old peer, who earlier testified that his financial road had been rocky during recent years, showed no emotion as sentence was pronounced. His attorney indicated an appeal would be filed immediately. Testifying today in the case which arose from his pawning of jewelry allegedly not his property, the duke said 'I have been bankrupt twice.'

LONDON, May 9. (AP)—King George told members of parliament who came to congratulate him today on his Silver Jubilee that he prayed his country could continue to pursue the cause of freedom and progress. "In these days when fear and preparation for war are again astir in the world," the monarch said, "let us be thankful that quiet government and peace prevail over so large a part of the earth’s surface." King George also expressed gratitude "that under our flag of freedom so many millions eat their daily bread in far distant lands and climes with none to make them afraid." Referring to Westminster Hall where he received the Lords and the members of the House of Commons as "the very cradle of our envied parliamentary institutions" the king said: "Here is the anvil on which our common law was forged to become the joint inheritance of the United States of America and of our own community of

LONDON (UP) — Britain is prepared to fulfill her obligations under the Locarno treaty and extend military aid to France if the latter is attacked by Germany, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today. Members plied the government with questions about whether Britain would use her military force with France if Germany further repudiated the Versailles treaty by violating the demilitarized Rhineland. Sir John evaded the direct issue by saying Britain would faithfully fulfill her obligations under the Locarno treaty, which provides for military assistance in case of unjustified attack, but not for such assistance in case of violation of a previous treaty.

LONDON, May 10 (UP),—The Duke of Manchester was sentenced in Old Bailey court today to nine months’ imprisonment on a charge of fraud. The Duke, who is 58, is the ninth of his line. He was convicted by a jury of obtaining money under false pretenses by pawning jewelry which did not belong to him. The jewelry was owned by the late Consuelo, Duchess of Manchester, the American-born mother.

DUDLEY, WORCESTERSHIRE England, May 10.—(4)—Girls with bare legs and painted lips were banned from the parish church at Sedgley near here today by order of the vicar, the Rev. Harold Marley. The pastor warned his feminine parishioners that he not only would eject from the church all girls who neglected to don hosiery, but that he also would refuse to administer the sacrament to women with carmined lips. The Rev. Mr. Marley's admonition was contained in an article in the parish magazine. "I consider the girl who thrusts her unclothed flesh before the attention—frequently the close attention, because of the near in the pew—of the male sex is doing a catty trick. "The male mind, being what it is, is bound to be diverted. If it be said, ‘well I don’t think much of the male mind,’ my answer would be, ‘it is as it was made.’ "Woman was given those fair limbs to attract man, but only so that sh

1935-09-13.text: [Capone 2985 by the, Asmacatad: Poa} DO PA., Sept. 12} The honey-haired, blue-eyed little Evelyn Hoey, singer of torch songs to Broadway, Paris and London, was found shot to death early today on the floor of a bedroom of the country place of Henry Huddleston Rogers, Jr. At her feet lay a pistol, on the bed was another. And in a corner of the room, leaning against the wall, was a sawed-off shotgun. District Attorney William H. Parke, of Chester County, said today the fatal shooting of Evelyn Hoey, actress, “looks like a suicide.” Rogers, 29-year-old son and namesake of the late Standard Oil multi-millionaire who died last July, was brought to jail here for questioning and was held on a technical charge of suspicion of murder. With him, and held as a material witness, was William J. Kelly, of Union City, N. J. Denies Guilt Both Rogers and Kelly said the girl had killed herself after a viol

Geneva, Sept. 13. (#)—Premier Laval of France places France in the ranks with Great Britain, Russia and the smaller nations of Europe in defense of peace obligations of the League of Nations covenant. "Our obligation is inscribed in the covenant," Laval told the League. "France will not evade it." To this French stand, opposed to immediate war between Italy and Ethiopia, was added a warning to the delegation from the dominion of South Africa. It was forecast that it might lead to a racial conflict between the blacks and whites. Theodore Te Water, delegate from Union of South Africa, warned that Africa will arise in the case of an Italo-Ethiopian clash.

LONDON, Sept. 12—(AP)—Great Britain is rushing additional troops to reinforce its garrisons at Malta, a strategic post in the Mediterranean, a high source disclosed today. Three battalions stationed at Catterick, England, are being sent to the tiny island, which has already become the focal point of Britain's Mediterranean defense plans. A British battalion normally is composed of four companies of 250 men each. The units ordered to embark are the Lincolnshire regiment, (Continued on Page Two.)

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 12. (/P) Emperor Haile Selassie today expressed his profound gratitude for the British stand at Geneva backing the League of Nations covenant and opposing aggression. "The tide seems to have turned," said the emperor, and smiled, "We face the future with renewed confidence. God, justice and the great powers appear to be on our side. Our prayers for peace may yet be answered. "We will not be the first to draw blood, but if war must come, we are prepared. We will yield nothing further in the way of economic, political or territorial concessions to Italy. Our delegation at Geneva is so instructed." One of Haile Selassie’s closest advisers said that if Italy attacks Ethiopia without a formal declaration of war, as Japan did in Manchuria, the emperor would give Luigi Vinci-Gigliucci, the Italian minister, his passports and that all other Italians remaining after the beginni

Barnsley, Yorkshire, England, Sept. 12 ()—Trapped behind a wall of flame, 16 miners met an agonizing death and nine others were burned seriously after an explosion rocked the North Gawber colliery tonight. "The deadly blast roared through a 200-yard gallery in the mine, cutting off the men working at the far end. One of the survivors, Donald Brook, who escaped with his clothes smouldering, described it graphically, "I was working just below the place where the explosion occurred," he said. "Suddenly there was a boom, my electric torch was blown out of my hand and I was flung down in the darkness. "A cloud of choking coal dust blew down the workings and everything was blacked out. I never thought I'd get out alive."

BY WAAL ae Crikey, United Press Staff Correspondent (Copyright, 1935, by United Press) GENEVA, Sept. 13—(U.R)—France stepped to the side of Great Britain today with a clear declaration that both are agreed on the necessity of joint international action to prevent war. "It must be clearly understood that there exists no disagreement between France and Britain," Premier Pierre Laval told the assembly of the League of Nations, thus endorsing the previous declaration by Sir Samuel Hoare along the same lines. Neither specifically pledged his country to enforcement of penalties against Italy if she invades Ethiopia, but their call for full and complete enforcement of League regulations could be so construed. Laval's speech created a profound impression, as did the succeeding warning by Charles T. Te Water of South Africa that war on Ethiopia might cause a general African uprising of blacks aga

ROME, Sept. 13. — ( - England's reinforcing of her Mediterranean and Red Sea bases and sending of additional battleships to the Mediterranean is “placing in a state of alarm Italy's position in the Mediterranean and Red Sea,” the semi-official Azione Coloniale said today. The publication said in a front page editorial that this move by England could not but give rise to special measures by Italy. “The moment must come,” said the publication, “to demand what end England is pursuing in the Mediterranean Sea — our sea for geographical reasons, for military security and for necessities of provisioning.” It said the presence in the Mediterranean of a “never before seen number of units of the British fleet” constitutes a political act of undoubted significance.

Great Britain’s foreign secretary pleaded with hate tonight "in the words of w fre tor a peace that will do peace alike for Ethiopia’s national rights, and Italy's claims for expansion. Sir Samuel Hoare, in a speech broadcast to his own empire but meant for the ears of T uee, delivered a fervent appeal for a neat settlement of the bitter conflict between Italy and Ethiopia.

1935-10-01.text: NEW YORK—The British steamer Ariguani was standing by in a calm sea Monday to take off the passengers of the Rotterdam, Holland-America line steamer, aground on a reef 5 miles southeast of Kingston, Jamaica. "Everybody well and quiet; no danger" said a wireless message to the Associated Press from Captain Van Dulken, commander of the 21,000-ton vessel. The liner, which left New York Sept 21, had been plowing northward from Venezuela behind the hurricane which lashed Jamaica and part of Cuba during the week-end. Weather reports indicated she was "not directly in the storm's path when she went aground" for the hurricane early today was moving toward Bermuda. It had taken an estimated 37 lives in Central Cuba and had caused heavy property damage. COLUMNIST DIES CAMBRIDGE-UPI A veteran reporter and columnist for the Cam-

By United Press PARIS, Oct. 1— Britain and France moved a stage nearer to complete unity today in the face of the growing menace of war, and an official spokesman said the chances were three to one that France would support Britain. This development came after "vitally important" talks between Premier Laval and Sir George Clerk, British ambassador, and a meeting of Laval and the Prince of Wales with Maurice Gamelin, generalissimo of the French army, at the British embassy.

MIAMI, Fla. (UP) — The tropical hurricane that raged up the coast last week from Cuba caused heavy property damage at Bimini, a British island lying 43 miles east of here, but no lives were lost, it was reported today, in the first message from the island since the storm. The small island felt 125 mile an hour winds, it was estimated, by residents as the vicious hurricane swirled across it on an erratic course away from the Florida mainland. Weather officials believed the center of the hurricane passed very close to Bimini Saturday night. If conditions there appear serious from observations a small plane will fly from Miami to ascertain the needs of relief. Breathing freely again as they emerged from safe places sought when the hurricane warnings were hoisted for 17 hours from Ker

Ethiopian situation: ADDIS ABABA: American missionaries, deciding to stay at posts, are equipped with gas masks against air raids. Hillside dugout prepared for 65 American residents of capital. PARIS: Italy, fearing England will close Gibraltar, specifies 120,000 tons of coal ordered from France must be delivered overland if necessary. Prince of Wales talks with French officials. GIBRALTAR: British battleship Queen Elizabeth arrives to reinforce Mediterranean fleet. ROME: Italians await news of fighting in Ethiopia, expecting it momentarily. VIA ASMARA: Aduwa, scene of Italy's crushing defeat in 1896, will be first Italian objective, Webb Miller finds on visit to front. LONDON, Sept. 36—(UP)—Recurring reports that Great Britain has resorted to secret, back-stage diplomacy to bulwark her position against Italy in the Mediterranean Sea went unconfirmed and un denied in official circles tonight. A “hush-hush” attitude greeted the reports, from both Paris and Geneva, that Great Britain has addressed an inquiry to France to learn what the latter would do in the case of an unprovoked attack on the British navy in the Mediterranean Sea. The official refusal to discuss the matter in any form led to immediate speculation in diplomatic circles, where it was pointed out, however, that this official silence was the only thing lending credence to the reports.

PARIS, Oct. 1 (UP)—The Prince of Wales was host to Premier Laval and the ministers of marine and post offices at a British embassy lunch today which followed a conference between Premier Laval and Sir George Clark, British ambassador. Both conversations were regarded as developments of major importance in the Italian-Ethiopian dispute, coming at a time when Great Britain is seeking to gain French support in the crisis and France seeks in return to win Great Britain’s agreement to act with similar firmness in any crisis involving European nations, meaning Germany.

Memel, Sept. 30 (4)--German Memelanders, angered by the prolonged voting in the territory's Diet election, sent a telegram of protest tonight to the Geneva delegations of Great Britain, France and Belgium, signatory powers to the Memel convention. Despite this new dispute, the territory concluded its second day of voting on German or Lithuanian candidates for 20 Landtag seats with only minor brawls reported. Rumors, wholly without confirmation, were spread that Reichsführer Adolf Hitler would make a surprise appearance at Tilsit, just across the Prussian frontier, tomorrow for an important political speech. Still another day will be devoted this week-end to voting in the district of Juknaiciai, where a polling station was wrecked in an election row Sunday. This meant still more delay in announcement of the results of the balloting.

Rome, Sept. 30. (INS).—After having been slowed up temporarily by the League of Nations and British moves in the Mediterranean, Premier Benito Mussolini, to-day, ordered full speed ahead as he plunged Italy forward toward war with Ethiopia within a few days. The unexpectedly solid league front formed at Geneva in opposition to an Italian invasion of Ethiopia and the surprising action of Great Britain in rushing warships and fighting planes to the Mediterranean two weeks ago compelled Il Duce to pause and consider his projected war again. Now, after considering the situation in all its aspects, Premier Mussolini has made it clear he meant what he said when he declared he would obtain what he wanted in East Africa “with the league, without the league, or against the league.”

1935-09-24.text: GENEVA, Sept. 23 (7).-Rumors swept through the League of Nations lobbies today that the Italian delegation, angered by the Italo-Ethiopian committee's attitude, might leave Geneva, These reports were heard after the British delegation took the position that Italy’s counter-proposals to a league plan for settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute were unacceptable, The league plan was accepted by Ethiopia. League officials said the danger of a hopeless deadlock was developing. The officials said they based their view on the fact that the committee of five which prepared the compromise plan had decided that an Italian communique and oral statements made by the Italians constituted a definite rejection of the plan. The plan was prepared by a committee composed of delegates from Spain, Great Britain, France, Poland and Turkey. The chairman of the committee, Salvador De Madariaga of Spain, rec

Latest developments in the Ethiopian crisis: ROME—Mussolini tells cabinet what he will do if nations apply penalties to Italy; shows no sign of weakening in determination to proceed with war on Ethiopia regardless of the attitude of other powers. Cabinet votes sweeping measures to prepare army, navy and air force for East African campaign. Italian test mobilization cancelled. Britain reassures Italy her fleet movement is not aggressive. Italian troops and war supplies continue to pour into Africa, GENEVA—Committee of five admits failure to settle dispute and throws problem back in lap of council. LONDON—British cabinet unanimously approves Britain's course in Ethiopian dispute, including Britain's stand at Geneva for complete enforcement of the League covenant.

Ballinrobe, County Mayo, Ireland, Sept. 23—(P)—Officers of the Irish Free State Air Force arrived today to undertake dismantling the monoplane of Felix Waitkus, American Trans-Atlantic flier, smashed in the forced landing which ended his 3,000-mile solo flight from New York. The 28-year-old aviator, uninjured in the crack-up and refreshed by a night's sleep, said his future plans were undecided pending a final report from engineers who are examining the plane, but that he considered resumption of his flight to Kaunas, Lithuania, out of the question. Earlier, the flier had laughed off his mishap with the words: 'I got quite a bump, but I can hardly wait to fly on to Kaunas.' While Waitkus had a long sleep, four civil guards kept an all-night watch over the craft. At Geneva: Rumors of an Italian break with the League of Nations deepened the pessimism as British spokesmen characterized Italy's counter-proposals to the League peace plan as removing all hope for conciliation. Italian delegates remained in Geneva, but would not say they would stay if the League council decides to act under article 15 of the covenant. At Rome: Italy made tentative preparations to evacuate sea-coast cities in case of necessity as 206,000 newly mobilized troops reported for duty. The official gazette announced 244 million lire had been appropriated for colonial expense. Ballinrobe, County Mayo, Ireland, Sept. 22.—-(AP)—The transatlantic solo flight of Felix Waitkus, 28-year-old Wisconsin aviator, ended today in a smashup in a rough field but the flier himself was uninjured. Fog-bound and buffeted by storms along the Irish coast, Waitkus, who had hoped to fly non-stop from New York to Kaunas, Lithuania, brought his white and orange plane down in a hazardous landing. Hits Tree Bouncing across the uneven field, the machine struck a tree and was badly damaged, but Waitkus, whom frantic villagers expected to find dead, climbed out of the wreckage and said he felt lucky to escape without a scratch. “I had been flying blind for a long time,” he asserted. “I had bad visibility all over the Atlantic and when I reached the coast I ran into storms and fogs. LONDON, (®)—The British cabinet Tuesday approved the action of its statesmen at Geneva regarding the Italo-Ethiopian situation and decided to continue in the firm support of the League of Nations’ covenant. An authoritative source, discussing this action, said the cabinet had decided not to make any further decisions for the moment. It further decided, it was said, to continue the imperial defense committee as a council of action empowered to take all necessary steps to keep Great Britain prepared for emergencies. It was said in authoritative quarters that the personal message of Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary, to Premier Mussolini, delivered Monday night by the British ambassador to Rome, Sir Eric Drummond, had received a friendly response. BALLINROBE, County Mayo, Irish Free State, Sept. 23 (UP).—Felix Waitkus, United States army reserve flyer whose attempt to make a non-stop flight from New York to Kaunas, Lithuania, ended with a forced landing yesterday, impatiently awaited repairs of his cracked-up plane today. The slim, 27-year-old aviator still was weary after his battle against fog and rain in his flight across the Atlantic, but was eager to resume his flight to Kaunas. He was uninjured when his monoplane overturned yesterday. “I had a most trying time over the Atlantic,” he said. “Most of the time I was flying blind. As I approached the Irish coast I struck particularly stormy weather. “I was delighted to see land because I was tired out from fighting the storm and my gasoline supply was getting low. “I decided to land if I could find a break in the fog. 1935-09-14.text: Geneva, Sept. 13 (#)—Europe presented a solid front to Italy in the interests of peace tonight after France chose to follow Great Britain and support the League of Nations wholeheartedly. In one of the most eagerly awaited speeches here since the World War, France's Premier, the veteran Pierre Laval, declared: “Our obligations are inscribed in the covenant. France will not evade those obligations.” Thus one of Italy's warmest friends sided with Britain in efforts to halt a threatened African war which might destroy the League. And a powerful European balance swung against Premier Benito Mussolini’s military plans. (An official spokesman in Rome said Italy would not swerve from her present path, despite Laval’s speech. He characterized the address as neither friendly nor unfriendly). Laval's oration was considered by League observers as a friendly admonition to his friend Mussolini that w

GENEVA, Sept. 14—Vast Soviet Russia, speaking for immense reaches of two continents, the little entente, the Balkan entente and the Baltic states, all raised their voices today before the assembly of the League of Nations in defense of the league covenant. Thus they joined England and France in swelling into imposing proportion the protest of the world’s nations against an Italian invasion of Ethiopia. Maxim Litvinoff, Russia’s spokesman, told the assembly that for his nation “there is only the question of defending the covenant as the instrument of peace. He warned, however that the “covenant is not enough” and created a sensation by saying that certain bilateral non-aggression pacts actually are designed for security and aggression. (By the Associated Press) ROME, Sept. 13.—Italy announced tonight she would go straight ahead with her plans in East Africa and at the same time a semi-official newspaper said the country would take "answering measures" to Great Britain’s concentration of a fleet in the Mediterranean. Not to Change Plans Commenting on the speech at Geneva of Premier Pierre Laval of France, in which he supported obligations under the covenant of the League of Nations, an official spokesman said it would not change Premier Mussolini’s plans. The cabinet will meet tomorrow in its regular session. Laval’s speech created an impression in official circles here that it was "neither favorable nor unfavorable." His general statements backing up the league pact were felt to be offset by his references to French agreements in January with Mussolini. ATHENS, ‘U.P)—Great Britain today asked an explanation of recent frequent calls of small Italian warships to Greek harbors. Sydney P. Waterlow, British minister, made the request. It was understood that Waterlow informed the government that in many places the incursions of the Italian warships into Greek territorial waters were regarded as threatening Greek integrity. The United Press reported on the basis of authoritative information two weeks ago that the cabinet had decided that in the event of an Italian-British clash, Greece would go wholeheartedly with Britain. Hence the British representations were friendly and apparently intended to lay the basis for further tightening of the web about Italy as it proceeds with its plans to make war on Ethiopia. London, Sept. 14. (#) — Dame Madge Kendal, noted actress of the earliest years of the century, died here today. She was 86 years old. An actress whose active career on the stage lasted more than half a century, Dame Madge Kendal was known as “the matron of the British drama.” Descended from a family that for generations had been connected with the theater, she was not quite five years old when, in 1854 in London, she played her first role. Through the rest of the century and into the next the stage was almost her home — in London, in the provinces and in America, where she made her first appearance Oct. 7, 1889 at the Fifth Avenue Theater, New York. She was made a Dame Commander of the British Empire in 1926 and a year later was given the grand cross of the order.
