Geneva, Sept. 14, (U.P)—Communist Russia, world's greatest military power, today joined Republican France and monarchial England, Russia's allies of czarist times, in a new triple entente against an Italian war on Ethiopia. Promising Russia's full, unqualified support of the league in the interest of peace, Maxim Litvinov, Russia’s brilliant, forceful foreign minister, indicated clearly that he had in mind this fact: That if the League of Nations imposes penalties on Italy in event of an attack on Ethiopia it might provide a historical precedent for league action against possible German aggression in future. His bold presentation before the League of Nations assembly of a new aspect of the league's struggle with a grave European crisis was matched by his statement on Russia’s position. “If all peace efforts of the league council fail,” he said, “and the Italian-Ethiopian conflict comes b

Geneva, Switzerland (INS)—Completing a virtually unanimous decision, Soviet Russia and more than half a dozen small countries today followed the lead of Great Britain and France to put in action the full peace power of the League against the Italian plans to invade Ethiopia. In addition to Russia, whose stand was announced by Maxim Litvinoff, Portugal, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Greece, Turkey, and Bulgaria all stepped into line with pledges of full support of whatever steps the League may take against Premier Mussolini if he carries out his intentions to make war on Ethiopia. Previously Belgium, the Netherlands and Scandinavian powers had taken similar stands. This left only Germany and Japan of the world’s important countries—as far as Geneva's representation goes—on the fence.

1935-09-17.text: LONDON, Sept. 17.—An authoritative British source tonight described the transfer of almost the entire British home fleet to Gibraltar and the Mediterranean as "precautionary." This disclosure came shortly after the cabinet ministers who virtually make up the imperial defense council had met at 10 Downing Street in answer to the summons of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin. They were in session one and one-half hours, and it was understood they considered general empire policies in view of the increasingly dangerous situation engendered by the Italo-Ethiopian crisis. The British public was in the dark concerning the movement of the great ships of the mightiest naval power. It was explained authoritatively that the situation now existing in the Mediterranean—where the Italian navy incidentally is holding maneuvers and through which thousands of Fascist soldiers are being moved to East Africa—

LONDON, Sept. 17, — (AP) Seven persons were known to be dead today as the result of the most violent gale of recent years. The gale, which swept the English coast, moderated toward nightfall, but heavy seas still surged at channel ports. The dead included a sea captain, a woman crushed by a chimney, and three cyclists swept along by the wind.

Both Italy and Great Britain marshalled their naval strength today as the hour drew near for the League of Nations council to make its decision in the Italo-Ethiopian dilemma. Mussolini recalled from the reserves Italy's two largest battleships, the Duilio and the Doria, both carrying 13 12-inch guns. The premier also sent orders to squadron commanders in the Mediterranean, Adriatic and Red Sea to shape the navy into compact fighting units. Small Home Fleet A strangely small British home fleet of only 19 ships steamed off Portland for maneuvers ordinarily held off Scotland, but doubt was expressed as to just where the tactics would take place or how many vessels would be involved. About 50,000 troops awaited orders in South England. Alexandro Lessona, under secretary of State for Italian colonies, said in an article written expressly for the Associated Press, that Italy "does not want a

Troop Maneuvers in England Also Reported, Statesmen Fear Fight May Momentarily Break Out Along Ethiopian Frontier. Events in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis moved swiftly toward a climax in Europe today. Outstanding events follow: The British navy masses in the Mediterranean in formidable force, including some of the largest fighting units in the home fleet and others from as far away as China. Forty thousand British troops, with 300 tanks and scores of airplanes start maneuvers in the near future.

New York, Sept. 16 ()—The S. S. Washington messaged tonight that the British steamer Mary Kingsley had sent a distress call, saying the ship was taking water in a heavy Atlantic gale and most of the crew was injured. The Washington reported that the captain of the Kingsley declined offers of several salvage tugs for towing purposes and that no ships were standing by. The Kingsley was off the Irish coast. The Belgian steamer Jean Jadot was communicating with the Kingsley and offered to proceed to her if needed. The British steamer Tamaroa reported she hoped to reach the Kingsley by 11:30 (Greenwich meridian time) tomorrow.

By The Associated Press Gibraltar, Sept. 17—Five of Great Britain’s mightiest cruisers which steamed secretly from Portland, England, Saturday night, slipped into Gibraltar today. The Renown, Hood, Neptune, Achilles, and Orion, accompanied by four destroyers, arrived after a fast voyage of about 1,200 miles. The ships sailed amid greatest secrecy, after assembling in Portland ostensibly to participate in home fleet maneuvers in Scottish waters. Their arrival confirmed a belief that the south coast of England squadron was en route here to assist in bolstering the line of ships which Britain has moved to the Malta and Suez region to protect the “life line” of the empire. The increasing tension in the Italo-Ethiopian crisis has already caused near record concentration of British ships and planes in the Mediterranean.

Great Britain and Italy moved to put their battle fleets into strategic position Monday night to meet whatever menace may come out of the tense Italo-Ethiopian row. Great fighting ships of the British home fleet slipped quietly away from Portland on the eve of scheduled maneuvers, presumably to reinforce those vessels already in the Mediterranean. Naval authorities swung a boom defense across the southern entrance of Admiralty harbor at Gibraltar. Passing through it was prohibited. From Rome came Mussolini’s reply. He ordered the Italian fighting maritime forces split into Adriatic and Mediterranean fleets with a “superior command” in each sea. At Geneva—Certain League of Nations members were reported reliably to have started on a preliminary plan for an economic boycott of Italy should she start an unprovoked war on Ethiopia. At Addis Ababa—Sources close to Emperor Haile Selassie said h

Hyde Park, N. Y., Sept. 16. (4) — President Roosevelt discussed the possibility of further naval limitations over the tea cups today with Norman Davis, American representative to the preliminary negotiations. Davis afterward expressed doubt of new agreements. With the British fleet steaming into the Mediterranean in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis, Mr. Roosevelt leisurely talked over the situation with Davis and Mrs. Davis at tea. Davis, upon his return to the temporary executive office at the Nelson house in Poughkeepsie, said that the foreign situation was discussed just like any other exciting news of the day but that there was no thought of American intervention. So far as the foreign situation is concerned, Mr. Davis said the British have taken the initiative. He said there was no indication of American involvement and spoke discouragingly of the possibility of future naval limitations

1935-04-16.text: Sirexa, Ualy, April 18.---(49—A determined unity among the three great western European powers was seen in conference circles today as the most significant contribution to peace resulting from the tri-partite conversations of Great Britain, France and Italy. Six points of agreement were listed in a communique issued after the meetings closed: One, a common line of conduct on the French appeal to the League of Nations council for consideration of Germany's rearmament moves. Two, pursuance of negotiations for "the development which is desired in the security of eastern Europe." Three, consultation in case of a threat to the independence and integrity of Austria and a summoning of a conference at Rome to conclude a Danubian accord; Four, further study looking to completion of the western European defenses air pact. Five, recognition that Germany's unilateral abrogation of the military claus

GENEVA, April 16.(UP)—Great Britain, France and Italy steamroller tactics today to force through the council of the League of Nations a resolution strongly condemning Germany for re-arming in violation of the Versailles treaty. "The three powers adopted a firm, united front and passage of the resolution tomorrow was virtually assured. The council adjourned without taking a vote. When the vote is reached, Denmark and Poland, who oppose such strong condemnation of Germany, probably will abstain. A unanimous vote is required, which the abstentions would permit.

Geneva, Apr. 16. — France, Great Britain and Italy today submitted to the extraordinary council session of the League of Nations the draft of a resolution condemning “any unilateral repudiation of international obligations” such as Germany's repudiation of the armaments clauses of the Versailles treaty. Pierre Laval, foreign minister of France, although faced with opposition to the resolution by several nations, notably Poland and Denmark, received the strong support of spokesmen for both Great Britain and Italy when he presented it to the council. The council received the resolution and, after a brief debate, adjourned until tomorrow.

Associated Press Foreign staff, LONDON, April 15.—(@)—Neville Chamberlain, the chancellor of the exchequer, painted a rosy picture today in the house of commons of Great Britain’s financial and trade position as he presented the British budget for 1935-36 with an estimated surplus of 5,610,000 pounds—about $28,030,000. The chancellor was buoyantly cheerful in outlining improved economic conditions and placed the estimated total of ordinary expenditure by the government at 729,970,000 pounds—about $3,649,800,000—with a total estimated revenue of 735,580,000—about $3,677,830,000. The difference between the figures is the surplus. On the expenditure side, Chamberlain pointed out a provision must be made for an additional 10,500,000 pounds—about $52,300,000 for defense services as already outlined in the army, navy and aviation estimates. He estimated the income tax would bring in 237,000,00

(Copyright, 1935, by the Associated Press) GENEVA, April 16—(4)—The “condemnation” by indirection of Germany for the repudiation of treaties and the regret of France, Great Britain, and Italy that Germany has failed to fulfill her agreements under the covenant were introduced to a private session of the League of Nations council today by Pierre Laval, foreign minister of France. Laval announced the resolution was made jointly by France, Great Britain, and Italy. A French spokesman informed the Associated Press that, in a further attempt to adopt a policy of conciliation, the French draft of the resolution was amended at the last moment so that Germany was not specifically mentioned in that phase which condemns the violation of treaties. It was understood, that, instead, the resolution condemns all unilateral repudiations of treaties.

| By The Associated Press - London, April 16—The British government announced today it is setting up a special department to deal with safeguarding the British Isles’ 46,000,000 people against air attacks. Sir John Gilmour, the home secretary, told the House of Commons the Home Office was setting up a special department and starting to work on the subject of air defense with a full staff May 1. The first task of the new department will be to circularize all local authorities outlining the public air defense policy and indicating the nature and the extent of the cooperation required from them.

(Copyright 1935. by The Associated Press) Geneva, April 15.—While the League of Nations council pondered the French protest on German rearmament, a reliable informant here disclosed tonight that the action of England and Italy in reaffirming the Locarno pledge to guarantee peace on the Rhine was made intentionally as a warning to Germany. This disclosure was made simultaneously with the intimation that the action was likely to have important bearing on the deliberations of the council on Germany’s treaty violation. Dodged The first day’s session of the council produced little in concrete results except a decision to put off Ethiopia's request for immediate arbitration of her dispute with Italy. The council recommended that (Continued on Page 2?)

London, April 15. — Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, pulled his fourth balanced budget out of the counting house today, offering new relief to millions of small taxpayers despite increased military expenditures for 1935-36 of £10,500,000—about $52,300,000. The smiling chancellor proposed to the House of Commons that the income tax be reduced in the lower brackets and announced the restoration of the final portion of pay cuts made in 1931. Even so he presented an estimated surplus for the year of £50,000, about $2,425,060. “Our program of cheap money, tariffs, remission of taxes and balanced budgets,” said the chancellor, “has made it possible for our country to recover 80 per cent. of its prosperity. Given peace abroad and fair times at home we should make a further substantial advance in the coming fiscal year.” The chancellor's total estimated expenditure of £729,970,0

1935-09-08.text: Anxious world statesmen shot nervous glances toward British and Italian fleet maneuvering in the Mediterranean as they studied the diplomatic moves at Geneva which may mean peace or war in Ethiopia. The Italo-Ethiopian crisis overshadowed all other problems as Dr. Barique Ruiz Guindazu of Argentina, turning over the chairmanship of the assembly of the League of Nations to the new president, Dr. Eduard Benes, confessed the world was “distracted with anxiety.” As Benes, foreign minister of Czechoslovakia, and one of the guiding spirits of the Little Entente, took office, authoritative sources confirmed the concentration of the British home and Mediterranean (Continued on page three)

SMO® ASSOCIATED Press. LONDON, Sept. 7. — Reuters (British) news agency reported today that Premier Mussolini of Italy had assured France that Italy will not resort to war so long as the Italo-Ethiopian dispute is under consideration.

ROME, Sept. 7—U.P)—A challenge to Britain’s strength and historic domination of the Mediterranean was seen tonight in plans for extensive Italian naval maneuvers in the eastern half of the sea. One of the most interesting phases of the maneuvers, designed to display Italy's new strength and Britain's changed position, is expected to be the operations of sixty submarines between Sicily and Italian Libya, on the north coast of Africa. Such a fleet could conceivably block all Mediterranean traffic and break the all-British commercial and military sea route to India, the Far East and Australia-New Zealand. Italian naval observers contend that the development of the Italian fleet and establishment of numerous air bases, with a heavy concentration of planes in the Mediterranean, directly affects the 150-year-old policy of Britain to maintain a naval ratio in the Mediterranean of 2 to 1 against

LONDON, Sept. 7.—How’s your Amharic (pronounced am-har-ick)? With names and places in Ethiopia becoming more important daily, language experts at the Ethiopian legation today gave reporters a short course in how to handle tongue-twisters, for the benefit of readers at home. It appeared to be only the spelling that frightened. To pronounce Ualual, the frontier oasis, for example, it is only necessary to look one casually and repeat, “well, well,” without fear or hesitation. The Ethiopian capital becomes: Ah Des (accent second syllable) Ah Bah Bah (accent first syllable). The first part is pronounced leisurely, the second as though you were going some place in a hurry. The emperor’s name to be pronounced correctly, must be Lek Still Loss’ See’ (accent syllables, respectively). The hissing sounds characteristic Continued on Page 8 Column 7.

ROME, Sept. 7—(Pi)— The authoritative Giornale D'Italia said tonight groups of armed Senussites (a North African Moslem sect) are concentrating on the border of Libya, an Italian possession, with "mysterious support." In an article directed against British influence in Egypt, the Giornale demanded to know who is furnishing the Senussites with arms and favoring their "aggressive" designs. The newspaper said the Senussites were hired fighting tribes who fled across the border into Egypt following the domination of Libya by Italian troops. It also was recalled that Premier Mussolini received Marshal Italo Balbo, governor of Libya, this week and promised to send him troops from the mainland. The newspaper demanded to know what measures were being taken by authorities in Egypt to keep that country neutral in the event of an Italo-Ethiopian war and to prevent Egypt from being drawn into it thr

(Copyright 1935 by United Press) GENEVA, Sept. 7—A League Council sub-committee today sent letters to Italy and Ethiopia asking them to refrain from hostile action while peace efforts were being made. The appeal was sent by the new committee of five nations which represents the last League of Nations hope of averting war. Salvador De Madariaga, Spanish chairman of the committee, explained: "We are going to ask Italy and Ethiopia not to make so much noise that we cannot hear ourselves. The letter, signed by me, will ask both governments to do nothing to complicate our task." But actually the appeal is direct to Benito Mussolini, defying the League and the world to stop him in his ambition to conquer Ethiopia. It is on Mussolini alone that the success of the plea hinges. The Ethiopian rains, according to latest predictions, may not end until early October, but League leaders fear each day

RUM, Sept. 1.— (A) —Pope Pius, referring to the Italo-Ethiopian conflict, delivered a plea for peace before 20,000 former service men at St. Paul's basilica today and announced, “From our latest information, we seem to see forming on the horizon a rainbow of peace casting its rays across the world.” The pontiff left his summer retreat at Castel Gandolfo early in the morning to celebrate a mass for an international convention of former service men which opened with the ceremony at St. Paul's. He recognized Italy's aspirations in Ethiopia, saying, “We desire that with peace the aspirations of good people, all their needs shall be satisfied, recognized and obtained but with justice and with peace; with justice because against justice there is only sin and sin makes the people miserable.”

Addis Ababa. Sept. 7.—(AP)—Italian Minister Vinci today ordered all Italian consulates in Ethiopia withdrawn. The minister acted on orders received from Premier Mussolini. The date for withdrawal was Sept. 15. Diplomatic observers feared closing the Italian consulates meant Premier Mussolini was determined to go to war to settle the Italo-Ethiopian dispute, despite decisions of the League of Nations council at Geneva. The five-power committee of the League of Nations council, dealing with the Italo-Ethiopian crisis today, in effect asked the disputants not to resort to force pending efforts to solve their differences peacefully.

1935-09-05.text: LONDON, Sept. 5--(#)--Two other ships today took 736 holiday passengers off the Doric, "Cupid's Ship" of the Cunard-White Star line, after its collision with the French freighter Formigny 70 miles off the coast of Portugal. Wireless messages said the Orion of the same line had taken off 400 passengers and the Viceroy of India, the remainder. Reuters’ (British News Agency) Lisbon correspondent said the 16,484-ton Doric was not seriously damaged. He reported the sea calm and the rescue accomplished without difficulty. The trim new Orion turned its maiden voyage into a rescue expedition, being the first to respond to the Doric’s SOS. The Doric was known as the "Cupid Ship," because nine couples announced their engagements while on a previous cruise. At the time of the collision she was bound from Gibraltar to London. The Formigny, 2,166 tons, was bound for Dunkirk, France, to Oran, a seapor

CALGARY, ALTA, SEPT. 4. (AP).--Trapped on a ledge high up on a mountain side in northern British Columbia, Paul Cardoni, a young surveyor, was in danger of death today. Rescue efforts were halted by darkness last night. Rescuers were making other attempts to reach him today. One thousand feet up the mountain and 600 feet from the summit, young Cardoni was held prisoner on a narrow ledge, unable to sit or lie down in a bitter cold northern night with snow swirling around the mountain peak. A member of a far north mining camp survey party, Cardoni found himself in a position where it was difficult to return down the precipitous slope and moved upward 1,000 feet, hoping to get over the top of the mountain and descend by another route. He reached the ledge and found he could neither ascend nor descend.

LONDON, Sept. 5, (?).—Two British liners today rescued the full list of 736 passengers from another British ship, the S. S. Doric, after it had collided with the French S. S. Formigny in the Atlantic off the coast of Portugal. The collision occurred in a fog. The sea was calm. The passengers accepted the interruption of their holiday cruise without a sign of panic. Instead, they sang as they waited their turn at the lifeboats and sang again as they pulled away to safety. No Casualties The Cunard-White Star Line, owner of the ship, announced: "There were no casualties. All passengers have been taken off the Doric and are being taken to London. The Doric herself is sailing for Vigo under her own steam." The rescue was accomplished by the Orion of the Orient line and the Viceroy of India of the P. and O. line. Captain A. C. Greig, commander of the Doric, took the helm of the ship last April

London, Sept. 5 (Thursday) (P)—An SOS call was flashed from the Cunard-White Star liner Doric today, saying the vessel had been in collision with the 2,160-ton French steamer Forminey. The Doric is on a cruise, en route from Gibraltar to London. The British vessel, of 16,484 tons, messaged that it was in collision at 41.19 degrees North, 9.34 degrees West. The distress call was picked up by the Lands End Radio Station, Lloyds said. The scene of the crash was off the Portuguese coast, about 70 miles off Oporto.

GENEVA, Sept. 4 (4).-Anthony Eden, British Cabinet Minister, assured the League of Nations Council today that there can be no question of any political or economic conflict between Great Britain and Italy. The British Minister stated such conflict was impossible because Italy had promised to respect Great Britain’s interests in Ethiopia “and Great Britain is sure these interests will be respected in the future.” Premier Laval of France pleaded for conciliation on the part of both sides. Italy had filed a protest against Ethiopian membership in the League. (The Italian memorandum charged that Ethiopia by her conduct “placed herself openly outside the League and rendered herself unworthy of the confidence of her when she was admitted. Italy had been justified—under the League rules—in resorting to war against Ethiopia.” The Italian told the representatives of the other nations that his gov

PORTSMOUTH, Eng. (#) — Four hundred passengers were rescued today from the British passenger steamer, Whippingham, after it signaled distress off The Needles, west of the Isle of Wight, in the English Channel. The rescue was made by other paddle steamers, which answered its call, while a British destroyer also went to her aid.

GENEVA, Sept. 5.—Great Britain and France prepared today to renew their offer for a compromise on the Ethiopian dispute, which Premier Benito Mussolini rejected when it was first offered at the three-power conference in Paris last month. The Franco-British offer, it was understood, would be made the basis for efforts of an Italian-Ethiopian conciliation commission which it was decided today to establish under league auspices. The offer, revealed for the first time at yesterday's council meeting by Capt. Anthony Eden of Britain, provides for 'collaboration' of the three powers, with the consent of Ethiopia, to guide that country’s national life in almost every field, including the economic. The special interests of Italy in Ethiopia would be taken into account. With the council in recess until tomorrow, today was devoted to hotel room negotiations. Premier Pierre Laval of France conferred

London, Sept. 5..UP)—The 736 passengers of the British S. S. Doric were safely taken aboard two other British liners today after their ship collided in the cold fog before dawn with the French S. S. Formigny. Both ships turned toward land under their own steam. The passengers, who were on their way home from a pleasure cruise in the Mediterranean, told how the ship’s dance orchestra and a girl pianist who banged out “Tipperary” cheered them in the dismal hours between the time the collision awakened them and their departure in lifeboats. The crash came about 3 a. m. The passengers quit their cabins but there was no panic. Most of them gathered in the main salon and sang as the girl played songs they all knew. The dance orchestra alternated with her in the entertainment. Capt. A. C. Grieg, himself the hero of a sea disaster, sent out an SOS. The Orion of the Orient line and the Viceroy of

1935-11-04.text: (Associated Press Staff Writer) Students of fascist Italy demonstrated anew against Great Britain today as Mussolini, defiant of the alliance of sanctionists against him, pledged his nation victory in Ethiopia. With the nation celebrating the anniversary of the victorious World War Armistice with Austria-Hungary, bands of students paraded through the streets of Rome, shouting: "Down with England!" They stripped English signs from buildings. Storekeepers hurriedly removed British signs and goods from display windows. At the Hotel Eden, they tore down the sign of the British-French automobile club. (In last week’s rioting, the students forced the hotel management to cover the sign, saying it painfully reminded Italy of the leadership of Anthony Eden, British minister for League of Nations affairs, in the campaign for sanctions at Geneva.) To the thousands who surged about his Palazzo Venez

ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 4 (UR)— Thirty women and 15 children were reported today to have been killed Saturday in the most intense aerial bombardment yet conducted by the Italians on the southern front. The bombardment was said to have been made on wells near Gorrahei. LONDON, Nov. 4 (P)— The British government has been concerned for several months over the question of whether the Ethiopian war will develop into a European war, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, said in a speech tonight. Britain also has been concerned over whether a war between the black and white races will break out, he added. He did not disclose what conclusions the government had reached on either subject.

ROME—Mussolini pledged Italy victory in Ethiopia. “The Italian people,” he said, “are invincible, united and irrevocably determined.” MILAN—Anti-British demonstrations were renewed. GENEVA—A League of Nations subcommittee on sanctions in principle placed steel, coal, iron and petroleum on a list of key products, exportation of which to Italy is forbidden by sanctionists. ADDIS ABABA—Emperor Haile Selassie, observing the fifth anniversary of his coronation, said his nation would revive a concession to American Standard Oil interests after peace is concluded. Military Maneuvers: On the northern front, 120,000 Italian troops marched on Makale, unresisted. The Ethiopian government said Italian bombing planes killed 30 women and children in an attack on Gorrahe in the southeastern sector.

Rome, Nov. 4—Demonstrations against Great Britain were resumed today as Premier Mussolini promised Italy another victory to celebrate the 17th anniversary of the nation's triumphant armistice with the Austro-Hungarian empire. Bands of students paraded the streets shouting “down with England” and stripped English signs from buildings. Storekeepers hurriedly withdrew English announcements from their windows. The fascist students paraded in Via Veneto, where the American embassy stands. Most of the signs they ripped down were the English and French announcements posted by the hotels. They made a second call on the hotel Eden and took down the sign of the British and French automobile club. Last Thursday they compelled the management to cover the hotel sign “because it recalled too painfully Anthony Eden and his leadership in sanctions against Italy.” Police followed the students ready to in

| WE SSAA Sore NOY. Tew SS denial that any secret understanding existed between the United States and Great Britain concerning efforts to check Italian conquest of Ethiopia was made by Acting Secretary of State William Phillips today. Phillips made the denial in connection with charges by the Rev. Charles E. Coughlin, radio priest, that such an understanding existed. Phillips said this government has no understanding with anyone, and reiterated that the State Department has been acting entirely on its own initiative throughout the European war crisis.

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS Rome—Anti-British demonstrations were renewed by students. British signs were torn down. Students also demonstrated in Milan. "The Italian people," Il Duce declared, "are invincible, united and irrevocably determined." London — Official circles said peace negotiations were deadlocked. Paris—Premier Pierre Laval will continue peace talks tomorrow. Some circles suggested the possibility of Pope Pius intervening in an effort to find means of settlement. Geneva—League of Nations sanctions sub-committee approved in principle the inclusion of coal, iron, steel and petroleum in the key products exportation of which to Italy will be prohibited by League sanctionists after November 18. League officials foresaw the possibility of sounding out the United States on this question. Washington—Some officials said these products might be included if exporters fail to abide by the

ATHENS, Nov. 4.—The Greek people voted overwhelmingly for the recall of former King George to the throne, it was announced officially today, with nation-wide results from yesterday's plebiscite giving 1,491,992 for the monarchy to 32,454 for maintenance of the republic. The foreign minister communicated the results to the former monarch, now in London, and announced that a delegation was proceeding to London. As the counting proceeded, crowds continued nightlong celebrations in the streets and cafes of many cities and towns. All were waiting for a message from George in London, where news of the royalist victory had been dispatched by Gen. George Kondylis, regent who took over the government Oct. 10 in a bloodless coup. In London, the monarch said: “I am delighted that my people want me to return to them.” M. Petralias, royalist leader, declared: “It will only be a matter now of the king

GENEVA, Nov. 4.—An economic sub-committee of the League of Nations penalties committee today approved in principle a proposal to deprive Italy of oil, coal and steel. Thus opened the second phase of the league’s task of penalizing Italy for warring on Ethiopia. The proposal was approved in principle, rather than in fact, because its success depends largely on cooperation of non-member nations and chiefly the United States and Germany, both of whom may (Continued on page 13, column 2)

1935-11-21.text: LONDON. Nov. 20.—Lord Jellicoe, British admiral and an outstanding naval figure during the World War, died today. Death came to the admiral in his 76th year. He was born Dec. 5, 1859. Lord Jellicoe rose to his greatest fame as commander of the biggest fleet ever concentrated in the history of the world at the battle of Jutland in 1916.

(By Associated Press) LONDON, Nov. 21.—The halt in plans for the establishment of an autonomous North China was said by an authoritative source today to have been due to pressure brought by Great Britain.

LONDON, Nov. 20.—(UP)—Lord Jellicoe, British admiral who commanded the biggest fleet in the history of the world against Germany in the battle of Jutland, died today. He was 78 years old. By coincidence, the immediate cause of his death was an illness contracted during the recent Armistice day celebration at the cenotaph here. His illness was not announced until November 17, when a bulletin said the earl had contracted a chill and would be forced to cancel his engagements for three weeks. Although one lung was affected by the chill, as late as this morning, his condition was reported to be satisfactory. He died at 4:30 p.m. in his home in Kensington, surrounded by members of his family, including Lady Jellicoe. The earl, whose long and distinguished naval career was climaxed by the gigantic battle of Jutland, became a viscount in 1918 and the title of Earl Jellicoe of Scapa was conferred

Rioting arising from a variety of grievances broke out in widely separated parts of the world today. In Cairo, the anti-British demonstrations of the past several days were continued by students and street ruffians, who observed a "day of mourning" by clashing with police and forcing shopkeepers to close their doors. Police fired over the heads of demonstrators to check a barrage of rocks. Arabs in Haifa, Palestine, incensed over the killing of three of their race by British police, quitted the funeral of the victims to attack police at a railway station. Two policemen and two members of the Arabs’ mob of 2000 were injured in the fight. Police bullets broke up the altercation. Students in Budapest smashed windows of Jewish-owned shops in an anti-Semitic outbreak which was quelled by police with drawn sabers. The students stormed the conservatory of music before they were dispersed and 10

JERUSALEM, NOV. 21. (AP).—Two British police constables were injured and two Arabs wounded in a demonstration at Haifa in which 2,000 Arabs took part. The Arab demonstration was provoked by the funeral of three Arabs killed yesterday in a clash with police. The three were alleged members of a gang which killed a constable last week as he was trying to track down grapefruit thieves. Today the crowd attacked the police at the railway station, injuring the two constables. The police fired in retaliation, wounding two and breaking up the demonstration.

Cairo. - (AP) — The number of dead from anti-British riots reached five today, in official figures, but Egyptian sources asserted twice that number had succumbed during the current disorders. The death of Abdel Hakam Zaglul, fourth student to die from wounds received in a clash with British police last week outside the city, caused more bitter feeling among the nationalists demanding an end to British influence in Egypt. Authorities estimated that 10,000 students of the powerful W. A. F. D. nationalist party joined yesterday in the funeral procession for Abdel Hakam Zaglul. Many in the procession, it was learned, were armed with revolvers instead of the stones with which the students thus far have fought the police.

Latest war developments: GENEVA: League considers means of cutting off Italy's supplies of oil, coal, iron and steel. Britain actively supports move, especially regarding oil. ROME: Mussolini to furlough 100,000 of his mobilized troops in Italy to aid agriculture and industry and fight sanctions. LONDON: Italy understood to be tying up British funds.

CAIRO, Egypt, Nov. 21, (UP)— Rioting spread in Cairo late today during a general strike against British rule and police fired on the mobs. During the morning police fired with buckshot into a mob in the center of the city, wounding one man. This afternoon the shooting was renewed when demonstrators who were breaking windows were dispersed. A boy was wounded in the abdomen. The strike had spread through the bazaars, which were almost deserted. Police, mounted, afoot, and in trucks, with rifles and bayonets, were spread all through the city.

1935-11-10.text: SINGAPORE, Straits Settlement. (UP) — Through dense jungles of the peninsula, and over the turbulent waters of the Andaman Sea, and the shark-infested Bay of Bengal, a gigantic search went on last night for Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith and J. T. Pethybridge, missing more than 48 hours on an England to Australian flight. Chief hope of finding the daring Australian aviator and his companion was based on the fact that Kingsford-Smith once pulled through after being lost twelve days when his plane was forced down in one of the worst parts of the Australian brush, a region inhabited by cannibals. The search yesterday centered from a point 150 miles off the Malavan peninsula where his ship was last seen late Thursday, and in the jungles of the peninsula, and the dangerous islands off the coast. Burma and Malayan natives beat the dark jungles, Chinese junks poked their way up creeks and inlets o

SHANGHAI, Nov. 10. (Sunday) (Pj)—Nearly 2,000 Japanese marines marched into a demilitarized section of Shanghai today after the assassination of one of their comrades and a “showdown” in critical Sino-Japanese relations appeared at hand. Colonels fixed, a battalion was mobilized from three Japanese warships in the harbor and hurriedly sent into the native quarter where the slaying took place. They appeared prepared to enforce the threat by the Japanese embassy of drastic action unless satisfaction is quickly forthcoming. Chinese, recalling the hostilities of 1932 when Shanghai was attacked, were panic-stricken. Political motives were assigned by the Japanese embassy for the slaying of the marine, Hideo Nakayama, 23. He was shot in the neck and fatally wounded, allegedly by a Chinese. The scene was in the Hongkew district, outside the foreign settlement. Embassy officials immediately call

Thousands of Ethiopian warriors rushed to the northern front today to halt the advance of Mussolini’s empire-building legions. Emperor Haile Selassie, it is expected, will have half a million well-armed troops on all fronts by Nov. 20. Long-range artillery equipment, rifles and ammunition are being brought to Addis Ababa almost daily and are dispatched at once to the field. The Ethiopian government said it had started its first major aggressive counter-offensive against the Roman invaders. In the far northwest of Walkait province, up against British Sudan, Dedijazmatch Ayelu has mobilized his forces for an invasion of Eritrea. This movement is designed to envelop the Italian forces now holding the area around Aduwa, Adigrat and Aksum, south to Makale. If successful, it would also serve to halt the Italian advance southward on the west end of the northern front. In this sector, the invade

Singapore, Straits Settlement—(Sunday)—(#)—An Indian ocean monsoon was feared tonight to have brought death to Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, noted Australian aviator, and his co-pilot, Tom Pethybridge. Nearly two days have passed since their plane disappeared. A ray of hope remained, however, for the safety of the airmen—lost while attempting to make a record flight from England to Australia—as it was disclosed the plane could remain afloat indefinitely if forced down on water. C. James Melrose, who saw Kingsford-Smith’s plane at about 2:25 a.m. Friday over the Bay of ______ but found no trace of the pair.

The blessing of world peace was beseeched today (Sunday) in thousands of pulpits as religious services opened observance of the 17th anniversary of the world war armistice—tomorrow. The Federal Council of Churches of Christ and many other denominational and non-sectarian groups had urged universal expression of the prayer. Pastors pointed to the conflict raging in Ethiopia and the still not completely extinguished threat of its spread to other nations as evidence that the lesson of the world war had not been grasped. For tomorrow's celebration of the termination of the great conflict in 1918, world war veterans everywhere planned military and memorial gatherings. In Washington, the traditional honors to the thousands of world war dead included an address by President Roosevelt at Arlington National Cemetery. The president was to start his speech at 10:46 a.m. (eastern standard time) and

By The Associated Press Washington, Nov. 9—With the administration still short of the half-way mark in its drive to provide 3,500,000 jobs, figures made public today showed it must double its recently accelerated work relief pace to meet the December 1 goal. Harry L. Hopkins, works progress administrator, said the number put to work in the week ended November 2 totaled 194,425, compared with 121,715 in the preceding week. The total given jobs in place of direct relief Nov. 2, however, was only 1,737,610, in contrast with the original plan to have the entire 3,500,000 employables at work a day earlier. If the new December 1 goal is attained, 1,762,390 jobs remained to be provided in the four weeks beginning Nov. 2, a weekly average of 440,597. Hopkins nevertheless expressed renewed confidence that the program would succeed. Simultaneously he cut four additional states — Ohio, South Caroli

CHICAGO, Nov. 9. — They gave the Rev. William A. (Billy) Sunday the kind of funeral he wanted today — a housing revival service. They sang the “Glory Song” with zest and pleaded with “sinners” to come down front and be “saved” at his last rites in Moody Memorial Church. “Don't put it off even until the end of this funeral service,” exhorted the Rev. Dr. John Timothy Stone, president of the Presbyterian Theological Seminary, in calling for converts to “Mr. Sunday's Savior.” Four thousand faithful followers said “goodbye to the boss” with a smile on their lips, but hardly an eye was not shiny with tears.

PEIPING, China, Nov. 9,—Japan, through General Kenji Doihara, head of its military intelligence service in China, today demanded an independent regime be set up in North China immediately. The demand, reportedly made at Tientsin, coincided with a new Sino-Japanese incident at Shanghai—the death of a Japanese sailor following an attack by an alleged Chinese civilian.

1935-06-01.text: KARACHI, India, June 1. (UP) — Survivors under leadership of British officers battled flames today in the earthquake stricken region of Quetta, where an estimated 20,000 lives were lost in one of the worst quakes of recent years. Messages from Quetta continued to add to the story of death and destruction on a gigantic scale. Official messages from Quetta confirmed that “about 200” British subjects were among the dead and added “it is impossible even to approximate the Indian casualties.

Sporadic relapses from the shattered NRA hour and wage provisions and a report that New England's textile industry will return to the 48-hour week were met today with renewed threats of strikes. Most of America’s employers continued with working conditions unchanged from the NRA standards, but labor representatives reported instances of adverse wage or hour changes and a few strikes. Such cities as Atlanta, Greenville S. C., Brunswick, Ga., and Monroe, Ga., were involved. At Providence, R. I., it was stated by leading mill operators that the New England textile industry probably would adopt a 48-hour week soon, compared to the present 40 hours. President J. Nicholas Danz, of the Connecticut Federation of Labor, said he had received a blanket order from the national federation to deal “severely” with cases of adverse hour and wage changes and “strike if necessary.”
LONDON, May 31—An official announcement tonight said King George was suffering “from a chill and had been advised to remain indoors as a precautionary measure.

LONDON, May 31—(UP)—George Percy Stoner, 18-year-old chauffeur, was convicted in Old Bailey court today of murdering Francis M. Rattenbury, 67-year-old retired architect. He was sentenced to be hanged. Mrs. Alma Victoria Rattenbury, 39, the widow, who was tried with her chauffeur, was acquitted. Mrs. Rattenbury admitted that Stoner had been her sweetheart and that he was jealous of her husband, who was killed with a mallet.

The important announcement was made to the House of Commons by Capt. Anthony Eden, brilliant young Lord Privy Seal, convincing many listeners Eden would succeed Sir John Simon as Foreign Secretary in the cabinet shake-up expected early next month. London May 31 — Authoritative sources said today a threatening resumption of hostilities between the Chinese and Japanese in northern China will find Great Britain prepared to defend her nationals in that area. Reports that the Japanese military authorities threaten to move their forces into the whole area north of the Yellow River aroused great concern here, particularly in regard to the international cities of Peking and Tientsin. British naval forces, as well as military units in the two cities, are ready for service in the event the situation becomes serious, it was said in official quarters. Information reaching the British authorities confirmed reports the Japanese had demanded the elimination of the Koumintang (government party) headquarters in north China, the dismissal of the Chinese governor of the province of Hopei, and the cessation of all anti-Japanese activity in that area.

Dublin, Irish Free State, June 1—(AP)—This list of 200 Americans were among the £40 drawn up until the luncheon recess today in the annual Irish sweepstakes draw on the Epson Downs derby. They were drawn on 40 horses, with 40 more horses to be drawn in the afternoon. A prize fund of £1,160,900 ($95,746,455), the lowest since the first draw in 1930, was announced today as the sweepstakes draw opened at the Mansion House. The fund—the lowness of which was attributed to Great Britain's new anti-lottery bill—will be divided into eleven units of £100,000 ($494,700) each and ten residual prizes of £5,090 ($30,145) each. Each person drawing a horse is certain of a prize of £454 ($2,247), Jack O'Sheehan, director of the draw, announced. Viscount Powerscourt, chairman of the hospitals committee under whose auspices the draw is being held, charged that "Sabre Rattling" in some places abroad, which

By Associated Press LONDON, June 1.—King George was able to continue his work today, although obliged to remain indoors because of a cold, it was announced officially. The cold, which prevented the King from attending a London County Council reception in his honor yesterday, was said to be slight. The King will be 70 Monday.

1935-05-21.text: Wool, Dorsetshire, England—(4)— Messages from many lands poured into this rural community today expressing sorrow at the death of the colorful "Lawrence of Arabia." Despite his acclaim throughout the empire, the funeral of Col. Thomas E. Lawrence, who emerged from hazardous wartime adventures only to be fatally injured in a cycling accident, will be extremely simple in keeping with his wish. It will take place tomorrow in the village church at Moreton, near the cottage where Lawrence sought seclusion under his adopted name, T. E. Shaw. So anxious was Lawrence in life to avoid all acclaim that he refused the decorations which France and Great Britain desired to confer on him for his achievements in Arabia. He enlisted as a private in the Royal Air Force after the World War under his assumed name, and when his identity was discovered, requested transfer to the tank corps. Lawrence's death

WOOL, Dorsetshire, Eng., May 21. (AP)—Whether or not a mysterious black automobile had anything to do with the death of the almost legendary 'Lawrence of Arabia,' a coroner's jury of seven men decided today that he met death accidentally. Corp. Ernest Catchpole testified he saw Col. T. E. Lawrence swerve his motorcycle at the time of the accident on May 19 to avoid an automobile, colliding immediately with a butcher boy on a bicycle. Lawrence, he said, was riding along the Dorsetshire country road at a speed of from 50 to 60 miles an hour. A lad who had been a companion of the butcher boy testified he did not see the automobile described by Catchpole.

By United Press LONDON, May 21.—Ramsay MacDonald has decided finally to resign as prime minister in favor of Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, the usually well-informed political correspondent of the Daily Mail reported today.

LONDON, May 21 (UP)—Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, was urged in the House of Commons today to consult the United States on an Anglo-American plan for world monetary stabilization. Sir Robert Hamilton suggested that Chamberlain consult the United States, which through Secretary of Treasury Henry Morgenthau recently indicated its willingness to cooperate in any stabilization move although the Roosevelt administration would not be expected to take the initiative. “See if the United States is ready to join us in leading toward world stabilization of monetary currencies,” Sir Robert urged the Chancellor.

VATICAN CITY, May 20 (P)— An invitation to return to the Roman Catholic church was extended to England today by Pope Pius. The holy father took advantage of yesterday's ceremonies marking the canonization of two Britons, Sir Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher, to voice his plea for England's reunion with Catholicism.

ST. ANNE'S-ON-THE-SEA, England, May 21 (P)—Playing like a champion, Lawson Little of San Francisco, the title-holder, today entered the third round of the British amateur golf tourney by defeating Eris Martin-Smith, 1931 champion, 4 and 3. Other United States players advancing included Tommy Tailer of New York, who beat A. Jamieson, 4 and 3; and Capt. A. Bullock-Webster of San Francisco, winner over Bruce Thompson, 3 and 2.

PARIS, May 2%. (4+-France is transferring her naval strength from Mediterranean waters, it was learned today, to protect herself against any possible danger from Germany's naval rearmament. The sea force which defends the British channel and the North Sea is being strengthened. Four torpedo boats and the destroyer Lynx are expected to be transferred from the Mediterranean to the channel fleet after maneuvers off Morocco in early June, along with other reinforcements.

Wool, Eng., May 21.—With ceremony as simple as he would have wished it, Lawrence of Arabia was buried in an evergreen lined grave in tiny Moreton village churchyard today. While all the British empire mourned one of its greatest heroes, Lawrence was laid in his final resting place as if he never had been any more than “Aircraftsman Shaw,” the underling of the British air force which he chose to be in the final years of his young life. Only 200 persons were present. The funeral followed a brief formal inquest at which it was declared Lawrence was speeding along a rural road at between 50 and 60 miles per hour when he received his fatal injuries, swerving his motorcycle to avoid hitting two boys on bicycles.

1935-11-05.text: LONDON, Nov. 5.—(4)—The press association reported today that a wreck located by the salvage vessel Orphir off the head of Kinsale on the Irish coast has been definitely identified as the Lusitania, torpedoed by a German submarine during the World War. The Orphir has been at work since early in the summer attempting to locate the Lusitania.

LONDON, Nov. 4. (#)--George II of Greece, former monarch whose throne was offered to him again as the result of yesterday's plebiscite in Greece, drew up a proclamation tonight to announce his imminent return to the throne. “I am delighted,” he said during the day, “that my people want me to return to them.” (The Greek government announced the plebiscite showed the people favored George II's restoration by about 45 to 1. It stated there were 1,491,922 votes for the monarchy and 32,454 for the continuance of the republic.)

coast, it was announced officially by the salvaging company. The wreck was located by the salvage ship Orphir, operated by a British company, which had been searching for the wreck for many weeks. The reported finding of the Lusitania wreck climaxed years of plans and futile attempts to locate the wreck of the famous liner, the sinking of which on May 7, 1915, has been cited as a major reason for the United States finally entering the World War against Germany. Many Americans lost their lives in the tragedy. Principal interest of salvage operators has been the nearly $5,000,000 in coin, foreign exchange, jewels, and other valuables believed to have gone down with the vessel. The exact amount of these valuables never has been determined. The Lusitania had been believed to lie about 240 feet below the surface about eight miles off old Kinsale Head, County Cork. The recent salvage operation

Y Nov. 5—King George, recalled to the throne of Greece which he lost in 1922, issued a proclamation today pledging his devotion to the Greek people. In a letter to General George Kons, head of the government, ending his exile in London, he asked that the following proclamation be published in the newspapers and posted throughout the nation: "I shall come to my country. The separation has been hard and sorrowful, I have hatred for no one. I look forward to the future with confidence. I am faithful to the regime. I will give all my force for the realization of our common sentiments, remembering my beloved father, King Constantine." "My heart is love for my people." The proclamation was signed "George I, King of the Hellenes." It was his first official declaration since the plebiscite Sunday when the country voted overwhelmingly to restore the monarchy.

DRIVE CONTINUED) ROME, Italy. (UP) — Italians went through their first meatless day, reconciled to combating the league penalties, but privately pessimistic as to prospects ahead. Possibility of conflict with Britain is strong in the minds of those who survey the European situation as it may develop. Though the army is pushing into Ethiopia with little difficulty, it is generally realized that Italy is still far from its goal, and that the materials and time required may be more than Italy can give. Students’ demonstrations against Great Britain have not yet begun seriously. They only partly reveal the country’s deep-seated resentment at Britain's attitude. Despite continued assurances, Italians believe firmly that Britain wishes to humiliate Premier Mussolini and destroy fascism. They feel that the British attitude will be even firmer if not milder, after the parliamentary election, bec

All financial and security markets in New York were closed today, election day in that state. The following foreign exchange rates are furnished through the courtesy of the First National Bank: England, pound, $4.70; France, franc, 6c; Belgium, belga, 1c; Spain, peseta, 12c; Italy, lire, 26c; Norway, kroner, 22c; Sweden, kroner, 22c; Denmark, kroner, 19c; Mexico, peso, 24c; Germany, mark, 35c; Holland, guilder, 60c; Canada, dollar, 5c.

ROME, Italy. (UP) — Dispatches from Djibouti, French Somaliland, reported today the almost complete destruction by Italian bombing planes of an Ethiopian caravan on the way from British Somaliland to Harar, with munitions and supplies for Ethiopia’s southern armies. The story was related, the dispatches said, by Ethiopian civilians who arrived at Djibouti terror-stricken. The dispatch quoted Ethiopians as saying that 500 Ethiopian soldiers were killed. No mention was made of any civilian casualties, though it was related that the whole column of mixed civilians and soldiers numbered 600. It was said that a caravan containing scores of motor trucks and hundreds of camels set out for Harar from Ververa, port of British Somaliland on a forced march with supplies for the army of Ras Nassibu in the Ogaden country. The caravan was reported to be the largest to leave British Somaliland since th

Seen eae NT ers ieee Rome, Nov. 5.—(UP)—Sir Eric Drummond, British Ambassador, conferred with Premier Benito Mussolini late today. The reason for the conference was not announced, but the government was expected to issue a communique later.

1935-11-06.text: By Associated Press, Mussolini and Great Britain, Paris diplomatic circles said today, have settled their differences in the Mediterranean, As a result, Premier Laval of France renewed his efforts for peace settlement to end the Italian invasion in East Africa—a settlement acceptable to the League of Nations and Ethiopia as well as to Il Duce, Mussolini, uneasy over the vast British fleet in the Mediterranean, bargained for its reduction with London today, Definite progress was being made, informed persons said, toward allaying the tense situation between Italy and England—a friction marked by frequent anti-British demonstrations in the fascist nation, If an agreement is reached between the two powers, it would probably be on this basis: Must Withdraw More Troops Il Duce would withdraw the bulk of his fascist legions from Libya, his province bordering Egypt on the west. In return, Great

LONDON, Nov. 6 (#)—The Duke of Gloucester, tall soldier son of the king and queen of England, and Lady Alice Montague-Douglas-Scott, 33-year-old Scot aristocrat, were married today in a quiet ceremony in the Crimson and Gold Chapel of Buckingham Palace. Lady Alice, dressed in pearl-shaded satin, and the 35-year-old duke, resplendent in the gold-faced blue tunic, scarlet breeches and black-topped boots of the ‘Tenth Hussars, were pronounced man and wife by the archbishop of Canterbury. With the plighting of this troth, the Prince of Wales became the British royal family’s only bachelor. This second royal wedding within a year—a ceremony stripped of pageantry because of the recent death of the bride's father, the Duke of Buccleuch—was in sober contrast to the brilliant marriage last November of the Duke of Kent and Princess Marina. Mellow sunlight flooded the palace chapel during the cerem

[BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] Mussolini, uneasy over the vast British fleet in the Mediterranean, bargained for its reduction with London today. Definite progress was being made, informed persons said, toward allaying the tense situation between Italy and England—a friction marked by frequent anti-British demonstrations in the fascist nation. The Mediterranean problem was reported in French diplomatic circles to be “settled,” leaving Premier Laval a free hand to discuss the settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian war with Rome and London. It was said in these circles that the British are expected to take (Continued on Page 15, Col. 3)

LONDON, Nov. 6 (UP).—The Duke of Gloucester, King George's third son, and Lady Alice Montagu-Douglas-Scott, daughter of the late Duke of Buccleuch and Queensberry, were married today in a simple ceremony by the Archbishop of Canterbury in the royal chapel at Buckingham Palace. The death of the bride’s father, October 19, caused cancellation of plans for an elaborate state ceremony at Westminster — with 2,000 guests. Because of the change in plan, only members of the families, Queen Maud, of Norway, and former King George, of Greece, attended the service in the tiny chapel which seats but 200 people.

(By United Press.) With the Italian armies in Ethiopia temporarily halted by rain, interest in the war crisis centered today in Europe, where Great Britain showed increasing signs of preparing for trouble in the Mediterranean. Britain’s diplomatic approach to Mussolini regarding the Mediterranean situation might be interpreted in one of two ways: Either Britain is anxious to avoid a clash by persuading Mussolini to take his army out of Libya or she believes a clash is inevitable and is paving the way to justifying her own position before the world when it comes. There is no sign of yielding on either side. Mussolini has withdrawn one division of troops from the Egyptian border region and told British ambassadors yesterday that it is now up to Britain to withdraw some ships. Sir Eric sadly told him that one division is a drop in the bucket compared to the number still remaining there and

LONDON, Nov. 6. (AP)--Postponement of a conference of naval powers from Dec. 2 to Dec. 5 was officially announced today. It was said the change was arranged to give Japanese delegates sufficient time to reach London.

TATOI, Greece, Nov. 6. (P)—Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, making a second attempt within a month to fly from England to Australia, arrived here at 4:30 p. m. today (9:30 a. m., Eastern Standard Time.). He left England eight hours earlier.

LONDON, Nov. 5—(AP)—Subdued gaiety filled London tonight on the eve of the wedding of the Duke of Gloucester, third son of King George and Queen Mary, to Lady Alice Montagu-Douglas Scott at Buckingham Palace at 11:30 tomorrow morning. The wedding, which will bring to a close the celebrations of the monarchs’ jubilee year, is likely to be the last royal marriage Britons will see in many years unless the Prince of Wales finds a bride. He will be the only remaining bachelor of the four royal sons. The populace will not see the elaborate ceremonies which had been planned for the event, originally scheduled to be held before 3,000 persons in Westminster Abbey. Because of the recent death of the bride’s father, the Duke of Buccleuch, only a private service will be held, in the small white-gold chapel at Buckingham Palace, the favorite place of worship of Queen Victoria. Only 120 close friends

1935-10-08.text: (Copyright, 1085, By The Amend Press) Geneva, Oct. 8 ()-A plan to give Great Britain a League of Nations mandate, by vote of the assembly, to supervise sanctions against Italy was discussed to- day by some league powers, rep- resentatives of non-European countries disclosed. The idea behind the move was that Britain, supported by other interested powers, should take the leadership in the sanctions pro- gram and that Britain would be requested to adopt the initiative in accordance with developments in the situation. The Italian delegation was ex- tremely incensed over yesterday’s refusal by the League Council to postpone discussion of the com- mittee of six which indicted Italy (CONTINUED ON PAGE FOUR)

(By The Associated Press) The League of Nations having de- declared Mussolini's Fascist govern- ment an outlaw among nations today pondered the nature of sanctions to be imposed against it. A mandate to Great Britain to supervise such sanctions by a vote of the League assembly was one plan discussed. Premier Laval, of France, hoped to keep any sanctions mild. The assembly meets tomorrow to carry out the sentence of sanctions passed by the council yesterday after convicting the Italian government of aggression against Ethiopia. If the sanctions are economic and financial the Italian government is prepared to make the best of it. Il Duce’s economists have pointed to independence adopted by Italy in recent months; the “corporative state” which provides bread, light- ing, fuel, transportation without de- pending on the outside world; monopolies on necessaries, raw ma- terials; in fact the co

London, Oct. 8—(4)—Ambassador Robert W. Bingham of the United States went to the British foreign office today, presumably to discuss with Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, the United States neutrality proclamation and the British viewpoint in connection with the Italo-Ethiopian war. An authoritative source said it could be assumed that the British government was taking the opportunity to inform Bingham of the line of action Great Britain had adopted and would adopt in the future in the League of Nations. The British said it was their policy to keep the United States constantly advised of their viewpoint on the war situation. The general viewpoint of the British government is that President Roosevelt’s action indicates the United States will not challenge or in any way impede the League of Nations in applying economic sanctions against Italy.

LONDON, Oct. 8. (U.P) — George Lansbury, faithful wheel horse of the chariot of peace and most beloved of Labor leaders, today resigned as leader of the parliamentary Labor party in the House of Commons, because he is out of sympathy with the party’s policy of urging that Italy be punished for her invasion of Ethiopia. Major Clement R. Attlee was elected to succeed Lansbury.

By The Associated Press Paris, Oct. 8.—France sent assurances to Great Britain yesterday she would give her armed aid on land, at sea and in the air in case Britain is attacked while preparing to enforce League of Nations sanctions, provided the British would come to the aid of France in a similar emergency. A French note to London fixing the conditions for aiding the British fleet if it is attacked in the Mediterranean during the Italo-Ethiopian conflict was officially described as bargaining for aid in similar circumstances involving Germany. The note, a reply to the British request for military cooperation, named these conditions: 1. Great Britain and France will consult each other before taking action. 2. Whatever measures are taken after consultation will not be considered provocation for attack by a third power; and 3. If either France or Great Britain is attacked for measures (Con

A condition of equal importance, it was added, is that the terms must be based on the full consent and agreement of Ethiopia. | London, Oct. 7.— (AP) —The League of Nations stamped bellicose Italy with the stigma of war-maker | tonight and thus prepared the full weight of economic sanctions for the shoulders of Benito Mussolini. Italy, consolidating her newly-won lines in northern Africa, is willing to pay the price of her conquest in economic sanctions, informed sources said at Rome. Nor does she intend to bolt the league because of today’s grave step at Geneva, it was indicated. Looks to U. S. FRANKFORT ON THE MAIN, Germany, Oct. 844) — Prince Franz Ludwig Hesse, 27, suffered serious head injuries today in an automobile accident and was taken to a hospital. The prince is a member of the Battenberg family and is related to King George of England.

1935-07-20.text: Santa Monica, Calif.—News! Papers say, ‘The market stood still.” Yes, and so did Congress. Rain and no war in Abyssinia. Heat not so bad as it was. Now that the AAA raised prices on all products they are about to say it’s not constitutional, England let our chorus girls out. Well, that’s all right. Every country should be allowed to protect its own labor, be nobody more broke up over it however than the English “Johnnies.” American Bar Association came out very strong against unethical and shyster lawyers. Looks like I been vindicated, Yours, WITT, ROGERS.

LONDON, July 20. (UP)—Great Britain has refused bluntly to accede to Italian demands for complete overlordship in Ethiopia and insists that any settlement be based on the Briand-Kellogg anti-war pact as well as other treaties, it was said on reliable authority today. Italy has persistently demanded complete political domination of the ancient empire in secret negotiations, it was said, and Great Britain has persistently refused to accede. The sharpness of disagreement has brought to a temporary stalemate diplomatic conversations in London, Paris and Rome. Italians Flee Army Service VIENNA, July 20 (UP)—Italians are fleeing by scores daily across the Yugoslavian and Austrian frontiers to escape army service, the United Press learned today. Refugees also reported important Italian military movements on the Yugoslavian border and construction of trenches which might be used if Austria, Euro

LONDON (IP) — Former King George of Greece has ordered a private six-passenger airliner to be ready at Croydon field for a long-distance flight on short notice, the Evening Standard reported here today. The plane selected is capable of flying to Athens in 15 hours. Cabinet shifts in the Greek capital yesterday indicated the royalist influence has gained power and a restoration might be expected in the near future. The former king, meanwhile, remained in seclusion in a west end hotel.

LONDON, July 20—(AP)—Former King George of Greece has ordered an airliner to stand by at Croydon air field to fly him to Athens, it was learned today when Captain William Ledlie, the pilot, confirmed that he was awaiting instructions. The pilot, who was making a flight to Deauville and return this afternoon, said he had expected instructions for the Athens flight tomorrow. It was reported that the former king was awaiting the arrival of the mayor of Athens, M. Kotzias, due late today, before taking a final decision. Neither the former king nor his aide, Major Levides, could be reached this afternoon. Earlier in the day Major Levides, commenting on Athens rumors that George was returning to Athens, said: "We know nothing more than what is in the papers." Agitation for the return of former King George to the Greek throne has been growing since the ill-fated revolution of former Premier Ele

Lahore, India, July 20—Four Mohammedans were killed today when British troops fired three volleys into the Moslem mob of 20,000 who were disobeying a curfew order and had refused to disperse when ordered. The mob had attempted to storm barricades which police had raised to prevent their progress. Troops were summoned immediately to assist the harried troops. Several demonstrators were arrested.

LAHORE, India, July 20 (P).— British troops killed two persons and wounded several others today when they fired into a crowd of 5,000 Moslems who were attempting to visit the Shahidguna mosque. The police made several hundred arrests. The mosque, which the Moslems claimed as their property, was undergoing demolition by Sikhs, which had caused a riot July 8.

BERLIN, July 20. (4)—German Catholic circles was informed today that Papal Nuncio Cesare Orsenigo presented a note from the Vatican to the German government protesting decrees Thursday suppressing 'political Catholicism.' This followed a swift series of decrees and acts aimed at absolute domination of Germany by which Nazism harassed with increasing force the Catholics, Jews and war veterans.

LONDON, May 29 (UP)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald intimated in the House of Commons today that Britain is prepared to join in an international currency stabilization conference if some other nation takes the initiative. In a reply to a questioner, MacDonald emphatically refused to make the first move. “We are not required at this late hour to take the initiative,” he said. “We have been trying to get the initiative taken and up to now have not been very successful.”

Undeterred, however, by this opposition, the premier said he would carry his appeal direct to the chamber tomorrow. Further carrying out the government's project of defending the franc against devaluation, Flandin said the prosecution of speculators was contemplated and that evidence already gathered had been transmitted to the ministry of justice. VIENNA (UP)—Chancellor Kurt von Schuschnigg, addressing the central diet, Wednesday demanded full arms equality for Austria. He rejected the demands of Adolf Hitler for a plebiscite to determine strength. His speech followed by one day that of Premier Julius Gömbös, of Hungary, likewise demanding equality. Germany and Turkey have armed in violation of World War treaties, and Bulgaria, last of the central powers, wants to. "Our demand for equality includes cancellation of all restrictions on the army," said Schuschnigg. "Only Austria shall decide if and when general conscription is to be introduced." Replying to statements he credited to Hitler, Schuschnigg said that Benito Mussolini of Italy never tried in the least to influence Austria’s internal policy. "Nazis are seeking to poison our relations with Italy," he said, "Those who demand a plebiscite boast of having vanquished parliamenta

St. John’s, N. F., (#)—The French trawler, Marechal de Luxemburg, was feared today to have foundered off the coast of Newfoundland with her crew of 40 fishermen. The trawler, which is owned at St. Malo, France, has not been heard from since May 18, when she reported she was leaking and trying to make St. John's. Search for the crippled craft has been fruitless. The French naval cruiser d'Ys was ordered from St. Pierre to the rescue, but a search along the fishing banks has been futile.

PARIS, May 29.—The position of Premier Pierre Etienne Flandin’s cabinet became increasingly precarious today as it became virtually certain the chamber of deputies finance committee would oppose his demand for dictatorial powers to defend the franc. Voices were raised in violent discussion when members of the committee conferred with the premier in his office prior to today’s parliamentary session. The conference was described as “emotional and sometimes dramatic.” Flandin asserted France might be forced to devalue its currency unless he is granted the full powers he demands. Members of the committee said, however, a majority was still adamant in opposition.

(Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) PARIS, May 28—The French cabinet was reported tonight to be so shaken at parliamentary opposition to its demand for dictatorial powers to defend the franc that its resignation was a possibility. Friends of Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin said, however, he might attempt to dissolve parliament and take his fight before the country in new elections. Some parliamentarians asserted the cabinet might resign tomorrow night unless opposition within the chamber finance committee and former Premier Edouard Herriot’s powerful socialist party was overcome. Devaluation became an open issue as the cabinet, its political life in the balance, asked parliament to grant it sweeping emergency powers to defend the franc.

1935-12-10.text: LONDON, Dec. 10 (P).—An authoritative source disclosed today that the international naval conference has decided to plunge immediately into the question of total tonnages of the world’s greatest navies. It was learned after the adjournment of the first session that the delegates, in conference at the Clarence House, requested that the Japanese make a detailed statement at tomorrow's meeting of the other powers—the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy. Informed sources expected the British to make the first move toward an agreement to replace the expiring Washington and London naval limitations treaties, and to prevent a world naval construction race. It was believed the British either would give a more detailed statement of their views or would present their full proposals for a definite program of reduction in sea armaments.

Tatstield, Kent, England, Dec. 10.—(/)—Eleven persons were killed today when a Belgium airliner crashed into a rain swept English valley. Seven of the victims were passengers, four were members of the crew, singing the English channel in a high wind accompanied by rain.

(Copyright, 1935, By The Associated Press) London, Dec. 9—The United States today proposed at the opening of the naval conference, a 20 per cent reduction in the world’s great navies but Japan immediately rejected the plan. Admiral Nagano said such a cut of the existing treaty tonnage would only prolong the ratio system by which Japan is limited to three-fifths the naval power maintained by either the United States or Great Britain and that therefore it was not acceptable to Japan. Norman H. Davis, the chief American delegate, told the representatives of Japan, Great Britain, France, and Italy, that President Roosevelt advocated the progressive reduction of sea armaments. Admiral Nagano demanded the abolition of the ratio system of naval limitation as a prerequisite to any naval agreement. It was a reiteration of Japan’s consistent demand for equality in sea power with the United States

But the favorable response from elsewhere raised little hope for the success of the 5-power conference, which began its deliberations in the historic Locarno room of the British foreign office this morning and in a setting dark for disarmament. A new Franco-British "united front" demanded today that Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy show his hand in his war with Ethiopia. A speedy East African peace or a possible European war, informed Italian sources said, may hang on the premier’s reaction to proposals for peace drafted by London and Paris. Great Britain, it was said, had made marked concessions. At the same time, Mussolini declared to his Senate today: "Italian interests, both African and European, will be defended strenuously." Mussolini made no reference to the new peace plan reported reached between Great Britain and France. Events of the next 36 hours were expected to determine the duration of the campaign in the African kingdom. Delegates of the smaller powers in the league announced the alleged plan to give Italy a portion of Ethiopia to end Premier Mussolini’s demands for territorial expansion gave a premium to aggression. It was added, however, that if he did accept the offer for discussion he would make the important reservation that, during the discussion, talk of new League of Nations penalties against Italy, particularly, an oil embargo, should be held in reserve. The league's “general staff” is to meet Thursday to choose a date for the oil embargo, and an accompanying embargo on coal, iron and steel. Hence there are two days in which Mussolini may act and Great Britain and France may agree with him on a method of procedure. Some delegates went to the limit of saying that if newspaper versions of the Anglo-French peace plan were confirmed, a grave crisis would develop within the league. The forecast that certain nations might even resign on the probable grounds that the league was being used to give a premium to aggression by strong powers against weaker. One delegate described the reason for the rebellion as saying his country had participated in the league sanctions against Italy to prevent aggression against Ethiopia and to establish a precedent for the future of collective security against war. 1935-10-18.text: ZEILA, BRITISH SOMALILAND, Oct. 17.—(AP).—Tribesmen reported today to the district commissioner here that the 17th British Camel Corps guarding the Somaliland frontier suffered casualties during an Italian advance in the Ogaden desert. (The desert of Ogaden province runs along the border of British Somaliland close to the point where Italian Somaliland joins with the British territory. Italian forces have been reported penetrating northwestward, close to the British Somaliland border, in a drive directed at the Addis Ababa-Djbouti railroad.)

London, Oct. 18—(4)—Tension between the British and French mounted today as the British government let it be known plainly that recent events have shaken the British public confidence in France's loyalty to the League of Nations. Want Unconditional “Yes” The restoration of this confidence, authoritative sources said, hinges upon an unconditional affirmative French reply to the British query as to whether France will back up Great Britain if the British fleet in the Mediterranean is attacked by Italy.
