Peiping, China, Nov. 18. All doubt that a move is in full swing to separate North China from the control of the Central Chinese government was swept away today by pronouncements from leading Japanese and Chinese spokesmen. General Kenji, "the Lawrence of Manchuria," announced that if autonomy for the north was not proclaimed, he was prepared to send five Japanese divisions into Hopei and six into Shantung to split those key provinces off from the rest of China. Puyi, former emperor of China, and now emperor Kang Teh of Manchuria, then would be brought back to the throne at Peiping from which he was driven by the revolution of 1911, Doihara, who is chief of the intelligence section of Japanese forces on the Asian mainland, explained. 1935-10-04.text: PARIS, Oct. 4--(?)—The French cabinet today accorded Premier Laval a vote of confidence giving him a free hand in the League of Nations' consideration of sanctions against Italy. The cabinet also approved the dispatch of a note to Great Britain stating the attitude of France in the event that the British fleet, now operating in the Mediterranean as a “precautionary” matter, should be attacked, but there was no immediate announcement as to the nature of this response. French sources said they believe that an application of sanctions against Italy would take at least six weeks, provided the league approves of such action. Laval went to his cabinet for the approval of a Franco-British program for economic and financial sanctions against Italy.

LONDON () — Large crowds milled through Downing Street before the Prime Minister’s residence today as British warships patrolled 3,000 miles of the empire's traditional sea lanes, on guard against an interruption of empire communications through war in East Africa. The men in the street were heard to ask, “What next? Is it war? Where will it lead? Will England be drawn in?” Street bulletins were displayed throughout London declaring: “Aduwa Bombed—Italians Advance.” Authoritative sources said the government felt the whole future of the British empire depended on its ability to defend its own interests in case of attack through the spread of the Italo-Ethiopian conflict or as the result of league restraints. Paris, Oct. 3. ()—Great Britain and France today agreed on a joint program before the League of Nations which calls for the immediate severance by League members of financial and economic relations with Italy and possibly financial help to Ethiopia. The third of the three points of the agreement, French officials announced, favors prohibition of purchase of Italian goods by League members or sale of goods to Mussolini's nation, including war munitions and their transportation. Premier Pierre Laval after an hour's conference with Anthony Eden, British minister of League of Nations affairs, which preceded the agreement, stated: “Mr. Eden and I talked over the order of the day for the council of the League. This action followed an hour's conference between Premier Laval and Anthony Eden, British minister for League of Nations’ affairs. At the conclusion of their conference, Laval stated: “Mr. Eden and I talked over the order of the day for the council of the league. We have considered various methods of procedure. We will continue in close collaboration at Geneva.” Agree on Three Points. Officials said at the end of their conversation, Eden and the French premier had agreed on the following three points: 1. LONDON, Oct. 4—(UP)—British warships churned under forced draft from all parts of the world toward the Mediterranean Sea and Gulf of Aden today, while Malta, Gibraltar and Egypt fortified themselves against dreaded eventualities of the Italo-Ethiopian war. Authorities at Malta, 60 miles from Sicily, where Italian submarines and bombing planes reportedly are based in numbers, frankly and almost frenziedly prepared for siege. Wholesale grocers were ordered to report monthly the supply of foodstuffs on hand. Military orders plunged the great Rock of Gibraltar into darkness for 20 minutes last night while sirens wailed, a practice warning of a bombing raid, and great searchlights played out over the cloud banked straits commanded by the fort's guns. It was reported that Egyptian troops occupied all exposed areas, including Alexandria, and 300 Italian employees of British air fields in Egypt

Official Ethiopian reports of unsubstantiated bombing raid into Ethiopia today signalized, in the opinion of authorities of the League of Nations, the long-feared beginning of war in East Africa. A British source characterized the alleged bombing as the “declaration of war—the only declaration there will be.” Although Italy officially denied the bombing, it also announced that Italian troops had moved into advanced positions beyond our lines. Fighting Reported Reports of fighting poured into Addis Ababa. The wild Danakil tribes were said to have engaged the advancing Italians in Tigre province. There were reports of fighting in Ogaden province. Emperor Haile Selassie was quoted by Reuters as saying that Cross nurses have been killed and wounded at Aduwa. LONDON, - Oct. 4, —The Addis Ababa correspondent of Reuters reported today an Italian plane had been shot down near Aduwa, apparently during a second aerial bombardment.

London, June 25.~-(AP)-—Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, First Lord of the Admiralty, announced in the House of Commons today that Germany had agreed she would never again resort to unrestricted submarine warfare. Germany also was willing, Sir Bolton announced, to adhere to the rules and regulations regarding submarine warfare set up in part four of the London naval treaty, accepting them for herself irrespective of the attitude of other powers.

(Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) ROME, June 25.--Great Britain’s minister for League of Nations affairs, Capt. Anthony Eden, made a preliminary survey of the Ethiopian question with Fulvio Suvich, Italian Under-secretary for foreign affairs, this morning preparatory to a meeting with Premier Mussolini which may be one of the most important encounters of the year. The British diplomat and Suvich drove to Castel Fusano on the coast for luncheon. Although the idea of a formal conversation on foreign affairs in Rome was abandoned, the statesmen managed to cover many subjects during the 45-minute drive and later, at the table. British sources said the object of Eden's discussions today with Mussolini was to make no offers, but to find out from Il Duce what the premier wants from Ethiopia before he will give up the idea of an expedition into the African empire. LONDON, June 25 (#).—Great Britain today claimed the possession of the first entirely robot airplanes in the world. The air ministry revealed that a number of pilotless machines were in regular use for gunnery practice over land and sea. The airplanes are called the “Queen Bee” type, are operated completely by radio, fly more than 100 miles an hour, and reach an altitude of more than 10,000 feet. An air ministry official said: “They can be controlled so finely that without anyone aboard they will take off from the land or ships at sea and perform a flight limited only by fuel and the distance from the wireless station, then descend again with complete accuracy.”

Nanking, China, June 25, (U.R)— Dr. Alfred Sao-Ke Sze, outstanding Chinese diplomat, has been appointed ambassador to the United States, it was announced today. Washington recently raised its legation in China to the rank of embassy, in common with Great Britain and Japan.

| LONDON—(AP)—Helen Wills Moody began her campaign to regain all-England tennis championship today by eliminating M. Baumgarten of Hungary, 6-0, 6-1, in a first round match on Wimbledon’s famous courts.— Helen Jacobs, the American champion and old rival of Mrs. Moody's, also advanced into the second round in easy style, whipping Nelli Adamson, Belgian champion, 6-3, 6-2.

EDINBURGH, SCOTLAND, JUNE 25. (AP).—Seven men found guilty of creating a breach of the peace today were given the alternative of paying fines of ten pounds ($50) or serving jail sentences of one month as a sequel to religious riots which flared through Edinburgh's streets last night. Police patrolled the streets on guard against any recurrence of the turbulent scene when a crowd estimated at 3,000 hurled bottles and stones at Catholic women and priests attending the eucharistic congress. The disorders cropped up after Protestants gathered at Waverley market, where the Catholics were holding an open air mass meeting in connection with the Congress.

Paris, June 24. ()—Speedy completion of warships under construction and “prospective accords” with Great Britain and Italy constitute France's answer to Germany's projected fleet. Francois Pietri, minister of the navy, told a delegation of the navy committee of the chamber of deputies today Adolf Hitler's naval program was “serious” but not a “catastrophe” to this country. He outlined the plan which he will present to the full committee tomorrow, Pietri’s idea, committee members said, is to hasten the construction of the Dunkerqué, now nearly completed, and then to lay the keel of a 35,000 ton dreadnought in October. Work on many small craft likewise will be speeded without exceeding the Washington limitation treaty but with everything prepared for heavy building if needed when the pact expires Dec. 31, 1936. A pact with England, Pietri said, could assure cooperation in the north Atlanti

1935-06-27.text: Rome (P)—Official sources intimated today as Captain Anthony Eden departed for London that the British diplomat’s conversations with Premier Mussolini had not in the slightest respect changed Il Duce’s determination to make a “complete solution” to the Italo-Ethiopian problem. Captain Eden's farewell, if anything, was cooler than the cool welcome he received upon his arrival. He had a short talk with Fulvio Suvich, undersecretary for foreign affairs, at the railroad station. Few functionaries were present and there was no demonstration of any kind.

BEVERLY HILLS, Calif, June 25—In schools they have what they call intelligence tests. Well, if nations held ’em, I don't believe we would be what you would call a favorite to win. The chain letter thing lasted just two days in England. Over here it took us a whole month to figure it out. And Mexico laughed the thing out of their country before lunch. Then there was “tennocracy” which we took serious for over three months. There is still a lot of monkey in us. Throw anything you want to into our cage and we will give it serious consideration. Yours,

LONDON, June 27—()—Jean Borotra, France's bounding Basque of the tennis courts, assured All-England Club officials today that he would not permit his dueling engagement in Paris to interfere with his scheduled appearances in the Wimbledon championships. “One must fight as a point of honor,” said Borotra, “but I also am honor-bound to play at Wimbledon, and that must come first.” Friends of Borotra, who accepted a challenge from Didier Poulain, Paris newspaper tennis expert, revealed that secret arrangements are being considered by the two men's seconds whereby both principals would shoot in the air when they meet. These friends said the situation had reached a point where the duel could not be avoided but that, in the eyes of fifty million Frenchmen, nothing else would do. Under the French code of honor, the duel must be fought within 48 hours of the time of the challenge—issued Tuesday

| PARIS, June 27.—()—Official French sources said today France expects Great Britain, as "atonement" for making a separate Anglo-German naval deal, to put pressure on Germany for a reduction of the Reich's army. Premier Laval, according to these sources, told Capt. Anthony Eden of Great Britain frankly this morning that France wants Great Britain's help in seeking to induce Reichsführer Hitler to cut his proposed army well below the 550,000 troops announced. When Laval and Eden resumed their conversations, interrupted for a few days while the British diplomat talked with Premier Mussolini in Rome, their policies still were wide apart. Although Laval had demanded before Eden went to Rome that the British cabinet declare England hereafter would negotiate only in a collective peace system.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) PARIS—The immediate fate of a proposed five-nation air defense league to safeguard the peace of Western Europe was at stake today in a conference between Premier Pierre Laval and Anthony Eden, British cabinet envoy. Or instructions from the cabinet, it was learned Eden sought to persuade Laval that negotiation of an agreement for the league at the earliest possible time would be desirable. As an inducement, Eden was understood to have suggested coincident negotiation of an Eastern Security Treaty, which would be linked with a series of non-aggression treaties among eastern nations including Russia, Germany, and the Baltic States. The air defense league would include Britain, France, Belgium, Italy, and Germany. Each member would be pledged to attack any other member which made war on one of the five. MUIRFIELD, Scotland, June 27.—(?)—Battling a stiff head wind that at times reached gale strength, Henry Cotton, the defending titleholder, today yielded the lead in the second round of the 72-hole British Open golf championship to Charles A. Whitcombe, 40-year-old veteran British Ryder Cup team player. Players with scores of 153 or lower for the first 36 holes qualified for the double-round stretch drive tomorrow. Thus six Americans made the grade easily. Henry Picard of Hershey, Pa., and Robert Sweeney, New York amateur now living in London, qualified with totals of 145; MacDonald Smith of Glendale, Cal., and W. Lawson Little Jr., of San Francisco, had 146 aggregates, and Joe Ezar of Waco, Texas, and Fran Ball, formerly of Atlanta, Ga., made the grade with 151 totals. With 153 the borderline, 62 players were admitted to the final grind.

LONDON, June 27.—(4)—America's two women stars, Helen Jacobs and Helen Wills Moody, battled their way into the third round of the All-England tennis championships at Wimbledon today but John Van Ryn of East Orange, N. J., was eliminated in the third round of men’s singles by Fred Perry, of England, the defending champion, 4-6, 6-1, 6-3, 10-8. * Sidney Wood, chief American hope in men's singles, eliminated D. H. Williams of England, 6-3, 9-7, 6-2.

DUBLIN, June 27.—Communists throwing leaflets demanding the release of Tom Mooney tried to rush the automobile of Alvin M. Owsley, new United States minister, today. The car was approaching the entrance to Dublin Castle, bearing Owsley to present his credentials to President Eamon de Valera. Police beat back the communists and forced them down a side street. Owsley presented his credentials and left without further incident.

STRESA, Apr. 11.—(AP)—A clash of opinion between British and French delegations developed at today’s inaugural sessions of the Tri-Power conference here, authoritative quarters said tonight, after France moved unexpectedly to get British and Italian support for her appeal to Geneva against German rearmament. The French, it was learned, tossed into the midst of the afternoon session their memorandum of Adolf Hitler’s alleged repudiations of treaties. Pushed into the background by the French move were other, broader issues of security, even though Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain at the morning session had outlined his nation’s desire for an inclusive system to safeguard the continent’s peace. France withdrew her strong resolution of censure for German rearmament in the face of firm opposition by both Great Britain and Italy. It was indicated efforts are to be made to get Germany into the peace system and back into the League. Assembled statesmen today discussed what measures might be taken against nations which scrap treaties. Agreement among representatives of France, Britain and Italy as to program they shall follow in next weeks League of Nations council session in Geneva was reached today, Pierre Laval, French foreign minister said.

An Italian delegation at the British-French-Italian conference issued an unexpected communique saying Dr. Konstantin von Neurath, German foreign minister, had informed Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador in Berlin, that Germany was ready to enter a pact of non-aggression in eastern Europe. Germany offered to enter the pact "even if the other signatories to such a pact had already formulated separate agreements amongst themselves for reciprocal assistance." 1935-08-18.text: By The Associated Press Paris, Aug. 17—Differences and delays threatened tonight to wreck the tri-power conference attempting to settle the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. It was deadlocked, with the French and British on one side and the Italians on the other disputing whether there was any plan before them. The British were impatiently waiting word from Premier Mussolini as to what he wanted, while the Italians insisted procedure was up to the French and English. French officials explained a Franco-British plan was submitted for communication to Il Duce offering Italy certain concessions in Ethiopia. The Italians, however, denied that they were waiting for any word from Mussolini and insisted that no proposition had been submitted to them. Staff Sergeant Stanley Morgan, in charge of the army’s radio station at that bleak outpost, Point Barrow, wirelessed the story to the war department today, telling how a native ran 15 miles from his sealing camp to gasp out the message of the plane crash. Post had brought his plane down on a small river near the Eskimo’s camp and “two men climbed out, one wearing ‘rag on sore eye’ and other ‘bik man with boots.’” Rogers called to the native, asking directions to Point Barrow. Hanks Hinkel, Nazi commissioner of culture, with Dr. Paul Joseph Goebbels, propaganda minister, announced strict regulations for reorganizing Jewish cultural groups into one “life union of Jewish cultural societies.” Provision was made for their close supervision. Weary Senate and House conferees drove in an overtime session tonight, and arranged a Sunday meeting; in an effort to reach an agreement on the tax bill. -HYDE PARK, N. Y. (AP)—President Roosevelt looked forward Saturday to an early adjournment by Congress and a possible statement to the people. While keeping strictest silence during his week-end trip at home, it appeared he might give a talk over the air this week to the gathering of Young Democrats at Milwaukee, Wis. Should he go on the air then, it is believed possible Mr. Roosevelt might review the work of this busy Congress and outline some thoughts for the future. The presidential thoughts meanwhile are concerned with the fulfillment of his legislative program now at the crux in the closing rush of Congress.

1935-01-31.text: London, Ont.—John Labatt today identified David Meisner, in the courtroom where the latter is on trial, as one of three men who kidnapped him last August. The wealthy brewer, on the witness stand, was asked by Chief Crown Prosecutor J. C. M. German, who one of the trio was who stopped him on a lonely road between Sarnia and London. Labatt answered, "the accused." "Where is the accused?" asked the prosecutor. "In the prisoner's box," Labatt replied. Meisner, the former Cincinnati and Detroit bookmaker, sat quietly in the prisoner's box.

Sheffield, England, Jan. 31 (AP)—Henry Ross, 69, an unemployed workman, was called into police court today to answer to a kidnapping charge 31 years old. He was accused of abducting John William Whitnear, when Whitnear was four years and ten months old, and taking him to the United States. The warrant on which he was arrested was issued in 1904. “Whitnear, now 36 years old, will be one of the prosecution’s witnesses. He was found near Newark, N. J., five years after his alleged abduction and brought back to Sheffield, where he received a civic welcome. Ross, his attorney said, returned from the United States two or three years ago.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 31—The Yungkong native bank failed today as all China awaited efforts of government leaders to save the nation’s monetary system from collapse. The bank was the first institution to close its doors since the crisis developed. The Yungkong loss was estimated at $1,500,000. It had $3,000,000 in deposits. While other financial institutions strove desperately to obtain silver from a rapidly dwindling supply to meet demands for China's basic metal, Gen. Chiang Kai-Shek, recognized leader of the national government and his associates sought remedies for the situation in a Nanking conference. They closed one possible avenue to a new deal in Chinese monetary affairs by announcing definitely that they do not contemplate a Sino-Japanese economic bloc. It had been reported that Japan would make a large loan to China, that China would then go on the gold standard and that the Japanese

Tokyo, Jan. 30 ()--A warning before the Japanese House of Representatives today that disputes along the Manchoukuan-Siberian border “may cause serious trouble” at any time, was underscored tonight with reports of new fighting along the Manchoukuo-Outer Mongolia border. Rengo (Japanese) News Agency, in dispatches from Hsinking, Manchoukuo, said Japanese-Manchoukuan troops yesterday occupied Kalkha Miao on the Manchu-Mongol frontier, driving Mongols before them. “The new clash along the northwest frontier of Manchoukuo, nominally independent but Japanese-advised empire, was regarded as significant in the light of Japanese contentions that Soviet penetration into Outer Mongolia has resulted in virtual confiscation of that vast territory.” Japan's war lords pointed again to the Soviet “menace” to Manchoukuo to explain to the House of Representatives, considering the biggest war budget in Jap

TOKYO, (AP).—Fresh hostilities between Mongols and Japanese and Manchoukuan cavalry were reported today along Manchoukuo’s vague frontier bordering outer Mongolia. Dispatches from Hsinking, Manchoukuo, to the Rengo (Japanese) news agency, said the cavalry detachment was pursuing a band of Mongols fleeing across the frozen Steppes in 30 below zero temperatures. Japanese general headquarters of Hsinking announced that Japanese cavalry was participating in the expedition. Its purpose, the announcement said, was to “expel invading Mongols from Manchoukuo territory.” Although no Soviet troops were reported to have been involved in the fighting, the Japanese contend that the territory in which troops are active is ten miles north of the Kalkha river, which they assert forms the Manchoukuan-Mongolian boundary.

MUNICH, Germany, Jan. 30. — Notes he jotted down about the famed Dachau concentration camp, Richard Roiderer's friends said today, led to the high treason charges against the former Cleveland man who is a United States citizen. Roiderer was stoutly defended by his friends, who described him as “more a thinker and student than one obsessed with political intentions.” His nerves were reported to be badly frayed because he has not seen his aged mother who is dependent upon him for support. She is in a nursing home at Kaiserslautern.

VIENNA, (U.P)--King Carol of Roumania has made a five star final decision to renounce red-haired Mme. Magda Lupescu, for whom he once gave up his right to the throne, it was reported today. Carol was said to have given his word within recent days to several men high in Roumanian politics that he would seek a reconciliation with his divorced wife, Princess Helen, and ask her to remarry him. What the effect of a reconciliation would have as concerns the beautiful Mme. Lupescu was problematical. There were hints that Carol's affection for her remained undiminished, but that at the urgent demand of political leaders he would at least renounce formally this attachment. Carol's decision was said to have been dictated by reasons of State alone. It was asserted that his advisers told him his throne was endangered because of popular resentment.

1935-02-05.text: LONDON, Feb. 5—(P)—Great Britain has informed all other interested powers, including the United States, that unless Reichsfuehrer Hitler's response to the Anglo-French proposals is favorable, Germany will be isolated by defensive air alliances. The British government has asked the United States through Ray Atherton, counsellor of the United States embassy, to agree to repeal the military clauses of the separate peace treaty signed between the United States and Germany, provided settlement of Europe's problems is reached on the basis of the Anglo-French proposals. The military clauses of the Versailles treaty were duplicated in the American pact.

LONDON, Feb. 3.—()—An agreement between Britain and France on a proposal to legalize German armaments and an inclusive scheme for simultaneous settlement of all important European problems increasing the "dangers of war" was officially announced today. At the same time it was revealed that Britain and France, in their "momentous bi-lateral conversations, have agreed to a military air alliance. Under this alliance, each country would be bound to come to the immediate assistance of the other if it is "the victim of an unprovoked aerial aggression." The stamp of British approval also was placed upon the recent Italo-French accords, and in an official communique Britain reiterated its positions among the "which will consult together if the independence and integrity of Austria is menaced." In the field of aviation the new accord was regarded as the most binding alliance undertaken between na

Paris— (.) —Great Britain and France have agreed on a complete pact of mutual defense, Premier Pierre Étienne Flandin told the chamber of deputies today. In a declaration to parliament on the accord just reached in London on Germany's rearmament, Flandin said: “We have provided for reciprocal and complete assistance between France and Great Britain. We believe other nations should likewise be interested in removing the danger of aggression and therefore we decided to call for the participation of the nations which signed the Locarno pact.” PRINCIPLES PRESENTED Of the London accords, Flandin said further: “They must not be misunderstood. They are principles presented with a view to later conversations, as the two governments must act together again when they receive replies to their invitations.” Outlining the reasons for the accords, Flandin reiterated that Germany’s secret rearmament an

HUNTERDON COUNTY COURTHOUSE, Flemington, N. J., Feb. 4.—(U.P)—A story of how an English serving girl from aristocratic Englewood, N. J., supposedly joined a German fur worker from the swarming sidewalks of the Bronx to kidnap the Lindbergh baby was unrolled today. Bruno Richard Hauptmann’s lawyers drew it from witnesses with brief, sharp questions which usually could be answered with a simple “yes” or “no.” Then they left it there in the court record to sink into the minds of the jurors, and passed on to other matters, Fog of Suspicion Tonight, a fog of suspicion hangs over the graves of Violet Sharpe and Isidor Fisch—one in Brookside cemetery, Englewood; the other half a world away in Germany. Most of the day Edward J. Reilly, chief of the defense staff, worked to make a well-rounded narrative out of his theory that Bruno Richard Hauptmann is sitting here on trial for his life only beca

BERLIN, Feb. 4.--(INS) Long drawn out and “exceedingly difficult” negotiations were predicted by a spokesman for the Hitler Government today as the way was opened for a new disarmament convention by the Anglo-French accord achieved at London yesterday. Conceding that the way was now clear for negotiations, the Reich Government admitted it is now sanguine over the possibility of an early agreement in the arms dispute between Germany and the former allied powers.

Paris, Feb. 5—First steps toward effecting the French-British agreement on German rearmament may be taken this weekend, it was indicated today. There was an increasing tendency to see in the agreement, providing for a British-French, Belgian-German aerial defense treaty, with Italy perhaps also included, the germ of the international army of which some statesmen have dreamed for years. Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, may come here Friday for a dinner of the British Chamber of Commerce, it was understood today, and remain to discuss with Premier Pierre Etienne Flandin and Foreign Minister Pierre Laval the reaction of Germany and other nations to their joint announcement of their agreement. Establishment of direct negotiatory contact with Germany presumably had not been decided upon. There were apparently inspired reports that Simon, or Anthony Eden, chief British disarmament del

Chancellor Hitler, it was said in both English and French quarters, is "non-committal," refusing to indicate whether he will accept the direct approach negotiating to European security. The pact was presented, diplomatic quarters said, almost as a "last alternative to prevent bilateral alliances from forming against Germany." German officials said frankly and flatly the Accord, with its air clauses, its League of Nations proviso and other elements, is not acceptable. 1935-03-29.text: Moscow—(AP)—With a plan for United States collaboration with other powers in the Far East reportedly under discussion, Capt. Anthony Eden, British Lord Privy Seal, faced Joseph Stalin, Soviet chief, in the latter's private office in the Kremlin today. A high source said that Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinoff had suggested to Eden the formulation of a Far Eastern pact to include the United States, Great Britain, Russia, Japan, China, and France, and that Stalin, too, supported this suggestion. London—(AP)—Reliable quarters said today that Maxim Litvinoff, Soviet Commissar for Foreign Affairs, has proposed a Far Eastern pact to Capt. Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal, during the conversations of the diplomats at Moscow. Such an arrangement, Litvinoff is said to have pointed out, should include the United States, Britain, Russia, Japan, China, and France, as the powers having interests in the F

London, March 28.—The British government, facing a decision of grave import at the tri-power Stresa conference April 11, tonight studied still another European security scheme in an effort to save something from the wreckage of Anglo-German conversations at Berlin. Authoritative sources said Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, failed completely to get Adolf Hitler’s assent to fundamentals of the present security draft plan, worked out at Anglo-French discussions in London early in February. An alternative arrangement, therefore, will be sought, compromising differences between the Reich and other powers; it may be presented to France and Italy at the Stresa conference. Germany will not be present at that meeting, Sir John told the House of Commons today. Little Information He vouchsafed little other information about his mission, mentioning “considerable divergencies of opinion” b

MOSCOW, Mar. 28.—(AP)— Over tables groaning with the richest food in Soviet Russia, British and Russian statesmen tonight pledged their respective governments to bend every effort toward solution of the present European crisis. A brilliant banquet Maxim Litvinoff, Soviet commissar for foreign affairs, gave in honor of his British visitor, Capt. Anthony Eden, at Spiridonovka House was marked by the host’s declaration: “Never since the World War have there been such misgivings for the fate of peace as now.” Replying, the young British lord privy seal expressed the hope that the nations would “stand firm and so sustain the cause of this peace.” Lifting glasses of Soviet-made champagne, the two, who spent much of today over the council table, said their governments would do everything possible to solve the present grave problems. The banquet followed a reception at which men wore full dress

NEW YORK — Pp — Luck showered approximately $2,700,000 on American and Canadian sweepstake winners today in the running of the grand national steeplechase at Aintree, England, which was won by Reynoldstown. In addition to the money divided on the actual running, consolation prizes of more than $240,000 and residual prizes of an equal amount were given to American ticket holders. Beyond these amounts, there was a division of more than $1,000,000 to holders of tickets on "also rans," each of whom received $3,978, bringing the grand total to Americans approximately to $2,700,000. Four Americans and one Canadian won $143,475 each as holders of tickets on Reynoldstown, the 22-to-1 shot who came in first. They were: Roy Gold, The Bronx, N. Y. Alm Goldberg, 4906 Rorer street, Philadelphia, Pa. "Five Glasses," 1921 North Wanamaker street, Philadelphia. (Continued on Page 28, Col. 3)

MOSCOW, March 29.—(UP)— Russia urged on Great Britain today the absolute necessity of a treaty to guarantee the peace of Eastern Europe, and argued that if Germany and Poland refused to adhere, it would be because they wanted war. Anthony Eden, British cabinet envoy, continued his talks with Maxim Litvinov, Russia's brilliant foreign minister. The privilege of an appointment to meet Josef Stalin, leader of the Soviet, was accorded him. Stalin, secretary general of the Communist party, though titular head of the government, rarely sees foreign visitors. There seemed no doubt from the tenor of the negotiations that the visit of Eden would mean cementing relations between capitalist Britain and Communist Russia on a firmer basis than they have seen since the Bolshevik revolution. For the first time since the inauguration of the Soviet government, King George's health was officially toasted

By The Associated Press London, March 29—The collapse of the League of Nations beneath pressure from a new series of alliances similar to those of pre-war days unless the current European situation improves was forecast in diplomatic circles today. The Daily Herald quoted a confidential diplomatic source as saying: “The future of the league is at stake. If Great Britain does not stand by the league, a system of collective security alliances will begin to spring up in Europe, due to growing fears of Germany.” Conspicuously for the last few days on the Anglo-German conversations at Berlin, the government-inspired Times today devoted more than a column to editorial comment on the discussion among Reichsfuhrer Hitler, Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and Captain Anthony Eden, lord privy seal. The Times hinted the British government's policy in the face of Hitler’s rebuff of the pro

Blue Prince was second and Thomond II, only American entry to finish in the money, third. Reynoldstown paid: 22 to 1. Blue Prince 40 to 1 and Thomond II 9 to 2; Golden Miller, the Hon. Miss Dorothy Paget's brilliant eight year old gelding which won last year, fell at one of the treacherous jumps and disappointed thousands of backers who stood to win some $5,000,000 had he crossed the finish line ahead of the field. Reynoldstown dropped fortunes of $150,000 in the laps of four American ticket-holders in the Irish hospitals sweepstakes. Those who held tickets on Blue Prince came away $75,000 richer each and Thomond’s lucky holders benefited $1,000 apiece. But the thousands who had s

French officials, however, were described as despairing of getting Germany into any effective peace system, believing the only way to curb the Reich’s military power would be return to the old system of armed allegiances. If Hitler's reputed demands—economic union with Austria, air parity and some Czechoslovak territory among them—are true, and if any attempt is made to enforce them, the French said, the result will be war. France served notice upon Germany, the League of Nations disclosed, that she will not allow Nazi brownshirts to occupy the Rhineland.

1935-02-24.text: By The Associated Press London, Feb. 23—After one withering blast at Attorney Edward J. Reilly, Betty Gow went into hiding tonight. A diligent search of London hotels failed to locate the pretty Scot girl who, as Baby Charles A. Lindbergh’s nurse, was the last person to see him alive and one of the star state witnesses in the Hauptmann murder trial at Flemington, N. J. Miss Gow was believed to be with her mother, who met her at Southampton. The Lindbergh baby nurse broke her customary silence to take bitter exception to what she termed “brutal and unjust” attacks upon her by Hauptmann’s defense lawyers. Reilly, she said, “went too far. To insinuate that I knew more about the tragedy than I made known to the court was unjust. I am sure he would not have been allowed to do that in Britain. He should not be allowed to do it in America.” Reports that she became engaged to be married while in

BERLIN, Feb. 23— (AP) — Franz von Papen, German minister in Vienna, came to Berlin today to help Adolf Hitler solve the problem of Germany’s future policy toward Austria. The former vice chancellor’s arrival served to stress the dilemma in which the Anglo-French security proposals, involving Germany's adherence to the central European non-interference pact drafted at Rome, have placed Hitler. Great Britain has agreed to be “among the powers which will, as provided in the Rome agreement, consult together, if the independence and integrity of Austria are menaced.” France and Great Britain asked for “the direct and effective cooperation of Germany.” If he wants to play with the other powers, Hitler must give up his dream of guiding, either directly or indirectly, the destinies of the land of his birth, Austria. No longer may lieutenants of his harangue the Austrian public over the Kinnich r

ROME, Feb. 23—(AP)—Soldiers of Italy, more than 10,000 strong, moved tonight aboard a fleet of seven ships toward Africa and the theater of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Aboard the Vulcania, which sailed from Messina as huge crowds cheered, were four generals including General Rudolfo Graziani who is expected to take supreme command. Five thousand soldiers are aboard the Vulcania, bound as are the other ships for Eritrea and Italian Somaliland.

Associated Press Staff Writer. PAWNEE, Okla., Feb. 23.—Twenty-five years in state penitentiary is the penalty 19-year-old Phil Kennamer must pay for the slaying of John F. Gorrell, Jr., 23, in Tulsa last Thanksgiving night. The well-knit, dark-haired son of Federal Judge Franklin E. Kennamer stood up in district court room here today and accepted the long term, levied by Judge Thurman Hurst, without a change of expression. The state had asked 99 years. Judge Hurst said: “I do not feel that you should be accorded any special treatment because of your father. My idea is that the son of a federal judge or of the President should be treated just like any other person.” The defense immediately announced intention to appeal. Judge Hurst granted four months for its preparation. Previously, he had denied an eloquent appeal for a new trial. Bond for the youth, convicted of manslaughter last Thurs

NEW YORK, (AP).—The man whom poverty had never bothered, but whom money made mad, strained Saturday night at his straight jacket and cried out for his .315 hat. Saturday morning, not long after midnight, Frank Greges went violently insane and cried out that he was God. “I can look at a man and kill him with a look,” he screamed. He did look at a man, and the man— Michael Gryzwacz — fell dead. They said Saturday down at the little hotel on the Bowery where he had a room that Greges had been acting strangely for several days. “Once,” said the hotel manager, “the old fellow went to his room, knocked on the door and then waited until he invited himself in.” The little Lithuanian is 67 years old. “The most I ever had at one time was about $200 which I once was able to lay up in the summer time against the jobless months of winter,” he once said. He didn’t mind. He didn't want wealth for he di

Snow, sleet, violent winds and swirling dust storms darkened the world’s weather map yesterday, killing and destroying on both hemispheres. Howling gales pounded distress calls out of seven vessels in both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and battered an airplane under the waves, while inland storms swept over the east and southwestern parts of the United States, and through south and central France. At least ten deaths were counted in the East during the 24 hours ending Saturday night as a result of snow, hail and sleet. The slick highways caused numerous fractures, sprains and other injuries. Six persons were killed and five others injured when a windstorm swept through France, toppling chimneys, unroofing houses and disrupting communication. Planes Grounded Airplanes were grounded and other transportation slowed as the season's first dust storms swirled over western Nebraska, Colorado,

BETHLEHEM, Pa., Feb. 23.—(7)— A reported plot to kidnap Eugene G. Grace, president of Bethlehem Steel Company, and hold him for $250,000 ransom, was under investigation last night. The investigation is connected with two bank holdups and a series of other holdups, made a statement regarding the alleged plot.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 23. (P) — The administration's power experts today hastily drew plans aimed at having the supreme court overturn—at the earliest possible moment—the adverse decision against the TVA in Alabama. The comment from supporters of the TVA ranged from concern to consternation. There was no doubt that the New Deal would use every effort at its command to remove the threatened obstruction of its plans. Henry T. Hunt, general counsel of the PWA, said he would join with attorneys for the Tennessee Valley Authority in appealing the ruling of Justice W. I. Grubb. No Authority Grubb, the same federal judge who recently held the NRA unconstitutional, ruled that TVA had no authority to dispose of surplus power generated at the hydroelectric plants on the Tennessee River. The man who drafted the TVA act, Senator Norris (R-Neb), said today that the effect of the opinion was to virtually n

1935-05-09.text: London, May 9 (UP)—An imperial monetary conference among the British dominions and Great Britain was urged today by the British Empire Federation of Chambers of Commerce. Washington, May 9 (UP)—Patman bonus forces carried their battle to the country today, urging the people to flood the White House with 1,000,000 telegrams requesting approval of the inflationary measure. Washington, May 9 (UP)—The Senate appropriations committee approved today the $459,606,846 naval budget, setting aside $100,000,000 for construction of 24 warships. The bill has passed the House.

LOS ANGELES, May 9 — Elissa Landi, film star and writer of fiction and verse, today was granted a divorce from John Cecil Lawrence, London barrister, whom she charged with causing her great mental suffering by his alleged unconventional views on married life. Miss Landi, who brought the suit under her legal name, Elizabeth Marie Lawrence, told Superior Judge William S. Baird her husband told her of his asserted affairs with other women and suggested he would not object to her conducting herself with similar freedom with other men. Miss Landi testified she was greatly shocked at her husband's suggestions, which she said he also made concerning her to her mother, Countess Caraline Zanardi-Landi. A solicitor for Lawrence notified the County Clerk the barrister had filed suit for divorce there, and contended the Los Angeles court had no jurisdiction. The solicitor said Lawrence would not pay

PARIS, May 8. (?)—Former King George II of Greece was quoted Wednesday in dispatches from London to the Newspaper Excelsior as saying he was ready to return to the throne should his people summon him. “If the will of the Greek people clearly calls me back,” he was quoted, “I will return to my dear country, taking for my inspiration the constitutional and liberal principles my grandfather, George I, founder of our dynasty, applied during the years of a happy and fruitful reign.”

OMDIYY Denn, WLASSACN USES, May 3, 1935. I was surprised to find on my return home how discouraged people are in New England at the present time. This section is a hotbed of indignation against the New Deal Cotton program. One old Yankee mill after another has been forced to close its doors, throwing thousands of workers onto public relief. At the same time, big growers and shippers in the South are alarmed by the fifty percent drop in American cotton exports since a year ago. So the cotton program is caught between the crossfire of the mills and the growers. Russia’s “Man of Steel,” secretary of the all-powerful Communist Party and Soviet dictator, stressed three key points in those pronouncements. 1. (Copyright, 1935, By United Press) PARIS, May 9—(UP)—Three Army pursuit planes sped over France today bearing to Rome a mission charged with concluding the first specific aerial defense alliance in history. Gen. Victor Denain, Air Minister, led the mission. With him were Gusicard D’Estaing, his Chief of Cabinet, and aeronautic engineers and other experts of the Air Ministry. Two of the rocketing Potez 56 planes were piloted by trans-Atlantic flyers—Maurice Rossi, co-holder of the world straight line distance record, and Jean Mermoz, who has made the South Atlantic an aerial ferry line. The third pilot, Capt. Paul Girardot, also is an ace. Rossi piloted Denain's plane. They left Le Bourget Field at 7:57 a.m. and will halt at Marignane Airdrome, Marseilles, for the night and proceed to Rome at 10 a.m. tomorrow for a six hour flight. Copenhagen, May 8.—(AP)— King Christian of Denmark became a grandfather today with the birth of a daughter to Princess Caroline Mathilde and his youngest son, Prince Knud. Prince Knud and his cousin, Princess Caroline Mathilde, were married Sept. 8, 1933. The prince is 85 and his wife, 23.

1935-07-08.text: London—()— George Washington Hill, 50, president of the American Tobacco Company, married his 39-year-old secretary, Mary Barnes, in the Caxton Hall register office Monday. The ceremony, which was witnessed by nine persons, was performed by J. P. Bond, deputy-registrar.

Storms and raging floods spreading over wide areas in New York state, New England and Canada took at least 11 lives Monday, caused millions of dollars damage, forced hundreds of families to leave their homes and marooned hundreds of others in water-blockaded trains, buses and automobiles. United Press dispatches showed 11 deaths attributed to the most serious storm in New York state in more than a decade. Tentative estimates put property damage at over $10,000,000. Hundreds of people were completely or partly inundated and at least 150 cottages were carried into open water. Crops suffered heavily. An automobile carrying four persons was swept from the highway into a flooded creek. Virtually all of the flood victims were drowned, eight of them in or near Ithaca. The storms extended from western New York to Ontario and New England and varied from turbulent floods in the New York state area

LONDON, July 8.——Great Britain has been brought to at least a temporary halt in its effort to prevent Italy from waging war on Abyssinia. Both Italy and France have buffed British suggestions and efforts at compromise, and the United States’ refusal to invoke the pact of Paris—the Briand-Kellogg anti-war treaty—has left the government, for the present at least, empty of ideas. Joseph A. Avenol, secretary general of the League of Nations, was due here today to discuss with government leaders the possibilities to be expected when the league council next considers the Italian-Abyssinian crisis July 25. Avenol has engagements to see Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, and Anthony Eden, minister for League of Nations affairs, tomorrow. The cabinet will consider the situation Wednesday and Hoare is to make a considered statement on it to the house of commons Thursday. Italy has rejected all B

SAN DIEGO, Calif., July 8 (AP). A reunion of four women who had not been together since 1922 today ended in the death of all when their automobile plunged down a 35-foot embankment at Point Loma and landed in the surf. Later, in attempting to salvage the wrecked automobile, William F. England, a garageman, was fatally injured when a crane cable broke and struck him. The women victims of the tragedy were Mrs. Victoria Alberta Murphy, 45, of San Diego; Miss Mary F. Roome, 60, of King Cove Beach, Mass.; Mrs. Helen Billings, Pond View Avenue, Jamaica Plain, Mass., and Miss Constance Billings, her daughter.

Residents fled their homes in New York state today when torrential rains brought floods that set homes adrift, washed out bridges, marooned week-end vacationists and took two lives. The floods and storms spread destruction over widely scattered areas in New York, New England and part of Canada. A train was many hours overdue at Elmira, N. Y., in a region where many bridges were washed out. Shipping was greatly delayed by fog at Boston. Public services were suspended in New York areas as the water backed from swollen streams and rivers to cover highways, farmlands and town streets from one to several feet. Damage Totals Millions Damage will run into millions of dollars first estimates indicated. Loss to crops and trees was reported throughout the area. Homes, bridges, transportation lines and communication systems increased the damage. Twenty families left their homes along Sawkill Creek,

Lambie of the Abyssinian mission service said today, there is likely to be little fighting in the impending war with Ethiopia. ()-~-Italy stepped up its concentration of troops for action in eastern Africa today and some observers predicted that the war between Ethiopia and Italy may be started before the rainy season ends in September. The black shirt divisions, it was disclosed, have been increased in strength from 12,000 to 15,000 with four divisions completed and another to be completed soon. Rally To Mussolini. 1935-05-18.text: Wool, Dorsetshire, England, May 18--Wild rumors flitted about Col. T. E. Lawrence today as the famed World War figure lay for the fifth day, unconscious from a motorcycle accident. The reports were more fantastic than many of the legends linked to Lawrence’s Arabian adventures. One was that Britain would be in peril if Lawrence died because his brain holds the country’s war plan. A. W. Lawrence, brother of the man who changed his name to T. E. Shaw, when he joined the Royal Air Force in 1927, said the reports were “utter nonsense.”

Wool, Dorsetshire, Eng, May 17 (A)--Extraordinary measures for official secrecy surrounding Col. T. E. Lawrence, lying near death in an army hospital, led to reports tonight that the motorcycle accident in which he was injured resulted from an attempt on his life. The world-famous Lawrence of Arabia remained in critical condition and unconscious for the fourth day since the motorcycle he was riding collided on a public road with a bicycle ridden by a child. Physicians announced there was faint hope for his ultimate recovery.

WASHINGTON, May 18. —(#)— With British authorities turning a cold shoulder toward hints that this government might welcome overtures looking to international currency stabilization, financial circles wondered today if the lead in such a move might come from another quarter. Some observers said one possibility was that stabilization advocates might seek to persuade the Bank for International Settlements to submit a plan which could be used as the basis for a lasting agreement. An international parliamentary conference recommended recently that the World Bank make a study along these lines, holding that an end to international monetary uncertainties would contribute to a revival of trade. Only a few days ago, however, Leon Fraser, retiring president of the bank, declared that stabilization was “squarely up to Great Britain.” It was said in some quarters in the capital that the next move mi

WOOL, England (Pp) — Fantastical rumors, all declared to be without foundation, flourished Saturday about Col. T. E. Lawrence—Lawrence of Arabia—who is still unconscious five days after a motorcycle crash in which he suffered a fractured skull. The rumors included: That the man in hospital here was not Lawrence who actually is on secret service duty in the east. That Great Britain would be imperiled if he died, because in his brain alone was stored British war plans. This, it was said, was the reason office officials and high members of the government were concerned lest he died. That Lawrence recently went to Berlin, and after his return asked police protection. That King George personally telephoned the hospital frequently to ask anxiously about Lawrence's condition. Lawrence's condition was still unchanged Saturday. There was little apparent mystery about his accident. He was going at

VATICAN CITY, May 18 (UP) A plea to England to return to the Roman Catholic Church will be contained in the homily which Pope Pius will read at the canonization of Thomas More and John Fisher at St. Peter's on Sunday. The pope’s plea, it was understood, will be on the grounds that England should return to the Roman Church to make one flock under one shepherd.

LONDON, May 18. (#)—-A Reuters (British) News agency dispatch from Moscow tonight said 47 persons were killed when the Maxim Gorky, world’s largest airliner, crashed at the Moscow airport today. The dead comprised 11 members of the crew and 36 passengers, the dispatch added. The pilot of a smaller machine which collided with the huge aircraft also lost his life, the report said.

LONDON, May 18 (UP).—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Munich today reported "serious rioting" when organized bands of Nazis tried to prevent a collection for a Roman Catholic church. The dispatch said the Nazis molested the collectors and thrust into their hands copies of newspapers reporting the sentencing of Sister Katharina Wiedenhofer to five years imprisonment on charges of smuggling currency out of Germany. The conviction of the nun was the first of 50 cases of priests and nuns charged with violating reich laws. The Nazis displayed banners which said: "Don’t give a penny to the foreign exchange smugglers." "No German should give to the Roman Catholic traitors."

London, May 18.—The giant Soviet air liner “Maxim Gorky,” the world’s largest land plane, crashed near Moscow today according to a Reuter dispatch. Details were lacking but it was reported the huge plane cracked up after colliding with a smaller machine. Completed in 1934, the “Maxim Gorky” represented the ultimate achievement of the Soviet in air transport development. The big plane, named after Russia's first writer, was used by the government for distributing propaganda.

1935-07-25.text: By The Associated Press London, July 25—Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, announced in the house of commons today the British government will not for the present grant licenses for the exportation of arms from Great Britain to either Italy or Ethiopia. He said that the transit across British territory of arms destined for Ethiopia would be permitted, however. “The government,” said Sir Samuel, “is doing its best to make possible the peaceable outcome of the present dispute and would not wish to do anything which might prejudice the situation.”

BEVERLY HILLS, CAL. — Wiley Post and I have been blathering about flying over to a ranch in New Mexico, and some guy with poor slant on geography got it mixed up with Siberia in Russia. Looks like New Mexico has got a suit. England says the old armament treaties of Washington in 1922 are dead, that it wounded the pride of nations to hold that they were inferior. That's right, a nation can be small but it don’t want to be put in treaties that it's small. Besides it's the little nations that should be allowed the most armament: lack of armament got nothing to do with wars, Abyssinia has just got so many nine-foot ones. Yours,

London, July 24. (P)—An authoritative British source said tonight that Mussolini plans to use at least 500,000 troops in a projected campaign against Ethiopia. This source said some foreign governments have been advised that the Italian government intends to send whatever additional number of troops is needed to make up that number into East Africa before the present rainy season has ended.

(By the Associated Press) The British government has decided to forbid the exportation of arms and ammunition to both Italy and Ethiopia, the House of Commons was officially informed. “Sir Samuel Hoare, Foreign Secretary, explained, however, that a treaty with Ethiopia gave that country the right to receive arms shipments across territory owned or controlled by the British Empire. Great Britain and France, two of the most powerful forces in the League of Nations, planned separately today their campaigns of procedure to be undertaken next week at Geneva in an effort to stave off the threatened war between Italy and Ethiopia. The respective cabinets studied the situation and both governments were reported as favoring a league solution of the problem. Meanwhile, in Italy, public interest in what relationship Japan has with Ethiopia, if any, ran high, although a Japanese foreign office spoke

NEW YORK. (?). John F. McNamara, reputed to be the first American to have sunk a German submarine in the World War, died suddenly from a heart attack at his Garden City home. He was 36. McNamara, who was a United States Navy aviator, was attached to the American naval base in England. He dropped a bomb on the submarine while on a scouting flight over the North Sea. He was awarded the Navy Cross.

Pennsylvania on Thursday reopens its long fight to regain the New England soft coal market from southern operators. This time the operators will be joined in the battle by the Public Service Commission and officials of several state departments. They have been asked to tell the Interstate Commerce Commission about conditions in southwestern counties once one of the nation's biggest coal producing regions. The Keystone State delegation will charge present freight rates are unfair and a hardship on the mine owner, the operator and the miner and his family. The rates, the Pennsylvanians will contend, have permitted the soft coal fields of the south to ship the millions of tons of coal formerly sent from this state to New England. The Public Service Commission will seek to show that only a reduction of the preferential rates now enjoyed by southern operators will remedy the Pennsylvania situ

SOUTHHAMPTON, L. I., July 25, (INS)—Col. Henry Huddleston Rogers, oil millionaire, died today at Southampton hospital where he underwent an operation yesterday. Hospital attendants had reported Rogers was “getting along very well” after his operation, the fourth of a series in an illness extending over several months. Prior to the operation, he was given a blood transfusion. He came here a little more than a month ago from Baltimore, where he underwent the third operation at Johns Hopkins Hospital.

(Copyright. 1935, Associated Press) LONDON, July 25.—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and leading members of his cabinet were represented today as favoring full league action, provided other powers agree, as a last resort to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia. The time limit for appointment of a fifth arbitrator to the ‘deadlocked conciliation commission expires tonight, apparently killing all hope of settling the crisis by direct negotiations. Some circles said that Anthony Eden therefore will go to Geneva for a League of Nations council session about July 31 empowered to announce that Great Britain is ready, if no other alternative can be found, to stand by all its obligations under the league covenant. Political circles said Eden, an ardent champion of Geneva as Minister for League of Nations affairs, has been given virtually a free hand to present Britain’s views at the momentous ses

1935-06-07.text: London — ()— Stanley Baldwin, twice prime minister of Great Britain, accepted that post again today from King George after Ramsay MacDonald, who has served as head of government for the last six years, resigned. MacDonald, then Baldwin, by royal summons, conferred with the king in turn at Buckingham Palace. The retiring prime minister, who is leaving his high post because of failing health, handed over his portfolio to the king in his majesty’s private apartment. Their audience lasted almost an hour. King Calls Baldwin MacDonald recommended to the king that Baldwin succeed him and Baldwin, as lord president of the council and leader of the majority party, was summoned as soon as MacDonald had left the royal presence. A group of only 10 women which watched MacDonald go forth from No. 160 Downing Street to make his resignation, swelled to a large crowd by the time Baldwin had started out a

London, June 7 (UP)—James Ramsay McDonald, the Scottish Pacifist of war-time days, who rode into power in 1925 as England's first labor prime minister and has guided the country during the stormy days since 1929, resigned today, entailing with his resignation that of the entire British cabinet. MacDonald will remain in the cabinet, it was expected, but more or less in an advisory capacity. Stanley Baldwin, stocky leader of the conservative party, will take over the reins of the national union government, comprising representatives of all parties except the straight labor, until the general election late next year. Few new faces are expected to appear in the next cabinet.

BOSTON, JUNE 7—(AP)—New England’s most ruthless gang of killers, the Millen-Faber machine gun trio, paid for four wanton killings early today in the electric chair at state prison. Murton Millen, 25, his brother, Irving, 21, and their college graduate pal, Abraham Faber, died within a space of 30 minutes, after midnight for their brief but bloody career of crime. They were sentenced for the machine gun slaying of Patrolman Forbes McLeon during a $14,500 robbery and hold up of the Needham Trust Company on Feb. 2, 1934. While they died, Murton’s 20-year-old bride, Norma, was sleeping in her cell in Dedham jail, where she has been confined since last September as an accessory. The widow, the pretty daughter of a former minister, may be freed immediately. She was ordered confined by Judge Nelson P. Brown, until such time as her husband’s career “no longer was a matter of public interest.” A

LONDON, June 6—(AP)—A new cabinet, with Stanley Baldwin at its helm, will take over the governing of Great Britain tomorrow—unless all predictions go astray. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald will call at Buckingham Palace to resign the office he has held continuously since 1929 and Baldwin, now lord president of the council and leader of the conservative party, will take his place. It will not be long, political quarters predicted tonight, until the veteran MacDonald, staunch champion of the cause of peace and erstwhile laborite, is out altogether. Another cabinet shake-up will take place immediately after the forthcoming general elections, in which the national government will go to the country with Baldwin its titular as well as its active leader, and the white-haired MacDonald will be forced to retire, these quarters said.

LONDON, June 7 (AP) — The Exchange Telegraph Company reported today that a severe earthquake had occurred at Srokushow in Taichu Province, Japan. The report, dated Tokyo, said that there were 1,700 casualties. The market building and the grammar school were reported to have been wrecked and 450 dwellings demolished or damaged.

LONDON, June 7.—(AP)—Members of the House of Commons cheered today when Clement Richard Attlee, deputy leader of the opposition, declared that if Italy intended to use force against Ethiopia "she ought to be told quite plainly that in that event she would not have the use of the Suez Canal." His declaration was made in a debate in which Capt. Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal, told the legislators that Italian newspaper allegations that Great Britain was encouraging Ethiopia to adopt a hostile attitude toward Italy were "mischievously absurd." "Nothing could better please the British government," said Captain Eden, "than a peaceful and lasting settlement of the dispute and the restoration of friendly relations between the two countries." Captain Eden said he regretted the "wild accusations" against Great Britain. He said assertions that Great Britain for years had some form of protectorate o

| By The Associated Press Weybridge, England, June 7.— Helen Wills Moody entered the final round of the St. Georges Hill tennis tourney today with an easy 6-1, 6-4 victory over Billy Yorke, of England.

LONDON, June 7 (UP)—Warning that attacks by Italian newspapers upon Great Britain over Abyssinia might affect relations was made in the House of Commons today by Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal and cabinet disarmament expert. Eden described as “mischievously absurd and fantastic” the “wild accusations lately directed against the British government in the Italian press.” The newspapers have accused Britain of coveting Abyssinia to complete its line of domination from Cairo to Cape Town. “It is unfortunate that such misrepresentations have been allowed to appear, particularly because of the effect they may have on the truly excellent relations between the two countries,” Eden added.

1935-07-12.text: LONDON, July 10 (INE) The British government, persisting in its efforts to head off hostilities between Italy and Ethiopia, sought today another solution to the crisis. Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, called Joseph A. C. Avenol, secretary general of the League of Nations, to a conference at which informed circles said some new way out of the impasse might be advanced. The gray-haired Avenol, on a mission to avert war in East Africa and to bolster the league, also arranged a second conference with Anthony Eden, England's secretary for League of Nations affairs. France Side Steps With France sidestepping the situation and the United States expressing “extreme misgivings,” it was generally believed any key to possible peace still lies in London. It became clear, however, after Sir Samuel's exposition of foreign policy to the House of Commons yesterday, that Great Britain will not act a

LONDON, July 12- (UP) —Britain tackles the job of keeping the peace in Africa with better heart tonight, convinced Sir Samuel Hoare's speech before the House of Commons yesterday ‘had eased tension in Rome and Paris. A slightly strained atmosphere in both capitals due to what the British said was misunderstanding of their past efforts had hampered the work of this nation’s diplomats. Today, however, the air of modified hopefulness was obvious in Whitehall as a result of the generous reception given the foreign secretary's moderate-toned address reviewing recent developments in British foreign relations and devoting especial attention to the Italo-Ethiopian situation. To Investigate Arrest ROME, July 12.—(AP)—The Italian government made ready tonight to investigate fully the circumstances of the arrest at Gondar, Ethiopia, of the wife of the Italian consul, Signora Raifacle di Lauro, and

LONDON, July 12 (UP)—The United States and British governments were understood today to have concluded arrangements for cooperation in evacuation of nationals from Abyssinia in event of war between Ethiopia and Italy. The London and Washington governments arranged to instruct their respective legations at Addis Ababa to cooperate in the task of getting Americans and Britons safely out of the country "in event of an emergency." ROME, July 12 (&).—The temporary arrest of the wife of the Italian consul at Gondar, Ethiopia, the arrest of some servants of the Italian military attache in Addis Ababa, and a number of more minor incidents were reported tonight in a communique issued by the Italian government.

Rome, July 12.—(4)—The temporary arrest of the wife of the Italian consul at Gondar, Ethiopia, the arrest of some servants of the Italian military attaché in Addis Ababa, and a number of minor incidents were reported tonight in a communication issued by the Italian government. - The official statement said that Ethiopian soldiers stopped the wife of the Italian consul as she was traveling outside of Gondar on her way to Eritrea, the Italian colony. It was declared she was ‘furnished with a regular Ethiopian pass but that she was not permitted to proceed on her journey for two days, until after protests had been presented by the consulate.

ROME, July 12—(UP)—Secretary of State Hull's concern over the Italian-Abyssinian crisis is unwelcome in Italy and is regarded as unjustified, authoritative sources made it plain today. It was said frankly that the dispute is not an American problem, and no effort was made to disguise the surprise felt at the news that Hull had expressed concern to Ambassador Augusto Rosso at the danger of war. On the contrary, the speech in the House of Commons of Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, was welcomed as indicating a change toward a realist policy which would bring British support of Italy's claim to overlordship in Abyssinia. There was no reference to the once famous pact of Paris, sponsored by the United States, under which nations including Italy and Abyssinia renounced war forever in favor of peaceful settlement of disputes.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) Paris—Police in a series of raids in working class quarters today seized a quantity of army rifles from second hand dealers apparently in precaution against riots Sunday when left wing and fascist groups plan rival demonstrations. Twenty thousand police, mobile guards and republican guard were being reinforced by heavy contingents of provincial constabulary for Sunday's demonstrations and all soldiers of the Paris district who have not been detailed to parade will be kept in barracks ready for an emergency. The occasion for the demonstrations is the national holiday, Bastille day.

(by Associated Press) GRASSE, France, July 12—Ha Du Berrier, former American commercial air pilot, announced today he had recruited 12 American fliers to fight for Ethiopia. Duberrier said Maj. Granville Pollock, the famous veteran of the old Lafayette Escadrille, was aiding him to raise a force to form a nucleus for an Ethiopian air corps. He refused to divulge the names of the other pilots.

PARIS, July 18 (AP)—Alfred Dreyfus, chief figure of one of the most sensational and momentous trials in all French history, died yesterday. He was 75 years old. The Dreyfus case, originating in 1894, shook France to its foundations, well-nigh wrecked the republic, did unmeasured harm to the French army and turned the questioning eyes of the world upon French justice. A young Jewish officer in the French army, Dreyfus, who served on the general staff with the rank of captain, was convicted of betraying French military secrets to Germany. He was sentenced to Devil's Island for life, publicly drummed out of the army, and disgraced. Four years after his arrival at the notorious penal colony off the coast of French Guiana, Dreyfus was returned and again tried by court martial. To the astonishment of an entire world he again was convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison. The president of F

1935-06-06.text: London, England, June 6.—(U.P.) —Viscount Byng of Vimy, former governor-general of Canada whose name was associated with some of the most brilliant exploits of the World War, died today at his home in Essex. He was 72, and for 48 of his years he served the nation as soldier, statesman and administrative executive. He returned to England at the end of February after vainly seeking restored health at Pasadena, Calif. He suffered a heart attack there and returned to England. He went to his country home, Thorpe Hall, at Thorpe-Le-Soken, and became ill Monday night. An emergency operation was performed Tuesday night for an internal disorder and he died early today. Nearly all Englishmen knew of and admired him, but particularly World War veterans to whom the name Byng of Vimy meant much more than those of most commanders. He was a son of the 2nd Earl of Strafford, descendant of soldiers and o

Hollywood, Cal, June 6.—The United States finally got an even break with all Europe today; Americans won $2,745,000 and all the rest of the world combined only $2,966,000 on the big Irish sweepstakes, a lottery on the English Derby. They're going to try to retain the best features of the NRA by persuasion, hours and wages. You got to admit Roosevelt is trying to get a semblance of fairness. But they wouldn't even do it by law, so this scheme seems doubtful. Yours, o ae :

London, June 5. (P)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald presided today over what the politically informed believe will be his last cabinet session as head of the government. The Scottish statesman, who became prime minister for the second time six years ago and has since held the office without interruption, is expected to visit Buckingham Palace Friday to offer his resignation to the king. It is believed King George will then summon Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council, and request him to take over the reins of government. Baldwin, who has been prime minister twice before, is said to have been quietly preparing for his return to Downing Street and is believed ready to announce the composition of a new ministry Friday night... MacDonald’s withdrawal probably will be based on the eye trouble from which he has been suffering.

Rome, Italy, June 6. (7P)—The daily newspaper “Ottobre” appeared this afternoon with an article saying England could have war with Italy if she wanted it. All copies of the publication were quickly seized by authorities. Rome, June 6. (4)—The Giornale d'Italia in a three-column front page editorial today said England wishes to gain possession of Ethiopia and for this reason is opposing Italian penetration of that country. Similar accusations have appeared in other newspapers. Messaggero accused Britain of arranging a subsidy with Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia in order to give his troops regular pay. Despite British denials to the contrary, the authoritative newspaper reaffirms a previous statement that England is concentrating troops along the Sudan frontier.

ROME, June 5—(m—The newspaper, Messaggero, today published a front page accusation that England has arranged a subsidy with Emperor Haile Selassie to give the Ethiopian troops regular pay. The accusation was a highlight of a series of violent anti-British articles published by the entire Italian press:

LONDON, June 6 (CINS) - Field Marshal Viscount Byng, famed commander of the Canadian corps at Vimy Ridge in 1917, died at his home in Essex county today following an operation. A former governor-general of Canada, the 73-year-old warrior attracted wide attention early this year when he and Lady Byng, visiting Hollywood, accepted one of Mae West's famous invitations. They had tea with Miss West, and Lord Byng found her a "fine woman and typical American." Son of the second earl of Strafford, Lord Byng was surrounded by military traditions, and won the rank of major in the Soudan expedition of 1884. As colonel, he fought in the South African war and later in Egypt. World War Hero At the outbreak of the world war, Byng was in command of the third cavalry of the British expeditionary force, which saw heavy action in the first part of the conflict. The following year he commanded the third ar

London, June 5 (AP)—Reaching one of his rapid-fire decisions, Sir Malcolm Campbell announced today he would take his mighty Bluebird to Utah within a few months in an attempt to boost the world land speed record to 300 miles an hour. The famed British sportsman, who set the present automobile record at 276.816 miles an hour at Daytona Beach, Fla. last March, will try for a new mark on the dry bed of the Great Salt Lake near Salduro. Apparently happy to get the vexing problem off his mind and get started on a new adventure, the veteran dare-devil first declared he would be ready to shoot by July but later amended that to “or maybe August or September.”

1935-08-13.text: London, Aug. 72. Lord Robert Cecil said today the British government faces a tragic sequel to 1914 through its failure to make clear to Italy that England is not bluffing and is prepared to uphold its obligations under the League of Nations covenant "even if it means war." "Only plain speaking can save us from a repetition of the fateful blunders of 20 years ago!" the former under secretary for foreign affairs said in an interview on the Italo-Ethiopian crisis. Earlier in the day he expressed his attitude at a special meeting of the executive committees of the League of Nations union, Points To Danger The committee adopted a resolution pointing out the danger of any British uncertainty and insisting that collective action by the league members is "indispensable" if war is to be prevented between Italy and Ethiopia, The resolution also urged that the British government communicate to memb

Aug. 13—(UP)—Premier Pierre Laval today awaited a secret note from Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia which may provide a basis for French-British-Italian negotiations opening Thursday. In anticipation of the negotiations, Laval asked Dr. Tecla Hailé, chief delegate to the League of Nations, to find out how far Haile Selassie was willing to do toward meeting Italian demands on his country. The emperor's reply is expected before the allied negotiations start, offering what is believed to be the last hope for peace. (Continued on Page Five)

ADDIS ABABA—Women take over jobs of men recruited to army.

Kinsale, Ireland, Aug. 12.—(P)—Her supplies replenished after a month’s fruitless effort to locate the sunken Lusitania, the salvage ship Orphir sailed tonight for further attempts with high hopes of success. The Orphir has been systematically surveying the ocean floor. The searchers believed they had come within a quarter of a mile of the hulk of the Lusitania, but this theory was scouted by the crew and divers of the salvage steamer Arpione, which has been working here for 18 months. The Orphir already has located four large hulks, none of them the Lusitania.

Copenhagen.—(AP)— Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz-Reventlow and her husband escaped injury today in an automobile accident. Their car collided with another with slight damages as they drove from Hardenberg toward the ferry on their way to Paris. (Prince Alexis Mdivani, former husband of the countess who is heiress to the Woolworth millions, was killed August 1 in an automobile accident in Spain).

BERLIN, Aug. 13 (?)—The storm troopers, after a year’s eclipse, are being reorganized as a quality unit of Nazi defense against the “state enemies” of Semitism and “political Catholicism.” The fate of the Reich's Steel Helmet veterans meanwhile became increasingly uncertain. That something is going to happen to the Steel Helmets, whose leader is Franz Seldte, minister of Labor, was indicated by publication of the bare announcement that Reichsführer Hitler had discussed their future with Seldte. “The ion was regarded as significant in that the helmets are now held as “reactionaries.” The former Sturm Abteilung, new standard-bearers of the Hitler policy, led by Ernst Röhm, is leading the troops who are rebuilding the organization, eliminating all but “ideal” members for Der Führer.
