International affairs are now so interrelated an apparently trivial incident may have immense unexpected consequences. The elements constituting the present menace to world peace as a result of the dispute between Italy and Ethiopia may be summarized as follows: 1. The covenant of the league

(Copyright, 1935, By Associated Press) TILFORD, Surrey, England. — Philip Snowden, former chancellor of the exchequer, broke a lifetime rule Wednesday night and gave an interview in which he said Europe is on the brink of a new world war “too terrible to contemplate.” Asks U.S. Aid Viscount Snowden appealed to America to bring its influence to bear to help prevent a catastrophic clash of nations. “Mussolini has, for all practical purposes, already declared war,” the former government leader declared. “He has been massing his troops on the borders of Ethiopia for months and is only waiting for suitable conditions to launch an attack. “His aim and ambition will not stop short with the conquest of Ethiopia. If successful in this enterprise his next move will be to absorb Austria. That attempt will bring Germany into war and as European nations are now bound together with innumerable allianc

Los Angeles —(4)— Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith will retire from active flying——after he makes one final gesture, a flight from England to Australia. “I’ve reached that age,” said Sir Charles, conqueror of oceans and continents in airplanes today, “where 7,000 flying hours in 19 years beckon me to take my place in the development work in the interest of mail and passenger air service. “It has been my ambition for some time to enter commercial aviation. I may make other long flights, but I will not be out to make fast time or break records. I am done with all that. “I think my flights from England to Australia were the hardest, that is physically. They were more tiring. Those between Australia and the United States required more skill and possibly were the most dangerous.” The flier said he would devote his energy to perfecting a new Zealand-Australian air service.

Londen, Aug. 14,—AP--David Lloyd George charged today that Great Britain, France and Italy have “completely destroyed” the power of the league of nations and are preparing “to deliver Ethiopia to Italy. In an address to the National Trade Union Club on the current disarmament conference in Paris the former prime minister asked: “What are they discussing? Are they discussing how they are to prevent Mussolini from destroying the independence of a friendly power, which is a member of the league? “That is not it at all, they are just discussing what measure of economic, strategic and political control can be given to Italy without war, how they can deliver Ethiopia on the cheap to Italy—that is the question being discussed.” “Ethiopia,” he continued, “the very country whose integrity and independence was challenged, has been ruled out from the conference that is discussing its very existence

1935-05-04.text: LONDON, May 4 (#)—Carnival reigned king in London tonight as another king—George V—stood on the threshold of the silver jubilee of his sovereignty. Despite touches of rain, the largest throng since the Armistice Day celebration jammed the streets, turning traffic into seething, milling, laughing confusion. More rain was threatened by gray skies, but the enthusiasm of the celebrants, many of them come from Britain's far-flung domains, was undampened. The weatherman has forecast mostly bright, springlike weather for the king’s solemn procession to St. Paul’s Cathedral Monday morning. There may, however, be local showers. With the spirit of holiday already holding sway among his subjects, the king worked as usual today, holding, however, a special jubilee meeting of the privy council, at which he signed a proclamation calling for the issuance of three special jubilee coins. Nearly all work

London.—(AP) -- Jubilee visitors stormed London today and captured the city’s streets with a barrage of merriment unparalleled since the signing of the armistice. "The old metropolis, beflagged to celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of King George's accession to the throne Monday, was a cross between a Latin-American festival and a North American harvest festival." Visitors from all parts of the globe—300,000 were estimated to be here already—choked the city. Hordes more were expected before Monday’s great celebration. Traffic conditions were a nightmare for the police. Taxicabs did well to travel three miles an hour in the jammed streets. Pedestrians trod on each other's heels. The visitors made most of the noise. Londoners, for the most part, meandered agape at the transformation of the city into a far-reaching bower of color. Weather conditions were uncertain, with unsettled skies

(Copyright, 1935, by The Associated Press) London, May 3.—A high British source said tonight Britain must spend $116,000,000 for 600 fighting planes if she is to fulfill the government’s pledge to maintain air equality with Germany. That authoritative estimate was put forward shortly after receipt of authentic information from Berlin that Germany now has facilities for building 100 planes monthly for replacements, and may soon speed the pace to 200 planes each month.

the arma situation in brief LONDON — Informed quarters say Britain must spend £2414,008 (€118,000,000) to match Germany in air BERLIN—German press sees new hope for peace after British commons debate PARIS—Text of France Russian mutual assistance pact made public: France to help Russia build roads and railways in west WARSAW — Poland trades woman spy, two others, to Germany for Baron George Sosnowski, Pole

BERLIN, July 5.—(#)—Eight persons were killed and four injured today when an airplane plunged through the roof of a house at Britz, a Berlin suburb near Tempelhof airdrome. Six, including the airplane pilot and five mechanics, died outright in the crash. The other two, residents of the house, were trapped in the resulting fire and were fatally burned. Four other persons were taken to a hospital.

Istanbul, May 3 ()—A fresh series of earthquakes sent inhabitants of the Kars district on the Tureo-Russian frontier fleeing in terror today and brought the dead in the two-day disturbances to 599. More than 1,300 homes were reported laid waste and 1,200 persons injured. For the second night the populace planned to sleep in the open, fearing further tremors. Five earthquakes rocked the region today and although not as intense as the first shock yesterday, widespread damage was feared. While relief was speeded to the stricken zone, the wreckage of homes in more than a dozen towns was searched for further victims.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, May 4.—(P)—Two more violent earth shocks spread further destruction in Turkey's quake-torn area today where the killed and injured now are estimated at 2,006, with 1,600 houses destroyed. Seven strong shocks have been felt in the last few days besides numerous minor ones. Twenty-five villages were destroyed. Red water was rushing through yawning crevices 36 feet wide in some places.

| ISTANBUL, 414" -- Mount Ararat, | traditional resting place of Noah's Ark, was reported Saturday to be | showing volcanic activity following violent earthquakes which did widespread damage in Turkey, _ Fresh anxiety spread to the quake area upon receipt of volcanic reports. Three days of quakes and tremors brought the estimated killed and injured to 2,000 with 1,400 houses destroyed. The activity on Ararat was said to have begun since the first major shock in the Kara region near the Turco-Russian border. The mountain, which towers to a height of 17,000 feet, is perpetually covered by snow.

1935-02-20.text: LONDON, Feb. 19.—(AP)— Richard Bennett, the actor, is in a serious condition in a London nursing home, it was learned today, as a result of having recently been thrown from his horse.

Berlin, Feb. 20.—(AP)—The ominous shadow of the executioner's ax fell today upon two more convicted spies held in Ploetzense prison. The two, who may follow the same path to the block taken by Benita Von Falkenhayn and Renate Von Natamer, are men. One, it was learned, is a former naval technician, but the identities of both were concealed by official secrecy. The condemned pair are close to those in which the two noblewomen spent their last hours. They had no knowledge of their fate other than the grim tradition that no prisoner emerges from Ploetzense's walls alive and free. Several days may elapse before the official executioner is notified to sharpen his medieval battle-ax and don his formal garb again. Meanwhile, the prisoners may cling to the hope that Reichsführer Hitler will intervene to modify their death sentences. Unlike the two women spies, the men were tried several weeks ago

(Copyright by The Associated Press) Berlin, Feb. 20—(Wednesday)— Two men, one unidentified and the other a former naval technician, caught in the ever-tightening Reichswehr espionage net, are marked to follow the two women spies who lost their heads Monday on the block at Ploetzense prison, it was learned early today. Now knowing definitely the fate awaiting them, the two men were spending their last hours before decapitation in cells near those occupied by Benita Von Falkenheyn and Renate von Natzmer, who died silently and without a show of emotion. Their only inkling of what is to happen to them comes from the knowledge that nobody leaves a death cell in grim old Ploetzense prison alive and free. The identity of the second man could not be learned. Their names were expected to be announced later.

(By The Associated Press) Naples, Feb. 20—Approximately 1,000 regular officers and soldiers sailed aboard the S. S. Montenegro for Italy’s east African colony today at the moment when Italian newspapers were expressing fears of further incident on the Ethiopian frontier.
SHANGHAI Feb. 18 (4).— Chinese press reports from Foochow today said the Chinese SS. Fulung had sunk off Wuhuko with a loss of more than 100 lives.

DUNEDIN, N. Z., Feb. 19.—vA— Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd thought a clash of temperaments would arise if he had a companion to his lonely vigil in the Little America advance camp, he said here today. The explorer declared a belief that two persons constitute neither company nor a crowd during the long, cold, dark days and nights, but he decided to go alone rather than risk a temperamental clash after plans for two others to accompany him failed. Capt. A. Innes Taylor, in charge of the dog teams and sledges, revealed that two others had planned to join Byrd in last winter's adventure. He said landing operations on the barrier were so delayed that no time was available to stock the post with sufficient food for more than two men. Decided to Go Alone Byrd then considered the situation and decided it was psychologically impossible for only two men to live through the period of unbroken darkn

An eye witness to the execution of Benita von Falkenhayn and Renate van Natzmer, who were put to death before dawn yesterday in the bright glare of Goodlights illuminating grim old Ploetzenses prison’s courtyard, told the Associated Press today: . “What impressed us most of the two women’s behavior during their last minutes of life was that neither one of them murmured a single word.” Bodies Erect, Heads Held High Both went to their death with outward calm and bravery, he said, their bodies erect, their heads held high. The execution of the two, charged with betraying Germany's military secrets, took only six minutes, the informant said. “Frau von Falkenhayn was the first,” he related, “When she was led into the lights x x x she walked first to the improvised

PARIS, Feb. 20 (U.P)—Seconds for Bertrand De Jouvenel, French journalist, and Julien Duvivier, movie director, conferred today in a formal effort to avert a duel between the two. Both principals have refused to apologize, however, and it appeared likely they would meet with swords, probably at dawn Friday.

1935-10-22.text: The British government, a leader in League of Nations sanctions against Italy for its aggression in Ethiopia, left the way open today for an end to hostilities in East Africa. Opening debate in parliament on the Afro-European crisis, Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare declared Britain never had turned its back on a peaceful solution. “There is still breathing space before the economic pressure can be applied,” he said. “Can it not be used for another attempt at such a settlement?” As if in a direct plea to Mussolini not to press further in Ethiopia, the foreign secretary continued: “Italy is still a member of the League. “I welcome this fact. Cannot this eleventh hour be used to make it unnecessary to proceed farther along the unattractive road of economic action against a fellow member, an old friend, a former ally?” Sanctions imposed by the League would virtually isolate Italy economic

LONDON, Oct. 21.—(4)—Eight ships searched today for 37 men feared lost after abandoning a foundering freighter in a raging storm which killed 13 and injured scores in the British Isles. The crew of the 6,735-ton freighter Vardulia took to their lifeboats in tempestuous seas 400 miles west of the Hebrides after sending SOS calls Saturday.

By A.S. MANNING, Associated Press Developments today in the Italo-Ethiopian imbroglio seem to have lessened the possibilities of a European war growing out of the conflict. Italy and Britain, who have been viewing each other dourly through the sights of big naval guns, were said to have reached a friendlier understanding through diplomatic discussions. At the same time it was widely but unofficially reported that Mussolini was ready to talk peace. Italian suggestions for peace terms were said to have been placed in the hands of Premier Laval of France who has been laboring untiringly to bring about a cessation of hostilities. From Italian sources, too, came the report that Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia was ready to make terms. The Conquering Lion of Judah, however, was silent on this point. Recently he declared that there could be no peace while Italian soldiers remained on Ethiopia

(Copyright 1935, United Press) Rome, Oct. 22.—Trustworthy quarters expressed belief today that Premier Benito Mussolini soon would be ready to open negotiations for settlement of the entire Italian-Ethiopian dispute. Mussolini was said to be willing to settle the dispute on condition that Britain withdraw its Mediterranean fleet, the League of Nations postpone action of penalties and Italy be permitted to 'consolidate' territory already conquered. It seemed obvious that the conditions would not be acceptable to Great Britain, the League of Nations or to Ethiopia. But after negotiations, it is indicated that even such a feeler was put out here. It is felt that the first necessity is to make sure that tension in the Mediterranean really is eased as the result of last week's Italian-French-British negotiations. Italians seemed looking toward Paris for a lead. The army, whose activities must

KINGSTOWN, St. Vincent, B. W. I, Oct. 22 (AP).—Rioting broke out again on this West Indian island today while armed marines from a British warship enforced martial law after three rioters were fatally wounded during the night. The disorders, the outgrowth of labor troubles which had gone on for months and were increased by tension due to the Italo-Ethiopian war, reached a head in a series of battles with police last night, in which three of the rioters received fatal wounds. Eight of their companions, including two women, were wounded; and six police had been injured in the wild, club-swinging fights that raged through Kingstown yesterday after a mass demonstration of laborers before Governor Sir Selwyn Grier. The governor's car was smashed, as were those of a supreme court judge and of the island’s attorney general, and homes and stores were looted and wrecked before police guns subdued

| LONDON (UP) Great Britain hopes to localize and halt the war between Italy and Ethiopia without applying military sanctions, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, told a crowded house of commons Tuesday in opening a three-day debate on foreign policy. | Sir Samuel declared Britain does not intend to act alone and military sanctions are not practicable because there has been no collective agreement at Geneva to apply them generally. He indicated Britain will rely on economic pressure which is intended to limit and shorten the war. | Solemn Atmosphere Sir Samuel spoke in the most solemn and tense atmosphere that the house of commons has seen in years, The debate is expected to provide a basis for calculation of possibilities for the future—rearmament, Germany's role in any realignment of British policy and the fate of the Locarno treaty. A feeling that peace might be at hand was dampened, however, by the disclosure by high sources that Britain is not talking peace with Italy, that Britain does not anticipate any actual developments for many weeks and that she has not ruled out the possibility of application of military sanctions against Italy. DORKING, England, Oct. 21, UP —Laura La Plante, American film actress, narrowly escaped death today in a fire which badly damaged her home, a house formerly occupied by James J. Walker, one-time mayor of New York. Miss La Plante, wife of Irving Asher, film director, was ill in bed when the fire started. Her physician carried her to the neighboring house a short time before the roof fell in.

1935-09-23.text: LONDON, Sept. 23—(4)—Speculation as to whether further important military moves in the Mediterranean were contemplated was aroused today by the action of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in summoning the members of the imperial defense council to his office in advance of tomorrow’s cabinet session. It was immediately recalled by observers that the doubling of the British fleet strength in the Mediterranean began shortly after the cabinet meeting and defense council consultations one month ago. Authoritative sources said that Great Britain was not withdrawing any of the extensive naval and military reinforcements recently sent into the Mediterranean. This assertion came despite the view expressed in official quarters that the Anglo-Italian situation had been eased by the conversation held last Friday between Sir Eric Drummond, the British ambassador to Rome, and Fulvio Suvich, the Italian u

LONDON, Sept. 23. (U.P.) — Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin today summoned an important cabinet meeting for tomorrow morning to consider the Ethiopian crisis. Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary; J. Ramsay MacDonald, Neville Chamberlain and Sir John Simon conferred jointly on the situation today at No. 10 Downing Street.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) LONDON, Sept. 23.—An official communique on the reason for British fleet concentration in the Mediterranean disclosed today the real gravity of Italian-British relations. Intended as an assurance to Italy, the communique said the concentration, and military and naval measures generally, were not intended as a “maneuver” or anything like that but “as a natural consequence of the impression created by the violence of the campaign against the United Kingdom which has been conducted by the Italian press during the last few weeks.” The Italian press is closely controlled by Benito Mussolini, hence the significance of the statement.

Addis Ababa, Sept. 22 (4)—Emperor Haile Selassie took heart today as he studied week-end telegrams offering hope that war might be averted. The conciliatory tone of the Italian rejection of the League of Nations’ peace proposals and the British naval display in the Mediterranean encouraged him as he read reports of important conversations of ambassadors at Washington, London, Paris and Rome. The Emperor's advisers contrasted the moderate tone of Premier Mussolini's League reply with the bluntness of former communications refusing all compromise offers.

By International News Service ROME, Sept. 23.—In an atmosphere officially described as “calm” and reported to be due to personal intervention of King George of Great Britain and King Victor Emanuel of Italy, a government spokesman today declared Italy awaited new peace proposals from the League of Nations for settlement of the Ethiopian quarrel. “The doors are still open,” the spokesman said. “We are awaiting fresh proposals from the League which may form a minimum basis for discussion which the last proposals did not provide.” The proposals referred to were those of the committee of five rejected flatly by the Italian cabinet Saturday.

LONDON, Sept. 22—(4)—The British government officially placed full responsibility for its rapidly-increasing naval and military concentrations in the Mediterranean Sea squarely upon the controlled Italian press tonight. The foreign office, shortly after Prime Minister Baldwin had cut short his weekend at Chequers to return to Downing Street, issued a communique stating the unprecedented massing of warships from Haifa to Gibraltar and the increasing land and aerial defenses at such points as Malta and Gibraltar was caused by “the violence of the campaign against the United Kingdom” in Italy. As all members of the British cabinet gathered in London for their first full meeting since August 27, official assurances were received from Rome that Premier Mussolini has not yet slammed the door on further attempts at conciliation of his dispute with Ethiopia. The critical full dress session of th

| By International News Service. DUBLIN, Sept. 23.—With or without big plane—damaged in landing after a 22-hour flight from New York, during which he came at least once perilously close to death—Felix Waitkus, former United States Army pilot, planned today to continue to Kovac (Kaunas), Lithuania, as soon as possible. His machine, which he flew bad through rain and fog most of the way, rested on a hillside near Ballinrobe, County Mayo, one wing smashed, the propeller buckled, and the undercarriage torn away. It will be brought to Dublin airport, but may prove beyond repairing. A lowering gasoline supply forced Waitkus to end his projected non-stop flight to Lithuania, he said, revealing that once during the trip a frozen carburetor forced him steadily down toward the uncharted water, but that he was able to melt the ice in time.

GENEVA, Sept. 23—Great Britain side-stepped France's proposal for an international conference on monetary stabilization at a meeting of the economic commission of the League assembly today. Dr. E. L. Burgin of Britain welcomed France's offer to reduce customs barriers but said nothing about stabilization.

1935-08-09.text: LONDON, Aug. 9— Great Britain has almost abandoned hope of a peaceful settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian dispute and is preparing to safeguard its interests in northeastern Africa in the event of war, it was reported today. The cabinet was reported to be preparing to strengthen police and military patrols on the frontiers of Somaliland and Kenya colony and send a formidable body of troops—probably Sikhs from India—to the Sudan. August 16—a week from today—was fixed for the French-British-Italian conference, which is regarded as the last real hope for peace. If this conference fails—possibly even before—Great Britain may lift its provisional embargo on arms for Ethiopia. French opinion, like British, is almost despairing. But Britain intends to do all it can to preserve peace. So grave is its view of the possibilities of an Italian-Ethiopian war that the cabinet is reported on reliable a

WASHINGTON, Aug. 5.—America will have an observer and unofficial envoy in Europe during the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, it was revealed today. Senator James P. Pope, Democrat, Idaho, member of the Senate's foreign relations committee, sails next week for London, Paris, Geneva and Rome. Pope has scheduled important interviews with Premier Mussolini and Premier Laval, as well as with other European statesmen concerned with the threatened hostilities. Confirmation Lacking While official confirmation is lacking, it was understood Pope will represent the views of the United States in these conversations. He has discussed the situation with Secretary of State Cordell Hull and plans a conference this week with President Roosevelt. Pope's rise to eminence in the field of America’s foreign affairs has an added interest because of the long dominant role which his colleague, the senior senator from Ida

London, August 9. (INS).—Falling from a yacht mast to the deck, Greta Garbo, film star, suffered a painfully sprained ankle to-day, Reuter’s reported from Stockholm. She was a member of a yachting party off Baggenfjaerden, one of the numerous islands near Stockholm.

LONDON (4) — Published reports purporting to disclose that the United States is taking an active interest in the Italo-Ethiopian controversy preceded Anthony Eden’s return to London today to make final preparations for tri-power conversations, British press reports said James W. Gerard, former United States ambassador to Germany, was hastening to Rome at the request of the American government to talk over the situation with Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy. Ignoring the fact that Gerard retired from the American diplomatic service 18 years ago and presenting no positive authority for their statements, the newspapers pictured Gerard as an unofficial observer and possible mediator. Gerard was recently in London and has been vacationing on the French Riviera. (State department officials at Washington said they were not acquainted with any order sending Gerard to Rome as an official America

London, Aug. 9.—(Friday)—(@)— London morning newspapers published dispatches today asserting James W. Gerard, former United States ambassador to Germany, has gone to Rome at the instance of the American government to discuss the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Gerard left Antibes, France, for Rome yesterday and was reported to have an audience with Premier Mussolini scheduled for today.

PARIS, Aug. 9—(AP)—With troops ready but out of sight, the French government today ordered police forces to clean up agitation centers. Premier Pierre Laval ordered the Prefects of all France’s 86 departments to confer with him immediately. It was the first such conference in the history of the French Republic. A somewhat easier attitude prevailed as the laborers in the government arsenals at Toulon and Brest went back to work and the French line employees at Le Havre voted to end their strife. The object of the Prefects’ conference was understood to be the development of a more favorable attitude on the part of government employees toward the pay cuts which the government deems necessary for reasons of economy.

ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 9—(AP)—Daba Birrou, former foreign office official, left for Japan today accompanied by an unidentified Japanese on a secret mission. It was reported without confirmation that the mission had to do with the purchase of arms and ammunition from the Japanese. A reliable source said Birrou would establish the first Ethiopian consulate in Japan, probably at Tokyo. In connection with the arms and ammunition report, it was said Ethiopia would attempt to obtain credit for at least 56 percent of the value of the order.

Associated Press Foreign Staff ROME, Aug. 9.—Italy, shocked by the destruction of one of its most modern airplanes and the death of Public Works Minister Luigi Razza, applied itself with undiminished zeal today toward perfection of its military power. The disaster to the tri-motored craft which crashed on an Egyptian desert Wednesday night while on an inspection flight to Eritrea, killing seven persons, was viewed with particular concern since the plane was of the type designated for ‘East African service.

1935-11-08.text: By The Associated Press Singapore, Straits Settlements, Nov. 8—Darkness fell over the Malacca Strait tonight without any further word from Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, missing on a flight from England to Australia. The noted Australian pilot and his co-pilot were last sighted over the Bay of Bengal. Royal Air Corps pilots will start a search tomorrow.

(Copyright, 1935, United Press). SINGAPORE, Straits Settlement, Nov. 8 (U.P)—Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, Australian aviator, was many hours overdue on a flight from Allahabad, India, today and it was feared he was lost in the shark-infested Bay of Bengal. On his last long flight, from England to Australia, the conqueror of oceans was seen by a fellow aviator fighting a fierce storm over the bay, 150 miles from shore, flames shooting from the exhaust of his plane, the Lady Southern Cross. Kingsford-Smith and his co-

LONDON, Nov. 8 (#)—The foreign office announced today that the United States had formally accepted an invitation to attend the international naval conference Dec. 5. Italy is the only one of the five big powers concerned which has not replied. The British government has received acceptances from France and Japan also.

London, Nov. 7 A campaign to establish “the right of persons suffering from incurable disease to die” was announced today after an English doctor was reported to have admitted five “mercy slayings.” A “kindly-faced elderly family doctor,” said the Daily Mail, told of the slayings in a “confession.” “I've taken life on five different occasions. My conscience never pricked me. I still carry with me memories of those cases and the happy faces before they died.” Lord Moynihan, one of Britain's most distinguished surgeons, disclosed a campaign to give incurables “the right to die.” “This is a serious proposition,” said the peer, who has been an advocate of the formation of a “voluntary euthanasia legalization society.” Lord Moynihan announced the group to which he and other influential members of the medical profession and clergymen belong has called a meeting December 10 at headquarters of t

The Italians made two important conquests in Ethiopia today, capturing Gorrahei on the southern front and Makale on the north. In still another military movement they drove "deep" into the region leading to Lake Tana, in which Great Britain is interested because it feeds the river Nile. Mussolini has often disavowed having any ambitions toward Lake Tana. The advance of his troops in that area, however, may indicate a change in his views and a determination to make his conquest of Ethiopia complete. In capturing Gorrahei, a strategic center, the southern Italian army has removed another stone from its path toward Harar, the walled city of Ethiopia. Traitor Is Rewarded. Makale, like Aduwa, Aksum and Adigrat before it, fell without resistance. Swaggering in the van of the invading troops was Ras Haile Selassie Gugsa, the Benedict Arnold of Ethiopia. He went straight to the castle of former

MAKALE, Ethiopia, Nov. 8—Runners from the Italian army corps of Gen. Pietro Maravigna reported today he had sent “raking squadrons” deep into the regions leading to Lake Tana, headwaters of the Nile, in which Great Britain is vitally interested. Lake Tana is 160 miles southwest of Makale, which the Italian army took today. The runners said the squadrons had entered the Adiabo territory, dispersing groups of the warriors of the Ethiopian commander, Ras Seymoun. They brought word that one of Gen. Maravigna's light infantry columns, backed by mountain artillery, had left the Italian line along the Setit River, where they had been facing the Ethiopian Ras Burro's troops. One column of light infantry operating near Makale was reported late in the afternoon to have occupied Donghea Pass, which commands the approach to Selicot. The latter town is fifteen miles from Makale along the 40-mile rout

Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, Nov. 7.—(AP)—A belief that the United States and Great Britain would agree to continue their naval parity, no matter what happens at the forthcoming apparently ill-fated naval conference, was expressed today by authoritative quarters. Indications that the two powers already may be in general accord for continued equality, as the result of preliminary talks held in recent months, came from these sources. Pessimism prevailed, however, that any other very substantial agreements would result from the conference of naval powers, already postponed from Dec. 2 to Dec. 5—an attitude attributed to the somber international situation. A spokesman for informed naval quarters pointed out that parity would not necessarily mean the United States and Britain would build ship for ship and keep their navies in exact counter-balance. Rather, this source said, under co

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) LONDON, Nov. 8 (U.P) — Great Britain and Italy have reached a naval agreement which vitally affects naval construction and disarmament plans, the United Press was informed today. As a result of Anglo-Italian naval parleys, Britain, according to authoritative information, has abandoned its opposition to Italian construction of two 35,000-ton battleships. The move was regarded by naval experts as ending for all practical purposes the long British campaign in favor of reducing tonnage but not the gun-calibers of capital ships. The naval talks were held preparatory to the December conference, instead of December 5 at the request of the United States. The British experts, however, intimated their hope that Italy will refrain from further construction of battleships exceeding 25,000 tons.

1935-06-22.text: WASHINGTON, June 22.—()— Police tonight dug into mysterious circumstances surrounding a five-story plunge which left Mrs. Lucille English, 28, wife of an officer of the Byrd Antarctic expedition, near death in a Washington hospital. They questioned Harold Payne Starr, former NRA attorney, regarding his story that he had been called to the English apartment a short while before by Mrs. English, who asked for information on the divorce laws of the District of Columbia. They also were curious about four .38 caliber pistol cartridges found in his pocket. In the apartment, police reported they found evidences of a scuffle, an empty whisky bottle and one partly filled. At the same time, an employee of the Italian embassy, Clifford W. Brown, said he saw Mrs. English crawl out from the window sill onto a ledge as though trying to reach the next window, when she lost her grip and fell. Says He Sa

PARIS, June 22. “—Premier Pierre Laval and Capt. Anthony Eden, Britain’s traveling negotiator, appeared today virtually to have healed the Anglo-French breach over the British separate naval accord with Germany. Today's final talk between the two brought what Laval said was an agreement ‘to recognize that France and England should remain faithful to their common duty of working together in the closest manner for the achievement of the peace of Europe through increasing collective security.” After reaching what seemed to be a deadlock earlier in the day on the question of mutual assistance by air, Captain Eden telephoned London and it was his telephone talk which apparently brought the sudden agreement after the well-defined breach.

LONDON, June 22. (4.—The Sunday Dispatch said today former Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald would leave England shortly “on an important mission” to the United States. “It has been definitely decided to send MacDonald to America,” the newspaper said, adding: “He will discuss with President Roosevelt war debts, navies and currency stabilization.”

PARIS, June 21.—Premier Pierre Laval flatly told Captain Anthony Eden, of Great Britain, today that France was dissatisfied with the Anglo-German navy agreement and their conversation was interrupted in the middle of the afternoon. The premier avoided anything approaching an open breach, but reported the French note and renewed his reservations regarding the accord by which Great Britain granted Germany a fleet 35 per cent as large as her own. Dissatisfaction Voiced Having expressed his strong dissatisfaction to Eden, Laval raised a question on the conclusion of a general armaments pact, saying France is ready to proceed toward a general peace agreement. He was understood, however, to have insisted that France must have England's support for a higher naval ratio than at present in the face of Germany's 400,000 tons. He did not say whether he had declared France's intention to build a nav

DUBLIN—(AP)—Irish Free State and British statesmen are preparing for a formal reconciliation; high government quarters indicated today. President DeValera, whose recently friendly speeches regarding relations with England started the ball rolling, expects to be called to London soon to discuss commercial.

LONDON (pP)— Still unmarried, and apparently quite contented as a bachelor, the Prince of Wales celebrated his 41st birthday Sunday. As a special staff sorted hundreds of cablegrams, telegrams and letters of congratulation at Fort Belvedere, his country home, many of his future subjects saw it as the occasion the reason for renewed speculation on his wifelessness. No wife, no heir; and an unmarried crown prince or a bachelor king is almost unheard of in England. King George was 70 June 3. His wealth is delicate. At present, the second heir is the Duke of York, second of the king’s four sons, and his heir is nine years old Princess Elizabeth. The fourth heir is Princess Margaret Rose now nearly 5. The Duke and Duchess have been married 12 years. Unless the duke has a male heir, or the Prince of Wales marries, Princess Elizabeth will be queen in her own right, and any man she may marry wil

Three disputes, two of them international and one internal, held Europe's attention today. Foremost in importance was the Anglo-German navy agreement under which Germany can build a modern navy 35 per cent as large as the British fleet. Downing Street sent out a trouble shooter, Captain Anthony Eden, Minister for League of Nations affairs, in an effort to calm down the French who claimed that Great Britain had agreed to the wreckage of the Versailles treaty. To Rome Next. From Paris, Captain Eden goes to Rome to seek peace in another dispute—the conflict between Italy and Ethiopia. Italian sources have warned that Italy may withdraw from the League of Nations if the Geneva body interferes in northeast Africa. London, however, refused to consider there was any danger Italy would bolt the league. Yugoslavia was without a cabinet following the government’s resignation and German and Italian

PARIS, June 22—France and Great Britain, apparently having studied a naval agreement, were at odds today on how to negotiate a European pact of mutual assistance by air. This subject came before Premier Pierre Laval and Captain Anthony Eden, British secretary for League of Nations affairs, as they resumed their discussions. A rift between the two powers over the Anglo-German naval accord apparently was closed by an agreement on a course of “close cooperation.” France's protest against the pact still stands, however. French objection to separate negotiations of an air pact was so strong that Captain Eden talked with London officials before meeting M. Laval again today for lunch. Slight possibility for an agreement was seen before Captain Eden goes to Rome. M. Laval firmly insisted an air pact must be negotiated simultaneously with the eastern European and Danubian treaties, as France, Bri

1935-05-20.text: Wool, England, May 20,—Lawrence of Arabia, one of those figures whom fate plucks from the crowd of their fellow men to make history, lay a shattered corpse in the small chapel of Wool military hospital today. As an archeological student of 36 years, it fell to him to organize the unruly Arab tribes against Turkey in the World War, and win for Great Britain and its allies a great area of the Near East. He died yesterday after being unconscious six days from terrible injuries he suffered when, racing a motorcycle along a country road, he swerved to avoid killing two bicycling boys. There was widespread mourning for him throughout England. He was remembered as Col. T.E. Lawrence, his original name under which he organized the Arabs. As T.E. Shaw, disdaining the proffered rewards of the government for his services, he enlisted as a mechanic in the Royal Air Force. The best surgeons the gover

WOOL, DORSETSHIRE, Eng., May 19 (*)—England’s “Lawrence of Arabia”, one of the most romantic, yet enigmatic personalities of modern times, died today. Death came to Col. T. E. Lawrence, 46, shortly after 8 A. M. He had lain unconscious in a little military hospital in the countryside for 142 hours following upon a motorcycle collision. For more than an hour doctors attempted to revive him with continuous use of oxygen. Crashed Last Monday Since the crash late Monday they had waited constantly for an opportunity to operate in an attempt to save the one-time “uncrowned king of Arabia,” but Lawrence died without regaining consciousness. A post-mortem this afternoon disclosed that Lawrence’s brain was so badly damaged that had he recovered he would have regained only partial use of his speech and eyesight. His funeral will be held Tuesday. In accordance with the simplicity and selflessness o

ST. ANNES-ON-THE-SEA, Eng., May 20.—(4)—Meeting with an unlooked for stern test, W. Lawson Little, Jr., of San Francisco today was compelled to make some sensational recoveries to win his first round match in defense of the British amateur golf championship. Little defeated T. H. Parker, a Briton, one up. Three other Americans—John Porsman of New York, Robert W. Knowles, Jr., of Brookline, Mass., and Captain A. Webster-Bullock of Monterrey, Calif.—also gained the second round. The advance of Little and his compatriots, although rivals for the title he won last year at Prestwick, was contrastingly marked by the

Vatican City, May 19. (AP) Pope Pius besought the return of England to the Roman Catholic church today in a sermon to 50,000 persons attending the canonization of two Britons. Sir Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher, executed 400 years ago by order of Henry VIII for opposing his marriage to Anne Boleyn, were made saints by Pope Pius XI in a gorgeous ceremony in St. Peter's. The pontiff urged his audience to pray that England might return to Rome, declaring: "We desire that with your ardent prayers invoking the patronage of the new saints you ask of the Lord that which is so dear to our heart, namely that England, in the words of Saint Paul, ‘meditating the happy consummation which crowned the life’ of two martyrs, may ‘follow them in their faith’ and return to the Father's house ‘in unity, faith and knowledge of the Son of God.’"

LEPC OD PLC ICI. ANEW S ser y ice: Ff WOOL, DORSETSHIRE, England, May 20.— A great spontaneous movement to lay T. E. Shaw, “king-maker” of Arabia, among Britain's kings in Westminster Abbey swept a mourning country today, but for the time being the legendary hero's wish for the obscurity in death that he could never attain in life will prevail. Attended only by immediate members of his family and a few friends who fought with him in his incredible “revolt in the desert”, funeral services will be held tomorrow for Shaw, “Lawrence of Arabia”, in the village church of Moreton, near where he lived in a quiet cottage. Lawrence will probably be interred there, but later the demand that he rest in Westminster Abbey with the unknown soldier and Britain's other great warriors, writers, and statesmen, for Lawrence ranked high in all their fields, may know no denial. SEATTLE, May 4.—The steamer Denali ran aground on a lonely rock island in British Columbia waters today, but all passengers and crew members were reported safe, with a Coast Guard cutter standing by, guard headquarters here announced. The passengers, number undisclosed, and members of the crew were removed from the stricken ship to the little island, the reports said. It was added that the captain, the chief engineer and one crew member remained aboard. The skipper was represented as reporting the ship was buckling near the Number 2 hold and asking the aid of salvage tugs.

Vatican City, May 20. (UP)—Roman Catholic churchmen awaited today British reaction to a plea to members of the Church of England to return to the mother church. Pope Pius made the plea yesterday at a service at St. Peter's in which the blessed Thomas More and John Fisher were made saints of the church—the first Englishmen to be honored since the Reformation. London. May 20. (UP)—Politically the difference between the Church of England and the Roman Catholic church is that between constitutional government and "Mussolinism," the Rev. W. J. Carnegie, sub-dean of Westminster, said today in discussing Pope Pius’ plea for the Church of England to return to the Roman Catholic church. If the Church of England ever reunited with the Roman church, Canon Carnegie said, it would have to be on a much broader basis than was first apparent.

VATICAN CITY, May 20—five new saints, St. Thomas More and St. John Fisher, were numbered in the Heavenly host of the Catholic Church today and because they died for the unity of the church, Pope Pius XI signalized their canonization with a strong call for reunion with the Church of England. Pointing to the martyrdom of the two Englishmen because they refused to recognize King Henry VIII as head of the Reformed Church, the Pope, in an impressive ceremony, asked Britain to “return to the father's house.” Hundreds of high British Catholic clergymen and other pilgrims, including Thomas More Byanton, a descendant of the martyr, attended the rites. 1935-10-24.text: Times in the international field are likely next year and Britain finds it necessary to increase her defense forces, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin told the House of Commons today, continuing the three-day foreign affairs debate. "In the interests of world peace," Baldwin told the crowded house, "it is imperative that our defensive forces should be stronger than they are today." He then announced that Parliament would be dissolved on Friday and a general election held on Nov. 14. As the government benches cheered the announcement, Baldwin explained: "A lull in international affairs seems to have arrived, whereas if we postponed the election until January, we might find the country facing a more difficult time than today." Shuns Unemployment. Baldwin refused a Laborite request for a debate on unemployment. "The international situation is of paramount importance," he said, "and while unemp

LONDON, OCT. 24. (AP) —The British government sent out invitations today for a conference of the great naval powers on naval limitations to be held at London December 2. Thus the government set in motion a new move for naval restriction directly on the heels of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's announcement that he wants the country to give him a mandate for re-armament in the elections to the House of Commons November 14. The naval conference which the British government expects will be attended by the ambassadors of the United States, Japan, France and Italy and representatives of Great Britain, will meet 24 hours before the new parliament is called in after tomorrow's close of the present parliament.

LONDON, Oct. 23,—Gloomy predictions that the end of the Italo-Ethiopian war is months, even years away resounded in Congress today after Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin announced he would seek re-election on a rearmament program. — Parliament will be dissolved Friday, the general elections be held Nov. 14 and the formal opening of parliament Dec. 3. "In the interests of world peace it is essential our defensive services should be stronger than today," Baldwin said. Baldwin Applauded "I will not pursue a policy or be responsible for the government of this country if I am not given the power to remedy those deficiencies that have occurred in our defensive services since the war." This statement was heartily applauded. But government opponents immediately challenged the rearmament issue in a bitter debate in which the efficacy of economic sanctions against Italy was termed doubtful and dange

The diplomatic front: Mussolini pressed Paris and London for an answer on his peace terms, which demand a protectorate over much of Ethiopia. Premier Laval of France transmitted the terms to London. But in neither London nor Paris was there much optimism over acceptance of the terms. Italian officials expressed a desire for delay in enforcement of the League of Nations boycott, pending the outcome of peace parleys. Peace, British statesmen reaffirmed, must be concluded between Il Duce and the League; not between Rome and London or Rome and Paris. The war front: Italy’s two armies, northern and southern, were ready for a drive on Harar. Addis Ababa, Ethiopian capital, had reports of a great battle raging in the Webbe Shibeli river sector. These were denied by the governor of Harar province.

A ten-day truce in the European diplomatic field prevailed today, with France and Britain anxiously awaiting Premier Benito Mussolini's reaction to the speech of Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary. An open bid for peace, the speech nevertheless was an implied warning to Mussolini, designed to force his hand. Sir Samuel, warning that the Ethiopian war must be halted without fighting in Europe, made two important points: 1. Britain has no intention of fighting Mussolini alone, or of taking individual action such as a blockade or closing the Suez Canal. 2. As a corollary, action to stop the war must be collective, the implication being that if the powers at Geneva decide on force, Britain will act with them. Sir Samuel pointedly invited Mussolini to do something about it before Oct 31, when the League fixes a date for application of the financial and economic penalties already vote

LONDON (P)—An Ethiopian attack on the Italian line between Aksum and the Sudanese border was repulsed early Thursday after loss of more than 100 men by the attackers, according to an exchange telegraph dispatch from a correspondent with the northern Italian forces. Haile Selassie’s warriors, reportedly under the leadership of Ras Siyoum, were attempting to cut the Italian right wing and also to divert Italian troops to Aksum from points further east on the Italian line. Several forays were made against the Italians and it was believed that renewed attacks were being planned Thursday. Dorking, Surrey, England, Oct. 23 (4?) — Former Mayor James J. Walker may sail tomorrow to end a two-year self-imposed exile from the sidewalks of New York but his plans tonight were surrounded by uncertainty. Walker has booked passage on the S. S. Manhattan, sailing tomorrow, for himself, his wife, the former Betty Compton, musical comedy dancer; and her mother. "I hope to get away tomorrow but still do not know whether I can," Walker said tonight. "The fire caused us considerable trouble and I do not know whether we can straighten out our affairs so as to be able to leave." He referred to the burning two days ago of the house of his mother-in-law, Mrs. Frederick Compton.

ROME, Oct. 23.—Premier Benito Mussolini has requested France and Britain to delay application of sanctions to facilitate current diplomatic negotiations for settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian dispute, it was learned tonight. Great Britain was understood tonight to have rejected Italy’s request for an immediate, appreciable reduction of its Mediterranean fleet concentration, “pending a closer approach

1935-10-05.text: - LONDON, Oct. 8 (*)—The capture of Edagahamus, 10 miles beyond Adigrat, by Italian troops was reported today by the Exchange Telegraph correspondent with the Italian army in Ethiopia. Almost at the same time, the agency's home correspondent reported official Italian sources had stated that the Italians had not yet entered Aksum, another goal of the advancing troops.

London, Oct. 4. — An authoritative source stated tonight the British delegates are prepared to walk into the League of Nations headquarters at Geneva tomorrow demanding that the League council sit in immediate judgment on Italy's guilt or innocence in the invasion of Ethiopia. It was likewise stated that Great Britain wants the council to render a quick verdict, thus paving the way for the application of Article XVI of the covenant — the article concerned with the application of sanctions, punishments, against any nation which violates the peace of member nations. It was suggested that the council might reach its decision before sundown tomorrow and call upon the League assembly to sit in judgment Monday as to what penalties, if any, should be assessed against Italy. The British government was stated to be determined to strike while the iron is hot in an effort to make the League an inst

MYINTION, Oct. 4 (UP)—The chances are three to one that there will be war in Europe before the end of the year, according to the men who figure risks for Lloyd's. War risk insurance today, on the basis of any two European nations becoming involved in conflict, was being offered on the basis of a 75 per cent premium. In other words, the man who wants to protect himself against war must pay a premium three-quarters of the full amount he would receive if war came.

Associated Press Foreign Star Geneva, Saturday, Oct. 5.—The League of Nations council committee adjourned early this morning with its report on the Italo-Ethiopian conflict ‘practically finished.’ Anthony Eden, British minister for league affairs, was reported by an informed source to have insisted on a strong report clearly spotlighting facts “pointing to war guilt.” It is not the function of the committee report, it was pointed out, however, to name specifically the

PARIS, Oct. 4 (P)—The Havas News Agency announced tonight it had learned France has promised to support Great Britain with land, air and sea forces against any attack coming from preparations Britain may make for enforcing sanctions if they are voted in the Italo-Ethiopian crisis. The promise was made in a French note being delivered tonight in London, the agency declared. In return, France said Britain must pledge similar aid to France in analogous circumstances, it was reported. In either case, the pledge would be valid, the note was reported to have stated, only so long as sanctions had already been considered at preliminary talks between the two powers. Premier Laval was reported authoritatively to share the view of many in parliament that neutrality alone would be dangerous for France, which should make an effort at Geneva to keep Britain and Italy as close together as possible. | By The Associated Press LONDON, Oct. 4.—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin made a new appeal to Italy tonight and the British government pressed for a quick decision upon war guilt tomorrow at Geneva and the immediate discussion of sanctions. Cheered by the French cabinet’s firm support of Premier Laval and his backing for league action, authoritative quarters here expressed the hope the question of whether Italy is guilty or innocent of a violation of the league covenant will be decided tomorrow night, paving the way for possible applications of sanctions. Speaking to the conservative party convention of Bournemouth, Baldwin asked Italy “even at this hour” to refrain from action which would make the league’s task more difficult. London, Oct. 4.—The Ethiopian commandant at Aduwa has sent a message to the government: "I can not hold Aduwa much longer," the Exchange Telegraph Addis Ababa correspondent reported today. The correspondent said Ethiopians admitted a heavy reverse on the northern front. Italian troops hold the Shire hills dominating the Aduwa plain about 10 miles from the threatened city, the dispatch added. LONDON, Oct. 5. -- Sir Roger Backhouse, commander-in-chief of the British home fleet, was injured last night when an amphibian plane returning him to Portland from London capsized on landing in Portland harbor. Sir Roger had conferred in London with high naval officials.

1935-10-09.text: London — Great Britain, where the arrival of a royal child is something more than another name in the registration books, rejoiced today over the birth of a son to the Duke and Duchess of Kent. The new prince, third grandson of King George and Queen Mary, is seventh in line of succession to the throne. The mother is the former Princess Marina of Greece, whom the duke married last November.

LONDON, Oct. 9 — The cabinet has decided to summon parliament to meet Oct. 22, a week before its original schedule, political quarters understood today. Some believed it would be for the purpose of approving any penalties against Italy adopted at Geneva. It was also believed the summons would presage a general election in November. The cabinet held an important meeting today and discussed the problem of penalizing Italy. The entire situation was reviewed but any fresh decision on policy was deferred pending Geneva developments.

LONDON, Oct. 9 (Wednesday).— A son was born to the Duchess of Kent early today. The baby ranks seventh in line of succession to the throne of Great Britain. He was born to the former Princess Marina of Greece early this morning at her London home, No. 3 Belgrave Square. The Duke of Kent, fourth son of King George, and Princess Marina were married last Nov. 29.

| LONDON, Oct. 9.—The son born | early today to the Duchess of Kent, former Princess Marina of Greece, yelled as lustily as any day-old baby in his parents' home in Belgrade Square today as the British Empire celebrated the advent of another heir to the throne. - The condition of the pretty young mother of the youngest prince of the House of Windsor was reported to be as satisfactory as that of her child. | “I’m the happiest man in the world that it’s a boy,” Prince George, the baby’s father, told prominent Britons who called at his home to congratulate the family. “The event was the quietest matter for all concerned and the Duchess is as well as could be expected. So is the boy.” The birth of the child who ranks seventh in the line of succession to the British throne is acclaimed in today’s newspapers in headlines as large and as black as those recording the progress of the war in Ethio

| LONDON, Oct. 9 (Wednesday)— A son; the seventh in line of succession to the British throne, was born early today to the Duchess of Kent, An official announcement said the birth occurred at 2:15 a. m., and the glad news was telephoned at once to Sandringham, Norfolk, where King George and Queen Mary are in residence. The proud father, youngest son of the king, had waited up all night with his parents-in-law, Prince and Princess Nicholas of Greece, at No. 3 Belgrave Square. Both Doing Well Both the mother, the former Princess Marina of Greece, and her royal son, were doing well, it was learned. The Duke of Gloucester and his fiancée, Lady Alice Montagu-Douglas-Scott, heard the tidings at Sandringham, and the Prince of Wales and other members of the royal family immediately were informed. LONDON, Oct. 9.—A mass of conflicting unconfirmed reports and dearth of reliable news from the front characterized the Italo-Ethiopian war dispatches received in London today. Evidence of the scarcity of first-hand war news was the fact that Floyd Gibbons, war reporter for International News Service, had been unable to get any news into London since Sunday night when he filed a dispatch on the fall of Aduwa. Official news from Rome was equally light. Apparently the Italians were merely consolidating their positions awaiting new orders before continuing their advance. News from Addis Ababa was severely censored but the government admitted it had only very poor communications with the various fronts. In the face of these, rumors flew thick and fast.

AOUNLUIN, Sh Oy UE Pee VO Wee a cabinet meeting, an authoritative source disclosed today that Parliament will be summoned Oct. 22 — one week earlier than the regular date—should the international situation necessitate such action. The government ministers were in session two hours and 10 minutes. No plans were announced for any other meeting before the cabinet's next regular session, expected Oct. 16. Reports said that a general election would be called for late in November. It was understood that the cabinet did not make a definite decision on the question of shortening the Parliamentary recess by one week but that the ministers expressed the opinion that the events at Geneva may make an earlier meeting necessary. They were well aware that the official government opposition, the Labor party, had requested a speedy meeting of Parliament in view of the Italo-Ethiopian war.

By International News Service. ROME, Oct. 9—The government-controlled Italian press today bitterly attacked the policies of the United States regarding the Italo-Ethiopian war, intimating it has been influenced by Great Britain. For many weeks the Italian press has been attacking the stand of Great Britain on the East African crisis but until now has largely refrained from commenting on the position of the United States. Regarding the Monday statement of Secretary of State Hull, in which he said President Roosevelt made his neutrality proclamation entirely on his own initiative, the newspaper Tribuna commented ironically that he was “excusing himself for something he has not done.” The paper cast ridicule on the statement the United States was acting solely on its own initiative, implying there was significance in the visits of Ray Atherton, councillor of the American embassy in London,

1935-10-02.text: | France unexpectedly ordered military maneuvers strengthened on German border defenses as time for Germany's withdrawal from the League of Nations, set for Oct. 21, approached. The French were reported seeking British aviation help against any German threat. In return, the French would reinforce the British Mediterranean fleet in the event of Italo-British trouble. It was believed Emperor Selassie might order mobilization this week. The Italian minister at Addis Ababa ordered five Italian consulates at Aduwa and Harat provinces to evacuate immediately. Italian sources called Ethiopia's impending mobilization a “menacing threat” of war. It was said Italy's East African army was braced against an Ethiopian attack. George Lansbury, aged leader of the labor party in the British House of Commons, repudiated the party policy for military sanctions in the event of aggression in the Italo-Ethio

KINGSTON, Jamaica, Oct. 1 — The 450 passengers of the RMS liner Rotterdam were set ashore today by the British freighter Arugani. All were happy and none the worse for their experience. The Arugani also brought 100 members of the Rotterdam’s crew. Capt. Jan Van Volken and 296 members of his crew were left aboard the 24,000 ton vessel held fast on a coral reef at Morant Keys, 60 miles southeast of Jamaica. The Arugani’s decks and cabins were crowded to capacity for the 7-hour trip to Kingston. The passengers slept and rested as best they could, but all were cheerful and glad to be ashore. Five hundred and fifty men and women were transferred from the stranded liner to this freighter late yesterday. The transfer was accomplished in the same glassy-surfaced Caribbean in which the Rotterdam piled up on the reef early Monday morning. There was no difficulty, no danger, no discomfort or injury

LONDON, Oct. 2. (#)—Reports from Bombay that the British army in India is preparing for eventualities in Africa went undenied Wednesday by the government as the cabinet met in a two-hour session to discuss the Italo-Ethiopian situation with Anthony Eden, British spokesman at Geneva. The British army strength in India is approximately 60,000 troops. Authoritative quarters admitted having heard such reports but said they are not to be stressed at this time. The reports said plans have been made quietly for the quick transfer of large contingents of troops to Bombay for quick embarkation to East Africa in case of war. Officers have made plans, the reports continued, for concentration of the forces in British territory near Ethiopia where the strain of the campaign is expected to be. By The Associated Press LONDON, Oct. 1.—October, the month many observers predicted would see the outbreak of war between Italy and Ethiopia, found those nations steadily preparing today for just such an eventuality. Expect Mobilization Emperor Haile Selassie was believed preparing to call a general mobilization. He received assurances from woman leaders of the country they would do their share at the front. Because of the increased tension, the Italian minister to Ethiopia ordered Italian consulates in the provinces of Aduwa and Harar evacuated. Other consular agents in the interior are en route either to Addis Ababa or points outside the country. Increasing uneasiness was noted in Rome over the fact the British fleet is still massed in the Mediterranean. Anglo-Italian tension was relaxed recently through mutual assurances but the Rome press today resumed its bitterness against London.

London, Oct. 2, (U.P) — Cabinet ministers assembled at historic No. 10 Downing Street today for a meeting on whose decisions the peace of England and Europe may depend. Just before the meeting Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, went to Buckingham Palace for a long talk with King George. No sooner had he left than Lord Halifax, secretary for war, was received by the king. Both audiences were significant of the urgent gravity of the Italian-Ethiopian crisis. (Copyright 1935 by United Press) PARIS, Oct. 2—France has informed Great Britain unofficially that it will reply in the affirmative to the British appeal for French aid in the event that an Anglo-Italian incident in the Mediterranean leads to war, the United Press learned today from high sources.

PARIS, Oct. 1. (4P)—Negotiations between France and Great Britain for a mutual assistance agreement, inspired by complications of the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, today found both powers side-stepping specific pledges, officials said. France, these officials explained, is unwilling to go any further for Britain in the event of an Italian attack on the British Mediterranean fleet than it expects the London government to go in case of an air attack on France by Germany. The official French answer is expected to be drafted at Thursday’s cabinet meeting. At the same time, France authorized immediate military measures.

1935-04-07.text: Indications in London and Paris today were that three premiers will meet Thursday when the tripartite conference opens at Stresa, Italy. Premier Mussolini, as host, will represent his nation, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald will represent Great Britain in company with Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin was reported as likely to head the French delegation. Meanwhile Soviet Russia served notice through its official newspaper, Izvestia, that she would not consider any decisions reached at Stresa binding if they conflict with the Russian views of Europe's peace needs. Benito Mussolini's "realist policies" will be stacked against Great Britain's diplomatic "idealism" when representatives of three world allies sit down at Stresa, Italy, Thursday to decide what to do about Germany’s rearmament in violation of the Versailles treaty. Rome —(4)—(Copyright)— High Italian quarters Saturday night expressed irritation with England and doubt of France in connection with the tri-power conference at Stresa which opens next Thursday. At Stresa foreign ministers of the three nations will consider Germany’s rearmament, European problems arising in its wake and the old problem of security against war. Italy’s attitude can be summed up thus: 1. Annoyance with England because England apparently believes in a conciliatory attitude toward Germany, wants a general European accord and does not want an alliance. 2. Doubt of France because France, believed here to be under England’s influence, is seemingly moving toward the idea of a general accord. 3. (By the Associated Press) Premier Mussolini will ask Foreign Secretary Simon of Great Britain and Foreign Minister Laval of France at the Stresa conference beginning next Thursday, to discuss an accord to allow Austria, Hungary and Bulgaria to rearm, it was reported in high Italian sources Saturday. France continued mindful of her eastern border, announcing plans to man its steel and concrete fortifications with 60,000 troops ordered held under arms three months beyond the normal conscript period. Rome — Official quarters said Italy’s viewpoint concerning the Stresa conversations may be summed up thus: “Do something strong and concrete—with or without Germany.” Paris—The ministerial council approved plans to keep 60,000 conscripts under arms in order to maintain the army’s strength at the 350,000 considered the minimum for safety.
