By The Associated Press Free City of Danzig, April 8— The Nazis failed by 17,594 votes yesterday to create a dictatorship in this free city in their drive to unite it with Germany. Final official figures showed that they polled only 59.1 percent of the vote instead of the 66 and two thirds needed to gain control.

By The Associated Press Addis Ababa, April 6.—Ethiopian soldiers, with no rattling of sabers or rolling of tribal war drums, trudged along dusty roads to the border tonight as Emperor Haile Selassie’s answer to Italy's concentration of troops in Africa. The king of kings, the conquering lion of Judah and the descendant of the Queen of Sheba summed up the Italo-Ethiopian frontier dispute to an interviewer thus: “We have tried to negotiate directly with Italy, or through an intermediary. Unfortunately Italy has declined arbitration and has not replied to our proposals. Therefore we have broken off negotiations and submitted the matter to Geneva.” (The League of Nations announced receipt of Ethiopia’s demand for urgent treatment of the dispute, the Ethiopian note citing reports that thousands of Egyptian workmen are being employed to build roads to the Ethiopian frontier of Italy’s colonies

Taking no chances of a surprise invasion of her eastern frontier, will man her concrete and steel defense fortifications with 60,000 soldiers who today were ordered held under arms for three months beyond the normal period of service. As part of the steadily-growing program to bring the great fortress barrier against Germany up to full strength, trained men are to be kept in the ranks while their younger brothers, called to the colors under the new army program, will receive preliminary training to fit them to take over full duties as soldiers.

| PARIS, April 6.—France further strengthened her army today and at the same time prepared to reject Adolf Hitler's plan for a series of separate non-aggression pacts in Europe based on the Polish-German non-aggression treaty. France insists on a system of general security, with or without the inclusion of Germany, which would bind the signatories to protect any member attacked. Great Britain is fixedly opposed to committing herself to military action on the continent, although willing to join a mutual air pact. Highly reliable sources said tonight that if the British propose to the British-French-Italian conference at Stresa, Italy, next Thursday the adoption of Hitler’s suggestion, France will definitely reject it. France's determination to show Hitler that she is prepared to defend herself to the last ounce of her resources was emphasized today when the cabinet ratified yesterday's de

BERLIN, April 6—WPR—A Royal Dutch airliner crashed at the village of Brilon, near Kassel, tonight, killing seven persons including two passengers. One of them was said to be M. De Vaught, son of the Amsterdam burgomaster. Cause of the crash was not determined. The plane, the Leeuwerick, flagship of the recently inaugurated Prague-Amsterdam line, burst into flames, incinerating the two passengers and a five-man crew. The pilot was M. Soer, who last December established a record of four days and four hours for a flight from Amsterdam to Batavia. The ship crashed during a snow storm, apparently when visibility became so low that M. Soer was unable to find his way. The new service was launched only a few days ago. It linked Prague and Amsterdam by airline for the first time.

1935-10-16.text: ADDIS ABABA: Ethiopian tribal warriors invade Italian Somaliland, GENEVA: Britain proposes immediate boycott of Italian goods, CANBERRA: Australia adopts league penalties, PARIS: European political complications coincide with Laval’s peace move; France and Britain diverge on penalties, ROME: Italy denies talk of peace plan; public giving gold to aid treasury. LONDON: Cabinet rejects French suggestion for withdrawal of fleet from Mediterranean. WITH ITALIAN ARMIES: Northern army set for new drive; way to south reported open. HARAR: Maimed Italian prisoners may be pardoned in Harar, DJIBOUTI: Anti-foreign feeling flares in Ethiopia, refugees say. ALEXANDRIA: Italy masses 200 airplanes near Egypt’s frontier. WELLINGTON: New Zealand sends cruiser to aid British. ADDIS ABABA: Ras Gugsa’s surrender admitted.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) Paris, Oct. 15. (UP)—Premier Pierre Laval has asked Great Britain to withdraw its home fleet ships from the Mediterranean as a gesture to enable him to seek a peaceable settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian crisis, an official source said today. The disclosure was a sequel to a series of conferences by which Laval was understood to have embarked upon a new attempt to bring the war to a peaceful end. Gesture to Italy No gesture to Italy could be so attractive perhaps, as withdrawal of the great fighting ships sent from home waters in the British Isles to guard the entrances to the Mediterranean from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. It was understood that Laval made his fleet request through Sir George Clerk, British ambassador, after a long talk with Vittorio Cerruti, Italian ambassador, last night. It was said that Cerruti agreed that a more conciliatory atm

Paris, Oct. 16.—Officials disclosed today that France and Great Britain are asking Washington if the United States is willing to restrict its imports from Italy in case a sanction against Premier Mussolini's nation is applied by the League of Nations. The same authorities also stated that a similar question is being asked of other powers including Germany, Japan and Brazil which are not members of the league. It was stated that the exploration is being conducted through the ambassadors of those nations. The attitudes of the non-member countries is sought because of the fact that Yugoslavia, Austria, Spain and certain other countries including the Scandinavians are regarded as opposed to the plan for a restriction on purchases from Italy.

London, Oct. 10 (A’)—Italy’s Fascist legions advanced on both Ethiopian fronts under cover of aerial bombardments and scouting flights today and the League of Nations moved toward economic sanctions to choke off the African warfare. A tense situation on two continents saw a huge British fleet hold maneuvers off the shores of Alexandria, near the mouth of the Suez Canal. Bomb Detachments Italian airplanes commanded by Count Galeazzo Ciano, son-in-law of Premier Mussolini, bombed Ethiopian troop detachments at the key city of Makale, on the northern front, while the left wing of the Italian army advanced from the north, press dispatches said. The Fascist fliers were reported to have destroyed an ammunition dump near the town of Alaji. Frightened by the sudden appearance of Il Duce’s air squadron, the population of the important southern city of Harar fled in panic to the hills when the pla

LONDON, Oct. 16—(U.P)—The British Cabinet today decided to reject a French suggestion for withdrawal of the home fleet from the Mediterranean as a gesture of conciliation to Italy. The Cabinet adhered to Britain's repeated stand that her Mediterranean concentration is not a threat to Italy, but a purely precautionary measure; also that there is no need for private negotiations outside the League, since the problem is entirely in the League's hands. Developments since the invasion of Ethiopia, the Cabinet decided, particularly reinforcement of Italian troops in Libya, did not justify any suggestions for a fleet withdrawal. Andre Charles Curbin, French Ambassador, visited the Foreign Office this afternoon.

Geneva, Oct. aa Great Britain formally proposed to the League of Nations today an immediate complete boycott of Italian goods. The proposal was made by Anthony Eden of Great Britain. As soon as the economic subcommittee of the “general staff” which is framing penalties for the big league penalties committee had begun its meeting today, Eden handed in a resolution proposing the boycott. Under the British plan all league nations would pledge themselves to cease buying Italian goods of every character as punishment for Italy's war on Ethiopia. Continued on Page 2.

(Copyright by The Associated Press) Geneva, Oct. 16—(4)—Captain Anthony Eden of Great Britain backed energetically at a meeting of the economic sanctions committee of the League of Nations today, a proposal that league states buy nothing from Italy, but no decision was taken by the committee. The proposal originally advanced by the British for a boycott by League nations of purchases from Italy, was also supported warmly by the Netherlands and Belgium. Rumania, Sweden, Russia and Turkey also favored it. The British minister for league affairs emerged from the session in good humor and sources close to him said no real opposition had developed to this additional form of pressure against Italy. While pursuing relentlessly their erection of sanctions against Italy, league delegates heard from reliable sources that Premier Laval of France contemplated suggestion of an East African peace plan

LONDON, Oct. 12—(AP)—Quadruplets, all of them boys, were born at the Royal Free hospital tonight and all are surviving. The first baby arrived at 10:23 p.m. and the last one at 11:11 p.m. They were described by hospital attaches as of “a fair size.” The mother is Mrs. Victoria Harmsworth, wife of a metal polisher.

1935-02-23.text: LONDON, Feb. 22—(4)—Two farewell notes, their contents un-divulged, held the death secret of Jane and Elizabeth DuBois today. Coert DuBois, United States consul general at Naples, father of the attractive young women who plunged to their deaths yesterday from an airplane, was en route here with his grief-stricken wife to receive his daughters’ messages. The two notes, found on a seat of the airliner after the sisters had leaped from it at an altitude of 3,000 feet over Upminster, Essex, were in the custody of the American consul here. He declined to divulge the contents to anyone except the parents.

En route with President Roosevelt to Cambridge, Mass., Feb. 23.—(P)—A new ship subsidy program to supplant the present government policy of ocean mail contracts engaged the attention of President Roosevelt today as he traveled toward New England for a visit to his alma mater, Harvard University. Favoring direct grants to American steamship lines rather than aiding them by indirect subsidy through mail contracts, the president studied a report of a committee of experts who made an investigation of the whole subject. There were indications he would put the finishing touches on a message covering his recommendations which may be sent to the capital for transmission to Congress before he, himself, returns to Washington. Although his trip is being made primarily to watch his son, Franklin, Jr., initiated tonight to the exclusive Harvard Fly Club, the president will extend his weekend from Was

1 LONDON, Feb. 22. (AP)—A coroner's jury will investigate Monday the death plunge of Jane and Elizabeth Dubois from an airplane over the English countryside yesterday. Contents of two notes the girls left in the airplane were kept secret, awaiting the coroner's action. It was reported the notes explained the girls wished to die because two Royal Air Force aviators in whom they were interested perished in an air disaster in Sicily last week. Their parents are en route here from Naples. The mother was unaware of the circumstances of their deaths.

LONDON, Feb. 26. (AP) - Embittered at what she termed “brutal and unjust” attacks upon her by the Hauptmann defense, Betty Gow, former Lindbergh nurse, was resting in London today before continuing to her home in Glasgow. “I probably will send Betty away for a short holiday before deciding what she will do,” said Betty’s mother. Betty said she could never forget nor forgive the insinuations against her by Edward J. Reilly, Hauptmann's chief defense counsel. “He went too far,” she said. “To insinuate that I knew more about the tragedy than I made known to the court was most unjust.”

Walker; once mayor of New York writing a column for the London Sunday Dispatch, supplied one paragraph that he probably wrote: "Others might remember, 'Alter the counting of time, it is not so important as making time count.'" Is money more plentiful? Are prices lower? Is not money scarce, is not everything dearer, on the contrary? Who knows anything about money? Nobody. Senator Thomas, of Oklahoma, for instance, says the United States is still "on the gold basis." Former President Hoover wants to go back to the gold basis, even if we have to be content with a sixty-nine dollar based on the new kind of expensive gold. Dr. E. A. Schurmann, obstetrician of the University of Pennsylvania,

(AP) — Betty Gow, former Lindbergh nurse, arrived today on the S. S. Berengaria. A large crowd was about the dock attempting to get a glimpse of the woman who had been one of the star witnesses in the Hauptmann trial, but she refused to see anyone except her mother and a few friends who went on board. She entered an automobile and drove away to an undisclosed destination.

LONDON. A tour of eastern Europe's capitals was envisaged for Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, after Great Britain opened direct negotiations with Russia, Germany and Italy in furtherance of her security scheme. These negotiations, it was officially admitted, are to determine whether the visit of the British statesman to Berlin, Moscow and possibly Warsaw would be useful. Accompanying Simon is his projected crusade for the inclusive security plan drafted at Anglo-French conversations here early this month will be Capt. Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal and disarmament expert, it was indicated. The diplomatic conversations between London and Rome, officials said, are for the purpose of keeping Benito Mussolini informed on the Anglo-French discussions as to the best way to meet Adolf Hitler's willingness to join the western air pact and unwillingness to accept other engagements propo

Glasgow, Feb. 23. (UP) — Betty Gow's neighbors awaited her today as a returning heroine after her testimony in the trial of Bruno Richard Hauptmann for the murder of Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr., whom she nursed until his death. An all night party was held by residents in the modest three-story apartment house where Miss Gow lives. The house was decorated and illuminated. Police took precautions to protect Miss Gow from unwelcome publicity. With the cooperation of railway officials, arrangements were made for her to leave her train both here and at Motherwell, half an hour’s ride from Glasgow in order to discourage crowds. Motor cars were detailed to await her at both stations. On the Berengaria between Cherbourg and Southampton yesterday, Miss Gow said that the United States always called her back and that she might return later this year. Miss Gow said she was hurt more than anything by t

1935-07-07.text: By The Associated Press Events seemed to be marching today irresistibly toward war between Italy and Ethiopia, Addis Ababa.—The American legation told 125 resident Americans to leave the country, London—Britain contemplated one more effort for peace, with little hope it would succeed, Salerno, Italy—Benito Mussolini, speaking to 15,000 blackshirts leaving for East Africa, said: ‘We have decided upon a struggle in which we will not turn back.’ Rome—Italy continued her warlike preparations, Mussolini's two young aviator sons signed up for service. Washington—The state department in effect has refused Emperor Haile Selassie’s request to find some way to make Italy abide by the Kellogg anti-war pact,

Darlington, England, July 6. (P — Hundreds of persons ran for their lives in the streets of Darlington today after mischievous youths released three young lions at a carnival. Two of the lions were quickly recaptured, but the third, after touring the town, broke into a house. Occupants locked themselves in the bathroom. The animal finally was cornered and captured.

ROME, July 6 (UP)—The wireless antenna of Premier Mussolini's seaplane was struck by lightning today as Il Duce piloted it toward Salerno but neither the Premier nor other occupants of the plane were injured. LONDON, July 6 (UP)—A Reuters (British) news dispatch from Salerno, Italy said that lightning struck a seaplane piloted by Premier Benito Mussolini but that Il Duce was unharmed. The wireless operator in the plane fainted but other passengers were not affected, the dispatch said.

Wimbledon, England, July 6.— Climaxing the greatest effort ever vouchsafed by a woman in competition here, Mrs. Helen Wills Moody reclaimed the throne of women’s tennis today by defeating Miss Helen Jacobs, her bitter rival, in the finals of the all-comers singles before a roaring, raving mob of 18,000. The scores were 6-3, 3-6 and 7-5. Nothing quite like this finish ever was seen here. Mrs. Moody being seemingly beaten while trailing at 5-2 in the final set, but suddenly calling upon all resources to race through the last five games to the set and match, while the greatest crowd of Wimbledon’s history literally went mad. It was Mrs. Moody's seventh title at Wimbledon and marked just one more time when Miss Jacobs, the sad-faced lady from the same town, Berkeley, Calif., saw hope and ambition fade here. She has yet to win at Wimbledon.

London, July 6—Diplomatic circles this evening said they had heard Britain was following the United States’ lead in advising her nationals to leave Ethiopia, as the British government faced the next step in her efforts to avert an African war. The British were given advance information of the action of the American delegation at Addis Ababa in counseling American residents to depart at once, the diplomats said, and planned to follow suit.

LONDON, July 6 ()—Britain’s government will try again next week to avert an Italo-Ethiopian war, but without much hope of success. This was learned tonight. High diplomatic quarters said Britain was ready to follow the United States in urging all her nationals in Ethiopia to leave at once. Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, and Captain Anthony Eden, secretary for League of Nations affairs, will talk the situation over with J. A. O. Avenol, league secretary-general, who arrives Monday. League's Future at Stake What form Britain's new drive for peace would take remained obscure but unofficial observers—recalling many recent hints from Rome that Italy would forsake Geneva if the league “meddled” in her Ethiopian dispute—agreed that the entire future of the 15-year-old peace body was bound up in it. If Italy resigned from the league because of any future action of the Geneva body, it would

Salerno, Italy, July 6.—Premier Mussolini, mounted on a cannon, told 12,000 blackshirts ready to depart for East Africa today that “we have decided upon a struggle in which we as a government and people will not turn back. The decision is irretrievable.” Earlier, en route here from Rome, the wireless antenna of Il Duce’s big seaplane had been struck by lightning but none of the occupants of the plane was injured. Today's speech was addressed to the volunteer blackshirts of the “January 3” division who are expected to sail shortly for Africa. Il Duce told them the eyes of Italy were upon them and exhorted them to do their duty. “Remember,” he said, “that Italians have always defeated the black races. Adua (where Italy suffered a severe defeat in an invasion of Ethiopia in 1896) was an exception only because of the difference in proportion between the forces. There were only 4,000 Italians

ADDIS ABABA, July 6 -- The American legation today ordered all Americans to leave Ethiopia, Diplomatic circles took the action to mean that the United States expects there may be immediate developments between Ethiopia and Italy.

1935-10-26.text: Active sources said today that a stalemate had been reached in efforts to end the Italo-Ethiopian war and that there were no hopes for an early cessation of hostilities. At the same time, the treasury department ordered that Great Britain's financial sanctions against Italy be placed in operation next Tuesday. The official treasury explanation said financial sanctions were being applied under Article III of the league covenant and refers to loans and credits to or for the benefit of 1. The government of any Italian territory; 2. And a person (not being a body corporate) of whatever nationality resident in such territory; 3. Any person (wherever a resident) being a body corporate incorporated under the law of any such territory. Informed sources said that the progress of the peace negotiations of Premier Mussolini of Italy and Premier Laval of France had virtually broken down and that the

Premier Benito Mussolini's African adventure, which has succeeded thus far, apparently led him into a diplomatic blind alley from which he is trying to back out as gracefully as his position as a dictator will allow. From London came an official admission that Great Britain has received a series of proposals for a solution of the Italo-Ethiopian crisis. Now Marking Time. | tle Steff Correspondent) London, Oct. 2.—Great Britain has received a series of proposals for solution of the Italian-Ethiopian crisis, based on conversations in Paris, it was said officially today. It was believed that the proposals were not acceptable either to Great Britain or France. The proposals were communicated to London by Premier Pierre Laval of France, it was disclosed. They were based on conversations between Laval and Vittorio Cerf, Italian ambassador in Paris. Official admission of the proposals, called in Paris a “summary” of Premier Benito Mussolini's ideas of a proper settlement, came after reports that negotiations had been brought within the framework of the League of Nations for the first time even though they were not acceptable in the present form. Delaying Possible As a result, reports that it might be possible to postpone enforcement of further League penalties

PARIS, Oct. 26. (UP)—Great Britain was reported today to have refused an Italian request for postponement of League of Nations penalties pending diplomatic negotiations to end the crisis. Diplomatic quarters reported that Mussolini was assuming a more conciliatory attitude because of a bad financial and economic situation in Italy. It was this situation, according to the reports, that induced him to ask postponement of penalties during negotiations. A report current in Paris that Laval would go to Geneva Monday to ask postponement of penalties was denied by the foreign office.

LONDON, Oct. 25—(?)—a prediction that League sanctions against Italy "absolutely will go on" came from authoritative quarters tonight after King George, expressing his "gravest concern" over the Italo-Ethiopian war, had prolonged the eighth British Parliament of his regime. Recurring the unconfirmed reports of Premier Mussolini's "peace soundings" to Premier Laval of France met a cool reception and apparent dissatisfaction as the national government went to the country for a new mandate from the electorate—principally on the issues of rearmament and foreign policy. Officials stood on their statements that any suggestions for peace must be satisfactory to both the League of Nations and Ethiopia. And well-informed persons said no such suggestions yet had come from Il Duce. In fact, these persons insisted that nothing tangible had been received from Italy through M. Laval, and that there wa

ROME (*) — Great Britain has fumbled a chance to reinforce European peace, it was asserted in authoritative quarters today. This pessimism displaced the optimism of two days ago as a consequence of Britain's failure to respond to Italy’s withdrawal of a Libyan division with a reciprocal reduction of the British Mediterranean fleet. Speedy return of the fleet to its home quarters would serve more than anything else to restore amity between Italy and Britain, it was said in official sources. The time to do this is at once, these sources continued, if the effect is to be spontaneously wholesome. The British delay in acting is now viewed as having minimized, if not destroyed, Italy’s “Libyan gesture.” It was emphasized again in official quarters that there is no bargain between Italy and Britain for a joint reduction of their military and naval strength, yet there was no concealment of the I

PREDICTS ANOTHER WAR WASHINGTON—William B. Shearer, big navy advocate and once the center of a notable controversy, predicted that the world was going to see another major war. How soon? "It depends upon how long England can keep the lid on," he said. Target of senatorial investigators, Shearer was accused of 'breaking up the 1927 Geneva naval conference while in the employ of private shipyards. He said he helped save the United States 'from a naval limitation treaty that would have left her far behind Great Britain.

LONDON, Ont. Oct. 25 (P)—John Basil Bannon, one-time border rum runner, was convicted tonight by a jury on a charge of kidnapping John S. Labatt, London, in August 1934, and was immediately sentenced to 15 years in prison. David Meisner, former Cincinnati bookmaker, is serving a 15-year prison sentence for the same kidnapping.

1935-06-08.text: (Copyright, 1935, By Associated Press) LONDON, — White-haired Ramsay MacDonald, veteran fighter for peace stepped out as Great Britain’s prime minister Friday and Stanley Baldwin, who typifies “John Bull” himself to Americans, stepped in. The leader of the conservative party, who has been prime minister twice before, lost no time in reconstructing the cabinet, — in which MacDonald took Baldwin's former place as Lord President of the council. Five new faces appeared in the ministerial line-up, which retained the “national government” complexion. Three former ministers retired, one of them, Sir Edward Hilton Young, outgoing minister of health, to be raised to the peerage. So smoothly was the cabinet shift accomplished that only four minutes intervened between MacDonald's presentation of his portfolio to King George in His Majesty’s private apartment at Buckingham Palace and Baldwin's arriv

WASHINGTON, June 8 (UP)— Governments may rise and governments may fall in Europe, as they have been doing over there recently, but the debt defaults go on in the same serene way, if not forever. This fact was borne forcibly upon the United States today with receipt from the British government of a brief note formally announcing its intention to default the June 15 installment of its debt to the United States, amounting to $85,670,765.05. Administration officials were fully reconciled to the fact that this undoubtedly was the first of a series of such notes from the other debtor governments, except Finland, announcing another general default. The chorus of the debtors’ semi-annual song, “we owe you but you know us,” will cost the United States treasury $180,734,248.65 this June 15. The Finnish government has deposited with the National City Bank of New York $167,000 for payment of its Jun

WEYBRIDGE, Eng., June 8. (P)—Helen Wills Moody captured the St. George’s Hill tennis tournament today, trouncing Mrs. Bisle Goldsack Pittman of England, in the final round, 6-0, 6-4. Playing in her first tournament since a back injury forced her to default to Helen Jacobs in the final round of the American championships in 1933, Mrs. Moody overpowered her British opponent with a siege-gun attack for which Mrs. Pittman had no adequate defense. It was the third successive tournament in which Mrs. Pittman has been a finalist and the third in which she was beaten.

Himley Hall, Eng., June 8. (7) — Great Britain’s new government plans to strengthen its national defenses and will continue a standstill policy on the question of currency stabilization, Stanley Baldwin announced today in his first speech since taking over the premiership. “We do not believe our defenses are in the condition yet that will enable us to speak with the voice we should in favor of collective security, which gradually is commending itself to the people of this country. “We are fighting hard at Geneva to bring Europe, either piecemeal or wholly into collective security. The time has come to get limitations of arms, particularly with regard to air, but until such limitation could be got we must safeguard our people.” Baldwin contrasted England’s “great stability” with conditions in the United States and France.

London, June 8. (AP)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin started building political fences today for the forthcoming general elections as one section of the British Press viewed with misgivings the easy shakeup of the cabinet. Under such headings as “the musical chair” and “the same old firm?” the morning papers agreed that the changes will make little difference in the government's policy at home or abroad. Baldwin in his first speech at Himley Hall tonight was expected to make this clear and at the same time emphasize the importance of continuing the national government in the general elections.

WASHINGTON, June 7 (AP) - Hinting at the possibility of a future war debt settlement parley, Great Britain at the same time today notified the United States that it would default on war debt instalment of $85,670,756, due June 15, and payment in arrears amounting to, roughly, $380,000,000. Sir Donald Lindsay, the British ambassador, informed Secretary Hull in a formal note that the British government had given a comprehensive explanation in a note delivered last June why his government had been unable to make payments in the past "pending the negotiation of a final revised settlement." "His Majesty’s government’s note today said, "have constantly given most careful consideration to the matter, but they regret that it does not appear to them that the essentials of the situation have changed since that note was written. "They observe with appreciation the readiness of the United States gov

Rome, June 7.—(4)—A greatly increased guard was set about the British embassy today as the Italian press, reveling in the “lid off” order it received this week, continued its bitter attack on England's opposition to Italy's African policies. (In London Capt. Anthony Eden, retiring lord privy seal, told the house of commons that Italian newspaper charges that Britain was encouraging Ethiopian hostility against Italy were “mischievously absurd.” (The British legislators cheered loudly as Clement Richard Atlee, deputy leader of the opposition, declared Italy “ought to be told plainly that she would not have the use of the Suez canal” if she intended to use force against Ethiopia.)

PARIS, June 8.—The senate approved Premier Pierre Laval’s decree powers to protect the franc by the overwhelming vote of 233 to 15 today after the emergency measure had been grudgingly passed by the chamber of deputies. Previously the senate finance committee had approved the decree bill after disclosing a budget deficit of 6,500,000,000 francs (approximately 415,000,000) and the treasury faces the difficult task of finding this huge sum. The deficit, because of railroad obligations, was estimated in the chamber yesterday at 19,000,000,000 francs. The senate committee concluded the emergency powers were urgently needed to avoid devaluation. The powers, withheld from others, were granted within 24 hours after Laval took the helm of the government. The Premier, the third to face the chamber in eight days, wrung decree powers from the legislative body by a vote of confidence of 324 to 160.

1935-07-29.text: WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 29 —(/P)— England won the coveted Davis Cup—emblematic of the world’s tennis supremacy—for the third straight time today when the new doubles combination of George Patrick Hughes and C. R. D. Turkey defeated the American pair of Wilmer Allison and Johnny Van Ryn, 6-2, 1-6, 6-8, 6-3, 6-3, in the challenge round doubles match. The victory gave England the necessary third win in the five match series. The Britons’ victory was the final crushing blow to America’s hopes of recapturing the cup lost to France in 1927. The first blow was delivered Saturday when H. W. (Bunny) Austin pulled out a five-set victory over Allison in a singles match in which the veteran Texan was favored.

WIMBLEDON, England, July 29.—(UP)—England today completed its second successful defense of the Davis Cup, emblematic of world supremacy in amateur tennis, when its double team of Hughes and Tuckey scored a surprising 6-2, 1-6, 6-8, 6-3, 6-3 victory over the American team of Wilmer Allison and Johnny Van Ryn. The double victory, coupled with a clean sweep of Saturday's two opening singles matches, gave England the three points necessary.

London, July 29—(4)—Great Britain sought Sunday the cooperation of France to persuade Italy to reconsider the rigid conditions it has made governing its attendance at the League of Nations council called to attempt settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian controversy. Premier Mussolini's insistence that the discussions must be limited to the conciliation procedure which now stands deadlocked on the Ualual incident has thrown the British plans into disorder. Efforts to gain the full cooperation of France in persuading Italy to discuss broader issues are understood to be hampered by France’s desire to have the league council hand the problem over to the three powers—Italy, Great Britain and France—signatory to the 1906 Ethiopian treaty.

(International News Service) WIMBLEDON, Eng. July 29 America's collapse in the Davis Cup Challenge round became complete today when the team of Wilmer Allison and John Van Ryan was defeated in a five set doubles match by Pat Hughes and C. R. D. Tuckey of England. The final scores were 6-2, 1-6, 6-8, 6-3, 6-3, the English coming gamely from behind to win even as did 'Bunny' Austin in Saturday's 'key' match of the singles against Allison. The victory today, wholly unexpected, completed one of the greatest disasters an American international team has ever suffered, the English sweeping the first three matches played to take a lead of 3 to 0 and assure them of definite possession of the trophy for the third straight year.

PEIPING, July 29.---(UP)—Dr. Herbert Mueller, German newspaper correspondent, and Gareth Jones, British correspondent for the Manchester Guardian and International News Service, were held for ransom today by bandits. Ransom of $100,000 and 200 Mauser rifles was demanded. The German chauffeur for the two men said they were captured by uniformed soldiers. The British embassy was trying to communicate with the assistant military attache, who is returning from Mongolia to open negotiations for their release.

WASHINGTON—(AP)—A charge that the President and state department are dominated by the British foreign office was coupled yesterday by Rep. Tinkham (R., Mass.) with a demand for neutrality legislation. "Both the President and the department of state, dominated and controlled by the British foreign office," he said in a statement, "are opposed to legislation providing for strict neutrality of the United States in the next war, a war which is already beginning to loom on the European horizon." The House foreign affairs committee recently approved a bill providing for the assembling of statistical information on the arms traffic. But he contended the President, through the state department, opposed an amendment to bar arms export to any country engaged in a war in which the United States is not a party. The amendment, he said, would have meant "strict neutrality" for this country. "The Briti

Berlin — The tension among Jews, Roman Catholics and the world war veterans of the “Steel Helmet” was considerably eased today by the news of a “social” visit of Gen. Werner von Blomberg to Reichsfuehrer Hitler. Von Blomberg, minister of war, called on Der Fuehrer in the latter’s Bavarian mountain home for a long talk. The general feeling prevailed in political circles that Von Blomberg had pointed out to Hitler the international impression created by the drastic measures in the last fortnight against “political Catholicism” and the Steel Helmet and by the personal attacks upon Jews. Von Blomberg and Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, head of the reichsbank, are understood to be the two men chiefly pressing their energies toward moderation with the assistance of the foreign office. Some Success. That Von Blomberg’s efforts are not without success is indicated by

ROME, July 29 (U.P)—Italians believed today that war with Ethiopia was near. They saw in League of Nations efforts to solve the crisis only a waste of words and increased confusion. Stevedores were loading ten steamships with war materials at various ports. Additional thousands of soldiers were awaiting embarkation. War spirit was high, and the country was ready to fight. No Results Achieved— It was said frankly that diplomatic negotiations with Great Britain and France had achieved exactly nothing after ten days of spirited effort. There was no approach at all between Britain and Italy, and the limits of British and Italian concession remained far apart. Ethiopia’s note of yesterday to the League of Nations maintaining its position, caused no surprise, for no concession was expected. But it was received as tending merely to prolong diplomatic discussion between Italy and Ethiopia, and s

1935-09-26.text: Associated Press Foreign Staff ROME, Sept. 25—Improved relations between Great Britain and Italy resulted tonight in cancellation of the sailing from Naples tomorrow of 10,000 soldiers for Libya. Because of the decline in tension between the two governments, it was explained, the reinforcements in Libya, which borders upon Egypt, are not necessary. “The better feeling resulted from assurances between Premier Mussolini and Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary. It was emphasized, however, that the departure of troops for East Africa will continue unchecked. The Italia sailed from Naples today with 1,200 men and tomorrow the Colombo and Merano depart with approximately 2,800 soldiers. Italy will never take the first step in transforming the Italo-Ethiopian conflict into a European one, said a government statement today. This was part of a communique which disclosed that Sir Samuel, i

LONDON (iP) — Great Britain brought its defensive measures nearer home today, to teach London residents how to act in the event war should bring bombers over the city. Seven thousand men and women already were trained for emergency duty. Plans were pushed forward for instructing fathers and mothers in the east end how to protect their families from the effects of gas attacks. The program followed the elaborate air raid rehearsals in Mediterranean possessions, with the Italo-Ethiopian crisis apparently close to the breaking point.

London, Sept. 26 (Thursday). (Pj)—London’s most spectacular fire in years was choked out early today after it had razed a two-story riverfront warehouse and caused damage estimated at 1,409,000 pounds (about 35,000,000). Leaping 100 feet in the air, the flames, fed by stores of raw rubber, raged along the Thames Colonial wharves at Wapping in East London. Stores of rubber, tea and spirits were wiped out. Four hundred firemen, wearing gas masks, manned 58 fire engines to combat the flames. They poured water from nine water-towers on the streets and three fire floats in the river on the inferno. Flaming geysers of molten rubber shot into the sky and descended in cascades resembling a mammoth display of fireworks. Blazing cases of rubber bounced along the foreshore, endangering the firefighters, and an iron crane melted in the terrific heat. The great mass of molten metal crashed to the jet

RO THE ASSOCIATED PRESS LONDON, Sept 25.—Assurances of good will between Great Britain and Italy served to remove tension in Europe today in the Italo-Ethiopian situation. Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Rome, gave Premier Mussolini a message from Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary, in which Hoare said London is “particularly desirous of eliminating every useless misunderstanding between the two countries.” Never Take First Step In return, Italy told England she would never take the first step in transferring the Italo-Ethiopian dispute into a European conflict. While this development was encouraging both to Rome and London, pessimism deepened in Geneva. A spokesman of the Italian delegation said Italy is rapidly losing interest in what action the League council will take. The committee of five nations, which attempted in vain to solve the dispute, will report to the co

GENEVA, Sept. 26.—With the seat of the Italian delegate vacant, the League of Nations council today acted to outlaw war between Italy and Abyssinia, a move equivalent to sanctions against an aggressor and backed by renewed French and British pledges that they "would support any measures the council decides are indispensable." The council calls itself a "committee of the whole" to draft recommendations under Article XV. If Italy rejects the measure, then punitive measures under Article XVI are the next steps.

PARIS, Sept. 25.—VP}—French newspapers reprinted a story from the Sunday London Referee today saying Prince Umberto, heir to the Italian throne, is opposed to Premier Benito Mussolini’s conflict with Ethiopia. (This report was branded ‘utterly false in Rome’ and London’ by authoritative Italian spokesmen.) There is a possibility, the story said, of General Italo Balbo, governor of Libya and Italian air hero, leading a revolt against Il Duce. “Balbo, whose relations with the royal family are excellent, is also opposed to the Ethiopian campaign,” the story asserted. “A large number of Italian superior officers share his view.” The article was reprinted without comment from the communist newspaper Humanite.

Alexandria, Egypt, Sept. 26.— One hundred and seventy British royal air force airplanes have arrived since last Friday, it was learned today, en route to Aboukir, northeast of Alexandria, where Nelson routed Napoleon's great French fleet at the battle of the Nile. Of the planes, 70 arrived on one ship charted by the air ministry. Stringent control has been imposed on the port here. Three Italians, seen watching the unloading of planes and taking notes, were arrested and handed over to Italian authorities.

Paris, Sept. 26, Rumors of dissension — within Premier Mussolini’s cabinet over the Ethiopian campaign were published by the leftist press today. These newspapers speculated as to the possibility of a revolt in Italy and hinted that England would like to see a more friendly government in power in Italy. The newspaper L’Oeuvre printed a report from Geneva that Luigi Federzoni, president of the Italian senate, had made “a courageous criticism of Il Duce’s policy” at Tuesday’s cabinet meeting in Rome. The newspaper added another report that Marshal Badoglio, in a visit to the king during the evening did not hide his misgivings as to the final success of the Italians in Ethiopia. The newspaper Republique said: “The former Italian ambassador to Paris, Count Carlo Sforza, now an exile, is close to Dino Grandi, the Italian ambassador to London, and it is no one's secret that Grandi is maneuveri

1935-01-25.text: | PEIPING, Jan. 25. ?)-New Japanese bombing raids into Chahar Province killing 44 Chinese, were reported today by Chinese sources, indicating apparently a renewal of the Japanese attack. Chinese military authorities stated Japanese fliers dropped three bombs into Tungchetze and eight into Tuhsikow. The dead included five civilians; the others were militiamen and police.

FALL RIVER, Mass., Jan. 23 (P)—In the largest postal robbery in the history of New England, five bandits today held up a United States mail truck and tonight had apparently made good their escape with $129,000 in currency. The bandits were armed with machine guns and pistols. Apparently in conformance with a carefully prepared plan, a sedan was driven ahead of the small truck, forcing it to a halt. Two of the sedan’s four occupants jumped out and leaped aboard the truck. At pistol point, Herbert B. Reid, 43, for 20 years a postal employe, who was transferring registered mail from the railroad station to the post office, was forced into the sedan, bound and blindfolded. Convoyed by Sedan The truck then was convoyed by the sedan, out of the city to South Somerset, a distance of about 2½ miles, where a fifth member of the gang waited in another car. The truck was driven thrice its length of

Winter played a symphony across the continent Thursday, and as the stinging cold and paralyzing snowstorms began to subside the nation counted more than 175 dead in traffic mishaps, flood and fire and sub-zero weather. On opposite shore of the continent, British Columbia and New England dug their way out of snow drifts that had isolated cities and towns, wrecked communication lines and blocked roads. The mercury sank to 60 below zero in Quebec province, and zero weather moved into the eastern states for the night, but the grip of subzero temperatures was breaking in the middle west after a siege that caused days of intense suffering. Landslides and floods menaced (Continued on Page 2)
) GRIMSBY, England, Jan. 24 (P). After drifting badly damaged and helpless in a violent gale off the coast of Iceland, the trawler Jeria was believed to have gone down today with its crew of 14.

J.) By FORD MADOX FORD FLEMINGTON, N. J., Jan. 24.—(?)—The most impressive—as it was indeed the most satisfactory feature at Flemington, was the personality of the judge. His Honour Supreme Court Justice Thomas W. Trenchard is a heavy, greying, fresh-complexioned man and deliberate. Above all deliberate. To the verge of a slowness that is almost insupportable. But when he speaks to an objection—when the words reach you the sensation is one of supreme satisfaction. He speaks reasoningly, even a little tentatively, but what he says strikes you as the only thing that could be possibly said—by justice that is at once supremely impartial and benevolent. There is about the trial a lack of

Landon, Jan. 23—(UP)—Sir Jola Simon, foreign minister, today repudiated allegations that he was financially interested in armament and announced that he would criminally prosecute anyone who thereafter repeated the allegation. The repudiation came at a time when Great Britain is preparing for an arms investigation as have other countries since the United States' naval investigation was begun. Sir John made it through his attorney, Norman Birkett, in the course of the settlement of Simon's suit for slander against the Rev. Bond, Methodist minister of East Durham. Bond, addressing a church assembly last November, alleged that Simon was opposed to a “peace ballot” of the League of Nations union because “his money is invested in armaments firms.” Today Simon consented to settlement without damages or costs when Bond wrote an apology, admitting he based his allegation merely on hearsay. Simon

(Copyright. 1936, by Associated Press.) SHANGHAI, Jan. 25.—The looting and destruction of property by the American Evangelical church at Tungjen, Kweichow province, by Chinese national government and provincial troops was reported here today. News of the looting, suppressed by national government censors, was received here through Chinese and foreign sources. The troops, pursuing communist bands in western China, were said to have gotten out of hand and forced entry into the church’s mission properties. Witnesses related that the soldiers broke into and occupied the mission hospital at Tungjen, the residences of physicians and nurses, and a boys’ school which was looted and destroyed.

* ROME —(UP)— Benito Mussolini cleaned house in his cabinet Thursday to give new fascist figures their chance at government. He ousted six ministers—those of public works, agriculture and forests, national education, justice and cults, finance and communications — and ten under-secretaries. Il Duce, however, remained the majority in the cabinet. The premier holds seven cabinet posts. In these, there were no changes. The cabinet shake-up, the first general change since November 1933, was effected to give outstanding figures an opportunity to participate in the national government, officials explained. Favors Balanced Budget Foreign observers immediately picked the change in the finance department as the most significant. Jung, who visited the United States in the spring of 1933, has been in favor of stabilizing the lira at the present rate of exchange. He has urged balancing of the budget

1935-01-20.text: London, —(#)— Former Queen Helen of Roumania, divorced wife of King Carol, was reported to have accepted a proposal of marriage from an Italian prince, according to a special dispatch published in the Sunday Express today. The Italian prince was identified merely as an ex-cavalry officer, member of the princely Roman House of Columna. The paper published a rumor that Helen was about to enter the Roman Catholic church. A rumor from Florence added that the step was preliminary to a marriage and that the Vatican, which does not recognize divorce, may consider annulment of her marriage to King Carol.

San Francisco Winter in One OF the most savage moods swept the Pacific coast today, bringing snow, hail or rain and lower temperatures to five states and British Columbia. Eight deaths were reported. A game warden was missing in an isolated area 50 miles from Reno. The storm, which blew in from the northwest Friday, sent the thermometer skidding downward. At points in British Columbia it dropped to 56 degrees below zero, 59 degrees colder than it was in Juneau, Alaska. The heaviest snowfalls in years covered the area. The snow blanket at Norden, summit of the Sierras, was 183 inches and at Soda Springs 149 inches. Elk City, mountain village in Idaho, was isolated. Telephone lines to the town were down. Snow plows from Grangeville, Ida. started to cut a path to bring food to the village.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 19. iP—China’s heavenly dog swallowed the moon tonight. A firecracker barrage from the native population was occasioned by a total lunar eclipse, which was interpreted as a mythical celestial canine devouring the moon. As the eclipse receded, credulous ones considered that the firecracker attack had scared off the heavenly dog, saving the moon for Shacarina.

BERLIN, Jan. 19. — German Nazis, victorious in Sunday's Saar plebiscite, today turned speculative eyes toward Memel, another bit of pre-war Germany lost to her in the peace treaties. A sensational report published with singular uniformity by all Berlin's Nazi-controlled newspapers to the effect that Lithuanian troops were massing at Taurow, near the German frontier, was accompanied by expressions of the view that Memel (or Kisipeda), now nominally an autonomous city, should be restored to the fatherland.

MADRID, Jan. 19.—(UP). — Archaeologists believed today that they had found a Spanish Pompeii beneath an ancient olive grove in Andalusia. Excavations on the site of the Roman city of Italica, founded in 206 B.C., near what is now Seville, have brought to light streets, villas, a gymnasium, carved bricks, columns, beautiful mosaics, ceramics, shops, a bakery and nine taverns. Only a small part of the city has been uncovered, but Juan De Mapa Calliazo, professor of history at the University of Seville, who has been named to direct the excavation, believes that the find is one of major historical importance. It may be possible to restore to a measure of its grandeur much of the ancient city. Lucio Mumio, conqueror of Corinth, brought to the Roman city a great amount of the rich spoils of war, inscriptions on monuments have shown. The city thrived, and must have been one of great splendor. T

Geneva—(#)—The League of Nations Saturday apparently averted another international crisis by inducting Italy and Ethiopia to settle their African border difficulties in direct negotiations. A private session of the league council ratified an agreement, previously accepted by representatives of the two nations, whereby they pledged themselves to avoid new military conflict. If the controversy is not settled by May, the agreement provided, it will come up for discussion before the council session.

ROME, Jan. 19 (P)—A spokesman for the ancient Colonna family tonight said the family knew nothing of the reports that Helen, former queen of Rumania, was engaged to marry an Italian prince of the Colonna line. He admitted the possibility, however, that the divorced wife of King Carol of Rumania might be engaged to some member of one of the more remote branches of the family. (A Rome dispatch to the London Sunday Express said the Grecian princess had accepted an offer of marriage from an Italian prince, identified only as an ex-cavalry officer and member of the noble Colonna family.)

Washington, Jan. 10.---(/P)--An agreement for making available in a lump sum to be administered by the president the $4,000,000,000 requested by the administration for the new work relief program was reached today by President Roosevelt and Congressional leaders. It was agreed however that congress would specify how the regular annual $230,000,000 public works appropriation would be spent. Chairman Buchanan, of the house appropriations committee, said the huge work relief measure would be taken up in due course. It will be preceded by a deficiency measure to provide for emergency expenditures. The congressional conferees indicated the proposal by the President for authorization to spend $886,000,000 of unexpended balances in meeting direct relief needs for the next few months would be handled as a separate bill. 1935-02-01.text: Hongkong, Feb. 1.—(AP)—Two Russian guards aboard the S. S. Tungchow, carrying 75 American, British and Scandinavian school children, were killed by pirates, according to a report today to the China Navigation company agents in Shanghai. All the children were reported safe. The British second engineer of the ship, which is under British registry, K. McDonald, was reported wounded. The casualties were presumed to have occurred during the battle for the vessel. The British Naval Intelligence in Shanghai was advised that the vessel headed for Junk Bay, Hong Kong, after its release and was due to arrive late tonight. The Shanghai agents for the China Navigation company, owners of the Tungchow, refused to divulge any information concerning the vessel’s seizure, but asserted that all the passengers on board were unharmed. Word of the steamer’s safety came while British war vessels combed the Ch

LONDON, Feb. 14.—French circles reported today a communique has been drafted reaffirming Germany’s right to arms equality within a system of general security, and will be issued at the conclusion of the Anglo-French ministerial conference tomorrow. The British foreign office declined to comment. The British intimated, however, that an official statement may be expected tomorrow indicating how the British and French intend to proceed in their efforts to ease the tension in Europe. It was understood also that Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, and Pierre-Etienne Flandin, French premier, will have an opportunity to discuss stabilization at a week-end party given by Sir Gomes.

SHANGHAI, Feb. 1 (P)—The missing steamer Tungchow was located today in Bias Bay where pirates had abandoned her after killing one of the crew and wounding two others. None of the 40 school children aboard was harmed. The children, most of them British, were returning from a holiday visit to Hongkong and Shanghai. They were en route to Chefoo on the Shantung promontory when the pirates, members of the notorious band infesting Bias Bay, attacked the ship, overcame the crew and ransacked her. The man killed was an engineer. The wounded were Russian guards. Three British warships and a host of British seaplanes had been searching the coast from Shanghai to Chefoo for the vessel, which left here January 29.

LONDON, Feb. 1—(UP)—Four of Europe's leading political figures today began a two-day series of talks they hope will prove to be the first step—however short it may be—toward stabilizing European armaments. Prime Minister Ramsay Macdonald and Sir John Simon, foreign minister, represented Great Britain; Premier Pierre Etienne Flandin and Foreign Minister Pierre Laval represented France. The talks were started at No. 10 Downing Street, Macdonald's official residence. Flandin and Laval motored from their quarters at the Savoy Hotel and were met by Macdonald, Simon, Stanley Baldwin, Lord President of the Council, and Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal and chief British disarmament negotiator. As the meetings began today, British sources said that no hard agreement was sought, because Germany might interpret it as a joint French-British demand. Flandin and Laval, it was said, sought to ensure that

LONDON (PP) Pirates attacked the steamship Tungchow as it conveyed 70 school children, some of them possibly Americans, across the China Sea, but abandoned it after killing at least one ship's officer, according to unconfirmed dispatches Friday. The dispatches came from the Hong Kong correspondent of the exchange telegraph and the Shanghai correspondent of the Evening Standard. It was the Hong Kong correspondent who reported the attack and the abandonment of the ship by the pirates. He said it was reported also that the Tungchow was proceeding to Chefoo, its destination, under escort of British naval ships who had been seeking it. A Russian guard on the ship was reported injured by the pirates, the correspondent said. The Evening Standard Shanghai correspondent asserted that Americans were among the school children on the ship, returning to Chefoo after a holiday at Shanghai.

Copyright, 1935, Associated Press Berlin, Feb. 1.—The Saar plebiscite heralded as an important factor for the pacification of Europe, bids fair to start trouble among those many Germans of central Europe, who live beyond the boundaries of the Third Reich: In Danzig the Nazi district leader, Albert Forster, declared at a mass meeting in celebration of the event: "The result would be no different in Danzig, if the way were open for a return to Germany. The entire German population of Danzig would unequivocally vote loyalty to the Reich." A little farther to the east, in Memel, the Saar result kindled hopes that some day a plebiscite might be ordered for this strip of territory to determine whether it should remain under Lithuanian stewardship or be returned to Germany. The German press has assiduously nursed this hope, although Lithuanians say there is no occasion or prospect of a plebisci

SHANGHAI, (JP) — Shanghai banks pooled their dwindling silver resources Friday in efforts to weather a monetary crisis which within 24 hours has closed two large native banks here. A third failure was averted temporarily by a pool in which six financial institutions participated. Further closings, however, were predicted generally as the economic situation steadily became more serious. Bankers and merchants dreaded the approach of Feb. 4—Chinese New Year and "settlement day" when custom dictates that Chinese debtors settle their accounts and begin a new year free of debt. Unless the debtors can obtain silver, basic currency in a country where paper money is practically worthless, many merchants may be forced into bankruptcy. Government leaders were conferring at Nanking seeking a way out of the crisis. A reorganization of the ancient monetary system, based on silver, was considered. Deva

Rome, Feb. 1.—(UP)—Strength counts in international relations, Premier Benito Mussolini said today, enjoining his fascists to be strong and his fellow countrymen to be workers and soldiers at the same time. Clad in his corporal’s uniform with a new type of blue gray helmet, Mussolini shouted to a great gathering of his men. “Today's celebration brings our minds back to my 'armored tank' speech, namely, the Italian people must be workers and soldiers at the same time. “It is more than ever true today (Continued on Page 6)

1935-12-05.text: LONDON, Dec. 5— (UP) — Great Britain is ready to join in an oil embargo against Italy, and feels that as long as the Ethiopian war continues "there is little to be gained by resuming the discussions of the reduction of armaments," Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today. His statement was made during a debate on foreign affairs. At Paris, French and British foreign experts have completed the broad outlines of a proposal for peaceful settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian war, it is understood. It is intended that Premier Laval and Sir Samuel Hoare shall perfect the plan at a talk at Paris Saturday, and send it on to Premier Mussolini next week. At Rome, an unofficial government spokesman said today that Italy sees no foundation for recent foreign optimism about the possibility of an Italian-Ethiopian settlement. (DY ASSOCIATED Press) London, Dec. 3—Great Britain, in a tense atmosphere of European sanctions and what they may mean, stiffened her capital defenses against possible air attacks last night. Immediate reorganization of anti-aircraft defenses in the London area was announced. An entire division of four anti-aircraft groups was formed and charged with the defense of the city against any assault from the skies. Each of the four groups within the division is larger than an infantry brigade. Each will have headquarters where it can best cooperate with the Royal Air Force, which itself was expanded recently. The move followed upon today’s Cabinet meeting—a session which brought widespread predictions that oil shortly will be added to the long list of economic measures the League of Nations has taken against Italy. LONDON—Hoare considering important speech in Commons on Italian-Ethiopian crisis; British see series of swift peace moves; two battle cruisers, four destroyers, leave Gibraltar for cruises in Atlantic. ROME—Mussolini watching French-British moves and east African situation; offensive expected at any time; Bank of Italy and treasury formally suspend statements of condition. CAIRO—British continue to strengthen forces in Egypt. UNDATED—A dual clash, ostensible reason for Italian-Ethiopian War, occurred a year ago today.

Paris, Dec. 4--A joint Anglo-French request to Premier Mussolini to submit his peace terms before the League of Nations is forced to vote on an oil embargo was reported as a possibility tonight in informed circles. This move might be drafted when Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary, confers with Premier Laval here Saturday on the war situation. Only stony silence thus far has met Laval's efforts to have Rome indicate on what basis it will negotiate or even whether Italy is ready to negotiate at all. Favors Joint Note Laval is said to favor a joint note with the British minister in the belief a further sign of Franco-British solidarity would make Mussolini more willing to disclose his desires. Although it was suggested in some quarters that Laval might ask for a week's delay in application of the oil embargo, an informed source said “the embargo undoubtedly will be imposed.” Diffe

| LONDON, Dec. 4,-(INS)—The British Cabinet today put the finishing touches on a plan for peace in East Africa, which perhaps significantly, is expected to be acceptable to Premier Benito Mussolini but not to Emperor Haile Selassie. Whereas previous proposals associated with the British Government have been more acceptable to Ethiopia than to Italy, the plan now under consideration is declared in authoritative circles to contain strong elements of satisfaction for Il Duce but concession pile which the Negus may find hard to swallow.

CANBERRA, Australia, Dec. 5.—(@) The Australian government announced today it was equipping two air force planes with wireless, floats and skis to be used in an Antarctic search for Lincoln Ellsworth and his pilot, Herbert Hollick-Kenyon. Prime Minister Joseph A. Lyons telegraphed President Roosevelt that this act was a gesture of friendship for America. Ellsworth and Hollick-Kenyon have not been heard from since their radio failed on a trans-Atlantic flight Nov. 23. The New York Times and the North American Newspaper Alliance in a copyrighted article said F. Truhee Davison, president of the American Museum of Natural History, announced plans to rush emergency rations to Antarctica for the explorer and his pilot. Davison said a sister ship of Ellsworth's plane, “Polar Star,” has been acquired to leave for Magallanes, Chile, tomorrow or Saturday and then sail for the Antarctic aboard the

WITH THE ITALIAN TROOPS OF MAKALE, Ethiopia, Dec. 3.— (AP)—Italy’s Eritrean troops met the main body of the Ethiopian northern army face to face today in a brief clash at outposts on the Dolo-Makale line. The fighting was over quickly, the Ethiopians retiring almost immediately. One Italian white soldier was reported wounded. The enemy losses were not known. Authorities said the skirmish was not the big St. George's day battle for which they were prepared. However, they considered it significant because it indicated strong forces on both sides now are within reach of each other. Coincident with the initial clash, it was announced a number of lieutenants of Deggiac Kassa Sebat, who fought against the Italians recently at Azbi, were submitting to the Fascists. Large Ethiopian forces are advancing towards the Makale front, reports to Italian headquarters said.

1935-03-18.text: The European situation at a glance: Great Britain formally protested Germany’s rearming as threatening the peace of Europe. Germany replied it was willing to discuss the Anglo-French peace system for Europe as scheduled in Berlin. Concerted action of France, England and Italy appeared in abeyance. In Germany conscription of soldiers was under way and the storm troops were reported disbanding. The President of Russia warned that “war may break out unexpectedly” and called on his armed forces to be prepared.

LONDON, March 20. (4)—Even though she has decided to cast off her princely husband, Barbara Hutton Mdivani still wants to be called “princess.” Hotel flunkies serving her were under strict orders Monday to continue to use the title, although she has announced she is going to speed to Reno as fast as she can to make the third “marrying Mdivani” prince a free lance. Hotel employees have been almost the only persons to have contact with Princess Barbara the last two days, during which the five-and-ten cent store heiress has remained in seclusion in her suite. Even her “kid cousin” as she likes to call gangling, pink-cheeked Jimmie Donahue, went off on pursuits of his own Sunday night, remaining out on a party until the wee hours of Monday morning. In announcing her divorce plans, Princess Barbara insisted her prince was not going to get a nickel of the Woolworth fortune to which she is heir

Europe, jolted by Adolf Hitler into the realization that war is inevitable unless preventive action is taken promptly, went into action under Great Britain's leadership today to meet Germany's overthrow of the Versailles treaty. The British cabinet considered a strong note to Germany which was understood not to argue about Germany’s rearming, but to ask Hitler, in effect, if he would not talk terms and cooperate with the other nations to avert war. France consulted the other powers and favored joint representations to Germany. At the same time, she intended to go ahead with her plans for treaties of mutual security in Europe, with or without German participation. Other Nations to Follow. London, March 17.—()—Barbara Hutton Mdivani, 842,000,000 American princess, insisted Sunday that when she gets her divorce from her Georgian prince she will not have to settle a single penny upon him—he is going to have to shift for himself. "This has been mutually agreed upon," said the princess with a determined air. "Besides he has property himself in Spain and other places in Europe, and of interests in the United States. "He will continue to fill in a position in the Georgian legation in Paris." Princess Barbara denied reports that she had ever granted Alexis a separate allowance during her less than two years of married life. She announced Saturday night that she had instructed her lawyer in New York to institute divorce proceedings. The Woolworth heiress seemed composed Sunday, although she smoked innumerable cigarettes. Paris, Mar. 18 (AP)—France today sought a “union of peaceful peoples” as a war dike around rearmed Germany. The British view was regarded authoritatively as what would determine whether the old allies would protest jointly against Reichsfuehrer Hitler's scrapping of the peace treaty. But government officials said it was inevitable that “an alignment if not an alliance” of Great Britain, France, Italy, and possibly others would be sought for a defensive working agreement. A solemn pledge among the three powers that they fight together in the event of a new European war was proposed in French military circles as perhaps “the most efficacious guarantee of peace.” Hope For Russia's Aid France also is hopeful of support from Soviet Russia whose army is being made one of the most powerful in Europe. A joint protest to Berlin is regarded as certain by officials. They said it would follow consul

London, May 1, (U.P) — An anxious cabinet met today to formulate Great Britain’s policy in an armaments crisis whose urgent gravity is only now becoming apparent. Immediate protest to Germany against its submarine building program or prior consultation with France and Italy were alternatives to be considered. The government’s decision is to be revealed—if not before—at a debate on foreign policy in the House of Commons tomorrow. The cabinet met with a picture drawn by intelligence agents of the allied powers, which convinced them that a rearmed Germany is not a threat but a fact. How earnestly statesmen of Great Britain, as well as France and Italy, view the German rearmament threat may be gathered from the following summary of reports.
