{associated Press foreign staff) Berlin, March 12.—(?)—The German public received its first official information today that the Reich’s military air force is already in existence. Wilhelm Goering, minister of aviation, confirmed the long prevalent rumors and announced he would head the air force as ‘general of fliers.’ “It also became known that Germany's civilian ‘Air Sport’ Association has been placed under the direct orders of the Reichswehr (regular Army), thus becoming an integral part of the Reich’s defense forces. It was declared on good authority that the action departed from the provisions of the air clauses of the Treaty of Versailles. Military attaches of the powers signatory to the treaty, it was said, would be officially informed of the change March 23. In acknowledging that Germany has an air fleet, Goering said: “Our willingness to participate actively in safeguarding worl

1935-01-13.text: (By the Associated Press) Cold weather today brought relief from flood danger to all New England except a tiny hamlet in New Hampshire which was faced with isolation as an ice jam threatened to carry away a bridge at its main entrance. Five deaths—four in Connecticut and one in Vermont—were left in the wake of the swollen rivers which receded rapidly under the influence of freezing temperatures. Ice piled up in the Ammonoosuc River for distances of 200 feet above and below a bridge leading to Stark, N.H., a community of 30 souls, and residents feared that if the ice was suddenly released it would carry away the structure. Only two narrow country lanes provided other access to Stark, and one of them is already under water and the other almost impassable at this time of year. Another ice jam further upstream threatened ominously, for if it gave way townsfolk feared it would sweep the lower

Paris, Jan, 12—(4)—Twelve hundred communist hunger marchers converging upon Paris with cries for overcoats and an increased dole were defeated in a clash today during the season's first snow storm. The communists were dispersed by a wall of steel-helmeted mobile guards near the city gates. A column of demonstrators from the west broke ranks and trickled into the city in groups to attend three mass meetings this afternoon. Police barred the way of smaller columns from other directions. The demonstrators engaged in a general scuffle with the gendarmes but found themselves no match for their well-fed opponents. Quickly dispersed, the communists said they would make another attempt to enter the city later today after they had been reinforced by additional marchers from the neighboring department of Seine-Etoile.

Paris, Jan. 12.—( #) —A snow storm combined with massed battalions of police broke up a march of discontented jobless persons on the capital in defiance of the government's prohibition of demonstrations today. There were skirmishes in which a number of heads were cracked, but no fatalities. The marchers, estimated to number 1,200, never reached the chamber of deputies, which was their goal, but were scattered by police at the meetings at widely separated halls in the city. Cries of "Work or bread!" and the chant of "The Internationale" accompanied the charges of demonstrators on massed police in suburban Paris. Red workers from communist strongholds in the capital and suburbs were among those wounded in the clashes with police. Delegations were selected at the various meetings to carry petitions to communist deputies in the chamber, which was not in session.

PARIS, Jan. 12 (UP).—Thousands of unemployed demonstrators clashed with police in the suburbs of Paris today while other thousands met inside the city to demand relief measures. More than a score were injured in the fighting and half a hundred were arrested. Unemployed marchers who came through a snowstorm and bitter cold from northern France joined hundreds of others in half a dozen suburbs, where strong police forces used nightsticks freely to prevent the crowds from entering the city. Police also guarded three halls in Paris where a total of about 11,000 unemployed met to demand relief. The demonstrators held outside the city in Cour de Vincennes, Saint Denis, and other suburbs continued their efforts to enter.

(Copyright. 1935, by the Associated Press) FLEMINGTON, N. J., Jan. 12.~ Bruno Richard Hauptmann’s defense put its handwriting experts to work on the Lindbergh ransom notes today in an attempt to show they were written by wraith-like Isador Fisch. Taking advantage of a weekend recess in Hauptmann’s trial for life, the defense authorities also sought flaws in evidence presented by the state that the notes were written by Hauptmann himself. ° Edward J. Reilly, urbane chief of defense for Hauptmann in his trial for the murder of the kidnapped Lindbergh infant, said: “We will prove that Fisch not only collected the ransom but also wrote the ransom notes.” Rival Claims Made. Ever since his arrest, the Bronx carpenter has insisted that the $14,600 in ransom money found in his possession was given to him by Fisch, his former business partner who died obscurely in Germany. “The state produced evi

TRENTON, N. J., Jan. 12, UP) Defense counsel said today they would investigate reports that a “double” for Bruno R. Hauptmann, charged with the Lindbergh baby murder, had been found and might be able to refute prosecution testimony that Hauptmann was seen near the Lindbergh home on the day of the crime. FLEMINGTON, N. J., Jan. 12, UP) New Jersey will trace a total of $49,600 to Bruno Richard Hauptmann and prove that it is all but $400 of the $50,000 Col. Charles A. Lindbergh paid to ransom a baby already dead, the prosecution claimed today. This staggering blow against the taciturn German carpenter charged with kidnapping and murdering the Lindbergh baby was planned even while the state marshaled a great array of experts who will prove beyond doubt, the prosecution said, that Hauptmann wrote each and every one of the ransom letters sent Colonel Lindbergh and his intermediary, Dr. John F.

NEWTON, Mass., Jan. 12. ()-- Threat to “destroy” the six-year-old son of Thomas P. Beal, president of the Second National Bank of Boston, was revealed today. Demands for $25,000 and warnings that Thomas O. Beal Jr. would be “destroyed” unless immediate payment was made, were received first by the Beal family two months ago. Federal agents have been working on the case secretly. Meanwhile, telephone threats repeating the first written demand have been received.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 12. — Though President Roosevelt will lay a broad general program for social security before Congress next week, leaders understood today he would place upon them the responsibility of drafting the detailed legislation. Under this procedure, it will be left to Congress to decide, for instance, whether the payroll tax to finance unemployment insurance will be three or five per cent, and whether the fund will be financed entirely by employers or partly by employees. Generally, it is understood on the Capitol Hill, the report of the committee on security which the President will lay before Congress, will point toward a bill of the kind introduced last session by Senator Wagner (D-NY) and Representative Lewis (D-Md), on unemployment insurance. Recommendations on old age pensions were being even more

1935-03-23.text: DETROIT, March 23.—(4)—Martin J. Insull, freed of charges which developed from the collapse of the utilities empire built by his brother, Samuel, was deported to Canada today as a British subject. Insull, who had lived in the United States forty years, was ordered deported more than a year ago when he was extradited from Canada to face charges of embezzlement in connection with the receivership of the holding company which he headed as president. He was acquitted.

_ Copyright, 1935, Ass'd Press PARIS, March 23.—France, Italy and England agreed today to stand together ‘in complete unity of purpose’ in dealing with the German arms crisis. At Britain’s insistence, the tri-power parley held here to ‘prepare the way for Anglo-German conversations in Berlin Monday and Tuesday agreed to proceed cautiously and survey the ground thoroughly before forcing the issue before the League of Nations. Capt. Anthony Eden, who will accompany Foreign Minister Sir John Simon to Berlin tomorrow spoke for Great Britain; Foreign Minister Pierre Laval, who yesterday demanded ‘re-grouping of the allies’ against Germany, represented France; Under-Secretary of State Fulvio Suvich was Italy's spokesman. Even as the three met, the French general staff announced the transfer of some 30,000 troops to garrisons nearer the Rhine. Italy, through Premier Benito Mussolini, summoned 2

(By The Associated Press) London naval circles heard today that Germany would demand a navy equal to that of Italy or France to complement her newly-created air and land forces. While the diplomatic representatives of France, Italy and Great Britain prepared to journey to Paris for tomorrow's tri-partite conference, the eyes of all Europe were turned to the forthcoming conference at Berlin between Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and Reichsfuehrer Hitler. On the success or failure of the Berlin negotiations was expected to depend the entire policy of Western European powers with regard to preservation of stability upon the continent. LONDON -—= "The possibility was seen that failure of the Berlin talks would result in a system of European alliances to encircle rearmed Germany with an “iron wall.” PARIS—While diplomats went forward with their plans to seek a peaceful solution of

Paris. Mar. 23.--(4)--The three power conference here between France, England and Italy announced this afternoon that “complete unity of purpose” among their governments was apparent from the day long conversations on Germany's rearmament. It was agreed that Sir John Simon's talk with Hitler would follow the line of the London declaration following the Anglo-French agreement and would be of “exploratory character”. Mussolini's three power conference to determine international policy after Sir John's visit to Berlin will be held at Stresa, Italy, on April 12 it was announced. The Stresa conference will be held after the visit of Captain Anthony Eden to Moscow, Warsaw and Praha, Czechoslovakia and after the visit to the Rumanian foreign minister to Paris and London so that the views of the various countries and the little entente will be available.

Parts, March 23.—Complete unity of purpose among France, England and Italy was announced late today as a result of the daylong three-power conference on German rearmament on the eve of Sir John Simon's momentous visit to Berlin. Backed by Premier Mussolini's autocratic order mobilizing 220,000 additional men and official French admission of the transfer of troops to the Rhine frontier, the conference announced agreement that the British foreign secretary's talk with Hitler will follow the lines of the London declaration following the Anglo-French agreement and will be of exploratory character. Mussolini's three-power conference, after Sir John's visit, was set for April 11 at Stresa, Italy. France was understood to have proposed at the conference that public discussion on penalties for Germany take place at a meeting of the League of Nations, the penalties suggested being mainly economic

Associated Press, Copyrighted 193%. Paris, March 22.—France tomorrow will endeavor to plant England firmly within a united front with France and Italy against a re-armed Germany. Capt. Anthony Eden, British Lord Privy Seal, who came here today for a tri-partite conference preparatory to Anglo-German conversations in Berlin, almost certainly will be asked to drop the role of mediator for that of ally. Foreign Minister Pierre Laval, who will confer with Eden and Italy’s Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs, Fulvio Suyvich, himself told the Chamber of Deputies today: “France seeks to regroup the allies.” Elsewhere influential quarters alarmed at the Reich’s swift rearmament and angered at her cool reception of the French protest note, were calling for “action rather than words.” French officials said Laval would warn Eden against Sir John Simon's “going or promising anything” in his conversa

LONDON, March 23.—A hint of British isolation from continental quarrels appeared on the turbulent European scene today as Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, prepared for his momentous talks with Reichsführer Hitler in Berlin. Sir John himself, in a speech to constituents in the Spen Valley near Leeds last night said, "we cannot indulge in every sort of foreign adventure over all the world or pledge our activity to everybody’s quarrel." The foreign secretary previously told the House of Commons Britain has no enthusiasm for special pacts and insisted he was not contemplating a special agreement with any nation. Nevertheless Simon awaited the draft of questions Italian, French and British officials framed in Paris today which he is expected to put to Hitler. These in effect, are expected to demand whether Germany intends to enter or remain outside of a new system of security for Europe. Th

UNITED front against Germany's rearmament seemed unlikely than ever Saturday with the scheduled start of tri-power conversations at which France seemed certain to try to get Great Britain to drop the role of mediator and assume that of ally. With world attention on Sunday's visit to Berlin by Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and Capt. Anthony Eden, lord privy seal, Eden flew to Paris for preliminary explorations with French and Italian statesmen. Evidencing France's lack of faith in the prospect of the British getting Germany into any security agreement was Foreign Minister Pierre Laval's assertion Thursday that France "must regroup the allies" and reported preparations to move 25,000 French troops from the Italian to the German border. 1935-01-27.text: SEATTLE, Jan. 26. (A) — Gigantic earth slides and floods in the wake of a near record-breaking storm added eleven deaths tonight to the growing list of casualties and losses in the Pacific Northwest. The additional fatalities were reported in water-soaked British Columbia, bringing to 15 the number of dead in the Canadian province. Previously four persons were listed as dead in British Columbia and ten in American territory, bringing the aggregate to 25. Several Missing. Several persons were missing. Some of these were believed to have been buried deep under countless tons of earth and water unleashed by the storm. Many others were injured, Hundreds remained marooned. Several villages were evacuated and cities and towns still were isolated. Sunshine warmed the flood-stricken.

DEATH TOLL IS 30 | BOSTON, Jan. 26 (P)—New England’s death toll resulting directly or indirectly from Wednesday's blizzard mounted to 30 today. Seven additional deaths were reported overnight, all from Massachusetts. Clear and colder was the forecast for tomorrow:

SEATTLE, Jan. 25—(UP)—The Pacific northwest’s death toll in eight days of snow, cold and floods reached 20 tonight, as floods abated in western Washington and British Columbia where property damage was estimated in the millions of dollars. Four deaths were reported today. Three men were killed when an avalanche of snow roared over a workman's camp near Revelstoke, B.C. Mrs. Letta A. Cooper, 77, was killed by snow and ice that cascaded from the roof of her residence at Bonner’s Ferry, Idaho, as she was dislodging icicles.

DOORN, Holland, —-?)—sSor- rew over the Mohawk disaster tonight marred the former German Kaiser’s preparations to celebrate his 76th birth anniversary. Hale and hearty and feeling younger than in years, Wilhelm II, last of the German emperors, was engrossed in the fate of the hapless steamer’s victims and the disasters attending America’s cold wave even more than in the approaching celebration. “Grandfather is deeply shocked,” the prince said, “at the Mohawk disaster. As to the weather, he displayed the greatest interest in the stoppage of streetcars, the widespread area of the snowstorm and other details of the American weather situation.

MOSCOW, Jan. 26 (4)—Thousands of workers trudged through Moscow's great Hall of the Columns today to look upon the body of Valerian Kuibesheff, the second member of Russia's “big ten” to die in the last two months. Kuibesheff, who was 47, died suddenly yesterday of arteriosclerosis. He was vice president of the council of people's commissars and member of the all-power political bureau of 10 which guides the communist party and, hence, the destinies of the Soviet Union.

OSLO, Norway, Jan. 26.--(U.P)—Prof. Klaus Hansen, of Oslo University, underwent blood and other tests today so that he and other scientists might find out whether he is ‘going to emerge’ unharmed from his experiment in drinking “heavy water.” Nobody knows certainly whether the heavy water is ‘poisonous to human beings. Prof. Hansen joins in the growing belief that it is not—with some reason—for yesterday he drank, with apparent impunity, the largest dose any man has taken... “But he is determined to find out beyond doubt. To this end, if today’s tests show him to be normal, he intends to drink more doses, each dose a larger one, until he is able to take a dose of three ounces, which will cost $1000. Prof. Harold Clayton Urey, of Columbia University, New York City, discovered heavy water in 1931, and was awarded the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work. The water is used principally

DOORN, Holland, Jan. 29—Wilhelm the second, the former German kaiser who will be 76 tomorrow, looks with apprehension upon the nazi government's effort to crush the remaining spark of monarchism in the reich. He read with misgivings a recent statement by Dr. Joseph Paul Goebbels, minister of propaganda, in which Goebbels insisted “Germany needs no emperor.” It has been reported to him that monarchists in December and also this month, have gone into hiding for days at a time because of persistent reports a general raid would be made on persons of known monarchistic leanings.

By The Associated Press MADRID, Jan. 26.—Jose Sanchez Guerra, 75, former premier of Spain in the days of the monarchy, died today. Late in 1932 he suffered a paralytic stroke from which he never entirely recovered.

1935-12-11.text: Londen, Dec. 11—(AP)—The British government tonight made public the text of a note delivered by the British embassy in Washington to the state department again stating that Great Britain declines to make the semi-annual payment due on its war debt to the United States. The amount due Dec. 15 is $117,670,765.05. In its note calling attention that payment was due the United States expressed its readiness to discuss any proposals which the British government might desire to put forward on the question. In his reply the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, said, "It does not appear to my government that circumstances have so changed since their note of June 4, 1934, as to enable proposals to be put forward at the present time which would be acceptable to both governments. "They wish to repeat, however, that they will be glad to resume discussions whenever the situation warrants the hope t

(Associated Press Staff Writer) The program of Great Britain and France for peace in East Africa encountered an early obstacle today, Ethiopian officials asserting Emperor Haile Selassie would lose his throne if he dared to accept the proposal. The Addis Ababa government authorities said northern Tigre Province must be kept by Ethiopia lest native chieftains, ordered to retreat, rise in revolt on grounds that they ‘could have defended the province successfully. These officials described the peace plan and its reported provisions for exchange of land between Italy and Ethiopia as a “reward for Italy for breaking covenants, and another device to delay further sanctions.” Haile Selassie’s Paris minister, Wolde Mariam, conferred with Premier Pierre Laval on the terms, as did Premier Mussolini's ambassador, Vittorio Cerruti. Il Duce generally was expected to accept the proposals. MORE PENALTI

‘DY Associated Press} London, Dec. 11—Japan’s long diplomatic campaign for a navy equal to any came to a climax today with Admiral Nagano ready to make an emphatic demand to the international naval conference for equality with the United States and Great Britain. The Japanese delegation between adjournment of the conference yesterday and its meeting this afternoon evolved a detailed presentation of their argument for abolition of the 5-3-3 ratio system and substitution of the same tonnage for each power. The spokesmen for other delegations described this afternoon's meeting as an “extremely important session.” The consensus of opinion among observers was that it opened the most critical period of the parley called to find a new agreement to replace the Washington and London naval limitations treaties expiring at the end of next year. The Japanese demand was that a tonnage limit should be

LONDON. (UP). Japan, demanding naval equality with Great Britain and the United States, suggested at the five power naval conference that the three navies be reduced to the lowest possible level, entailing the scrapping of warships. The Japanese spokesman, Adm. Osami Nagano, head of the Japanese delegation, told the conference he was urging parity for the United States, Britain and Japan only on a total tonnage basis. He thus rejected the British and American thesis that navies should be limited by specifying the number and size of ships each nation can build in any given type of fighting craft.

(Copyright, 1935, By Associated Press.) "CAIRO, Dec. 11.—The cabinet of Premier Tewfik Necim Pasha, under nationalist pressure to end the British influence in this nominally independent kingdom, decided today to resign. The resignations will be submitted to King Fuad tomorrow, and it was understood authoritatively the king would accept them. Immediately after the cabinet's decision was reached, the Premier, accompanied by Mohamed Mahmoud Pasha, leader of the liberal constitutionalists, went to the home of Former Premier Nahas Pasha, chief of the powerful Wafd (nationalist) party. They held a council of peace, drawing up plans to present a united front in seeking changed British influences in Egypt. This was the first meeting of the tri-

LONDON, Dec. 10.—(AP)—Delegates of four powers, in a surprise agreement with Japan today, squarely met the major obstacle of the international naval conference by placing the question of total tonnages on the program as the first order of business. This issue is the danger point of the deliberations; because it contains Japan's demand for naval equality with the United States and Great Britain and the scrapping of the ratio system. Quick acceptance of Japan’s request for immediate discussion of the tonnage issue left the Orientals momentarily nonplussed. They had expected the British to challenge their views in an effort temporarily to sidetrack the grave issue. Instead, however, today's session, the first business one, was reported to be notably decorous and businesslike, with no hint of the clash of views known to lie ahead. The development, however, did not mean that either Great Brit

(By The Associated Press) The London silver market, which suffered a collapse yesterday, was still stalemated today, and one Democratic United States senator hinted British financiers are trying to halt America's silver-buying policy. No price on silver was fixed in the London market. It was the third successive day that, at the usual time, the price went unannounced. Brokers were awaiting further information from America.

(By The Associated Press) Washington, Dec. 11—Senator Borah, Republican of Idaho, struck out today at the Franco-British proposal to end the Italy-Ethiopian war as a plan which would leave Mussolini “the most powerful figure in Europe” and give him more than he sought in the beginning.

1935-08-21.text: By the Associated Press Vienna — Official government newspaper, Wiener Zeitung, declares Austria backs Italy in Ethiopian attitude. Addis Ababa—Reliable source says Emperor Haile Selassie has hidden war funds; tribal warriors hold sham battle. Paris—Laval negotiates secretly with Mussolini to limit war measures if they cannot be halted. Rome—Fascist cabinet members await call to serve in ranks with army in East Africa. WASHINGTON — The United States Senate adopts resolution designed to safeguard American neutrality in event of foreign war. LONDON—British inform United States of developments in Italo-Ethiopian situation, but make no appeal for review of American policy; British cabinet to outline British policy.

LONDON, Aug. 21—(P)—Seven leaders of the British cabinet today tentatively approved a policy demanding financial and economic action against Italy if that country attacks Ethiopia. The ministers had been called into a special, informal session by Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin. They conferred two hours. Their decision, although tentative, calls for a strong British stand at Geneva, in the forthcoming League of Nations session, for financial and economic sanctions. This idea will be taken up by the full cabinet tomorrow in an emergency meeting. Throughout the day there were indications Great Britain might seek American cooperation outside Geneva for a solution of the Italo-Ethiopian crisis.

(Copyright, 1935, United Press) London, Aug. 21, — Great Britain has appealed to the United States government to review its policy toward the Italian-Ethiopian dispute in the light of acute danger of war, it was learned officially today. Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, made the appeal personally last night to Ray Atherton, charge d'affaires of the American embassy, in a 45 minute conference at the foreign office. News of Hoare's appeal came after Ramsay MacDonald, lord President of the council and until recently prime minister, said on his arrival from his home at Lossiemouth, Scotland, for tomorrow’s emergency cabinet meeting: “I regard the present situation as the most serious we have had to face since 1914,” Representatives of the chief opposition groups in parliament and of Australia, New Zealand and Canada, were called into consultation with Hoare and Anthony Eden, minister for

LONDON, Aug. 20 (#)—Great Britain's foreign experts, an authoritative source indicated Tuesday night, have agreed to recommend to the cabinet Thursday adoption of proposals for economic sanctions by members of the League of Nations against Italy if she fights Ethiopia. This far-reaching decision, it was said, was reached by Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, and Anthony Eden, minister for League of Nations’ affairs. Joint economic and financial sanctions would prevent goods, cash and credit from reaching Italy. Smaller powers and France, it was said, would support the British government should it urge Geneva to adopt this course. If the League fails to act, Britain must then determine upon its own unilateral steps in the face of what it regards as an Italian challenge of England's prestige and dominance of the Mediterranean and Africa.

(Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) London, Aug. 21—Premier Stanley Baldwin and seven of his key ministers tentatively decided late today plans to make a strong British stand at Geneva for economic sanctions against Italy in the event of war. This policy will be placed before an emergency meeting of the full cabinet tomorrow. At the same time the British government did everything but specifically ask the United States to give its full support to London's policy and by implication tried to prompt Washington into voluntarily stating its official views. Report Is Denied (The United States Senate adopted a resolution designed to safeguard American neutrality in the event of a foreign war.) Ray Atherton, American charge d'affaires, had expected to be called to the foreign office tonight, but later went to the country for the night without the British government’s making any formal approach on

ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 21—The British legation today took steps to construct bomb proof shelters for British troops which protect the legation in event Italy attacks Ethiopia. British diplomats purchased 6,000 square yards of heavy corrugated sheet iron for shelters. These also will provide quarters for British civilians. A dispatch detachment of native Indian troops to reinforce the British legation guard at Addis Ababa was announced at Simla today. Reliable sources said Emperor Haile Selassie has a large secret fund of gold and silver to use in fighting Italy in event of hostilities. Money, amounting to several million dollars, was left by the late Emperor Menelik for defense of the country.

WASHINGTON—(UP)—President Roosevelt today said so far as he knows nothing in the way of a request from Great Britain asking the United States to join in efforts under the Kellogg-Briand pact in an effort to avert the Italo-Ethiopian conflict has been received. Mr. Roosevelt dismissed questions concerning the anxiety felt in Europe over the Ethiopian situation with that statement, made in response to the first question fired at him at his semi-weekly press conference. Mr. Roosevelt was equally non-committal regarding his opinion on neutrality legislation. Sen. Gerald P. Nye, R., N. D., by threats of filibuster, has obtained an agreement in the Senate that a vote on sweeping neutrality proposals will be taken before the end of the session. Nye and other sponsors of the legislation cited the threatening Ethiopian situation as a prime reason for immediate action by the Senate.

(By the Associated Press) Indications that Great Britain might urge economic pressure against Italy if she goes to war with Ethiopia arose Tuesday night. London—An authoritative source indicated Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, and Anthony Eden would recommend to the cabinet Wednesday a program whereby League of Nations members would be asked to adopt coercive measures against Rome in the event of hostilities. Rome—Members of the cabinet, other high government officials and Fascist party leaders will go to East Africa for active service. Addis Ababa—Emperor Haile Selassie, who appears tired and worn, is pushing defense measures. Paris—Although pessimistic following the breakdown of the tri-power conference, Premier Pierre Laval has not abandoned his efforts to avert warfare. Djibouti—Djibouti, Ethiopia’s only outlet to the sea, is booming with activity. Huge stocks of munitions consi

1935-12-17.text: A counter-attack on critics of the Anglo-French plan for ending the Italo-Ethiopian war is in preparation by the British government. In receipt of a crescendo of protests against what sharpshooters of the plan contend is a formula for dismembering the kingdom of Haile Selassie, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, informed sources said Monday, is collecting material for presentation to the House of Commons. The British cabinet, in token of the seriousness with which Britain has received the storm of criticism at Geneva and in various European capitals evoked by publication of the Paris scheme for ending the war, met in an emergency session. He made this statement to Admiral Osami Nagano, the chief Japanese delegate, directly across a private conference table. Davis told the assembled conferees that the usefulness of the Washington treaty of 1922—which set the British-American-Japanese navies on a 5-5-3 ratio—had been fully demonstrated and that there was no reason to change the existing system. BALTIMORE (AP)—Lizette Woadsworth Reese, NY, poetess and writer of “Tears,” described as one of the most perfect sonnets in the English language, died early today. Miss Reese died at 4:28 a.m. at the church home and infirmary. She had been a patient there for several weeks, announcing when she entered the hospital that she was going to take a rest cure.

Italy, apparently not content with Franco-British peace proposals which have stirred criticism in those countries for being too generous, was reported to have countered Monday night with new demands. Although Benito Mussolini let it be known in Rome he must wait on the Fascist Grand Council before replying formally to the two-power plan, diplomats in Paris said he had asked Premier Laval, through his ambassador, for wider concessions. The Paris reports said he demanded the holy city of Aksum, which the Anglo-French plan would give to Ethiopia; that he wants a colonization zone with no strings attached and with Italian-controlled police; that the seaport of Assab, Eritrea, must remain in Italy’s hands, with mere free-port rights for Emperor Haile Selassie. LONDON, Dec. 17 (W.P) - Popular apprehension in Japan over the possibility of a naval war with the United States was candidly described today by Admiral Osami Nagano, chief Japanese delegate to the naval conference. Nagano made his statement at a private conference between the Japanese and United States delegations at Claridge’s Hotel. He made it clear that because of the fear of the Japanese people for their safety in the event of a naval attack, Japan must reject President Roosevelt's suggestion for a general 20 per cent reduction in the strength of all navies. Japan, Nagano said, believes that the proposed cut would maintain existing ratios - 5 for Britain and the United States and 3 for Japan - and cause continued Japanese uneasiness over the superior strength of the United States. A becalmed African warfront appeared headed for new and bigger battles Sunday night. Optimism for the success of a Franco-British plan was conspicuous by its absence. And from the southern theater of war three Ethiopian columns of 40,000 men were reported only 30 miles from the Italian positions at Dolo, with the zero hour for an Ethiopian attack long overdue. Gen. Rudolfo Graziani, commander of the Italian Somaliland armies, promised to “drive straight and hard” at the foe when the opportunity presents itself. In the north, too, officers predicted a smashing campaign before long under the leadership of Marshal Pietro Badoglio, their new commander-in-chief. LONDON, Dec. 17.—(#)—A British retreat from active support of the Hoare-Laval plan for peace in Ethiopia was strongly indicated today as the government, in a cabinet meeting, outlined its position. Leaders of the cabinet met in the drawing room of Sir Samuel Hoare, the foreign secretary, consulting as to the British policy. As Anthony Eden, minister for League of Nations affairs, departed by train for Geneva at 2 p.m., authoritative quarters stated it was unlikely he would withdraw from his statement at Geneva last week: "If the League of Nations does not agree with our suggestions, we shall make no complaint." The cabinet’s attention, however, was understood to be principally concerned with repairing the badly shattered government defenses in Parliament in preparation for Thursday’s debate in the House of Commons. (Copyright 1935 by United Press) LONDON, (UP).—The cabinet met in emergency session today to decide its policy in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis. This policy entails success in three problems: 1. To achieve unity in the cabinet itself, 2. To decide on the manner of the government's defense when the House of Commons debates Thursday the French-British proposals for settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian war. 3. Great Britain's future course as regards the Italian-Ethiopian crisis, its relations with France and Italy, and its activities in the League of Nations.

(By the Associated Press) Geneva, Oct. 27.—France notified the League of Nations today she has accepted economic sanctions against Italy. Thus she joined Great Britain in a drive to isolate Benito Mussolini because he has made war on Ethiopia. Both France and Britain now have announced their readiness to enforce the most powerful sanction—an economic boycott of Italy—by agreeing to buy nothing from the Fascist state and by stopping the exportation to Italy of certain key products, especially those needed in the manufacture of armaments, munitions and implements of war. Laval Wires Acceptance Premier Pierre Laval telegraphed the French acceptance of economic sanctions. He informed League officials these would be applied on the date to be fixed by the League, but asked four days’ time to take the necessary steps. Great Britain and France are prepared, when the League of Nations penalties committee meets Thursday to continue the program of penalizing Italy for its war. It was said on reliable authority that the British government believes that if Britain and France push the penalties program with sufficient vigor, penalties can be made an effective deterrent to Italy’s campaign in Ethiopia. London, Oct. 28—Twin boys born to Lady Charles Cavendish and her titled husband on Saturday lived only a short time, it was announced today. Lady Cavendish is the former Adele Astaire, sister of Fred Astaire, the dancer. She and Lord Cavendish were married in May, 1932. The death of the babies was the second bereavement to visit the Cavendish home in a little more than two years. In October, 1933, their first child, a girl, died when only three hours old. Lady Cavendish and her brother were a popular dancing team both in the United States and England before her marriage.

London of San Diego, Cal., was found in her room several hours later near death from a brutal beating. County hospital physicians said the woman, about 30, had suffered a skull fracture and internal injuries. They said she probably would die. | Hotel attaches found the woman lying in a gore-spattered bed. A piece of blood-stained gas pipe lay beside her. One of her two purses was in an areaway below the window of her room. It contained a round trip bus ticket from San Diego to New York, but no money. Twelve dollars in cash was hidden in a cold cream jar among the victim’s effects. Employes at the Santa Fe Trails System bus depot said the woman arrived about midnight aboard a bus from the west. Communist Russia, foe of Fascism, joined with France and Britain today in the economic punishment of Fascist Italy for its invasion of Ethiopia. The Soviet Union's pledge reached the League of Nations as Italy’s armies, prepared for any counterattack by the Ethiopian tribesmen, drove deeper into the interior of Haile Selassie's empire. Moscow notified Geneva of its readiness to impose an embargo on the exportation of key products to Italy and gave its pledge to abide by the “Buy Nothing From Italy” boycott. France and England had previously notified the League they would impose such sanctions. Numerous smaller powers had given similar notice. The league's sanctions staff of 52 nations meets Thursday to set the date for laying down such penalties. Wolverhampton, England, Oct. 28 (UP)—Great Britain will never approve a blockade of Italy without an assurance of at least sympathetic support of the United States and Germany. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin said today in a general election campaign speech. Baldwin pointed out the danger of war inherent in the League's procedure in the cause of peace. Therefore, he said, he would never make himself responsible even for joint action under the League without adequate defense measures. “There is no question of huge armaments,” he said. “What we do want and must have is to replace our navy ships constructed before the war with the most modern ones.” The risks that may come from the fulfillment by the League of its obligations under the covenant will come at some future time, he continued. “The risk is not coming now,” he said.

1935-07-15.text: KINSALE, Irish Free State, July 15 (®)—Jack MacCarthy, 76, a baker who baked all night and hunted all day, died today. When he was a young man, MacCarthy decided that people lost too much time sleeping. So he gradually cut down on his own sleeping until he said he was able to forego slumber entirely. He boasted that he slept less in 50 years than the average man does in six months. As to how he did it, he always declined to say.

ROME, July 1—(7)—Mrs. May Katherine Thompson, 40, of Brooklyn, N. Y., and H. N. Scott, British subject and director of the American Express company in Italy, today were found dead in the sulfur baths at Acque Albule, well known Roman bathing resort halfway between Rome and Tivoli. While the cause of their deaths had not been officially ascertained, doctors expressed the opinion that they might have died of sulfur inhalation. The two went to Acque Albule yesterday afternoon with friends to swim in the sulfur waters. Their bodies were found yesterday evening. Police and the American consulate were notified, the former opening an investigation. Mrs. Thompson, whose husband is Edwin F. Thompson of Brooklyn, arrived in Italy nearly 10 days ago as a tourist. She came to Rome after spending several days at Naples. Here she gave her occupation as an artist. She had planned to go to Florence last

Rio de Janeiro, July 14.—(/)— The police arrested an English pied piper today as he prepared to lead a children’s crusade for gold and diamonds into the wilds of Brazil's Matto Grosso. Ten boys, ranging in age from 13 to 17, were identified as among his followers. Frantic parents were calling on police to ask regarding their lost offsprings. Harold Boddy was the name the sallow, sullen man gave the authorities. They said he had been figuratively piping his fabulous dream of gold and diamonds to youths in Rio de Janeiro the past two years. He was released after close questioning. One of three boys who formed a vanguard for the crusade has returned disillusioned after a trek to Sao Paulo, 285 weary and dusty miles away. Rome, July 1:—44)—The Italian public was convinced today that Benito Mussolini's aggressive East African policy remained intact despite the collapse of a conciliatory commission's British maneuver for further league jurisdiction and an Ethiopian appeal to America for invocation of the Briand-Kellogg pact. Well-informed circles feel that any further efforts by outsiders to moderate Italy's policy toward Ethiopia are sure to meet with coolness from this government. Italy, they said, has made clear that Il Duce’s insistence upon what he calls an “integral solution” of the quarrel with Ethiopia is justified. She is not indifferent to her future status as regards the League of Nations, but feels that France and England should accede to Ethiopia's expulsion from Geneva or at least a modification of the African kingdom's independence. Rome, July 15—With war between Italy and Ethiopia increasingly regarded as inevitable, Mussolini today ordered the mobilization of another regular army division and the creation of an additional division of black shirt militia. Il Duce also ordered the immediate construction of 10 new submarines. An official communique which announced the new preparations for possible hostilities in East Africa said “the accelerated fever of military preparations by Ethiopia forces us to proceed with additional measures of military character.” Today’s order brings the number of regular army divisions, designed for East Africa to five. Five black shirt divisions also have been created. This means Italy will have at least 250,000 men for service should war begin. The communique said Mussolini had called out special experts of the classes of 1902-1910, 1912 and summoned new quotas of pilots and specialists

Dartmund, Germany (AP)—Ten miners were killed, 32 injured and an undetermined number trapped underground today when an explosion 2,400 feet below the surface set fire to the coal shaft in which they were working. Fourteen hundred workers are employed by the mine. Half that number were working when the blast occurred. Refusing to divulge the extent of the disaster or say how many were trapped, the director of the mine said: "We are forbidden to talk in detail about the explosion. The management is preparing a statement for the press which will be announced through official channels."

Amsterdam, July 15.—(?)— Authorities ordered a rigid investigation today into the series of disasters to the Netherlands' air liners after Sunday's tragedy in which 6 persons were killed at the Schiphol air-drome. The giant American-made Fokker plane which crashed into a dike and burst into flames yesterday soon after taking off for Hamburg was the third “flying hotel” of the Netherlands wrecked in a little more than six months.

DORTMUND, Germany, July 15 (UP)—Ten miners were killed and 32 injured when an explosion wrecked the Adolf Hansemann coal mine in the suburb of Mengede today. BUDAPEST, July 15 (UP)—Four miners were killed and scores of others were endangered today by coal, gas and dust ignited by fire sweeping the Tatabanya collieries, northeastern Hungary.

1935-04-22.text: PARIS (#)—France rejected all suggestions today of entering into direct negotiations with Reichsführer Hitler to ease the strained European situation. High authorities said the government was ignoring an obvious campaign to bring about separate German conversations with Great Britain, France and Italy. They indicated they considered the effort a German move to break up the united three-power front formed at Stresa and at Geneva. “The three powers will continue to work together,” one official source said. The Nationalist Press strongly criticized the recent visit to Berlin of Georges Scapini, the blind deputy, who conferred with German veterans in an effort to bring the two countries together. The unfavorable comment said such negotiations hold grave danger for France and asserted the French veterans were being used as catspaws.

LONDON, April 22 ()--A high authoritative source disclosed today that Great Britain, France and Italy have made a strong joint protest to Lithuania regarding the treatment of the German element in Memel. The three powers as principal guarantors of the Memel statute, the source said, dispatched a note couched in firm language Friday calling Lithuania’s attention to the fact that administrative affairs in the territory are now in the hands of Lithuanians—and urging that Germans be given their share of places on the statute directorate.

Tokyo, April 22--(A.P.)—Governor General Nekagawa of Formosa in a radio-telephone interview with the newspaper Tokyo Asahi said the deaths from yesterday's earthquake probably would reach 3,000. Official figures as reported by the Exchange Telegraph (British) News Agency placed the death toll at 3,003. These figures included 1,831 in Taichu province and 1,172 in Shinchiku province. It was feared the number of casualties would be increased materially when figures were obtained from the region inhabited by aborigines in the interior which relief officials have not yet been able to reach. In Berlin, from which Hitler had sent protests against the League of Nations Council’s action in censuring Germany's rearmament, a well-defined campaign was seen to increase German armament to forestall a “hazardous attack” against the nation. LONDON, April 24.—Major Robert Hemphill fell to his death Monday from a 70-foot cliff in Cornwall, and his wife, summoned frantically by their 15-year-old son, fell after him, suffering fatal injuries. Major Hemphill, commandant of the Royal Military Academy hospital at Woolwich, was trying to photograph a buzzard’s nest when he lost his footing and plunged downward. Their son, Peter, frantically shouted and ran for his mother, who was close by. In a futile attempt at rescue, she slipped off the same cliff. When his mother disappeared, the orphaned lad clambered down the cliff and found her crumpled form. She lived only a short time. The major had fallen into the sea and his body was carried away by the outgoing tide.

LONDON, (UP).—Lucy Lady Duff-Gordon, who as an internationally famous dressmaker gave the world the Merry Widow hat before the World War, died yesterday. She was a sister of the novelist Elinor Glyn. Lady Duff-Gordon was 71. She had been in retirement for years. She founded the firm of society dressmakers, Lucile. She was well known in the United States. Lady Duff-Gordon was the forerunner of the dress designers of today. She emancipated the women of London from the woolen substituted glamorous chiffons and silks. She coined the word “chic” as it related to clothes, created the split skirt for comfort, and was the first to stage a mannequin show.

LONDON, April 21—Lady Duff Gordon, one of the last of the dwindling survivors of the ill-fated Titanic, and elder sister of Elinor Glyn, the novelist, died today at a Putney nursing home. With her husband, the late Sir Cosmo Edmund Duff Gordon, Lady Duff Gordon figured as a witness in the inquiry conducted in England into the 1912 disaster. Both had escaped the sinking ship in a lifeboat. Formerly a well-known modiste, Lady Duff Gordon urged adoption and maintenance of the short skirt. In 1910 Lady Duff Gordon opened a dressmaking establishment in New York, Lucile, Ltd., which eventually involved her in financial difficulties and litigation. When in court during the hearing of a suit in 1919, she was asked if she had bought any Liberty Bonds: “Why should I buy any?” Lady Duff Gordon replied, “This country means nothing to me. (By Associated Press) TOKYO, APRIL 22 — THE RENGO NEWS TODAY OFFICIALLY ANNOUNCED THAT 3,045 PERSONS HAD DIED IN THE EARTHQUAKE WHICH DEVASTATED SEVERAL FORMOSA COMMUNITIES SUNDAY.

1935-05-06.text: LONDON, (®). A tumultuous roar, "God save the king," burst from the throats of 50,000 jubilee rejoicing British subjects and welled over London as King George and Queen Mary appeared on a balcony of Buckingham Palace. Rewarding the patience of the throngs which crowded about the palace from dawn to dusk, charging through police lines once to witness the colorful spectacle of the changing of the guards, their majesties came forth for ninety seconds. The roar of acclamation rode higher than the shouts of communists who marched on Hyde Park earlier in the day chanting: "The jubilee celebration is war preparation." Attempting to disrupt a meeting of 30,000 laborites in Hyde Park, called to demonstrate the solidarity of the working classes, the communists mixed in with the workers and sought to drown out their speakers. | LONDON (P)—Britons led an empire that embraces one-fourth the world’s area and population Monday in a joyous celebration of the twenty-fifth anniversary of King George's accession to the throne. Millions of people, massed in the streets in carnival mood, shouted themselves into a frenzy of enthusiasm as the king and queen in state procession went to St. Paul's cathedral for a thanksgiving. On their return to Buckingham Palace, they stood on a Buckingham Palace balcony for six minutes in the bright spring sun while a crowd massed there, blocks deep, cheered, waved and sang “For He's a Jolly Good Fellow.” There was here perhaps the greatest celebration that London has seen, and there were celebrations by men, women and children of all the races on all the continents and islands dotted throughout the world united in rejoicing that the king had reached his silver jubilee year. GALWAY, Irish Free, May 6.—(UP)—A sea serpent something—arriving before the usual summer season, lay on the Galway coast today and people wondered what to do with it. John Crowley, keeper of Mutton Island lighthouse, shot and killed a big scaly head and a long scaly body ending in two knife-edged tails. It weighed four tons, Crowley said. Seamen were mystified. The monster had been breaking fishermen’s nets with its knife-like tail, and one party had just returned for repairs when they heard five shots ring out. It leaped from the water, the fishermen said, with a lashing of the sea into miniature tidal waves. Crowley had seen one of its fins as he tended his lights.

LONDON, May 6. (UP)—An empire that covers one-fourth of the earth's surface and includes one-fourth of its people celebrated today the 26th anniversary of the accession of King George V to the throne. Men, women and children of all races on all the continents and on islands dotted throughout the globe united in rejoicing that the King had reached his silver jubilee as King-Emperor. He succeeded to the throne at 11:45 p. m. May 6, 1910, at the moment that his father, Edward VII, died of heart disease in his presence after a two-day illness. Today's 25th anniversary opened three months of celebrations which it was apparent to anyone of the millions in London were to be unprecedented. By dawn, there was a deep crowd along the route of the King’s and others of the seven state processions from the West End to massive St. Paul's Cathedral. London, April 1.—-(P) —The color and gaiety of bygone days will return to England this summer in celebration of the 25th anniversary of King George's accession to the throne. Every city, town and village will be emblazoned with flowers, flags and bunting for the high carnival centering around May 6, the actual anniversary, which will be a national holiday. Buildings will be floodlit, and there will be parades and pageants the like of which England never saw before. The official period for the celebration is a fortnight, but most of the decorations—which are to be weatherproof, incidentally—will remain weeks longer. Manufacturers of flags and bunting are working overtime. Various boroughs of London have approved expenditures of more than $100,000 for decorations, while Brighton, England's favorite seaside resort, has set aside $30,000 for fireworks and other frills. New London, Wis., May 6-=(P) Theodore Knapstein gently rubbed his left foot where his great toe used to be and solemnly vowed today that he would do no more sleepwalking. Knapstein's toe was severed from his foot when he slammed a door on it, believing as he walked in his sleep in a nightmare, that he was shutting burglars out of his home. He tells the story himself, somewhat sheepishly: “I had a dream that there were burglars in the house and got out of bed. Thinking to shut them out of my room, I slammed the door. Suddenly I came to, snapped on the light and found I was on one side of the door, and my toe on the other.” Dr. C. J. Pfelfer, Knapstein’s physician, said the door did a neat job of amputation. Knapstein was confined in a hospital only one day and returned to work today.

ATHENS, May. 6.—(4)—Former Premier Eleutherios Venizelos, exiled leader of the ill-destined Greek revolt, was under sentence of death today for the part he played in the uprising. A court martial passed sentence on the veteran political leader yesterday and at the same time condemned to death General Nicholas Plastiras, who commanded the rebel troops. Both Venizelos and Plastiras fled the country after the failure of their attempted coup. Venizelos is now living with his wife and son in exile in Paris.

ISTANBUL, May 5.—(AP)—Tens of thousands of inhabitants of the Kars region on the Turco-Russian frontier, terrified by recurring earth shocks rumbling in the wake of a disastrous earthquake, wandered dazedly over the countryside tonight. Many were in dire need of food and medical attention. Scores of corpses were still believed buried in the debris of shattered homes and many towns and villages. Parliament voted 50,000 Turkish liras to speed relief work and build temporary shelters for countless victims of the quake, whose homes were destroyed as 35 villages were demolished. The Red Crescent Society opened a nation-wide drive to collect funds and immediately began dispatching food and medicine to the quake-blasted areas.

In a meeting of vital import to the world and Ethiopian situation, the ministers decided Italy will not abandon the League until the League itself assumes full responsibility for measures against Italy, and then declared: “Italy’s policy has no immediate or remote aim which could injure Great Britain’s interests.” The government, a cabinet communique disclosed, has communicated to Great Britain its readiness to negotiate for further accord which would harmonize with the legitimate interests of Great Britain in East Africa. Rome, Sept. 28.—Italy will not leave the League of Nations until the League has assured full responsibility for measures concerning Italy,” a cabinet communique read. The communique said also: In a gesture to Great Britain today. “Italy has no immediate or remote aims which might affect British interests.” Italy will do nothing to extend the Italian-Ethiopian conflict across Europe, it was added. Departures of soldiers for East Africa will be accelerated, the cabinet announced “because of the intensification of Ethiopia’s mobilization.”

"Italy’s policy has no immediate or remote aims which could injure Great Britain's interests," the ministers, meeting with Premier Mussolini, announced. The cabinet, however, took sharp issue with League of Nations procedure in the Italo-Ethiopian dispute and struck a new blow at Ethiopia's alleged lack of good faith. Despite the warning that "grave events" were impending, the League Assembly adjourned, but was ready to meet instantly in the event of an SOS call in any new Italo-Ethiopian emergency. Home, Sept 28—-(AT)—Premier Mussolini stretched a friendly hand forward to Great Britain today and announced he had already offered to negotiate accords to quiet her tears over the African problem. At the same time, he disclosed Italian troop movements to Africa are “being accelerated,” and warned the assembly of the League of Nations to keep its hands off. (The conferees are now negotiating for a settlement). Italian Offer Speaking through a communique of the fifth and closing September cabinet session, Il Duce sought to localize the apparently imminent Ethiopian conflict by an agreement with Britain. The cabinet made four points: 1. Italy offers to make accords with Great Britain. 2. Italy warns the League assembly not to interfere. 3. London, Sept. 28. (AP) — Great Britain speeded up plans for emergency naval construction to bring her fleet to safety limits, and began to call today for bids on 21 ships allowed by the 1935 naval building program. At the same time Great Britain has approached the French government to find out what manner France is to assist in carrying out the threats here. The bulk of the British fleet is now assembled in the sea for preparedness in the event that anything should come from the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Ten million pounds or 50 million dollars will be required by the 1935 construction program, it was estimated. The program is within the limits of the Washington naval treaty.

LONDON, Sept. 27 — New and grave issues took their places alongside the Italo-Ethiopian dispute tonight to worry an already worried Europe. The shadow of little Memel, backed by the larger one of Germany, loomed on the horizon as Geneva strove to keep peace between Italy and Ethiopia. Memel, once under Germany, but now under Lithuanian sovereignty, will hold a heatedly-contested election Sunday for the landtag (territorial assembly). Assurances Asked Guarantors of the Memel statute, Italy, France and Great Britain, sent identical notes to Reichsführer Adolf Hitler asking for assurances nazidom would aid in keeping the election tranquil. But Berlin officials, who have accused Lithuanians of unfairness, said the three former allied powers were trying to "excuse" Lithuania's methods. Fort Lauderdale, Fla.--(AP)— The British steamship Wanderer wirelessed just before 1 p.m. today she was aground on Point del Birril, off the south coast of Cuba. It was not immediately ascertained whether the Wanderer is a freighter or a passenger vessel. The United States Coast Guard base here intercepted the wireless message. It was not a distress signal, the ship merely reporting herself aground. Her master radioed he was emptying his ballast tanks.

1935-08-19.text: London, Aug. 20.—(#)—British ministers hurried home today quitting their holidays at continental spas and golf links to face the gravest international crisis since the world war days of August 1914. An emergency meeting of the cabinet was called for Thursday. A British policy presumably will be established for the meeting of the council of the League of Nations at Geneva Sept. 4. As the cabinet was summoned, because of the breakdown of the tri-power conference in Paris which met to find a solution for Italo-Ethiopian peace, fear swept the smaller nations of Europe. Stirred by apprehension that the League of Nations is on the verge of destruction as a result of Mussolini’s death blow to the Paris parley the little nations are reported planning a united front to save the league. “Where would the brave little Belgium of 1914 be today in view of the great powers seeming failure to prevent in

PARIS, Aug. 19 (AP).—Another diplomatic effort to prevent the impending war between Italy and Ethiopia ended today in an outburst of general recriminations. Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy, who had conveyed Premier Mussolini's "no" to French and British peace proposals, told Premier Laval "au revoir" and prepared to go back to Rome. Anthony Eden, British minister for League of Nations affairs, told the French government the same and prepared to return to London. A high French official said privately that Europe "faces a crisis like that of 1914" and "France must resign herself to losing Italy's friendship." A member of the Italian delegation blamed the breakdown of the conference on "the lack of English good will and their unbending position." War Inevitable A British spokesman commented: "Nothing can be done at Geneva to prevent war." The same source said that Premier Laval had assured Ede

Liverpool, Aug. 18.—(4?)— Six seamen perished and five others were injured in a bow-to-bow collision of the Cunard liner Laurentic and the Blue Star Steamer Napier Star in the fog-shrouded Irish channel today. The Laurentic, carrying 620 disappointed passengers and the Napier Star limped back to Liverpool in the tow of tugs, and docked safely this afternoon. Both were damaged badly. In Fog The ships collided in a dense fog 60 miles out of Liverpool early this morning, a few hours after the Laurentic had embarked on a fortnight’s cruise of northern capitals. The Napier Star, partly loaded with cargo, was en route from Glasgow to Liverpool to complete the loading. They locked with a grinding smash, that tore a long hole down the Laurentic’s bow side, crushing her crewmen as they slept in their bunks. Copyright 1935 By The Associated Press. London.—Alarms of war rang through Great Britain today as its people awaited Anthony Eden's report on the torpedoed peace parleys in Paris. The British press commented darkly on the possibility of war, and informed sources saw in Italy’s action a challenge the League of Nations may not survive. The British were eager to hear from their minister for league affairs the possible consequences of Mussolini's emphatic “No” to Anglo-French suggestions for compromise. But, more important, they hope to learn from him how far France will back Britain in the critical League of Nations council session in Geneva September 4. League Life At Stake. Britain is gravely concerned about the breakdown of the talks; negotiations in Paris. One option which may be considered by the cabinet is lifting of the arms embargo against Ethiopia, which would be regarded by Italy as an affront and would mark Britain’s first move to brand Italy as the aggressor in any war. WASHINGTON, Aug. 13. — The six New England states of Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut would go Republican if the presidential election were held tomorrow or the day after. That, at least, is the private opinion of the strategists of the Democratic political machine. They suspected as much, even before the Republican congressional victory in Rhode Island. Now they're virtually convinced. Rhode Island Democrats occupying administration posts, including some smart politicians, were predicting weeks ago that Judge Risk, the Republican candidate, would defeat Mr. Prince, the Democratic candidate. But they didn’t expect quite such a hard wallop. The size of the G. O. P. majority surprised them. LIVERPOOL, Aug. 19—(#)—Two British liners, the Laurentic and the Napier Star, were docked safely at Liverpool today following a crash in the Irish channel which cost the lives of six seamen. The Laurentic’s 620 passengers, whose scheduled fortnight’s cruise of northern capitals was ended abruptly early Sunday morning but 60 miles out of Liverpool, returned to London. The seamen who perished in the bow-to-bow collision of the two ships, as well as five others who were injured, had been sleeping in their bunks, situated scarcely 20 feet from the Laurentic’s first class quarters. The bow of the Napier was smashed in for 20 feet and her forecastle housing was carried away. The forward winches were still hanging over the side when the boat arrived in dock.

Rome, Aug. 19—Benito Mussolini’s goal of 1,000,000 men under arms by October is his answer to those who say he will weaken his position at home by warring on Ethiopia. While French and British negotiators waited two days in Paris for his reply to their peace proposals, Mussolini was inspecting Fascist divisions bound for East Africa. Today, while the next step was discussed in world capitals, Mussolini was concerned solely with his plans to dominate Ethiopia and achieve what he called Saturday a Fascist empire. Every expression of opinion in Italy leads to the impression that Mussolini believes there will not be war in Europe for three years. Has Biggest Army But at the same time he has the biggest army in Europe, except for that of Soviet Russia, ready for instant action. Talk here today was not of the Paris conference. A reliable source said the British cabinet understands that the government of Premier Flandin of France will be more liberal toward Germany and stand ready to accept Germany's allegedly illegal armaments as legal. It was understood furthermore that the British cabinet has decided to urge every reasonable concession toward bringing Germany back into the league even to recognizing the legalizing her armaments. () — The British cabinet, meeting today, was understood to be discussing a tentative proposal that Germany be given equality in armaments in return for a re-entry into the League of Nations. An authority stated that the cabinet was of a unanimous opinion that the time was ripe—provided the Saar basin territory has voted to return to Germany, and it is believed such is the case—to press for Germany's return to the league on the basis of equality. It was reported that Germany's cooperation in a treaty for arms limitation is also one of the essentials in the consideration of equality for Germany. | ROME, Jan. 14.—Princess Beatrice of Spain, elder daughter of former King Alfonso, was married today to Duke Alessandro Torlonia, son of the former Mary Elsie Moore of New York. Former Queen Victoria, the Princess’ mother, remained in England, refusing to attend the ceremony because, it was understood, she emphatically disapproved of the marriage of another member of the royal family to a non-royal person. Princess Beatrice and Alessandro will leave late today for Naples, to embark for a honeymoon in the United States. The brilliant marriage ceremony at the Church of Jesus, with Cardinal Segura y Saenz, archbishop of Toledo, officiating, was the result of a love match which probably deterred the princess from entering a convent. MIAMI, Fla., Jan. 14. UPI—Flying the same fast monoplane he used in the recent London to Melbourne air race, Col. Roscoe Turner hopped off from here today for New York after attending the all-American air races. Turner denied a statement by United Air Lines officials in New York that he would attempt on the flight to better the record between the two cities of 5 hours 36 minutes established last November by Capt. Waddie Rickenbacker.

Covington, Ky., Jan. 14—(P)—A man registered as Kingdom Pete Murray, a Covington salesman, was arrested by a Department of Justice agent and Covington detectives today on a Canadian warrant charging him with the kidnaping of John S. Labatt, wealthy Sarnia, Ont., brewer. ROME, Jan. 14.—Prince Alessandro Torlonia, son of the former Elsie Moore of New York, and Infanta Beatriz of Spain, daughter of former King Alfonso, were married today in Rome's magnificent old Church of Jesus. They were surrounded by the scions of Europe’s proudest royal families during the ceremony. Hundreds of persons jammed adjacent streets to catch a glimpse of the bride but she entered the church by a rear door. The wedding was performed by Cardinal Pedro Segura, exiled cardinal primate of Spain. First among the guests in the royal pews were King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy, Queen Elena and the princess of the House of Savoy. Former King Alfonso of Spain headed the princes of the blood of the Bourbon family who gathered to see their young relative wed. (Continued on Page Seven)

THE HAGUE, Jan 14 (UP)—The Hague court of justice today ruled against the validity of the gold clause in bonds of the Royal Dutch Oil Company floated in New York and Amsterdam. The decision was to the effect that because of the Roosevelt suspension of gold payments, interest on the bonds need not be paid in gold dollars, as stipulated.

BERLIN, Jan. 14.—(UP) — Nazi Germany awaited today with mingled confidence and concern the announcement of the vote which Saarlanders cast yesterday to determine national status. At 8 A. M. tomorrow, when the vote is announced at Saarbrucken, Josef Buerckel, Nazi Saar commissioner and governor designate, will inform Adolf Hitler by wireless of the result. The whole nation has been asked to listen for the statement, and there will be a spontaneous national celebration if there is a big majority for return to Germany. Everybody is convinced that the Saar is essentially German and that the vote will be for Germany. But beneath this confidence, there is an unexpressed question whether the vote against Nazism—rather than against Germany—may be sufficient to determine the League of Nations from awarding the territory integrally to the Third Reich. 1935-11-29.text: (By The Associated Press) A virtual French ultimatum, warning Benito Mussolini directly and officially that any unprovoked attack on the British Mediterranean fleet would be regarded as an attack also on France was disclosed by high sources in London and Paris Friday night. This action by Premier Laval of France was regarded as dashing Italian hopes for further delay in imposition of an embargo on oil shipments to Italy — something which high fascist sources have conceded may seriously affect the Ethiopian war. In Geneva, discussion of the embargo by the League of Nations sanctions committee was set officially for December 12. Premier Laval, at whose request the original discussion was deferred from Friday, was said by league officials to have asked that the meeting be held on December 12 instead of on December 5. Washington — Carrying a mandate to oppose increases in the world’s burden of naval costs, the American delegation sails tonight for the London conference on limitation of fighting fleets. Departing from New York aboard the liner Aquitania, the delegation is due at Southampton at noon Dec. 6, the day the conference opens. It plans to speed directly from the boat to the Locarno room of the British foreign office. Around a table there, the world’s sea powers will hold conversations that may determine whether there shall be a tremendous naval building race, or some limits on the war fleets. The objective of the parley is to reach some agreements to succeed the Washington and London naval limitation treaties which end Dec. 31, 1936.

A direct accusation that the Japanese army was in large measure responsible for the north China autonomy movement was made today by the Chinese government. Japan was reported at the same time to have made evasive answers to queries by representatives of western nations—notably Great Britain—as to Japan's future plans in North China. The Nanking government, in a sharp note of protest, said the move for separation of North China from the central government was planned by “disgruntled elements, acting in connivance with Japanese military officers,” and asked the Tokyo government to halt such activities of its army men. Nanking also proposed to settle North China troubles by diplomatic action, and, in another note, requested the Japanese to complete withdrawal from the important railway junction of Fengtai, which they seized early Wednesday. (By Associated Press) Rome, Nov. 29—A new European crisis arose today over the League of Nations projects for an oil embargo against Italy for which responsible sources asserted Premier Mussolini has evolved a counter program including a swift thrust at the British fleet. Responsible persons, not officials, but holding high connections, said a fresh conflict, perhaps another World war, would result if the League applied the oil embargo in addition to its present sanctions to cut short the Italian warfare in Ethiopia. Mussolini's program in reply to an oil ban was said by these persons to include withdrawal of diplomatic representatives from "enemy countries;" resignation from the League and an attack on Britain’s Mediterranean fleet by Italy’s aerial "death squad." These sources said the three-point program was adopted by Mussolini and the Fascists’ grand council at the Nov. 18 midnight

LONDON, Nov. 29 (U.P) — Some competent diplomatic observers believed today that the question of war or peace in Europe would be decided within the next ten days. The present situation between Italy and Great Britain and other European countries is most serious. But many believe there is a good chance for peace. The view is taken that Premier Benito Mussolini would not be able long to combat such penalties as an embargo on oil, coal, steel and iron, and that despite threats, he is likely to think long before adopting warlike measures involving him not only with Britain but with all league nations. Listen To Reason— Hence there is some disposition to believe that Mussolini may yet, as it is put here, listen to reason because nobody wants a war with Italy. MASSOCK (Associated Press Foreign Staff) (Copyright, 1935, The Associated Press) Paris, Nov. 29.—(AP)—Great Britain was reported by informed sources today to have achieved its long-sought assurance of French support in case of an Italian attack on the British in the Mediterranean. It was stated that Premier Laval, who previously delayed League of Nations action on the proposal of an oil embargo against Italy, had given in to the British demand for action on the subject, thereby wrecking Italian hopes for further delay. Yielding to the insistence of British Ambassador Sir George Russell Clerk, these sources said, Laval made clear to Italian Ambassador Vittorio Cerruti that if Il Duce did anything 'desperate' in the Mediterranean, France and other League of Nations powers would stand solidly and unreservedly behind Britain. Italy is ready to attack the British Mediterranean fleet if the League of Nations imposes an oil embargo on her, informed but unofficial sources at Rome said. France was reported in official quarters to have advised Italy it will back Britain to the hilt if Premier Mussolini does anything "desperate" in the Mediterranean. Ethiopian officials were quoted as saying their forces had recaptured Walwal, near the Italian Somaliland border. Dispatches to Rome, confirmed by an official Ethiopian communique, described an aerial bombing of Daggah Bur, strategic fortress between Italy's southern armies and their objectives of Jijiga and Harar. The American government required all manufacturers, importers and exporters of arms and ammunition to register with the national munitions control board.

London, Nov. 20.—(UP)—The Japanese government officially advised the British government tonight that it refused to accept responsibility for developments in North China. Authoritative sources said this viewpoint was advanced to A. F. I. Wiggin, the British charge d'affaires in Tokyo, in a talk he held yesterday with the vice minister of the Japanese foreign office. It was said that the vice minister declared Japan considers the movement for the autonomy of North China to be entirely Chinese in character and wholly spontaneous. (Chinese authorities in Nanking have stated that the autonomy movement was Japanese-inspired.) The vice minister added that Japan, as an interested power, was watching the developments in China. Contrary to earlier belief it was learned that the missing ace’s plane could remain afloat indefinitely if he had been forced down, with his Co-Pilot Tom Pethybridge, on the Bay of Bengal, where they were last seen fighting through a monsoon. Scan Stormy Waters Royal Air Force planes soared north, nearing the Siamese frontier, to start a systematic scanning of the stormy waters from Victoria Point, above the Malay Federated States. C. T. Pethybridge, feared lost on an England-Australia flight. Wireless messages flashed out to liners and freighters in the Andaman sea and the Bay of Bengal seeking to trace the Lockheed monoplane Lady Southern Cross in which the great Australian aviator and his co-pilot were seen late Thursday fighting for life over shark-infested waters, only 200 feet above a stormy sea, 150 miles from the coast of the Malayan peninsula. Singapore, Straits Settlements, Nov. 9.—(Saturday) — (4) — Two Royal Air Force flying boats returned today from a dawn flight over the Bay of Bengal and coastal jungle islands to report they had found no trace of Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, missing for 36 hours on a record flight from England to Australia. James Melrose, the airman who last saw the famous flier and his companion, Tom Pethybridge, battling a monsoon over the Bay of Bengal, joined the search. A squadron of bombing planes was standing by, ready to aid if necessary. Hours passed without word of the crack long-distance pilot, whose monoplane was equipped with a wireless. Ships at sea had been warned to keep a sharp lookout. Aviation officials here pointed out that if the veteran pilot landed in water without crashing he might be able to lighten his plane sufficiently to remain afloat for at least two days. The extent and speed of Italy’s occupation of Ethiopia will be limited only by the military judgment and patience of Mussolini’s general officers, it appeared today. Little more than a month has elapsed since Italy crossed the Eritrean frontier. When the present military phase of the advance has been completed, Italy will hold an estimated 25,000 square miles of Ethiopian territory—approximately one-eighth of the East African Kingdom. These immense territorial gains have been accomplished without a single major or bloody battle. The steady, sure advance of the Italian armies in the north, northwest, and south has been without conspicuous Ethiopian resistance. Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, has claimed that its strategy consists in guerilla warfare until the Italians are lured into a favorable spot and then a general ambush patterned after the Aduwa victory of 1896.
