Geneva. Feb. 14 ().—Hugh Wilson, United States minister to Switzerland, told a special committee of the disarmament conference today that the dearest hope of the United States is a general convention for the limitation of armaments.

1935-11-12.text: MANILA, P. I., Nov. 12—A far away typhoon reared its head today as the U. S. Navy sent another destroyer to the rescue of 54 persons marooned on a wave-lashed rock by the wrecking of the British freighter Silverhazel. However, naval officers expected to have the entire party rescued long before the typhoon, forming off the island of Yap 1200 miles due east of the wreck, reached the Philippines. Government forecasters here said it would be two or three days before the tropical storm would strike the islands. To Join Rescuers The destroyer Blumer which left Manila at 2:19 p. m., with special life-saving equipment, was due early tomorrow at the scene of the wreck, 350 miles from Manila by water at the southern tip of Luzon Island. It will join the destroyer Peary which attempted in vain all day yesterday to reach the castaways in small boats.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, Nov. 12 (AP) - The Turkish steamer Inebou sank in the Smyrna harbor last night during a severe storm. Ninety of the more than 200 passengers and crew aboard were reported drowned or missing. The British freighter Polo rescued 111 persons in the darkness.

Rangoon, Burma, Nov. 12—-(AP) Crews of the planes seeking Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith and his co-pilot, Tom Pethybridge, lost on an England-Australia flight, reported today that the search was "virtually hopeless." Two royal air force flying boats arrived here from Singapore, Straits Settlement, where the Australian pilots were due last Friday, after a fruitless search over a wide area off the coast and over the Bay of Bengal. Officials announced, nevertheless, that the hunt would continue,

MANILA, P. I. — Three members of the crew of the British freighter Silver Hazel were picked up from a little raft on the storm-ridden southern coast of Luzon today. Word of the rescue was radioed to Manila by the United States Navy destroyer Peary, standing by in pounding seas to render assistance to fifty-two wreck refugees marooned on a barren, rain-drenched rock near San Bernardino island. While the Peary and two merchant vessels stood by, the U. S. S. Bulmer raced toward the scene from Manila carrying line-throwing equipment with which it was hoped the remaining passengers and crew may be rescued. Repeated attempts to launch rescue boats have been defeated by heavy seas and adverse tides. For more than twenty hours the wreck victims have clung to the rock, exposed to the full fury of the tropical rainstorm. The Silver Hazel grounded on a reef and broke in two yesterday. No casualties

Manila, Nov. 12—(Tuesday)— An unsigned message saying “so far all is well” was flashed here by radio early today from the site of the wrecked British freighter Silverhazel, ashore in treacherous San Bernardino Straits with 54 crew and passengers. The message, received by A. G. Henderson, vice president of the Silver Java Pacific line, said the crew of 49 had been contacted on the bleak rock against which the vessel crashed and broke in two. Destroyer Stands by No mention was made of the one man and four women passengers, but it was assumed here reference to “all is well” indicated they were in no immediate danger. Henderson received the message at 6:33 a. m. (5:33 p. m., Monday, Eastern Standard Time) shortly after word came that the United States destroyer Peary had reached the wreck and was standing by for other rescue vessels. Heavy seas previously had damaged one rescue ship, the Jap

LONDON, Nov. 12 (Pi)—Justice Atkinson of the King's Bench division today awarded judgments totaling £39,500 (about $197,000) and interest to the British plaintiffs in the long drawn out Chrysler motor shares case. Included in the award was £3,500 and interest for Arnold De La Poer against Walter P. Chrysler, the American automobile magnate, and his associates, Stephen D. Briggs, Bernard E. Hutchinson, Joseph Fields, and the Chrysler Corporation. There was also a judgment of £36,000 and interest against the same defendants on behalf of the Suffolk Investment Company, Ltd.

Manila, Nov. 12. (Tuesday) (®)— Trapped on a bleak rock against which the British freighter Silverhazel crashed and broke in two, some 54 sailors and passengers were believed alive today as rescue craft battled treacherous seas off Luzon island. Wireless indicated the five passengers, one man and four women, and all crew members were on the rock or the part of the broken ship wedged above water. The crew numbered 49. From Manila the United States navy destroyer Peary was reported nearing the scene after one rescue ship, the Japanese freighter Chicago Maru, sent word it had been badly damaged by heavy seas—and was steaming for Manila. Other ships standing by were the Steamer Tana, the Governor Taft, an interisland steamer, and the United States Steamship company’s New York. Life boats sent out by rescue ships were tossed about by the rip tide and heavy swells of San Bernardino straits, in

LONDON, Nov. 11—(AP)—Rome was the only Allied capital today where the 17th anniversary of the Armistice went unobserved. In striking contrast to misty London, where a deep stillness fell at the approach of 11 a. m., Rome watched armed legions, heavy artillery and tanks parade in the Coliseum through Caesar’s forum and cheered Premier Mussolini’s praise of the martial Italian spirit. Italy celebrated the Armistice a week ago on the anniversary of the peace with Austria. "The occasion was the 66th birthday of King Victor Emmanuel, who spent the day in his country palace. Il Duce told his followers Italy could take care of herself in Europe along with Africa. In Paris a march of 25,000 veterans to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier under the Arc De Triomphe was marred by nationalists and anti-Fascist rioting. A dozen encounters occurred, but police reserves and mobile guards quickly quelled th

1935-08-28.text: LONDON, (UP).— A sanguinary raid into Ethiopian territory by natives of French Somaliland, in which 60 were reported killed, spread consternation tonight in European political circles, already on a nervous edge over the critical situation. The raid shifted the zone of potential dynamite in Africa to a new sector—the border of Ethiopia and the French territory of Somaliland, hitherto quiet. French Somaliland, containing the vital seaport of Djibouti, lies between Italian Eritrea in the north and British Somaliland in the south, all of them bordering on Ethiopia and cutting her off from the sea. The raid was reported to Addis Ababa by the governor of the Ethiopian border province of Aussa, a fertile, well-watered country on the edge of the desolate Danakil desert of Ethiopia. Complete details were lacking.

By The Associated Press Principal developments in the Ethiopian situation: Rome—Annual furloughs of all the military personnel — army, navy and aviation — have been suspended. London—The trade union congress, meeting next week, will review plans for general strikes and boycotts reported under way to combat Italian war moves. Addis Ababa—Emperor Haile Selassie will introduce gas masks at an air raid rehearsal. Paris—Premier Laval will receive a free hand by the cabinet to carry on mediations at Geneva.

Laborites of both England and the continent it was reported, are planning general strikes and labor boycotts against Italy to prevent a war in East Africa. Guglielmo Marconi, radio inventor, will direct the telegraph, telephone, and wireless communications of the Italian armies in East Africa. The government announced all furloughs suspended in a move to marshal all its military strength in event of a crisis. The Italian and French cabinets were meeting to consider their lines of policy in the East African dispute with Pierre Laval of France reported to be receiving a free hand to mediate the controversy at the League Council, Sept. 4. Emperor Selassie ordered a gas mask drill to acquaint the natives with the devices and continued passing out reserves of arms hidden in secret underground chambers. The Italian war maneuvers close to the Austrian frontier were to end today, Mussolini makin

LONDON, AUG. 28. (AP).—Europe-wide general strikes and labor boycotts to combat Italian war moves today were reported being planned by British and Continental laborites, who are considering joint action in the event hostilities break out in East Africa. The reported plans, which are to be reviewed by the trade union congress at Margate next week, include strikes against handling supplies consigned to Italy. When C. R. Attlee, deputy opposition leader in the House of Commons, conferred in Paris recently with Leon Blum, French socialist leader, he carried out instructions from George Lansbury, leader in the opposition party in Parliament, to exchange views and possibly lay groundwork for future joint action in the industrial field. Results of cabinet meetings today at Bolzano, Italy, and Paris were awaited with keenest interest at Whitehall, where Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, and A

(Editor's Note: All avenues to peace in Europe have now apparently been closed as Premier Mussolini plans shortly to hurl his legions against Ethiopia, H. R. Knickerbocker, noted foreign correspondent of International News Service, writes in the following graphic summary of the situation. Mr. Knickerbocker is now in London en route to Ethiopia to cover hostilities for International News Service.) By H. R. Knickerbocker Staff Correspondent (Copyright, 1935, By International News Service) London, Aug. 28 (INS)—Europe sweated with alarm today as Premier Benito Mussolini met his cabinet in the full panoply of that war which this continent fears. That war is not an Italo-Ethiopian conflict. It is a general European war. Today’s concern has ceased to be the fate of ten million Ethiopians. Today's concern is the fate of four hundred million Europeans. That is the concern of the French cabinet a

Fall River, Mass. Aug. 28—James Sinclair, a leading figure in the New England textile industry and president of the Fall River Cotton Manufacturers Association, died suddenly last night at his summer home at Horse Neck Beach, Westport, Mass. Mr. Sinclair was about 66 years of age and had been prominent in textile affairs for years.

LONDON, Aug. 28 — The British Minister at Addis Ababa is advising the early departure from Ethiopia of all British subjects who can get away, it was understood tonight. A report from Djibouti that “Britons have been ordered to leave Ethiopia within four days” was denied authoritatively.

Providence, R. I—(INS)—Joshna Crane, 42, World War ace, and prominent New England aviator, was killed today and Arthur Howe, 26, of Philadelphia, airplane company observer, was critically injured when their airplane was thrown out of control by high winds at a height of several hundred feet, the plane nose diving to the ground at the Hillsgrove state airport. Howe was dying of a fractured skull and internal injuries. Arthur L. Johnson of this city, owner of the monoplane, who was to join Crane and Howe in a trip to Maryland, witnessed the fatal accident with a group of ERA workers.

1935-08-12.text: ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 12 (UP).— Emperor Haile Selassie I appealed in a speech to his people today for the support of the world powers, especially Britain and France, against the impending war with Italy. The danger of war is very near, he said, but Ethiopia still hopes the powers will effect a settlement. Regarding the peace efforts now in progress, he said: “It is impossible to foresee the result. The end of the rainy season approaches while diverse means are being tried to regulate the conflict pacifically. Italy continues ceaselessly to send troops and war materials into her bordering colonies. “The danger of war increases. Nevertheless, Ethiopia still nourishes strong hope for a pacific solution of the regrettable conflict. “Let us remember the role played by our fathers in safeguarding the integrity of our land and the glorious past of our country.” The emperor emphasized the need for p

By WEBB MILLER | (Copyright, 1935, by United Press) London, Aug. 12. (UP)—An internal struggle within the Nazi party in Germany is going on today between extremists and conservatives, in what is the most important internal political situation since the "purge" of June 30, 1934. The answer to questions being asked about the real reason for the four-front Nazi drive against Jews, Roman Catholics, war veterans and Free Masons is: Regime Not Endangered The Nazi regime in Germany as such is not endangered and its complete mastery of the country is not shaken to any appreciable extent and is not likely to be. Adolf Hitler’s personal prestige is not weakened and it presently is higher than at any time since he took power because of his sensational successes in the foreign diplomatic field, such as his defiance of the Versailles treaty and his reconstitution of the German army. The division betw

London, Aug. 12 (UP)—Prince Anuvatana of Siam, chairman of the regency which governs for boy king Ananda on Siam, died today the Exchange Telegraph Bangkok correspondent reported. Prince Anuvatana was a first cousin of the ex-king of Siam, and a grandson of King Rama IV.

NEW YORK, Aug. 12.—General Motors Corporation announced today in conjunction with a financial report indicating worldwide progress toward economic recovery it has begun a $50,000,000 program of plant modernization in the United States, England and Germany. Pres. Alfred P. Sloan said the program was the result of a “more assured outlook for profitable development.” Most of the expenditure will be for machinery in plants in Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Tennessee. Sloan predicted, in a statement accompanying the financial report for the first six months of 1935, that consumption of motor cars and trucks in the United States this year would be 70 per cent of consumption in 1929, the industry's record year.

BANBURY, Oxfordshire, England, August 11 (#)--Maddened by a domestic quarrel, Wilfred Gibbs, blacksmith and expert marksman, opened fire with a rifle on a midnight bus last night and killed three persons. Then he committed suicide. The victims, all passengers on the bus, were his wife; his sister-in-law, Iva Cora Goode; and Thomas Messenger. Another passenger, William Messenger, was wounded in the knee by the first bullet, which killed Mrs. Gibbs. There were nine passengers on the bus.

TOKYO, Aug. 12.—(4)—Lieutenant General Tetsuzan Nagata, director general of Japanese military affairs, died today of sword wounds, which the war office stated, were inflicted by Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa during a fight in Nagata's rooms. The incident was said to have grown out of recent transfers of army officers. Gen. Senjuro Hayashi, minister of war, was said to have prepared his resignation as a result. General Nagata was one of his strongest supporters. The director general was wounded in his rooms in the war office where Aizawa called on him this morning. There was a fierce argument during which the lesser officer drew his sword, the war office said, and inflicted the wound. The war office, after reporting the incident, immediately imposed a strict censorship on details. There has been a growing dis-

ROME, Aug. 12.—(#)—Orders distributed today indicated the mobilization of an Italian force of 500,000 men for war maneuvers in northern Italy Aug. 24, bringing the total Italian army to a strength approaching 1,000,000 men. Today's orders varied from the usual formula in that they failed to state the date upon which the mobilized men could return to their homes. This fact led informed quarters to believe Premier Mussolini will be prepared during the last week of this month to strike at any developments in East Africa with the full weight of a mobilized army which will be close to the 1,000,000 man total he set as his objective for October. The mobilization of Aug. 24 has been announced as designed for maneuvers in the Brenner pass area, Observers said there obviously

By GUENIAER USDBEUARENI, (Associated Press Foreign Staff.) Berlin, Aug. 12.—(AP)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler, whose silent retreat to his Berchtesgaden home led to reports that others were directing recent Nazi religious restrictions, stood forth today as the backer of the housecleaning of “state enemies.” Der Fuehrer broke his self-imposed silence in a speech at Rosenheim in which he declared that the Nazi party would smash its opponents. Other leaders added to the disquiet of the Jews with threats of future strictures. “By fighting we conquered Germany,” Hitler said, “and by fighting we shall preserve it. Those standing up against us shall not deceive themselves about us. “We have never fled from a fight either in the past or today. We shall smash them so they will forget to continue their opposition for the next 15 years.”

1935-08-31.text: Addis Ababa, Aug. 31—Francis M. Rickett, a British promoter, told a correspondent yesterday that Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, seeking to stop an expected Italian advance into Ethiopia, deeded more than half his empire to Anglo-American interests for exploitation and development just before Thursday midnight. I saw the original charter, signed by the emperor with his official title “anointed king of kings.” Duplicate versions, one in English, the other in Amharic, carried the great imperial seal of the “conquering lion of Judah.” By this remarkable document the sovereign turned over an area of 150,000 square miles (more than the combined areas of Indiana, Illinois and Iowa) to the Standard Oil Company and British industrial interests under a 75-year charter. The charter authorized its holders to exploit the oil and mineral resources and to develop the country. Rickett said the empe

LONDON, Aug. 31 ().—A Reuters (British) News Agency dispatch from Ronzone, Italy, said Premier Mussolini declared, in speaking to his troops, that 200,000 more troops will be called to the colors in order to face any eventuality that might arise. "The world must know once again that while there is talk so absurd and provocative of sanctions, we will not give up a single soldier, a single sailor, or a single aviator, but will bring to the highest degree the power of all armed forces of the nation," the dispatch quoted Il Duce. Concluding a 200-word speech, Mussolini was quoted as saying: "You have given during the last few days evidences of the very high morale with which you are inspired, making us certain that if tomorrow the country calls you to accomplish harder tasks, you will undertake them with enthusiasm, courage and resolution, determined to the end."

(World Copyright, 1985, by The Associated Press) ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 31.—Emperor Haile Selassie, seeking to block Italian penetration into Ethiopia, has deeded more than half his empire to the Standard Oil company and British interests for exploitation and general development, says Francis M. Rickett, a British promoter. In addition, the promoter said, the emperor has entered negotiations to grant a corporation known as the Lake Tana Conservancy Syndicate the right to perpetuity to construct dams and pumping stations at the famous Lake Tana. Rickett said an initial investment of $60,000,000 would be made in the oil and mineral exploitation enterprise, to be controlled by an African exploration and development company owned by the Standard Oil company. The affairs of the corporation, the promoter said, would be managed by an American board under an American president. The Lake Tana project

London, Aug. 29. (?—The British government intends to proceed with its own strong policy at Geneva, informed quarters reported today, regardless of what Benito Mussolini has to say. Failing in efforts at Geneva to avert war, Britain hopes the United States and France jointly will call a consultation of all signatories of the Briand-Kellogg peace pact in an effort to prevent war. Il Duce’s proclamation last night was termed just another of his customary strong public statements by these sources. Downing Street, it was said, officially ignored the long statement and refuses to be stampeded into a reply now. Mussolini's statement that British interests are not imperiled by his plans got a lukewarm reception here. It was emphasized the main thing Britain is after is not a statement about its own affairs, but an affirmation of Italian intentions not to resort to war.

London, Aug. 31—The British government warned Emperor Selassie today to cancel the oil concession granting rights in his kingdom to Anglo-American interests. The government instructed its minister at Addis Ababa to advise the emperor to “withhold the concession.”

LONDON, Aug. 21—(AP)—The foreign office announced today the British minister to Ethiopia had been authorized to inform Emperor Haile Selassie the British government advises him to withhold oil concessions granted yesterday. An official communique, after a day of silence, said: “His majesty’s government have as yet received no confirmation of reports in today’s press of a grant of concessions for oil and mineral rights in Ethiopia, but have felt it necessary to inform his majesty’s minister to Addis Ababa such concessions would undoubtedly be a matter for preliminary consultations by his majesty's government, the French and Italian governments under article 2 of the tri-partite treaty of 1906. “In these circumstances Sir Sydney Barton has been authorized, if the report is true, to inform the emperor that his majesty's government must on their part advise him to withhold the concessions.”

LONDON, Aug. 31--()—British aircraft factories plunged into a 24-hour schedule to speed up the production of fighting planes today in the wake of reports from Rome that Italy was concentrating air forces and submarines in Sicily, directly opposite the vital British naval base of Malta. The Air Minister sounded an urgent call for more pilots to operate 2000 new planes. He announced five new training camps will be established within six months.

PORTSMOUTH, England, Aug. 31 — The British battleship, Ramillies, today brought in the bodies of three German sailors and rescued members of the crew of the North German Lloyd steamer, Eisenach, victims of a collision between the two boats near Dover last night. North German Lloyd officials said two of the dead seamen were engine room hands on the Eisenach named Jagow and Hinsrich. They said an unnamed oil room trimmer had been badly injured and that still another sailor was missing. Flags on the steamship offices at Bremen were flown at half-mast. The Eisenach, a small passenger vessel, was towed stern first into the harbor at Dover after the collision. The ship was badly damaged about the bow and was riding low in the water. Tugs had battled throughout the night to keep her off the dreaded Godwin sands. The ship’s dog was also among the rescued brought in on the Ramillies.

1935-03-14.text: CHICAGO, March 13 (®) — Evelyn John St. Loe Strachey, widely known British author, promised a “last ditch” fight today against government efforts to deport him as an alien Communist. While repercussions of his case riffled the calm of official and political quarters from here to London and evoked a number of protests from fellow liberals, the towering young economist boarded a train for Cleveland to continue his lecture tour. Posts Bond He appeared before Alfred J. Schlotfeldt, immigration inspector here, and posted a $500 bond to obtain his release on Federal charges of gaining entry to the country through false statements and advocating Communist doctrines. “The charges against me are absolutely false,” he asserted. “I will fight them to the last ditch.” Flanked by sympathizers and attorneys furnished by the American Civil Liberties Union, he spent 40 minutes in conference with the ins

By The Associated Press. CHICAGO, March 14.—Immigration officials agreed today to postpone the "trial" of Evelyn John St. Loe Strachey, British writer and lecturer, arrested here on the charge of "actively advocating Communism." A hearing into Strachey’s deportation as an undesirable alien was tentatively set for Thursday, March 21.

CHICAGO, March 14.—Evelyn John St. Loe Strachey hurried back to Chicago today from Cleveland, where he told 2,500 persons last night that “Communism offers a better life,” to fight a deportation order defining him as a dangerous Communist. Lawyers employed for the youthful British author and former parliament member by the American Civil Liberties Union planned to ask for a delay of a hearing but anticipated scant success. A delay, immigration men pointed out, would permit Strachey to reap a large return on the worldwide publicity which sent sales of his revolutionary books bounding overnight into best-seller figures. The huge Euclid Ave., Temple in Cleveland was jammed to standing room capacity last night when he appeared there. His smiling booking agents said that “this order is the finest thing that ever happened to us.”

PARIS, March 13—(4)—French government officials tonight were reported considering notifying Germany, with the expected support of Great Britain and Italy, that her proposed “official” air force constitutes clear violation of the Versailles treaty. Would Invoke Rome Accord If the action is taken, it was said, France would invoke the Rome accord and the Franco-British declaration at London in support of her move to keep the Reich from giving her air force official status. These understandings include the denial to any power of the right to modify an armaments agreement without the consent of other signatories. This denial, it is understood here, was intended to apply primarily to Germany, whose military forces the peace treaty restricted. Rome, London Consulted French officials were in consultation with Rome and London to see what could be done in the face of the forthright announcement of

(Associated Press Leased Wire) LONDON, March 14.—Sir Bolton Fyfes-Monsell, First Lord of the British Admiralty, told the House of Commons today that Great Britain was disappointed by Japan's denunciation of the Washington naval treaty of 1922, but that there was no need to treat the situation ‘too tragically.’ Sir Bolton said he hoped a naval conference would be held this year and introduced the government's naval estimates to consideration by the legislators.

LONDON, Mar. 13.—The Englishman's proud boast of pipe-smoking superiority was shattered today. A mere woman outlasted ten men in a pipe smoking contest at Covent Garden. She kept 1-12 ounce of tobacco alight for 20 minutes.

JERUSALEM, March 13. (Palcor Agency)—The discovery of porcelain archives 2,500 to 2,900 years old, apparently belonging to the leading prince of Judah, was revealed here today. The find was regarded of vast importance as corroboration of Bible stories during the pre-Solomon era. A British archaeological expedition headed by J. L. Starkey reported the find at Tel Adduwetr, midway between Beersheba and Gaza. The engraved Hebrew inscriptions give the names of the most famous Israelites mentioned in the Scriptures during the kingdom of Judah.

(Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, Mar. 14. 1945. Princess Barbara Huttan Mdivani is the kind of girl who insists on leading her own life—and that, she said today, is the reason she came to London alone “instead of tagging after” her husband, the polo-playing Prince Alex Mdivani, to Spain. “Bobby,” as she is known to her intimates, was wearing a cloth dressing gown, gold slip and a diamond solitaire as a man’s thumb when she received the Associated Press respondent in her hotel suite, # (Continued on page ten)

1935-06-17.text: IN ARMAMENT RACE LONDON, June 16, (4)—Europe is pouring millions into men and machines and there was little prospect today of an abatement of the land and air armaments race. Great Britain’s defense building program finds this government, customarily Europe’s leader in disarmament, in step, or rapidly trying to get into step, with the others. The expenditure of £23,000,000 (approximately $115,000,000) for air this year has been announced, with the prospect this sum will be greatly increased next year. An additional £100,000,000 is being spent this year on the navy and army. Although France hopes to get Germany into a network of peace pacts, she is appropriating 10,622,000,000 francs (approximately $690,430,000) for air, land and sea armaments and 3,331,000,000 more francs are authorized or are pending in Parliament. Germany is leaving no stone unturned in arming against her neighbors, bu

LONDON, June 16.—While rescue workers fought their way through tangled wreckage in search of further victims of a train collision near London which killed 14, another passenger train piled up near Glasgow today, injuring 21 persons. The second crash occurred at Gourock when a train from Glasgow loaded with passengers bound for pleasure resorts smashed against buffers at the end of the track. Instead of stopping at the platform, for some unexplained reason the engine hit the buffers with a crunching roar. Most of the passengers were standing, ready to get off, and were thrown into heaps on the floors of the coaches. Three persons were seriously hurt. Twenty-nine were injured in the first wreck when a train speeding northward with Sunday newspapers crashed into the rear of the Newcastle Express, a crack train which had been slowed down by signals at Welwyn station, a suburban resort. Conti

LONDON, June 17—(U.—British and United States oil concerns have decided to withdraw from the Manchoukuoan market because of the government monopoly, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, told a questioner today in the House of Commons. The companies are discussing with Manchoukuoan authorities the conditions for their withdrawal, Sir Samuel said. He said the Chinese economic situation is extraordinarily difficult and is complicated by...

QUEBEC, June 16 VPi—The 42,000-ton liner Empress of Britain, flagship of the Canadian Pacific fleet, collided in the foggy Gulf of St. Lawrence today with the collier Kafiristan, which was badly damaged by the impact. The liner escaped with minor damage to her bow and proceeded tonight on her voyage to United Kingdom ports. Fire broke out aboard the 5393-ton collier after the collision, but the crew extinguished the flames. The Kafiristan’s engines were out of commission and the ship suffered seriously from the impact. The east coast radio service was informed that the collier was attempting to make the nearest port.

LONDON, June 16 (/)—Political circles learned today Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin has decided to reject Lloyd George's proposed “New Deal” for Great Britain. Baldwin, it was understood, reached the opinion that the veteran Liberal leader’s plans for speeding up the economic recovery of the nation do not offer any advantages over the government's own program, which Baldwin considers has been highly satisfactory. A cabinet committee appointed by former Premier Ramsay MacDonald has been studying the New Deal, much of it taken from President Roosevelt's program, for several months, meeting often with Lloyd George.

MONTREAL, Que., June 17. (U.P)—Three men were drowned and five others injured when the Canadian Pacific flagship, Empress of Britain, collided with a coal-carrier during a heavy fog in the St. Lawrence River, it was announced officially today. The accident was reminiscent of the sinking of the Empress of Ireland in almost the same spot 21 years ago. Details of the collision were not available.

Landon, June 37.—(Monday)— Reuters (British) News Agency dispatches from Hongkong said 2 fierce artillery duel broke out early today between forts at Canton and two cruisers seeking to desert the Canton government. The cruisers Halchi and Hashen were reported to have been spotted as they attempted to slip out to sea and were fired upon from the Bacnlgris forts. The rebels were reported to have returned the fire successfully and to have run the gauntlet. It was understood they were making for Hongkong. The two vessels deserted the Nanking government in 1933 and went over to the Canton command. Recently they had expressed dissatisfaction over conditions and pay. Hongkong and Canton shipping was held up until the situation could be cleared.

| Rome, June 17— (JP) —Premier Mussolini told 7,000 war veterans Sunday “soldiers always prefer action to words and we are a nation of soldiers.” The destiny of modern Rome, he declared, may well be equal in greatness to that of ancient Rome. He spoke briefly from the Coliseum, imposing monument of the time when the city ruled all of the known world, to a reunion of grenadiers. As Il Duce spoke Italy marshaled her financial and economic resources, as well as her manpower, for a war with Ethiopia which almost the entire nation believes will break out in the autumn, after the rainy season. Arbitration proceedings designed to settle the boundary dispute between Rome and the African kingdom are now at a virtual standstill and the sending of war materials and workmen to Africa has been speeded up. No fewer than four ships sailed from Naples Saturday for the colonies. One reason for the “high

1935-08-08.text: WASHINGTON, D. C., Aug. 8.—President Roosevelt will stand pat on the new deal and go into the 1936 presidential campaign with issues repudiated Tuesday by Rhode Island voters in a by-election which revealed the administration to be slipping in a typical New England industrial constituency. Conservative Democrats have been grumbling for months against some phases of the new deal program. They would like to put the brakes on Roosevelt. The president is more or less opposed by a "conservative insurgent" group of Democratic senators and representatives just as the famous progressive Republican bloc heckled former Presidents Coolidge and Hoover. But the new deal group would permit the conservatives to bolt altogether before abandoning the reform and recovery policies which Mr. Roosevelt has prescribed to attain "a better social order." Expected Big Fellows’ Revolt. Postmaster General James A.

LONDON, Aug. 7. (UP)—Great Britain made strong representations to Italy on July 26 against violent attacks against Britain in Italian newspapers, it was confirmed officially today. Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, made the protests to Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador.

HATFIELD AIRDROME, England, Aug. 8 (WP)—T. Campbell Black soared away at 12:30 P. M. today on an attempt to break the airplane speed record from England to Capetown, South Africa. He flew a new, improved type comet plane, similar to that in which he and Charles W. A. Scott raced halfway around the globe in three and a half days to win the London to Melbourne air derby last October.

By £282 “SSS a fees LONDON, Aug. 1. -— Suburban London housewives became a defending force and fought with boiling water millions of flying ants which invaded their homes in clouds, ravaging their gardens and looting their larders. The insect scourge was described by A. Moore Hogarth, founder of the Institute of Micro-Biology, as the worst in 25 years. He attributed it to the abundant breeding of the moist spring and predicted it would be over in a few days.

London, August 8. (INS). — A sharp note, protesting still more vigorously against the anti-British onslaught of the Italian press, will be sent to Rome unless Premier Benito Mussolini soon gives a satisfactory reply to the strong representations voiced two weeks ago to the Italian Ambassador here, — it was learned to-day. Britain may even consider an “unofficial” economic and financial boycott of Italy, it was said in some quarters. Italian-British relations are being seriously impaired by accusations in Italy, British cabinet ministers feel. One charge brought in the Italian press is that Britain herself desires a protectorate over Abyssinia.

BERLIN, Aug. 8 ().—Reichsführer Adolf Hitler’s newspaper, Völkischer Beobachter, announced today that all Free Mason lodges throughout the Reich would come to an end Saturday. On that day, the newspaper said, the State Lodge of Saxony, the Dresden Great Lodge and the “German Brethren Chain” of Leipzig would be dissolved. After dissolution of the old Prussian Free Mason lodge July 21 and the gradual disappearance of smaller lodges in a year-long campaign, the Free Masons in Germany—first so-called “state enemies”—thus would be wiped out completely. Hitler’s organ, asserting the secret aim of Free Masonry was a Jewish world republic, said the forthcoming dissolution would “finish a special chapter in world history, and the guardian of the Nazi ideal will be alert.” Jews accused of trying to hide their race to escape anti-Semitism appeared to stand in the center of Nazi determination to pur

Rome, Aug. 8.—(U. P.)—Seven persons, including Luigi Razza, minister of public works, were killed in a crash of an Italian airplane near Cairo, it was announced today. The plane was en route from Rome to East Africa. It left early Tuesday and was wrecked shortly after refueling at Cairo. The plane left Cairo at 5:20 p.m., Wednesday.

Rome, Aug. 7.--(4)--The War department summoned more potential officers from home and abroad today as the populace, aroused anew by Premier Mussolini's order constituting three new divisions, acclaimed his Ethiopian policy. The press alternated in heaping praise on the “unwavering determination” of Italy and flinging de- Continued on Page *Three

1935-12-07.text: (By the Associated Press) Premier Mussolini or war girded Italy defied the 52 "sanctionist" nations trying to force his hand toward peace with Ethiopia today, even as Great Britain addressed a new appeal to him to end the rattle of gunfire in east Africa. Amid stormy applause in the chamber of deputies, which met coincident with a second air bombing of the Ethiopian emperor's field headquarters at Dessye, the Italian dictator said his nation would not relent in its fight against the penalties imposed on it by the League of Nations. "When we have reached the 365th day of the siege," he proclaimed, "we will still have the same courage, the same determination as on the first day." Continue Bombings At the war front, four Italian bombers swung low over Dessye and the palace of the emperor, giving leaden voice to the determination of the Italian dictator to pursue his campaign of occupation o

LONDON, Dec. 7. —(#)— The Japanese delegation to the forthcoming international naval conference advised the British admiralty Saturday that Japan demands naval parity with the United States and Great Britain in reality and not merely in name. Further, the Japanese told the British that no other questions can be discussed at the parley opening next Monday until Japan's demands for parity are met. This viewpoint was expressed to experts in the admiralty at a conference at which the Japanese were represented by Admiral Osami Nagano, Matsuzo Nagai, Rear Admiral Iwashita, and Taro Tarasaki, the — of the Japanese delegation. This means that the Japanese are standing solidly for a navy equal in size and strength to that of Great Britain and the United States, the stand which wrecked the long preliminary bilateral conversations early this year and led the Japanese denunciation of the Washington

Canberra, Australia, Dec. 1 - Hope for rescue of Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith and his co-pilot, Tom Pethybridge, lost on a projected flight from England to Australia, was abandoned officially today by the Australian government. Prime Minister J. A. Lyons announced no further hope existed for the fliers and the parliament adopted a motion recording its appreciation for Kingsford-Smith's achievements. The cabinet is considering some form of recognition for Lady Kingsford-Smith, whom Sir Charles married in 1931, and their three-year-old son. Kingsford-Smith and Pethybridge disappeared November 8 while flying over the Bay of Bengal from India to Singapore, and a persistent search since then has proved fruitless.

LONDON, Dec. 6.—The Chinese government, it was said in responsible quarters tonight, may take its dispute with Japan to the League of Nations, charging Tokyo with aggression in the northern provinces of China. The British government, an informed source indicated, also may act against Japan in an attempt to preserve the territorial integrity of China, guaranteed under the nine-power treaty. This source said Britain was considering representations to Tokyo, drawing attention to Japan's obligations under the nine-power act. Date Indefinite The date of China’s formal appeal to the League of Nations, it was reported reliably, depends on how the situation develops and how the signatories of the nine-power treaty react to the North China situation. The Chinese ambassador to London, Quo Tai-Chi, called the crisis to the notice of the British government early this week, pointing out Britain's obl

(By The Associated Press.) The British government made a new appeal to Premier Mussolini to end the war in East Africa. Italian bombing planes attacked Dessye, Ethiopian field headquarters and current residence of Emperor Haile Selassie, a second time. The attack coincided with the convening of the Italian parliament where Premier Mussolini may reply to British-French peace overtures. In Paris Premier Laval and British Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare planned a conference to draft a definite peace programme for submission to Italy and Ethiopia.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 6 (P)--A thriving trade with Italy was revealed today by commerce department reports, despite administration efforts to discourage the sale of potential war supplies to belligerent nations. The figures disclosed also a big jump in exports to Great Britain from which some sought to gauge the consequences to American business of that great customer should it ultimately become involved in war. At the same time, the interior department reported that despite a drop in exports of gasoline to Italy, exports of that essential military item—crude oil—to Italy were multiplied by more than six in October as compared with September. From the consular service, too, came word that Italian businessmen in most sections were finding it increasingly difficult to obtain credit, and that some importers were advancing government restrictions upon foreign exchange as an excuse for delaying th

| PARIS, Dec. 7(4).—Premier Laval and British Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare undertook today, in a personal conference, to draft a definite peace program for submission to Italy and Ethiopia. The French premier and the British government minister hoped, informed sources said, that Italy’s Premier Mussolini would break his long silence and indicate he was willing at last to consider ending his war for an “honorable peace.” Diplomatic sources asserted that if Il Duce failed to respond to this latest Franco-British plan, there was little chance of ending the Italo-Ethiopian hostilities before the spring rainy season. The League of Nations sanctions committee of 18 will meet at Geneva in five days to consider addition of the dreaded oil embargo to the war penalties already imposed on Italy. LONDON, Dec. 7, ().—It was officially announced today that the British government has addressed a new peace appeal to Premier Mussolini of Italy. The appeal, it was stated, was given directly to Il Duce this morning by Sir Eric Drummond, the British ambassador to Italy. The two conferred on the subject.

1935-03-17.text: (United Press Staff Correspondent) (Copyright 1935 In All Countries By United Press) London. -(UP)— Princess Mdivani, the former Barbara Hutton, five-and-ten heiress, today instructed her New York attorney to take preliminary steps to apply for a divorce at Reno, Nev. The New York attorney is Millard Tompkins. Princess Barbara herself revealed her decision to the United Press in an interview in her suite at the Dorchester hotel. "Alec and I have definitely agreed to part," the heiress, poet, and society beauty said. Still Are Friends — "But we agreed to part only legally," she continued. "I mean that as a result of this decision we today have greater friends than ever and intend always to remain so. "The fact is we have the greatest mutual affection and respect. "We always did have, even if we may have occasionally disagreed as most people must at some time or another in their lives. "Al

By Joe Associated Press. LONDON, March 16.—Barbara Hutton is getting ready to divorce her Asia Minor prince, Alexis Mdivani, after all. A laconic announcement tonight from her hotel suite, where she has been in virtual seclusion since she arrived from Paris this week, said her lawyer had been instructed to institute divorce proceedings. Only Thursday the Woolworth heiress, whose fortune has been estimated as high as $42,006,000, had issued another of her many denials that her marriage was near a break-up. “We are very happy,” she said then, “and have had no quarrel.” Just why she is divorcing her prince, whom she married in Paris June 20, 1933, her brief announcement did not say. Her maid, who with her akin was all the company “Bobby” had at her hotel, knew only that “she is apparently very upset and has acted very strangely since coming here.” “She very seldom leaves her room,” the maid

LAUSANNE, SWITZERLAND, Mar. 15. (?)—Prince Ananda, the 11-year-old king of Siam, will stick to his studies in a private school here for two more years before he returns to his native country for his coronation. A group of Siamese officials arrived today from London and paid homage to their newly-named sovereign, then announced that Ananda would remain in school although they will consider him to be the ruler of their nation despite the fact that he has not been crowned. The delegation interrupted the boy's school work but its members said later that they had been received with dignity and calm. The boy gave the delegation a message of greeting to the national assembly at Bangkok.

— London—(4)—(Copyright) — <% far-reaching “peace ballot” caused Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald’s administration increasing embarrassment Saturday as returns passed the 3,000,000 mark. No peace movement since the war has caused so much bitterness, observers say. Launched by the League of Nations Union, it is now sponsored by 38 national organizations. An overwhelming vote for abolition of private manufacture of armaments has been rolled up since a house-to-house canvassing began last November. The government has waged several fights in parliament against the proposal. Here are the percentage figures: For the League of Nations, 97.2; for disarmament, 92.8; for abolition of naval and military aircraft, 85.5; for abolition of private arms plants, 93.3; for security by non-military measures, 94.1; for security by military measures if necessary, 72.9.

Berlin, March 16—Moving swiftly to meet the rearmament of Great Britain and France, Chancellor Adolf Hitler today decreed compulsory military service for Germany, increasing the Reich's standing army from 10 divisions totaling 100,000 men to a ‘strong defense force numbering 36 divisions, estimated at 320,000 men. Automatically repudiating the military clauses of the treaty of Versailles, the Fuehrer acted with dramatic suddenness, breaking short a rest cure in Bavaria and rushing back to Berlin. The chamber of deputies voted an increase in the term of military service in the army of France. An official proclamation characterized the measure as unaggressive in tendency and necessitated solely by the inadequacy of the Reich’s national defense in view of British and French rearmament.

London, March 16.—()—Germany has not only wrecked the Versailles treaty but has openly announced her intention of establishing German military superiority in Europe by Hitler’s decision to introduce general conscription, an official British spokesman said today. Despite the reticence of Berlin officials to make public the numerical size of the army they are planning, it was stated authoritatively here that Hitler bluntly informed Sir Eric Phipps, British Ambassador to Berlin, that it will be 500,000 strong. This will be an army of 100,000 stronger than France has had at any time during the past five years, stated an informant here.

BERLIN, Feb. 16, (UP)—Two women, a Berlin society beauty and an unnamed girl secretary in the army—were sentenced today to be beheaded at dawn Monday for espionage. Two other girls, secretaries in the Reichswehr, were sentenced to life imprisonment. The sentences were announced in the "people's" court, a dreaded tribunal whose judges are mostly Nazi officers, as the mothers and families of the three girl secretaries wept hysterically. The society woman is Baroness Benita von Berg, a tall blond and one of the most beautiful women in Berlin society. She is the wife of Joseph von Berg, a well-known aviation engineer, and divorced wife of Richard von Falkenhayn, son of the late general of world war fame.

Berlin, March 16.—Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler, in a sudden, breathtaking announcement, today denounced the military clauses of the Versailles treaty and proclaimed immediate military conscription in Germany. Germany’s denunciation of the treaty clauses and institution of universal military service rocked a Europe already tense with the increasing momentum of an arms race among the big powers. France and Great Britain already had moved this week toward increased armed strength. Neither the Hitler proclamation nor the new law specifically said that Germany denounces the military clauses of the Versailles treaty; but the conscription law actually was a denunciation and violation of the treaty. The Hitler decision was disclosed in an atmosphere of drama and suspension at the propaganda ministry after the cabinet had approved. The law was entitled ‘strengthening the German defense arm’ and was

1935-01-15.text: Associated Press, Copyright, 1925. London, Jan. 14.—Great Britain is willing to enter a swapping deal with Germany—the abrogation of the military clauses of the Versailles treaty in return for Germany's wholehearted participation in a general pact for the limitation of armament. This announcement came from an authoritative source after the British cabinet met today and reviewed the European outlook in the light of the improved atmosphere resulting from the Franco-German agreement of Rome last month and yesterday's plebiscite by which it was conceded the Saar Basin territory voted for reunion with Germany.

Indianapolis—Fire of unknown origin in the English theater here early today destroyed scenery, properties and costumes of a touring company of Earl Carroll’s “Vanities.” James Carroll, manager of the company and brother of the producer, estimated the loss to the show at $55,000. Vince Burke, theater manager, estimated damage to the show house, located on Monument Circle in downtown Indianapolis, at $3,000. Carroll said the show will be put on in another theater here.

LE BOURGET, France; Jan. 15.—(AP)—An automobile containing the Duke and Duchess of Kent knocked down a little girl and injured her slightly today while they were hurrying to catch a plane here for London. The girl, Marguerite Ollier, 5, was crossing the street to school when the car struck her. She was covered with bruises but after emergency treatment at a hospital went home. The Duchess, the former Princess Marina of Greece, and the Duke, were alarmed by the accident, but a member of the British embassy staff induced them to continue while he remained behind to see that the child was taken to a hospital. He telephoned them at the airfield that the child was not seriously injured.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 15—Norman Davis returned from the futile London naval conversations exuding optimism and hope. The roving ambassador told newsmen he did not expect a naval race but confidently believed an ultimate agreement is probable. What he told them off the record cannot be repeated, but it is no violation of confidence to disclose that it was even more roseate. No one here will believe him—that is, no one in the state and navy departments and, perhaps, even the White House. There is a widespread suspicion that Mr. Davis’ optimism is a diplomatic pose, and that his hope is a diplomatic slush. The capable ambassador-at-large has been a diplomat so long that his best friends suspect he is beginning to believe the things he says. A fair statement of the way this government looks at the naval situation from the inside is this: If the British and the Americans would promise to give the

Covington, Ky., Jan. 14. (#)— Arrested today on a Canadian warrant charging the kidnapping of John S. Labatt, wealthy London, Ont., brewer, a prisoner who identified himself as Kingston P. Murray, 34, pleaded not guilty a few hours later. An agent of the division of investigation, United States Department of Justice, aided by two Covington detectives, nabbed him on a street corner. He offered no resistance. Arraigned before U. S. Commissioner Edward Pflueger, he entered his plea and officers were ordered to take him to the Covington jail in lieu of ($50,000) bond. A hearing was set for Jan. 23, on the question of his removal to Canada. The prisoner, known as 'Piccolo Pete,' contended he had not been out of Covington for 'five or six years,' and so could not have been near London last August 14 when the kidnapping occurred.

In an impassioned radio address, Hitler asserted he regarded the Saar vote as “a decisive step in the road to ending the most terrible and the most unfruitful fight that tore European nations asunder.” - The plebiscite, he said, “means that the indissoluble unity of the German people once again has been demonstrated. Germany thanks you from millions of hearts.” Church bells rang throughout Germany when the result was announced. Schools were closed for the day after a short and solemn ceremony celebra

(Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) BERLIN, Jan. 14—Germany has perfected every detail to enable the reincorporation of the Saar Valley into Der Fuehrer's reich within a month, Minister of the Interior Wilhelm Frick said today in an exclusive interview. Frick, the National Socialist Party’s floor leader in the Reichstag when the Nazis were a scorned minority, declared a month would be more than the necessary time to accomplish the technical and administrative tasks involved. The veteran associate of Adolf Hitler, as minister of the Interior for both Prussia and the Reich, is charged with the details of absorbing once more the rich coal region.

HESSALON, Ont, Jan. 14 (P) — William Gillespie, Thessalon farmer, said today he was investigating a report a white woman who might be his sister had been found among Indians of Little Lake, near the Ontario-Manitoba boundary, 46 years after she disappeared on a berry-picking expedition. Maude Gillespie, the sister, disappeared at the age of 1. A search failed to reveal her whereabouts. The mill of the Diamond Lumber Co. was closed two days to permit all employees to take part in the hunt. They found the cup which the little girl had used to pick berries. At the time it was feared the child had become lost and had perished in the bush. Gillespie entertains a faint hope she might have been kidnapped.

1935-12-03.text: London, Dec. 3. (UP)—Princess Victoria, 67, sister of King George, died today, causing cancellation of the state ceremonies at the opening of parliament. The immediate cause of her death was a stomach hemorrhage. She had been ill about three weeks. The fourth child and second daughter of King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra, Princess Victoria never married.

London—Britain strengthens London anti-aircraft defenses; quick off embargo predicted after cabinet meets. Addis Ababa—Ethiopia reported ready to hurl 400,000 against Italian Northern armies; offensive may begin at dawn. Rome—Italy beginning to feel sanction pressure, business leaders say; at least 470 Fascist dead in Africa. Geneva — Ethiopian troops to evacuate Harar, Selassie tells league to avoid air raid, Dessye, Ethiopia—Emperor, near front, to direct Northern and Southern armies from Dessye. By The Associated Press. Great Britain moved to strengthen its aerial defenses Monday after indications she was prepared to press for adoption by the League of Nations of an oil embargo against Italy. | LONDON, Dec. 3 (AP)—Princess Victoria, eldest of the two surviving sisters of King George V, died today after a severe stomach hemorrhage in her home in Ivor, Buckinghamshire. | “Her Royal Highness died a peaceful death at 3:35 a.m.,” said a bulletin issued at “Copins,” Princess Victoria’s modest home 18 miles west of London. She was 67 years old, three years younger than the Monarch. A blood transfusion gave her only temporary relief. Reports were that, as a young woman, she lost her heart to a man whom, under the more rigid social code of that day, a King’s daughter could not marry with propriety. She never married.

LONDON, Dec. 8 (Tuesday) - Princess Victoria, sister of King George, died early today. The princess, who was 67 years old, never married. She was the favorite grandchild of Queen Victoria, and was known as the favorite sister of King George. She was the fourth child and second daughter of King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra. Died at Home She died at her home in Buckinghamshire at 3:35 a.m. (10:35 p.m. Monday, E. S. T.), The official bulletin said: “Her royal highness has had a peaceful death.” The princess, never strong, had suffered from illness much of her life. Her death followed a critical ailment that developed Sunday night, when she was reported seriously ill from a stomach hemorrhage. She also is survived by one sister, Princess Maud Charlotte Mary Victoria, queen of Norway. The other sister was Princess Louise Victoria Alexandra Dagmar, who married the Duke of Fife. Paris, Dec. 3 (UP)—France and Britain today decided to submit a new peace plan to Italy before ‘embargoing oil and increasing the severity of sanctions. The French and British foreign offices concluding secret consultations decided upon a supreme attempt to bring about a peaceful solution of the war. The plan will be based upon proposals submitted to Italy late last August and rejected by Duce with an abrupt “No!” Basis for the plan was establishment of an international mandate for the development of Ethiopia under the League in which Italy would have a dominant share plus an exchange of territory that would give Ethiopia an outlet to the sea. (Copyright)

PARIS, Dec. 1—(UP Copyright)— League of Nations leaders waited today for Premier Benito Mussolini, of Italy, to make the next move in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis. It is the general opinion here and in London that Mussolini must make a statement of his aims and intentions before peacemakers can help Italy salvage something out of its costly Ethiopian venture. Both Premier Pierre Laval and Sir Samuel Hoare, British Foreign Secretary, have asked Mussolini directly to state his case. Laval went further and has asked Mussolini if he now regarded more favorably proposals which, framed here, he refused last August. These proposals provided for a League of Nations mandate over Ethiopia, to be administered by France, Great Britain, and Italy, with Italy having the preponderant role in Ethiopia’s commercial and economic development but sharing equally in policing and in legislative, judicial, and

PARIS, Dec. 3—(U.P)—France and Britain today decided to submit a new peace plan to Italy before embargoing oil and increasing the severity of sanctions. The French and British foreign offices, concluding secret consultations.

ON AE London, Dec. 3 LINS)—Declaring it “urgently necessary that deficiencies in my defense forces should be made good.” King George today advised Parliament that his ministers would soon present plans for increasing Britain's fighting forces. A renewed declaration that Britain will continue firmly to support the League of Nations in its sanctions against Italy, at the same time continuing Italo-Ethiopian peace efforts, was also emphatically made in the king’s address. In the absence of the king, due to the death of his sister, Princess Victoria, today, the speech was read by Viscount Hailsham, the lord chancellor, before a drab House of Lords and the new House of Commons, swept into power on just such policies as the king expressed. 1935-12-31.text: Charles A. Lindbergh, declared by members of the crew of their ship to have left the United States to avoid the execution of Bruno Richard Hauptmann, landed here today after a rough trans-Atlantic trip and went into immediate seclusion in a hotel suite in the heart of Liverpool. They dashed down the gangplank of the steamer American Importer, which carried no other passengers, and, escorted by a carload of detectives, drove directly to the Adelphi hotel. There the famous flier, his wife and their three-year-old son, Jon, passed swiftly through the lobby without registering and went directly to their rooms. Even the numbers of the hotel rooms were kept secret. Considerable Delay The American Importer, arriving off its Gladstone dock in the Mersey river at an early hour this morning, lay at anchor until 11 a.m. Then a tug puffed up the side of the vessel and started it through the locks. (Copyright, 1935, by United Press.) LIVERPOOL, Dec. 31.—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed on British soil today with their son, Jon, for whom they are going into voluntary exile. The United States liner American Importer, with the Lindberghs as only passengers, was warped into its dock by a tug just after noon today after its voyage from New York. The Lindberghs stood on deck in the fog and driving rain, Mrs. Lindbergh with Jon in her arms. Are Heavily Guarded. Scotland Yard men, local police and steamship line officials had boarded the ship as it lay at anchor off the docks, awaiting the turn of the tide. As the ship docked, the Scotland Yard men and the Liverpool men formed line on each side of the Lindberghs and rushed them ashore through a lane of policemen. LIVERPOOL, Dec. 31 The Lindberghs, Charles, Anne and Jon—reached Britain to stay, a family spokesman said, for some time, seeking privacy and security for their second son. While the famous little family rested in the seclusion of a Liverpool hotel following their arrival from the United States, a member of the J. L. Morgan family in Llandaff, Wales, disclosed the Lindberghs will be guests at the Morgan home. The Morgan spokesman said the family understood the Lindberghs were seeking some degree of privacy in England, fearful lest they meet the same fate as befell their first son, Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr., kidnapped and murdered in 1932. J. L. Morgan, at whose home the Lindberghs will reside, is the father of Aubrey Neil Morgan, widowed husband of Mrs. Lindbergh's sister, the former Elizabeth Morrow. Wellington, N. Z., Jan. 1 (UP)— The little British colony on Hanson Island, 414 miles southeast of here, had its big moment today— first to greet 1936. As 1 a.m. risers were throwing back the bed covers in the eastern time zone of the United States yesterday (6 a.m. Tuesday CST) the village church of Hanson Island tolled midnight and the New Year had arrived. In all some 200 shepherds and fishermen on Hanson and others of the Chatham Islands, celebrated the New Year. The Chatham Islands are nearest to the British admiralty date line from which all time is reckoned. The line curves east and west of the 180th meridian of longitude in such a way that it lies always in the ocean. The Chathams are just east of the line. GIBRALTAR (UP)—Great Britain, by a new admiralty order, made the semblance of a friendly gesture to Italy Tuesday and increased at the same time the strength of its fighting fleet in the Mediterranean. It was announced that the battle cruiser Renown would leave Thursday for Alexandria, which has become a gigantic fleet base at the eastern end of the Mediterranean. The battle cruiser Hood, the world’s biggest warship, will return for England about Jan. 8. | LIVERPOOL, Dec. 31 (Tuesday) (P)—As the hour approached when it was thought the Charles A. Lindberghs might arrive here, police early today suddenly threw a heavy guard around the dock at which the ship American Importer was scheduled to tie up. All motor cars, trucks and pedestrians were halted a mile away and not permitted to go unless they produced specially signed passes. Cars were carefully searched by police. Officers insisted no special precautions were being taken, but one of them remarked “You may be sure nothing will happen to the Lindberghs here.” It was thought the American Importer, whose only passengers were Col. and Mrs. Lindbergh and their son, Jon, might arrive at 5 A.M., Liverpool time (12 midnight Eastern standard time) but the harbor master said he was uncertain of the exact time of docking. CAIRO, Dec. 31 (4)--New violence flared here today with the opening of the International Surgical Congress in the Cairo University building. Two British outriders, escorting the motorcar of Premier Nessim Pasha, were roughly handled by a crowd which yelled “Down with England—Egypt for Egyptians!” The Egyptian minister of justice also was given a hostile reception and manhandled by the students. The premier was prevented from reaching the university by students who jumped on the car and damaged it. Sir Miles Lampson, the British high commissioner, and King Faud previously had cancelled their scheduled attendance at the Congress.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) LONDON (UP) — Anthony Eden, chief British delegate to the British-French-Italian conference on the Italian-Ethiopian dispute, may take to Paris proposals which will bring the entire European problem into negotiations, it was understood Monday. It is no longer denied that Eden will offer Italy entirely new terms if it abandons its plan to war on Ethiopia at the end of the rainy season next month, and it was indicated the terms would recognize officially what everyone already knows — that the Ethiopian crisis is inseparable from Europe's problems and, whether there is war or peace, will affect them vitally. KLAVIK (Northwest Territory) Aug. 12.—To the Editor of The Bakersfield Californian: Get your map out and look this up. The mouth of the McKenzie River, right on the Arctic Ocean. Eskimos are thicker than rich men at a Save the Constitution convention. This is sent from one of the most northerly posts of the Northwest Mounted Police. A great body of men, like the G-Men. We are headed for famous Herschel Island, in the Arctic. Old Wiley had to duck his head to keep from bumping it as we flew under the Arctic Circle. With no night, it's all day up here. Yours, WILL ROGERS.

(Associated Press Leased Wire) Paes, Aug. 10.—Premier Pierre Laval gave warning today that a dictatorship of France was not unlikely if present measures fail in the enforcement of his recovery decrees, which have already caused disorder and bloodshed. The warning, veiled but unmistakable, was contained in his insistent demands that his unpopular decrees be accepted. The fate of the regime and the life of the country are at stake, he told a gathering of all but one of France's 86 prefects. Lacking dictatorial powers himself, the Premier made the provincial governors share the responsibility of preventing the “dramatic situation.” Fear of further disorders over the government's effort to find a way out of the depression through deflation subsided, however, as investigating officials blamed a few professional agitators for the rioting at Toulon and Brest. BERLIN, Aug. 12—Adolf Hitler took the lead today in the Nazi drive toward “totality,” claiming divine blessings for Nazism and announcing his men would crush all who defied them. The Reichsführer, emerging after long silence from his mountain retreat in Bavaria, exhorted his followers to fight for their cause. He left no doubt that the Nazi drive against Roman Catholics, opposition-Protestants, Jews, Free Masons, War Veterans and Socialists and Communists would continue on an official basis. Hitler spoke to his Nazis through the “Old Guard”—men who were with him in the days when he was derided as a mountebank—at Rosenheim, Bavaria, last night. Along with his speech were reports which showed an important broadening of the attack against “political enemies” in the Catholic church. Addis Ababa, Aug. 10. Ur— The malodorous civet cat, which smells just as bad as the United States skunk and grows three times as big, was drafted for possible hostilities against Italy. Emperor Haile Selassie’s ministry of commerce not only ordered a speeding up in culture of the civet cat to obtain funds with which to buy badly needed munitions, but Ethiopian tribesmen were reported laying plans to harass the men of Il Duce by posting the animals at water wells that might be used by the Italians. Civet culture is a major industry of Ethiopia, for the “sachet kitty” gives off a secretion that is indispensable to perfume manufacturers (of all people). They are unable to imitate the fragrance of certain flowers without it. The essence is imported to the United States and France in large quantities.

Rome, Aug. 10. ()--—Premier Mussolini reviewed part of his navy today, ordering still more men to bear arms as he drove ahead with his huge East African campaign. He flew to the Spezia naval training station and there, from the decks of the flagship cruiser, Zara, he watched tactical maneuvers of the first naval squadron. A royal decree ordered subalterns and technicians of the air force classes of 1909 and 1910 recalled from the military reserves for an indefinite time. The bitter press campaign against England, which has brought representations from that country, continued unrelentingly with charges of British “hypocrisy.”

Paris, Aug. 10.—(/?)—Premier Laval, warning that the republic’s life is “at stake,” sought today to stir all forces into action in support of his emergency recovery program. He told the people, through the prefects, they must discipline themselves because ‘“the fate of the regime itself’ is in the balance. A dictatorship, he said, is not impossible if present measures fail. Leftists Aloof As the number of deaths in port riots of the past few days reached four, left-wing leaders hastened to wash their hands of the street battles and bloodshed. They counseled their followers against disorders, which were prompted by the government pay cuts. Prefects, who were told yesterday they would have plenty of “worries” if they failed to get busy and make the government decrees work, were back at their posts today with a program of action. ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 18—(P)— The Ethiopian government launched a campaign of education against gas attacks today and dispatched orders to Poland for shipment of gas masks and arms. Newly printed pamphlets, describing how to wear gas masks and take other precautions against the poisonous attacks, were issued to tribes through their chiefs. The Polish orders were the result of the visit of a sales mission of the Polish arms industry recently.

1935-10-15.text: ROME. (Copyright by AP.) Premier Mussolini apparently believes Great Britain means war and seems to have lost hope of avoiding a European conflict, former Senator Henry Allen of Kansas told the Associated Press after an interview with il duce. Allen was received for half an hour in audience Monday afternoon. He said he found Mussolini in excellent spirits, despite the depressing effects of the times. “In spite of the heavy international threat under which he is proceeding,” said the former senator, “il duce impressed me as being probably the calmest ruler in the world. Apparently he regards the die as cast and he has no domestic problem so far as consolidation of his support among the Italian people is concerned. He gave me to feel that he does not hope for avoidance of a European war. He continues to assert he will not leave the League of Nations unless military sanctions are employed.

(By Associated Press) Alexandria, Egypt, Oct. 15—Great Britain's navy began today its first large maneuvers off the coast, between here and the Port Said seaboard at the north end of the Suez Canal on Italy's route to East Africa. Two aircraft carriers, the Courageous and Glorious, and most of the larger vessels of the fleet which had been crowded into Alexandria's harbor left during the night for the exercises. Naval experts said that this stretch of coast would be the first object of an Italian air or sea attack in the event of the closing of the Suez Canal. Thirty vessels were estimated as participating in the maneuvers. Only about 53, besides tenders, remained in the harbor yesterday. The Piscatagua Stamp Club will hold its last meeting in October, the club meeting the first and third Tuesdays of each month. Dr. C. H. Savage will be one of the speakers.

Rome, Oct. 14—Premier Mussolini indicated a willingness today to overlook League of Nations “injustices” and to talk with France and Great Britain, under the aegis of the League, about peace in Ethiopia and Italy's needs in East Africa. Government sources said a League mandate over four provinces of ancient Ethiopia, with Italy in full possession of most of the remainder of present-day Ethiopia, could solve the problem to the satisfaction of Italy, the League, France and Britain. The Italian spokesmen made a distinction between the old provinces of Tigre, Amhara, Gojjam and Shoa, and the remaining two-thirds of modern Ethiopia, which they described as merely colonies conquered and appended to the original nucleus of the empire. (by United Press). London, Oct. 15. — London newspaper correspondents with the Italian Somaliland army and at headquarters of the Ethiopian force of more than 100,000 men opposing it, reported today that the greatest battle of the war is in progress in the wild Webbe Shibela river valley. The Daily Mail's correspondent at Djibouti, French Somaliland, reported ‘authoritatively’ that Tecla Hawariat, Ethiopian chief delegate to the League of Nations had been ordered home immediately to become generalissimo of all Ethiopian troops in an effort to halt the southern invasion. A group of European engineers caught in Ogaden province by the swiftly spreading guerilla war, told the same correspondent by telephone that 18,000 Ethiopian natives had been killed since Saturday by airplane bombard- Continued on Page 28.

NEWPORT, Monmouthshire, England—(—More than 2,000 strikers were underground in pits in England and Wales today as the outgrowth of a “stay-down” strike of 150 employees of the nine-mile point colliery here. More than 1,900 miners in the South Wales district went underground in sympathy with the nine mile point strikers, who are protesting employment of non-union laborers. Walkout above ground of others in the Monmouthshire district put more than 3,000 on strike in this vicinity.

(By The Associated Press) Italian airplanes flew over Harar and Diredawa, Ethiopia, both strategic points, and bombing planes dispersed troops with explosives south of Makale. Great Britain’s navy maneuvered at Alexandria, Egypt, where a formidable fleet is concentrated. Cruise of grand fleet to Greek waters is abruptly cancelled. Hordes of Emperor Haile Selassie’s black warriors marched barefoot to the southern front for an engagement with Italian Somaliland troops which may be the first major battle of the war. Henry J. Allen, former U.S. senator from Kansas, said after an interview with Premier Mussolini that the dictator is resigned to war in Europe. Premier Laval, tireless seeker of peace in East Africa, renewed conversations in an effort to learn Mussolini's terms for stopping hostilities. (By United Press). Geneva, Oct. 14.—The League of Nations sanctions committee of 18 today accepted a proposal by Captain Anthony Eden of Great Britain to make Oct. 31 the time limit for various governments to ratify the League’s financial and economic penalties against Italy.

Latest war developments: PARIS: France redoubles peace efforts, making detailed proposal for halting war. GENEVA: League takes up third step on penalties plan—economic boycott to strangle Italy's trade. HARAR: Ethiopian commander orders general offensive against Italians. LONDON: English correspondents report biggest battle of war in progress in south; Daily Mail gets roundabout report of heavy slaughter. ROME: Italian planes bomb Ethiopian camp of 300 tents and explode ammunition dump. Former Sen. Henry Allen of Kansas, after talking to Mussolini, says Duce believes Britain wants war. ASMARA: Bruno, 1½-year-old son of Mussolini, returned from flight with four bullet holes in plane.

1935-08-14.text: PARIS.—(AP)—A three-cornered effort to settle the Italo-Ethiopian quarrel without war was ready to start Tuesday night with the arrival of Anthony Eden, Great Britain’s minister for League of Nations affairs. Eden is reported to have brought with him one of the many expected plans to give Premier Mussolini control in effect but not in name over Ethiopia. A Rome dispatch said Italy's policy at the Paris conference would be one of “no compromise.” A reconciliation of French and British views is the first step in the negotiations, which begin formally Friday when Premier Pierre Laval of France, Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy, and Eden meet. Eden and Laval will talk Wednesday and Aloisi and Laval Thursday to smooth out the rough edges of their conflicting arguments.

LONDON, Aug. 13. (AP)—Great Britain has demanded that the League of Nations secretariat place the Italian-Ethiopian dispute first on the agenda for the league council meeting Sept. 4, it was learned today. Disclosure that the dispute was placed 22nd on the list of 25 topics for the council meeting was interpreted generally as foretelling an effort to delay consideration while minor matters were passed on. This would give additional days in which Italy could prepare for its expected attack at the end of the rainy season, which at the time of the meeting will be imminent. The government, it was learned, promptly informed the secretariat that it confidently expected the Ethiopian crisis to be first on the council’s list. This comprised advance notification to council members of Britain’s attitude. The council will meet in private to consider arrangement of items on the program. Britain’s mo

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) PARIS, France (UP)—Italy will be offered not only wide economic concessions, but colonization rights in the rich, sparsely inhabited areas of upper Ethiopia, it was learned today. The news came as British and French delegates began a series of talks primarily to try to negotiate a last effort to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia. It was understood the British plan would be effected by a mandatory scheme under the League of Nations covenant. Ethiopia was believed to be willing to grant the colonization concessions, particularly as it might get a seaport in return. If Italy refused to accept the concessions at the price of peace, it was reported Britain would seek to place blame for any war on Italy, when the League of Nations council meets September 4.

That information, the leader said privately, was conveyed to him by two New England Senators who told him they had reached such an understanding with Senate Democratic leaders. “The plans,” the House chief continued, “apparently are to get everything else out of the way in a hurry, scuttle the G cmap, emt am be ready to adjourn by next week.” When Chairman Doughton (D.-N.
