SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 13.—(UP)—A ‘sordid version of life in Alcatraz Island prison in San Francisco bay was told today by William Henry Ambrose, former narcotics dealer, who was taken from Alcatraz for deportation to England. Ambrose told a story of a prison almost continual silence, where even hard characters like Al Capone, one-time Chicago vice lord, are “burning up over the rules and regulations.” Ambrose, heavily guarded and accompanied by two San Quentin and two Folsom prison convicts, was aboard a prison car with 18 other deportees after spending a year in Alcatraz; he is to be sent back to England in line with a new federal policy. The prison-imposed silence rules, permitting the convicts to talk only once a week, and “kindergarten tricks” of Alcatraz guards are the hardest to bear of all the prison regulations, Ambrose said. He revealed that Al Capone, first of America’s “No. 1 pu

London, Aug. 14 ()--A Reuter’s (British) news agency dispatch from Athens said today that the Italian-owned Dodecanese islands in the Aegean Sea have been placed under martial law with a severe blockade in force. The island of Leros has been converted into a fortress. Visitors are not allowed to disembark at Leros, but are forced to go to Rhodes, where all are subjected to a close scrutiny. Private houses on the islands have been requisitioned for hospital service in the militarization program. The 13 islands of the Dodecanese are in the Aegean Sea, off the coast of Asia Minor. Rhodes is the best known of the islands. Formerly in the possession of Turkey, the secret treaty of London of 1915, which won Italy’s entrance into the World War, gave Italy sovereignty over the islands. This sovereignty was disputed until, in 1920, the treaty of Sèvres gave Italy full control. The island of Leros

Geneva, Aug. 14. (UP)—Japan’s right to retain privileges enjoyed by members of the League of Nations, despite her withdrawal from that body, was challenged by the League today for the first time. The mandates commission asked Great Britain why she is allowing Japanese products to enter Palestine, which is mandated to Britain, on an equal footing with products of League members. Publication of the mandate commission’s minutes showed that the commissioners twice sought to learn why Britain, as a mandatory power, is permitting the alleged dumping of Japanese textiles and other products into Palestine. British representatives replied that the Anglo-Japanese commercial treaty of 1911 prevented Palestine from taking action, although Japan, by resigning from the League, theoretically lost the equal rights which the mandate system guarantees to all members of the League. The commissioners retort

Paris, Aug. 14. (P)—Premier Laval of France and Anthony Eden, British minister for League of Nations affairs, played their first cards today in their negotiations to give Premier Mussolini of Italy what he wants by peace instead of war. Two threats hung over the momentous conversations which Eden engaged in at the foreign ministry. First was a war in Africa with its danger of arousing race hatreds throughout the world; the second was Eden’s rumored intention of announcing that Great Britain would wash her hands of the proposed European peace system if Italy conquers Ethiopia. Six diplomats began “an exchange of views” which French officials said may, in a few weeks, decide whether there shall be continued peace or a war that may further disturb the whole troubled European situation.

1935-05-01.text: Copyright 1985 by The Associated Press - LONDON—Police throughout Europe were alert today to quell any incipient disorders heralding tomorrow's celebration of May Day—the day originally designated for peaceful festivities of working men. Trouble threatened most seriously in Spain and Austria. A brief exchange of shots, during which a young woman was gravely wounded, developed from a communist demonstration in Madrid yesterday. Ten communists were arrested in Seville after authorities found subversive literature in their possession. Fascists Clash with Police. In Austria, Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg’s government offered free goulash and movies as a counter attraction to disorder. The attitude of the conservative peers came as a strong dissenting voice in the general chorus of condemnation and apprehension over Germany's course. “Germany is not the only power that has repudiated treaties,” said Viscount Esher. “The sins of omission of this country and France are little better than Germany's sins of commission. Britain repudiated the Versailles treaty by not making effective her pledge to disarm after the war.” (By United Press) London, May 1. — Intensive rearmament preparations in Germany will result in completion of the Reich’s first submarine — in defiance of the Versailles treaty — probably within six months, Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, First Lord of the Admiralty, told the House of Commons today. BOSTON, May 1--(/P)—Marked declines in the consumption of raw cotton in New England mills in February and March and a slight falling off in the level of general business activity in New England in March, after allowance for seasonal changes, were reported today by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston. In its monthly review of industrial and financial conditions the Federal Reserve Bank announced that during the first quarter of 1925, the amount of raw cotton used by mills in New England dropped by about 338,000 bales, or 12 per cent. An increase of 1.7 per cent in cotton consumption in January over the corresponding month in 1934 was followed with a drop of 12.4 per cent in February and a further decline of 24.3 per cent in March, as compared with the same months last year.

Hitler told more than a million persons gathered at his feet in Tempelhof airdome that Germany desires only peace with other nations. “Just as we restored peace within Germany,” he said, “we want peace abroad, because only then can our domestic work be a success.” It was a cold stormy day. The listening multitudes were lashed by a thunderstorm, but Hitler, bareheaded, stood high above them on a rostrum and pleaded for a closer union of the nation. His voice was husky but easy to understand as he spoke with solemnity through microphones which carried his voice to every section of the Reich. “May other nations understand,” said Hitler, “that the Germany of today is not the Germany of yesterday. Therefore, fellow citizens, I ask you to bind faster the band of the community. Do not forget that you are members of one people as ordained by God.” The Reichsführer proclaimed that the German nati

BERLIN, April 30, (U.?)—Germany is building small destroyers and torpedo boats at Baltic shipyards, it was reported today, in addition to “baby” submarines. Well informed, though private sources, said that construction of “coastal defense” warships such as destroyers and torpedo boats accounted for current activity at the yards, in addition, it was reported that Germany was fortifying a marine base on the island of List in the North Sea, No trespassing has been permitted near List, at the northernmost end of the island, since 1932 because a marine airport was established there. In the summer of 1933 more territory was closed to visitors on the ground a bird sanctuary had been established. Natives of the island, however, admit that gun emplacements have been built. It is known that there is a small gunpowder factory near List, liberally surrounded with huge “verboten” signs.

1935-11-07.text: LONDON, Nov. 7 (AP)—An unidentified English doctor has admitted, the Daily Mail said today, taking the lives of five private patients whom he could not cure. In what the newspaper called the doctor's “confession,” the medical man declared: “I've taken life on five different occasions. My conscience never pricked me. Berengeria off Ryde Isle of Wight. A passport and a wallet belonging to Scarborough, who was returning from a trip to New York, were found on the deck. Fellow passengers said the veteran foreign correspondent had appeared depressed.

LONDON, Nov. 6—(AP)—The stalwart Duke of Gloucester, third son of Britain’s monarchs, and his fair bride, Lady Alice Montagu-Douglas-Scott, whose Scottish ancestors once plagued English kings by cattle-rustling, were on their honeymoon tonight in the heart of England. Cheered on their way by the thousands in front of St. Pancras railway station, the 35-year-old duke and the new fourth lady of land, 33, sped to the seventeenth century Broughton Hall, an old family place of the bride’s ancestors, after they were married in Buckingham Palace. The royal couple had their first moment to themselves when they stepped into the flower-filled royal coach of the chromium-plated “Silver Jubilee” train which took them to Kettering. ALLAHABAD, INDIA, NOV. 7. (AP).—Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, flying from England to Australia, landed here at 5:25 p.m. local time (6:56 a.m. Eastern Standard time) today. His elapsed time to this point from Lympne, England, was 2 hours and 28 minutes, which is 167 minutes behind the record established by J. W. A. Scott and Campbell Black, who won the England-to-Australia air derby a year ago. The flier took off again at 6:25 p.m. for Singapore.

ALLAHABAD, India, Nov. 7 (*)— Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, flying from England to Australia, landed here at 5:25 p. m. local time, (6:45 a. m., C. & T.) today. (The British flyer started from Lympne, England, at 6:28 a. m., Greenwich time, (12:28 a. m. C. S. T.) Wednesday. Consequently, on his arrival at Allahabad he had covered something over 5,500 miles in 30 hours, 17 minutes).

She clung to the secret of her new fiance’s identity, however, saying: “You'll be amazed when you find out who it is—in about two weeks.” The Polish actress and star of American films expanded slightly on this description by stating: “He is a very famous statesman, a former member of parliament, and enormously wealthy. That is all I can tell you now because the elections are going on and it might make things difficult. “He is about 10 or 16 years older than I am and tremendously intellectual—and that’s what I want now, I want peace. “I want somebody who will love me and not fame; who will care for me and think for me. LONDON, Nov. 7 — UPR — Harold Scarborough, former correspondent in London for the New York Herald-Tribune, fell into the sea from the Liner Berengaria today and apparently was drowned, the Exchange Telegraph reported from Southampton.

| SOREST HILLS, N. Y., Sept. 11. —The two-year reign of Great Britain's great Fred Perry as United States singles tennis champion was ended this afternoon when Wilmer Allison, 31-year old Texas veteran defeated Perry in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3, 6-3 before a capacity crowd of more than 14,000 in the West Side club’s stadium. Allison will meet Sidney Wood, Jr., of New York in the finals tomorrow. Wood made his way to the final today at the expense of Bitsy Grant of Atlanta, winning in four sets, 6-2, 4-6, 12-10, 6-2.

| GENEVA, Sept 11th | Great Britain took a forceful stand in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis today, demanding, in the League of Nations assembly, that members fulfill obligations to resist as a unit unprovoked aggression. Confident of his country’s might and the support of the British public, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, opened the historic debate on the crisis with vigor and assurance. He exhibited complete inattention to Mussolini's threat against any who interfere. He repeated Britain's recognition of Italy’s need for expansion and raw materials, but he would not admit that these could not be obtained peacefully. So strong were Hoare’s words that delegates began at once to speculate whether Great Britain might even resign from the League of Nations if France and other nations deserted the covenant. GENEVA, Sept. 11--(/P)—Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary of Great Britain, gave the world warning in his address to the League of Nations today that the League must enforce a peaceful settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. He said League failure would wreck the “main bridge” binding England to the continent, and that Great Britain would back the league covenant “in its entirety.” He suggested advanced peoples should lend a helping hand to the “backward nations.” Tecle Hawariate, Ethiopian delegate, asked for the continued independence of Ethiopia. He asked the League to send a commission to Ethiopia to inquire into the charges against the Empire. At Rome, 50,000 more men were called to the colors in what is believed the last draft necessary to mobilize a million men this month. ROME—Fifty thousand more men were called to the colors in what military circles believed was the last draft necessary to carry out Premier Mussolini's promise to complete mobilization this month of 1,000,000 men. ADDIS ABABA—Ethiopian women, their offer of service accepted by Emperor Haile Selassie, began mobilizing ‘battalions of death.’ ROME—An official communique denied Italy had suggested conclusion of a non-aggression pact with Germany.

GENEVA, Sept. 11.—(INS)—In a ringing speech which heartened Ethiopia’s supporters in the League of Nations, Foreign Minister Sir Samuel Hoare today pledged Great Britain to observe the League covenant “in its entirety” and particularly to back collective action against “all acts of unprovoked aggression.” Meanwhile, League council members were studying a system of “graduated sanctions” including closing of the Suez Canal, against a possible aggressor in East Africa. Reports of an attempt on the life of Premier Laval were denied by the French foreign office today.

GENEVA, Sept. 11—Great Britain stands for steady, collective resistance to all acts of unprovoked aggression, Sir Samuel Hoare told the League of Nations Assembly today with clear allusion to the Italo-Ethiopia crisis. The British foreign secretary declared his government would hold firmly and adherently to the policy of collective maintenance of the league covenant in its entirety. To a question of Britain’s fidelity, he said, is “dangerously misleading.” Delegates in rapt attention and crowds which packed the galleries sat silently as Sir Samuel delivered what they felt to be a friendly warning to Mussolini that Britain would be strong in urging opposition to any unprovoked war against Ethiopia. It was understood they discussed the Italian Ethiopian situation. The meeting lasted two hours. Those present included J. Ramsay Macdonald, Sir Bolton Evres-Monseli, Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister, and Malcolm MacDonald, as well as Sir Robert Vansittart, permanent under foreign secretary, and Sir Edward Ellington, air chief marshal. Fontainebleau and Chantilly, in the Paris area, have been suggested as possible meeting places, alternatively to Nice or another Riviera resort. Fixing of the date for the meeting depends on the speed with which the British, French and Italian delegates to last week's League of Nations council meeting can complete reports to their governments, and cabinets can decide on a policy. French sources expressed hope that diplomatic exchanges incident to the negotiations can be brought by Thursday to a stage at which a call for the conference can be issued. London, Aug. 5—(AP) The exchange telegraph correspondent at Addis Ababa reported that he learned today Japan signed a contract Friday to supply a “very heavy consignment” of arms and ammunition for modernization of the Ethiopian army. Arrangements were said to be complete for dispatch of a Japanese military and commercial mission to Ethiopia.

NEW YORK, Aug. 6.—(4)—Helen Jacobs returned from abroad today and expressed delight when informed she probably would meet Mrs. Helen Wills Moody in the national tennis championships starting at Forest Hills Aug. 29. With six members of the British Wightman Cup team as traveling companions, Miss Jacobs, holder of the United States singles crown for the last three years, returned on the liner Majestic. “Oh, good,” was her only comment when told that Mrs. Moody had decided to play in the nationals this year. She would not say she felt confident of defeating Mrs. Moody the next time they meet “for no player in the world,” she said, “can meet a player of Mrs. Moody’s calibre and feel overconfident.”

(By United Press.) ROME, Aug. 6.—Premier Benito Mussolini has ordered mobilization of 65,000 additional troops for East Africa, it was announced today. The unit mobilized, it was announced, is a Fascist blackshirt division of Italians who have returned from abroad to volunteer for service in event of war with Ethiopia. Two regular army divisions were included in the order. With the addition of men called for service today, Italy will have 225,000 men in East Africa, on the way, or awaiting embarkation. Italy now has about 925,000 men under arms, including 700,000 in the home forces. In addition, there are 340,000 Fascist militia who may be called out, and the army class of 1912, numbering 200,000 men, is subject to call. Youths of the military classes of 1915, 1916 and 1917 will receive training each Saturday afternoon from Sept. 20 to Feb. 21, 1936, in preparation for army service.

ATHENS, Greece, Aug. 5 (#)-- Complete order has been restored everywhere in the rebellious isle of Crete, the government announced tonight, after a short-lived revolt by 4,000 strikers had taken a reported toll of six dead and nearly 40 wounded. The riotous strikers early today overwhelmed government forces in Candia, sacked the administrative offices and fought in the streets with stolen weapons. They capitulated late in the day. They were given until morning to surrender all the stolen arms or face drastic measures, General Bakopoulos, in command of the trouble zone, reported to Athens. Six strikers were reported killed.

While the government awaited news from Geneva of the reopening of the conciliation commission's discussions, informed quarters said the four conciliators might encounter difficulties at once in naming a fifth arbiter. The National Federation of World War Storm Troopers submitted to the government a request for admission into the East African service. The regular program for supplying Italy’s colonies with troops, workmen and materials proceeded apace. The steamer Nazario Sauro, which sailed from Naples last night, headed across the Mediterranean.

Berlin, Aug. 09—An avowal by Dr. Paul Joseph Goebbels to strike "into the dust" all "state enemies" sharpened today the Nazi drive on all who have stood out against party discipline. The minister of propaganda, addressing a demonstration at Essen, Sunday, fired a broadside particularly against the Stahlhelm (steel helmets) veterans organization, but turned also on Jews and "political Catholicism". Grave apprehension prevailed in Steel Helmet circles, especially after it became known that not only had its organ, Der Stahlhelm, been suspended indefinitely, but that Former Field Marshal August von Mackensen, an honorary member since its foundation, had resigned. Goebbels’ blunt assertion that "there is no organization beside the Nazi party entitled to own political 'life' in the Third Reich," was seen by many sources as an omen that an end of the veterans union of some 790,000 members may b

1935-07-22.text: ROME, July 22 (*)—Foreign diplomats at Addis Ababa were reported today to be arranging to move their legations as Italian officials expressed doubt that efforts by England and France would ward off an Italo-Ethiopian war. The authoritative newspaper La Stampa of Turin said diplomats have decided to go to Djibouti, French Somaliland, when growing resentment among Ethiopians to white men makes the situation too serious. The ministers and consuls of the United States, England, France, and Japan already have acquired legation buildings at Djibouti, the newspaper said, and have begun to send their archives there. The management of the Franco-Ethiopian railway between Addis Ababa and Djibouti was reported to have ordered a special train placed at the disposal of the consulate corps. British circles said they believed Sir Eric Drummond, British ambassador to Rome, would ask Premier Benito Musso

ROME, July 22.—(UP)—Benito Mussolini, defiant and in fighting mood, is due this week to give Great Britain and France the final word on peace or war with Ethiopia. If the week passes without an approach to pacific negotiation, it was indicated today, war will be almost inevitable. Britain and France, it was learned, were working on what they feared and Italy believed offered the last hope for peace. Sir Eric Drummond and Count Charles De Chambrun, the British and French ambassadors, have been engaged in consultations with Fulvio Suvich, Mussolini's undersecretary for foreign affairs. Up to Mussolini The consultations, it is under—stood on reliable authority, have reached a stage where Mussolini himself—his own foreign minister and the final authority—must be consulted and say the words that mean a precarious peace or certain hostilities when the Ethiopian rainy season ends in September.

LONDON, July 22. — (>) — Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, first lord of the admiralty, told the house of commons today that England was definitely abandoning the principle of naval ratios adopted in 1922 at Washington. Sir Bolton, who made his statement during a defense of the recent Anglo-German naval pact, declared Great Britain’s new policy had been adopted because some nations felt it wounded their national pride to accept permanent inferiority. (Under the Washington treaty of 1922, later supplemented by the London treaty of 1930, the Naval tonnage ratios of the leading powers were established at 5 for Great Britain to 5 for the United States to 3 for Japan—the famous 5-5-3 ratio. The navies of France and Italy, on the same basis, received a rating of 1.5 each.) Sir Bolton explained that other means are being sought to accomplish the same result of naval limitation. They would be based upon

New London, Conn., July 21.—(P)—The 110 passengers and part of the crew of the excursion steamship Yankee were removed by the coast guard tonight as she ran onto rocks at the mouth of the New London harbor in a dense fog. Although first reports said 250 passengers were aboard, coast guard officials said all had been taken off when the 110 reached shore. Stay Aboard Some members of the crew remained aboard to aid in attempts to float the vessel at high tide.

LONDON. (Monday). (UP), Wahabi warriors in Hejaz territory released Capt. Joseph Chamberlain, son of Sir Austen Chamberlain, and seven companions after holding them captive for a week, according to dispatches from Jerusalem. The men were released as the result of an appeal cabled by young Emir Saud, crown prince of Saudi Arabia, who is now in London, to his father, Ibn Saud, it was explained. The dispatches said the men had been “handsomely treated” and entertained, after they were reported to have unwittingly crossed the frontier while on a pleasure expedition from their post on the trans-Jordan frontier.

LAHORE, India, July 21—U—British troops were forced to fire on three occasions today in an attempt to disperse rioting Moslems who have been striving since yesterday to gain possession of the Gurwara mosque, which is being demolished by Sikhs. The total deaths since the outbreak of the trouble yesterday is estimated at 10. The actual number is not ascertainable due to the native custom of quickly removing the slain and wounded. Cavalry and armored car units were summoned today to support the Royal Scots guard who have been doing heavy duty under the blazing sun.

| WIMBLEDON, England. July 22 (UP).—Baron Gottfried von Cramm defeated Wilmer Allison of Austin, Tex., today to even the count at one match each in the interzone Davis Cup tie between the United States and Germany. Von Cramm won 8-6, 6-3, 6-4. The tie, which will determine the nation to challenge England for the cup later in the month, will be resumed tomorrow with a doubles match, and concluded on Wednesday by two singles matches. America, despite Allison's defeat today, still is favored to win the tie. The American doubles team is a heavy favorite to take tomorrow's lone engagement for a 2-1 lead, and Allison is liked over Henkel on Wednesday. The American champion will have to play better than he did today, however. Not once, during the entire three sets, did he appear a match for the fluent-stroking nobleman. Allison's showing was a severe disappointment. As America’s No. 1 man, and

LONDON, July 28 - The cabinet met in special session today to consider the Ethiopian situation and was understood to have concerns over Premier Mussolini's ambitions in Africa. A usually trustworthy source revealed that high government officials were apprehensive that Mussolini's colonial aspirations in Africa could extend beyond Ethiopia and even lead to direct conflict with the interests of the British Empire. It was understood the meetings prompted Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, to urge cabinet colleagues to work towards localizing the Italian-Ethiopian dispute. It was reported that members of the cabinet, including Anthony Eden, secretary of state for league affairs, presented arguments that the attempt to isolate the Italian-Ethiopian affair would undermine the League's authority. It could sound the doom of any European action through the League, they declared, and amount to r

1935-07-31.text: GENEVA, July 31.—Secret three-power negotiations by Great Britain, France and Italy emerged today as the chief hope of preventing war between Italy and Ethiopia while anxious League of Nations council delegates assembled for a portentous meeting. So grave was the situation, so far apart were the powers on policy, so real was the danger that a war in Ethiopia would spread inevitably if slowly to Europe and perhaps to Asia, that few cared to risk a ‘real show-down at the council meeting starting at 5 p. m. today. In an admitted emergency, authoritative British and French sources revealed a plan by which Anthony Eden and Pierre Laval, the British and French chief delegates, would contact Baron Pompeo Aloisi, Italian chief delegate, at once, and seek by direct negotiation to avoid a crisis. Arbitrate Border Clashes. If they succeed in reaching a basis for discussion, it is intended to try to

Geneva—League future seen at stake as council members arrive for momentous session on Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Paris—Anthony Eden of Britain, Pierre Laval of France seek way to peace; no progress reported. Rome—Italy sends diplomats north to Geneva, troops south to Africa. Addis Ababa—Field army of 10,000 leaves capital, reportedly for front; Ethiopians head Italian Somalis in revolt. London—Authoritative quarters say Britain to press Duce to accept economic advantages. Capetown—Reuters (British) news agency reports Emperor Haile Selassie wants all white volunteers sent to Ethiopia at once to officer army.

GENEVA, July 31 (P)—The League of Nations council, facing one of the gravest international controversies of the league's 15 year history, met in private session at 5 p. m. today to seek a way of averting an Italo-Ethiopian war. An open clash between Italy and Great Britain, despite the common front they achieved at Stresa in May, was predicted in view of Britain's authoritatively reported determination to have the whole African situation thoroughly thrashed out around the council table. Italy has indicated she merely wants to bring about resumption of the work of the Italo-Ethiopian conciliation commission. A British spokesman asserted it would be "futile, perfectly futile thus to limit the council's activity." Though Britain was said to be determined to get more than mere promises that the disputants would not resort to war, French circles said it appeared likely the council would adjou

GENEVA, July 31—(AP)—Premier Pierre Laval of France, Anthony Eden of Great Britain, and Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov of Russia failed tonight in a private meeting to reach an accord on the basis of a formula for an Italo-Ethiopian peace move. They had been assigned to the task by the League of Nations Council. The three diplomats are to meet again later tonight in another attempt at an accord. Baron Pompeo Aloisio, Premier Mussolini’s representative in the league, flatly told the League Council today that Italy would not discuss anything at this time except the arbitration question in its dispute with Ethiopia. Not In Talks The Italian representative declared he could not participate in any discussion which included other matters than the subject of arbitration. He was heard by the council meeting in private session which lasted less than one hour. It adjourned until 5 p.m. (liam. EL

{Copyright 1935 by United Press) LONDON, July 31 (P)—Great Britain has decided to dispatch Indian troops to Addis Ababa to reinforce the Legation Guard, it was understood today. The decision was understood to have been reached at a cabinet meeting this morning at No. 10 Downing Street, official residence of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin. The present legation guard consists of a white officer and 20 colored Colonial soldiers. It was expected that the additional force would consist of a company of the crack troops, among the toughest fighters in the world, and a contingent of machine gunners. Today’s news complements reports from Paris yesterday that Great Britain was preparing to defend British interests in the Lake Tsana region of Northwest Ethiopia in event of an Italian-Ethiopian war. This report said British Sudanese troops were ready to cross the frontier and occupy the Gondar regio

Geneva, July 31.—(Copyrighted by The Associated Press)—An open clash between the views of Italy and Britain over the League of Nations handling of the Italo-Ethiopian conflict was evident as leaders of various delegations carried out their preliminary conversations. Italy has indicated she is here merely to secure resumption of the conciliations commission while the British spokesmen asserted it would be "futile, perfectly futile" thus to limit the council's activities. The British spokesmen declined to reveal England's hand to be played at the council's proceeding except that it will go further than resumption of the conciliation commission and will devote its efforts to prevent an outbreak of war. The impression prevailed that England will at least insist on some pledge by both Italy and Ethiopia that neither country would resort to force during the conciliation proceedings. The Britis

Vancouver, B. C., July 31 (UP)—Two persons were killed and two were injured when a seaplane plunged into Atla Lake, north of Vancouver, in an accident for which British Columbia officials sought an explanation today. The dead are: R. W. Brock, dean of applied science at the University of British Columbia, and chairman of the Vancouver harbor board, and W. R. McClusky, pilot of the plane. The injured are Mrs. Brock and David Sloan, director of the Pioneer mine.

VANCOUVER, B.C. CU.—(/)— Dean R. W. Brock of the University of British Columbia and chairman of the Vancouver board of harbor commissioners, and Pilot W. McCloskey were killed Tuesday and two other persons were injured in an airplane crash near Alta Lake, about 10 miles north of here. Information reaching here Tuesday was that a seaplane owned by the Pioneer Mines nose-dived after taking off from Alta Lake, a point on the Pacific Great Eastern railway.

1935-10-27.text: LONDON, Oct. 26.—(P)— The British government marshalled a formidable battery of sanctions guns into position against Italy tonight. The treasury department ordered that financial sanctions against Italy be made effective next Tuesday. It was announced the arms embargo became operative yesterday, and that economic sanctions would be levied when the League council orders them, probably in early November. Everything Ready. The government announced everything was now prepared for the effective operation of sanctions. A distinct feeling that many weeks and months may elapse before peace can be secured in Ethiopia was apparent in British official circles. It brought an end to the week's bright hopes that Premier Mussolini would grasp the olive branch held out to him by British statesmen. Proposal Unacceptable, Definitively branding as unacceptable Mussolini's peace proposals, advanced in diplo

Rome, Oct. 26.—--()--Italy, disappointed that Great Britain's fleet is still massed in the Mediterranean, announced a huge appropriation to bolster her own navy. A government decree authorized 441,000,000 lire (about $25,721,000) as an extra appropriation for “new construction and transformation of naval craft.” Another decree set up a “high naval command” in Italy's Dodecanese Islands in the Aegean Sea. Hope Lost Italy was clearly disappointed that Britain had not withdrawn some of its fleet following Italy’s gesture of recalling a division of troops from Libya.

LONDON, (UP). A fire damp in the Akaike mine in Fukuoka prefecture buried 126 miners, an exchange telegraph dispatch from Tokyo said. Six bodies were recovered. Little hope was held for the remainder.

Latest war developments: ITALIAN FRONT: Final Italian advance on Makale expected tomorrow. ADDIS ABABA: Ethiopian sources report route of advance Italian detachment at Makale. GENEVA: League studying means of cutting off oil, coal, iron and steel from Italy, with cooperation of United States and Germany. ROME: Oil scarcity sends price of gasoline up nearly 30 cents to more than $1 a gallon.

(By The Associated Press): ROME—Premier Mussolini denounces sanctions and announces Italy will fight against them; new naval appropriations are made. MOGADISCIO, ITALIAN SOMALILAND—Fascist troops push toward heart of northeast Ethiopia, planning eventually to join Italy’s northern army. ADDIS ABABA—Italy’s minister to Ethiopia departs by train for home. ITALIAN NORTHERN ARMY—Reports indicated the southern Italian army soon may threaten Harar, important eastern city. -LONDON—Treasury department orders financial sanctions against Italy effective next Tuesday. - PARIS—Official circles indicate France will soon accept applications of sanctions.

Rome, Italy—(?)—Benito Mussolini lashed out at sanctions in a militant appeal to his fascist followers Saturday and warned that Italy would fight against this “most odious of injustices.” His warlike words were in his annual message to the blackshirts as a salute to the 14th year of fascism, opening Monday on the anniversary of the march on Rome. “Those who are ready to consummate against us the most odious of injustices will perceive that the Italian people is capable of heroisms like those of the soldiers who avenged Adwa with glory and carried civilization to the soil of Africa,” he said, referring to sanctions. “This is an epoch in which one must feel the pride of living and of fighting. This is an epoch in which a people measures upon a base of hostile forces its capacity of resistance and victory. “Before an economic siege which history will brand as an absurd crime, destined to au

ROME, Oct. 26.—(U.P)—Italy will fight against League of Nations penalties by organizing “the most desperate defense,” Premier Benito Mussolini told the nation today in a ringing proclamation commemorating Monday's thirteenth anniversary of the fascist march on Rome. Italy salutes the fourteenth year of fascism “with a war-like spirit and with flags unfurled,” Mussolini declared. In a veiled threat to those who impose sanctions, Il Duce said Italians will long remember such action and in the future be able to “distinguish between friend and foe.” The anniversary message to the black shirts was published in the order sheet of the fascist party, marking fascism’s most sacred anniversary.

Rome, Oct. 26—()—Italy thrust her military farter into Northern Ethiopia today, Italian correspondents with the invaders reported tonight, as native Eritrean troops captured two towns in a determined drive southward toward Makale. The troops which advanced from southward toward their goal, while those from the vicinity of Aksum cut across country eastward for 15 miles, the two Eritrean columns being respectively 35 and 60 miles from Makale. The dispatches received here said the Italian-trained natives occupied Debra Sion and Tecla-Aimanot (not shown on maps.) The first Eritrean advance column began its drive from Edaga Hamus, about 50 miles north of Makale, and filtered into enemy territory via mule trails leading to Makale. (Edaga Hamus is a village 15 miles southeast of Adigrat, one of the first Ethiopian towns occupied by the Italian northern army.) Other indigenous troops filed into

1935-11-19.text: LONDON (UP)—A British long-term loan to the Soviet Union, coupled with possible settlement of the debts of the old czarist regime is under official consideration, it was revealed authoritatively today. The plan is still in the stage at which the British foreign office, treasury and board of trade are considering various suggestions, but there have been preliminary discussions with the Soviet government. Formal Anglo-Soviet negotiations, however, will await further clarification of the British attitude. The Russian pre-revolutionary debts to Britain, according to British estimates, totalled 250,000,000 pounds (nearly $1,250,000,000).
LONDON, Nov. 19—(UP)—Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King has invited President Roosevelt to visit Canada, highly informed sources said today.

(By United Press). London, Nov. 19. -- The Exchange Telegraph reported in a dispatch dated with the Italian forces today, that 6,000 Ethiopians were killed or wounded in the Italian aid and machine gun raid south of Makale. The computation was based on estimates of bodies viewed from the air and on statements of the wounded and captured, the dispatch said.

LONDON, Nov. 19 (AP)—Dr. Hermann Gortz, a German, was arrested at Harwich, authorities announced today, charged under the Official Secrets Act. Gortz was remanded, the officials said, and will appear in the courts in the normal way. The Official Secrets Act is applied in cases where a leakage of secret information is suspected. The Daily Sketch called the arrest a sensational development, arising from reports circulating for some time in a number of naval ports and air stations in south and west England. This newspaper said it was alleged Dr. Gortz was in possession of documents contrary to the secrets set. The Sketch said Gortz was a wartime member of the German air force and a frequent visitor to England before and after the war.

Washington, Nov. 23.—The Far Eastern situation with respect to approaching Japanese domination of North China was discussed today by the British Ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, and William Phillips, Undersecretary of State. Phillips confirmed this at a press conference. He said Ambassador Lindsay presented nothing formally. Their conference was described further as having dealt with various matters but with nothing of particular importance. The Undersecretary said this Government had made no plans to invoke the nine-power treaty and that such a step was not now under consideration. The treaty to which he referred was made in Washington in 1922 at a conference of the nine powers most interested in Far Eastern affairs.
Bs United Press PARIS, Nov. 19.—The French note rejecting Italy’s recent protest against sanctions imposed by League powers was handed tonight to the Italian ambassador, Cittorlo Cirutti.

London, Nov. 19 (INS)—A sensation was caused in London today with revelation that Dr. Herman Gortz, a German who was arrested recently in England upon returning to this country from Germany, is charged with espionage in England under the Official Secrets Act. Gortz is now in prison under remand, and authorities refuse to give out any information regarding him. It is understood, however, that Gortz, who was a frequent visitor to England before and after the World War, was recently accompanied by a beautiful blonde, said to be his daughter or niece, who was working as his secretary. According to reports, he was found in possession of documents contrary to the Official Secrets Act.

Washington. — (7) — President Roosevelt was believed to be ready to announce today or tomorrow the names of the men who will represent the United States in the London naval conference beginning Dec. 6. Advance indications were that Norman H. Davis, the president's “roving ambassador,” and Admiral William H. Standley, chief of naval operations, would head the delegation.

1935-10-10.text: London, Oct. —-(P)—Premier Mussolini's invading armies consolidated their positions for a new offensive in the vicinity of the holy city of Aksum tonight and the Ethiopian government ordered the Italian minister to leave the country. These developments came as the world awaited action by the assembly of the League of Nations tomorrow on sanctions against Italy. Already Taken While Rome officials said the armies were preparing for a push beyond Adigrat, some press dispatches reported Aksum, in northern Ethiopia and once the capital of the empire, had already been taken. Ethiopians have made several attempts to recapture Aduwa, Italian officials said, but were refused on every occasion. One British agency reported the Italian capture of the hamlet of Edagahamus, 10 miles beyond Adigrat. A Reuters dispatch said Italians used gas for the first time near Aduwa yesterday, but there was no offi

London, Oct. 9.— (4?) —Austria and Hungary, key actors in another and never-to-be-forgotten drama of Mars, rudely jolted hopes for a common League of Nations front on sanctions against war-like Italy tonight. Those nations, Italy’s neighbors, yet her foes two decades ago, came to the rescue of Benito Mussolini in the setting of a grave, twilight session of the League assembly and threw Geneva into a turmoil. There were indications the assembly, when it takes up its task again tomorrow, will by majority vote uphold the League council's indictment of Italy as a war-maker. British cabinet ministers, in London, held hurried meetings. The government felt the League of Nations system was hanging in the balance. Italy and Ethiopia virtually broke off all relations. Their envoys in Addis Ababa and Rome were expected momentarily to leave for their respective homes. Great Britain continued her def

London, Oct. 10.—(UP)—Ethiopians fear that Dedjabmatch Haile Selassie Hugsa, son in law of Emperor Haile Selassie I, has been killed in a daring cavalry drive into Eritrea. It is learned that Aberas and Aile, two of Ras Suyoum’s trusted generals, have been killed in battle at Adigrat,” said a brief dispatch received in Rome today from Adigrat. Haile Selassie Hugsa, who married the emperor's second daughter, was the leader of the raid of 15,000 men sent by Ras Siyoum across the Ethiopian frontier, according to dispatches from Addis Ababa. The raid was started last Saturday while the Italians were preoccupied with the attack on Adigrat and Aduwa. The Ethiopian government had frankly expressed anxiety lest the daring raiders would be cut off and annihilated. The fact that the Italians mentioned “Ail

{By United Press. Paris, Oct. 16.—Two writers on diplomatic affairs reported today in newspapers of widely divergent policy that Great Britain will blockade the Red Sea within six weeks to isolate Italy’s African expeditionary armies from their homeland. Both writers intimated that the foreign office and the directorate of the Suez Canal, whose headquarters are in Paris, have been unofficially warned that the blockade may be necessary to enforce League of Nations penalties against Italy. Simultaneous appearance of the report in the semi-Fascist Echo de Paris and the left wing Oeuvre gave it an appearance of authenticity. The writers were André Geraud Pertinax, veteran of diplomatic correspondence for the Echo, and Geneviève Tabouts, one of the continent's best known correspondents on international affairs. Commentators cited much of a statement by the semi-official Lavoro Fascista in Rom

London, Oct. 10, (U.P)—Italian forces have killed 2,503 Ethiopians and taken 600 prisoners since the start of Premier Benito Mussolini’s campaign in Africa, the Exchange Telegraph's correspondent reported today from Eritrea, northern headquarters of the Italian armies. The correspondent said Italian casualties have been light. Only two of Il Duce's officers have been killed and 100 officers and men wounded, he reported.

LONDON, Oct. 10.—(/P)—The British government moved swiftly behind the scenes on three fronts today, authoritative sources disclosed, to repair the damage caused by the bolt of Austria and Hungary from the League of Nations’ sanctions proposals against Italy. The British action was described as: 1. Undisguised disapproval of the position taken by Austria and Hungary with a hint that moral pressure might be brought against them. 2. Making efforts to prevent such defections from spreading to other members of the league. 3. Exerting pressure to prevent the defections from weakening or nullifying the application of economic sanctions against Italy for breaking the league covenant. The stand of Austria and Hungary was frankly termed disappointing, although not wholly unexpected.

London, Oct. 10 (INS)—Ethiopian losses since the start of the Italian invasion were placed officially at 2,500 dead by Italian army headquarters in Eritrea today, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch received here. The dispatch said Italians claimed they had taken 600 Ethiopian prisoners. Italian losses were placed at two officers killed and only 100 officers and men wounded.
ROME, Oct. 9 (UP)—Dr. Jesus Atework, Ethiopian minister to Italy, received urgent instructions from his government today to leave Italy immediately.

1935-12-06.text: Great Britain and France have given Italy a “set of suggestions” for ending the Italo-Ethiopian war in east Africa with an appended comment which said in effect, “take it or leave it.” Diplomatic sources said today it represented the last word of London and Paris before an oil embargo is applied against the government of Premier Benito Mussolini. In the face of assurances by fascist sources that such an embargo would mean “fight,” Premier Pierre Laval of France was reported authoritatively to have given the “suggestions” to Italian Ambassador Vittorio Cerruti late yesterday. No Change Apparent. The conference at which the proposals were advanced was called presumably, said a spokesman for diplomatic circles, to discuss French desires that Mussolini make some move toward peace before the Dec. 12 league of nations meeting to consider oil sanctions. No change in the attitude of the Italian

WASHINGTON, Dec. 0.—Japan and the rest of the world were put on notice tonight by Secretary Hull that the United States government does not look with equanimity upon the autonomy movement in north China. England Heard From In a formal statement, which followed close upon a sharper and even more pointed warning to Japan in the British House of Commons, the Secretary of State called upon "all nations" to respect existing treaties. Hull did not mention the name of Japan, which generally has been credited with encouraging the move to separate the North China provinces from the Nanking government, but his meaning was clear. His equally obvious reference also was to the nine-power treaty, with Japan, Great Britain and the United States among its signatories. This pact guarantees both China's territorial and administrative integrity and the maintenance of the "open door" to foreign trade. Wide

WASHINGTON, Dec. 6 (UP).—Political observers today read into the simultaneous statements on far eastern matters by Secretary of State Cordell Hull and British Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare veiled warnings to Japan to have a care lest she become the next objective of the world’s peace machinery. Hull issued a formal and carefully worded statement “in regard to the ‘autonomy movement” in North China, Chinese and Japanese activities in relation thereto,” at almost the precise moment Sir Samuel was addressing the British House of Commons in an unexpected speech that called attention to Japan's military activities in North China. Both statements stated frankly their belief that these activities constitute a threat to the world’s peace, and both placed the Japanese government on formal notice that these two great naval powers have vested rights and interests, as well as treaty obligations

BY BEN BVSENISUN Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, Dec. 5.—(#)— A British warning to Japan against aggression in China and an overture to Italy to end aggression in Ethiopia were extended by Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, today as two of the Empire’s warships were withdrawn from the Mediterranean. Sir Samuel said the situation in North China might be harmful to Japan's prestige among other countries unless she quickly clarified her attitude. "I can only regard it as unfortunate,” he told the House of Commons, “that events should have taken place, which, whatever the actual truth of the matter may be, lend color to the relief that Japanese influence is exerted to shape Chinese internal political developments and administrative arrangements. “Anything which tends to create this belief can only do harm to the prestige of Japan and hamper developments, which we all desire, of the

(By the Associated Press.) Formal British representations to Japan because of the North China situation were understood to be under consideration today, following American and British expressions of concern. Informed London circles said the British government was contemplating drawing Japan’s attention to its agreements under the nine-power treaty, unless the North China autonomy movement was quickly clarified. Britain also was understood to be considering strong action to maintain China’s territorial integrity, guaranteed under the nine-power treaty. Signatories of the pact were Japan, the United States, the British Empire, China, France, Italy, Belgium, Portugal and the Netherlands. Japan takes the stand, said a foreign office spokesman, that the nine-power treaty was never fully effective because, he said, China failed to meet some of its obligations. (By The Associated Press) “Sanctionist” Great Britain sounded a new and fervent call for peace in Africa Thursday, Before a hushed and solemn House of Commons, Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary, openly asked Benito Mussolini to forget his suspicions, pledged “another great effort for peace” and paved the way for Anglo-French talks in Paris Saturday in an attempt to find a basis for Italo-Ethiopian settlement. To Play Its Part. But he made it plain that Great Britain and the League of Nations are pledged in principle to an oil embargo against Italy in the belief it may shorten “the war; that Great Britain will play its part in any collective action the League may take. Even as Sir Samuel spoke, two great British battle cruisers and four destroyers, part of the mighty armada of 150 warships which the empire has flung into the Mediterranean and Red Seas, got up steam to venture in

Rome. Dec. 5 (UP) — Italy sees “no foundation” for recent foreign optimism about the possibility of an Italian-Ethiopian settlement, an official government spokesman said today. The Franco-British conversations in Paris, the spokesman said, are purely technical and non-political and are entirely without Italian participation. “We do not know anything about them,” he said. “We have received no communications on them and see no foundation for the optimism reported in the foreign press.”

Latest War News ROME: Mussolini expected to accept Franco-British peace plan tonight as basis of discussion. GENEVA: Small powers bitter over “betrayal” of Ethiopia and league: oil embargo expected to be shelved. LONDON: Eden leaves for Paris and Geneva to fight for adoption of peace plan. PARIS: Laval determined to push program through; Ethiopian minister lodges bitter protest.

1935-11-13.text: CAIRO, Egypt, Nov. 14--(UP)-- Anti-British rioting flared out today in a spectacular battle between police and striking students on the Abbas bridge spanning the River Nile, in which one student was killed and an undetermined number wounded and a British officer injured. The students, shouting anti-British slogans and urging a national boycott of the British, advanced from the suburb Ghizeh across the river. At the bridge they encountered a strong force of Egyptian police mobilized to put down the rioting. British troops were not involved. A British officer named Lees was passing and was caught in the fight. He was slightly injured about the head. A constable was seriously wounded. The police then fired on the students who scattered in confusion. The number of students wounded was not ascertained. They were carried off in taxicabs. After the riot it was announced that all University facu

PEARY, OFF ISLAND OF LUZON, (Philippines)—Seamen of the United States Navy searched through the gloom of a gathering tropical storm today for two persons still missing in the wreck of the British freighter, Silver Hazel. The two still missing, out of fifty-six men and women, after a night of hysteria, heroism and death in raging sea off the southern coast of Luzon, were Capt. H. A. Lennard, the Silver Hazel’s master, and an unidentified person, believed to be a seaman. Two were known dead and fifty-two had been rescued. The castaways made a mad race on frail rafts to the safety of two Navy destroyers from a small rock jutting from a rain and gale lashed sea. Known victims were Mrs. Neil Williams of Pasadena, Cal., one of the freighter's five passengers, and Bernard Charles MacPherson, eighteen, Gloucester,

LONDON Nov. 13 (The spirited British election campaign ended today with disorders and a prediction by observers of victory for the present government. Tomorrow the voters will decide the popularity of the government's domestic and international policies. Political commentators predict Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's forces will receive a “workable” majority. The returns will establish the political division of the 615 seats in the House of Commons, the first revision since the general election four years ago when the national party gained a record-breaking majority of 521 to 1. As the campaign reached a climax, Winston Churchill, former first lord of the admiralty and mentioned for a cabinet place if he is elected to parliament, dodged stones thrown at his automobile. London, Nov. 13. (UP)—Great Britain is preparing to propose that all 52 League of Nations countries participating in penalties against Italy send a joint reply to Premier Benito Mussolini's note threatening reprisals, it was understood today. It was believed the reply, as Britain envisages it, would be a strong rebuff for Mussolini. Mussolini addressed the nations individually, and asked each to tell him what they proposed to do. Under the British plan the nations as individual units would ignore Mussolini and in their reply remind him that the full pressure of the League is behind all penal action, and that they intend to deal with him as one group of peace enforcing countries.

Chicago, Nov. 13.—(4)—Endorsement of England’s “mercy murder” movement by clergymen, including the famed “gloomy dean,” William Ralph Inge, was reported Wednesday by the London correspondent of the Journal of the American Medical Association. To meet possible objections on religious grounds, the former dean of St. Paul's cathedral signed a statement that “what is proposed is not contrary to Christian principles,” the Journal correspondent said in this week's issue. Other signers, the correspondent said, were Dean Inge’s successor at St. Paul's, the Very Rev. Walter Robert Matthews; Canon J. S. L. Sheppard, and Dr. T. Rhondda Williams, chairman of the Congregational Union. The Journal correspondent said the plan advanced by Lord Moynihan, president of the Euthanasia Society who is drafting a bill for the House of Lords, included an application form to be filled out by the patient seeking

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 12—LP)—Maj. L. L. B. Angas, British boom forecaster, predicted today the coming of an American “tidal wave of recovery and prosperity” in a speech prepared for delivery before the annual convention of the American Bankers Association. Major Angas declared: “Confidence already has returned to this country; fear has declined; monetary velocity will increase. The result will be an immediate boom—first, in consumer goods; second, in plant and machinery; third, in the housing industries. “America, in fact, has at last turned the corner, and even fears of elections and foreign wars are unlikely to check the tidal wave of recovery and prosperity.” Major Angas is credited with calling the turn on the present revival of trade and industry in America in his pamphlet, “The Coming American Boom,” published some months before the current upswing.

Manila, Re fe Cpibalinaear 2 Manila, Philippine Islands, Nov. 33 (Wednesday). — Wireless message from the U.S. Destroyers, Blumer and Peary, early today announced 27 marooned men from the wrecked British freighter, Silverhazel, had been rescued from rafts in San Bernardino Straits. Only the four women passengers of the Silverhazel and one unidentified man were left clinging to the rocks against which the steamer crashed Sunday, the messages stated. The destroyers had previously picked up 20 other men from rafts. No reason was given for leaving the women on their precarious perch, but it was believed here rescuers had been unwilling to allow them to chance the hazardous raft. They were thought to be in no immediate danger where they were.

LONDON, Nov. 13 (4)—An authoritative source said today that Great Britain, in a new rebuff to Premier Mussolini, has let it be known that it is not considering an individual reply to Italy's note protesting against the application of League of Nations’ sanctions. It was stated authoritatively that the British government, contrary to Italy’s request for individual replies, feels a joint answer by all countries should be framed through the League of Nations. The answer to Mussolini's threat of reprisals, it was pointed out in informed circles, is that all countries voting sanctions did so in full realization of the consequences, balancing them against the risks of inaction which might have involved the breakdown of the league machinery against war. 1935-07-26.text: (Copyright, 1935. By The Associated Press) | LONDON—The British government has ordered troops sent into Ethiopia to guard its legation at Addis Ababa. An authoritative source disclosed today that instructions have been dispatched to African military posts for transfer of 100 soldiers and officers to Ethiopia as quickly as possible. Informed quarters said an effort would be made to pick expert black troops under the command of whites, and that the company of the famed King’s African Rifles of the Kenya colony possibly would be selected. Emperor Haile Selassie has not yet officially approved a British request for the right to transport troops over Ethiopian territory, but this was regarded here as a mere formality. Plans have been made to send additional troops to Addis Ababa if the necessity arises, the government being determined that its legation must be fully protected throughout the I

Rome, July 26.—A new formula intended to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia has been offered by Great Britain and France, it was understood today. Reliable informants said the plan had met Italian sympathy and the diplomatic atmosphere was more hopeful than it has been for a long time. It coincided with an impressive manifestation of enthusiasm by 15,000 people, most Fascist blackshirts, who paraded to Benito Mussolini's Venice palace and cheered him repeatedly while bands played martial airs. In concern lest the crowd's cries against Great Britain and Japan lead hot heads to demonstrate before the British and Japanese embassies, 400 carabiniers were sent to the areas. It was learned the government would survey the situation anew in the case the League of Nations Council, soon to meet, was unable to halt threatened Italo-Ethiopian hostilities or one or more nations refused to abide by its League obligations. (Belgium joined Great Britain in refusing to ship arms to Ethiopia, Premier Van Zeeland announcing practical reasons concerning present circumstances dictated the embargo.) In announcing that arms exports would not be licensed to either disputant, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons Great Britain would permit transit of arms destined for Ethiopia across British territory. SANTA BARBARA, July 26.—One man was missing and believed drowned and $50,000 worth of motion picture equipment lay at the bottom of the ocean off San Miguel Island, 30 miles from here, after tragedy struck at a motion picture company. The exact replica of the famed quarter-deck of the British warship “Pandora” of the Colonial era built on a barge on which a Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer company was filming the story “Mutiny on the Bounty,” suddenly lurched on its side and sank. Clark Gable, Franchot Tone and Charles Laughton, stars of the picture which is nearing completion, were not on board the barge when the accident occurred. The man who is missing is said to be Glen Strong, assistant cameraman. Several other members of the cast of the picture and of the production staff sustained injuries, it was reported.

HAMMOND, Ind., July 25,— (AP)— Police Chief Tom Martinson announced late today that two Canadian witnesses whose names were withheld had identified James Parker, alias Michael McCardell, 42, as a member of the gang which kidnapped John S. Labatt, wealthy London, Ont., brewer a year ago. The identification, Martinson said, followed a tentative identification made by the two persons a week ago from photographs of Parker, under arrest here on a charge of armed robbery. Parker, who Canadian authorities claim is actually McCardell, a Canadian citizen, was brought here today from the county jail at Crown Point. He faced the two unnamed witnesses with Crown Attorney Norman Newton, and Inspector Hamor Gardner of the London police, and Sergt. Peace proposals and the setting of a date to hear them were today’s chief developments in the Italo-Abyssinian crisis. At Geneva the League of Nations Council’s session on the threatened war was called for July 31 or August 1. In London, International News Service learned, Great Britain has scored an initial victory for peace by getting Abyssinia to agree to an economic compromise which it is hoped will be a wedge for a general peace, In Rome the British ambassador discussed peace plans with the Italian foreign office. (Copyright 1935 by United Press) CALCUTTA, (UP)—Mahatma M. K. Gandhi moved Friday to swing India’s 350,000,000 people to the support of ancient Ethiopia in its threatened war with fascist Italy. From his retreat at Warha, in the central provinces, the wizened Mahatma, called by his people a lieutenant of God, appealed to the country to contribute money for an Indian Red Cross contingent for Ethiopia and said: “India cannot ignore Benito Mussolini’s threat against the colored people. “Although India is under British rule, she is a member of the League of Nations. “She is fully entitled to assist another nation, even in a non-combatant way.” There was no immediate word whether Gandhi would organize the contingent himself or participate in it actively. 1935-10-13.text: (By the Associated Press.) In England last night there were martial rumblings almost as ominous as the roar of guns in Africa. While the mailed fist of Mussolini reached out, today to add the bloody fields of Aduwa formally to the territorial possessions of the new Roman empire, the words of England's young and vigorous diplomat at Geneva, Capt. Anthony Eden, echoed in the British Isles. "What is needed is effective action—now!" he declared. Thus on the one hand the Italians in the Aduwa region were preparing to welcome their commander, Gen. Emilio de Bono, who was to make the gesture of annexation, and on the other the nations supporting the League's action in adopting sanctions, or penalties, against Italy, were perfecting arrangements at Geneva to hamstring the Roman war horse. ROME, Oct. 12. (®)— Premier Mussolini has moved to strengthen his naval defenses in the Mediterranean so that he would be able to meet Great Britain with her own weapons if necessary, it was learned Saturday night. Through a series of decrees he has put high naval officers to work studying defenses and how to strengthen anti-aircraft services, especially in Sicily and Sardinia. For anti-aircraft protection of the islands of lower Tyrrhenian he called specialists of the classes of 1909, 1910 and 1912. At the same time I Duce signed a decree holding over in service indefinitely 300,000 men of the class of 1914 who are about to complete their normal training period. Fascism’s anger at its “new enemy,” 49 league powers imposing sanctions, was shown clearly Saturday night. Italy will meet “threat with threat,” authoritative quarters disclosed. (UP) — Worldwide boycott of Italian exports was proposed to the League of Nations' little committee on penalties by Captain Anthony Eden today when 17 key nations began consideration of punitive measures to halt Italy’s illegal war on Ethiopia. Britain’s minister for League affairs, most strenuous advocate of swift and severe measures to check Benito Mussolini’s African adventure, offered the drastic proposal at a private meeting of the committee of 17 as soon as it assembled at 3:45 p. m. (8:45 a. m. CST). Approve Outline Earlier a sub-committee approved the general outline of a program designed to make it impossible for Italy to borrow abroad. The spread of the quota system, Eden said, had taught nations how to restrict commerce of other countries. He then urged that League members “reduce to zero” their import quotas on Italian goods. "ATHENS—Greece is ready to give King George II a tumultuous welcome next month in his expected return from England. The "crowned republic" already had bowed its knee to the monarchy officially through its minister at London. Government circles took the result of a plebiscite November 3 as a foregone conclusion in view of the general rejoicing over establishment of the regency.

GENEVA, Oct. 12 (*).—The financial sub-committee of the League of Nations’ general staff for sanctions today took the first definite step toward cutting Italy off the world pay-roll. It decided to recommend the immediate discontinuance of all loan bank credits to Mussolini’s government. In addition, it appointed a sub-committee headed by Demetrios Maximos, of Greece, to consider further steps in that direction. In view of yesterday's unanimity on the arms embargo, it is regarded in League circles as a foregone conclusion that the committee’s recommendation will be adopted by the full represented general staff committee, probably later today. The financial sub-committee voted that the basis of the formal resolution for the financial isolation of Italy should forbid the following: 1. Opening of credit to Italy in any foreign country; 2. Authorization of a public issue by Italy in foreign c

The League of Nations moved to strike at Italy's pocketbook Saturday by withholding all loan and bank credits to the fascist government. A financial sub-committee of the league's general staff for sanctions recommended this action, which is expected to be taken without delay. The league, with 49 nations on record for sanctions, already has placed an arms embargo upon Italy and lifted it from Ethiopia. Adjourned To Monday A sanctions committee of 17 adjourned until Monday without having reached a decision upon an economic boycott, which league leaders favor imposing upon Italy. The general tenor of the discussion was that the problems are exceedingly complicated and require further examination. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia — (4) — Italy's minister to Ethiopia, who defied an order of Emperor Haile Selassie to leave the country, was taken Saturday from the legation and conducted by troops to the home of Ras Desta Damtou, son-in-law of the emperor. The minister, Luigi Vinci-Gigliueci, refused to receive even his colleagues at Damtou's house, where he enjoys every luxury. Position Obscure His position was obscure Saturday night. Although Haile Selassie delivered an ultimatum demanding that the minister leave by 7 a. m. Sunday, it appeared possible he might relent and allow Vinci-Gigliueci to stay. Armed soldiers preceded and followed the diplomat when he was taken from the legation, where he was a virtual prisoner to the home. Haile Selassie was plainly outraged by the minister's action. In a defiant letter to the Ethiopian government, the minister said: "I am staying of my own free will

(By United Press). Harar, Ethiopia, Oct. 12.—A battle involving 150,000 men that will test the fate of Ethiopia appeared imminent today on the edge of the southern Ethiopian plateau. I have just returned from Jigjiga, 40 miles from this Djibouti-Addis Ababa railroad point, have seen thousands and thousands of savage tribesmen entrenching to meet the Italian army of 60,000 from Somaliland, and saw the veteran and formidable Ras Nasibu, commander of Ethiopian forces in the south, depart to take command of his front lines. Even as he rode out of Jigjiga at the head of a column of fast cavalry, cruisers brought him word that Italian airplanes were over the Webber Shebelle river valley, the great natural trail to Jigjiga and the interior, and had killed many natives. 1935-10-03.text: (By The Associated Press) Paris, Oct. 3—It was announced today that Premier Laval of France and Anthony Eden of Great Britain had agreed on League of Nations action for the immediate rupture of financial and economic relations with Italy.

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS LONDON, Oct. 2.—King George took a direct hand in the Italo-Ethiopian crisis today when he summoned his foreign and war ministers to the palace just before a cabinet session on the subject. The cabinet, which heard the report of Anthony Eden, minister for League of Nations affairs, on the situation in Geneva, in an atmosphere of extreme pessimism, continued to rest the responsibility for action in the Imperial Defense Council. Immediately after the cabinet meeting, the Defense Council went into session. King George conferred at length with Viscount Halifax, minister of war, in whose hands the responsibility for assembling Britain's gigantic land war machine rests. There were indications the machine is being made ready for action. Other arms of Britain's defense—the Navy and air force—already have been or are being mobilized in the troubled sector. LONDON, Oct. 3.—(?)—The Norwegian steamer Askild was drifting helplessly, with broken steering gear, amidst heavy seas in the north Atlantic today, said a message to Lloyd's from Valentia, Ireland. The American steamer City of Havre, answering an S. O. S. call, wirelessly reported that she sighted the vessel. German and British steamers were also hastening to the scene. The Askild’s position was given as latitude 50 degrees 10 minutes north, longitude 20 west (about 450 miles due west of Rannagh, Irish Free State.)

Premier Mussolini, in a militant address to mobilized Italy, told it yesterday he would go ahead with his East African program and an unofficial report said the long-expected fighting had already started. The newspaper Paris Soir reported from Addis Ababa that 25,000 Italian troops advanced into the Mussa Ali region of Ethiopia and engaged in combat with irregular Danakil tribesmen, with casualties resulting. Confirmation was not forthcoming, but Emperor Haile Selassie in a protest to the League of Nations charged Italy had invaded Ethiopian soil in that region. Haile Selassie will order a general mobilization tomorrow, expected to bring 10,000,000 men, women and children into military service. Already, nearly 250,000 warriors were reported on the march in Ethiopia, most of them toward Italian colonial frontiers. Church bells and sirens called Fascist Italy into one of the world’s greate

LONDON, Oct. 26 Anthony Eden, secretary for league affairs, left London today for Paris and Geneva, armed with full authority from the cabinet to maintain England's support of the league. In other words, to insist on the application of sanctions and penalties against any government breaking faith. Shortly after Eden boarded his train with a meeting with Premier Pierre Laval of France as his first objective, Dino Grandi, Italian ambassador here, called at the foreign office and conferred with Sir Robert Vansittart, government undersecretary. Cabinet in between were close-mouthed about any plans Britain may have for making sanctions effective in the event the League votes their application against Italy when the council meets Saturday.

LONDON, Oct. 3, (P).—The Reuters correspondent at Addis Ababa today quoted Emperor Haile Selassie as saying in an interview: “I have just received the news that the first bombs dropped by Italian airplanes on Aduwa fell on the Red Cross hospital there killing and wounding nurses. “We think the embargo on the export of arms to Ethiopia should be immediately raised, owing to the fact that Italy has not only menaced us but, also, according to the most recent news we have received, because Italians have crossed our frontiers at several points and bombarded the towns of Aduwa and Adigrat.”

Paris, Oct. 2, — Premier Pierre Laval, cautious in committing France to a definite attitude in the Italo-Ethiopian conflict in fear of what Germany would do, today received Adolf Hitler's assurance, transmitted through Great Britain, that the Third Reich has no intention of joining Italy, French officials said. Official circles learned of Hitler's reported promise not to attempt to “draw any profit from the present situation” as Laval conferred with his defense ministers over a new alarm—the reported invasion of Ethiopia by Italian troops. Anxiously Awaits Call The premier expressed the fear that sanctions are near and that the war feeling in Europe had been heightened. He anxiously awaited the league's call to such measures. French officials found nothing disturbing in Mussolini's speech, however, dismissing it as “nothing new.” The French welcomed it as having “cleared the air of too m

- London, Oct. 3—The town of Adigrat, east of Adowa in Northern Ethiopia, was razed to the ground by Italian bombing planes today, according to a dispatch to the Daily Express from its Addis Ababa correspondent. “Terrific” casualties were inflicted among women and children who were unable to evacuate when the warning was given, the dispatch said. The battle began at dawn in the region of Agame, a nearby town, the dispatch reported. Fifty thousand Abyssinians, led by Ras Kabada, right-hand man of Ras Siouma, were engaged with the Italians late today, according to the Express correspondent.

1935-10-17.text: The estranged relationship between France and Britain approached a definite show-down. Britain demanded of France a promise of unqualified aid for its fleet in case it were attacked in the Mediterranean while carrying out League of Nations penalties against Italy. Premier Pierre Laval, asking for time, decided to lay before his cabinet the whole question of how far France will go to aid Britain. Italy determined to keep out of negotiations of any kind. The League of Nations sanctions committee, for the second day, failed to agree on the British "buy nothing from Italy" proposal. PARIS. (UP)—Great Britain has issued a virtual ultimatum to France, demanding that she cooperate with Britain in the Mediterranean or lose British support on the continent, highly reliable quarters said today. The British indicated to the French, these sources said, that if Paris does not reply favorably to the latest British questions about the Mediterranean, Britain will consider Franco-British cooperation ended. When questioned, refused to confirm or deny the British demand, but admitted that such an attitude corresponds to that of the British government. It was understood from the highest source that after Britain had applied strong pressure to Premier Pierre Laval, the latter declared he will reply definitely on Monday, after Sunday’s senatorial elections have been held.
