LONDON, July 11 U.P)—An immediate conference to find means of averting war in Abyssinia has been proposed secretly by Joseph A. Avenol, secretary general of the League of Nations, it was learned on excellent authority today. Under Avenol’s proposal, an unsuspected ray of hope of a new war, Premier Pierre of France would summon the three-nation meeting, which would be held at Paris.

CHESTER, Ill. (Tuesday.) Three youths died in the electric chair at the southern Illinois penitentiary early Tuesday for the murder of a 66 year old street car motorman, John Krul, 21, was the first to go to the chair, being pronounced dead at 12:14 a.m., three minutes after the first shock of electric current was sent through his body. Five minutes later, the youngest of the trio, Edward Balling, 19, was sent to his death. Van Buren Dedmon, 25, was the last executed. They had been convicted of slaying William C. Moss when he resisted their attempts to rob him the night of Feb. 22. Governor Horner's denial of clemency pleas made by attorneys and relatives of the condemned men was based on a unanimous recommendation of the state pardon board.

LONDON, July 10 (4---A comprehensive program for protecting Britain's population against air raids went out today to all local authorities in England, Scotland, and Wales, accompanied by assurances that “the need for these measures in no way implies risk of war.” The government's circular, which made plain that local authorities would be responsible in the final analysis for protection of the public, also pledged the government to continue striving for peace.

1935-03-09.text: BEVERLY HILLS, March 8.— To the Editor of The Californian: It's the usual custom for a writer or speaker to tell how much better England or France or Zululand have handled their money than the U. S. Well in yesterday’s paper France is prohibiting the shipment of gold out of their country, and still they say they are not going off the gold, no, but they are not letting the gold off them either, then last week England had to put up millions of pounds to stabilize their money. So I guess over there they are pointing to the excellent way our system is working. Your own country always looks like they are the only one doing the wrong thing. This thing called money has got the whole mess of ‘em buffaloed, money, horse racing and women are three things the boys just can’t figure out. Yours, WILL ROGERS.

LONDON, March 9 (Saturday).—(AP) A dispatch to the Daily Express today from its Belgrade correspondent said that Yugoslavia has issued a stern warning to Bulgaria. “If a single Bulgarian soldier enters Greek territory,” the dispatch asserted, “the Balkan pact will come into force and Yugoslavia, Turkey and Rumania will go to the aid of Greece.”

MANCHESTER, England, March 8 (?)—Fierce hand-to-hand street fighting broke out tonight as the climax of a speech in the town hall by Sir Oswald Mosley, British fascist leader. The disorder was touched off when intruders sang the communist “Internationale” at the same time those in the meeting sang “God Save the King.” Three persons were injured in the ensuing clash, which saw police, anti-fascists and the blackshirts in a three-sided battle.

MIAMI, Fla., March 9 (UP).— The yacht Nourmahal is expected to arrive here tomorrow to await the coming of President Roosevelt for a fishing cruise in Bahaman waters. Aboard the yacht, arriving from the British West Indies, are Vincent Astor, Mrs. Astor, and Mr. and Mrs. James Roosevelt, with a party of friends. Roosevelt is expected to arrive late this month or early in April.

- LONDON, March 9.—(UP)—Cecil Swaniand, 47, an artist, was remanded until Tuesday at Croydon Magistrate's court today, charged with the theft from the airport's strong room Tuesday of £21,000 in gold. ($100,432). Three other men were sought as accomplices. Swaniland was well dressed in a pinstriped navy blue suit with a spotted silk handkerchief in his breast pocket and a multi-striped muffler.

Tokyo —(?)— The House of Peers enacted the 1935-36 budget Friday, giving final approval to the demands of Japan's army and navy leaders for the largest military appropriations in the empire's history. The budget totals 2,210,000,000 yen (about $600,000,000). From this sum the army will receive 490,000,900 yen (about $142,000,000) and the navy 530,060,000 yen (about $154,000,000).

Marseille, France, Mar. 9—Police questioned three terrorists today in efforts to track down the mysterious blonde “Gun Girl” sought as a conspirator in the assassination of King Alexander of Yugoslavia. Joseph Paul von Cour, fiery former premier who will represent the monarch's widow in the trial of the terrorist, demanded the authorities find Maria von Draceck, the missing blonde. The gun girl has been sought by police of a dozen nations. Although many months have passed since the crime, few facts about her have been uncovered. The three confessed aides of the king’s assassins, awaiting trial, deny she ever existed.

Athens, Greece (47)—Reports of a rebel advance on Salonika evoked grim expectancy of a possible climax in the week-old Greek revolt today, but loyal forces were assured by the government that the presence of General George Kondylis in the area would make empty the alleged threat against the stronghold. The roar of artillery fire was reported heard on the Salonika plains as government forces prepared to meet the rebels on the Struma river front, reported to be under the command of the son of former Premier Eleutherios Venizelos, leader of the civil strife. The government placed its faith in Kondylis and the existence of harbor guns and extensive mining of the Salonika gulf. For the moment at least the bitter winter weather held in check major activities of loyalists and rebels as the struggle entered its second week. The government's present inability to make effective its reiterated prom

1935-06-16.text: London—(/)—Great Britain Saturday ordered eight battalions to be formed immediately on a wartime basis for anti-aircraft defense. The surprise war office announcement, culminating the nation’s air force expansion, said five units will be made over into searchlight battalions and three more, including the famous Royal Fusiliers, will become anti-aircraft artillery brigades. The order by the army council provided only for the London area, and organization of similar units for the great midland manufacturing cities was expected. The war office emphasized the necessity that the new units be “ready for action immediately on the outbreak of war or even earlier.” The eight new units were ordered to enter a strenuous course of training for a first line of defense. The program will be financed by a fund of about $2,250,000, set aside March 18 by the house of commons for anti-aircraft defense.

London, June 15.—-(AP)—At least 17 persons were killed tonight as a fast train laden with newspapers plowed into a stationary section of the London-Newcastle express at Welwyn station, in the metropolitan area. The official report telephoned from Welwyn said 17 were killed, but two London newspapers placed the death roll at “80 so far.” This could not be confirmed but it was believed many victims still were in the wreckage. Two score persons, all aboard the express which had stopped at Welwyn, were seriously injured. The agonized screams of the dying, pinned in the wreckage, added to the horror of the scene as the noise of an explosion which followed the crash died away. Rescue work was hampered greatly by lack of lighting facilities.

(Ape fn ASSOCIATE Press) China has resorted to an appeal to western powers for help against Japan, diplomatic quarters in London asserted, her ambassador to Great Britain protesting to the foreign office against Japan's penetration of North China. Two series of Japanese demands confronted Chinese authorities, while Japan poured fresh troops into Tientsin and Peiping and massed forces at the sea end of China's Great Wall. Lt. Gen. Toranosuke Hashimoto, vice minister of war at Tokyo, asserted the North China demands "contain nothing the Chinese government cannot accept if it is sincerely interested in furtherance of peace in the Far East." Chinese government authorities conferred at Nanking with General Ho Ying-Chin, Chinese minister of war, concerning the demands.

LONDON, June 15 (The Vienna correspondent of the Exchange Telegraph company today quoted the Salzburger Chronik of Salzburg as reporting that an attempt had been made upon the life of Adolf Hitler while he was staying at his villa near Berchtesgaden, Germany. The report was immediately denied in secret circles. According to the Salzburger Chronik, Hitler escaped injury in the assault but one companion was wounded.

LONDON, June 16. UP)—(Sunday)—Thirty bodies had been removed from the wreckage of an express passenger train and a fast freight which were involved in a collision at midnight near Welwyn, Hertfordshire, it was announced officially early today. It was one of the worst disasters in English railroad history. At least 70 others injured were taken to hospitals. It was feared many of them would die. The accident occurred at Garden City station where the train had halted. The freight train crashed into the rear of the passenger carrier, telescoping the rear coaches. The impact was terrific. Debris intermingled with dead and dying along the tracks. Garden City residents hastened to the scene, formed rescue crews and extricated victims. The injured were cared for in Garden City hospitals.

. Metz, France, June 15— (AP) French pursuit planes today chased two German ships, which were hovering over frontier fortifications, back into German territory. Military officials said the German craft were first observed over the defense works known as the “Petite Roselle,” northwest of Metz. Several French planes set to guard against such excursions promptly took to the air but the German airmen turned tail and fled, escaping over the border before their pursuers caught up with them.

ROME, June 15—The Italian government tonight ordered the recall of silver money circulating in the country. Official and financial circles said the reason for the drastic monetary step was the ever greater necessity for supplies of this metal in connection with Italy’s preparation for possible hostilities with Ethiopia. Silver coins are the sole medium of exchange in both of Italy's African colonies, Eritrea and Italian Somaliland, and Ethiopia.

- New York.—(#)—The body of little Jackie Kaul, 5, was recovered from the East River Saturday, ending a frantic search which began June 6 when the boy disappeared from a playground in fashionable Sutton Place on Manhattan's East side. The body was identified by the missing boy’s father, John Kaul. The body, taken from the East River in The Bronx, roughly 10 miles from where he was last seen, was viewed in the Fordham hospital morgue by the father. He collapsed after making the identification. Recovery of the body ended a police search that has progressed on two theories since the child’s disappearance. One theory, believed by his mother, was that he had fallen into the river. Police also believed he might have been seized by a woman of frustrated maternal instincts.

Vital decisions on raising the present embargo on arms against Italy and Ethiopia, and on the course to be taken at the League of Nations council meeting next Wednesday will hinge in large measure on the interpretation. The foreign office is awaiting a copy of the complete neutrality bill as passed by the United States Congress just before its adjournment. With the copy will be a report from the British embassy at Washington. Legal and diplomatic experts here will be assigned to analyze the bill, and if there is still uncertainty, the government will seek clarification from the American State Department. The all-important question to Britain is exactly what the embargo imposed by the bill on belligerents covers; whether merely "visible" munitions of war such as arms and a

Premier Laval of France, with a “free hand” authorized by his cabinet, went to the quiet of the country to make up his mind whether France should support Italy or Great Britain in their opposing stands on the Ethiopian question. The League of Nations council will meet next week on the subject. Italy wants the other nations to keep their hands off. Great Britain wants a showdown opposed to armed invasion of Ethiopia. The Italians frankly prepared for war, and artillery threw barrages of real shells over the heads of its soldiers maneuvering in the north of Italy in order that they might become accustomed to the sound of flying steel. They have assured their nationals that they would have plenty of notice in case hostilities broke out. In London, the Ethiopian legation posted a notice that it “gratefully receives all contributions to the Ethiopian cause.” British statesmen, meanwhile, prep

ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopia. (UP) — The Ethiopian government Friday stopped all railroad transportation of merchants’ goods in order that the army may utilize railroad facilities for the movement of soldiers, munitions, and foodstuffs. The British, French and Greek legations here are understood to have been assured that there is no need for panic and have been promised at least a two weeks’ warning in the event of danger of an Italian invasion.

British, French and Greek legations are understood to have given assurances there is no present cause of alarm. LONDON - A notice posted at the Ethiopian legation acknowledges that contributions to the empire's cause are “gratefully received.”

WITH THE ITALIAN ARMY, BOLZANO, Italy, Aug. 29.—(AP)—Benito Mussolini was off to the mock wars along the Austrian frontier today, leaving Italians and foreigners to ponder the denunciation of Ethiopia, the warning to Great Britain and the exhortation to Italians he voiced after last night’s cabinet session. One prominent Italian banker told the Associated Press that the four economic steps the cabinet took last night are about the most important ever taken in Italy. He said the provision for limiting the profits of corporations and requiring companies to invest any excess profits in government bonds which they cannot sell for three years, might be considered a temporary sequestration of the entire. Bond Conversion Forced The forced conversion of foreign securities into Italian government securities was rendered necessary by the outflow of gold to pay for foreign purchases. The provision

LONDON, Aug. 30 (®—A Reuters (British) News Agency dispatch from Moscow today said Barbusse, noted French writer, had died. He was 61. The dispatches said he had been in the Kremlin hospital for several weeks suffering from pneumonia.

LONDON, Aug. 30.—(14)—Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, is awaiting President Roosevelt's final decision on the congressional neutrality act and an official copy of the act for determination of just what actions the United States proposes to take in event of an Italo-Ethiopian war, it was learned today from informed quarters. There has not been the slightest indication, however, that the government is reserving decisions on policy to be pursued at Geneva next week pending Mr. Roosevelt's signature or rejection of the act. The policy to be followed at the league council session was agreed upon at last week’s cabinet meeting. There has been no sign it is contingent upon anything the United States does but rather, dependent upon what other members of the league agreed to do. The government, it was learned authoritatively, has decided to pursue the strongest course of collective action at

1935-03-06.text: SANTA MONICA, Cal, Mar. 4.—Greece got some kind of a little cotton tail revolution on over there. I flew through Athens in January, ‘32, coming from India and went up with one of our officials there and had a couple of hours chat with this old statesman Venizelos. He speaks good English (better than me), got a lot of humor, and is a mighty interesting old gentleman. They call him the Grand Old Man of Greece. You see he is about the last one outside of Lloyd George of England, that was with President Wilson during those historic old Versailles days. Greece has got a lot of old ruins, but he is not one of ‘em.

LONDON, March 4.—(?)—Authoritative British quarters stated today that Italy had reached an agreement with Ethiopia on the proposed neutral zone between the African empire and the Italian colonies of Somaliland and Eritrea. These quarters understood that the Italian envoys to Addis Ababa had been instructed to consult the Ethiopian government immediately regarding details of the neutral zone. An official source said that although Italy's action meant only an acceptance in principle of the neutral zone idea, it was believed that it would lead to a peaceful settlement of the dispute between the two nations, thereby averting hostilities.

LONDON, March 6.—A $97,000 gold-bar robbery was reported today from Croydon Airdrome. Three bars of gold, worth approximately 20,000 pounds ($97,330 at par), were reported stolen during the night from the strong room of the airdrome, which is London's chief airport and the terminus of the main London-Paris air lines. It was understood that the gold taken was intended for transport to Paris this morning, and it was reported that the owners were Americans.

Dery, DAAP, Greeyee pera ei Va hie clals ndmitted today that the British white book on German armaments, rather than the throat trouble of Reichsführer Adolf Hitler, was the guiding influence behind Berlin’s postponement of Sir John Simon's visit. There was little effort today to conceal the fact that the Führer’s cold is more diplomatic than real. Sir John, British foreign secretary, was to have come to Berlin tomorrow to discuss European peace problems with Hitler. “It was blow for plow,” one official of the Wilhelmstrasse said, “The white book was a blow for us and we replied with another blow.” Hitler was working as usual today, and was not confined to his apartments. The propaganda ministry said “his indisposition is very slight.”

mnie? reese stall Correspondent (Copyright. 1935. by United Press) London, March 6.—Naval estimates calling for $224,000,000 comprised Great Britain’s response today to German anger over charges that Germany's military spirit forced Britain to re-arm, The estimates were issued just twenty-four hours after Adolf Hitler, on the plea of a cold, cancelled a visit set for tomorrow from Sir John Simon, foreign minister. Belief here that the cold was a diplomatic one was strengthened by bitter comments in the closely controlled German newspapers over the charges of Nazi militaristic sentiment. The building program under the estimates calls for twenty-eight new ships as follows: Three cruisers. One flotilla leader and eight destroyers. Three submarines—one mine laying, one general service, one patrolling. One submarine depot ship. Four sloops—three mine laying, one convoying. One surveying ship.

(Copyright. 1935. By Associated Press) BERLIN — A “slight cold” Adolf Hitler developed after publication of the British white paper criticising German rearmament Tuesday caused him to postpone— perhaps forever— the visit of British statesmen in the interest of European peace and unity. It split German public opinion sharply into two sections. One charged that Der Fuehrer, in suddenly postponing his conference with Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, set for Tuesday, may have lost an historic opportunity for ensuring world cooperation. The other, which included Hitler’s most ardent adherents, took the view that the new Germany, as personified in Hitler, once again showed the world it won't stand for any belittling. Hitler’s followers seemed confident Great Britain would somehow excuse herself for the white paper and thereby pave the way for some later meeting.

LONDON, March 5 (®)—The fate of Britain’s European scheme apparently hung in the balance tonight as the government strove energetically to learn just why Adolf Hitler suddenly postponed Sir John Simon's visit to Berlin, scheduled for Thursday. Plans to expand air defense went into high gear with the announcement of 1935 estimates providing for addition of 11 new air squadrons to the home defense force. Britain’s ambassador at Berlin investigated two possible explanations of the Führer’s surprise decision not to see the British foreign secretary: —Hitler may be gravely ill, more so than the German government cares to admit openly just now. (A “slight cold” was Hitler's official explanation of the postponement.) —The British white paper, defending Britain’s armaments increases and criticizing German rearmament, either stirred Hitler's resentment or caused him to decide to give it extensive

New York, March 5.--(AV)—President Roosevelt's remarks concerning the value of the dollar at his press conference today were followed by a brisk rally in the stock market and a moderate surge in U.S. government bonds. Furthermore, a fresh decline in the British pound, which has been disturbing Wall Street as a possible deflationary influence, was quickly checked. The pound had dropped to a new low since 1933 at 4.72%, of nearly 4 cents, but it quickly recovered its loss. President Roosevelt merely stated that he did not think the debt burden had yet been sufficiently relieved by the shrinkage in the purchasing power of the dollar, and discouraged queries as to whether he was intimating further devaluation. Nevertheless, this was sufficient to give a boost to the share market. Some quarters in Wall Street regarded the President's remarks as a strong hint to British monetary authorities th

1935-06-28.text: ) London, June 28.——(Copy- wight by The Associated Press.) —On this 21st anniversary of the assassination of Arch Duke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo—the shot which precipitated the world war—Great Britain suffered a setback in her role as peacemaker. Her traveling salesman of peace Captain Anthony Eden was back from his continental tour today bearing a report on the avowed intention of Premier Benito Mussolini, of Italy, to go to war against Ethiopia in East Africa. Before reporting to a cabinet meeting the only comment of the young secretary for League of Nations affairs concerning further security negotiations was: “It is on the knees of the Gods.” Although the Italo-Ethiopian crisis relegated other questions of European security to the background the British diplomats discussed other prospective moves on the chess board of world peace. These were for an eastern European pact, a Danubian

MUIRFIELD, June 28.—(#)}—Alfred Perry, 30-year-old British Ryder Cup team player, won the British Open Golf championship today with final rounds of 67 and 72 for a record-equaling total of 283. Perry's finishing rounds, collectively representing five strokes under par and made in the face of a wind that at times approached gale force, brought to an end the meteoric reign of Henry Cotton, winner at Sandwich a year ago. Cotton completed the 72-hole grind over the Muirfield course with rounds of 76 and 75 for an aggregate of 293. Perry, who previously had failed to finish in the money in the open championship, had a 12-foot putt on the final green to set a new low score for the tournament. He putted boldly for the cup and a birdie three, but the ball slid inches past. As it was, he tied the winning record score of 283 hung up by Gene Sarazen in 1932 and duplicated by Cotton last year at San

LONDON, June 28. UP)—A fresh disagreement between Great Britain and France was reported today over terms of the British-German naval agreement. France, it was understood, was unwilling to accept a British invitation to send naval delegates to London until it learned the details of German naval building intentions for the next seven years. Germany, it was understood, held that details of her naval program for these years should be disclosed to France and other powers only after they had made known their own programs to Britain. British quarters admitted that under their agreement, the German program must be kept secret from other powers until the powers had tabled their own programs. It is the British plan that France, Italy and Russia shall send delegations to London and that these delegations will receive details of German intentions as soon as they disclose their own.

MUIRFIELD, Scotland, June 2% Equalling the record low aggregate of 283, Alfred Perry, English Ryder Cup player, today won the British Open golf championship. Perry blazed home with a 67 to tie Muirfield course record in the morning play, and, when the pressure was on in the afternoon finale, held his shots true for a par 72.

Paris, June 27.—(AP)—France, her breach with Britain over the Anglo-German naval agreement still unhealed, moved independently today to perfect further her own defenses. Capt. Anthony Eden, Britain’s traveling negotiator, left for London by the night plane after talking two hours with Premier Pierre Laval. Both admitted existing differences had not been reconciled. For Defense Almost at the same time the chamber of deputies finance committee voted more money—about $92,500,000—to build up the army, navy and air forces.

Murifield, Scotland—Col. Lawson Little, San Francisco, father of the United States and British amateur champion, was robbed of a $1200 letter of credit and $320 in cash by a pickpocket today while he was among the gallery following his son in the British open tournament. Little withheld the news from his son for fear of spoiling his game. Lawson was still competing in the open when the robbery occurred. When the tournament started the course was placarded with notices warning against pickpockets, and plain clothes detectives mingled with the crowd.

Dublin, Irish Free State, June 27. P—The United States was represented by a full-fledged minister to the Irish Free State for the first time in more than a year today. Alvin M. Owsley of Dallas, Texas, former commander of the American Legion, presented his credentials to President Eamon De Valera. Irish Communists seized upon the occasion to conduct a demonstration against the new American envoy. Hostile leaflets were distributed while Owsley was being received in St. Patrick's Hall.

By ALBERT W. WILSON. Associated Press Foreign Staff. Copyright, 1935, by The Associated Press. London, June 28.—Stabilization of the world’s currencies on a gold basis will be discussed with United States government leaders and bankers by Johannes Postmus, the governor of the South African Reserve Bank, who departed from London today on a hurried trip to the United States and Canada. Postmus’ presence in London apparently was not discovered by the British press, although he had several long talks with Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England, and will present both his own and Norman’s view to the Americans, It is understood they are mainly interested in obtaining more detailed information regarding the motives underlying the recent (Continued on Page Seven)

1935-06-18.text: Santa Monica, June 16,—They have such a thing among nations, like they do among people, called “chickens come home to roost.” England and all the big nations are awful sore at Italy about Abysinnia, and Italy is just as wrong as she can be, but all these others have gobbled up something at some time and Mussolini reminds ’em of it, and that makes ‘em sorer than ever. Reading history has put all these ideas in Japan's head. Us giving back the Philippines may ease our conscience a little. It almost pays a nation to remain small, and point with pride that they haven't gobbled up anything. Copyright McNaught Syndicate,

Copyright 1935 by The Associated Press LON June 18.—(?)—A final agreement between Germany and Great Britain on all important points of a treaty to maintain the German navy at 35 per cent of the British strength was announced officially today. It was stated officially that the principle of the 100 to 35 ratio “should in general apply to each category.” It was understood that this means Germany will be allowed some latitude in building submarines because of the French and Italian undersea fleets which are larger than the British. It was stated that Germany would be allowed to make a limited transfer of 35 per cent of her tonnage from one category to another but that the ratio would be strictly maintained in regard to the entire under-age “effective” fleets of the two nations.

LONDON, June 18. — Responsible American quarters have heard unofficially that the government intends to send former Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald on a good-will mission to Washington. No official intimation has been received that MacDonald might visit the United States, and authoritative British quarters described reports of a possible visit as fiction. It seemed possible, in view of conflicting statements, that some British leader, probably MacDonald, might visit Washington if the idea were encouraged. Reports in usually well-informed newspaper circles first mentioned the idea, and said that members of the cabinet were considering it in line with their policy of seeking close American co-operation in view of pending world problems. It was understood in American quarters here that if the suggestion for a visit by MacDonald were made officially, he would be assured a cordial

London, June 18. — Great Britain and Germany have reached agreement on relative naval strength, it was announced officially today. The agreement is based, it was announced, on the concession to Germany of a fleet 35 per cent as strong as Great Britain's. There are to be further meetings on technical matters in the next few days. The conversations are expected to end Friday. The agreement provides that in no circumstances shall Germany's fleet exceed in total tonnage more than 35 per cent of Britain's tonnage. The same principle, in general, applies to each class of warship although a certain latitude is allowed Germany for transferring tonnage from one class to another in accordance with her needs. Any transfer would always be inside the 35 per cent limit.

London, June 17 — Reliable sources revealed today that Great Britain has asked both the Japanese and Chinese governments to clarify reports that Japan insists upon controlling the appointment of new officials in North China. Semi-official circles said they believed this move by the British government indicated a serious view was being taken of the Chinese situation and it was considered that this particular part of Japanese activities might lead to representation under the nine-power treaty which was signed by nine nations agreeing to respect the independence of China, including Japan.

London—(#)—Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, announced in the House of Commons today that the Lausanne agreement, virtually cancelling the German war reparations, cannot be finally ratified by the World War allies until their war debts to the United States are settled. William Mabane, liberal member, asked whether the chancellor would propose to France, Italy and Belgium that this condition be waived preceding ratification of the Lausanne agreement, "giving final authority to the instrument which now is capable of being disturbed by the independent act of any one of six governments." Chamberlain replied: "No. His Majesty’s government is not prepared to depart from the view that ratification of the Lausanne agreement is bound up with the problem of war debts as a whole." Pressing his point, Mabane asked: "In view of the international situation would not the position be eas

Basel, Switzerland — (7) — An entente between the United States, England and France to stabilize world currencies was discussed Monday by bankers assembled for a meeting of the Bank for International Settlements. The confidence that such an entente, designed to include Japan eventually, would be sufficient to bring stabilization of monetary systems. The proposal from the United States treasury for an international stabilization conference came too early in view of Great Britain's reluctance.

(Associated Press) LONDON, June 17—A reliable authority said today that Great Britain alone will regulate the actual sizes of both the British and German navies under the terms of a hitherto secret provision of their 100 to 85 ratio agreement. By this step, allowing Great Britain to be the virtual dictator of the new Nazi navy, Reichsführer Hitler was said by this authority to be regarded as having taken a bold move toward winning the confidence and support of Great Britain. It was said that Germany accepted the role of being merely a consultant in determining the tonnage strengths of the two fleets in return for the British approval of her having a navy far in excess of the Versailles treaty limitations. In other words, Germany is regarded as having given up to Great. (Continued On Page Two)

1935-05-28.text: Los Angeles, Cal., May 26.—The sporting pages were where the news was this Sunday morning. Dear old Babe Ruth, God bless him, stepped into three fast balls and put ‘em all out of bounds. Lawson Little, a Stanford boy, for the second year in succession collected a small portion of the British debt, with a golf club. A Mr. Owens, a colored lad of 21 years, from Ohio State University, broke practically all the world records there are, with the possible exception of horseshoe pitching and flag pole sitting. Congress laid dormant, Hitler was refueling, and Mussolini was changing records. But a man in California sued his wife for non-support. Copyright McNaught Syndicate,

LONDON, May 27 (?)——Well-informed quarters said today that the British government was considering the possibility of holding a seven-power naval conference before the end of this year. This statement followed a confirmation of an announcement in Berlin that Anglo-German naval talks would open here June 14. These talks are expected to determine whether Germany and Russia could be included successfully in a round-table conference with the five naval treaty powers—the United States, Great Britain, Japan, France, and Italy. Great Britain is regarded as adhering firmly to the view that a conference of at least five powers must be held in 1935 as required under the expiring London treaty and also under the Washington treaty of 1922 in view of Japan's abrogation last year of the latter pact.

LONDON, May 27— (#) —Great Britain will “call” Adolf Hitler on his offer to abolish submarines when Anglo-German naval talks open here June 4, well-informed quarters said tonight. Hitler, in his speech to the Reichstag last Tuesday, offered to meet other powers in curbing armaments, even to the scrapping of U-boats, dreaded German weapon during the world war.

PARIS, May 27. (U.?)—The cabinet agreed today to ask full powers from parliament to deal with the most serious financial situation since the late Raymond Poincaré saved the franc in 1926. It was decided, at a 3 1/2 hour meeting, to demand full powers to protect the currency and balance the budget. Members of the coalition cabinet were reported in full agreement, including Louis Marin, minister without portfolio and representative of the right wing. A communique described the cabinet’s project for meeting the financial crisis as designed to give the government “extended power” in financial matters. It is necessary under the project to find means to overcome a prospective budget deficit of 10,000,000,600 francs ($658,300,000) and generally to strengthen the financial situation. The powers which the government seeks would center in

Paris...(AP)--The French cabinet today offered battle for the gold standard, announcing the government's life would be staked on the defense of the franc. A demand by Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin for “full powers” was approved, and the council of ministers, with President Lebrun presiding, is expected formally to adopt his program tomorrow.

Copyright 1935 by The Associated Press PARIS.—The Bank of France launched a hot fight against “international speculators” in the franc today by raising its discount rate for the third time within one week as Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin prepared to go before parliament in quest of dictatorial powers by which he may keep France on the gold standard. The bank increased its re-discount rate to 6 per cent from 4 per cent, after raising it to 3 per cent last Thursday from 2 1-2 per cent and then increasing it to 4 per cent last Saturday. Lean Rate on Gold Hiked. Similarly, the loan rate on gold bars was increased today to 7 per cent from 5 1-2 per cent, on securities to 6 1-2 per cent from 4 1-2 per cent, and on 30 day rate to 5 per cent from 4 per cent. The bank’s challenge was issued immediately after the full cabinet appealed unanimously to the council.

(Copyright, 1935, by The Associated Press) PARIS, May 28.—With a government demand from Parliament for full power to restore France's finances, Louis Germain-Martin, minister of finance, revealed to the Chamber of Deputies today that the gold reserves of the Bank of France had been diminished by nine billion francs—about $594,000,000—in the last two months. The finance minister told the legislators that the rhythm of withdrawals was steadily increasing, the bank losing three billions between March 29 and May 17, three billions more during the week ending May 24, and an additional three billions in the last three days. His plea to Parliament followed by a few hours an announcement by the Bank of France that it was making an increase on its rediscount rate to 6 per cent from 4 per cent.

TOKYO, May 27 (AP)—A strong hint that Japan regards herself as the “target” for the sea power of the United States was contained in a pamphlet distributed today by the navy's propaganda bureau in connection with the empire’s celebration of navy memorial day. The occasion was the 30th anniversary of the Japanese navy’s victory over the Czar's Baltic fleet in the Russo-Japanese war. “Then (in 1908) Russia was the rival and the danger,” said the navy office's brochure, “Today that is changed. We have had to face in another direction. We are confronting another great sea power which is increasing its navy with Japan as the target.” Although “the great sea power” was not specifically identified, observers had little doubt that the reference was to the United States. The pamphlet continued with an exposition of Japan’s demands for naval equality with the United States and Great Britain. “We ne

1935-11-28.text: LONDON, Nov. 27 UP)—British authorities, receiving reports that an Italian expeditionary force may soon invade the Lake Tana region of Ethiopia, intimated today such an incursion would be regarded as a violation of Italian government assurances. This development came simultaneously with a full meeting of the British cabinet at which the government reaffirmed its determination to enforce an oil embargo against Italy. Also it was revealed that the government officially assured the United States that imposition of the embargo will be considered by the League penalties committee at Geneva shortly. The Lake Tana matter is regarded with gravity. The lake, in northwestern Ethiopia, comprises the headwaters of the Blue Nile and is vital to England's vast irrigation projects in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan.

New York..(AP)--The British two-masted schooner R. L. Borden was found in flames by the steamer Exilona today, several hours after the Borden's master and five of the crew were rescued by the Italian freighter San Pedro about 610 miles east-southeast of New York. The Exilona’s wireless report, Mackay Radio announced, said she had reached the side of the stricken vessel after having seen the flames while four hours distant. Neither the San Pedro nor the Exilona gave any word of the cause of the fire.

PARIS, Nov. 28. —(AP)— Diplomatic sources said Thursday that Premier Mussolini, declaring Italy is ready to “oppose an oil embargo by every means,” has threatened to reenforce Italy’s troops in Libya again unless Great Britain withdraws her ships from the Mediterranean. Premier Laval of France, who considers the proposed oil embargo a danger and seeks the quick resumption of peace efforts in view of the new tension in Europe, talked to Ambassador Vittorio Cerruti Thursday morning. The Italians were said in authoritative quarters to be offended at Great Britain’s failure to withdraw some of the home fleet from the Mediterranean after the British elections. It was added that the Italians were threatening to send back the division of troops ordered out of Libya in anticipation of the British curtailing their display of naval force. The British, for their part, were reported to have delayed

LONDON, Nov. 28— Pp — War clouds hung heavy over Europe today as the tension between Great Britain and Italy continued grave. Anxiety reminiscent of the Summer of 1914 was evident in all capitals as a result of Mussolini’s defiant measures to discourage Britain and other members of the League of Nations from shutting off Italy’s supply of oil, cotton and metals, vital necessities for her war with Ethiopia. England's assurance to the United States that the league's general staff of 18 would meet Dec. 5 to extend anti-Italian sanctions to an oil embargo revived the tension that has more or less been dormant for the last three weeks. Some observers claimed war between the two nations hinged on application of the oil embargo. They pointed out that Italy is entirely dependent on the outside world for petroleum and without it Mussolini would have to abandon his East African campaign. Significa

SANTA MONICA, Calif. — All the excitement in London, The Prince of Wales has adopted a new style in trouserings called the “Straight Cut.” With no desire to be morbid, I've gone into the fascinating details, I glean from the cablegrams that they touch the wearer in but one place, and only then if his Royal Highness is sitting down. When walking, he has to take two steps while the trousers are taking one. It's as though Slim Summerville swiped my things and was trying to escape with the goods on. I shall not follow the royal example. As a snappy dresser I never seem to get anywhere, somehow. George Ade once said no matter what I put on I still looked like Paducah, Ky., and when I read what the well-dressed man will wear I sorrowfully admit there's nothing correct about me except my back collar button and I'm not so sure about that. Winchester, Eng., Nov. 27 (4)—A British soldier was sentenced to death upon his conviction today in one of the strangest murder charges on record in England, that of running down a girl cyclist while driving a stolen automobile. Arthur Charles Mortimer, called the “terror man,” with trembling lips heard the foreman of the jury declare him guilty of the murder of Mrs. Phyllis Mary Oakes, beautiful private secretary of a well-known novelist. Authorities said he attempted to kill three other girls in the same manner. The six-foot Mortimer is a lance corporal, stationed at Aldershot barracks. He was convicted of killing Mrs. Oakes by deliberately running her down August 8 in a stolen car. Mrs. Oakes was dragged 40 yards, entangled in her bicycle. She died three days later, on the eve of her twenty-first birthday. The defense contended that even if the jury was satisfied the tall soldier drov

As the American delegation made last minute preparations to sail Friday, naval experts summarized these demands as threatening to wreck the conference and launch a naval construction race. 1. France insists upon a navy equal to the combined naval strength of Germany and Italy. 3. Italy demands the right to build a navy equal to France. 4. ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 28.—Emperor Haile Selassie left his capital by automobile with a great military escort today, heading for Dessye to take personal command of his armies against the Italian invaders. It was the second visit by the King of Kings to his defending forces since the Fascist invasion began. He returned only recently from an aerial tour of inspection to the southern front. His second sally directed him to Dessye, 170 miles to the northeast, the Ethiopian field headquarters between the northern and southern fronts. The Ethiopians said their attacks on the Italians were progressing on both the northern and southern fronts. The emperor himself, the Abuna (high bishop) of Ethiopia's Coptic Christian church, said: "I leave without knowing when I shall return or if I shall die for my country. But if I never return, I shall be happy knowing that you, my father, are in my place. Give m

1935-08-10.text: London, Aug. 10. —(UP)—An effort to impose a boycott on Italian goods by means of chain letters among British housewives has been started by Lady Harris, wife of Sir Percy Alfred Harris, liberal member of the House of Commons, it was learned today. The move coincides with a demand by liberals all over the country that the government stop the threatened Italian-Ethiopian war and in any event remove at once its ban against export of arms to Ethiopia.

Addis Ababa—A one-man Ethiopian mission left for Japan, presumably to seek credits for the purchase of war materials, Rome—Italians killed in a plane crash en route to Eritrea were hailed as “heroes” of the East African campaign. London—Britain may lift her arms ban against Ethiopia if tri-power conference in Paris fails. Paris—Outlines for the tri-power conference began taking shape and officials were less pessimistic over the outlook for war. SEEKS CREDIT Addis Ababa, Aug. 9 (#)—A one-man Ethiopian mission hastened toward Japan tonight, presumably in an effort to secure credits for the purchase of war supplies, another indication of the developing bonds between the two countries. He was Daba Birrou, former foreign office official, who departed on his secret trip accompanied by an unidentified Japanese. News of their departure led to speculation as to whether Emperor Haile Selassie, cut

LONDON, Aug. 5 (Pr)—Great Britain's temporary ban on arms shipments to Ethiopia may be immediately lifted in the event of a failure of a tri-power conference in Paris next week on the Italo-Ethiopian dispute, it was learned tonight. The British are convinced the conference with France and Italy will definitely determine whether there will be war or peace. If no solution is found the government may decide to let arms go forward.

ROME — Italy strengthens its military power by summoning to service officers and technicians of the air force reserve. ADDIS ABABA — France acquires barracks for additional troops in French Somaliland near the trouble zone. LONDON — Reuters (British) news agency said Ethiopia had armed a quarter of a million men and planned to put seven armies totaling 600,000 men in the field if there is a war. GENEVA — Neutral league commissioner for Ethiopia seen as possibility, agreement reached on Aug. 16 meeting on conciliation commission in Paris. ROME — Dispatches from Tripoli said 600 Libyan cavalrymen and horses sailed for East Africa. INNSBRUCK, Austria — South Tyrolians reported permitted to choose between domestic and African service. LONDON — Diplomatic circles rate odds for war at 5 to 1 seek full statement of Italy's aims.

International News Service Staff Correspondent LONDON, Aug. 10—Coincident with cabled reports from Addis Ababa that Ethiopia will have more than half a million armed men ready to take the field against Italy, the British government today crystallized the stand it will take next week in Paris at the Franco-British-Italian parley on the threatened war. The British attitude was finally cemented at a conference between Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, Foreign Minister Sir Samuel Hoare, and Capt. Anthony Eden, minister for League of Nations affairs, who will head the British delegation to Paris next Wednesday and Thursday. Await Italy's Presentation The government would not admit a specific plan had been decided upon as a final drive for peace, and made it clear that Italy first ought to present her case. (By Associated Press) Rome, Aug. 10—Italy summoned 48 new units of its reserve military power to the colors today. A royal decree was published in the official gazette ordering the subalterns and technicians of the air force classes of 1909 and 1910 recalled for service for an indeterminate time. Indicative of the efforts Italy is making to safeguard the welfare of its soldiers and workmen in East Africa, the official gazette also published a royal decree ordering employers to provide insurance for the workers. The insurance will compensate them if they fall ill of malaria or other tropical diseases, or otherwise suffer any ill effects from their stay in the colony.

PARIS, Aug. 9. — tA -- Premier Pierre Laval, unrelenting despite widespread disorders and bloodshed, told all save one of France's 86 prefects today to enforce firmly his unpopular deflationary decrees. One prefect was missing from the meeting called here by Laval, unprecedented in French history. He was the prefect of war, in which Toulon is situated. He took charge of troops patrolling the streets there after yesterday's rioting. One thousand guards were sent to Toulon as reinforcements to prevent a recurrence of last night's fighting when two were killed and from 50 to 200 injured. Other ports seemed to settle down to normal work today. Communists were blamed by officials for disorders among arsenal workers over 10 per cent government pay cuts.

BERLIN, Aug. 9.—(4)—Germans got a two-sided picture tonight in which a reduction of 122,000 in unemployment lists spoke of domestic well-being, while disorders and agitation showed difficulties abroad. Save for brief reports of actions against Jews and Catholics in the provinces, newspapers turned from these worries to cheer unanimously a cut in unemployment during July of 1,754,000. This figure does not include 168,000 officially classified as “emergency workers,” such as those sent to farms who are earning a pittance. More building and improvement in some industries helped the employment situation, in addition to army recruiting and labor services. The number receiving doles was reduced by 63,000 to 904,000. At the side of the optimistic reports were articles of communistic disorders and strikes in many parts of the world. A shortage in certain food sup-

1935-11-15.text: CAIRO, EGYPT, Nov. 14— A British officer shot one rioter to death and wounded three others shortly today, it was announced officially, amid tension arising from serious anti-British demonstrations. Earlier reports said all four demonstrators died under the fire of the officer, who sustained minor head injuries himself in a clash with a party of Egyptians advancing on Cairo from nearby Giza. Authorities said the officer involved in the incident was named Bimbashi Lees. The advancing body, armed with sticks and branches and estimated by authorities to number 1,000, was met by a force of 200 police whose warning shots failed to halt their march. A British officer, leading the police, fired into the crowd, and one person was killed. The marchers promptly turned and fled. The shooting brought the total number of deaths in the anti-British manifestations to four. A re-check of the casualties i

London, Nov. 15, (P)—The National government, strongly Tory and pledged to support international action against any war-maker, won the general election today with a safe majority in parliament. At 2 p. m. the government passed the 308 seats necessary for a majority and its victory became more pronounced as returns continued to come in. Labor headquarters, in admitting a clear-cut government victory, said it expected the government majority to be between 200 and 250 seats. Labor made gains, but not as much as expected. It will have a stronger voice in parliament than in the last session, but never enough to upset the government. The Liberals slipped and Labor's gains were made from all parties, including the Conservatives. The defeat of Sir Herbert Samuel, leader of the main branch of the divided Liberal party, left David Lloyd George, former Liberal leader, in a stronger position, with a

Pope Pius sought postponement of sanctions against Italy today, informed ecclesiastical sources said in Rome, as anti-British rioting continued in Egypt. Sources close to the pope represented the Holy Father as still hopeful league of nations powers would delay imposition of trade bans in the interest of world peace. One Egyptian died before a police gun as a column of protestants against England’s domination of Egypt marched on Cairo from Giza. The gunfire brought casualties in two days' melee to four dead and 150 injured. Armed police patrolled Cairo streets. More than 100 members of the powerful Wafdist party, leaders in the anti-British demonstrations were sent to hospitals. The Wafdists demand the resignation of Prime Minister Twefik Nessim Pasha. If he does not step down, they declare, the party will refuse to cooperate with the government and British authorities. The riots started

London, Nov, 15 (Friday) (4) Labor gains of nearly fifty seats marked available returns early today from Great Britain's general elections, but the national government, with great reserve strength throughout the country, apparently was not threatened in its control of parliament. The standing of parties at 3 a.m. showed: Conservatives, 166; National Labor, 3; National Liberal, 14. Total for the government, 155. Labor, 77; Liberal, 9. Total for opposition, 86. Independents, 1. The popular vote: Government, 1,444,697; opposition, 4,138,558. MacDonald Beaten? From the national point of view, observers asserted that Labor victories could be interpreted as a sign of political health because all the old leaders who were beaten in the national government landslide of 1931 were re-elected. CAIRO, Nov. 15.—(#)—Armed patrols of police brought quiet to prevail today over the anti-British demonstrations which resulted in death to four persons and injuries to 150 in their two-day course. Cairo itself was calm, with no evidence of the tension which mounted Wednesday with the original “Independence Day” disorders and developed Thursday into a clash between police and demonstrators in which one Egyptian student was killed. Despite the insistence of Egypt's powerful Wafd nationalist party for the resignation of Prime Minister Tewfik Nessim Pasha and a halt to British influence in Egyptian affairs, officials said the situation was “under control.”

(By The Associated Press) The second day of anti-British rioting in Egypt, partly stimulated by strong opposition to sanctions against Italy, today raised the death toll to four, with 150 injured. At the same time, Pope Pius was represented by informed ecclesiastical sources in Rome as seeking postponement of economic sanctions against Italy. Gunfire from police, who faced a crowd of Egyptians opposing Great Britain's control, killed one of the natives as they marched on Cairo from Giza. More than 100 members of the strong Wafdist party, who led the anti-British demonstrations, were in hospitals, as armed police guarded against further outbreaks. A large section of the Egyptian population has opposed the government's adherence to Great Britain's application of sanctions against Italy. Sources close to Pope Pius said the Holy Father, strongly wishing maintenance of world peace, hoped impo

Pernambuco, Brazil —(#)— Miss Jean Batten, New Zealand flier, passed high over this city on her England-to-Brazil flight today, having covered the 186 miles from Natal, Brazil, in one hour and 15 minutes, a speed of 148 miles an hour. Miss Batten, who became the first woman pilot ever to fly the south Atlantic when she landed at Natal yesterday, is expected to cover the 1,736 miles from that point to Rio de Janeiro by nightfall, unless she stops en route. In adding this new accomplishment to her many aerial honors, Miss Batten crossed the 1,231 miles from Dakar, Senegal, to Brazil in 13 hours and 15 minutes. Her total elapsed time from her starting point, Lympne, England, was 61 hours and seven minutes.

LONDON, Nov 15.—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin today gained a 3-to-1 decision on his demand for a mandate on rearmament and reconstruction. Late returns from yesterday’s election showed the national government commanding a clear majority of the 615 seats in the next house of commons, with the likelihood that its final lead would be at least 200. The labor party more than doubled its strength and ousted the former head of the national government, Ramsay MacDonald, in Seaham, together with his son, Malcolm the colonial secretary, who ran in Bassetlaw. Rural constituencies, reporting late today, were swelling the number of government seats. Opposition liberals suffered heavy losses as the voters chose between the national government and the labor party. The vote count up to 3 p.m. showed 366 national government members had been elected to the commons and that the popular vote for national g

1935-03-22.text: (Copyright, 1935, By The Associated Press) LONDON, March 21—A warning that Germany’s rearmament leads ultimately to “war and the destruction of civilization” echoed in the British parliament today as the Reich spurned vigorous French and Italian protests against her treaty violations. Nevertheless, Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, told the House of Commons his plans to visit Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler Sunday are unchanged. If the Anglo-German talks prove fruitful, Simon said, all Europe’s major powers, Germany among them, will be called into conference to work out an inclusive security system. Developments in the increasingly tense situation included: Germany’s foreign minister, Konstan Von Neurath, told shocked French and Italian envoys “the German government must decline to entertain the protests” presented in formal notes. LONDON, March 22.—Germany will demand from the European powers the right to a navy at least equal to the size of Italy's and possibly comparable with that of France, according to reports naval circles received today from Berlin. The German navy now totals approximately 150,000 tons with 26,000 tons new building. Italy has approximately 375,000 and France 550,000 exclusive of vessels now being built. The reports circulating in naval circles were that the Reich desires a fleet of at least 375,000 tons, possibly more. Great Britain Leads Naval authorities recalled that Great Britain leads in naval tonnage with 1,160,000, with the United States second with 1,060,000 tons. (BY Associated Press) London, March 22—Great Britain is opposed to any discussion of the return of former German colonies to the Reich during conversations between Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Adolf Hitler, it was officially said today. In reply to a question as to whether the subject of colonial restoration would come under discussion at Berlin Monday, a government spokesman said the subjects not being covered in the Anglo-French proposals for security last month should not be entered on the conversational program. The German naval question, however, will not be barred, and reports to naval circles from Berlin indicate the Reich will demand a fleet at least equal to Italy's and possibly comparable to that of France. An official emphasized, however, that Britain will be unable to make a decision on naval matters, since the navy proposals would have to be discussed later by nava

GENEVA, March 22—(UP)—Tewfik Rushdi of Turkey, president of the council of the League of Nations convoked the council today for the first week of April to consider the French protest against Germany. Tewfik will announce the exact date shortly, it will be immediately after the conference of Britain and Italy in northern Italy.

The word “war” figured in discussion of German rearmament at four European capitals yesterday as events moved swiftly in Europe’s arms crisis. LONDON—George Lansbury, labor leader, told the Commons the Reich's arms policy, if unchanged, leads to ‘war and the destruction of civilization” as Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, promised his best efforts to get Germany into an inclusive security system. ROME—An enthusiastically cheering Chamber of Deputies heard Under-secretary of War Frederico Baistrocchi, referring specifically to the East African situation, declare Italy's high-speed military machine ready for war. PARIS—Minister of War Louis Felix Maucin told the Chamber of Deputies' arms committee that the French general staff has its plans ready in case of war, which, however, he said he did not expect. CHICAGO, March 21--(4)—Arthur Garfield Hays, veteran New York lawyer, vigorously objected today to the manner in which Evelyn John St.-Loe Strachey's deportation hearing was conducted. Hays, defending the young British economist, and William J. Zuker, immigration inspector presiding at the sessions, engaged in a heated clash after Zuker had summarized the evidence by which the government seeks to expel Strachey from the country as an alien communist. Zuker's introduction of communist pamphlets with the request that the defendant advance his opinions on them spurred Hays’ outburst. “On what theory,” he demanded, “are you pulling out communist material and asking Strachey to state his views on them?” “Put your objections in a brief,” Zuker rejoined, “and they will be submitted to the secretary of labor for a final decision. LONDON, March 22—A new system of alliances to build an ‘iron wall” around rearmed Germany was seen as a possibility today in the event of failure of the negotiations next week between Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Reichsführer Hitler. A strong hint of the likelihood of such a policy was given by Sir John in the House of Commons last night. “A system of select and special combinations, for assistance against the danger in our midst,” the foreign secretary said, was bound to be the alternative if it proved impossible to bring Germany back into the councils of Europe. Sir John added, however, he had strong hopes such a necessity would not arise as the alternative was one for which Great Britain has no enthusiasm since it is opposed to special pacts of the sort. LONDON, Nov. 26. ©. %)—Great Britain remains in favor of collective action to enforce an oil embargo against Italy, it was announced officially today. The announcement followed immediately upon a full dress meeting of the defense committee of the cabinet at which, it was believed, the danger of a direct Italian-British conflict in event of an oil embargo was under consideration. The announcement, a blunt challenge in effect to Premier Benito Mussolini to make good his threats, puts the situation back where it was during the recent Italian-British tension in the Mediterranean.

Washington smoked out Great Britain on its attitude towards depriving Italy of oil today. Intimations came from Washington that the government felt that after it had tried to discourage American oil men from exporting to Italy, it had been “left out on a limb” when the powers postponed acting on the oil embargo at Geneva, and might change its position. Prompt reaction came from London in the form of an official statement that Britain still favors a general embargo. In Rome, Premier Benito Mussolini moved to fight a possible ban by ordering the country’s oil tanks filled almost to capacity by Dec. 15. The war situation in Ethiopia remained static, with various minor engagements reported on northern and southern fronts.

LONDON, Nov. 26—High British quarters showed concern today over what effect the League of Nations’ delay in action on oil sanctions against Italy might have on public opinion in the United States. A British source made the terse observation that the United States “is left holding the bag.” What action the league will take on the project for shutting off oil from Italy—as the United States has recommended from both Italy and Ethiopia—still had not been determined. Although American diplomatic and trade officials were watching the situation closely, it was authoritatively stated that there had been no exchanges between the two governments. At the same time, British sources expressed suspicion that Premier Mussolini of Italy had at last succeeded in driving a wedge between Premier Laval of France and Great Britain. Winchester, Eng., Nov. 26. (P— Admiral Sir Edward Eden Bradford, 76, retired British naval commander who headed the third British naval squadron during the World War, died today.

London, Nov. 25 (INS)--The United States stood alone today in efforts to cut down on abnormal oil shipments to Italy after the powers, fearing grave consequences, postponed increasing sanctions. This action coincided with the revelation of a dramatic new peace move by Premier Stanley Baldwin of Britain, who personally appealed to Premier Benito Mussolini to outline Italy's idea of a solution of the Ethiopian problem. While awaiting Mussolini's answer, Britain is understood to be considering its own definite peace plan, eliminating cumbersome mandates machinery and giving Italy outright economic and territorial concessions. Backed by a mandate from the British electorate, Premier Baldwin is taking direct steps, but still adheres to the principle that a settlement should be brought about through the conciliation committee of five of the League of Nations, and must be satisfactory to the Le

PARIS. Nov. 26—(4)—Premier Pierre Laval today yielded to the demands of the Leftists for the disbanding of Nationalist forces, such as the War Veterans’ Croix De Feu, to save the franc and to defend his cabinet against threat of overthrow. The cabinet agreed on a proposal, now pending in parliament, to appeal to the chamber of deputies’ “patriotism” for immediate discussion of Laval's financial measures. This decision means Laval will demand an immediate vote of confidence for his decree laws which are intended to defend the franc against speculation and the budget uncertainty now causing a heavy outflow of gold, with danger of eventual collapse of the franc. The premier will ask the chamber to take up the battle against political troops after he disposes of the interpellation of his financial policy. The cabinet's decision to support a proposal to disband “seditious leagues” was, withou

ROME, Nov. 26.--(#)—Italy is reported to have an aerial “death squad” of 125 men pledged to die, Friends of certain aviators said today that these men are volunteers who will go to certain death if they are ordered to attack a hostile naval fleet, To each of these men, it was said, has been assigned an airplane carrying one gigantic bomb. Each man of the “death squad” would pick an enemy warship, and dive down as a living projectile. The bomb would be big enough to wreck a warship.

1935-01-10.text: Hull, England, Jan. 9.—(#)— Thirteen persons were believed to have drowned tonight on the sinking steam trawler Edgar Wallace, which struck a sand bank in the fog-bound River Humber. Three of the Edgar Wallace's crew of 16 were rescued. Most of the victims were trapped below decks in a sudden inrush of water.

Sosion, Jan. 10—Rivers of northern New England, swelled by a steady rainfall, rose rapidly today, overflowing lowlands, blocking highways and flooding cellars as they approached freshet and moderate flood stages. Scores of roads in Vermont, New Hampshire and western Massachusetts were under water and a low-hanging fog hampered rescue and coastguardsmen who sped to the aid of helpless fishing craft. The Weather Bureau predicted freshet conditions in Vermont and New Hampshire while in Maine "moderate floods" were forecast. The Coast Guard cutter Mojave continued its search for the trawler Plymouth, reported to be disabled 250 miles east of Boston, and the cutter Argo was summoned out of Newport, R. I., by distress calls from the Nova Scotia fieldwood, whose rudder was disabled in Vineyard Sound. Two Chatham fishermen, missing in their motorboat for two days, were picked up early this morni
Berlin — Germany Thursday declined the invitation of Great Britain to send a representative to Geneva for the League of Nations Council meeting next week following the Saar territory plebiscite.

(Rye The Associated Press) Bombay, Jan. 9—Seven Moslems were killed and twenty injured today in Ajra, in the state of Ichalkaranji, when police fired into a crowd of 300 Moslems attempting to prevent the arrest of one of their compatriots.

He calls himself Finn Johansen now.
