The suggestion of German collaboration in an agreement for disarmament came from an authoritative source, which said France and Italy have chosen the Italian disarmament memorandum of last January as the basis for granting Germany partial rearmament, provided she returns to the League of Nations and enter

OSLO, Norway, Jan. 10. (UP)— Henry (Red) Johnson, former Sweetheart of Betty Gow, will not return to the United States to testify in the Hauptmann trial, he told the United Press today. Johnson, a Norwegian, and living here under his Norwegian name, Henrick Johanson, was held soon after the Lindbergh kidnapping because of his friendship with Miss Gow and finally was deported. Recently married to a Norwegian girl, Johnson is operating a fruit store here.

1935-12-23.text: | NEW YORK, Dec. 23.— Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and his wife have fled to England with their three-year-old son Jon to protect the baby from kidnappers, the United Press learned today from a friend of the family. | The Lindberghs left secretly on a boat on which they are the only passengers and will be at sea over Christmas. | The Lindberghs sailed last Saturday night, the United Press learned. | The United Press was informed the colonel was determined to remain in England permanently if necessary for Jon's protection. He had been disturbed recently by the revival of publicity in the case of Bruno Richard Hauptmann, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering his first son, Charles Augustus, Jr. Plans for their departure were kept secret from all except members of the family and intimate friends. It is believed in England the Lindberghs may go to the home of Mrs. Lindbergh's brother-in

LONDON (7) — Japan's stubborn, unswerving determination to have a navy equal to any regardless of world opposition emerged clearly today as seapowers’ delegates debated the merits of British compromise proposals. While American, French and Italian conferees after a recess for study and consideration voiced approval of the principle of the British proposal that each nation set a limit on new construction based on naval needs instead of “rights,” the Japanese made no secret of strong objections. The preamble of the tentative draft of the plan recognizes the right of each power to possess naval strength necessary to assure security but specifies each base construction on the minimum adequate to obtain security.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press.) LONDON, Dec. 23 (UP).—British and French general staff officers of the army and navy have conferred secretly on co-operation in a possible European emergency with results that are regarded as satisfactory, it was learned today. The conversations were a part of Great Britain’s reinsurance policy against a “mad dog” act by Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy. The British staff officers went to Paris, where they held their meetings. They have returned to London. It was learned that the conversations—and the satisfactory results—did not involve other officials in France. As this revelation was made, it was said on authentic authority that the appointment of Anthony Eden as foreign secretary means: 1. Great Britain will support the league in its penalties campaign against Italy. 2. No more peace proposals to Italy are contemplated. 3. The government assumes t

(Copyright 1935 by United Press) ROME, Dec. 23 (p)—Italians learned today that Anthony Eden, regarded as Premier Benito Mussolini’s arch enemy, had been named foreign secretary of Great Britain. They told each other that Britain had taken off the mask at last, and wanted war. They expressed the opinion also that if Eden—as they expect him to attempt—succeeds in obtaining application of an oil embargo against Italy, it will mean war. Reinforce Army— Mussolini's first reply to the appointment, regarded as an open challenge, was expected to be reinforcement of the army in Libya and a new effort to speed up the military campaign against Ethiopia. Only a few days ago Mussolini was awaiting the proper moment to accept French-British proposals as a basis for peaceful negotiation of the Italian-Ethiopian dispute. During the weekend he informed Sir George Clerk, British ambassador, that he was re

The war scare was more acute in Europe today than at any time since Italy invaded Ethiopia. Appointment of Captain Anthony Eden as British foreign secretary was received in the various capitals with acute interest. Because he is an avowed advocate of stern League penalties against Italy, it was regarded as indicating Britain intends to increase the pressure at Geneva. In Rome, the Italians were reported to be enraged and to feel that Britain has “taken off the mask” and wants war. Ominous rumors were circulated in Cairo. In the wake of the disclosure a few days ago that the British are strengthening their tanks corps and barbed wire defenses on the Libyan border, came unconfirmed reports that an actual border clash had occurred, and the population of the strategic town of Matruh in Egypt had been ordered evacuated. The approach of the Christmas holiday, which in Britain lasts until Frida

(UOPYyTignu Dy &. IN. O- New York, Dec. 23.—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, with the little brother of the murdered Lindbergh baby, today were aboard a vessel whose identity is closely guarded, bound for England to seek sanctuary following receipt of threats against their son. They especially wanted to be away from the United States, “this next month”, a close friend of the family revealed when Bruno Richard Hauptmann, convicted slayer of their first born, is scheduled to die. While Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh have gone away with Jon, their three-year-old son, to seek residence in the British Isles, they were particularly anxious to be out of this country before the Bronx carpenter walked his last steps to doom, it was said. Having made up their minds some months ago that they could not bring up their son in an atmosphere of tension, constantly subject to the prying eyes of strange

ROME, Dec. 28--The appointment of Anthony Eden as Great Britain's foreign secretary, said a source in close touch with Italian government opinion today, proves that the disagreement in Europe is between Italy and Great Britain, and not between Italy and the League of Nations. The peace formula prepared by Premier Laval of France and Britain's former foreign secretary, Sir Samuel Hoare, was rejected by the British, it was said in this quarter, before the League showed its opposition to it. The British, through Eden, said this source, still take the leadership against Mussolini. Leader of Sanctions / Italian Fascists asserted the appointment of Eden—the man they consider the chief operator of the Geneva sanctions machine—as foreign secretary diminished any hopes for early East African peace. Even before the elevation of the British minister for League of Nations affairs to the leadership o

(Copyright 1935 By United Press.) LONDON—War talk spread throughout Europe today, to mix sober thought of what may be ahead with the gaiety of the Christmas season. Reaction from capitals all over the continent left no doubt that the appointment of Anthony Eden as British foreign secretary, more than a diplomatic sensation, was regarded as a curt warning to Premier Benito Mussolini that Great Britain is prepared for any emergency. His appointment coincided with an announcement that the British army will undergo the most extensive reorganization in its history and be mechanized to the minute. Italian troops were reported ready to leave to reinforce the army already in Libya, west of Egypt and the Sudan. Premier Nahim Pasha of Egypt asked railway executives to tear up sufficient railway tracks on active branch lines to insure immediate ex. (Turn to Page 12—No, 4.)

1935-06-03.text: London, June 3. (AP) KNE George V, astride a gentle bay horse, rode with his four sons at the head of a column of crack cavalry and foot soldiers today in the ancient ceremony of trooping the colors as a mark of his completion of the biblical span of three score years and ten. All the British Empire celebrated the King's seventieth birthday anniversary as a holiday, but the ceremonies centered here around the King himself. His Majesty wore the scarlet and gold uniform of Colonel-in-Chief of the Irish Guards. He saluted right and left with a white gloved hand as he rode from Buckingham Palace to the Horse Guards Parade and back again. From all sides came from the crowds cries of “God bless you, sir!” “Many happy returns!” “Long may you live!” The Prince of Wales, the Duke of York, the Duke of Gloucester, and the Duke of Kent, like their father, wore military uniforms and the blue ribbon o

LONDON. June 3 (UP).—Dr. A. R. Dafoe, physician to the Dionne quintuplets, was recognized by King George today in the list of honors granted on the occasion of his seventieth birthday. Dr. Dafoe was made an officer of the Order of the British Empire. John Masefield, poet laureate of England and one-time porter in a New York saloon, was made a member of the Order of Merit; Lord Bledisloe, former governor general of New Zealand, was made a viscount and six barons were named.

WEYBRIDGE, England, June 8—(UP)—Mrs. Helen Wills Moody of California, completed successfully the first step in her comeback campaign today by wrestling the St. George's Hill tennis title from the defending champion Mrs. Elsie Goldieack Pittman. Mrs. Moody defeated Mrs. Pittman in the final, 6-0 6-4.

LONDON, June 8.—Germany's bid for rearmament reached another stage today with the opening of preliminaries to British-German conversations in which the Nazi government seeks a navy 35 per cent as strong as Great Britain's. The conversations will start formally tomorrow, with Joaquim Von Ribbentrop, special ambassador, leading the German delegation and Sir Ernle Chatfield, first sea lord, in charge for Britain. Ribbentrop today conducted a series of preparatory talks with British leaders, while his aides prepared to argue their case. The conference opens as British salvage crews prepare to raise the last warships of the German grand fleet, scuttled by their crews in Scapa Flow, in the Orkney islands, north of Scotland, upon the surrender to Britain after the World War. Germany's Desire Germany seeks the right to build ships of any character it likes up to around 400,000 tons. The British

LONDON, June 3, (P)—Dr. Alan Roy Dafoe, whose achievement in nursing the Dionne quintuplets through one year of life made medical history, has been appointed an officer of the order of the British empire. The award was conferred on the little Canadian physician in King George’s birthday honors list, which extended recognition for meritorious services to men famous in artistic, literary and scientific fields throughout the empire.

ALGIERS, Algeria, June 2 (P)—A searching party found the bodies of an Englishwoman and an Englishman on the scorching Sahara sands today and rescued two Frenchmen near death from thirst. The woman, Mrs. Knight, the widow of an English aviator who committed suicide recently at Agadez, French West Africa, had slashed her wrist, apparently in an attempt to end her torture from thirst and heat. A party of four, including Mrs. Knight, Peyton, an English resident of Switzerland, and two Frenchmen, Kneebret and Chavexus, left Agadez by truck May 22 for Tamanrasset, Tawarek. After the quartet were missing four days a searching party left Agadez for them. It found the Frenchmen on the fifth day of the search in a serious condition beside the truck near a dried-up river bed, 30 miles north of Ingessam. When the Frenchmen were revived they said they had run out of both gas and water. A day later, d

LONDON, June 3.—(#)—The German delegates to the Anglo-German naval conversations were reported in diplomatic circles today to oppose any British suggestions for the restriction of war vessels by categories. Formal negotiations start tomorrow. It was understood the Germans regard their offer to keep their navy under 35 per cent of the British strength as the only restriction the Reich can accept. They were expected to insist that the manner in which Germany distributes her tonnage is a matter for her to decide alone. Although Reichsfuehrer Hitler's proposal for the abolition of submarines undoubtedly will be discussed, there is little belief that anything more than a tentative agreement may be concluded here. Italy and France, both with larger fleets of undersea craft, must be consulted, it was pointed out, before any final accord of this nature may be reached. Hitler sent Joachim von Rib

ALGIERS, Algeria, June 3. (4) Two Frenchmen, rescued from a horrible death in the scorching Sahara, were recovering today in a Tamanrasset hospital from the effects of an experience which cost the lives of two companions, an Englishman and an English woman. Tamanrasset authorities telegraphed the governor general here that the Frenchmen, Kneebret and Chavezus, were out of danger, although suffering from the tortures of thirst and exposure to blistering heat for five days. The survivors related that they set out on a desert expedition in a truck with a Mrs. Knight, widow of an English aviator, and another British subject, a Mr. Preyton. They left Agadez May 22 for Tamanrasset, they said, after arranging with the company from whom they hired the truck to send a party in search of them, in accordance with desert law, if they should not reach their destination within a specified time. The tr

1935-05-31.text: LONDON, May 31.—(#)—An authoritative source stated today that the British military forces at Tientsin and Peiping, China, are prepared for defensive measures if fighting between the Chinese and Japanese threatens those cities. This source stated the British government had been aware for some time of the danger that warfare would be renewed in North China and had received official dispatches confirming that Japanese military authorities had complained that the demilitarized zone south of the Great Wall was not being maintained by the Chinese. Officials were informed that the Japanese demand the ousting of the Chinese magistrate in Hopei province and threatened action to extend the demilitarized zone to Tientsin and Peiping. The information indicated that the Japanese military forces were impatient with the efforts of the Japanese foreign office to appease the Chinese and therefore were ta

Yondon, May 20.--Adolf Hitler today offered Europe his draft on an "air Locarno"—the first specific German proposal for peace bulwarks on the continent. Copies of the draft were sent simultaneously to Britain, France, Italy and Belgium, the four governments which with Germany signed the original Locarno convention designed to guarantee western Europe's frontiers. Attitude of British Tonight the British foreign office was giving the German plan, details of which were kept secret, close study, but authoritative sources said Britain's answer would demand that Germany, simultaneously with signature of the air convention: 1. Join some general armaments and security agreement, and 2. Return to the League of Nations. Those, with the air pact proposal, were the principal points involved in the Anglo-French security system. (Continued on Page 6)

London, (4) — George Percy Stoner today was convicted of the “triangle murder” of Francis Mawson Rattenbury, architect, and sentenced to death. His co-defendant, the murdered man's widow, Alma, was acquitted. The verdict ended one of the most sensational murder trials the Old Bailey has ever witnessed. The couple—the boy aged 18, and the woman aged 38—were tried for the murder of the woman's elderly husband, Francis Mawson Rattenbury. The jury of 10 men and two women gave heed to the defense contention that Stoner struck the blow with a mallet that inflicted fatal injury to Rattenbury, but disregarded the plea that the youth was insane with drugs and jealousy at the time.

Karachi. India May 31 (CINS)— One of the most disastrous earthquakes of the 20th century razed the entire city of Quetta today, killing an estimated 20,000 persons. The quake, which laid waste a large section of Baluchistan, destroyed the important British military post at Quetta, where 43 members of the Royal Air Force were killed. British and Indian troops worked feverishly to extricate the dead and injured from the debris of tens of thousands of homes, including those of a modern British quarter which had many up-to-date, western style buildings. Answering a radio relief call from Sir Norman Cator, governor general’s agent from Baluchistan, who himself narrowly escaped death, scores of trains set out for Quetta from provincial capitals bearing doctors, nurses and medical supplies. The radio was the only line of communication not wrecked by the quake. One train left Karachi with a cont

(Copyright, 1935, by Associated Press) PARIS, May 31.—With Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin forced out by an overwhelming parliamentary vote of lack of confidence and with the premier-designate, Fernand Bouisson, apparently unable to form a cabinet, political quarters said today that Edouard Herriot probably would be called upon again to serve as premier. Herriot, who already has held the premiership three times, would be called upon to face the financial emergency which resulted in the chamber of deputies voting against Flandin 353 to 202 early this morning. Herriot himself was overthrown after four days as premier in 1926 when the collapse of the franc caused Raymond Poincaré to be called to the rescue. Bouisson, 69-year-old president of the chamber of deputies, was asked by President Lebrun to form a government succeeding that of Flandin. Bouisson undertook the task against his own wish

PARIS, May 30.—The towering Premier Pierre Étienne Flandin was overthrown heavily tonight in his demand for dictatorial powers to defend the franc, and Fernand Bouisson, presiding officer of the chamber, attempted immediately to form a new government. The government, seeking to stem the flood of gold from the Bank of France, launched simultaneously police action against speculators, closing at least one "financial establishment." Devaluation of the franc, which Flandin predicted would follow his fall, remained an ever-present threat. Bouisson is committed to support of the franc, but Flandin declared in his farewell speech from the rostrum of the chamber that devaluation was inevitable if his successor failed to get the dictatorial powers which were denied to him. The Flandin government was overthrown by a vote of 353 to 202. The premier had already tossed aside Louis Germain-Martin, his

ROME, May 31. (4).-The Italian government today announced mobilization of 44,000 additional troops for East Africa service. It was stated Ethiopian officials had arrested Italian diplomatic couriers carrying mail to the Italian consulate at Donar. Couriers were released after representations were made by the consulate. The communique said "partial mobilization of Ethiopian forces and arrival in Ethiopia of additional war materials require us to adjust new defensive measures to guarantee security of our colonies from attack."

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) Paris, May 31 (UP)—Fernand Bouisson, president of the chamber of deputies, sought today to form a cabinet and prevent a grave financial crisis. He accepted from President Albert Lebrun a mandate to form a wide national union or coalition cabinet, of sufficient strength to prevent a grave flight of capital and save the franc. The seriousness of the situation was attested by the night-long conferences that followed the defeat in the chamber of deputies at 1 a.m. of the government of Pierre Etienne Flandin, who sought plenary emergency powers to govern by decree until October 31. Bouisson accepted the task of forming a ministry after working through the night unofficially, and seeking particularly to win support of the socialists, who with the communists comprise the extreme left wing. He was received by President Lebrun at 2 a.m., an hour after the chambe

1935-11-22.text: CAIRO, Egypt, Nov. 21. (P)—Fifty rioters were arrested and seven native policemen injured in short-lived disorders today on Cairo’s anti-British “day of mourning.” Tram windows and street lamps were smashed and some shops damaged by several thousand hooligans and a few students. For three hours paving stones were tossed about freely, but order was restored tonight and the rioters vanished. Students, who called the “day of mourning” for their comrades slain in last week's anti-British riots, failed, however, to effect a hoped-for general strike. Lawyers’ Strike Fails Egyptian nationalists did not join in the demonstrations as groups. A projected lawyers’ strike failed, many barristers doing business as usual. In the native quarter, some merchants draped their doors in mourning and when the correspondent drove through the district his Arab Dragoman was kept busy shouting: “American—not Bri

LONDON, Nov. 22.—(UP)—Lord Halifax has been appointed lord privy seal in the government which Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin is forming, it was announced today. He succeeds former Premier James Ramsay MacDonald, who was defeated for re-election in the November 14 general election. MacDonald remains lord president of the council, it was announced. Halifax replaces Lord Londonderry. Malcolm MacDonald, son of the former premier, has been appointed dominions secretary; J. H. Thomas colonial secretary and Duff Cooper secretary of war. Viscount Halifax was war secretary in the outgoing cabinet.

London, Nov. 22, (U.P)—Foreign exchange dealers refused to make quotations for the Italian lire today as the result of Italy’s action in holding British owned deposits. The refusal caused a sensation in the market.

(International News Service) LONDON, Nov. 22.— Ethiopian warriors were reported to have killed 300 Italians in a fierce battle at Womberta, north of Makale on the northern front, November 12, a Central News Dispatch from Addis Ababa stated today. An Exchange Telegraph Dispatch from Addis Ababa said the Italians, marching from Makale to Kolel, were wiped out. A Reuter Dispatch from Rome, however, said the Ethiopian claims that 300 Italians had been wiped out referred to a day-long engagement between the “mystery” Danakil column of Italians and troops under Ras Kassa November 16, in which the Italians were ambushed by the Ethiopian warriors. Reuter stated the Italians admitted four officers including a colonel were injured in the fight and 50 Askaris were wounded. Rome also reported today an encounter between Italian and Ethiopian forces, but said it was near Amba Betlem, southeast of Maka
London, Nov. 22 (UP) — Herbert Carmichael, religious classical painter of the Victorian era, died yesterday at the age of 79.

By EDWARD W. BEATTIE ‘United Press Staff Correspondent (Copyright 1935 by United Press) ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 22.—“Operations to date on the southern front have demonstrated that my armies are capable not only of resisting modernized troops but even of defeating them,” Emperor Haile Selassie told the United Press today. He made his statement in a self-written interview, in response to my questions, after an airplane flight to the eastern-southern front. “We saw no Italian airplanes in the course of our trip,” said the emperor. “But their presence was signaled from Jijiga, Harar and Diredawa—and there was another escadrille over Arussi—immediately after our departure from the front.” Jijiga and Harar, south of the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, are the chief eastern-southern air bases. Diredawa is on the railway. The Arussi country is south of the railway and west of Harar. Otherwise, the empe

WITH THE ITALIAN ARMY AT MAKALE, NOV. 22. (AP).—Ras Seyoum, beaten off by an Italian column at Abaro Pass yesterday, circled and attacked the Italian rear guard today but was repulsed again after a hot skirmish. The leader of the Ethiopian northern army was reported in dispatches from the Italian command in the Tembien region to have engaged 15 battalions of Italian native troops who formed the head of the column now attempting to reach Amba Alaji. Four Italian battalions of infantry and a squadron of cavalry reported yesterday they had smashed through an Ethiopian ambuscade after several hours’ fighting. It was the rear of the same column that Ras Seyoum and his men attacked today, apparently after a fast overnight march. The Italians, however, were awaiting the maneuver and were prepared. They said they had repulsed the rear guard attack without loss. Several casualties among Italian o

(Copyright, 1995, Associated Press) Tokyo, Nov. 22 (Friday) (/P)—Sources close to the government said Japanese militarists and opposing civilian leaders faced a showdown today over the North China situation with the life of the cabinet possibly in the balance. The issue is expected to be debated at a cabinet session with Koki Hirota, the Foreign Minister, leading the civilian group, and Gen. Yoshiyuki Kawashima, Minister of War, representing the militarists. Hirota, informed sources said, favors a compromise on the North China issue which would allow the Chinese National government to retain a considerable degree of authority in the five northern provinces. This plan was recommended by Akira Ariyoshi, ambassador to China, who conferred with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, Chinese National government leader, in Nanking yesterday. (Chinese dispatches said Japanese officers in China were imp

1935-12-04.text: [COPYRIGHT 1935 BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] Emperor Haile Selassie of war-torn Ethiopia has made another bid for peace with Italy, an authoritative religious source in Cairo divulged today. While Premier Mussolini created a “brain trust” to remodel the Italian diet along wartime lines and the British treasury offered two gigantic loans—part of which may be used for defense—it was learned the king of kings has appealed to the supreme authority of the Coptic Christian church for aid. Another king, George of Britain, conveyed to his parliament the warning: “The fulfilment of our international obligations under the (League) covenant, no less than the adequate safeguarding of the empire, makes it urgently necessary that deficiencies in the defense forces be made good.” Intervention Sought Ethiopia’s ruler would have the patriarch Johannes intervene with the Italian government to establish a basis fo

London, Dec. 3, (U.R)—King George pledged Great Britain forcefully and unequivocally today to the government’s firm policy in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis. In a speech from the throne of the House of Lords at the state opening of parliament, read in his absence by the Lord High Chancellor, the King committed the country 1—Firm support of the League of Nations, 2—Fulfillment in cooperation with other countries of the league covenant, with its Article XVI providing for penalization of a war maker. 3—Exertion of its influence in favor of an Italian-Ethiopian peace acceptable to Italy, Ethiopia and the league. 4—"Urgently necessary” strengthening of the national defenses in order to fulfill its international obligations under the covenant and to safeguard the empire. The state opening of parliament was to have been one of pomp and pageantry with the king reading his speech in the House of Lo

Copyright 1935, By Associated Press LONDON, Dec. 3. (#)—The United States has undertaken preliminary work for a reciprocal trade agreement with her greatest foreign customer—Great Britain, an authoritative source disclosed tonight. This move follows upon conclusion of a trade agreement between Washington and the Dominion of Canada. It was learned that surveys are under way in London and Washington to determine the practicality and benefits of a reciprocal agreement. While the Canadian negotiations took two and a half years to complete, it is believed the Anglo-American work may be speeded up with a possibility of a conclusion next summer. Officials here recognize the great obstacles that confront the two countries because of the many interlocking British trade agreements with other countries, but it was agreed the time is ripe for an Anglo-American treaty. The Ottawa empire agreements, w

LONDON, Dec. 4.--Great Britain and France are expected this weekend to make the strongest effort since the outbreak of the Italian-Ethiopian war to end the crisis peaceably and avert the necessity for a dangerous and possibly disastrous trial of strength between Italy and the League of Nations. Diplomatic activity in London, Paris and Rome was more intense today than it has been at any time during the two months since Italy attacked Ethiopia. This activity will reach its climax when Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, goes to Paris this weekend to talk to Premier Pierre Laval (of France regarding (first), terms for a peace agreement which would be acceptable to France, Britain, Ethiopia and the League; (second), the best means of bringing Italy into direct negotiations, and (third), imposition of an oil embargo against Italy probably before Christmas if peace efforts fail. Up to Mussoli

LONDON, Dec. 4.—General Yin Ju-Keng, head of the autonomous regime set up in northern Hope province and in part of Chahar, has been assassinated, Chinese newspapers reported today, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Tientsin. Yin obtained much of his early education in Japan. He has a Japanese wife and his brother-in-law is a high officer in the Japanese army. Chinese loyal to the central government at Nanking have openly accused him of being a tool of the Japanese army. Reports yesterday stated that a mob had demonstrated before Yin's headquarters at Kungchow, a few miles from Peiping, demanding relief from taxes and threatening his life. The reports said Yin had fled in disguise.

Washington. —(UP)— Secretary of State Cordell Hull said today that the possibility of a trade agreement between the United States and Great Britain was being discussed. While no formal discussions have taken place, he said that a casual exchange was taking place from time to time in accordance with the reciprocal trade agreement program. He indicated that world conditions were such that the question of an agreement was in doubt at present. Regarding reports of an agreement for Italy to obtain oil from abroad through American controlled firms, Hull said the department had not had time to find out as yet regarding the reported facts. He indicated that the state department had not got in touch with the Standard Oil company in connection with the reported agreement.

Copyright, 1935, Associated Press Paris, Dec. 4 — A spokesman for diplomatic circles said today Premier Laval would seek an agreement with Sir Samuel Hoare on how much Ethiopian territory to offer Premier Mussolini as a basis for peace in East Africa. French and British experts, studying a possible plan for an Italo-Ethiopian settlement, were reported to have split over terms for a peace proposal, leaving the problem up to the foreign office heads. The French favored giving Italy the territory in northern and southern Ethiopia already occupied by Il Duce’s troops, but this suggestion was rejected by the British as too generous, informed sources said. The British were reported willing to propose merely an exchange of lands between Ethiopia and Italy, whereby Ethiopia would give Italy part of its territory and would receive an outlet to the sea. The deadlock was generally considered hopele

BOSTON, Dec. 4—(P)—Governor James M. Curley’s decision to seek the toga of U.S. Senator Marcus Coolidge next year presaged today, even to the non-politically minded, a rough and tumble Democratic primary campaign. Curley, New England’s original “Roosevelt for President” man who has broken with some state Democratic leaders, announced his intention last night to the Total Abstinence Society at Rockland.

1935-02-02.text: (By Albert W. Wilson—Associated Press Foreign Staff London, Feb. 2—(A-P.) — The Anglo-French conversations unexpectedly turned to discussions of stabilization today and it was revealed that England and France are both worried over the future of the pound and the franc because of the uncertainty of the United States dollar's position. The uncertainty here was admitted in official circles after it became known that Premier Pierre Flandin of France and the British financial expert, Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, had discussed stabilization at a long session during the forenoon. Additionally, the British cabinet met at 10 Downing Street during the morning, indicating the significance of new developments in the Anglo-French discussions. Previously the talks had centered upon armament problems and general matters of European security. It was learned Great Britain will formally invite Germany to joi

HONG KONG, Feb 2—A British airplane roared over the coastal steamer Tungchow at noon yesterday while her passengers, prisoners of pirates, cheered wildly and the outlaws, who seized the ship soon after she sailed from Shanghai, Tuesday, fled for shore. That was the dramatic story radioed to Hong Kong today as the Tungchow—the 75 American, British and Scandinavian school children aboard her safe and sound—made for this port after 66 hours in the hands of the pirates. The pirates, numbering 12, boarded the ship at Shanghai and seized control at 6 P. M. Tuesday, the radio advices said. A Russian guard, one of six employed to protect the vessel from piracy, fought off four men until finally he was shot down. Passengers saw him alive 20 minutes later when the brigands, they said, brutally killed him. When the alarm was sounded, Second Engineer K. MacDonald rushed from his cabin only to fall s

HONG KONG, Feb. 2--Forty British and American school children, more thrilled than frightened by their four-day adventure in which they were at the mercy of Chinese pirates, reached here unharmed today aboard the S. S. Tungchow. The pirates released the Tungchow yesterday in Bias Bay, notorious outlaw rendezvous, when British airplanes approached in search of the missing ship. Most of the children, members of missionary families, carried cartridges and pieces of cloth as souvenirs of their exciting experiences. The Tungchow was en route to Chefu of the Shantung Peninsula when pirates seized the steamer Tuesday. Apparently the outlaws had boarded the craft at Shanghai and waited until she reached the open sea before. J. N. Duncan, a mission schoolmaster in charge of the children said he heard a scuffle outside of Woosung and went on deck in time to see the pirates shoot and kill I. V. Thin

London, Feb. 2—(P)—Important decisions were reported to have been reached today by a surprise meeting of the British cabinet which discussed a series of rapid developments in Franco-British negotiations toward strengthening European peace. The cabinet meeting was called suddenly after Premier Pierre Flandin of France had delivered to Britain a secret memorandum which was prepared hastily last night. Flandin and British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald have been discussing for two days the possible ways and means of solving the German re-armament and other problems affecting Europe’s future. Last night Rene Massigli, the French expert, and other members of Flandin's party worked until 2 a.m. on a memorandum which was believed to summarize the French attitude at the conclusion of Friday's Franco-British conferences. The memorandum was said to outline concessions and guarantees which France

London, Feb. 2, —(UP)—A painting for generations hanging unrecognized on the wall of a country home was hailed today as the art find of the century and one of the most important in art history. The painting is a life-sized portrait group of three persons, painted probably about 170 years ago by Thomas Gainsborough, whose Blue Boy brought the highest price ever paid for a painting. Experts believe this one is worth at least £250,000 and might bring $1,000,000—more than the Blue Boy. About 1765, when Gainsborough was attaining great fame, he painted a portrait, eight feet high, the Byam family—George Byam, of Appas Court, Surrey; his wife Louisa and their three-year-old daughter Selina. It passed down through the generations to H. C. Hony, of Ogbourne, Wiltshire, a lineal descendant.

Hongkong (/P)—Pirates who plundered the steamer Tungchow threatened to massacre the 75 mission school children aboard if the British plane which roared overhead attempted a bombing, those aboard the ship said today. The marauders held the children and their elders in a state of terror for three days before the plane from British aircraft carrier, Hermes, frightened them away yesterday. Police broadcast a warning that another gang of pirates was proceeding toward Santon with the object of attacking a ship running for Shanghai.

- BOSTON, Feb. 2 (?)—Ten persons were forced to flee into the street today when a two-alarm fire of undetermined origin badly damaged the four-story stone residence of Joseph P. Carney, Manager of the New England branch of the Federal Reconstruction Finance Corporation, at 80 Marlboro Street. Carney, whose permanent residence is in Gardner, rescued two maids, Miss Sadie MacAskill and Miss Katherine MacNeil, who were trapped in their rooms on the fourth floor by smoke. Making his way through the skylight of an adjoining home, crossing the roof and down into his home, Carney assisted the two women to the street. Mr. and Mrs. Carney and their two daughters, Betty, 23, and Ruth, 20, reached the street safely without assistance. Mr. and Mrs. Charles P. White, who live at 78 Marlboro Street, were driven from their home by smoke and firemen carried their two small children, Robert, eight, and C

BERLIN, Feb. 1.—(UP)— Eight passengers and three members of the crew were killed when the regular Moscow-Berl in passenger plane crashed near Stettin, Pomerania, it was announced today. The crash occurred at 7 p. m. yesterday. It was understood all the passengers were Germans.

1935-04-01.text: London, April 1.—(#)—Unconfirmed British press reports said the German military class of 1915 totaling 580,000 young men would respond to the new conscription law today by reporting for their medical examination. These same reports said a total of 8,500,000 men is likely to be called up eventually for military training in pursuit of Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s program to reestablish Germany as a first line military power.

LONDON, April 1. (U.P)—Great Britain, France and Italy have issued a strong warning to Lithuania against abuse of her rights in the Memel Territory, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, informed the House of Commons today. The three powers, Sir John told questioners, told Lithuania that “the present situation in Memel is incompatible with the principle of autonomy guaranteed to the territory by the Memel Statute and they consider it the duty of the Lithuanian government to terminate the situation without delay.”

MOSCOW, April 1—(UP)—Anthony Eden, British cabinet envoy, sped to Warsaw today to ask Polish leaders to join an Eastern European treaty that would impose peace by military force. He was a diplomatic salesman. If he can sell Poland he may alter the whole trend of negotiations in Europe’s arm crisis. He left Moscow last night after a three-day visit which cemented Russia-British relations on a basis firmer than since 1914. The 37-year old British war veteran and the Bolshevik leaders found themselves in complete agreement on means to preserve peace in Europe. Now it is his job to win Poland to the idea of joining with Russia and other nations in a treaty under which each would pledge its aid to any other that might be attacked. It was Poland’s opposition to such a treaty that hardened Germany's attitude against it—and today made it appear that such a treaty would be signed by France, Russi

Moscow, March 31.——(#)——Capt. Anthony Eden of Great Britain is in agreement with Joseph Stalin and Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinoff that the nations should go ahead with building up a European security arrangement on the basis of the London peace plan, a joint communique announced tonight. - The first official account of the joint conference here, issued as Eden was leaving for Warsaw to continue his peace tour, followed by a new blast at Germany in the Soviet press with the sharp warning that the Reich has plans for revenge on France, Belgium and Czechoslovakia. Imperative Tonight’s communique said all parties in the conference finished yesterday were of the opinion that ‘it is more than ever necessary to pursue the endeavor to promote the building up of a system of collective security in Europe as contemplated in the Anglo-French communique of February 3 and in conformity with the Lea

LONDON, April 1.--The mysterious warning that death was imminent for Reichsfuehrer Hitler, reportedly made by a gypsy a month ago, turned out to be an April Fool joke today for all concerned except possibly the London insurance companies. The underwriters were reported to have cleaned up several thousand dollars "easy money" on the strength of the tale. Several British firms trading in Germany were said to have decided to take out insurance after the gypsy story began to circulate. The premiums demanded were small, one insurance broker said, and after a while the scare died down. The version of the Hitler death prognostication story which was prevalent in London involved a motorist who was said to have been told by a gypsy to whom he gave a ride: "There will be a dead man in your car by evening as sure as Hitler will be dead before the month is out." That night, the story ran, the motori

Pope Pius denounced the spirit of warfare Monday while Capt. Anthony Eden, British diplomat, turned from Russia toward Poland in an endeavor to obtain her adherence to an eastern European peace pact. Russia is willing to form an alliance to “resist aggression” in the east. To make the circle around Germany complete, sanction of Poland and Czechoslovakia is necessary. Eden, therefore, will visit Prague after he has conferred with Polish statesmen at Warsaw, after which the way will be opened for an informal conference of representatives from Great Britain, France and Italy at Stresa, Italy. Although the far eastern situation was not mentioned in the Russian communique announcing the results of Eden's conferences, the fact that there was no conflict or diversion of views between Britain and Russia was taken to indicate agreement had been reached for an anti-aggression understanding in the

BY H. R. KNICKERBOCKER (LN. &. Staff Correspondent) (World Copyright, 1935, by I. N. S.) (Reproduction in whole or part strictly prohibited). LONDON, April 1—(NS)—Germany was engaged in the creation of her first conscript army since the war today and while initial groups shouldered their wooden trunks and marched to barracks the rest of Europe marched toward an alliance to hold the Germans in check. Just sixteen days after Hitler's challenge to the Allies, Europe now is an armed camp, whereon moves and counter-moves follow with bewildering rapidity and trumpet calls drown out the feeble tones of peace. Within a fortnight, the continental scene has suffered amazing alterations and the outlines of an anti-German bloc can already be discerned. As it grows clearer, chances for a general collective system including Germany recede. The chief factor is Britain’s consequent history-making change

LONDON, April 1 (UP)—Count Haugwitz of Denmark today denied reports that he might marry Princess Barbara Hutton Meivani, heiress who is divorcing Alexis Mdivani at Reno. “I saw the princess here,” Haugwitz said, “but I have not heard from her since. There is no foundation to any rumor of matrimonial intentions on my part. I am not engaged, never have been and am unlikely to be.”

1935-03-04.text: CRANLEIGH, England, March 4—King Prajadhipok of Siam, until a short time ago one of the world's few remaining absolute monarchs, is plain Prince Sukhodaya today, one of England's country gentlemen. The adamant little sovereign, who would not brook his parliament's determination to modify his power of life and death over his 10,000,000 subjects, formally abdicated his throne last Saturday. Prajadhipok named no successor. It was explained Siamese laws provide for the present contingency. Studies At Lausanne Eleven-year-old Prince Ananda, the former king’s nephew, now studying at Lausanne, Switzerland, generally was expected to become Siam’s sovereign. At Bangkok, Siam, it was said no definite reply has been received from Prince Ananda yet. The announcement that the king had relinquished his royal estate was made yesterday by his secretary at Prajadhipok's country residence here. Later the

CRANLEIGH, England, March 2. (¥)—Prajadhinok of Siam, ruler until today of 10,000,000 people, has abdicated the throne without designating a successor and retired to private life as plain Prince Sukhodaya. Three simple sentences, "It's all over, The king is no more, He has abdicated." informed the world that the stubborn, diminutive, brown-skinned monarch has stepped down, bringing to an end months of wrangling with the home government over his royal prerogatives. He signed the abdication document Saturday afternoon at his temporary country residence at Knowle. This announcement by his secretary, M. R. Smaksman, was delivered this afternoon. Later the king gave his first interview since coming to Britain on his present trip. After posing for photographs, «Continued on Page 2, Col. 8.).

LONDON —(WUP)—An 11-year-old boy, reared in Boston, was expected today to succeed to the golden lotus throne of Siam which King Prajadhipok gave up because his parliament would not restore his power of life and death over his subjects. While Prajadhipok remained at his country estate near London, it was reported from Lausanne, Switzerland, that the Siamese minister to France visited Prince Ananda, the 11-year-old heir presumptive, and asked him to go to Siam to take the throne. Ananda and his mother, Princess Songkla—living at a modest Lausanne boarding house during his education—were willing, although the boy’s health is delicate and he was forced recently to interrupt his studies at a private school to go to Villars for winter sports. A statement from the government at Bangkok was expected Tuesday, probably announcing that Ananda

CRANLEIGH, Eng., March 3—(47)—Prajadhipok, diminutive King of Siam, has given up his throne, it became known today. He signed the abdication document Saturday afternoon at his country residence at Knowle. The man of many titles, including the “Possessor of Twenty-Four Umbrellas,” finally made good his months in dealing with a military government in Bangkok. Prajadhipok and his wife henceforth will be known as “the title under which they are traveling incognito.

London, Eng. (INS)—In a document that dealt in frank unblushing terms with the increase in military strength in Germany, the United States, Soviet Russia and Japan, Great Britain today disbanded universal armament as a key to peace and announced she was building up her armament to a point in keeping with national security. Anxiety over German armament was admitted as one of the causes,

LONDON, March 4.—French speculators turned on the American dollar today and forced it down toward levels where gold imports from New York would be profitable. Weakness of the dollar was viewed with a further abrupt decline of the pound and an advance to a record high in the London gold price for attention. The exchange situation was becoming acute. French financiers were worried. British continued complacent. Washington was silent. Speculators Control Neither the American nor British control funds were in operation and exchange rates were swayed by the will of the speculators. British operations in the pound and dollar were discerned. Continental investors, frightened by the pound’s recent abrupt decline, continued to repatriate their funds from London. French continued to buy London gold and it was reported they took the entire amount offered today, £674,000 ($3,196,445). Paris exchange

FOLKESTONE, England, March 4.—#)—Recovered from an operation on his jaw performed last Saturday, Leopold III, King of the Belgians, decided today to terminate his brief English visit and return to Brussels. The greatest secrecy surrounded the short stay here on the Belgian Monarch and Queen Astrid, giving rise to varying reports concerning his illness.

London, March 4. (UP) —Great Britain announced officially today that, since other nations are re-arming at a rapid rate, she finds it necessary to strengthen her naval, land and air forces immediately. The announcement was in the form of a “white paper”—which is Britain’s way of making such a proclamation official and final as a matter of government policy. The “white paper,” in effect tore the mask off all the futile talk of peace and disarmament in recent years and called for a showdown, with the British lion in effect showing his teeth and declaring “if you are preparing to fight, I will defend myself.” It coincided with publication of increased estimates for the army, navy and air forces for the coming fiscal year. The “white paper,” one of the frankest and most significant documents in modern diplomacy, emphasized especially the fact that Germany is re-arming, recalling the recent s

1935-12-21.text: Premier Mussolini of Italy directed his Blackshirt troops to proceed with their campaign of conquest in Ethiopia today, and Great Britain again took up the challenge to "sanctionist" nations with a warlike appeal for aid. The Italian dictator, scorning to reply to the now dead Franco-British proposals for peace, urged his "unshakably united" people against the "disorganization and contradictions" of the nations seeking to penalize him for taking up arms against Ethiopia. At Birmingham, England, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer who has been mentioned as a possible new foreign secretary, told an audience of conservative party workers: "I trust the nations of the league will show that they are prepared to make themselves resist any attack which may be made on any one of their number." Thus were the lines drawn taut between a resumption of the explosive-filled economic battle

Copyright, — the Associated LONDON, Dec. 21—The British government was stated by a reliable source today to be considering further precautionary measures against the possibility of a warlike act on the part of Premier Mussolini of Italy because Great Britain's determination to reinforce sanctions against Italy. A meeting of the council of the League of Nations to discuss the question of mutual defenses against an act of desperation on the part of Italy was mentioned in government circles but was not confirmed officially. In government offices, however, it was authoritatively confirmed that steps have been taken to see what support by other nations could be mobilized in the event of a warlike move. It was said that the inquiries thus far had been encouraging. Thus far the British government has confined its approach to Mediterranean powers.

Great Britain was believed to possess definite assurances of support from the Mediterranean powers today in event of any attack on her by Italy. It was indicated that Britain asked for these assurances, and received them, early this month—before Sir Samuel Hoare went to Paris to negotiate Italian-Ethiopian peace proposals with Premier Pierre Laval. Diplomatic quarters disclosed yesterday that Britain had asked assurances of France, Spain, Greece, Yugoslavia and Turkey. The disclosure had been made already on the floor of the House of Commons, along with the news that assurances had been received. Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, made the disclosure in the House of Commons late Thursday night. He said the government had not only asked the assistance of France in the event Britain was attacked in the Mediterranean. He continued: “We received from all—France particularly—th

Rome, Dec. 21.—(AP)—Premier Mussolini showed his disdain for the discarded Franco-British proposals for peace between Italy and Ethiopia today by refusing even to reply to them after ordering the East African campaign to proceed. An official spokesman said the decision of the fascist grand council issued after a session last night, constituted Italy’s only answer to the peace plan. This decision referred briefly to British “repudiation” of the proposals and said Italy would go on to the “goal” designated by Il Duce as the nation’s destiny. In directing confidentially that his armies press on for conquest of Ethiopia, Mussolini posed his “unshakeably united” people against the “disorganization and contradictions” of sanctionist nations. He declared his conviction that fascism would triumph over both Ethiopia and league sanctions.

In a militant death wake for discarded peace proposals, Great Britain rallied friendly powers Friday night to assure quick help if her Mediterranean men o' war are attacked. Already, said dispatches from London and Paris, Britain has been assured by France, Turkey, Greece and Yugoslavia that they will come to her aid. United Front Sought She wants a united front of collective defense by League of Nations members against possible unprovoked assault by Italy, now that the Anglo-French plan for African peace is dead. Recent movements of French troops, ships and airplanes took on added significance as informed Parisians said France was ready to defend both herself and Great Britain if there is a European war. International observers in Geneva suggested that the league council, meeting again next month, consider asking member states for armed ‘contributions’ to uphold the league covenant. Whe

Rome, Dec. 21, (WP) — Premier Benito Mussolini has decided not to reply to the late British-French proposals for settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian war, an official spokesman announced today. The decision, the spokesman said, was made because Great Britain repudiated the proposals.

ADDIS ABABA: Ethiopia claims military successes along northern front, reporting Italian casualties at over 600 and the capture of several Italian positions. ROME: Mussolini will not reply to the now defunct Anglo-French peace proposals. Strong guard established around British embassy. LONDON: Britain reportedly possesses definite assurances of support from Mediterranean powers in event of any attack on her by Italy. PARIS: Ethiopian "publicity counsellor" says Ethiopia is ready to give Italy occupied territory between and north of Adigrat and Aduwa and section of Ogaden in exchange for seaport.

NATIONS HELD RESPONSIBLE Paris, Dec. 21.—()—If Premier Laval fails to stave off a European war, authoritative quarters disclosed Friday night that France is prepared to defend herself and aid Great Britain in the event of an Italian attack. Recent movements of French troops, ships and airplanes were disclosed as significant in responsible circles, following a disclosure in London that Britain has asked Mediterranean powers what precautions they have taken. Others Give Support Diplomatic sources said Turkey, Greece and Yugoslavia also have indicated willingness to take military and naval precautions against any possible Italian attack because of sanctions. The newspaper L’Ordre asserts that Il Duce would “be glad to see the colonial war degenerate into a general war” because he realizes it “will finally alienate the Italian People” from Italy’s former allies. Vittorio Cerruti, the Italian

1935-03-11.text: | LONDON, March 9— (Saturday) —(AP)—The Daily Herald under a flaring five-column headline “Mussolini Behind the Greek Rebellion” cited British “diplomatic circles” today as the source of a story claiming diplomatic intrigues of Il Duce caused the Greek revolt and trouble in the Balkans. “Every responsible statesman is convinced that the Venizelist revolt is encouraged by Italy, supported by Italy, and is part of the Italian campaign to break up the Balkan Pact,” said the Daily Herald. “Venizelist pro-Italian Greece linked with pro-Italian Bulgaria would break the bloc and give Italy strategic control of the Balkans. “There is even suspicion that the mobilization of Italian divisions for Africa is connected with events the Italian government knew were impending in the Balkans.”

- LONDON, March 11—%)— ~W. J. A. Grant, the 84-year-old explorer who celebrated the approach of death with a big party fourteen months ago, is dead at last. He died yesterday in his little cottage at Hillersdon, Devonshire. Death came quietly to the man who had spent a lifetime defying it. Grant participated in nine expeditions to the Arctic and many big game hunts. In January, 1934, he gave a “swan dance” in Exeter and invited in 600 friends and a bevy of dancing girls. It was his last fling at life, he said. But he did not die and, subsequently, made a voyage to the Amazon,

Daytona Beach, Fla, G#)- Str ‘Malcolm Campbell turned the half century mark today, still hoping for conditions that will give him an opportunity to realize his greatest ambition—to travel 300 miles an hour in an automobile. The British nobleman saw his 60th birthday dawn with little prospect that he might be able to take his Bluebird onto the beach in an effort to raise his own speed record from 278.816 miles an hour. The track still was bumpy in spots, too rough to travel at the hazardous speed he hopes to attain.

ATHENS, MAR. 11. (AP).—Government sources said today rebel forces, battered by a terrific bombardment from government artillery, withdrew from their strongly fortified position in the town of Seres. News of the rebels’ reported withdrawal was made public at the same time the government was informed the rebel cruiser Helle had been abandoned in the port of Kavalla by the officers and crew. Shortly after the rebels evacuated Seres, the government report said, capture of the town was completed, a detachment of cavalry entering its streets at the head of the main body of government troops. Word received by the government said 3,000 rebel officers and soldiers have surrendered to loyalist troops, while others are leaving their commands to shift for themselves and fleeing northward toward the Turko-Bulgarian frontier. Unofficial reports said the casualties in the bitter fighting of the last 48

ATHENS Greece, March 15 (UP) - The Greek government appeared to be winning today in its fight to crush the Venizelos revolution after 10 days of civil war that has taken a heavy toll of life: Gen. Geo. Condylis, war minister and the head of the government, closing in on rebels on all sides in Macedonia, ordered his aircraft to cease bombing and avoid unnecessary bloodshed, in view of the collapse of the rebels. The loyalist army of Gen. Chliastas, moving westward from Thrace was reported to have cut off rebels who were attempting to flee to the sea. Gen. Camanos, rebel leader, was reported to have retreated from Tavalla to a point not far from the Bulgarian border accompanied by 10 of his men. The rebel warship had surrendered. Hundreds were reported to have...

(Copyright, 1935, by the Ass Press) ATHENS March 10—Government in their slashing drive in Macedonia when the rebels rallied seven miles from their stronghold of Seres and halted the advance. This was admitted by the government, which earlier had claimed gains along a wide front in its major push. Gen. George Kondylis, military leader in an Official communique late tonight said his troops struck unexpectedly strong resistance when the rebels rallied near Seres. Other reports indicated also that the rebels were showing strength as the fighting raged in Macedonia’s mud and snow. Vivid red flashes of government artillery lighted up the Struma river valley before dawn in the beginning of General George Kondylis’ big push. Reports tonight said there were answering flashes from mountain artillery brought into play by the rebels. The government tightened its belt another notch in the life-and-de

VIENNA, March 11—(#)—Dispatches to Vienna newspapers today from Athens said 4,000 men were killed on both sides in the battle along the Struma river between the Greek government and rebels. Rebels retreated slightly, the dispatches added, but were showing a vigorous resistance.

Athens, Greece, Mar. 11—The collapse of the Greek revolution on land was claimed by the government today. Rebels were reported in full flight after loyal troops had captured a wide area east of the Struma River, including rebel stations at Seres, Drama, Demichisser and Kavalla. The government announced the capture of 3000 persons at Seres. The remainder of the rebels were said to be retreating towards the mountains in the east.

1935-10-31.text: By The Associated Press Concessions to Mussolini to end his invasion of Ethiopia, high British sources said today, would be discussed at Geneva tomorrow when the League of Nations sanctions staff meets to fix a deadline for imposing the economic penalties against Italy. Sir Samuel Hoare the British foreign minister who will go to Geneva to survey possibilities of peace with Premier Pierre Laval of France declared, however, any basis of peace must be “an honorable settlement of the dispute acceptable to the three parties concerned—the League, Italy and Ethiopia.” No Change In Policy Sir Samuel vigorously proclaimed there has been no change in British policy. Other British sources saw such a change, however slight, in the renewal of discussions for settlement. Informed circles in Paris said British and French navy, army and air chiefs were drafting a plan for full wartime cooperation betwe

Rome, Oct. 31,—(4%)—Students demonstrating against Great Britain stormed stores they believed to be British owned last night following a morning demonstration in front of the British embassy. Shouting “Down with England!” they broke a big lamp hanging in front of a tea room and pasted a map of Aduwa, Ethiopia on the window. The place had signs printed in English and students thought it a British restaurant. The students, some of whom carried banners denouncing British action against Italy in relation to the sanctions, marched through Rome and were frequently cheered by the population. Italian officials, seeing their World War friendships fading, expected Germany and Austria—enemies of Italy in the Great War—to furnish coal, iron, steel and other products needed by the nation. Authorities said they were watching closely the attitude of new world countries, the resources of which might see

London. Oct. 29.—Efforts of Anglo-French experts to agree upon a plan for settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian war have failed, it was confirmed officially tonight. On the heels of this disclosure, Anthony Eden, Great Britain's “International commuter” prepared to return to Geneva to push London’s determined drive for quick operation of sanctions against warring Italy. But his portfolio contains no peace scheme to put up to the league, high sources revealed. Sir Samuel Hoare, Foreign Secretary, will follow Eden 24 hours after the latter leaves. Hoare's unexpected return, it was emphasized, indicated no change in Britain’s policy of firmness and there is no likelihood of three-power conversations with France and Italy.

PARIS, Oct. 30 (AY) — The newspaper “La Liberte” tonight printed a dispatch from its London correspondent reporting a “secret agreement” between Premier Mussolini of Italy and Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia. The dispatch said the alleged “accord” specifies all the details of Italian military operations and calls for a pretense of resistance (on the part of Haile Selassie) “to satisfy the demands of national honor in both countries.” The dispatch adds that military hostilities will end the day Italy considers she has gained enough to ask the League of Nations to recognize her position. In exchange, the correspondent stated that Emperor Haile Selassie would receive important financial and “moral” concessions.

Rome, Oct. 31.—Italian students shouting “Down with England” demonstrated outside the British embassy today as Italian authorities looked toward Germany and Austria for working agreements in steel, coal and other products in Italy’s hour of trial under League of Nations sanctions.

BERLIN, Oct. 31 (4--The Nazi regime's recent coolness toward Great Britain was given concrete expression today in orders to the German ambassador at London to protest attacks on the party and on Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler by Winston Churchill. Not only Churchill, but other prominent statesmen in England have spoken recently of the German government in a vein construed in official quarters here as unfriendly. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and Sir Samuel Hoare, the British foreign secretary, are among those accused by the Nazis of making provocative remarks.

LONDON—Great Britain has decided to keep her mighty fleet in the Mediterranean until its relations with Fascist Italy improve radically, the United Press was informed today. It also was learned the French naval experts now in London for discussions preliminary to the forthcoming naval conference probably are examining the practical effectiveness of Premier Pierre Laval's recent pledge of French support to Great Britain in the event of an attack on the British fleet. In other words, the French and British naval experts were understood to be discussing the exact form French aid would take if Britain should ever claim to have been victimized under Paragraph 3, Article XVI of the League of Nations covenant. Among the questions to which the British sought specific French answers are: Would French battleships come to the support of British warships? Would France give British ships permission t
LONDON, England. (UP) — An Italian supply train was annihilated in the Danakil desert, an exchange telegraph dispatch received today stated. The report was not verified from any other source.

1935-11-17.text: LONDON—Economic sanctions against Italy, approved by 51 League of Nations members, took effect. Italian goods will be barred from their markets and they will not export certain raw materials to Italy. ROME—Troops guarded the British and other embassies as students paraded, denouncing sanctions, some shouting: “Down with England!” The Fascist grand council was to meet tonight to consider Italy’s resistance to sanctions and perhaps discuss peace plans which came from diplomatic negotiations. Gen. De Bono reported progress of the Italian troops in the North, with the Ethiopians retreating beyond the Takkaze river, as the Ethiopian southern army was said to be withdrawing to Harar. ADDIS ABABA—One authority said Haile Selassie would go to the northern front within 10 days, after which a major battle could be expected. Another report said he would leave tonight. NAPLES—Marshal Pietro Badoglio

London (/P)—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin undertook the task of rebuilding his cabinet today, secure in the knowledge he would be backed by a heavy government majority in the House of Commons. At his official residence, he had a number of weighty problems to solve. Among them was a means of countering the sensational defeat of his lieutenant, former Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald.

(Rv United Press): Italy’s most important military move since the black shirts and native Askaris crossed the Eritrean border was taken today when General Emilio de Bono, commander-in-chief of the East African armies, was relieved of his post and recalled to Italy. Successful generals are not relieved of their commands during the heat of a campaign. This old military adage may be altered to some extent by political and civil influences, but its truth remains strong. Although de Bono's recall to Rome was gilded over by his promotion to a marshal’s rank, even the cables from Italy admit that Marshal Pietro Badoglio was appointed in his place because he is considered the more able tactician and now is the time when increased Ethiopian resistance may be expected. Several explanations may be made for the switch in command. They are: 1. Dissatisfaction with the conduct of the war to date. 2. A

The date fixed by Great Britain is that upon which economic and financial sanctions as instituted by the League of Nations go into effect against Italy. BERLIN, Nov. 16.—(AP)—The German government protested to London today against British regulations on German goods exported to England after Nov. 18. An official communique said the requirement that these products must be accompanied by certificates of origin "is not in harmony with certain provisions of the German-British trade agreement." Britain’s action, to take effect the same day that economic and financial sanctions against Italy go into force, was considered an attempt to prevent exports from Italy entering Britain through a nation not joining in the League of Nations' sanctions.

New York, Nov. 16.—(?)—Clark Gable’s favorite partner on Broadway excursions, says the Daily News, is Elizabeth Allan, pert British film star who has announced her intention of divorcing her husband, W. J. O'Bryne of London. Gable and Miss Allan appeared together in the film version of “Men in White.” Since his return from South America, the Daily News says, he has showered her with flowers and has accompanied her frequently to cafes and night clubs. Gable left for Connecticut to visit friends after his impending separation from his wife was announced.

CAIRO, Egypt, Nov. 16/—Anti-British rioting broke out in Egypt again today as the death toll in previous disorders was raised to six. A government communique said police fired at the legs of students with whom they clashed at Zagazig, and that two students were sent to a hospital. Six policemen, it was stated, were injured as the students hurled stones during the melee. Police broke up a demonstration in Cairo by firing into the air. Two students who fought police Thursday died today.
London—(AP)—Butler Aspinall, 74, noted barrister practicing in maritime arbitrations, and chairman of the British and American joint arbitration board in 1929, died today.

Honolulu—(4)—Rescue was virtually in sight today for the crew of the schooner Seth Parker, which was apparently out of distress again this morning despite its S O S of Sunday evening. The British cruiser, Australia, carrying the Duke of Gloucester, third son of King George of Great Britain, was expected to reach the adventure ship almost momentarily. "Things are looking pretty favorable," said a message from the schooner’s master, Philips H. Lord, American radio star known as Seth Parker, at 4:45 a.m. (10:15 a.m., B.S.T.) today. Through Friday night and much of Saturday the exact condition of the schooner was in doubt. Sunday morning the Australia reached her, only to find everything in order and to be told assistance no longer was needed. The Australia radioed a report expressing "considerable satisfaction" at the situation, and we were only to be stopped at 7:00 p.m., Monday, E.S.T. by

SANTIAGO, Chile, | Feb. 11.—(#) —It took Ralph Codina, young English adventurer, one month to convince Bolivian authorities that he was not a spy, then they made him a lieutenant in the army and sent him into the Chaco Boreal to fight against Paraguay. “What is the worst of the fighting?” I asked him. “The thirst and the heat,” he said. He called the Chaco a solid waste of brush, shadeless trees, and giant cacti. Nature takes 60 per cent of the war's thousands of dead, preying on the men with heat, mosquitoes, malaria, cholera, dysentery, unbearable thirst, and venomous snakes and insects. There is danger from the enemy bullets, said Codina, but there is worse danger, when you hack your way through jungle, from the deadly coral snakes, no bigger than a pencil, whose bite is regarded as certain death. Not so deadly, but much more numerous are rattlesnakes and the reptile called the asp. A

LONDON, Feb. 12. (AP) — Indications that the labor party was planning a parliamentary vote of censure against the government for its administration of the dole caused widespread talk in political circles tonight of possible early reorganization of the cabinet.
