The air fleet, which has been under the command of Gen. Italo Balbo, the leader of the mass flight to Chicago two years ago, took off from Cyrenaica for Eritrea. Balbo himself is to come to Rome tomorrow to attend a grand council meeting which has been called for Thursday. The three classes have been called to the colors to assist in the transportation of troops to Eritrea and Italian Somaliland. The soldiers called in include the complete military class of 1911—numbering 225,000 men—and two divisions—numbering 8,000 men each. Another squadron of airplanes will leave t

ROME, Italy, Feb. 11 (UP) — Italy mobilized two divisions of troops on a war basis today as the result of an attack by Abyssinian tribesmen on Italian native troops in disputed territory between Abyssinia and Italian Somaliland. It was said authoritatively that an ultimatum would be sent to the Emperor Haile Selassie I., Abyssinia’s “king of kings,” unless Italy received complete satisfaction. Premier Benito Mussolini's action today came as a portentous climax to the announcement last night he sent a forceful protest against the alleged attack and called some 75,000 picked men of mechanized military units to the colors. No doubt was left that he is determined to end by war, if necessary, the raids by frontier tribesmen.

BERLIN, (7). If all efforts to come to an arms agreement fail Germany would have to prepare for war and call as many men to the colors as possible, reichswehr (regular army) circles said. The statement came as the reich followed with close attention Adolf Hitler’s deliberations over his reply to Anglo-French proposals, made after conversations in London last week, for an inclusive European security agreement. Hitler, faced with one of the most momentous decisions of his career, has retired to almost complete seclusion to work out his answer, an answer, the reichswehr sources said, that may involve Germany’s entire future course in military matters. Aside from the Anglo-French proposals, army men list the French movement for lengthened army service and the enigma of Russia as likely to influence that course. So long as these three factors remain unknown quantities, they said, it would be

VIENNA, Feb. 10 ()—Rioting broke out tonight in the factory suburb of Floridsdorf as radical anti-government demonstrations began in connection with the anniversary Tuesday of last year’s socialist civil war. Despite the bitter cold, hundreds of workers suddenly swarmed into the streets, shouting defiance to the fascist government. Strong detachments of police swept down upon them, however, and quickly dispersed them. Ten persons were jailed.

1935-02-27.text: ABOARD S.S. EUROPA. IN MID-ATLANTIC, Feb. 27—(UP)—The luxury liner Europa and two other rescue ships abandoned the search for the British freighter Blairgowrie today and continued on their courses. Their masters had concluded that the Blairgowrie went down, carrying twenty-six men to death. Only one faint hope remained—that the crew of the Blairgowrie had taken to lifeboats and were afloat somewhere on the Atlantic which was whipped by gales of hurricane force. The Cunard-White Star liner Olympic will pass through the stretch of waters where the storm-broken freighter presumably sank. The Olympic wirelessed that she was keeping a sharp lookout for boats or wreckage. But this hope was of the vaguest. Masters of the Europa, the United States liner American Banker, and the Dutch ship, Blommersdijk, were convinced the Blairgowrie was down with all hands before they ordered their vessels back

LONDON, Feb. 27. (AP)—Private James Baker of the Welsh Guards was found fatally shot today in the Bank of England—the world famous "Old Lady of Threadneedle Street." The usual secrecy attaching to even the most ordinary accidents at the old bank added to the mystery of Baker's death immediately after the discovery of his body. Bank of England officials would say only that Baker was dead when found at his post in the bullion yard and the War Department said it would announce nothing until after an inquest. It was perhaps the first violent death in the bank since 150 years ago, the bank staff stood off rioting attackers with muskets, melting down their pewter inkstands for bullets. There were several versions of Baker's shooting. It was certain only that he died in hospital from a rifle bullet wound soon after he was found lying at his post behind the bank's loopholed walls. The guard was

London, Feb. 27 (AP) — A 22-year-old Welsh soldier standing guard in one of the key sentry posts in the bullion yard of the Bank of England was mysteriously slain in the early morning darkness today. Tight-lipped police and military authorities declined to comment on whether the guardsman’s death was an accident or suicide, but it was understood one cartridge was missing from the victim's ammunition belt. Authorities said the dead man was James Baker. The silence which settles over London's financial district after nightfall was broken shortly before dawn by the crack of a rifle shot. Baker was found lying on the ground, a bullet wound in his head. He died soon afterward. The young soldier, unmarried, had been in the army only a year. The Bank of England has been guarded nightly by a detail composed of an officer, a sergeant, two corporals, 24 men and a bugler since the institution was r

London, Feb. 27.-(AP)-The fate of the British freighter Blairgowrie, disabled by a howling mid-Atlantic gale, was a mystery today as the liner Europa and two other vessels hunted her in vain through mountainous seas. The failure of any of the three ships which sped to the craft's aid to report they had reached the freighter’s side gave rise to apprehension that the Blairgowrie may have foundered, carrying its crew of 26 to their deaths. The Europa, the American Banker and the S. S. Blommersdyk, a Netherlands vessel, all rushed to the position given in the Blairgowrie's distress message but found no trace of the freighter. Reported Hold Filling. The crippled ship's last report gave her position as about 760 miles due west of Brest, and 1,000 miles east of Newfoundland. She said her steering apparatus had been carried away and her hold was filling. The 5,259 ton freighter was ten days out

London, Feb. 26.-- (4?)-—Austria’s chancellor and foreign minister left for home tonight confident Great Britain would press for Germany's adherence to the Rome pact designed to guarantee Austria's independence, While British sleuths peered and poked under their railway coaches for fear radicals had placed bombs, (Continued on Page 2)

HOUSTON, Feb. 26. (#)— Dr. Stockton Axson, professor of English at Rice Institute, died today. He suffered a stroke Monday. Few men knew President Woodrow Wilson so intimately or admired him so greatly as Dr. Axson, his brother-in-law, an educator, lecturer, philosopher and writer. Dr. Axson, head of the English department of Rice Institute here and professor of English literature, came to Houston in 1914. Before that time he had studied under and taught with Mr. Wilson. If Dr. Axson had not dropped by an aunt's home for a duty call on his baby sister when he was a lad of 15 he might have become a prosperous Georgia merchant instead of a well-known educator. The courteous teacher's eyes always twinkled a little more than usual when he recalled that incident. Up to the time his father asked him to go see his sister, young Stockton’s mind had feasted solely on dime novels and adventure sto

Portsmouth, Eng., Feb. 0—UVr— An admiralty court martial today acquitted Rear-Admiral Sidney Robert Bailey, the first officer of his rank to go on trial since the World War, of responsibility for the recent collision of the battle cruisers Hood and Renown. Nine naval officers, ranging in rank from admiral to captain, exonerated the commander of His Majesty’s battle cruiser squadron from the charge of having “hazarded” the two big warships by improper orders during naval maneuvers off the Spanish Coast Jan. 23. The trial was of intense interest in England, for H. M. S. Hood and Renown are two of the most famous ships which carry the Union Jack. Three hundred spectators, half naval men and half civilians, packed into the courtroom to watch the proceedings. The court sat around an oval table.

Peiping, Feb. 27—Shensi provincial authorities today ordered the 7th division of the Chinese Republican army to attempt the rescue of two British missionaries who many sources believe already have been killed by their bandit captors. No definite word came from either Shensi or Nanking concerning the fate of the Rev. S. C. Frencham, a native of Melbourne, Australia, and his wife, a former resident of Ledbury, England.

1935-03-02.text: Manchester, Eng. — () — Freed from jail and from the noose by an act of mercy rare in British annals. Mrs. May Brownhill, 62 years old, who was condemned to die for the "mercy murder" of her imbecile son, returned to her home in Burnbridge today. The frail mother put her son, Denis, "to sleep" forever with sedatives after nursing him for 30 years. Her release was by order of the home secretary, whose prerogative it is not only to grant reprieve from death sentences but also to decide if prison terms shall be served. Mrs. Brownhill spent most of her time in a hospital ward while in prison and soon must undergo a serious internal operation. The home office thus has given fullest effect to the recommendation of the jury for mercy when the death sentence was passed. She was sentenced to be hanged on Dec. 1. The judge ignored the recommendation for mercy, but it was endorsed by sympathetic pe

Cranleigh, Eng., March 2.--(4)— King Prajadhipok Friday night framed his formal abdication of Siam's throne while a phonograph in his study played American dance music. Reports from Bangkok, meanwhile, said Prince Ananda, 11-year-old nephew of the king, probably would succeed to the throne in the event of the monarch’s abdication. King Is Through At Knowle house, his great country mansion, M. R. Smaksman, the king's private secretary, assured the Associated Press that his ‘father,’ as the king is known in his native land, is absolutely through. The phonograph never stopped playing while the little monarch’s secretary made the announcement. There was little about the grounds to indicate a great change was taking place which will affect Siam’s 10,000,000 persons. The king’s chauffeurs were playing a spirited game of darts in the garage. A smiling bobby, one of those delegated to guard the

London,—(AP)—Much interest was evident today in coming sales of art treasures of J.P. Morgan in London as the financier proceeds with partial liquidation of his estate. England's tastes, concentrated wealth and nearness to continental centers provided a good market for such objects. Should Morgan come here to live he would have no househunting to do. For many years he has maintained both a London town house and a country home. He is a well-known figure at Watford, Hertfordshire, site of his country estate maintained in the fashion of any English landed baron. There are many farm agents, gamekeepers and servants. Fine blooded stock is but one of the features of the estate. Hogs have been entered a number of times in the neighboring shows which correspond to the American county fairs. The Morgan town house is located in a quiet square of exclusive Mayfair.

SIAN, Shensi Province, China. An inland mission worker was reported killed by Chinese soldiers today and missionary searchers gave up hope of finding his young wife, a London girl, who set out a week ago on foot from Nanklang. The death of Frenchan, a young Austrian, was reported by troops from Nanklang, the seat of his mission.

LONDON, Mar. 2. (WUP)—Gold again soared to a record high today, silver made a six-year high and the pound sterling dropped to a record low in terms of the devalued American dollar. Speculators reportedly withdrew large sums from London. Sharp and almost sensational declines in the pound both in dollar and franc terms continued to cause worry over the future of gold bloc currencies. There was no evidence of operation of either the American or British control funds. British leaders seemed unperturbed by the decline in the pound which would give the country an advantage in trade. In Paris, however, the situation was seen as dangerous. If the decline should gain such headway that the British control could not check it when it considered the time ripe to intervene, the gold bloc might be forced into devaluation, it was said. Rumors were circulated that the United States, hampered by Britain’s

CRANLEIGH, Eng., Mar. 2.—(?)— King Prajadhipok of Siam remained in the seclusion of his counting room at spacious Knowle house today, but he wasn’t counting out his money. He was counting himself out as ruler of Siam. The diminutive monarch was busily framing his formal abdication, presentation of which is believed to be inevitable, and it was believed he would have a formal draft ready for presentation to the government and the legation here early next week. There was no apparent reaction here to the latest advices from Bangkok, the king declined to comment on the report that he has polled only five votes in parliament.

CHANGTEH, China. (UP). Two British missionaries, R. A. Bosshardt and A. Hayman, captured by communists in Kweichow province last October, have been executed by their captors, according to Chinese reports reaching missionaries here. A Chinese asserted he saw the hacked bodies of the two missionaries lying in the street in the village of Fengchiangkan, ten miles west of Tayung in northwestern Hunan province. He reported the alleged double murder occurred Christmas day and said the incident had not been reported sooner because of the remoteness of the village and the difficulty of penetrating red army lines. The eyewitness declared Bosshardt and Hayman were slain along with other captives after the time limit specified in the ransom demands had expired. SIAN, Shensi, China, (?). VALETTA, Malta, March 1 (A)— The British submarine Oxley, fire in her control room, raced for Gibraltar tonight as the British Navy counted three damaged ships in maneuvers of its Mediterranean fleet. In addition to the Oxley, the destroyers Witch and Whished were damaged in collision at sea and returned to this port. The fire breaking out in the Oxley’s control room brought orders to two other vessels to stand by. Later the submarine was instructed to try to make Gibraltar.

Anthony Eden and called “betrayal” by one newspaper, drew fresh fire today from the British press. The most outspoken critic was the isolationist Daily Express, which said editorially: “British men and women, wake up! With stern reference to Captain Eden, “British minister for the League of Nations at £3,000 per annum,” the Express asserted: “To please Geneva and prop up the crumbling structure of the League of Nations, British citizens are to be transferred to alien rule. “Mr. Eden dares to make virtue of the fact that he would ask that the grazi

WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 2 —()—Dorothy Round, England’s top-flight player and defending champion, passed from the All-England tennis championships today in a quarter-final upset but America’s Helens—Mrs. Moody and Miss Jacobs—gained the semi-final with a strong likelihood they will renew their long-standing rivalry in the final. Joan Hartigan of Australia, displaying one of the most powerful and accurate forehands seen here in years, accounted for the highly-favored Miss Round in three sets, 4-6, 6-4, 6-3. The Australian player, seeded eighth, will meet Mrs. Moody in the penultimate round. Mrs. Moody was in her old-time form as she disposed of Mme. Rene Mathieu of France in straight sets, 6-3, 6-0, running her opponent ragged from corner to corner with deep baseline drives. Miss Jacobs romped through the first set against Mile. LONDON, July 1—(AP)—Government opponents raised a short storm in the House of Commons when it was disclosed today Great Britain had offered to hand over a strip of its territory to Ethiopia in an effort to avert a war between Italy and the African kingdom. Capt. Anthony Eden, diplomat who just returned from fruitless conversations with Benito Mussolini, explained the offer to cede the land. He said Il Duce had turned thumbs down upon the proposal. The idea was for Britain to give Ethiopia a seaport in British Somaliland and the latter was to make concessions which would satisfy Il Duce and make him call off his warlike preparations. Opposition leaders immediately demanded to know if the House would be consulted before British territory was given to foreign powers. Bluntly, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, replied: “The Commons must trust the executive department in these matters; if

Regina, Sask., (CP) — Three thousand relief camp strikers, who battled Royal Canadian Mounted Police in a riot during which a municipal officer was beaten to death, were subdued today by tear gas and gunfire. A second officer and a striker were injured critically. Five more police and a score of strikers were hurt before police quelled the crowd, arresting 27 persons in pursuing them through the streets.

Sidney, N.S., July 2. — Three young survivors of an Atlantic gale that cost the lives of their companions—a Boston yachtsman and his two sons who sought to save him—took refuge in port today, still suffering from their experiences. Their 54-foot ketch, Hamarah, her rigging and sails damaged, rode safely off the Royal Cape Breton Yacht Club but her 21-year-old navigator, Charles Tillinghast of Providence, R. I., said it might be several days before they could put to sea again. Tillinghast and his two companions, Roger Weed, 25, and Sheldon Ware, 19, both of Boston, brought their crippled craft into Sydney harbor yesterday and reported that Robert Ames, 55, Boston realty broker and sportsman, had been washed overboard by a mountainous wave. His sons, Richard, 23, and Harry, 20, were lost in a vain attempt to rescue him.

SIDNEY, N. Y., 8.—Seamen inspecting the tragedy yacht Hamrah today marveled that her three man crew had been able to bring her to port after losing the master and his two sons in a fierce storm in the North Atlantic. The three survivors told a dramatic story of filial heroism. The two sons gave up their lives in vain efforts to save their father, Robert Russell Ames, socially prominent Boston real estate man and yachtsman. The sons, who share with their father a watery Atlantic Brave, were Richard, a recent Harvard graduate, and Henry, a Harvard sophomore. Ames, with an amateur crew composed of his sons, Forster Tillinghast, Providence, R. I., Robert Weed, of Milton, Mass., and Sheldon Ware, of Boston, was racing his yacht to Norway. The Hamrah, a ketch, and the yachts Varmarie, Mistress, Stoertebeker, Stormy Weather, Sandejord and Vagabond, sailed from Newport June 8 for Bergen, Norway.

MOSCOW, July 2. (©P)—Russia, angered by repeated dangerous incidents on the Siberian-Manchukuoan frontier, today awaited a reply from Japan to a strongly worded note of protest. In the note, delivered to the Japanese foreign office yesterday by Ambassador Konstantin Yurenev, the government complained of eight recent violations of Soviet Union territory by Japanese-Manchukuoan military forces. There was a hint in the note, apparently, that if border violations continued Russian military commanders might be given orders to revise their present policy of leaving diplomats to settle them. The note asked Japan to affirm its intention to maintain peaceful relations on the border and to take prompt, energetic measures to prevent such provocative action as that complained of. Diplomatic circles discussed the possibility that the government suspected in them efforts to precipitate a real crisis.

REGINA, Sask., July 1—Two persons were killed and more than a score injured tonight when a squad of steel helmeted Royal Canadian mounted police and city police broke up a mass meeting of 3,000 striking relief camp workers. The police, traveling on horses and in trucks, swept down on the meeting, scattering the strikers into streets and alleys. Tear gas bombs were hurled into the crowd when some of the men became unruly. Constable Charles Miller of the city police was killed. The other dead man was Dan McGee, identified as a striker.

1935-12-01.text: (By the Associated Press) Franco-British collaboration has eased international tension in the Mediterranean, informed sources in London said today. Talk of a crisis in the relations of Great Britain and Italy over the question of an oil embargo on the Fascist domain by the League of Nations simmered down on the heels of France's frank warning to Italy against any unprovoked attack on Britain's Mediterranean fleet. Has Il Duce Changed Tune? One commentator referred to “Mussolini’s change of tune,” but on the war front new evidence cropped up to support the belief that the Italian premier intended pushing his campaign of occupation in Ethiopia to a swift conclusion. Only yesterday well-informed Italian sources said Il Duce planned to attack the British fleet in Mediterranean waters if Downing Street, mainspring of the League sanctions movement, pressed for the imposition of an oil embargo

Talk of peace in East Africa, the purpose for which sanctions were imposed, languished as Britain's attention turned to an oil embargo to freeze that nation into submission to the will of her sister states in the League of Nations. A two-fold program was before the British leader in the sanctions drive: 1—Should an embargo on oil shipments to Italy be imposed at Geneva? Commentators little doubted the cabinet would approve the move and transmit its decision to the league. 2—If the embargo goes into effect and Italy makes good her threat of reprisals, what course shall Britain pursue? Paris, Nov. 20.—(UP)—Great Britain has moved to seek a basis of negotiation with Italy and thus to avoid the gravest potential crisis since the world war, it was learned today. Strengthened by a big majority in the recent parliamentary election, the British government has suggested unofficially a meeting between Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, and Premier Pierre Laval to discuss the possibility of a peaceable settlement before an oil embargo is applied against Italy. France has replied, also unofficially, that it will agree to the meeting if Britain makes its suggestion an official one. Hoare is to be in Paris at the end of next week en route to winter sports in Switzerland. A foreign office spokesman told the United Press that Laval was most eager to meet Hoare then, believing a conversation would be very useful. Laval saw Vittorio Cerruti, Italian ambassador today, and it was assu

HANNIBAL, Mo., Nov. 30—Today is the 100th anniversary of the birth of Samuel Clemens — Mark Twain. But a celebration of the Missouri humorist’s centenary has been in progress nearly a year. At one time or another the entire world has joined in. John Masefield, Britain's poet laureate, only yesterday proposed the erection of a monument on the Thames to honor the American writer. The celebration will end tonight at Hannibal, Twain's boyhood home. He was born Nov. 30, 1835, at Florida, Mo., 30 mi. inland from this Mississippi river city, but moved here with his parents when a child.

PARIS, Nov. 30 (UP).—Great Britain and France today moved for a final joint effort to reach a settlement with Italy before an oil embargo is imposed, with its attendant threat of war in Europe. As in previous efforts of the same nature, only faint hope was held that it would succeed, because of the difficulty of reconciling Premier. (Continued on Page 12, Column 8)

(By The Associated Press) ROME—Cabinet adopts further defense measures, calls another session Tuesday. LONDON—Authoritative sources say: tension has lessened, following French warning to Italy against attacking British fleet. ADWA—Fascists report Ethiopian counter-attacks have been beaten off; strong enemy forces said to be moving toward Italian lines. ADDIS ABABA—Ethiopia announces 183 Italians were killed when column was surprised in east. DESSYE—Emperor Haile Selassie arrives to establish general military headquarters.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 30—(P)—With the zero registration hour all but on, the nation’s holding companies today maintained their virtually unbroken front against the New Deal’s utilities act. The New England Power Association and the New England Public Service Company, two major units, registered today with the securities commission to become the only big systems agreeing to obey the act. Utility spokesmen here contended, however, that this indicated no real break in the line. The New England Power Association stated it was filing “under duress,” claiming the act to be unconstitutional and reserving full rights to attack its constitutionality at any time in the future. This accords with the commission’s frequently reiterated suggestion. Most companies, however, have refused to accept it. The registration deadline is midnight tomorrow, after which the commission contends many of the activities o

a en a Ce ee Se ee ee | League Sanctions, Rome, Dec. 2.—Italian business leaders said today that trade was slackening and that problems of labor and business credit were developing as the result of League of Nations sanctions. They said that the imports and exports, which normally total about 1,000,000,000 lire (about $80,000,000) monthly, were being cut to a point where estimates as to the probable damages were impossible. They suggested that if this trade were only halved, the reduction would be equivalent to the wages paid monthly to nearly 1,000,000 men. Small firms manufacturing for export or dependent upon foreign material, said these leaders, may soon be confronted with a critical situation unless they can use their facilities for other types of work.

1935-11-27.text: LONDON: British officials intimate if Italy invades Lake Tana region it will be regarded as violation of Italian assurances and treaty pledges. Government assures United States oil embargo will come up at Geneva soon. BERLIN: Hitler, in interview, says Germany will never abandon claims to lost colonies, and as a major power is entitled to army of first rank. GENEVA: League reveals sanctions net around Italy is rapidly tightening. ADDIS ABABA: Capital hears 1,000 white Italian troops are being evacuated from captured Makale, indicating increased use of natives as better able to stand diet and climate. ROME: Government regulates flights of civil aircraft in Italy and near Egyptian border of Libya.

Paris. —-(AP)-- The newspaper L'Oeuvre said today it had learned in reliable sources that Great Britain has offered to serve as intermediary in peace talks between Italy and Ethiopia. The paper stated it understood Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary, had sent a memorandum to Premier Mussolini, informing him Britain was ready to take this role in direct discussions to settle the conflict.

London, Nov. 27 (p)—The British cabinet assembled today for its first meeting since the general election maintained the national government in power, and informed sources foresaw steps toward further defense measures. The principal tasks confronting the ministers were to review the foreign situation and to draw up a legislative program to be presented in King George's speech at the formal opening of parliament December 3. A second cabinet meeting was contemplated for Friday at which the government attitude toward extension of League of Nations war penalties against Italy would be discussed. Political sources expressed belief today's session would result in a declaration of the government's desire to reach an effective agreement with other naval powers at the forthcoming London conference concerning the future sizes of their fleets. ROME—Movement of civil aircraft over strategic points in Italy and on the Libyan-Egyptian frontier was restricted closely today by an air ministry decree. The decree follows by 24 hours an announcement at London that Great Britain still favors an embargo on oil which would be calculated to cripple the country’s industries and paralyze its army in East Africa. The ministry’s decree—Premier Benito Mussolini is his own air minister—prescribes that no civil airplane shall fly: 1, In the Rome area except in the immediate vicinity of the civil airport, 2. Outside of specially appointed routes about Venice, at the top of the Adriatic sea; through the Strait of Messina which separates Italy and Sicily, or on the Sicilian coast further south between Augusta and Syracuse naval base. 3. Chicago, Nov. 27. (AP)—Depression was explained today as a flurry in economics caused when the Bank of England called in all of the gold to settle the mythical Sir Francis Drake estate when M. A. Aasgaard, printer of Boone, testified in the mail fraud trial of 41 persons charged with working in the Drake swindle. He said he was told that in 1931 by J. Vern Carlson of Boone, one of the defendants.

By United Press ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 26.—The Italians have evacuated the southern towns of Gorrahei and Gellogubi, it was announced officially today, and the Ethiopians are preparing to re-occupy them. The Italians have made much of the occupation by their advance patrols of the two towns, which are on a line extending eastward from the Fafan River. The announcement was hailed here as evidence that Ethiopian resistance, coupled with the heavy rains, have halted the Italian advance toward Harar, their main objective near the Addis Ababa railway.

(Copyright by The Associated Press) Shanghai, Nov. 27—(4)—Japanese troops moved in North China by the trainloads today while northern Chinese leaders waivered on the issue of secession from the centralization government, Troop trains bearing 3,000 Japanese soldiers and war equipment arrived at Tientsin. At Peiping, where the Japanese garrison has more than doubled in the last 24 hours, the Fengtai railway junction a few miles east of Peiping had been seized. Officials asserted the Fengtai occupation became necessary because of rumors that rolling stock on the Peiping-Mukden railway was being moved south, threatening to isolate the Japanese forces at Peiping.

NANKING, China, Nov. 27. (Wednesday) (2)—A high government official told The Associated Press today the Chinese government had determined to meet with force any move to impose the autonomy program on the territory south of the borders of Hopei and Chahar provinces. (Yin Ju-Keng, administrative commissioner of the North China demilitarized zone, already has proclaimed an autonomous state in 25 counties in East Hopei and Chahar provinces.) The nation’s militarists, meeting in Nanking, have adopted a plan to defend Shantung and Hunan provinces against encroachment from the southern Hopei border, the government informant stated. This border has been adopted as the first line of defense against any autonomy movement from the north—political or military—he asserted. 1935-11-20.text: By the Associated Press The Japanese foreign office today attributed to the British and American currency policies in China the necessity for the internal political campaign to sunder north China from the government of Nanking. The United States’ silver purchase policy has intensified China’s economic troubles, the Tokyo government department explained. This and Great Britain's support of Nanking currency reform were looked upon as spontaneous stimuli to the movement for autonomy in north China. This authority also insisted north China’s impending declaration of self-rule would not affect China's territorial status and hence the nine-power treaty, guaranteeing China's sovereignty and territorial integrity, cannot be invoked. Administration officials in Washington betrayed a deep concern over the events in north China, however. American business firms have large holdings in the affected t

WASHINGTON, Nov. 20.-- (Pp The Roosevelt administration's surprise move in naming William Phillips, undersecretary of state, as a delegate to the London Naval conference opening Dec. 8 was interpreted today as a sign the parley is considered of major importance. Phillips, a career man with long experience in international affairs, will be a member of a delegation headed by Norman H. Davis, "roving ambassador." Admiral William H. Standley, the navy's highest ranking officer, was selected as another member. The first indication of the policy to be upheld by the American delegates was given last night by President Roosevelt. It is a policy of opposition to any increases of naval strength beyond present limits. The United States, Mr. Roosevelt said, will oppose the building of navies that cost nations more than they cost today. Whether this meant that the United States would oppose Japan’s l

WASHINGTON—(® —Enunciating a definite policy of American opposition to any increases of naval strength beyond existing limits, President Roosevelt Tuesday named a three-man delegation to the forthcoming London Naval conference. Headed by Norman H. Davis, America’s roving ambassador, others on the delegation will be William Phillips, undersecretary of state, and Admiral William H. Crandall, chief of naval operations.

CAIRO, Egypt. (UP) — A general strike was proclaimed today for tomorrow, a climax to recent disorders in protest against British influence in the government. Students announced that they would enforce the strike themselves. They planned to march to the Bazaars and force dissenters to close. Thirty newspapers, comprising the entire Arabic language press, announced that they would not publish tomorrow, in protest against press restrictions, the outgrowth of student riots. Foreigners in Cairo were apprehensive, in view of the students’ animosity over killings in the recent disorders. Police are taking extraordinary precautions against a dangerous outbreak. In their editions today, the newspapers indirectly and discreetly — in view of the repressive ordinances — call on natives to cooperate against alleged British dominance of the government.

LONDON, Nov. 20 (UP) — Coal miners of the United Kingdom have voted more than 14 to 1 in favor of a nationwide strike to enforce their demand for a wage increase of 50 cents a day and a national wage agreement, it was announced today. The strike vote, threatening the most serious industrial dispute in Britain since the general strike of 1926, was announced by the executive committee of the mine workers federation, which also communicated the result to Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and asked him to meet with it at the earliest possible moment. The committee authorized its officials to continue negotiations with mine owners for settlement, but it also decided to convene the miners federation for the purpose of effectuating the ballot. In view of the overwhelming majority in favor of a strike, it would appear that the ballot could be effectuated only by calling the strike.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 19—(# Supposedly imminent seizure by Japan of control over North China, a matter of growing administration concern, today precipitated a joint Anglo-American canvass of the crisis. For half an hour, Sir Ronald Lindsay, the tall British ambassador in Washington, discussed the Sino-Japanese developments with the U.S. Secretary of State, William Phillips. Any possibility of joint action by the two governments was discussed; however, it was kept a carefully guarded secret. Both governments have an interest in the five North China provinces which Japan seeks control. More than 1,000 American citizens are reported to be living in this section, excluding military forces. Extensive American business interests and investments are seated there. The British population and investment is even heavier. Concerning his conference with Ambassador Lindsay, Phillips said at his press confe

(Copyright by The Associated Press) Tokyo, Nov. 20.—VP—The campaign for political independence of North China from the Nanking government was attributed in part by a Japanese foreign office source today to American and British currency policies. A summary of Japan's position, issued by this source, said the United States silver purchase policy, intensifying China’s economic troubles and Britain's support of Nanking currency reform were among the factors “stimulating the spontaneous popular movement for autonomy of North China.” No Treaty Violation The question of application of the nine-power treaty, guaranteeing China's sovereignty and territorial integrity, this summary set forth, could not arise in connection with North China’s impending declaration of self-rule because the new regime would not affect China's territory status. The Japanese government denies responsibility for separati

London.—(U.P)—Earl Jellicoe, Britain’s naval leader in the World War, who bottled up the German fleet in the Kiel canal, squashed the U-boat offensive, and led the fleet at the Battle of Jutland, died today. Lord Jellicoe was 75. He had long been in poor health and never recovered fully from bronchitis contracted in 1931 after staying too long in a Turkish bath. The immediate cause of his death was understood to have been a chill caught while attending outdoor exercises on Armistice Day.

1935-07-21.text: ROME, July 22.—(4)—The Italian press, apparently by general order, printed violent attacks against Japan Monday, using phraseology not unlike that employed against England a few weeks ago and against Germany last year. The basis for the attack was an alleged dissimilarity between statements made to the Italian foreign office by Ambassador Sugimura of Japan concerning Ethiopia and by a Japanese foreign office spokesman. The Japanese embassy cabled long extracts from these press comments to Tokyo and well-informed sources said they were convinced that the bitter tone of the editorials was certain to elicit a diplomatic protest from the Japanese. Il Tevere said: “One has the sensation of finally learning why so many races have been created with only one image and likeness of the Creator and why, among other variously-colored ones, one is of the color of betrayal. “The Japanese believe the s

LAHORE, India, July 20 (P).—A day and night of rioting in Lahore left nine Moslems and one British trooper dead tonight, with further serious trouble expected before dawn. Most of the deaths occurred when British troops, of the Royal Scots Guards, fired into 2000 Moslems charging toward the Shahidguna mosque in an effort to halt its demolition by Sikhs. An undetermined number of persons were injured. The trooper was killed when he was knocked from his horse in the mad melee raging around the mosque, which the Moslems claim. Balked in their efforts to reach the heavily-guarded building, the natives adopted Mahatma Gandhi's "passive resistance" tactics, squatting in the streets in protest.

By The Associated Press London, July 20.—Whether Ex-King George of Greece is or is not ‘ready to fly back to Athens—that was the question here tonight, An airplane pilot said he was, ‘The king’s aide said he was not. ‘The monarch could not be found for comment. The pilot, Capt. William Ledlie, asserted the former king, whose (Continued on Page 2)

Berlin, July 22.—(#)—Fresh bans against Catholic youth organizations were issued in the Palatinate today with indications that similar restrictions may soon be expected throughout Germany. The full machinery of the Nazi press was invoked in a general fight against political Catholicism and Jewry with both Catholic organizations and Jews included in the term "reactionary." Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s newspaper ranks political Catholicism as "Public Enemy No. 1" while Nazi antagonism against the Jews was displayed at increased heat. From the Palatinate came word that Catholic youth organizations can no longer wear their distinctive garb in public and may not display flags and emblems. They also were forbidden all athletic activities as organizations. It appeared but a question of time when all Nazi district leaders throughout the Reich will have issued the same bans on Catholic youth organizati

(Copyright, 1938, by The Associated Press) ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopia, July 20—Emperor Haile Selassie flung another ringing challenge at Italy Saturday as Italy's diplomatic representative here vigorously protested the “bitter tone of attacks on Italy” in the emperor's fighting speech before Parliament Thursday. Count Vinel, the Italian minister, called at the foreign office to protest verbally against the address without waiting for written instructions from Rome. The King of Kings said in an interview: “Ever since her crushing defeat by our army about 49 years ago Italy has nourished the desire to attack us. This desire has assumed a more acute and more menacing form, which Italy has proclaimed to all the world.”

By MELVIN K. WHITELEATHER Copyright 1935 by The Associated Press BERLIN, July 20.—(P)—A new Nazi “purge” of “reactionary” opposition—thus far bloodless—swept through the Reich with increasing impetus today, its chief victims or threatened victims Jews, clergymen and war veterans. Nazi publications and official spokesmen lumped Hebrews, Catholic and Protestant men of the cloth, and members of the steel helmet veterans organization with hated communists and other “reactionary” or “subversive” elements in the determined fight to make national socialism the faith and religion of unified Germany. Day’s Developments The day’s developments included: 1. Julius Streicher, leading Jew-baiter and publisher of the bitterly anti-Semitic newspaper “Stuermer,” announced he himself would head the drive to oust all Jews from Berlin or segregate them in ghettoes. 2. A decree issued by the ministry of the

LINDSAY, Ont., July 20 (?— Five children of Mr. and Mrs. Guy Wallace were thrown into the Scugog River tonight and three were drowned before rescuers could reach the scene. Police placed the mother of the children under arrest. They announced she was being held temporarily under a vagrancy charge. The drowned children were Catherine, 9, Agnes, 7, and William, 4. Gavin, 11, and Mary, 2, were saved. Three of the children were dragged from the water by Clarence McGee, 14, who was swimming 150 yards from where the screaming children were thrashing about in the water, but two, he said, were dead when he reached safety. Gavin, according to McGee, crawled up on the river bank and ran to his home nearby. Young McGee dived and pulled out Mary, Catherine, and William, but only Mary was alive when he brought them to the bank. The pretty, 36-year-old mother ran from the river bank and summoned a pri

Barcelona, Spain—Ten gunmen entered a nudist camp today with revolvers and forced them to open the lockers where their clothes were kept. In the clothes they found watches, money, and such items as must be kept in pockets. The total loot was about 50,000 pesetas—$7,000. Then they burned the clothes to prevent the nudists from pursuing them.

1935-05-24.text: St. Anne’s-On-The-Sea, Eng. May 24—William Lawson Little Jr., of San Francisco tonight stood on the threshold of doing what no other American ever has done and which only two Britons have accomplished in 50 years—winning the British Amateur golf championship two consecutive years. The husky 25-year-old Pacific coast shotmaker, who won the title in his first bid for it a year ago at Prestwick and also holds the American Amateur championship, qualified today for the 13-hole finals tomorrow when he will be matched against Dr. William Tweddell, himself a winner of the crown in 1927. In the quarter-finals this morning the defending champion made short shrift of George L. Q. Henriase, a 32-year-old stock broker who had the sensation of the early rounds, winning by the lopsided score of 6 to 4. This afternoon Little put out Robert Sweeney Jr., formerly of N. Y., and a resident of London for man

LONDON, May 74—()—The youth of Great Britain was responding with enthusiasm today to the government's appeal for recruits for the suddenly expanded Royal Air Force. Recruiting stations here and in other parts of the British Isles from Plymouth to Glasgow and Belfast had a rush of applicants for the 22,500 posts created under the new aerial program designed to give Great Britain parity in the air with every other European power. Of the additional personnel some 2,500 will be pilots and the others skilled and unskilled workmen.

LONDON, (Copyright by AP). The Royal Air Force launched its greatest recruiting campaign in history to back up Britain's warning to Adolf Hitler that she will not be outstripped in the air. A large recruiting station was established in downtown London, with ten others planned for other parts of England, Scotland, Ulster and Wales, to enlist the 2,500 pilots and 20,000 skilled and unskilled men the Air Ministry wants. Simultaneously Lord Londonderry, Secretary for Air, appealed to the nation’s youth to answer the call to arms. Mincing no words in letting Reichsfuehrer Hitler know Britain would spare no effort and brook no delay in speedily executing plans to treble her first line home defense air forces, Lord Londonderry said: “We welcome Herr Hitler's offer of limitation (made in his speech to the German Reichstag Tuesday night), but at the same time we are carrying out our declared poli

GENEVA. (Friday), (®). The outlook for settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute changed from despair to one of bright hope when Italian quarters reported a compromise had been reached. While British circles failed to confirm a compromise and said the situation was still confused, there were indications the outlines of such a compromise have been approved in principle at least. The French delegation said the changed situation looked promising and that the negotiations were likely to result satisfactorily.

Conference Still Possible Berlin, May 24—A conference to negotiate an aviation pact and an interview between Reichsfuehrer Hitler and Pierre Laval, French foreign minister, appeared to be possibilities today as Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador, asked the German foreign office to clarify several points in Hitler's recent speech to the Reichstag. Germany is pushing hard on both possibilities. Ambassador Francois-Poncet of France has returned to Paris for three weeks’ vacation in which it is understood he is to help Laval persuade the French government to permit the foreign minister to meet the German leader to talk things over. Sir Eric's questions were made on instructions from London and were understood chiefly to concern the air pact to which Hitler referred in his speech somewhat sarcastically because the powers had not acted on what he described as his long-standing readiness to li

Rome, May 24 —(AP)— Premier Benito Mussolini told massed thousands of soldiers and civilians today: “Italy now is ready for any trial,” His declaration came in the course of observance of the twentieth anniversary of Italy's entrance into the World War, a ceremony which included the presenting of battle flags to regiments which replace units assigned to East Africa. His listeners packed Venezia Square, in front of his office. They heard him say: “The words of an unknown Italian soldier scrawled on the wall of a house demolished by a shell, ‘It is better to live one day as a lion than 100 days as a lamb,’ are not merely an order—they are gospel for us. “We swear to respect this sacred injunction everywhere and in spite of anyone.” He added: “Let no one in Italy or abroad delude themselves. Italy will consider carefully before arriving at a decision, but when the decision is reached, then

Stockholm, Sweden, May 24—Pretty Princess Ingrid of Sweden was married today to Crown Prince Frederik of Denmark. Archbishop Erling Eidem, of the Lutheran church, performed the ceremony in the castle church at 12:30 a.m. (5:30 a.m. est). There was national rejoicing in Sweden and Denmark, for aside from the fact that the marriage links more closely the two royal houses, Ingrid and Frederik have been sweethearts, apparently for years. She is the third girl of the Swedish royal family, the romantic house of Bernadotte founded by Napoleon's brilliant marshal, to marry a crown prince. A cousin, Astrid, is queen of Belgium. Another cousin, Princess Martha, is wife of Crown Prince Olav of Norway. More than three score members of the European royal houses, including the kings and queens of Denmark and Belgium, attended the ceremony and remained to join in the gay activities with which the event

ROME, May 24 (UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini proclaimed to the world today that Fascist Italy will proceed with the course it has determined on and will brook no interference from other nations. At a moment when the powers are putting pressure on Italy at Geneva to modify her demands on Abyssinia, Mussolini addressed a crowd in front of his Venice palace and re-affirmed his stand on the problems facing Europe. “Let it be known here and abroad,” he said, “that once Fascist Italy has taken a position we march direct. We do not turn back. “Once an obscure infantryman, one of a million who fought, suffered and won, said: “It is better to live one day as a lion than a 100 years as a sheep.’ This is our thought.” Mussolini's speech was a part of an elaborate celebration of the 20th anniversary of Italy’s entrance into the world war. Rejects Compromise GENEVA, May 24 (UP) — Premier Benito Mussoli

1935-02-25.text: Romford, England. Feb. 25 (#)— Elizabeth and Jane Du Bois, who plunged from an airplane to death last week, visualized their suicides as a “pretty straight” corollary to the dead men they loved. A coroner's jury today returned a joint verdict of “Suicide while of unsound minds” after it had heard the contents of two letters which the girls had intended only for their father, Coert Du Bois, United States consul general in Naples, and their mother. The father, tight-lipped and white-knuckled, attended the inquest. The mother stayed alone at a hotel, still unaware of the complete details of her daughters’ plunge from a commercial transport ship. The letters were read publicly over the protests of Franklin McGowen, United States consul. The coroner said he only did his duty in reading the letters as with- (Continued on page two)

London, Feb. 25 (AP).—Two legs severed from a man’s body were discovered today stuffed under the seat of a train arriving in Waterloo station. Railway police, mystified by the find and unable to determine at first even the sex of the human being from which the legs had been chopped, called in Scotland Yard detectives. The criminal investigation division operators announced within a few minutes that the legs undoubtedly had belonged to a man.

London, Feb. 25.—()—Buffeted by New York creditors and English police regulations, James J. Walker, former New York mayor, told a chancery court today that he was so broke his present wife, Miss Betty Compton, had to pay their joint traveling expenses out of her savings as an actress. The dapper Jimmy was still dapper but he was worried when he was called to answer to two judgments against him for bills allegedly run up by his first wife in New York. Then he emerged to find that his status as a legal resident of Great Britain was in jeopardy because of his failure to comply with regulations and register with the police in London. Such failure subjects one to the possibility of fine, imprisonment or deportation—on occasion, all three. Informed of this last straw in the steadily mounting burden of grief, Jimmy exclaimed: 'I am willing to do anything except give up my citizenship.'

Hy Marry Flory United Press Staff Correspondent ROMFORD, England, Feb. 25 "Pp — Farewell letters written by two heartbroken American girls revealed today the story of their decision to follow their British aviator sweethearts in death by plunging, hand in hand, from an airliner soaring over the English countryside. The letters were read at the inquest on the broken bodies of Elizabeth Du Bois, 26, and 23 years old, only daughters of Coert Du Bois, American Consul. After their evidence over the formalities, others told of their arrival at Stapleford airdrome and of their leap from the airliners, in which they had reserved all seats from London to Paris at cost of $135. Read Letters But it was left for the letters to tell the story. They were read at the end of the inquest. There were two letters, one to Du Bois, the other to the girls' mother, who was unable to attend the inquest. Each gi

LONDON, Feb. 25.—Earthquakes in Greece today killed eight persons and injured five. The casualties took place in the Candia and Crete districts. Considerable property was damaged according to advices received in London. Other earthquakes are reported to have occurred today at Cairo, Egypt, and on the Island of Malta, British naval base, in the Mediterranean Sea.

DORCHESTER, England, Feb 25 Farmer George Chell’s cattle are getting extra-fine fodder these days—and why not? While grazing the other day, the cattle kicked up a half dozen gold coins which started the farmer digging in his pasture. He unearthed more than a hundred coins dating back 200 years. The treasure, worth about $5,000, is believed to have been buried during the reign of the Stuarts.

(By the Associated Press) Five ships sent out distress calls yesterday (Sunday) as gales continued to lash the North Atlantic and the Bay of Biscay and swept into the Mediterranean. A Greek steamer believed to be the Delphoi, drifting helplessly with damaged engines, and the British freighter Hillcroft, with a broken rudder, were reported in trouble in almost the same position, off Cape Finisterre, Spain, in the Bay of Biscay where four ships sent out SOS calls last week. The United States Shipping Board freighter Oakmon, out of Mobile, Ala., was reported in distress though in no immediate danger from a lost rudder 700 miles northwest of the Azores, with the S.S. end of Newport News standing by. An SOS from the Australian steamer Speitro in the Mediterranean was picked up by Casablanca radio station. The disabled British vessel, Ottinge, messaged that assistance was “urgent” when the tow

i aN. Feb. 24 PF Purmer Mayor James J. Walker of New York, once a noted spender, dresser and bon vivant, admitted in chancery court today that he is broke and cannot pay his bills. Walker testified that his income is $105 a week from newspaper writing, 40 percent coming from a collaborator on 4 projected books; that he is living with his wife and her mother-in-law in the latter's house, and that his wife, the former Betty Compton, paid for their recent trip to Spain.

1935-09-16.text: (Copyright, 1950, By the ‘4°)) PORTLAND, England, Sept. 16. —The bulk of Great Britain's home fleet has disappeared from here on the eve of its scheduled maneuvers off Scotland. Although no officials would discuss the present location, the street talk is that these ships are steaming for the Mediterranean.

GENEVA, (UP) — Eamonn De Valera, president of the Irish Free State executive committee, made an impassioned appeal to the League of Nations assembly today to call an immediate peace conference to prevent an Italian-Ethiopian war. For once in complete agreement with Great Britain, De Valera pledged the Irish government to join fully in imposing the league covenant on any aggressor. Soon after the speech, the assembly closed its general discussion of the crisis. Even as De Valera spoke, events in the crisis were speeding to a climax of historic importance. By this weekend Benito Mussolini is expected to have committed himself irretrievably — by acts, not words — to a war policy. League of Nations leaders, anticipating months of crisis, intend to keep the league council in permanent session until Christmas, recessing occasionally for brief periods. Italy’s rejection, regarded as ‘absolutely

LONDON, Sept. 16 (P) Lloyd's underwriters today cancelled the war risk clause at present included in general policies. The move, apparently made because of the growing Italian-Ethiopian war threat, applies to all contracts. After ten days' notice, merchants contracting with Lloyd's must take out separate war risk contracts if they desire such protection, a notice issued by the underwriters said. These policies are to be made at special rates. At present, the general policies automatically include war risk insurance.
Rome, Sept. 16.—Premier Mussolini tonight reorganized Italy's fleet, dividing it into east and west superior commands, in answer to the British fleet concentration in the Mediterranean Sea.

LONDON, Sept. 16.—(UP)—Lloyd's underwriters today cancelled the war risk clause at present included in general policies. The move, apparently made because of the growing Italian-Ethiopian war risk, applies to all contracts. After 10 days notice merchants contracting with Lloyd's must take out separate war risk contracts, if they desire such protection, a notice issued by the underwriters said. These policies are to be made at special rates. At present the general policies automatically include war risk insurance. General application of the new plan was made, according to good authority, in order that the Italian-Ethiopian situation be not too much emphasized. However, the rates for war risk on Mediterranean shipments are expected to be substantially higher than elsewhere.

Rome, Sept. 16.—(AP)—Just how Great Britain may react if Germany tries to win back the Memel territory from Lithuania was viewed with interest by official Italy today. A government spokesman explained that while Italy, in general, was indifferent to yesterday's speech by Reichsführer Hitler, in which he mentioned an increasing German anxiety concerning Memel, she was interested in observing what Great Britain's reaction may be. The spokesman said it now would be significant to observe whether Great Britain would pursue her same policy of fidelity to League of Nations principles in the face of Hitler’s pronouncement of interest in Memel. An official source said that if Great Britain is not to lay herself open to the accusation of inconsistency, she must oppose German designs on League-guaranteed territory with the same firmness that she has displayed toward Italy's East African policy. Latins. Sent. 15—The League of Nations council committee on the Italo-Ethiopian dispute will complete a peace plan Monday or Tuesday, a well-informed source said tonight. Other sources described Dr. Edouard Benes, president of the League Assembly, and British representatives as voicing pessimistic predictions as to the outcome. The preamble, it was understood, will refer to the Italo-Ethiopian memoranda already submitted to the league while the detailed plan itself will be an amplification of the Paris proposals of August 16. At a meeting in Paris of diplomats representing Britain, France, and Italy, the two former nations outlined a plan by which Il Duce could obtain wide economic concessions in Ethiopia in exchange for a promise not to go to war. Italy rejected these proposals, asserting concessions could mean nothing unless she was given the right to occupy Ethiopia with military forc

Geneva, Sept. 16.—(4A’)—Reliable sources disclosed tonight that a preliminary plan for an economic boycott against Italy in case that nation should launch an unprovoked war is being worked out among certain members of the League of Nations. This disclosure came after a day in the league assembly in which Poland had snubbed Soviet Russia, her delegates walking out on a speech by Maxim Litvinoff, Russian foreign commissar—and in which Panama, the Irish Free State and Haiti had warned the league it must prevent the conquest of a smaller nation by a larger. The sources in question said the British delegation to the league had suggested the idea of a general economic blockade against Italy in case she attacks Ethiopia and that the plan for such a blockade had already been previously mapped out. The suggestion regarded as a preliminary and precautionary project, was understood to be a sequel t

1935-11-14.text: LONDON, Nov. 14—(AP)—Thirty-one million voters told the British government Thursday with ballots what they think of its domestic and foreign policies. The seventh general election since the World War was expected in political quarters to give Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's conservative forces a majority of approximately 159 in the House of Commons seats. As the electorate chose the 615 members of the lower house of parliament after a rowdy campaign, political observers forecast two possibilities: 1. The labor representation may be increased through reduction of the conservative majority, largest in history in the last parliament, although laborite victories hinge largely on the choice of liberal voters. 2. Some outstanding candidates, was accused of deserting the labor party, of which he was a leader, when the national government was formed.

London, (AP)—King George II of Greece left today for Paris, first stop on his journey homeward to resume his throne. Members of the British royal family, headed by the Prince of Wales, waved farewell to the restored monarch as his train pulled out from Victoria station at 11 a.m. King George planned to visit in Paris, and then go to Italy to stop at the graves of his mother and father, King Constantine and Queen Sofia. An official Greek delegation will join his party before he reaches his country. King George's return, officially requested by the Greek people on Nov. 5, restores Greece from a republic to a monarchy. The Royalist forces, headed by Gen. George Papandreou, actually took over on Oct. 10 and made Kondyltis regent, pending the plebiscite. More than 95 per cent of the ballots favored the Royalist cause. Republican leaders forced King George into exile after a plebiscite in 1924

(International News Service) DAKAR, Africa, Nov. 13—Miss Jean Batten, New Zealand aviatrix, took off at 5:30 a.m. (1:30 a.m., New York time) today on a flight across the South Atlantic to Natal in her attempt to set a new record from England to Brazil.

| Manila, P. I— (4)— Bedraggled and ill, survivors of the wrecked freighter Silverhazel were treated Thursday as they told of horror and heroism on the wave-lashed rocks off San Bernardino straits where they were marooned four days. Of the 54 aboard the 3,091-ton British vessel when it was wrecked Sunday, four were dead. Two were badly injured. Two had pneumonia. The rest were suffering from exposure and wracked nerves. Peary Brings 43 The destroyer Peary landed 43 survivors Thursday. The others were aboard the destroyer Bulmer. Unable to approach within 1,000 feet of the treacherous rocks, rescue craft could only pick up the survivors as they drifted from the rocks on rafts built from the wreckage. Capt. H. A. Lennard perished while trying to reach a raft with his pet dog, after giving his life belt to a member of his crew. Mrs. Neil Williams of Los Angeles drowned. Ship's Doctor E. L.

London, Nov. 13.—Great Britain's swift but stormy general election campaign ended tonight with the main interest in how badly shaken Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's National government will be after the nation votes tomorrow. A victory by the National regime was expected by party leaders. They predicted a reduced but sound working majority in the House of Commons, probably of around 150, although there were unknown elements, such as how Liberals will vote. Several outstanding personalities, including former Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, were likely to be beaten in their constituencies. MacDonald, now lord president of the council, is accused by the Labor party of being a “traitor” to it. Others thought in danger were Sir John Simon, Liberal and present home secretary, and Sir Herbert Samuel, Liberal leader. Disorders and rowdyism, especially in the industrial sections of the north an

LONDON... (UP) British voters chose today the men and women who will shape the country's destinies in the House of Commons in months or years to come. It seemed certain the conservative-liberal-national labor coalition of Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin would win a comfortable, if reduced majority, on a platform which calls for loyalty to the League of Nations covenant, pursuit of the present policy in the Italian-Ethiopian crisis, and a big rearmament program which will cost between $500,000,000 and $1,000,000,000. Something more than 20,000,000 of the 14,780,261 men and 16,525,246 women voters were expected to cast their ballots. An accurate forecast of the complexion of the new house should be possible tomorrow morning.

Angas, British financier, addressing the American Bankers’ association, says: “Confidence has now returned to the United States, fear has declined, monetary velocity will increase. It will soon speed up and “revolve,” or change hands thirty-five times a year. If Lloyds would insure the accuracy of the major’s prediction, a good many would buy policies. - United Press Cable Editor: Britain’s motives behind her stand in the Italian-Ethiopian dispute became clearer after the outbreak of violent anti-English rioting in Egypt. Egypt is vital to the empire, its trade routes and domination of the Mediterranean. Britain without doubt would sooner go to war than lose control of Egypt to a foreign power. The fine Italian hand of propaganda may be seen in the Egyptian disturbances. Italy has used the newspapers and radio to encourage the Egyptian nationalists in their demand for complete independence. About a month ago, Britain protested to Rome against Italian broadcasts in Arabic from southern Italy, and arranged to open her own radio station in Palestine to counteract them. Britain’s status in Egypt is this: After the World War, she released Egypt from Turkish domination and set up a protectorate. In subsequent years, she proclaimed Egypt a so

1935-01-06.text: , NEW YORK, Jan. 5 (U.P)—Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito today challenged the right of America and Great Britain to have navies which could make war in Asiatic waters while limiting Japan to a navy which had no chance of attacking them at home. He contended in an address to the Foreign Policy Association that such was the effect of the existing 5-5-3 Naval ratios. Japan gave notice last week of withdrawal from the Washington Naval Treaty which established that ratio. Japan believes, he said, that fairness and mutual security require all navies be reduced to a common level with elimination of the big vessels capable of aggression. He expressed Japan’s willingness to see the size of her navy drastically reduced if such steps were taken.

NEW YORK, Jan. 5 (UP)—Fire in a cotton-laden hold of the huge Cunard-White Star liner Georgic was brought under control today an hour after it was discovered by prompt action of ship officers and city fire apparatus on land and water. Thick smoke billowed from the vessel, one of the largest British-built ships afloat, as firemen fought to confine the flames to hold No. 2, in which a quantity of baled cotton was stored.

- LONDON, Jan. 5. (U.P)—Earthquake shocks in widely separated areas of Europe and Asia Minor caused alarm in the past 24 hours but apparently little damage and no loss of life resulted. - Tremors were reported from Turkey, Bulgaria and Holland. - Three separate shocks were felt in Turkey. Those at Istanbul, although not of major severity, were reported the worst since 1874. - Houses and apartment buildings were shaken,

Rome, Italy, Jan. 5.—(U.P.)—Premier Benito Mussolini and Foreign Minister Pierre Laval of France reached complete agreement at the first of a series of conferences today on means of guaranteeing Austria’s independence. They hoped that in further conferences over the weekend they would prepare the way for an alteration of the diplomatic map of Europe to safeguard peace. Under the Austrian independence agreement, Italy, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia, Germany and Hungary would guarantee Austria’s independence, as neighbors of the nation which is the crossroads of Europe. Hungary would be permitted to make reservations in adhering to the agreement. Rome, Jan. 5.—(4)—Benito Mussolini and Pierre Laval, representatives of two of Europe’s most powerful nations, tonight publicly pledged them to friendship and active collaboration in the cause of peace. “The peace of Europe remains precarious,” France’s foreign minister said at the brilliant banquet Il Duce gave him in the Venezia palace, “and requires attentive care of statesmen.” “The continent’s peoples,” Laval said, “are not willing to wait any longer for peace.” In stirring speeches, Mussolini and his French guest foreshadowed the signing of Italo-French accords designed to guarantee Austria’s independence, fortify the structures of peace and wipe out long-standing differences between the two nations. “We have given rise to great hopes,” Laval said. “We will not receive them. Peace must be maintained and consolidated. “Our civilization cannot disap- (Continued on Page 3)

Bruno Hauptmann's aged mother, Frau Pauline Hauptmann, wept unrestrainedly today as she reiterated her faith in her son's innocence of the charge of Kidnapping Col. Charles A. Lindbergh's baby, crying “No, it cannot be true.” “There’s no rest for me in the world,” the septuagenarian woman exclaimed, sobbing and wringing her hands. “Oh, Lord, why must such disaster come over us?” “Every night I spend praying that the Almighty may change my Bruno's terrible fate.” “Cheer up my boy in his prison cell,” she added, while tears rolled down her furrowed cheeks, “by telling him I'm praying for him every night.” Kamenz townfolk, who knew Bruno Hauptmann in his youth, were avidly reading newspaper reports of the Flemington trial. There was little inclination to discuss the case, however. “We are sick and tired of talking about

Berlin—(4)—Lesser lights in the Nazi party were reliably described Saturday as living in fear that they will be eliminated from the party rolls before the middle of April. “The cleansing has already started,” a non-German official declared Saturday, “although in a different way from the ‘blood purge’ of June 30. “Some have already been ousted, but the big clean-up is expected in many party circles, including the ranks of the storm troopers, within three months. “Prussian Premier Hermann Wilhelm Goering recently asserted publicly that there won’t be another June 30, so a ‘blood purge’ is not to be expected.” The statement was an outgrowth of a new crop of reports circulating in well-informed circles as a result of Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s mysterious meeting last Thursday, which was said unofficially to be a consultation on Hitlerism’s immediate domestic and international plans.

FLEMINGTON, Jan. 5 (AP)— Mr. Einstein, your attention, please: How does one get into the courthouse for the Hauptmann trial? The problem is this: To get into the courthouse one must have a pass, The only one who issues passes is the sheriff, The sheriff's office is in the courthouse. It resolves itself, Mr. Einstein, to this: One cannot get into the courthouse until one has already got into the courthouse to get a pass to get into the courthouse, Please mail your solution to Mr. and Mrs. John Q. Public who are to be found between the hours of 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. on the courthouse steps.

Ministers headed by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald informally discussed the legality of the latest gesture of Reichsfuehrer Hitler in defiance of the Versailles treaty and arranged for consultations with France and Italy. There were indications that a protest, probably in the form of a note, was under consideration, and also possible joint action of the powers at Geneva. London, Apr. 30—An authoritative source said today the proposed naval conversations between Great Britain and Germany have been “postponed” pending an expected announcement by Reichsfuehrer Hitler on Germany's foreign policy. It was said the British government was complying with Hitler's desire for the postponement of the conversations and that it had agreed on the basis that until the atmosphere was further cleared with a more definite statement of policy on Hitler's part that it would be unsatisfactory to proceed with the conversations at this time. The postponement, however, is expected to delay the talks only a few days. The conversations, originally planned to begin during the second week of May, now probably will start during the following week since Hitler is expected to tell the world of his latest stand in the international field in a speech May 15. Members of the Cabinet subcommittee on Foreign Affairs discussed the revelation of German submarine construction plans, and formed the basis for an outline of government policy to be decided at a full cabinet meeting tomorrow. Then on Thursday will come, in the House of Commons, one of the most important debates of the session—a full dress discussion of foreign policy. WASHINGTON, April 30 (A New England trio, a governor, a manufacturer, and the head of a huge labor organization—urged a special cabinet committee today to provide immediate assistance for the cotton textile industry. Governor Green, Rhode Island Democrat, told the committee that a serious condition existed in the industry. Thomas F. McMahon, president of the United Textile Workers, who last September conducted a general strike in the textile industry, added his voice to the clamour for assistance to the cotton mills. Harry H. Dutton, manager of the Lonsdale company at Providence, R.I., was the third member. The appearance of Green and McMahon in the same group recalled an incident during the general strike last fall when the Rhode Island governor asked for federal troops to maintain order in his state. Governor Green submitted several recommendations including re-enactment of the Nationa

LONDON, April 29.—Prancing thoroughbreds from the royal mews thrilled thousands of spectators on Park Lane today with an old-fashioned two-reel runaway. It served as an unofficial prelude to the great jubilee procession in which “the king's horses and the king's men will march down the street and march back again.” Out for a practice spin near the marble arch, one of the royal coaches was suddenly jarred out of its dignity today when a double-decker bus bumped one of the smartly trotting Windsor greys which traditionally has drawn the king’s coach with decorum. From then on for a few minutes, all was practically chaos.

(By United Press). Rome, April 30.—The Giornale D'Italia claimed today to have authoritative information that Germany will have 170,000 tons of warships within three years. (The Italian navy is 378,858 tons and the British 1,095,400. Germany has proclaimed her right to a navy one-third as big as Britain’s, or more than 300,900 tons.) - The newspaper said 95,100 tons of the total will be ready by the middle of next year. Submarines, it continued, will vary from 250 to 500 tons each. The number of submarines is not known but is believed to be considerable.

London, April 30.—(U.P.)—King George motored into London today to prepare for the celebration of his 25th anniversary as sovereign. With Queen Mary, the king arrived at Buckingham Palace after a stay at ancient Windsor Castle. All along the route, the cheers of the people attested to his popularity. London is crowded with visitors from all over the world, representing officially or unofficially the 14,000,000 square miles of territory and 493,000,000 people in the empire—one-fourth the world’s land area and population. The anniversary of the king’s accession, as successor to his father Edward VII, is next Monday. The day will be the occasion of the greatest celebration in a generation. King George and Queen Mary will drive in state procession to a special thanksgiving service, and thus will start months of joyous observances of the king’s reign. Startled and angered by disclosures of Germany's 'U-boat' plans, the wartime allied nations took new steps yesterday toward isolating Germany, now arming in three segments—land, sea and air. Members of the British parliament, visualizing Reichsführer Hitler's newest plan as a direct blow at England, demanded quick cabinet action in concert with France and Italy, and the cabinet was considering a protest and possible joint action of the powers at Geneva. LONDON—A group of cabinet ministers arranged for consultations with France and Italy while informally discussing the 'legality' of submarine construction in Germany. The British people were thoroughly aroused, keenly remembering wartime U-boat horrors. A newspaper printed a report that Germany has built a great new sea-plane and submarine base in the North Sea. 1935-03-25.text: BERLIN, Mar. 25. UP——The return to Germany of her lost territory of Memel arose as a key issue today when Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler and Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon of Great Britain started their momentous conversations on peace and security in Europe. An issue such as Memel might well prove to be the key point of the entire negotiations leading to an agreement which would bring Germany back into the family of nations. The Memel territory has an area of 943 square miles and a population of 150,000. It lies on the Baltic between East Prussia and Lithuania. It was taken from Germany by the treaty of Versailles and was first made League territory, and then turned over to Lithuania. Quarters close to the German foreign office speculated on the possibility that Hitler might be offered a plebiscite in Memel in return for his concessions on other points touching re-armament and security. SHANGHAI, Mar. 25. (U?)—The Rev. and Mrs. S. C. Frencham, British missionaries, today notified the China Inland Mission by telegraph that they were safe and unharmed. The message dispelled fears for the safety of the missionaries who previously had been reported kidnapped and slain by bandits.

(Copyright, Lysa, Associated Press) BERLIN, March 24—A two-hour talk between Britain’s two smiling peace envoys, Sir John Simon and Anthony Eden, and the German foreign minister tonight increased optimism in the government camp. It was said in circles close to governmental chieftains that Germany feels the atmosphere is clearing now that the British are here. The two Englishmen have not yet seen Reichsführer Hitler, and may not until tomorrow or Tuesday. They arrived by air late this afternoon at Tempelhof Airdrome and went to the British embassy, where the conversations were begun with Baron Konstantin von Neurath. The greetings were extremely cordial on both sides. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador, and a battery of secretaries. Baron Konstantin von Neurath, Reich foreign minister, introduced the British foreign secretary. Hitler previously had met Captain Eden, as the youthful British diplomat had negotiated an agreement with the Reichsführer more than a year ago limiting Germany's army to 300,000 men. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain told the House of Commons that, while he believed Germany intended not to observe certain military clauses of the Versailles treaty, only those clauses were affected and that the treaty as a whole could not be considered as denounced. In Geneva the League of Nations called a special council session for April 15 to discuss France’s appeal against Germany.
