The long awaited conference between Great Britain and Germany got under way today when Adolf Hitler of Germany talked personally with Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and Captain Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, in the chancellery in Berlin. Hitler told his guests of Germany’s program and desires. Their talks will continue through tomorrow. Hitler, it was reliably reported, insisted that Germany needs an adequate army and a navy capable of controlling the Baltic with a large air fleet as well in order to defend western European civilization from invasion by Russian bolshevism. Official Italian circles in Rome said Italy is willing to participate in diplomatic negotiations with France, Great Britain and Germany provided the latter is willing. Berlin, Mar. 25—British and German negotiators today began their task of finding means to dissipate Europe's grave arms crisis. Adolf Hitler unexpectedly joined his Foreign Minister, Baron Konstantin von Neurath, and his disarmament expert, Joachin von Ribbentrop, at a conference with Sir John Simon, British Foreign Minister, Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal, and Sir Eric Phipps, British Ambassador. The talks with the British, which will continue throughout today and tomorrow, at once assumed added importance because of Hitler's immediate participation. It had been planned that Simon and von Neurath would start the conversations, with Hitler joining later. But the first conference developed into a full dress one. It was held at Hitler's Chancellery, starting at 10:15 a.m., and was expected to continue all day except for a brief midday recess. The conference opened in an atmosphere of optimi

Optimism grew in Berlin as German officials inaugurated vital conversations with British statesmen on European peace proposals. Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Capt. Anthony Eden spent two hours with Foreign Minister Konstantin von Neurath after their arrival in Berlin, the first emissaries from a foreign power to visit that city since before the World War. The two did not see Adolf Hitler, but were expected to confer with him Monday or Tuesday. At Rome, officers were busy carrying out Premier Mussolini's call to the colors of the 200,000 members of the military class of 1911. Military circles said the class probably would be moved to northern cities. France pushed ahead with its proposed eastern European mutual assistance pact while awaiting the result of British talks in Berlin. 1935-11-25.text: Postponement of the League of Nations Sanctions Committee meeting to consider an oil embargo against Italy next Friday was “arranged” Sunday night, leading to the hope in Geneva that peace negotiations between Italy and Ethiopia may soon result in an agreement. Action of Great Britain, a strong supporter of projected oil sanctions against Mussolini's government, in agreeing with France to recommend a postponement caused this reaction. The League Committee of Eighteen was to have considered adding other “key products,” as well as oil, to the list of raw materials which cannot be exported to Italy by League members. In London an authoritative source said that Great Britain agreed to the postponement at the request of Premier Laval, reported to have said he would be unable to leave Paris because of the internal situation in France. Paris, Nov. 25 (P)—A blunt warning by Premier Mussolini and doubt over the ability of the United States government to halt oil shipments, informed sources said today, prompted France and Great Britain to seek a delay in imposing an oil embargo on warring Italy. The two nations agreed to recommend postponement of the League of Nations sanctions committee meeting called for Friday to discuss an oil embargo, authoritative sources said, after a conference between Premier Laval and the British ambassador, Sir George Russell Clark. This agreement was attributed further to a desire by Laval to be at Geneva when a decision is made on the proposed addition to the League's war penalties against Italy. Observers considered it impossible for Laval to leave Paris Friday.

Kiome, Nov, ¢ (P)—Italy's preparedness against a possible clash with Great Britain continued tonight—overshadowed, but not halted, by war with Ethiopia and the sanctions sweeping in Europe. British declarations have brought some reassurance to Italy for continued peace in the Mediterranean. Benito Mussolini, on his own part, made the gesture of withdrawing a division of troops from Libya to lessen what Great Britain considered a threat against Egypt as a reprisal to the presence of the big British fleet in the southern sea. The fleet remains. But the fact remains, Italian naval experts say, as much of a threat as ever. At sea clustered about Alexandria, too far away for planes to fly from there to bomb the warships and return. But if that physical separation offers hope for peace, Italian observers contend the actual presence of the fleet complicates "incidents" considerably. Significant

Coughlin again directed critical comment toward the League of Nations in his regular radio broadcast Sunday with the charge that “the League of Nations and its sanctions exist for but one single purpose—to act only and when British interests are at stake.” He charged that this country had made an informal agreement to support league sanctions. “A semi-secret ambassadorial agreement was made with the League of Nations in 1935 that America would support the league in its sanctions against any ‘aggressor,’” he said, declaring that the agreement was made by Norman Davis, a European observer for the Roosevelt administration. The priest said the “agreement was a factor in England's decision to impose sanctions on Italy.

GENEVA, Nov. 25.—(#)—The League of Nations announced today Friday's session of the sanctions committee of 18, called to consider an oil embargo against Italy, would be postponed to a date not yet fixed. The postponement followed a meeting at Paris between Premier Pierre Laval and British Ambassador Sir George Russell Clerk in which they agreed to recommend the delay, lest early oil sanctions aggravate dangerously existing political tension. By EDWARD W. BEATTIE (Copyright, 1935, By United Press) ADDIS ABABA, Nov. 25.—Ethiopia claimed the rout of three Italian battalions on the northern front today, with more than 100 Italians killed. An official communique said that the fight occurred near Hawale, north of Makale on the northern front. The three Italian battalions, it was asserted, had plundered a village and had encamped preparatory to feasting on captured cattle. Ethiopians under the Dedjazmatch Woress, it was said, surprised the Italians in a defile in the mountains, attacked furiously and killed the commander and more than 100 men, according to the estimate of those present. The rest of the Italians were put to flight, it was asserted and eight horses and 13 mules laden with ammunition were captured. This claimed victory was impossible to confirm, as usual.

ATHENS, Nov. 25—George I, King of the Hellenes, returned to Athens today after twelve years of exile to reascend the throne he fled on December 18, 1923. The returning head of the house of Glucksburg is the first deposed European monarch to recover a throne since the World War. He was greeted by Prince Paul, his uncle, Gen. George Kondylis, who has been acting as regent since the Nov. 3 plebiscite restored the monarchy, and a large group of national officials, as he left the launch of the cruiser Helle, which brought him from Brindisi, Italy, to Greece. From that moment on, it was a day of triumph. The motorcade in which he entered his capital, escorted by ten mounted generals, was cheered wildly along its route. The crowds began their demonstration the moment the booming of guns in Athens announced the king had landed and enthusiasm never slackened until a hush fell as George entered th

GENEVA (UP)—Augusto De Vasconcellos, chairman of the League of Nations general staff, today postponed a meeting set for Friday at which leaders were to consider putting an embargo against oil, coal, iron, steel and possibly copper to Italy. The meeting, Vasconcellos announced, was postponed at the request of Premier Pierre Laval of France. Laval pleaded he could not get here for the important meeting because the French parliament meets Thursday. However, the result of the postponement is to delay action on the new penalties, notably as regards oil, and it gives Laval another chance to seek a basis for diplomacy. (Turn to Page 10—No. 5.)

1935-11-16.text: London, England—(4’)—Returns from Thursday’s general elections showed Friday the national government retained its majority in the House of Commons, although Ramsay MacDonald, Lord President of the Council and the first leader of the national government, went down to defeat. The voters apparently had returned 415 national government members to the Commons, assuring the government 200 more seats than the opposition. There are 615 seats. Ramsay MacDonald received 17,882 votes in Seaham, while his labor party opponent, E. Shinwell, received 38,380. Shinwell was Minister of Mines in the first government MacDonald headed as Prime Minister. Defeated with his father was Malcolm MacDonald, Colonial Secretary. F. J. Bellenger gained the seat in the Bassetlaw division of Nottinghamshire for labor by a plurality of 1,139 votes. Anthony Eden, Minister for (Look for FOUR on Page Six)

| London, Nov. 15 (4)--Stanley Baldwin's National Government retained control of Great Britain's destinies in the general elections and prepared tonight to continue a firm stand in efforts to halt the Italo-Ethiopian war. But Ramsay MacDonald, founder of the National Government four years ago, was dropped overboard from the ship of state. At 7:50 P. M., with only 19 scattered districts unreported, the government had a commanding majority in the House of Commons of 242. It captured 419 seats in the new Parliament, exceeding most all forecasts. The combined opposition won 176 seats, with one independent also marked up. MacDonald Defeated The entire cabinet except for MacDonald and his son, Malcolm, were re-elected. They had the posts of Lord President of the Council and Secretary for the Colonies, respectively, following upon the veteran MacDonald's resignation as Prime Minister several mo

LONDON, Nov. 15.—(INS)—British voters, giving Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's national government an overwhelming endorsement in its pro-league, anti-Italian policies and returning it to power for another five years, nevertheless tossed out of office two of its best known members. Former Prime Minister James Ramsay MacDonald, Lord President of the Council, and his son, Malcolm MacDonald, Minister for the Colonies, were defeated by Laborites in yesterday’s election. On the basis of latest returns, the government had won 419 of the 615 seats in the House of Commons, and the opposition 177.

LONDON. Nov. 16.—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and his cabinet, immeasurably strengthened by the general parliamentary election were expected today to embark at once on a broadly envisioned effort to consolidate world peace. Informed political observers predicted that the policy would be: unwavering determination to seek a solution of the Italian-Ethiopian problem only within the framework of the League of Nations covenant. To consider the imposition of military penalties under the League covenant’s article XVI only in event of the most extreme Italian provocation against League members. To do everything possible to minimize the possibility of an Italian-British clash. Most rapid strengthening of national defenses. To seek further to cement British-American good relations as a means of promoting a stable, peaceful world.

TOKYO, Nov. 16, (4?)—Japanese delegates to the London naval conference left Tokyo today with instructions to stand pat on demands for parity with the United States and England. A cheering crowd waved farewell to Admiral Osami Nagano and Matsuzo Nagai, the delegates who are expected to arrive in London about December 1, 2.

| LONDON, (UP).—Secretary of State Cordell Hull’s new warning to American merchants against trading with belligerents in the Italo-Ethiopian war was hailed as most timely by official British circles today. The prediction was freely made that, as a result of the United States stand, the league will almost certainly impose further embargoes on exports to Italy. It was emphasized that the question of embargoing shipments of oil to Italy depended almost entirely upon the attitude of the United States.

LONDON, Nov. 15 (4)—Former Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, somewhat bitter and by his own admission a “done in old man” sat in his Hampstead home today, too weary to discuss his future plans following his defeat in the British elections. At the same time his victorious opponent, E. Shinwell, Labor candidate, issued a statement that MacDonald’s defeat had brought the national government hurtling to the ground. Recovering from the combined shock of his own defeat and that of his son, Malcolm MacDonald, the former prime minister said he was too surprised by his loss and that he was glad he had made his fight for re-election in the Seaham district. MacDonald first entered parliament 29 years ago.

BERLIN. Nov. 15 (Pi)--Jews were stripped of all political rights by the Nazi government today and were forbidden to marry gentiles. Official decrees put into effect the sweeping citizenship and racial laws approved by the Reichstag at its Nurnberg meeting in September. Thus Germany's Jews are deprived of the right to vote, to hold public office or even to be employed by the government. Only a special dispensation from Adolf Hitler himself can exempt Jews and part Jews from these restrictions. The decree also forbids the employment of female Aryan servants under the age of 35 in Jewish households. 'The Jews cannot be a Reich citizen, cannot vote or occupy public office,' said the decree, 'Jewish functionaries of the government will be pensioned December 31, 1935.'

1935-02-06.text: LONDON, Feb. 5 (#)—A startled House of Commons tonight heard King George, his youngest son and his newest daughter-in-law called “parasites.” J. McGovern, the same fiery labor member from Glasgow who set the house by its ears when he interrupted the king’s speech May 21, 1933, hurled the almost unprecedented epithet at the royal house during the debate on the Bill to reorganize the dole system. ‘We pay King George £10,750 a week, and one shilling a minute to the Duke of Kent and his wife,” the left wing laborite declared. “These parasites are living on the wealth of the country.”

LONDON, Feb. 6.—(UP)—John McGovern, 47, plumber M.P., from Glasgow, added another purple paragraph to his parliamentary record today after a speech in the House of Commons in which he called King George and his newly married son, the Duke of Kent, “parasites.” His outbursts, in an unemployment insurance debate last night, sent 60 persons, said to be communists, charging toward the public galleries to hear him. Police whistles resounded in the old chamber as policemen ran up to drive out the intruders. McGovern said last night that it cost the country $53,750 a week to support the king and $125,000 a year to support the duke. He was contrasting allowances to unemployed with grants to the royal family, “We pay King George £10,750 ($53,750) a week,” shouted McGovern. “That's £64 ($320) an hour. We pay the Duke of Kent £25,000 ($125,000) a year—these parasites living on the wealth of the cou

LONDON. (7. Great Britain told the world Tuesday that Germany’s refusal to enter the new Anglo-French peace framework will mean her isolation by defensive air alliances. The alternative facing the reichsfuehrer, the most critical test his spectacular foreign policies have faced since he and his nazis came to power two years ago, has been communicated to all the world’s interested powers, among them the United States. If Hitler says “Yes” to the Anglo-French proposals drafted at the weekend conversations of French and British premiers and foreign ministers, Germany will: First, join France, Britain, Belgium and Italy in defensive air pacts requiring all signatories to lend immediate assistance if one of them is attacked by another from the air. Second, enter the proposed central European non-interference pact drafted at Italo-French conversations in Rome, and designed primarily to secure

COLUMBUS, O., Feb. (—The proffered resignation of Wilam F.P. Amrine, veteran superintendent of the London prison farm, threatened today to have far-reaching repercussions. Action on the resignation may decide whether or not Mrs. Margaret Allman, state welfare director, is confirmed by the senate. Amrine offered to resign after Mr. Allman insisted on knowing the political affiliations of employees at the prison farm. She requested the information on instructions from Governor Davey's office. Amrine, who has worked in various state institutions since 1912, has built up a reputation as a penologist during his administration at the prison farm since 1925. Unofficial polls in the senate indicated that the 17 votes necessary to confirm Mrs. Allman as welfare director could not be mustered yet. Administration leaders in the senate held up action on her confirmation. Governor Davey, who saw "not

Sutheld, Lug., Led, by Nine policemen were injured and 20 to 30 persons arrested yesterday when several thousand persons clashed with police during a meeting of protest against the new reorganized dole system. The crowd tried to get the city council to receive some of its members and, when the council refused, the demonstrators surged around the city hall, throwing stones at the building and breaking windows. Police, both mounted and on foot, charged into the rioters but suffered 9 casualties in restoring order. The protest was directed against the new method of dole payments which are the subject of wide opposition, complainants claiming there is inequality in the system.

(By The Associated Press) London, Feb. 6.—Sir James Heath, 83-year-old colliery proprietor, and Dorothy Mary Hodgson, 36, were mar- ried today at the registry office. The marriage is Sir James’ fourth, his third with Sophie Mary Elliot-Lynn, an aviatrix, having been dissolved by divorce in Reno in 1932.

PARIS, Feb. 6 (UP).—Street disorders marked the anniversary of the bloody Stavisky riots today as strong forces of armed mobile guards and police massed to prevent demonstrations. Police clashed in the Place St. Michel with 1,000 students who howled insults at them. Royalists, the die-hard fascists, booed Premier Pierre Etienne Flandin as he left the heavily guarded Notre Dame cathedral after a requiem mass for the 25 persons killed in the riots a year ago today. “Assassins,” they shouted until the police massed in the vicinity forced them back. Because of the nervous temper of the crowds, the king and queen of Denmark, arriving on their way to the Riviera, were heavily guarded. Police estimated 10,000 persons were massed about Notre Dame.

(By The Associated Press) S.S. Jacob Ruppert, At Sea (Via Mackay Radio), Feb. 6.—The Byrd Antarctic expedition, its men and supplies aboard the S.S. Jacob Ruppert and the Bear of Oakland, left Little America, Antarctica, today, headed home to the United States.

1935-07-28.text: MOUDL SLTyY WASHINGTON, July 29. —()— Navy quarters today expressed interest in a London Daily Herald article which said Britain plans to build almost a new complete fleet by 1942 at a cost of $750,000,000. Some naval men said they were reluctant to believe the British admiralty planned such a move. It was said that it would mean the danger of a world-wide building race would be increased. The suggestion was made that perhaps the craft referred to in the London newspaper are paper ships which might be used to bargain with other naval powers at some future conference on limitation of sea armaments. Naval circles also expressed interest in the 1942 date reported as the time for completion of the British program. This is the year the United States plans to attain present treaty strength. GENEVA, JULY 29. (AP)—League of Nations circles said today Ethiopia made a major concession in its dispute with Italy by refraining from insistence that the council dig to the bottom of the controversy. Emperor Haile Selassie in his latest communication to the League, contented himself with getting back to the arbitration attempt. He asked at its session three days hence that the League council define the powers of the deadlock conciliation commission. In answer to the Italian contention that the commission should restrict discussion to frontier incidents, however, Ethiopia demanded that no such limitations be imposed. “The king of kings” had the right to call for a council investigation of the East African crisis under article 15 of the League covenant, under which the council eventually would make recommendations for a settlement. Varese, Italy—()—With a terrific blast which shook villages and broke windows in buildings for miles around, the Bickford-Smith munitions factory at Taino blew up Saturday afternoon, taking an estimated toll of 50 lives. Scores of workers were injured. Officials of the factory and municipality refused to answer questions concerning the explosion. Villagers, however, expressed the opinion the first blast occurred in the packing warehouse. They said many girls were working in that building. The families of the approximately five hundred employees of the plant hovered around the outskirts of the factory grounds until late at night, awaiting reports from squadrons of militiamen who were rushed to the scene. Witnesses said several smaller explosions followed the first tremendous blast, which caused a heavy pall of smoke and dust to obscure almost completely the immediate vicinity. Late Saturd

BERLIN, July 27 (4).—Nazism’s big offensive against reactionaries struck new terror into Jews and steel helmet war veterans today but Catholics, heretofore under heavy fire, thought they discerned indications of an imminent truce. Uneasiness increased among the Reich’s 505,000 Jews. An olive branch was held out to Catholics by the official organ of the Hildesheim bishopric. It said: “We consider true peace between the state and the Catholic church quite possible.” Rumors grew apace. The city buzzed with reports that widespread changes in state and party leadership might take place.

By The Associated Press Rome, July 27.—Italy sent the League of Nations today an implied threat to quit the council session starting Wednesday if it discussed phases of the Italo-Ethiopia quarrel Italy did not want talked about. A telegram to J. A. C. Avenol, league secretary-general, said Italy ‘would not “have any difficulty in participating in the session” if its work were confined solely to “studying the most opportune means of placing the commission of conciliation and arbitration in position to resume its labors.” (The Italo-Ethiopian commission adjourned at Scheveningen, the (Continued on Page 9)

BERLIN. (AP). The official Ger- man press service announced Ger- many considered her commercial treaty with America terminated. The press service communique said the treaty was broken by the action of Mayor LaGuardia of New York in refusing to license a German resident there as a mas- seur because of alleged anti-Jew- ish acts by the Nazis. “This constitutes a clear breach of the German-American friend- ship, commercial and consular treaty of Dec. 8, 1923,” the com- munique said. “It is up to the American federal government to give instructions to officials con- cerned to observe the treaty.” Officials here said no diplomatic steps had been taken in the mat- ter but stated they hoped the com- munique would “be read by re- sponsible authorities in America.” The German press also called for diplomatic action and an apol- ogy from the United States be- cause the German flag was torn from th

BERLIN, Germany (UP)— Mayor Fiorello H. La Guardia’s refusal to grant a license permitting Paul Kress, a German national, to operate as a masseur in New York City, constitutes a violation of the German-American treaty of 1928, it was charged last night in a formal statement issued by the official German news bureau. The statement came as German newspapers throughout the country expressed outrage over the incident.

GENEVA, July 27—(UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini pointedly informed the League of Nations today that he expects the council, at its meeting next Wednesday, to deal solely with the revival of arbitration of border incidents in the Italian-Ethiopian dispute. “Should this not be the case,” the Italian dictator said significantly, “The Italian government will state its observations on the subject.” The latter sentence was interpreted here as a veiled warning that Italy might withdraw from the League. There was also a veiled intimation that Italy might not even attend the council's session if its desires are not met. The text of Mussolini's telegram, as published by the league follows: “In my telegram dated July 25, 1935, the Italian government has the honor to inform the secretary of the League of Nations that it had addressed two communications to the Ethiopian government, on July 14 and July

1935-12-13.text: (Copyright, 1935, by The Associated Press) LONDON, Dec. 12.—Japan’s demand for equality in naval strength was rejected at the International Naval conference today by the four other great naval powers and the British dominions. American, British and Italian delegates flatly rejected the Japanese proposal, and had the support of the British dominions, while France expressed opposition chiefly on grounds of procedure. It was understood the British took the lead in opposing the Japanese demands. The meeting broke up at noon with the Japanese leaving hastily. Although they are usually the first to depart, their hurried exit created the impression at the moment that they were walking out of the conference. Well-informed sources said, however, the Japanese merely wished to submit certain questions to Tokyo, French Ask Full Rights French and Italian opposition to Japanese equality was understood

Geneva, Dec. 12.—(4)—Plans for settling the Italo-Ethiopian war were thrown into the hands of the League of Nations council late today after oil and other new sanctions had been sidetracked at a meeting of the league’s sanctions committee of eighteen. British delegates announced the league council would meet Wednesday to discuss the whole question. An implacable stand against any big concessions to Italy at the expense of Ethiopia's sovereignty took form Wednesday night among smaller powers of the League of Nations.

By The Associated Press London, Dec. 13.—Japan granted Soviet Russia the right to a fleet equal to its own in arguing for tonnage equality for all nations before the international naval conference, authoritative quarters disclosed today. This widening of the scope of Japan's position was regarded as one of the most significant developments of the conference. Japan’s delegation previously maneuvered to win the support of France and Italy. The Japanese had revived their plan for a common upper limit on naval tonnage to include the five powers: Japan, the United States, Great Britain, France, and Italy, instead of the first three only previously suggested.

Geneva. —- (AP) — Emperor Haile Selassie asked the League of Nations to call a special meeting of the League Assembly on the grounds that the Franco-British peace plan violated the spirit of the League Covenant. The plan, which it was understood offers about half of Ethiopia to Italy in exchange for peace, already has resulted in a call for a session of the Council next Wednesday. Many of the smaller nations in the League were represented as opposed to the plan on the grounds that it would give Premier Mussolini his objective in East Africa.

Atay RED SASSUIa Od LPO, The inflammatory issue of an oil embargo against Italy was put aside for the time being by the League of Nations Thursday night. Instead, the league decided to take over the widely-bombarded Franco-British peace plan, which was handed to it with a weary air by Premier Laval and Anthony Eden, Britain’s minister for league affairs. A session of the council of the league was called for next Wednesday to study the Italo-Ethiopian situation from A to Z. Delegates meanwhile will acquaint themselves with the carefully guarded details of the peace formula. As a result of the day’s developments, a rebellion by small powers against the Franco-British moves apparently died down. Both Laval and Eden gave assurances that their only object was peace, within the framework of the league, and that Geneva and Addis Ababa would have their say as well as Rome. There were strong indi

LONDON (UP) — The naval conference was thrown into confusion today when Admiral Osami Nagano was understood to have revised Japan's proposal that fleet equality be limited to the navies of the United States, Great Britain and Japan. The head of the Japanese delegation was reported to have said today that Japan would not object to a “common upper level” for the fleets of other naval powers as well, Animated discussion ensued during which the British dominions, apparently in an attempt to discredit the Japanese suggestion, asked whether they also would be entitled to fleets as strong as those of the three leading sea powers. The debate ended inconclusively, leaving some delegates with the impression that Nagano’s intention has been to extend the parity principle only to France and Italy. Nagano was reported to have raised the question whether the British Empire was attending the conference

- LONDON, Dec. 12.—(P)—Scarlet garbed peers of England today acquitted Lord De Clifford, 28 years old, of a charge of manslaughter arising from an automobile accident. The verdict of innocence was returned by the members of the house of lords after six hours of judicial pageant such as had not been seen in England in the last 34 years. The verdict—"Not guilty upon mine honor"—was pronounced one by one by the assembled peers with their right hands over their hearts following the taking of evidence. Lord Hailsam, serving as attorney for the defense, told his brother lords: "There is no evidence of criminal negligence or even negligence." Consequently, he argued, there was no case against De Clifford. The case arose from an automobile accident at Kingston-on-Thames in which Douglas George Hopkins, a commoner, was killed.

London, England, Dec. 13.—(2)— Japan's delegation to the international naval conference maneuvered today to win the support of France and Italy in the Asiatic empire’s demand for sea power equality. The Japanese revised their request for a common upper limit on naval tonnage to include the five powers—Japan, the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy—instead of the first three only, as previously suggested. The French and Italians opposed the Japanese demands yesterday because they were not included. However, informed sources said they did consider the new tactics would prove successful, although they will bring the French and Italians more into the general debate. As a result of the new Japanese plan, the French and Italians are expected to present more detailed viewpoints when the session is resumed Monday after a week-end of conferences within the delegations. 1935-02-18.text: London, Feb. 18.—(LP)—A decree nisi of divorce granted in July to Mrs. Thelma Colman against Ronald Colman, motion picture star, was made absolute today. Both now are free to remarry.
LONDON, (UP)—The United States dollar dropped in value today after announcement of the gold decisions. From a previous quotation of $4.86 5-16 to the pound, the dollar went to $4.89.

BOSTON, Feb. 18 (P)—Alexander Kaminski, 24-year-old New Britain, Conn., youth, convicted of slaying a Springfield jail guard during an escape, will die in the electric chair at state prison shortly after midnight tonight. Warden James L. Hogsett was to notify the youth this afternoon. Prison officers said Kaminski dined heartily yesterday and appeared unconcerned over his future. He devoted an hour to writing a letter to his counsel, Edward L. Fenton of Springfield.

Fall River, Mass., Feb. 18-()— Ten year old Alyce Jane McHenry, of Omaha, today ends her long trip to New England in search of health. The Truesdale Hospital, where she will be operated on for an unusual ailment that has turned her stomach upside down, receives her today. Despite intense pain, Alyce has remained cheerful throughout her journey. A rare muscular strain has inverted her stomach, pushed the heart across her chest to the right side and impaired her left lung, and has caused a hernia of the diaphragm. Danger of death through strangulation is ever present.

(BERLIN, Feb. 17—(4)—Sentences for divulging military secrets, passed by the dreaded people’s court upon four German society women and one man, will be made public tomorrow, an official of the propaganda ministry said. He professed ignorance, however, as to whether the death penalty would be imposed. Apparently that rested with Reichführer Hitler himself, to whom the Nazi cabinet recently delegated the final word in death sentences. Two of the women, Frau Von Berg and Frau Renate Von Natzer, are to pay the death penalty, according to non-official sources, while Fraulein Von Jena and Fraulein Zandersch, also said to be implicated in the plot, are to be sentenced to hard labor for life. Baron George Sosnowski, Polish nobleman who is accused with the women of making German military secrets available to Poland, is likewise to be sentenced to life imprisonment, it was said unofficially. (International News Service Staff Correspondent) BERLIN, Feb. 18.—The headsman’s axe descended today, upon the necks of two beautiful German noblewomen—put to death for espionage activities against the Nazi regime. The victims were the beautiful blonde Baroness Benita Von Berg, former wife of Baron Von Falkenhayn, son of a German world war general, and Baroness Renate Von Matzmer, Captain Ulrich Von Sosnowsky, Polish nobleman and leader of the spy ring, was sentenced to life imprisonment at hard labor, together with Frau Irene Von Jena. The aristocrats, who sold their birthright and lives by divulging military secrets to a foreign power, were executed at dawn after a year's imprisonment. Announcement of their execution was deferred for almost eight hours by the ministry of propaganda, The women were tried and convicted by the dread people's tribunal in connection with the alleged espiona

PARIS (UP)—Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi, veteran French aviators, discussed their plans at Porto Praia, Cape Verde islands, today after an escape, through cold nerve and good fortune, from almost certain death at sea on a Paris-South American flight. Starting Saturday in their famous monoplane Joseph Lebrix to fly as far down the South American coast as possible, in hope of breaking their own world long distance flight record, all went well until they reached mid-Atlantic. Then the oil pressure in their motor began to fail. They were hundreds of miles from either coast; there were almost no ships in their course. They decided to run for the Cape Verde Islands, off the African coast, and arriving over Porto Praia at 1:15 p.m. yesterday (8:15 a.m. S.T.) they circled the flying field and landed 15 minutes later. During their grim race back over the sea, the flyers exchanged calmly drafted m

ABOARD ADMIRAL BYRD'S FLAGSHIP, At Sea. Feb. 17.—(Via Mackay Radio)—Beards and long hair got a trimming today as members of the Byrd Antarctic expedition prepared for their first glimpse of civilization tomorrow in 15 months. The flagship at noon was only 240 miles from Dunedin, N. Z., the first port of call, and expected to dock there about 3 p. m., tomorrow. The barkentine Bear of Oakland was about 160 miles astern. A feeling of excitement took possession of the ship. Amateur barbers were busy clipping beards that had been permitted to grow unrestrained in the Antarctic. Clothes which were considered good enough for Little America were shed and dropped overboard. Commenting on his second expedition, Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd said, “What is most gratifying to me, overshadowing the accomplishment of the mission we set out to fulfill, is the fact that we are all coming back with no liv

1935-09-27.text: LONDON, SEPT. 27. (AP).—The United States today asked formally for a clarification of British views on holding an international naval conference before the end of this year as required under the Washington naval treaty of 1922. A conference between American diplomats and foreign office officials on the subject of such a parley followed close on the heels of British press reports that the British government soon would advise the United States it was terminating the Washington treaty. This report, however, was emphatically denied in official quarters. Ray Atherton, counselor of the United States embassy, accompanied by Captain Walter Anderson, the United States naval attache, called on R. L. Craigie, the head of the American section of the foreign office and expert on naval affairs. They asked of him what the British government view might be on the stand which must be taken by the mandator

LONDON, Sept. 27.—(Friday)—(AP)—The British government, sections of the London Press announce today, intends to send a note to the United States government this week-end informing Washington and other signatories to the Washington naval treaty that it intends embarking upon a big naval program. Empire responsibilities and foreign commitments, it was understood, will be given as the reasons. The Express asserted this action was equivalent to denunciation of the London and Washington naval treaties. The London Daily Mail announced that the new British naval program would likely be made public soon after the assembling of parliament next month. Japan denounced the Washington treaty, providing a 5-5-3 ratio in naval tonnage for the United States, Great Britain and Japan, respectively, last December. The treaty was signed in 1922. Japan's abrogation of the pact takes effect Dec. 31, 1936. The

Rome, Sept. 26 (4)—The League of Nations’ proposal for a three months’ truce between Italy and Ethiopia got a cool reception in Rome tonight and “freedom of action” was the official watchword. The British navy, whose presence in the Mediterranean is the cause of grave anxiety here, failed to modify Il Duce’s intentions in East Africa. A government spokesman reiterated that the Ethiopian problem is for Italy, not the League, to solve. Italy has “been very patient” while the League Council sought a solution, he said, but he rejected the idea that Italy, by “listening” to Geneva, in any way has surrendered what she considers her right to act as she sees fit.

LONDON, Sept. 27 (P) — Lord Edward Montagu, second son of the Duke of Manchester, was found guilty in an Old Bailey court trial today on all six counts, charging theft and forgery of a check. He was sentenced to nine months’ imprisonment.

Quebec, Sept. 26 (#).—Harry K. Thaw, returning from a trip to Europe, was taken off the liner Empress of Britain today and rushed to Hotel Dieu hospital. Attendants said he was critically ill with double pneumonia. Physicians gave Thaw an even chance to recover. The once prominent New York night life figure was reported ill when he boarded the ship at Cherbourg and his condition became steadily worse. On his arrival here he was in a semi-delirious state. - He was en route to Springfield, Mass.

a mutual assistance agreement to cope with any European war threat, French officials said today, The proposed pact, now in the discussion stage, is said by these officials to be an outgrowth of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. It was also stimulated by the promise of Sir Samuel Hoare, British foreign secretary, before the League of Nations, that Britain would stand by the League “at all places and at all times.” The pact, interpreted as the British reply to the French request for more precise reaffirmation of 'Hoare’s speech, was officially described as “very satisfactory and just what we wanted.” “Premier Laval,” one official said, “now has no fear of going ahead with Great Britain.” This bilateral mutual pact would be similar to the Franco-Soviet agreement concluded earlier this year, officials explained, but whether the two nations would sign a formal treaty was regarded as questionable.

London, Sept. 26. (AP)—The Council of the League of Nations warned Italy and Ethiopia today that they cannot begin a war in Africa before December 4 without violating the league covenant. Such violation calls for punitive steps by other league members since it is considered an act of aggression against them all. Adopting a course of procedure in the grave crisis, the council decided to seek a solution under the article XV of the covenant. This requires the council to draft recommendations for a settlement. A cold reception was given the league proposal for a truce until this winter in Rome and government officials let it be known Italy feels she has “freedom of action.” “Italy will listen to what the League of Nations says,” said one official, but “without promising to wait after the boggy path to Addis Ababa becomes dry enough to support its army.” Italians Walk Out Prior to the council

LONDON (U.P.) - Britain Thursday night refused to give France advance assurance of military support against Germany or any other possible European aggressor. The statement was made in reply to French inquiries as to whether the British attitude on sanctions, expressed by Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare on the Ethiopian situation, would apply to a continental European emergency. The foreign office handed a note to French Ambassador Andre Charles Corbin which emphasized that Britain's attitude generally favored collective action against an aggressor but that theoretical future situations must be met when they arise. France's query was understood to have been preliminary to a decision on whether or not to join Britain in support of sanctions against Italy if Ethiopia is attacked. 1935-08-16.text: London, Aug. 16 (AP)—The British government announced today that it has invited the United States, Japan, France and Italy to a preliminary naval conference, planned to be held in about October. - The conference would follow the bilateral discussion which Great Britain has scheduled with France. These discussions with France, Italy and Russia are expected to begin in September. Purpose of the preliminary discussion is for a possible agreement on the naval limitation for all as provided in the Washington treaty in 1922. It was stated here that the date for the formal conference which was to be in 1935, was still as indefinite as ever. Consequently the preliminary conference would decide the fate of the formal conference. On authoritative sources it was disclosed that invitations had been issued early this month.

PARIS, Aug. 15 (AP) - Baron Pom- peo Aloisi, head of the Italian delegation to the tri-power conference opening tomorrow, informed the British representative, Anthony Eden, tonight that Italy’s minimum demand for peaceful settlement of her dispute with Ethiopia was occupation of Ethiopia by the Italian army. Aloisi said Premier Mussolini would require this condition in order to provide for the enforcement of economic privileges. Italy, he said, would not be able to accept the British plan for economic concessions in Ethiopia unless Italy could make Ethiopia respect them. This, he said, would mean Italy must keep armed forces in the East African country. After the meeting it was said in informed quarters their positions were as ‘irreconcilable’ as before the meeting.

London, Aug. 16. — Great Britain, in a formal note to the United States, Japan, France and Italy, today proposed an informal naval conference during October, preliminary to a formal naval limitation conference. The Washington and London naval limitation treaties expire December 31, 1936. The Washington treaty limits capital ships — battleships, aircraft carriers and battle cruisers — and the London treaty limits auxiliaries — cruisers and lesser craft. France and Italy are not signatories to the London treaty as they could not agree on their own relative strength in auxiliaries. Prospect for renewal of the treaties has been poor because of Japan's demand for absolute equality with the United States and Great Britain. Continued on Page ?.

(Copyright 1235, By United Press) Paris, Aug. 16—A new, important compromise plan by Premier Pierre Laval was expected today as the first move in a three-power French-British-Italian conference to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia, Reports that Laval had a compromise plan ready were circulated soon after the delegates of France, Great Britain and Italy met at the foreign office for the start of their three-power negotiations, One possible proposal mentioned was the creation of a neutral zone between Ethiopia proper and a colonization zone which Britain had proposed should be given to Italy. This would create an area which neutral troops—probably natives from adjacent French, British and Belgian territory—would police under League of Nations auspices. This would ensure respect of Ethiopia’s sovereignty without the Italian military occupation which, it was learned, Italy now demands, A

Paris, Aug. 16.—(U. P.)—Great Britain has informed Italy that an invasion of Ethiopia will result in the collapse of the League of Nations and the resumption of dangerous pre-war "balance of power" in Europe, authoritative sources said today. Representatives of Great Britain, France and Italy conferred here in an effort to avert war and its threats to peace in Europe. Great Britain was said to have informed Italy that the East African situation is likely to result in the small nations breaking away from their present protective alliance, leading to a general resumption of the pre-war political situation, with Italy perhaps isolated if the war causes a collapse of her financial system.
By Associated Press LONDON, Aug. 16.-The British government announced today that it had invited the United States, Japan, France and Italy to a preliminary naval conference "about October."

LONDON (#) — A Reuters (British news agency) dispatch from Peiping reported today that Gareth Jones, British journalist and former secretary to David Lloyd George, who was captured by bandits near Kalgen, Chahar province, Inner Mongolia, a fortnight ago, had been killed by his captors. It was said his body was found near Paochang. Gareth Jones, correspondent for the Manchester Guardian, was seized on July 29 with Herbert Mueller, German journalist, and held for $40,000 ransom, arms and ammunition. Mueller was released August 1 to negotiate for the ransom of Jones. On his arrival in Peiping he expressed the belief that Jones would be released through negotiations between the bandits and Chahar province authorities. When Mueller was released he was warned that, unless the ransom for Jones was paid, the British journalist would be killed. The amount had been reduced to $20,000.

BY RICHARD G. MASSOCK Associated Press Foreign Staff Paris, Aug. 16—(#)—Three men met today in a secret session which may result in the alteration of the map of Ethiopia and a change in the African empire's economic life. The men were Premier Laval, of France, Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy, and Anthony Eden of Great Britain. They conducted their talk in the ante-chamber of the clock room of the foreign ministry where their countries, in 1928, signed the Kellogg-Briand pact ‘outlawing war.’ Their avowed intention is to prevent war between Italy and Ethiopia. Experts Sit Outside Door For a few minutes, Robert G. Vanstittart, British permanent foreign under-secretary, sat in on the conference but, for the remainder of the meeting, the three diplomats were alone. A group of 12 other experts and secretaries sat outside the ante-chamber until an hour and a half had elapsed and they were called

1935-04-08.text: By The Associated Press London, April 8—The sudden illness of Captain Anthony Eden, lord privy seal and British ambassador for peace in the recent arms discussions, upset yesterday Britain’s plans for facing a hard battle at the Stresa conference April 11 over the powers’ future policy toward Germany. The brilliant young statesman is suffering from heart strain. An official foreign office announcement revealed that physicians have ordered him to take a com- (Continued on page 3)

LONDON, April 8 (AP)—The Munich correspondent of Reuter’s reported today that Gen. Erich Ludendorff, breaking a long silence on the eve of his 70th birthday, proudly styled himself “an anti-Christian and a heathen” and placed the blame on Christianity for Germany's collapse in 1918. Erich Ludendorff's open fight against Christianity today caused the Roman Catholic Church and the Protestant Confessional Synod to decline to display flags tomorrow in honor of the general's 70th birthday, although Reichsfuehrer Hitler himself ordered all government buildings to fly flags. 70 Years Old Tuesday BERLIN, April 8 (AP)—Whether Reichsfuehrer Hitler will go to Tutzing in Bavaria tomorrow for the celebrations marking the 70th birthday of General Erich Ludendorff was a question many Germans asked today. LONDON, April 8 — I telephoned to some of the principal European bureaus of the United Press today to find out what nations are preparing for war, to what extent and against whom. “They all are preparing. Alignments are uncertain, but every nation is taking precautions against attack by every other nation. Neighbors distrust neighbors. There is more militarism in the world than at any time in its history. Here is the picture: Tear Gas Attacks. The common people of Europe in recent weeks have become infected with the fear of war. Here in England you meet people in the street who tell you they are buying gas masks and considering constructing private bomb shelters in their cellars. In France, many are buying a pamphlet describing what to do in case of air raids or gas attacks. LONDON, April 8 (AP) — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced today that he and Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, would form the British delegation to the conference with Italy and France at Stresa Thursday. The prime minister made the announcement himself in the House of Commons in reply to a question by Austen Chamberlain, former lord privy seal, who referred to the sudden illness which has sent Capt. Anthony Eden, the present lord privy seal, to bed for a complete rest. Chamberlain said to the prime minister, "May I express what is the general feeling of sympathy with the lord privy seal and also express the hope that he will splendidly recover?" MacDonald replied: "The British representatives will be the foreign secretary and myself. Conservative, labor and liberal members felt that in their decisions might rest the entire future of negotiations with Germany. They had the danger of war in mind. It was said authoritatively that the keystone of their policy would be to try to make Britain mediator among European nations whose interests are in conflict. 4 associated Press foreign Staff LONDON April 8—(?)—The orders of two physicians threw an- other obstacle today in the path of Great Britain’s search for a happy formula to remove all threats to Europe's peace, Captain Anthony Eden, Great Britain's young diplomat, in whom she placed much reliance in working out the perplexing security problem, was sent to bed and instructed to remain there to recuperate from a heart strain, Eden’s indisposition prevented him from making a personal report on his European trip at today’s crucial cabinet session, It also will eliminate him from the list of Great Britain's representatives at the tri-power conference.

1935-04-02.text: Milan, April 2—Premier Benito Mussolini today demanded that France, Great Britain and Italy adopt a united course of action in face of possible war. The forceful Duce, tired of what he called “the European diplomatic circuit” of statesmen’s visits to each other, demanded that at their conference at Stresa April 11 the foreign ministers of the three allied countries unite for action. His demand was made in his newspaper Popolo D'Italia, which he founded in 1914, when the World War broke out, to become the mouthpiece “that was to lead him to the heights of power. In an editorial, branding the diplomatic visits as a “circuit,” he warned against over-optimism regarding the Stresa conference, at which he will be host and on which, he said, “the usual castles of Mussolini are being built.” This was a reference to the speculation that at Stresa it will be possible to make an offer to Germany th

Warsaw, Apr. 2. (—Captain Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, began his conversations today with Polish statesmen who, it was hinted by the semi-official Gazetta Polska, may propose changes in the League of Nations. It was assumed that the conversations would amplify views leading to a new proposal for allaying mutual distrust among European nations and that the scheme might take the form of a re-named eastern European security pact that would satisfy Poland’s preferences for limited agreement, meet Germany’s opposition to the mutual assistance clause, and soothe the Russian fear regarding Polish-German intentions.

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) Warsaw, April 2 (UP)—An eastern European security treaty which will either include Germany or ring it with potentially hostile nations emerged today as the keystone of immediate armament negotiations. Captain Anthony Eden, special British cabinet envoy, began a two days series of talks with Polish leaders who will define their attitude toward such a treaty. Make It a Battlefield It was indicated at the outset that Poland is not prepared to enter the treaty originally proposed—a treaty which would seek to impose peace by military force and might make Poland a battlefield for contending Russian and German armies. London, Apr. 2. UPX—A naval petty officer who cut a shipmate’s throat was hanged today in Wadsworth jail while two airplanes hired by an anti-capital punishment group headed by a wealthy widow circled overhead. The airplanes trailed huge yellow banners reading “Stop the Death Sentence.” In the street in front of the jail, trucks drove back and forth with the strains of “Abide With Me” blaring forth from loudspeakers. Sandwich men distributed handbills to all who passed. Despite the noise and confusion outside, Petty Officer Leonard Albert Brigstock was dropped through the trap. He had killed Chief Petty Officer Deggan aboard the warship Marshal Soult January 19 at Chatham. Mrs. Violet Vanderlst, the Kensington widow who has declared war against the death penalty, organized the demonstration. (By The Associated Press) Warsaw, April 2—A hint that Polish statesmen may propose strengthening of the League of Nations in their talk with Capt. Anthony Eden was contained today in the Gazetta Polska, whose information is regarded as officially inspired. The visit of the British diplomat, the organ said editorially, comes at a time when the European symptoms, based on the Geneva organization, “begin to shiver.” “One must either modify and fortify the League or create a new system,” Gazetta Polska said. “The latter proposal is very difficult because such a new plan would have to be general and elastic to prove effective.” A full day was outlined for Eden beginning with preliminary conferences with a British mission. He will lunch with President Ignace Moscicki and join Marshal Joseph Pilsudski, the Polish dictator, for tea in the afternoon. There the principal discussions for which he c

By The Associated Press. Warsaw, April 1—Capt. Anthony Eden, Great Britain’s Lord Privy Seal and traveling salesman of peace brought to the capital of this "buffer" country tonight Russia's and Germany's plans regarding European security and found a cordial welcome in Poland. It was reported that Eden would discuss agreements. A Polish foreign office spokesman previously had said that while Poland was opposed to the pact in its present form any modification Eden might suggest after his arrival would be heard with interest. Poland's participation in such a pact is known to be one of Britain's chief desires.

Rome, April 2. (INS).—Ordering his people to take a realistic view of the European arms muddle, Premier Benito Mussolini to-day sensationally toppled the “castle of illusions” being built up around the Stresa conference. Britain, France and Italy, the nations that will send representatives to Lago Maggiore April 11, have not been in “complete unity of thought” since German rearmament was openly announced, and the only hope for Stresa was that their “identity of viewpoint be consecrated,” Il Duce said.

Warsaw, April 1 (#)—A loophole in Poland's opposition to the proposed eastern Locarno pact was tacitly offered by the foreign office today while the nation prepared a cordial welcome for Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, now on the home stretch of his European peace pilgrimage. Although emphasizing that Poland is opposed to the eastern pact in its present form, a foreign office spokesman said any modification Eden may suggest after his arrival tonight from Moscow would be listened to with interest. Poland's participation in such a pact is known to be one of Britain’s chief desires. The opposition of Poland's statesmen generally was pictured as that of champions of peace and status quo. The aged Marshal Joseph Pilsudsky, war minister and virtual dictator of Poland, will take the lead in the conversations, with Foreign Minister Joseph Beck assuming an active role. 1935-04-19.text: (Copyright 1935, by the Associated Press) Berlin, Apr. 19.—Warned by Great Britain and Italy that they will oppose any move to refortify the demilitarized Rhineland zone, Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler deliberated today on what stand he would take in face of international reproof for Germany's treaty repudiations. The ambassadors of the great European powers planned to stay close to Berlin during the Easter weekend awaiting what one envoy described as a colored Easter egg containing a serpent. Considerable surprise is felt in diplomatic circles that der Fuehrer has not acted before this time, at least for the purposes of counteracting at home the bad taste left by the Geneva resolution. Hitler's arrival at Munich to confer with his advisers led many to believe a statement may be forthcoming today or tomorrow, his 46th birthday. BERLIN, April 18—Great Britain and Italy, it was revealed tonight, have warned Germany she must let the demilitarized Rhineland alone. Ambassadors of the two powers yesterday presented their joint Stresa decision to maintain the status quo in the Rhineland, and Germany met that with “sizzling” diplomatic protest to Great Britain against League of Nations censure of the Reich’s rearmament. Nevertheless, Nazi officials today were inclined to look upon yesterday’s action at Geneva more calmly, partly because the British and Italian ambassadors, in response to pointed questions, gave the Foreign Office assurances of their government’s intention to fulfill to the full their obligations under the Locarno treaty. While the Foreign Office strove to pour oil on troubled waters and the press received instructions to handle the situation with gloves, Reichsführer Adolf Hitler left his Bavarian moun

BERLIN, April 19—(UP)—Adolf Hitler prepared today to give his birthday present to the world—a declaration of his views on the Stresa conference and the League Council's condemnation of his treaty violation. Following up a verbal protest to Great Britain and Italy against the League Council vote, Hitler intends tomorrow, on the occasion of his 46th birthday, to declare his views. It was indicated unofficially today that regardless of the strength of his protest against the course which the allied nations of Great Britain, France, and Italy are taking over German rearmament, Hitler would not bar the way to further negotiation. But it was learned that during the Council meeting, when its vote might have been foreseen, the government informally submitted to the French and Italian governments a series of questions concerning the proposed Danubian conference at Rome. LONDON, (UP) — All England started a four-day holiday. There were no newspapers. Stores as well as offices were closed, and there was almost a complete stoppage of normal activity in observance of Good Friday. Black Saturday, tomorrow, will be devoted entirely to sport. Stores will be open, and there will be newspapers, but most offices will remain closed. There will be Easter parades Sunday, and Monday is a bank holiday, with all business still paralyzed.

BERLIN, April 18 (P)—A “sizzling” diplomatic protest to Great Britain against League of Nations censure of Germany’s rearmament was followed tonight by calmer estimates of yesterday’s action at Geneva. One reason for this was the assurances the British and Italian ambassadors gave the foreign office last night that their governments intend to fulfill to the full their obligations under the Locarno treaty. At Mountain Retreat - Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler remained at Berchtesgaden, his Bavarian mountain retreat, closeted with several close collaborators to consider what form his reply to the League council's resolution shall take, if he decides to make any further pronouncement. While the foreign office strove to pour oil on troubled waters and the press received instructions to handle the international situation with gloves, it was revealed Bernard W. Von Buelow, foreign under-secretary,

An Anglo-Italian warning to Germany to keep hands off the demilitarized Rhineland was met by Germany’s vigorous protest to Britain against League of Nations disapproval of German rearmament, it was disclosed yesterday. Britain and Italian envoys Wednesday communicated to the Reich their governments’ joint decision at Stresa that the Rhineland's status quo must be continued, the former receiving in return a “signaling” expression of German displeasure at the Geneva action. Help to Clear Air Sensational, though they were, the two developments helped clear the air and German officials seemingly viewed the situation more calmly, the more so because Britain and Italy reiterated their determination to carry out fully their obligations under the Locarno treaty. British officials, however, feared that another of Adolf Hitler's “bombshells” might be in the making at the Fuehrer’s secret conferenc

(Copyright, 1930, BY U. F.) Paris, April 19—A French-Russian military agreement first of a many intended to ring Nazi Germany, was submitted to the cabinet today and was due to be initialed probably tomorrow. Approval by cabinet members of the draft treaty was regarded as a routine matter. Maxim Litvinov, Russian Foreign Minister, was due here tonight to initial the treaty with Pierre Laval, French Foreign Minister. Formal signature was expected when Laval visits Moscow on his delayed trip late in May. The treaty binds France and Russia to mutual aid against an aggressor which could only be Germany. The treaty will be left open for signature by Germany or any other nation. Its articles, as now drafted, are three in number. They provide for invocation of articles XV, XVI and XVII of the League of Nations covenant to provide first economic and financial, then military penalties, against an

Berlin, April 19—The death penalty, it was announced today, will be invoked in Nazi Germany to exterminate Pacifism in time of war or national emergency. The German board of jurisdiction said capital punishment would be made a feature of the law for "protection of the 'spirit' of the German defense force," which is being formulated to supplement the existing military law. "One of the three articles," the board announced, "is directed against the destructive work of Pacifists and anti-military organizations. Persons arranging meetings as well as people attending will be punished. "During the time of war or danger of war, life imprisonment will be changed to death penalties for hard. "The board’s announcement said two other articles of the new law would be designed to suppress Pacifistic influences in the German army and provide penalties for refusal to undergo military service.

1935-06-05.text: LONDON—(UP)—Ramsay MacDonald is expected to resign as Prime Minister at an audience with King George Friday morning, and to be succeeded by Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader. It is understood that the audience already has been arranged at Buckingham Palace, and that Baldwin will be summoned immediately afterward to take MacDonald’s place. Baldwin is expected to announce his cabinet Friday morning. MacDonald, in ill health and long planning retirement, presided at 19 Downing Street, his official residence, over a cabinet meeting this morning. It was the anniversary of his formation of the coalition cabinet in 1929, and was expected to be his last regular meeting as Prime Minister. There has been much speculation as to probable changes. The conservatives, national liberals and national laborites will continue to make up the cabinet. MacDonald may take an advisory post if his health perm

LONDON, June 5.—(AP)—Sir Malcolm Campbell, British sportsman, will attempt to better his own world’s automobile speed record at Salt Lake City in July, he announced. Campbell said he would leave for Utah in July for a new record attempt that month. He lifted the record to 276.816 miles per hour at Daytona Beach March 1. “It's impossible to rely in the future on the beach if you wish to do anything in the region of 300 miles an hour,” the sportsman said. “You must have 100 per cent perfect conditions for high speed. We now are carrying out further tests in our attempt in July.”

BY TANE@ Associated Press Epsom Downs, England, June 5. — Bahram, the favorite of the Aga Khan's stable, today won the one hundred fifty-sixth running of the Derby. Robin Goodfellow was second, and Field Trial third in the field of 16. One of the strongest favorites in recent years, Bahram went to the post the choice at five to four as the King and Queen and a half-million of their subjects saw the race. Robin Goodfellow, a 50 to one shot, was two lengths behind with Field Trial another half-length to the rear. The victory was the second Derby triumph for the Indian potentate. His Blenheim won the classic in 1930.

LONDON — Conviction of the Duke of Frana was quashed by the Criminal Court of Appeal which granted the Duke's appeal after his counsel established that he had no intention to defraud. The Duke was convicted last year of pawning family heirloom jewelry, left to his mother, which did not belong to him.

CHRISTCHURCH, England, June 5 (AP).—The body of a woman who stabbed herself six times in the chest and flung herself into the River Stour last night was identified today as that of Mrs. Alma Rattenbury, freed five days ago of charges of complicity in the mallet murder of her aged husband. William Mitchell, herdsman, told authorities he saw the woman sit on the river’s bank, thrust a dagger into her body and then plunge into the water. He said he attempted to seize her as she jumped and barely missed clutching her heel. The dagger sheath was found by the river in a handbag which also contained several notes. Some of the notes mentioned George Stoner, Mrs. Rattenbury’s 19-year-old chauffeur, who was sentenced to hang for beating Rattenbury to death with a mallet. Mrs. Rattenbury was 31 years old and a native of Victoria, B. C. She was married twice before becoming the wife of the 64-year-o

EPSOM DOWNS, Eng., June 5.— Justifying the odds that made him one of the shortest priced favorites in English turf history, Bahram, flaunting the silks of the Aga Khan, wealthy Indian potentate, drove to a smashing victory over 15 other three-year olds in the 156th running of the derby today. Held at 5 to 4 in the betting, the son of Blandford finished the one and one-half miles two lengths clear of Sir Abe Bailey's Robin Goodfellow, a 50 to 1 shot, as the king and queen and upwards of a half-million of their subjects packed every inch and corner of the rain-soaked downs. A half-length back of Robin Goodfellow came Lady Astor’s Field Trial, held at 9 to 1, showing the way to Theft, also a member of the Aga Khan's stable. Stretched out far to the rear were the others, including the third of the Indian potentate’s powerful entry, Hairan, (Continued On Page Four)

LONDON, June 5 (UP) — Mrs. Alma Victoria Rattenbury, beautiful black-haired songwriter, acquitted five days ago of the mallet murder of her rich, aging husband, walked slowly into the river Stour last night to drown after stabbing herself six times. Her body was identified by police and by Miss Irene Riggs, her former companion. On the body was found a note to George Percy Stoner, 19, the Rattenbury family chauffeur and her confessed lover, awaiting execution June 15 as the murderer of the husband, Francis Mason Rattenbury, 67. Mrs. Rattenbury, 31, was acquitted at the famous Old Bailey criminal court here May 31. Stoner was convicted and sentenced to death.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, June 5 (®).--Fourteen American fortunes in the Irish Free State Hospital Sweepstakes worth a total of £400,000—nearly $1,500,000—rode with Bahram, Robin Goodfellow and Field Trial, the horses that came in first, second and third in the English Derby today. Americans held seven winning tickets on Bahram, four on Robin Goodfellow, and three on Field Trial. Tickets on Bahram, worth $148,500 each, were issued to the following in the United States: "Past Due," Brooklyn, N. Y.; F.C. Prall, Buffalo, N. Y.; T. O’Berle, New York City; Miss Hocken and three others, Oakland, Pa.; Joseph Taymoe, Allston, Mass.; "Jack and Sondra Brody," Dorchester, Mass.; A. T. Tiethaway, and L. Hanser, Wilkes-Barre, Pa. 1935-10-20.text: (BY Associated Press) London, Oct. 19—Great Britain intends to maintain her battle fleet in the Mediterranean, authoritative sources said today despite an easing of the Italian-British tension and a definite understanding with France. The British government was represented as feeling that Premier Laval of France has definitely removed any misunderstanding which previously existed between Great Britain and France. These authorities said, however, that since no progress yet had been made toward the settlement of the main issue—the Italo-Ethiopian war—the Mediterranean fleet would have to remain at its present station, although it was possible that a few ships might later be removed from Gibraltar as a conciliatory gesture. It was stated in informed quarters that diplomatic conversations now in progress in Rome and in Paris were all designed to clear up side issues and that there had been n

(by the Associated Press) France, albeit still conciliatory, threw in its lot with Great Britain in the Afro-European crisis today; but the efforts of its premier, Pierre Laval, had lessened somewhat the tension between Italy and Britain. There was not the slightest indication the diplomatic conversations of the last few days had changed Dictator Mussolini’s intentions to push his drive into the interior of Haile Selassie’s Ethiopian empire. Push Boycott Plan, At Geneva, where the British stand firm in their efforts to punish Mussolini’s fascist government for this aggression, the League of Nations sanctions committee of 18 nations approved the British proposal for a “buy nothing from Italy” boycott. (Associated Press Staff Writer) The peace talk of Friday turns out now to have had ‘nothing to do with the Italo-Ethiopian war. It was peace talk about a non-existent war—the “war” many diplomats feared was brewing between Italy and Great Britain. The war of bombs and bullets, of dead and wounded, goes on. (Continued on Page 9, Col. 8.)

LONDON, Oct. 19.—(#)—A gale racing as high as 100 miles an hour in some sections of Scotland swept the British Isles early today, disrupting shipping and causing at least one death at Glasgow, Scotland. Five others were injured at Glasgow by falling debris. The anchor liner Transylvania, due to leave Glasgow for New York at 2 a.m. with 240 passengers, was held up by the gale, but officials hoped the ship could sail on the afternoon tide. Many small boats in the Clyde river, Scotland, were smashed and sunk. Telephone communications between Edinburgh and Newcastle were cut.

The Associated Press Maintenance of peace in Europe received tacit guarantee today, and establishment of peace in war-torn Ethiopia appeared to be more than a possibility. British diplomacy, hard at work in Rome and Paris, succeeded in easing the tension on international nerve centers, calming fears of extended conflicts at arms incident to the Italo-Ethiopian war. Crisis Temporarily Passed Negotiations among Italy, Great Britain and France revived hopes for a stilling of cubs in East Africa. Just when Italian-British tension over the question of Italy’s abandoning its Ethiopian campaign was becoming acute, Downing Street let it be known that the crisis, at least for the moment, was past, and that some of Britain’s vessels in the western Mediterranean eventually may be withdrawn. (By United Press) ROME—War clouds over Great Britain and Italy lifting as prolonged diplomatic maneuvers bring Anglo-Italian truce in the Mediterranean. Italy to reduce Libyan forces and Great Britain to withdraw some warships. ROME—Fighting in Ethiopia, which has been quiet, is about to start with renewed vigor as 200,000 Italian troops on the northern front make ready for an imminent “zero” hour which will plunge them deep into Ethiopia. GENEVA—General staff of the League of Nations penalties committee adopts proposal for complete boycott of Italian goods to take effect Oct. 31. PARIS—Great Britain receives promise from France of support. HARAR—Italy’s three columns pointed northward from Italian Somaliland drive slowly toward a common junction as desultory hostilities continue on three fronts. WORCESTER, Eng. 4. Premier Stanley Baldwin, voicing faith in the League of Nations, made what many interpreted to be a direct bid for the United States to join the league. Britain's leader told his political constituents that the failure of the league to end the war in Africa would not mean the end of the league itself. “I would say rather,” he asserted, “that if this first attempt by the world to secure peace fails let us see whether our machinery or whether our work may have been at fault; let us try again and let us see once more whether we cannot get those still outside the league to join the league.” Baldwin made a direct appeal to Italy to understand that Britain's eye to the Ethiopian campaign is motivated “solely” by concern for world peace, rather than any hostility toward Italy or a desire to overthrow fascism. Striking while the iron is hot in the wake of an apparent easing of

Great Britain and France reached an understanding on French aid for the British fleet in the Mediterranean should any emergency arise from the imposition of sanctions. The League of Nations sanctions committee approved a "buy nothing from Italy" proposal. It went to the full plenary committee of the League. The French premier, Pierre Laval, found some success in his efforts to lessen the tension between Italy and England. The British fleet, however, will remain in the Mediterranean. Perhaps later, a few ships may be withdrawn. None of the diplomatic conversations, however, brought any hope for an end to Italy’s conquest in Ethiopia. MILITARY MANEUVERS General Emilio de Bono, Italian commander-in-chief, announced the abolition of slavery in all Ethiopian territory held by Italy. 1935-08-04.text: GENEVA, Aug. 3 (UP). — The council of the League of Nations, feebly sparring for time in the international effort to prevent war between Italy and Ethiopia, adopted a compromise plan tonight designed to delay hostilities for at least a month. In the interval, Britain and France will do their utmost to divert the dispute into peaceful channels. The compromise is in two parts, as follows: 1. The two arbitrators named by Italy and the two by Abyssinia will resume their interrupted negotiations, naming a fifth and neutral member to cast the deciding vote. The commission’s work will be strictly limited in scope, however, and will decide only on responsibility for the border clashes at Ualual and elsewhere, in which each nation claims the other was the aggressor.
