LONDON, Aug. 3. (J.)—Paul Humphrey MacNeils, well-known inventor of infra-red ray instruments and native of Niles, Mich., announced today that he had been demonstrating devices similar to "death ray" machines to the British government for many months. It was asserted in apparently reliable quarters that one of MacNeils' devices for locating faraway airplanes by their engines’ heat was so delicate that MacNeils, demonstrating to the air ministry, was able to locate a hidden man by the heat of his body.

Ethiopia accepted today the League of Nations' formula to settle her quarrel with Italy. After hours of study, Emperor Haile Selassie late this afternoon made this brief announcement: “I have instructed my delegate to Geneva to accept the league's proposals as elaborated by Mr. Eden and Premier Laval.” Earlier, Selassie had expressed willingness to sit down at a conference table with Benito Mussolini in an effort to settle their difference. A foreign office official said the ruler was awaiting advancement of such a proposal by Rome or Geneva, but that thus far no such move had been made. His only stipulation, it was explained, is that the talks be held on neutral territory, possibly in France. Expressions of good will toward Ethiopia came from a number of quarters as the government considered a decision on the formula adopted at Geneva to settle the dispute. Owners of a number of newspap

(Copyright, 1935, By The Associated Press) Moscow, Aug. 3.—The Soviet Trans-Polar plane, carrying three daring airmen on a non-stop flight across the roof of the world toward San Francisco, headed out across the Barents Sea at 2:25 p.m. (7:25 a.m. E.S.T.). The plane, UR. S. 25, radioed at that time that it was heading out over the 2,391-mile stretch of water and polar ice and into the zone of continuous polar daylight. Pilot Sigmund Laveneffsky reported he was averaging about 110 miles an hour after reaching the sea. Roaring toward open water on their daring across the pole to America route, the Soviet Arctic fliers radioed at 11:42 a.m. Moscow time (5:42 a.m. Eastern Standard Time) that they were “approaching White Sea.”

MOSCOW, Aug. 3.—Oil trouble over the icy Barents Sea thwarted tonight the ambitious attempt of three Russians to fly non-stop from Moscow to San Francisco, across the North Pole. Disappointed, the fliers turned about when over the southern part of the sea and returned to Leningrad tonight, arriving at 10:30 p.m. Moscow time, 12:30 p.m. E.S.T. Dream Is Spoiled A defective oil line spoiled their dream of setting a new world’s non-stop record in a 6,000-mile hop to the Golden Gate from Moscow. A radio message, after eight hours of silence, said a line from the distribution tank began throwing off excessive quantities of oil and the crew was unable to discover the cause. They had made the first part of their flight—an 875-mile stretch from Moscow to the Barents Sea—at an average speed of 106 miles an hour, considerably better than had been expected. ATHENS, Greece, Aug. 5 (UP)— The revolt of workers on the Island of Crete was ended tonight. The strikers accepted a two-hour ultimatum requiring them to surrender their arms and dissolve unconditionally. ATHENS, Greece, Aug. 5 (UP)—Martial law was proclaimed today in Candia, Crete, to cope with a revolt against the government which started amongst workers and was joined by the Venizelists. The government, dispatching two destroyers and five bombing planes to silence the strikers, said the strikers had not captured the public buildings in Candia, as they claimed. Four thousand laborers gathered in front of the prefecture at Candia and clamored for higher wages. When they refused to disperse, police and troops charged them and there was sharp fighting. 50 were reported injured. The strikers still refused to disperse and members went to a gunsmith’s shop where they seized the entire stock

Moscow, Aug 3—The crew of the Soviet polar plane abandoned their projected non-stop flight to San Francisco tonight because of oil trouble and turned back. The craft was nearing the North Pole, over the Barents Sea, when the trouble was discovered. It wired officials here for permission to return, which was granted. Ejection of lubricating oil from the feeding tank caused excessive consumption of oil, it was explained. The fliers said they were unable to ascertain or remove the cause of this trouble. They turned about and headed across the Kola Peninsula towards Leningrad. A special commission was ordered to examine the airplane when it lands and investigate the causes of the trouble. 1935-06-10.text: Hollywood, Calif., June 8 — To read what all these critics of our country write, you would naturally think that everybody else was just sitting pretty. But France has offered their premiership to everybody over there but Chevalier, and they know he is too smart to take it. England just today traded horses right in the middle of Thames river. Half of Italy has gone to Africa with a gun on their shoulder. Japan is just looking over Chinese maps to see where to send their army. Russia must be in some devilment, we never hear of ‘em any more. So you see there are none of ‘em that we can point with pride to. It’s just a bad time to be in the government business anywhere. Yours.

CAGLIARI, Sardinia, June 8. (#) Premier Mussolini told soldiers departing for East Africa today, “We have an old and new account to settle with Ethiopia and we will settle with them. Speaking to 20,000 soldiers and a huge crowd of blackshirts, Mussolini made a sharp pointed reference to England. He said, “We will imitate to the letter those who try to teach us a lesson. They demonstrated that when they are creating an empire by defending it they never took into consideration world opinion.”

Mussolini hopes today to moderate the bitterness of their attack on Great Britain in connection with the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Although he did not command the press to suspend its anti-British comment entirely, the premier, acting through his son-in-law Count Galeazzo Ciano, under secretary of state for press and propaganda, enjoined publications to keep the tone of their campaign within certain limitations. Il Duce is said to have been startled by the extreme degree of antagonism reflected in newspaper articles and editorials in the last few days. The torrent of denunciation of Great Britain's attitude toward the East African crisis culminated in a front page editorial in the Super-Fascist Daily Ottobre in which the British were warned that if they wanted war they might have it. London, June 10.—-(#)--Word that Premier Mussolini has applied the soft pedal to the anti-British campaign

LAYTON, Mo., June 10 (UP).—Jack C. Coffee was a happier and richer man today. His new-born and prepaid twin daughters were alive and healthy and Lloyds of London were ready to pay the $1000 due him as a far-sighted father, who took out anti-twin insurance last January. Friday night Mrs. Coffee gave birth to twin daughters. Saturday night Coffee made application to collect on his policy, which stipulated that twins must live for 24 hours before the insurance could be collected. The girls, Cynthia and Carol, paid little attention to the financing of their existence. Reported as “doing all right” they acted much as all babies do.

St. Louis, June 10.—An incubator holds twin girls and their father’s hopes of collecting a $1,000 insurance policy on their birth. To protect himself against the financial woes of unexpected parenthood, Jack Coffey, 34, last February paid a $90 premium on a policy under which Lloyd's of London agreed to pay him $1,000 if twins were born to Mrs. Coffey. “We were so certain of twins, we named them in advance,” said Mr. Coffey, employed by a Detroit commercial motion picture company. He said the insurance concern had raised its premium from $50 to $90 after learning of other instances of twins in the family.

NEW YORK, June 10.—(1P)—The Jonker diamond, largest uncut gem of its kind, which was brought to New York from England by registered mail at 29 cents although insured for $1,000,009.60, will be taken in an armored truck today for appraisal at the customs house. The big chunk of crystallized carbon—the same substance as coal but with a different atomic structure—arrived aboard the liner President Roosevelt in an ordinary mail sack. Four men guarded the sack across the Atlantic. It was carried under guard to the main post office where it remained overnight. The stone, ellipsoidal in shape, two and three-fourths inches in length, one and one-half inches in height, about an inch across and weighing 726 carats, is owned by Harry Winston, dealer in precious gems. Winston purchased the stone in England at a figure in excess of 700,000.

TOKYO, June 10 — Chinese troops were reported in Japanese news dispatches today to have started their evacuation of North China, signalizing what the messages described as China’s complete surrender to the demands of Japanese military authorities. These reports said the threat of an occupation by General Jiro Minami’s war machine was sufficient to persuade the Chinese nationalist government to capitulate to the Japanese requirements for establishment of a new regime in North China. As a consequence, the Japanese press said, the Japanese troops concentrated in Hopei Province, although ready for action, will not be called on to move southward, at least for the present. The reports indicated that a precedent has been established conceding the Japanese army the right to indicate who shall administer and what troops shall be stationed in Hopei Province. HELSINGFORS, Finland, June 10.—(/)—Finland will pay its war debt installment due the United States June 15 in money already earmarked in the National City Bank of New York. (Finland is the only one of the war debtor nations which has paid the debt installments, amounting to about $52 million dollars. Risto F. Cit, governor of the Bank of Finland, responding to the semi-annual question as to whether Finland would pay the installment and why, replied: "Yes, because it is a contractual debt; because it is the natural thing to do; because Finland can afford to pay; because the debt, strictly speaking, is a post-war debt which brought relief to Finland when such relief was vital to the welfare of the country."

1935-03-28.text: (Copyright: 1935, Associated Press) Moscow, Mar, 28—Foreign Com- missar Maxim Litvinoff and Capt. Anthony Eden, British Lord of the Privy Seal, today discussed “the conclusions to which the Berlin negotiations are leading” during a two-hour conference on the peace of Europe. The British envoy, received with honors, talked to Litvinoff in the latter’s office in the foreign ministry and the description of the subject of their talk was made later by well-informed quarters. These sources were unable to say what nature of “conclusions” were meant. It was stated, however, that Litvinoff and Eden “have had no disagreement on the problems discussed.” Their parley was described as being conducted in “an extremely friendly atmosphere.” Captain Eden informed Litvinoff of the conversations he and Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, had with Reichsführer Hitler and other German leaders in

MIAMI, MAR. 2. (AP).—President Roosevelt cruised aboard the yacht Nourmahal in the clear blue waters of the Bahama Island group today on his annual fishing trip. Reaching the Bahamas yesterday, he received the Duke and Duchess of Kent, members of the British royal family honeymooning in this region, who were introduced by Sir Bede Clifford, governor of the Bahamas, and Lady Clifford. Mr. Roosevelt kept contact with Washington through temporary headquarters at the Miami-Biltmore hotel, where Marvin H. McIntyre, a secretary, was established with a staff. He was garbed today in clothes which included a somewhat spotted white sweater and a fisher’s hat, ready to try his luck for the game fish of this region. With McIntyre at the Miami headquarters was Federal Relief Administrator Harry L. Hopkins, who has the last minute executive instructions regarding the $4,000,000,000 work program now be

Cheers greeted Sir John from all parts of the House as he rose to reply to the inquiry of George Lansbury, laborite, on what happened at Berlin. The members were eager with anticipation as they waited to hear what Hitler proposed in his talks with the British envoys on the security system envisaged in the re- Germany made wide demands as a statement as to the position, which still is under investigation. "Unauthorized speculations such as have appeared in some quarters," Simon said, "may be disregarded."

French officials, meanwhile, urged strengthening of co-operation among France, Britain and Italy and looked forward to the tri-power conference at Stresa, Italy, early in April as offering an opportunity to encircle Germany with pacts. Berlin—British quarters hinted that Great Britain, by direction, might not regard unfavorably some German military rehabilitation to check France's hegemony and curb Russia’s power. Copyright, 1935, The Associated Press BERLIN, March 26.—Anglo-German security discussions ended late today apparently without providing a solution for any of the major problems imperiling Europe's peace. Britain's representatives were obviously disappointed, while the Germans seemed as determined as ever in their old demand for complete equality among nations. A brief, vaguely-phrased official communique revealed little other than the bare fact that the conversations, held "in the frankest and friendliest spirit," took up the matters "set out in the London communique of February 3." Highlights Are Cited Authoritative sources, however, said the highlights of the last day's parley between Sir John Simon and Capt. (By United Press). Moscow, March 28. — Great Britain and Russia got together today on peace in Europe and themselves in agreement on means of attaining it. After a two-hour conversation between Capt. Anthony Eden of Great Britain and Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov, it was learned from official sources that the two found themselves in agreement on all points discussed so far, The points were not enumerated but they obviously included an eastern Europe security pact and the problem of maintaining European peace if it is menaced by Germany's rearmament.

Dublin, Mar. 28 (UP) - President Eamonn De Valera directly snubbed the King of England today when he announced in the Dail that he had notified Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald he was unable to accept an invitation to the king’s silver Jubilee celebration this summer. De Valera said he had told MacDonald he could not attend “in the circumstances now existing.” John W. Dulanty will attend in his capacity as Free State high commissioner in London.

LONDON (WP) — Adolf Hitler has demanded restoration to Germany of at least one colony and formal abolition of the Versailles military treaty clauses, it was said Thursday of semi-official authority. He demanded also, it was said, that the League of Nations covenant must be separated from the treaty. These conditions, it was said, (Continued on Page Two.)

1935-03-21.text: (Copyright, 1935, By The Associated Press) LONDON. — A smashing vote of confidence in the French senate for the French government's determined efforts to curb German rearmament Wednesday followed closely decisions of the British, French and Italian governments to hold direct discussions of the problem. Great Britain, yielding to French and Italian insistence, agreed to abandon diplomatic negotiations and send Capt. Anthony Eden, lord privy seal, to Paris for the tripartite conference, to be held one day before Eden and Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, go to Berlin to confer with Adolf Hitler. France The vote of confidence given Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin’s stout resistance in the face of Hitler’s decision to renew compulsory military training in Germany gave additional evidence of the French determination to act alone in the face of the German threat, if necessary. Simultane

Washington, March 21.— (4%) President Roosevelt and his advisers on foreign affairs today studied a report from the American embassy in London giving the British official version of the situation created by Germany's rearmament plan. The first report to be made to this government on direct conversations on the subject, the dispatch came from Ray Atherton, charge d'affaires at London, who was called to the British foreign office by the foreign secretary Sir John Simon to receive. There was no announcement as to its specific contents nor any information as to official reaction to it here. Meanwhile the consultations with state department officials which have occupied a good portion of Roosevelt's time in the past continued today. From these, the president hoped to decide on the wisest course for the United States to pursue in the European crisis.

DAYTONA BEACH, Fla, March 21—(4)—Sir Malcolm Campbell decided today to abandon further attempts here this year to break his automobile speed record of 276.216 miles an hour. He ordered the Bluebird crated and will leave as soon as possible for England. The condition of the beach caused Campbell's decision. He will sail on the Berengaria from New York March 30.

LONDON (UP) — “We are marching towards war,” George Lansbury, labor leader, declared in the House of Commons today in opening full debate on foreign affairs and the European crisis. Lansbury was interrupted by cries of ‘no, no, not yet,' but he continued to declare that the citizens of Britain and other countries are living in a state of war mentality and demanded that European statesmen act. “Never have I observed such a feeling of dread expectation that something dreadful was go- (Turn to Page 6—No. 11.)

LONDON, March 21—Germany’s rejection of the French and Italian protests against her rearmament was regarded Thursday in unofficial but informed circles as an unexpected jolt which may cause another crisis before Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Reichsfuehrer Hitler meet in Berlin for their once-postponed conversations.

| BERLIN, March 21.—Flatly rejecting protests lodged by France and Britain against Reich rearmament, Germany staged a brilliant diplomatic counter march by accusing the former allies of violating the Versailles treaty and flouting the obligations. | The refusal was tantamount to a threat by Germany to the allies and took the form of a public warning that the Reich stands on a firm footing and will not be dictated to by the other powers.

NATIONAL BEACH, Flag. (fi. Sir Malcolm Campbell's 1935 speed trials are finished. The British driver took one last look at the beach today and told his mechanics to prepare Bluebird, his automobile, for shipment.

NEW YORK, March 18—The military minds of the world turned today to Europe's 17,000,000 mobilizable fighting men while England protested Germany's establishment of a conscript army of 500,000 men as an affront to the security of Europe. At a cost of more than three billion dollars yearly, Europe's leading military powers maintain their standing armies and lines of reserves so that if need be a greater complement of war forces can be put in the field than at any time in the world’s history. Military observers consider that foremost among the fighting machines—with the possible exception of the Russian enigma—is France. Standing on almost the same footing as France are England and Italy. Less strong are the smaller powers of Poland, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia. The two great mysteries are Russia and Germany. 1935-12-12.text: Ethiopia said “no” today to the latest effort to end its East African war with Italy by negotiation. Scarcely had peace terms agreed upon by Great Britain and France been dispatched to Addis Ababa before the empire's minister in Paris announced his government was unalterably opposed to any plan for settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian war which would “reward Italian aggression.” Ethiopia, he added, will adhere to the principle of its territorial and political integrity. The peace formula drafted in Paris by Premier Pierre Laval and Sir Samuel Hoare, Britain's foreign minister, was understood to encompass cession of considerable land to Italy in return for the latter's providing Ethiopia with an outlet to the Red Sea. The Italian government was silent, although high Fascists expressed the opinion the proposal delivered to the premier, whether completely satisfactory or not, was likely to for

GENEVA, Dec. 12.—The small powers, angered by the concessions made to Premier Benito Mussolini in the Franco-British peace proposals, won a tactical victory today as soon as the league’s penalties committee of eighteen assembled. In the first skirmish against the Franco-British plan, the small powers succeeded in forcing an agreement for a full debate on it when the council convenes next Tuesday. Opposition of Turkey and Poland obliged France and Britain to abandon their plan to submit the peace proposal to the council's committee of five, where, with the support of Spain, they would have a majority. The committee of five is composed of France, Britain, Spain, Poland and Turkey. Under those circumstances, the committee of five could continue negotiations with Premier Benito Mussolini and the emperor of Ethiopia as it wished. Consequently, it becomes necessary to submit the plan directly

(Associated Press Staff Writer) A tide of rebellion surged against the Franco-British proposals for peace between Italy and Ethiopia in East Africa today as British diplomacy sought to allay another crisis tangent to the war. With London’s consent King Faud of Egypt signed a royal decree restoring constitutional government to his nation. The relation between efforts to settle the war as quickly as possible and pour oil on the troubled waters of Egyptian politics was pictured in League of Nations circles as due to Britain’s worry over anti-British demonstrations in Egypt which complicated the Mediterranean imbroglio. Want “Front” Then, too, those circles said, Downing Street is anxious to re-establish quickly the damaged “united front” erected by Italy, France and Great Britain at the Stresa conference. London, Dec. 12 (UP)—Seven delegations, led by Great Britain and the United States, rejected Japan's demand for naval equality today. It was learned from the United States delegation after the conference adjourned until tomorrow that Norman H. Davis, head of the delegation, had presented three arguments against Japan’s claim. Plan Unworkable There were intended to show that the Japanese plan for bringing the navies of the three strongest naval powers to the same level—as outlined yesterday by Admiral Osami Nagano, head of the Japanese delegation—was both unworkable and unacceptable. In the first place the United States ambassador at large contended it would result in an increase rather than a decrease in naval building. Secondly, Davis insisted, it was learned, that the Japanese project would upset Washington and London treaty arrangements which he said had created an equilibrium based u

By The Associated Press London, Dec. 11 — Admiral Osami Nagano placed Japan’s demands for a navy as large as that of any other major world power squarely before the delegates to the international naval conference today. The admiral was the only speaker and the session was adjourned until tomorrow when the American and British delegates will reply to the Japanese demands. Non-Japanese experts said that because the British and Americans have not built up to treaty strength while the Japanese have, Japan already possesses a modern under-age fleet of considerably greater strength than the treaty 5-5-3 relations. British, American, and similar interests are opposing Japan’s party demands for a new treaty.

) CAIRO, Egypt, Dec. 12. (AP)— King Faud today signed a royal decree restoring constitutional government to Egypt. Great Britain consented to the move after a persistent nationalist anti-British campaign which has resulted in several fatal riots. The new constitution provides for a senate and chamber of deputies and takes control of the country’s internal affairs away from the British. It does not affect British control of Egyptian foreign affairs nor the present British military protectorate.

Emperor Haile Selassie, although much of his kingdom is occupied by enemy troops, appeared certain Wednesday to reject a plan put forward by Great Britain and France. Ethiopia's minister to Paris told Premier Laval his country would resist any move to give a "premium for the Italian aggressor." Officials in Ethiopia denounced the plan, saying its acceptance would cause a revolt forcing Haile Selassie from the throne. They were bitter toward France and incredulous that Britain had approved the plan. In quarters other than Geneva the formula evoked sharp disapproval. Smaller nations of the League of Nations said they would stand fast against any violation of Ethiopia's sovereignty and the league covenant. Geneva Officials Nettled. LONDON. (A deadlock threatened the international naval conference after Japan's demands for a fleet equal to that of the United States and Great Britain were formally put forward. Admiral Osami Nagano, head of the Oriental delegation, said a total tonnage basis for the three biggest sea powers should be fixed “as low as possible.” A French delegate, Jacques Stern, it was understood, told Admiral Nagano that naval strategists feel approval of Japan's demands would give Tokyo unquestioned naval supremacy in the Far East, leaving the interests of other nations there at the mercy of the Japanese. Americans made no comment. The three-day-old conference thus faces at its outset a supreme test of its ability to find a formula permitting nations to continue along the road to naval limitation, begun in 1922. 1935-06-24.text: ROME—(4)—Well-informed sources said today that Premier Mussolini, in conference with Capt. Anthony Eden of Great Britain, is prepared to demand the exclusion of Ethiopia from the League of Nations if the British diplomat raises the subject of the Italo-Ethiopian conflict and its effect upon the League. Official Italian circles said they hoped the subject would not be brought up between the two statesmen but British authorities said they considered its discussion inevitable. The two foregathered at Venezia Palace this morning and conversed for two hours on the Anglo-German naval pact and the proposed western European aviation agreement. Italian sources said Il Duce turned a deaf ear to Eden's explanations of Great Britain's naval accord with Germany.

ROME, June 24. (®)—Italian circles said Premier Benito Mussolini turned a deaf ear today to Capt. Anthony Eden's explanations of the Anglo-German naval accord. The Italians predicted freely that no results would come from the conference between Mussolini and Britain's roving representative, save possibly a European air accord. Concerning the Anglo-German naval accord, they said Mussolini told Captain Eden he couldn't approve the unilateral manner in which it was reached without bringing Italy and France into the final discussion.

(By The Associated Press) Labor disputes spread sporadically over the United States today. In New England, the United Textile Workers of America called out its members in mills operated by the Uxbridge Worsted company. Early reports said approximately 2,800 of the mills’ 3,375 employees answered the call. This was the first serious dispute in the frequently-turbulent textile industry in New England since the expiration of the codes. Ask Wage Increase The union issued the strike call as a protest against the alleged lowering of code operating standards and to enforce a demand for wage increases. The company’s mills were affected in Uxbridge, Mass., Putnam, Conn., Woonsocket, R. I., Pascoag, R. I., and Lowell, Mass. The demand for higher wages also brought a strike call from the International Seamen's union to members employed in oil tankers owned by the Cities Service company. Four tanker

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, June 24-()—The two governments of Ireland encountered open threats of serious trouble today—from Republicans in the south and Orangemen in the north. The Irish Free State already was a scene of violence, the Irish republican army and the Irish citizen army having come into conflict at Bodenstown, County Kildare, where urgent pleas for independence were uttered. A free-for-all, in which several casualties were reported, flared up Sunday as thousands of republicans cheered the challenge of Sean McBride, member of the republican army executive council, who asserted: “Republicans fill the gaols of the north and south, but the republican movement is on a rising tide, gathering strength.” McBride and Maurice Twomey, chief of staff of the republican army, came out of hiding to take part in the annual army celebrations at the grave of Wolfe Tone, famous Irish patriot, a

PARIS. — The newspaper DL Oeuvre published a report Monday that Col. T. E. Lawrence is not dead, but is acting as military adviser to Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia. The article, coming from Cairo, said "Lawrence of Arabia" was not killed in a cycling accident in England but arrived in Africa late in April with an assistant named Gardner, who aided him in his Arabian adventures.

ROME, June 23.-P}—Great Britain's roving diplomat, Captain Anthony Eden, arrived tonight in Rome, faced with a united Italo-French front in opposition to Britain’s methods of obtaining a naval agreement with Germany. His welcome was cool. Fulvio Suvich, under-secretary for foreign affairs, went to the station to meet him, but there was no demonstration such as usually accompanies a statesman’s arrival, and the customary top hats were missing. Shortly before Eden got here from Paris talks, Suvich received Charles De Chambrun, the French ambassador, who had just returned from Paris. Suvich, it was understood, told him the Italian viewpoint on England's accord allowing Germany to build up to 25 percent of her naval strength was identical with that of France. Both governments object to the unilateral manner in which London reached an agreement without taking into consideration the opinions o

| MUIRFIELD, Scotland, June 24; (#)—MacDonald Smith, the veteran Scot, who makes his headquarters at Glendale, Calif, laid claim early to the shot-making honors in the 36-hole qualifying round for the British Open golf championship today with a six under par, first round 66 fired over the neighboring Gullane course. The 45-year-old veteran, who has been seeking a major title for more than a score of years, toured the first nine in 34—one under par—and then came back in 32, displaying some of the finest golf ever shot in this weather country. Smith was one of the three early finishers to break par on the Gullane course. Percy Alliss of England and P. J. Mahon, a young Irish professional, reported sub-par 70's, while Frank Ball, formerly from Atlanta, Ga, came up with a par 72. Bad driving, rather than the heavy mist, contributed to a high first round 78 for William Lawson Little, Jr., the

(Associated Press Leased Wire) PROVIDENCE, R. I., June 24.--New England's first serious labor trouble since NRA’s demise centered today around the seven mills of the Uxbridge Worsted Company, with reports indicating that 2850 of the 3375 workers responded to a strike call. The strike, called by United Textile Workers of America officials, affected operations in six of the plants. Although officials of the company in the various strike areas contended they were unaware of any demands having been made on the behalf of workers, union leaders said they wanted a 20 per cent wage increase and equalization of the machine load. No disturbances were reported at any of the plants.

1935-03-05.text: BERLIN, Mar. 5.—()—Reichsfuehrer Hitler today postponed his scheduled conference with Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, “on account of a cold” but Berlin diplomatic circles expressed the opinion that Hitler was offended by yesterday's British white paper. These diplomatic circles characterized the side-stepping of the conference Thursday as a “diplomatic form” of canceling the long-expected talk completely. (The British white paper, given to parliament in connection with the British government's plea for an increase in military expenditures, alluded to charges that Germany was rearming and said: “This rearmament, if continued at the present rate, unabated and uncontrolled, will aggravate the existing anxiety of Germany's neighbors and may consequently produce a situation where peace will be in peril.”)

LONDON, (4%. Great Britain added $19,750,000 to the 1935 army budget estimates and blamed the increase on Germany's increased armaments. A new elastic policy of expansion for British empire defenses was initiated in a white paper presented to parliament by Prime Minister MacDonald almost on the eve of Sir John Simon's peace mission to Berlin. MacDonald, in an unexpected attack, attributed Britain's feeling of insecurity particularly upon German rearmament, but also included to some extent American, Russian, Japanese and other increases in arms. Added increases for the British air force and the navy will be made known during the week. The British government jumped on the force and spirit with which the German people are being organized, and warned that peace was endangered. While such criticism has been made before in various ways it takes on new significance just when Britain is trying t
Berlin Reichsführer Hitler today sensationally cancelled plans for a proposed conference with Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, attributing his act to a head cold.

| London, Mar. 5.—Great Britain made public today plans to meet Europe's winged competition by adding 11 squadrons to its home defense air force during 1935. _. (A British squadron consists of 12 airplanes.) | Estimates of this year’s air defense expenditures totaled 23,851,100 pounds (approximately $119,255,500), an increase of 3,685,500 pounds (approximately $18,427,500) over the figure for 1934. | The addition of 11 squadrons will bring the home defense force up to a total of 54 squadrons, 41 of which compose the regular air force and the rest auxiliary craft. It also is planned to increase the strength of the air force by adding 19 first-line aircraft. These new formations will raise the total strength of the royal air force to 106 squadrons, of which 93 will be in regular service. The estimates reflect the first stage of the expansion program which parliament approved last summer. T

London, March 5. (INS).—Piling up arms to new heights for the postwar period, the government announced to-day that eleven airplane squadrons, totaling 132 machines, will be added to the home defense force in the forthcoming year as the first phase of the air’s share of a co-ordinated land, sea, and sky security program. Air estimates for 1935-36 laid before the House of Commons called for an increase of $18,427,500, bringing the total to $119,255,500. Yesterday, warning that German rearmament “may produce a situation where peace will be in peril,” the cabinet asked for an increase of $19,750,000 in the army estimates. To-morrow more money for the navy will be sought. The eleven new home defense squadrons will bring that branch up to a strength of fifty-four squadrons, usually of twelve planes each. In addition, new units for the naval air force are planned, bringing the total strength of

The government announced today that an accord had been reached at Addis Ababa for the creation of a neutral zone along the Italian Somaliland border, the scene of hostilities which precipitated the Italo-Ethiopian crisis. The announcement was made following the receipt of a telegram from the Italian minister at Addis Ababa. "The basis of an accord for the construction of a neutral zone," the government spokesman said, "has been reached at Addis Ababa. The zone will be six kilometers (about four miles) wide."

VIENNA, Mar. 5.—(#)—A wave of apprehension swept through Vienna today when unconfirmed reports indicated Turkish troops were gathering on the Greek frontier because of the Civil war in Greece. The same reports said that the Bulgarian border guard had been strengthened in view of the situation in Greek Macedonia where loyal government troops are making a desperate drive to suppress the rebellion. Some refugees from the fight already are said to have arrived at Petritch in Bulgarian Macedonia.

ATHENS, (Copyright by AP.) (Tuesday.) After a smashing land victory, the government rushed mine layers to Saloniki early Tuesday to mine the harbor’s entrance and prevent any attempt by the rebel fleet to put in at the Macedonian fort. This action strengthened reports the government has determined to “smoke out” the insurgent fleet from Souda bay, off Crete, and force a decisive sea battle. Two destroyers and two submarines were steaming for Souda bay as an advance guard and four other warships were clearing their decks for action. No chances were being taken on the fleet's bombarding Saloniki, Macedonian stronghold, and combining with rebel forces in that section. A few hours earlier the government triumphed in interior Macedonia by driving rebels back across the river Struma after killing and capturing an unknown number. Badly armed, the rebels retreated in terror under fire from gover

1935-04-21.text: BERLIN, March 21.—Determined to override all opposition in its march toward full rearmament, the German government Thursday flatly declined to consider French and Italian protests against its unilateral abrogation of the Versailles treaty military clauses. After two separate visits to the German foreign office to deliver the communications of their governments, the French and Italian ambassadors, to their great astonishment, were informed in effect by Baron Konstantin von Neurath, that Führer Hitler would pay no attention to them. This action was interpreted in official circles as a further warning that Germany already feels so strongly confident of her military power that paper protests of her (Continued on Page Eight)

TOKYO, April 21. (®)—An estimated 130 persons were killed when a severe earthquake rocked the southwest section of the Island of Formosa early Saturday, said a Rengo (Japanese) News Agency dispatch. Shinchiku Province alone reported 45 dead and 85 injured, said a dispatch from the city of Taihoku. Nearly 600 houses were destroyed. Formosa is an island possession of Japan, lying to the east of southern China.

Yorkton, Sask., March 21 () — A farmer went wild with a revolver in the Roman Catholic mission here today, killing one priest, seriously wounding another, and then, facing capture by police, shot and wounded himself. The priest killed was the Rev. Father Delforgeo. The Rev. Father Bala was wounded. The farmer, who may not live, is Steve Elash. According to the police story, Elash entered the Ruthenian mission at 9:45 A. M., and asked for a priest. Father Delforgeo was instantly killed by a shot in the back of the head. Father Bala was the next to be shot,

BERLIN, April 20—(UP)—Adolf Hitler on his 46th birthday today challenged his self-appointed judges of the League of Nations council and firmly rejected their condemnation of Germany's rearming. In strong yet temperate notes to 14 nations represented on the council, Hitler denied the right of the council members to judge the Reich’s action, and spurned the council's action in the “firmest manner.” Hitler did not, however, close the door to future negotiations, restraining his bitter resentment, and indicated his willingness to cooperate in forthcoming efforts toward fortifying the peace of the continent. Sending of the note was the highlight of Hitler's nation-wide birthday observance, during which he was presented with 27 airplanes by Nazi troops and 14 by the League of War Veterans. This is part of the rebuilding of the German war machine which brought the Reich to a European crisis on

ROME, April 20. -P-—-Pope Pius himself will climax Easter celebrations in this center of the Roman Catholic world tomorrow by imparting his pontifical blessing to the thousands upon thousands of Romans already beginning to jam St. Peter's plaza tonight. Scores of persons will take up posts of vantage in the plaza before dawn tomorrow. They hope to be in the vanguard of the crowds which each Easter Sunday morning pour into the basilica and pack the huge circle.

BERLIN. (Copyright by the AP). Reliable quarters asserted intense military air activity "is rapidly placing the German army beyond undreamed of dimensions" since the announcement of conscription a month ago. A noticeably feverish rearmament increase was concentrated on improving the Reich’s position as to gas, airplanes, personnel and the storage of materials already at hand. New factories are being pushed ahead. Recruiting is progressing apace. War games are being played at the new airdromes. Intensified training is being given to special population groups. Not of the least importance is the propaganda. Seemingly the people approve conscription as a patriotic duty. One reliable quarter said that Germany now had 1,500,000 men in uniform, so that the beginning of conscription this autumn "will mean comparatively little, since by then the cream of able-bodied men will be soldiers and the i

ROME, April 20 (C%).—The flames of hundreds of new fires were kindled by flint and steel in Rome's places of worship today as church bells, mute since Thursday, signaled the end of Lent and the advent of Easter. Officiating at Holy Saturday ceremonies in St. Peter's this morning, Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli himself struck the new flame suggestive of the resurrection. Cardinal Pacelli also blessed the pope's traditional Paschal candle which was eight feet high and three inches in diameter. Meanwhile organs which had been stilled since Holy Thursday ushered in the morning period of Christ's death, once again resounded through Basilicas and chapels, and choirs sang the “Gloria in Excelsis” to welcome the Resurrection.

AMSTERDAM. (7). Rumors cir- culating here that former Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany is seriously ill were denied at Doorn castle. The rumors, which were not confirm- able, persisted that he had not been seen outside the castle for the past two days and that doctors have called there frequently. BERLIN. UP. Members of the Hohenzollern family in Berlin and Potsdam were represented as having no information other than that former Kaiser Wilhelm is well.

1935-01-29.text: LONDON, Jan 28.—(UP)—A riot in the House of Commons gallery and a demand from the floor that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald be horsewhipped from public view left Britons today looking back to the wild times of the suffragettes before the war for a precedent. There was a threat of another riot tonight, for more than forty labor party partisans, exiting rapidly up the steep gallery steps before the propelling arms of attendants, shouted: "We’ll be back!" The house was debating the government’s unemployment bill late last night. The galleries up in the rafters of the little old chamber were full. Labor partisans on the floor and in the public gallery became more and more angry as provisions of the bill for restricting allowances to the unemployed were discussed. LONDON, Jan. 28.—(AP)—Disorders broke out tonight in Britain’s staid House of Commons following a violent verbal attack on Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald over the new nationalized dole system. A score of men and women spectators in the public gallery, aroused by shouts of “down with the unemployment act!” had to be ejected with violence producing such a clamor that members on the floor could not hear each other for 20 minutes. With the greatest difficulty the gallery was cleared of men and women who joined in the melee. No one was reported injured. Laborite George Buchanan, a Scotsman from Glasgow, called Prime Minister MacDonald a “swine” and a “ratbag” during acrid debate on the new dole (Continued on page 5)

(RY the Associated Press) The winter's most bitter spell lingered over the northeastern states Monday, sending temperatures down to 2 below zero at Washington and 40 below in snowbound New England. It was the last vestige of the 10-day wave of sub-zero weather and snowstorms that had departed from most of the country, leaving mild temperatures in its wake. The disastrous Coldwater river flood in Mississippi had begun to subside, although still spreading toward the South and East. Its cost, still mounting, was estimated in the millions of dollars, and at least 20 dead were believed to have been found by the rescuers, who left the bodies to give their attention to the living victims. Trains Still Marooned Another death in British Columbia brought the total of flood and avalanche victims in the Far Northwest to 27. The high waters were receding, but the last of the trains marooned more than

London, Jan. 28 (f?)—While financial quarters awaited with deep interest the expected decision of the United States Supreme Court on the gold clause in bonds, the United States dollar took a sudden upward swing in European foreign exchange markets today. In London, the dollar gained one cent to the pound from Saturday, closing at $4.85 to the pound. In Paris the dollar gained 1042 centimes from Saturday, closing at 15.415 francs (6.487 cents to the franc) and in Berlin its value climbed over the week-end from 2.51 marks (39.76 cents to the mark) to 2.54 marks (39.37 cents). In the London market the trade in the dollar went through some surprising fluctuations, at one time touching $4.82 to the pound, its highest quotation since November, 1933.

GENEVA, Jan. 28--Official Japanese sources said today Japan and China are about to seek a far-reaching agreement for peaceful cooperation in the development of China. The first object of this agreement, they said, would be a common drive against Communism in China. The second object would be the development of China economically, thus enlarging the market for Japanese goods through an increased Chinese purchasing power.

BERLIN, Jan. 28.—German military circles declined to become excited today over news that in Geneva and other European centers uneasiness exists because of Germany’s attitude toward armaments. The Reichswehr (standing army) was represented to the Associated Press by a well-informed source as feeling: "We don’t believe any government would be so mad as to start war with us over our arms policy." Of the exact details of this arms policy, no Reich official will speak. Germans pride themselves on their almost brutal frankness, but when it comes to discussing their military affairs, they shut up like clams. All the world knows that Germany is re-arming vigorously, but one can no more get an admission of this obvious fact than he can get a dyed-in-the-wool Nazi to concede that Adolf Hitler isn't infallible. "The question of Germany’s armaments is a highly political one, to which Adolf Hitler al

Geneva, Jan. 28. (p)—An official Japanese spokesman at Geneva said today the nationalist government of China has invited Japanese officials to confer on the possibility of a Sino-Japanese accord for the economic and financial development of China. The spokesman, in line with the local conviction that Japan is moving constantly toward primacy in the Far East, said the first object of Chinese and Japanese cooperation would be a common drive against communism in China. Second would be the development of China economically, enlarging the market for Japanese goods through increased purchasing power among the masses of China.

Flemington, N. J., Jan. 28—Bruno Richard Hauptmann was confronted today by sketches of a window and a ladder in his own notebook. He denied the drawings, and then made admissions which virtually absolved the dead Isador Fisch from one of the chief implications of his defense—namely, that he might have copied Hauptmann’s handwriting in the Lindbergh ransom notes. Responding to a withering cross-examination, Hauptmann admitted he did not know Fisch before the time that Baby Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr., was kidnapped and murdered. He denied writing the telephone number and address of Dr. John F. (Jafsie) Condon, Lindbergh ransom intermediary, on a wood panel in his home, and on this his testimony was in direct variance with answers he is alleged to have made to Bronx authorities following his arrest. Baby Lindbergh was kidnapped on March 1, 1932. The state charges

1935-10-19.text: Paris, Oct. 19. — France’s “favorable” reply to Great Britain’s demand for assurance of aid, if the vast British fleet is attacked in the Mediterranean, was announced officially Friday night. It was dispatched to London, French officials said, after Premier Pierre Laval had been appeased by an assurance Great Britain has no present intention of taking military sanctions or erecting a blockade against Italy. It is not impossible, some usually well-informed persons added, that Great Britain might withdraw some of her battleships from the Mediterranean in exchange for Italy's reduction of her troop concentration in Libya, on the western border of Egypt. Officials, however, declined to comment on a report Premier Mussolini of Italy has indicated a willingness to submit to a peace with Ethiopia. The French note was reported reliably to have interpreted paragraph 3, article XVI, of the league

A joint Italian-British communique, expected to tell the world that the acute danger of war in the Mediterranean has been averted, is to be issued tomorrow morning, it was said authoritatively in Rome today. Staffs of the foreign office and the British embassy worked on the text today, harmonizing them. It was intimated that they would considerably relieve the Italian-British tension which has been increasingly acute. The United Press understands that the communique will reaffirm Great Britain’s declaration that it intends no independent action against Italy and also will say that Italy will reduce its army in Libya, bordering Egypt and the Sudan, and Britain will reduce the size of its fleet in the Mediterranean. The “general staff” of the League of Nations penalty committee meanwhile adopted a proposal for a complete boycott of Italian goods, effective Oct. 31. The proposal was referre

(Associated Press Summary) Rome displayed a conciliatory attitude toward Great Britain Friday night through an official communique declaring the doors to peaceful settlement of their differences over the African campaign "are not closed." Italy’s attitude was made public after France, yielding to unrelenting pressure by Great Britain, submitted to London a "favorable" answer to Great Britain’s demand for a "year-or-no" stand upon the question of French support in the Mediterranean. The answer was in the affirmative. The Franco-British "showdown" and Rome's tentative gesture toward conciliation followed a day of feverish diplomatic conferences in Paris and Rome. Although speculation in European capitals ran rife over possible concessions by both London and Rome, the Italian spokesman for Mussolini declared "there is nothing definite to report." Discussions between Premier Mussolini and Si

Rome, Oct. 18 (AP)—Italy let it be known officially tonight that ‘all doors are not shut’ to a peaceful settlement of her differences with Great Britain over the Ethiopian war. This terse hint, in the form of an official communique, was dropped suddenly into the midst of peace talks which, informed sources said, were getting down to “bed rock” in an attempt to halt the conflict in Africa. “Conversations in normal diplomatic channels are proceeding between Paris and Rome and Paris and London,” said the communique. “There is nothing specific at the moment, but the fact the conversations are proceeding shows all doors are not shut.” Simultaneously, a government spokesman conceded that a long conversation this afternoon between Sir Eric Drummond, the British ambassador, and Premier Mussolini likely had served to ease the tension. (An exchange telegraph dispatch from Rome said it was rumored

GENEVA, Oct. 19.—()—The League of Nations sanctions committee of 18 nations approved today the British proposal for a “buy nothing from Italy” boycott. With the consent of this committee for “immediate” sanctions to cut short the Italo-Ethiopian war, the projected sweeping boycott against all Italian goods now goes before the plenary committee of 2 nations for final approval. The boycott was discussed point by point by the smaller committee, and only Switzerland made reservations. Even this nation, however, did not abstain when the measure as a whole was approved. The committee decided that on Oct. 31 the larger plenary committee of all league States except Italy and Ethiopia should decide the exact date on which League nations would begin simultaneously enforcement of the boycott. A member of the committee said that while Switzerland pointed out some difficulties and made a slight reser

(By United Press). Rome, Oct. 19.—Great Britain will not act independently of the League of Nations in the Italo-Ethiopian war, Sir Eric Drummond, British Ambassador, assured Premier Benito Mussolini yesterday, it was announced officially today. The official announcement corroborated reports that Great Britain has reached an agreement with Italy whereby the danger of war in the Mediterranean will be averted.

LONDON, Oct. 19.—Italian-British-French diplomatic negotiations have removed—for the moment—the gravest threat of big scale war in all the months of the Ethiopian crisis, it was understood today. Great Britain has offered to withdraw part of its fleet from the Mediterranean on the basis of French assurances of support. It was said that Great Britain took the initiative, and offered to withdraw some ships if Italy reduced its army in Libya, adjoining Egypt and the Sudan. Italy agreed to these terms. France, it is understood, will replace any British ships withdrawn on the understanding that it is clearly defined where they shall be stationed and what their precise duties will be. WILL APPLY PENALTIES Great Britain and France—and the League of Nations—will continue with the work of applying against Italy, for the duration of the Italian-Ethiopian war, any penalties voted. LONDON, Oct. 10 (P)—Lloyd’s reported the British steamer Vardulia sent a wireless message today saying “now abandoning ship,” soon after asking for immediate assistance because of a dangerous list. The vessel was about 420 miles southwest of the Hebrides, an island group northwest of Scotland. She carried a crew of about 40 and no passengers.

1935-02-17.text: (Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) LONDON, Feb. 16.—Restoration of confidence—by peaceful or forceful methods—in order to restore prosperity, was revealed today as the single purpose of the Anglo-French-Italian accords. Now the focus of European diplomacy, the accords were originally conceived by Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon. They had one single all-important purpose for planning these pacts—to bring about a revival of economic prosperity, in order to make Great Britain’s traditional position in world affairs secure once more, by a restoration of confidence on the continent. If Germany enters the scheme in a co-operative manner, the confidence-restoring plan will take the peaceful road. If Germany chooses to keep aloof, Britain, France and Italy will form a powerful combination of armed forces to assure peace until normal trade makes the police

LONDON — Britain, France and Italy have joined forces to keep Europe's peace until the return of confidence makes their policing unnecessary, authoritative circles disclosed today. That, it was revealed, was the sole purpose in the Anglo-French accords drafted at London two weeks ago, to which Adolf Hitler was invited to adhere. If Germany ultimately decides to enter the accords, it was said this restoration of confidence will be achieved by peaceful means and international cooperation.

Not altogether satisfied with Germany's reply to the Franco-British security proposals, England and France moved today to formally consider Reichsfuehrer Hitler's offer to talk things over with London and his declaration that Germany is ready in principle to use her air forces to preserve the peace. The note said Germany agrees with the British and the French governments in desiring sincerity "to promote the safeguarding of peace" but specifically avoided mentioning the Eastern and Danubian pacts. PARIS...The German note met with keen disappointment in France, being regarded as a plain attempt on Germany's part to split up the London Security Pact, but the French were planning to discuss immediately with the London foreign office a joint Franco-British response. ROME, Feb. 16. Premier Mussolini broke his silence on the Ethiopian controversy tonight by urging all mobilized Italians to "be ready for any eventuality." In an address to the Fascist Grand Council, Il Duce for the first time made a definite reference to a "front." He congratulated the "virility of the men leaving for the African front". The statement, to which deep significance was attached, was made several hours after the first detachments of Italian troops sailed for Africa. Mussolini's council in a four-hour session approved his measures "for the security of peace" in East African possessions and those considered necessary "for control over Italian interests." Thunderous Cheers Thunderous cheers greeted the dictator's statement that 700 blackshirts have volunteered for service in East Africa since Feb. 2 and also thousands of other citizens and war veterans. The Grand Council's com

Berlin, Feb. 16. -(4P) -Adolf Hitler tonight studied death sentences passed by the peoples court on three women and one man, described as of aristocratic birth, for espionage. A responsible official of the propaganda ministry said the women, Frau Von Berg, Frau Von Natzner and Fraulein Von Jena, and the man, Baron Sosnowski, were sentenced for using their high social and reichswehr (regular army) connections to get German military secrets. These secrets, it was charged, they divulged to Poland through Baron Sosnowski. The three women were said to be young, attractive and members of the best social circles. Efforts to identify Frau Von Berg as the Baroness Benita von Berg met an evasive reply. Serious government officials were represented as believing that the alleged plot might involve not only Polish-German relations but also many persons high in German social and official life.

ROME, Feb. 16 (Hundreds of soldiers moved into Rome today from northern points, preparatory to embarkation for Africa in a possible campaign against Ethiopia. Reports that the first contingent would sail today failed to ruffle Negradas Yesus, Ethiopian charge d'affaires, who declared: “We will defend our homes with our lives.” ‘If Italy comes against us,” Yesus said, “her blood will be on her own head.” The troops entered the city for final inspection before leaving for Sicilian ports. Ready For Service The troops in the streets wore brand new uniforms, and ordinary trench caps, but the pith helmets of the tropics dangled on the soldiers’ backs. Hundreds of other reservists continued to receive mobilization cards, telling them to hold themselves in readiness for the moment the mobilization posters are pasted up. Many unemployed mechanics, motor experts, electricians, road and bridge buil
TROOPS LEAVE FOR AFRICA ROME, Feb. 16. (4)—An official communique said the first contingent of Italian troops embarked for Italy's African colonies today.

Istres, France (#)—Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi, holders of the world’s long distance flight record, were soaring over Morocco this afternoon, headed for a non-stop south Atlantic crossing to Buenos Aires, trying to hang up a new record. © They took off at 6:36 a.m. in the same “Joseph Lebrix” in which their heavily loaded plane, the one they flew from New York to Syria in 1933.

1935-06-23.text: Garden City, L. I—(#)—Two men were killed Saturday night when their monoplane crashed into a vacant lot off Nassau boulevard. Alfred Weisbord, who watched the plane hurl to death, told Garden City police the pilot was stunting. The pilot was identified as Albert Whitey, 45, a commercial artist of Garden City. He held a transport license. Frank Whitney, son of the pilot, tentatively identified the second man as Floyd Brink, 30, also a commercial artist. He said Brink's home was in Biching, N. Y.

PARIS, June 22.—France today won England back to cooperation, temporarily at least, in building the big, complex system of peace pacts this nation holds necessary to guarantee her against attack. A wide Anglo-French breach was bridged when Premier Pierre Laval induced Capt. Anthony (Turn to Page 4&5. Column 5.)

LONDON, Eng. (UP) British and German naval negotiators in three days of technical discussions have failed to agree definitely on three main points, it was understood Saturday. The British-German agreement calls for a 85-to-100 ratio of strength for the British and German fleets. Technical points on which it was understood the delegates had not agreed are: 1. The exact number of ships Germany intends to build by 1942. 2. The type of construction of ships built. 3. The sizes of the ships. Regarding the last point, it is reported that the Germans have accepted a limit of 25,000 tons and 12-inch guns for battleships, and 10,000 tons and 6-inch guns for cruisers. A final meeting of the experts was scheduled Saturday. The Germans expected to go to Berlin Sunday, having further exchanges to diplomatic channels.

MEAUX, France, June 22, (AP).— Three officers burned to death in a bombing plane which crashed early today into a woods near Lagny during a night practice flight. A fourth member of the crew jumped clear of the blazing plane with a parachute and escaped injury.

WASHINGTON, June 22—(AP)—New signs of undercover dissatisfaction with several New Deal measures arose today, leading some congressional chiefs privately to express fears of a major uprising in Democratic ranks unless the session ends soon or different tactics are adopted. Concrete evidence of the discontent included there: 1. Fourteen of the 22 senators who signed the petition for action before adjournment on share-the-wealth taxes were Democrats, some of whom expressed “off-the-record” fears that the President's advocacy of the taxes might have been only a political move. 2. Disclosure that an actual majority of house members had opposed the Wagner labor disputes bill, which was passed without a roll call. 3. The fact that members of the house ways and means committee were openly expressing doubts of the constitutionality of the Guffey coal bill, which is on the President’s “must” list.

Washington—(4)—A nation-wide campaign for legislation to deport approximately 6,000,000 aliens as a partial solution to the United States’ unemployment problem was pressed Saturday by 155 organizations, estimated by Representative Dies, (D-Tex.), to represent 5,000,000 people. Plans to organize 10,000,000 native born and naturalized citizens for a drive to get congressional action on the Dies deportation bill were reported by the tall Texan as he thumbed 50,000 letters and telegrams received in support of the measure. The organization is to be called "The Americans" and is to be organized in each state on a non-sectarian and non-partisan basis, he said. "At least 150 congressmen have pledged themselves in favor of the bill, which provides that no alien can hold a job in this country that can be filled by a citizen," he said. "It is about the same legislation as the alien deportation laws

Tacoma, Wash., June 22.—(P)—Another attempt by remorseful Mrs. Margaret Thulin Waley, 19, to plead guilty to "Lindbergh law" violation in the George Weyerhaeuser kidnapping was blocked today by Federal Judge E. E. Cushman after her attorney had expressed the belief she could not be convicted. "In my opinion," said Stephen J. O’Brien, her court-appointed attorney, "she could not be convicted if she went to trial." Plea Denied Sobbing and unkempt, the young wife of Harmon M. Waley, who pleaded guilty to the same charge yesterday and was sentenced to 45 years in prison, then was denied permission to plead guilty. Judge Cushman ruled the trial date would be set Monday. Without her swaggering, gum-chewing former convict husband whose last word in court was a plea in her behalf, Mrs. Waley seemed lost. Her eyes were red and puffed from hours of weeping. TACOMA, Wash., June 22 (UP)—Less than one month after he had prided himself on the success of his first major crime, Harmon Metz Waley, 25-year-old small town bad boy, began a 45-year prison term today for the kidnapping of George Weyerhaeuser, son of a Tacoma millionaire. PLEADS GUILTY—Through an apparent deal with the government agents who arrested him in Salt Lake City two weeks after the kidnapping, the gawky six-foot desperado pleaded guilty to the charges against him and received a sentence which spared him the life term he might have received under the Lindbergh law had he chosen to stand trial. Waley was taken to McNeil Island federal penitentiary in Puget Sound to begin his term. It was indicated he might later be transferred to Alcatraz Island or some other federal prison. 1935-12-14.text: The death of an American medical missionary in Ethiopia punctuated today the fretful aftermath of the attempt by Great Britain and France to formulate terms for peace between Italy and the empire of Haile Selassie. Dr. Robert W. Hockman was killed while handling an unexploded Italian bomb at Daggah Bur, on the southern front. Dr. Hockman, who was a United Presbyterian missionary to Ethiopia, had removed the detonator and supervised the digging out of the unexploded projectile recently. He had made a hobby of studying bombs. The Franco-British peace proposal meanwhile appeared to have precipitated only a protracted wrangle over the plan between its advocates and those nations aligned solidly against it on the ground that it threatened the foundations of collective security. A Crisis Britain was in the midst of a political crisis incident to the formulation of the scheme. Advices from Rome

London. (AP)--The inauguration of bilateral conversations, coupled with the announcement of a super-secret session Monday, attended only by delegates, was believed today to be ushering in one of the most significant, critical periods of the international naval conference. Both moves, it was learned authoritatively, were maneuvered by the Japanese on the grounds that general sessions were cumbersome and unsatisfactory in the negotiations to overcome differences and to reach a new agreement to replace the expiring Washington and London naval limitations treaties. Best informed sources said the British, who held their first separate discussion with the Japanese last night, acted only after urgent Japanese insistence. An authoritative British source said that, while a few more bilateral discussions would be held, they would be kept to an absolute minimum and no resumption of a general bilate

LONDON, Dec. 14.—A well-informed source disclosed today that Great Britain has suddenly moved to cultivate closer relationship with Reichsführer Hitler of Germany. The move was not explained in official circles, although it came obviously after six months of European turmoil over the Italian-Ethiopian hostilities. Sir Eric Phipps, the British ambassador to Germany, was assigned to take the initiative in Berlin, conferring with Hitler in a general discussion of Anglo-German problems. Sir Eric’s move followed closely on Hitler’s reception of the French ambassador. Conjectures The news gave rise to various conjectures including reports that Great Britain was taking the initiative to negotiate a four-power aviation pact. There were indications that Sir Eric’s visit was linked to direct reference made by Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, to Anglo-German problems in his speech of Dec. 5 in

The five-day old Franco-British plan to end the Italo-Ethiopian war seemed headed for summary burial Friday night. Stinging denunciations from Ethiopia, revolt in Geneva, London and Paris and misgivings even in Rome piled up against the proposals to give Benito Mussolini much of what he intends to seize from Emperor Haile Selassie by force of arms. At Geneva, Ethiopia flatly rejected the proposal, declared its opposition to "all secret negotiations," and demanded that the League of Nations’ assembly be called in special session on the ground the Franco-British plan violates the spirit of the league covenant. Designed to give Il Duce control or sovereignty over almost two-thirds of Ethiopia, the proposals, nevertheless, aroused no official enthusiasm in Rome. Italy would get the eastern part of Tigre province; the Ogaden region of the south and rights of colonization and development in a

United Press Staff Correspondent ROME, Dec. 14 (UP). Premier Benito Mussolini countered a French-British plan for settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian war today by asking for clarification of certain of its provisions. Thus he evaded a direct committal of his government on the acceptability of the plan as a basis for peace negotiation, and won further time to consider his course. Mussolini particularly requested clarification of the proposal for an Italian zone of influence in Southwestern Ethiopia, it was learned authoritatively. The query specifically asked in what manner the area was to be governed and the type of defense that would be afforded Italian immigrants to the zone. An official announcement of his action said also that he was unlikely to reply specifically to the French-British proposals before the meeting of his Fascist grand council, the supreme body of Italy, next Wednesda

London, Dec. 14.—Delegates to the naval limitation conference found themselves deadlocked today and began to discuss the possibility of complete failure of their effort to negotiate a treaty. The conference is to recess Dec. 21—a week from today—until Jan. 2. It was asked whether anything was likely to occur that would permit useful discussion for any length of time after the Christmas holiday. Japan has bid for naval parity in discussions in hope that some way may be found to start the conference on its way. The situation, however, is bad. It was anticipated, long before the conference met, that there would be complete disagreement on the Japanese claim to equality and on the limitation of classes of ships in each navy. But there was some hope that agreement might be possible at least to restrict the size of individual

LONDON, Dec. 13—(#)—British officials, in what some observers said was a significant and unexpected re-charting of Britain’s course as host to the International naval conference, inaugurated separate two-nation discussions among the powers tonight, conferring with the Japanese delegation. The surprise conference was held in the foreign office while members of the American delegation were in the country for a rest and the French were week-ending in Paris. Authoritative sources said the Americans were not informed of the development beforehand, and it was stated they were ‘unpleasantly surprised’ when the news became known. After the discussion between the British and Japanese officials, Japanese sources said the talks were frank, cordial and useful. Previously Japan, despite challenges from 10 delegations, doggedly maintained her demand for fleet equality, defending her thesis that only i

(Copyright 1935, by the Associated Press) Rome, Dec. 14.—A government spokesman disclosed today that Premier Mussolini has asked "clarifications" of the terms of the Franco-British plan for peace in Ethiopia. Il Duce probably also will discuss his peace or war decision with the fascist grand council before replying formally to the proposals, the spokesman indicated. For the time being, informed Italian sources believed, the Franco-British program encouraged negotiations. The peace proposals offered Premier Mussolini title to somewhat less territory than his troops have already occupied, in addition to economic rights in areas of Ethiopia which his forces have not yet won. Authoritative sources said Il Duce had the alternative of accepting this offer, if it survived league and Ethiopian opposition, or chancing the ability of his armies to seize even more territory against the combined opp

1935-03-16.text: By The Associated Press. | MESSINA, Sicily, Feb. 15.—Nine British officers and men were reported killed late today in a crash of the seaplane “Singapore” en route from Naples to Malta. The plane burned immediately after the crash.

| LONDON. — King Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia suffered a dozen slight wounds from bomb fragments, and his Crown Prince, Amir Saud, was wounded in the shoulder by a dagger, when three Yemenites tried to assassinate the Mohammedan fundamentalist leader yesterday, the Daily Mail reported today. | In a simple pilgrim’s robe, Ibn Saud and his entourage were kissing the sacred black stone of the ancient Kaaba — the stone, according to Islamic belief, given to Abraham by the Archangel Gabriel when three men rushed from the crowd. Each threw a bomb. The second burst in front of Ibn Saud and punctured his leg. None of the wounds was serious. Baring daggers, the three assailants rushed for the king. Amir Saud and the Bedouin Chief Nadi Fadhaliya hurled themselves in front of the king. Amir Saud was stabbed deeply, though not seriously, in the left shoulder as he grappled with one of the assailants. |

Rio de Janeiro.—-(AP)—-A Japanese financial and commercial mission to Brazil will sail for this capital April 7, it was said today, with the intention of fostering trade in Brazil and extending growing markets in the interior countries of the continent. French, British, Italian and United States business circles were discussing the visit and it was known that one large American bank was bringing in from Buenos Aires a Japanese technician, versed in the business life of his country. While the commercial mission headed by Hiosaburo Hirao, president of the Kawasaki Drydock Co., apparently has no connection with the large-scale South American plans of Japanese business as a whole, some commentators prominent in importing circles linked the mission with purported plans of the Tokio government to colonize in Paraguay.
LONDON, March 16 (LP) Speedy consultation between France and Great Britain was foreseen today after the German action in violation of the Versailles treaty.

EDITORS’ NOTE: In the following dispatch written for the United Press, Eamon De Valera, President of the Executive Council of the Irish Free State, sends his greetings to the United States. DUBLIN, March 16—(UP)—On the occasion of St. Patrick's Day I send greetings to our friends in America. During the past year steady progress has been made toward our respective national and economic independence. Our people once more have shown their power of endurance, their unconquerable national will, and their sound judgment. They have cooperated with the government joyfully in all its efforts. While agriculture in Ireland, as in all countries, continues depressed, the rapid expansion of secondary industries here is providing an ever-increasing home market for our produce. For example, we are now producing all our requirements in flour and 80 percent of our sugar requirements. We are producing a la

- Stockholm, Sweden, March 15 ()--All Sweden lifted glasses tonight in toasts to the engagement of its pretty 24-year-old Princess, Ingrid, to tall, handsome Crown Prince Frederick of Denmark. All other world events were pushed far into the background by the formal announcement of the “love match,” oft rumored and oft denied. Photographs of the couple’s betrothal kiss claimed wide public attention. A candle-lighted dinner table at the royal palace, meanwhile, saw the affianced pair drink to each other's health and happiness. (A British News Agency dispatch from Stockholm quoted palace circles as saying the wedding of Frederick and Ingrid probably would take place at Stockholm toward the end of May.) Internationally the match was held to be significant, in that it binds still more closely two nations already linked by racial and economic ties.

PARIS, Mar. 16—(4)—Official circles today said Germany's open defiance of the military clauses of the Versailles treaty threatens to toss the whole suggested scheme for European peace into the discard. The announcement at Berlin that Germany has decreed compulsory military service was regarded by the French officials as a direct answer to the French government's action in extending the compulsory military service to two years, approved by the chamber of deputies early today.

STOCKHOLM, March 16. (P)--- Rejoicing over the engagement of Princess Ingrid to Crown Prince Frederik of Denmark was halted today when Queen Alexandrine, Frederik’s mother, was taken to a hospital for a serious appendicitis operation. She was operated on at once, and it was officially announced she was progressing satisfactorily. | BRUSSELS, March 16.
