1935-08-20.text: (Associated Press Foreign Staff) LONDON, Aug. 19—(AP)—The British cabinet, faced with the necessity of deciding quickly half a dozen momentous problems arising from the failure of the tripartite conference in Paris on the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, was summoned to meet in extraordinary session Thursday as ministers tonight converged on London from widely scattered vacation points. Confronted by a situation considered by many as the most serious threat to world peace since 1914, King George personally took up the matter, summoning Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, to Sandringham. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin hurriedly made preparations to quit Aix-Les-Bains, where he arrived only yesterday to begin his vacation. Acting Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, ending a busy day of conferences at his native Lossiemouth, attempted to obtain a plane for a flight to London, but was forced to make tr

(Copyright, 1935, by United Press) LONDON, England. (UP) — The Italian program of expansion is regarded as a bold, direct threat to the power of the British empire by a considerable proportion of the British leaders, it was learned today. An emergency cabinet meeting was called for Thursday and ministers were urgently summoned home from vacation. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin announced at Aix Les Bains, France, that he would start for London tonight. Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign minister, and Anthony Eden, British chief delegate at the disastrous British-French-Italian conference at Paris, which precipitated the crisis, converged at the foreign office today on British policy. Ray Atherton, American charge d’Affaires, visited the foreign office yesterday to discuss the situation, it was learned. It is understood that strong reinforcement of British forces in all territory bordering Ethiopia

Italy, through her envoy to the shattered tri-power conferences in Paris, served notice Monday night that she expects "nothing from Geneva" in the way of averting her determined move on Ethiopia. Baron Pompeo Aloisi, leaving Paris after Premier Mussolini’s "no" to Franco-English suggestions for partial Italian control of Ethiopia had wrecked the tri-power parley, declared: "I see no basis for further discussion. Italy does not want to leave Geneva, but, if we are led to the door, we will have to leave." French officials were predicting storm clouds for Europe and a return to "jungle law" as a result of the failure of the conference. London—Great Britain's statesmen began consideration of her course of action at the League of Nations meeting Sept. 4 as diplomatic circles saw an Italian challenge to British supremacy in Africa and in the Mediterranean and a threat to British control of Lak

London, Eng. (INS)—For the first time in years, the summer vacation of British cabinet members was rudely shattered today as Premier Baldwin from his villa in France issued a call for a special cabinet session to consider means of halting Premier Mussolini's march on Ethiopia. All ministers including the foreign affairs expert who have seen each attempt to avert Ethiopian conflict wrecked, were ordered to assemble on Thursday morning. They will assemble in an atmosphere of gravest tension, unparalleled since the assassination of King Alexander of Yugoslavia threw Europe into a turmoil a year ago.

8 MISSING AFTER PORTION OF SUBWAY COLLAPSES IN GERMANY Workmen were reported missing today in the collapse of a portion of the Hermann Goering Street subway, now under construction. A section of the street near the Brandenburg Gate dropped away about 12:15 P. M., and one and three-quarters hours later, only four members of the crew which had been below had been brought up. All four suffered broken bones and internal injuries. It was hoped that some of the 18 workers believed still underground might have escaped crushing by running to safe ends of the tunnel. Police, firemen, first aid workers, and 300 regular army soldiers were sent to the spot in rescue attempts.

ROME. (WP) — Premier Benito Mussolini, deaf to the threats of the powers, increased his air force personnel by 67 per cent today in preparation for war on Ethiopia by adding 500 officers, 1800 non-commissioned officers, and 10,588 men to his force. He empowered the air ministry also to maintain 1500 officers, 1500 non-commissioned officers of air force reserve. LONDON. Fulda, Germany, Aug. 20. (P— The German Catholic bishops met in secret today to prepare a counter attack on the Nazi drive against “political Catholicism.” The conference, described by the Nazis as one that “will have a decisive influence on the relationship of the church to the national socialist state,” was regarded by Catholics as the most important assemblage of bishops in recent years. The entire German Catholic hierarchy—three cardinals, three archbishops and 19 bishops, presided over by Senior Cardinal Bertram of Breslau—discussed what Catholics call the “serious situation facing the German church.” The bishops meet in this old Catholic center of learning annually over St. Boniface’s tomb in the cathedral. They sit for three days, in private except for the opening and closing sermons, One of the main questions under discussion was how to protect the clergy from the order of Herman

Berlin.-()—The main building of Berlin’s radio city was a heap of smouldering ruins today after a spectacular fire which caused one death and injury to 26. The building, of wood construction, was the only one of the eight inter-connecting halls swept by fire, the origin of which has not been determined.

1935-04-03.text: (Copyright, 1935, The Associated Press) LONDON — Sir John Simon, foreign minister, revealed to the House of Commons today that Reichsfuehrer Hitler told him in Berlin that Germany already has an air force as large as that of Great Britain. Sir Charles William Cayzer, Conservative, asked whether Hitler during his conversations with the foreign secretary “gave any indication of the present size or strength of the German air force.” Sir John answered: “Yes. In the course of those conversations in Germany, the chancellor stated in general terms that Germany had reached a parity with Great Britain in the air.”

Copyright 1935 by The Associated Press WARSAW, April 3.—Great Britain and Poland today agreed to “the desirability of maintaining close contact” on the European situation, with authoritative quarters indicating a ‘Pan-European security system as a likely result. The agreement was reached with Polish statesmen by Capt. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, as he concluded two days of conversations concerned with the general peace of Europe and prepared to depart for Praha and more conferences. As the conferees parted; they gave each other mutual assurances described officially as concerning “the desirability of maintaining close contact in regard to future developments in the European situation.”

LONDON, April 3 (UP).—Poland has balked at entering the proposed eastern European security pact along the lines desired by Britain and France, it was indicated authoritatively tonight as Capt. Anthony Eden ended his mission to Warsaw. Informed quarters said the talks in Warsaw had been inconclusive and that Foreign Minister Joseph Beck had indicated Poland was unwilling to jeopardize her relations with Germany. Beck intimated Poland's readiness to join non-aggression and consultative treaties, but re-affirmed the government's refusal to join any pact which would entail the possible incursion of German or Russian troops on Polish soil. Under the proposed eastern treaty, any menace to security would involve armed action by the signatories against the aggressor.

(Copyright 1935, by the Associated Press), London, Apr. 3.—Plans for a pan-European security system with enforceable provisions against aggressor nations were stated by a British government spokesman today to be a requisite goal of the forthcoming conference of Great Britain, France, and Italy at Stresa. The spokesman said the recent conversations by envoys of the British empire in Berlin, Moscow, and Warsaw had convinced the government that a non-partisan plan open to the signatures of all nations including Germany was the only way to insure the future peace of the European continent. Such a plan, he said, would be suitable to all of the peace-loving nations, large and small, who now are frightened, and should be put into effect in the shortest possible time after its construction, probably through the agency of the League of Nations. In theory the pact would not be directed by name aga

LONDON, April 3.—On the word of Chancellor Adolf Hitler himself, Germany already has aerial parity with Great Britain, foreign secretary Sir John Simon told the House of Commons today. Reporting for the second time on his historic conversations with the Fuehrer in Berlin, Sir John startled the House by revealing Hitler had told him Anglo-German air parity already exists. (Editor’s Note: Estimates regarding Britain’s present air strength vary widely. Some estimates place Britain’s fighting planes at 1,593, with 472 more for the dominions, giving a total of 2,065, but the Statemen’s Year Book, a usually reliable authority, lists the total at 1,128.) A demand that Great Britain, France and Italy join forces in the face of German rearmament was made in Premier Benito Mussolini's newspaper, Il Popolo d’Italia, as observers at Warsaw thought they saw Poland swinging back from Germany to France. Belief that Polish sentiment is veering was based on reported progress Capt. Anthony Eden, British traveling statesman, made in inducing Poland to accept some modified eastern security agreement and Poland's surprise decision to invite Pierre Laval, French foreign minister, to visit Warsaw when he goes to Moscow this month. Another international conference on German rearmament was in progress at Copenhagen, where foreign ministers of Denmark, Sweden and Norway gathered. In Paris the French chamber of deputies adjourned until May 28 after hearing Premier Pierre-Etienne Flandin say France must keep her military strength at its utmost to oppose the

Athens, April 2—(4)—Thousands of students and others paraded the streets of Athens Wednesday, protesting against the failure of the government to sentence to death the leaders of the Venizelist rebellion. Athens resembled a beleaguered city. Armored tanks were stationed before the home of Premier Panayotis Tsaldaris and public buildings, While the mob shouted “lynch the traitors, lynch them!” thirteen rebel officers condemned to life imprisonment by court martial were publicly degraded: Thousands of citizens fought for places in the huge courtyard of the Athens barracks to see the insurgents humiliated. The crowd howled its approval as the presiding officer, armed with an American-made razor blade, ripped epaulets and insignia from the uniforms and caps of the prisoners.

| ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopia (4) — Ethiopia is moving troops up to her frontiers, authoritative sources report today, to meet what her government regards as a threat from Italy’s East African forces. The Ethiopian detachments were said to be moving in large numbers to the Eritrean and Italian Somaliland borders. Government sources were quick to explain the activities were solely for defensive purposes, ROME (#) — Italian military authorities said today Italy has been aware for some time that Ethiopia has been massing troops on both the Eritrean and Italian Somaliland frontiers and has made extensive purchases of war materials abroad. Italy now has about 75,000 Italian and native troops ready for action in East Africa, these sources said, a force they regarded as capable of coping with any Ethiopian attack. More than 30,000 men have left Italy for the East African colonies, according to offici

1935-04-05.text: Associated Press Foreign Staff Copyright, 1935, by the Associated Press PRAHA, Czechoslovakia, April 4. —Capt. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, received an assurance today from Dr. Edouard Benes, Czech foreign minister, that Czechoslovakia remains in perfect accord with Great Britain concerning the safeguarding of general peace and in attachment to the policy of the League of Nations. The British diplomat, who already had conferred on the European situation with Reichsfuehrer Hitler in Berlin, with Joseph Stalin in Moscow, and with Marshal Pilsudski in Warsaw, talked only briefly with Dr. Benes, the organizer of the Little Entente, on his arrival here today. Shortly later he left by airplane for London following the issuance of a communique which said in part: “Captain Eden and Dr. Benes had a cordial and friendly exchange of views on all questions contained in the London communiqu

LONDON, April 4—A busy week faced the British cabinet tonight as it awaited Capt. Anthony Eden’s return from his European peace tour to begin drafting compromise security proposals to be presented at Stresa next Thursday. The young Lord Privy Seal, “indisposed” at Cologne, Germany, after his tiring trip to Berlin, Moscow, Warsaw and Praha, was expected to reach London tomorrow at midday and go into conference with part of the cabinet shortly afterwards. His reports will provide the basis for the proposals Britain will offer France and Italy. Officials here hope they will allow all European nations to be brought into one firm “Pan-European” security set-up. Reports from Paris said Foreign Minister Laval, who is drafting the French proposals, would seek British and Italian support in an effort to “frighten” the rearming Reich, failing which France would try to link Russia and Czechoslovaki

Copyright. 1935, By Associated Press) LONDON.-Austria’s sudden decision to increase her army Wednesday night apparently added one more problem to those confronting the Stresa conference at which, sources said, Great Britain would do all in her power to weld Europe's nations into one far-reaching security system. British Surprised While British officials, surprised by the report from Vienna, declined to comment pending receipt of further information, first impressions were that the Austrian move would tend to create further difficulties at the Stresa conference. Observers received with interest, too, the reported decision of the Lithuanian government to protest to Germany against asserted Lithuanian demonstrations and threatened reprisals for the recent sentencing of 91 Nazis convicted of plotting to retrieve Memel for Germany. A “Pan-European” scheme with adequate enforceable provisions

LONDON, April 5. U.P)—European investors in American securities took their first step today in an attempt to get a reversal of the recent U. S. Supreme Court gold clause ruling. The London advisory protective committee for American investments authorized its counsel, Barnett Hollander, to communicate with corresponding French, Dutch, Swiss and Belgian bodies immediately for action toward that end. The London committee, headed by Sir Harry Armstrong, former British consul-general at New York, accepted Hollander’s legal opinion that a reversal of the gold rulings is possible. Corresponding committees in the other countries already have been formed into an international committee against repudiation of the gold clause.

BY j2 280° ASSOC A200 Press A proposal that France, Italy and Great Britain join forces to “frighten” the rearming Reich was reported under consideration in Paris yesterday as Europe’s attention focused on the tri-powered conference at Stresa, April 11. Foreign Minister Pierre Laval, the Paris reports said, will seek mutual assistance pacts with Russia and Czechoslovakia if Italy and Great Britain fail to fall in with his plan. The British cabinet awaited Capt. Anthony Eden’s return, expected tomorrow, to draft compromise security proposals Foreign Secretary Simon will present. Eden, after extraordinarily brief and cordial conversations with Czechoslovak statesmen at Praha, was “indisposed” when he arrived at Cologne. Authoritative sources at Addis Ababa, meanwhile, said an Ethiopian army numbering 100,000 men, well equipped, was moving to the borders of Eritrea and Italian Somaliland. A

LONDON, (P) — The House of Lords, highest tribunal in Great Britain, today, for the first time in history, quashed a murder indictment against a condemned man. Reginald Woomington, 21, a Dorset farm laborer, had twice before been found guilty of murdering his 17-year-old wife, Kathleen, with a sawed-off shotgun. The only other murder case ever heard by the House of Lords was 16 years ago.

Washington, Apr. 4 (4)--Eighteen years after the World War, a comparison of the national defense budgets for the United States and Great Britain, the two great English speaking nations involved, today showed that both are near peace time records. Although legislative action has yet to be completed in either country, government estimates virtually sure to be approved or even exceeded placed the projected expenditures for military and naval establishments for the coming year as follows: The United States, more than $800,000,000; Great Britain more than $480,080,000. The British figure, however, does not include maintenance of forces in Australia, Canada, the provinces and colonies in Africa, India and elsewhere. Both great powers are contemplating increasing their army personnel, air defenses and naval strength. The United States plans to lift its army enlisted strength from 118,000 to 165

WASHINGTON, April 5 — Organized labor surged into the already complicated textile situation today with a demand to the National Recovery Board for reopening of the cotton textile code and drastic revisions of the charter. While cotton manufacturers and groups of members of Congress from New England and the South battled for elimination of the cotton processing tax and prompt action for protection against increasing textile imports, the emergency council of the United Textile Workers presented to the board an eight-point program which contained demands for several of the objectives sought by the union in the general strike of last September. The delegation, led by President Thomas F. McMahon, included Tranos J. Gorman, organization director, and Vice Presidents Horace Riviere of New England, John Peel of the South, William F. Kelley of the Middle Atlantic division, and William White of Ne

1935-04-15.text: London, April 15 (UP)—A balanced budget with an estimated surplus of 5,610,000 pounds ($27,208,500) was announced to the House of Commons today by Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer. Chamberlain proposed to achieve the results without raising the income tax, customs duties, etc. He estimated total ordinary revenue of 735,580,000 pounds ($3,567,562,000), and total ordinary expenditures at 729,870,000 pounds ($3,540,354,500). Chamberlain's speech was optimistic. He said the year had shown excellent recovery and that trade improvements “have reached down to the purchasing power of the people.” He boasted that no country has shown such a measure of recovery as Britain.

LONDON— (UP) — An anarchist plot to assassinate Benito Mussolini of Italy and possibly Pierre Laval, French foreign minister, has been frustrated by French police, the Exchange Telegraph Geneva correspondent reported today. The correspondent said Marseilles police arrested Rudolph Gunscher, an Italian anarchist and his woman companion, Ida Caroni, April 5. Police asserted they obtained a confession that they belonged to two groups of anarchists who planned to cross into Italy and assassinate Mussolini, then go to Geneva to assassinate Laval.

GENEVA—(U.P.)—Great Britain and Italy are prepared to give military assistance to France if Germany violates the demilitarized zone along her borders, an authoritative source revealed tonight, saying the Anglo-Italian reaffirmation at Stresa of their Locarno treaty obligations implies military action under certain circumstances.

London, England, April 15—Miss Mary Lawson, British actress, today announced termination of her engagement to Fred Perry, British tennis star, and said Perry had advised her by cable that he would accept a Hollywood film contract. Miss Lawson said that Fred liked America and that she did not. Consequently, the romance between the two was ended.

For two years dust has been transforming once fertile wheatlands of a region large as New England into desert. Since February the storms have reached unprecedented intensity. The United Press sent a staff correspondent into the region worst affected, to report first hand what he saw and what he learned from the inhabitants. By FRANK McNAUGHTON. (Copyright 1955, By United Press) Clayton, N. M., April 15—The wall of dust, at least 10,000 feet high, boiled over the horizon on the wings of a gale and engulfed me and every animate and inanimate object in blackness laden with stinging dirt. I drove here from Felt, Okla., through a region once called the "bread basket of America." The storm broke suddenly at about 5 p.m. yesterday. Leaving Felt I heard cries of "Dust storm, dust storm." I saw men and women and children running toward their homes. Brave with inexperience I drove on. It is not fl

BOSTON (4) — Northern cotton goods manufacturers responded today to calls for two conferences on relief for the cotton textile industry in New England, its 100,000 employees and their families. Governor James M. Curley’s warning today “unless government aid is given to the textile industry at once, not a spindle will be turning in New England in six months,” sounded the keynote of the manufacturers’ campaign against the processing tax, Japanese importations, overproduction and North-South wage differentials. While manufacturers sought abolition of the processing tax and establishment of higher tariff barriers against Japanese importations, labor press and Governor Curley declared elimination of the wage differential would cure the ills of the industry. The governor estimated that the wage differential cost New England manufacturers $250,000 more per week for labor than it did southern mi

(Copyright 1935 by United Press GENEVA, April 15 — The Scandinavian nations started a strong movement at the council session of the League of Nations today to placate Germany and tone down a strong French resolution rebuking the Reich. Peter Munch, Norwegian foreign minister, on behalf of the Scandinavian nations, conferred with Sir Johan Simon, British foreign secretary, and urged a vague resolution not condemning Germany. The council, after a private session lasting only an hour, adjourned until tomorrow, when it will discuss the French appeal. GENEVA, April 15 — Germany’s violation of the Versailles Treaty was placed before the League of Nations council today with the implied demand that the League act to punish future violations. France called the meeting. She seeks a pronouncement from the council on treaty violations generally, and inauguration of action to punish promptly and seve

STRESA, April 14—The premiers of three great European powers participating in the Stresa conference announced today their sharp opposition to Germany's repudiation of the Versailles treaty which has “undermined the public confidence in security of peaceful order.” The three premiers, Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, Benito Mussolini of Italy and Pierre-Etienne Flandin of France, also announced in a communique closing the conference their complete agreement on a common policy of pacts to ward off war. Peace Hopes Shaken The communique said the magnitude of the declared program of German rearmament had invalidated the assumption upon which efforts for disarmament had hitherto been based, “and shaken the hope by which those efforts were inspired.” It strongly backed France's protest to the league to be taken up at Geneva tomorrow, but did not mention Germany's communique of yesterday whic

1935-05-17.text: LONDON, May 16 (4)—The possibilities of a shakeup in the British cabinet were discussed avidly today, not only in parliament lobbies, but in government offices. A strong attack launched against Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, by conservatives headed by Sir Austen Chamberlain and Winston Churchill has given rise to reports that Premier Ramsay MacDonald may become foreign secretary, a post he formerly held, with Baldwin resuming the premiership.

WOOL, DORSETSHIRE. Eng. May 17.—(#)—Physicians this afternoon kept constant watch over the little spark of life burning in the body of Lawrence of Arabia, as the fourth day since his motorcycle accident found him still unconscious. A hospital bulletin issued at 1 p.m., (8 a.m., E.S.T.) said Colonel Lawrence's condition remained critical.

Wool, England, May 17, UA—Col. T. E. Lawrence—Lawrence of Arabia—remained unconscious today and little hope was held for his recovery from the fractured skull he received in a motorcycle accident. No change in Lawrence’s condition was noted. He had remained unconscious since he was thrown 100 feet from his motorcycle Monday. Capt. C. P. Allen, a specialist, spent the entire night at Lawrence’s bedside at the military hospital here, expecting a definite turn in his condition.

LONDON, May 17.-(4) — Great Britain announced plans to develop oil fields in her own realm with the hope of freeing herself from dependence upon American and Russian sources for the supplies she needs to keep her fleet in operation in time of war. The project envisages a widespread oil prospecting stampede mildly resembling the Klondike and California gold rushes. The prospecting will be set in motion June 17 when the mines department starts issuing licenses. According to the plans, Great Britain will be mapped out into "oil areas," and licenses issued for plots of from eight to 200 square miles for fees ranging from 20 pounds (approximately $95) up. Both British and foreign individuals.

BALTIMORE. (P. Ed Howe, “the sage of Potato Hill,” is “mad” because he feels England, for which he says he has “never had any love,” is “beating us back to day.” “England is ahead of us,” asserted the emphatic Atchison, Kas., editor, now past 80, as he arrived here for an operation to restore his failing eyesight. “We need a big butter and egg man. If we found one, we'd make him dictator. It would make your head spin. What do I mean by a big butter and egg man? I mean a businessman who knows how to cut his suit according to his cloth. Roosevelt isn’t the man we want.”

London, May 17—Great Britain, France and Italy will hold private conversations at Geneva next week, it was stated authoritatively today, in an effort to find some way to settle the Italo-Ethiopian quarrel. Plans for these talks were revealed after Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and other British officials conferred with Sir Eric Drummond, the British ambassador to Rome, whom the foreign office hurriedly summoned home after Premier Mussolini's “hands off” Ethiopia speech this week. Sir Eric, it was understood, reported on his conversations at Rome Wednesday with Fulvio Suvich, the Italian under-secretary for foreign affairs. After Drummond's arrival, rumors ran about Whitehall that Il Duce, irate at Britain’s expressed intention to try to forestall war in Africa, had refused to receive the envoy. A dispatch from Rome last night said Drummond saw Mussolini briefly before leaving, the v

LONDON, May 17 (Ur) — Adolf Hitler's speech to the German Reichstag Tuesday night is expected to mark a definite turning point in the armaments crisis. It is to be followed on national defense in the British House of Commons. If Hitler's speech is temperate and offers any practicable basis for negotiations, indications were today that Great Britain will hasten to take advantage of it. “Any British opinion will be disappointed and dismayed if when Hitler faces his Nazi Reichstag at 8 p.m. Tuesday he does not make a speech which will give Europe another chance to turn toward peace. Like Benito Mussolini of Italy, he has often made such gestures at a time when his critics looked to him for explosive talk.

‘Copyright By Associated Press) BERLIN, May 17.—Persistent rumors that Pierre Laval, French foreign minister, will come to Berlin for a conference at the invitation of Reichsfuehrer Hitler circulated today despite official deprecation. A spokesman for the propaganda ministry said such a move was “hardly in the realm of possibility.” Diplomatic circles, however, asserted that Hitler is becoming increasingly apprehensive of the welding together of Russia, France and Czechoslovakia in pacts of mutual assistance. The developments of the past few days, they say, have encouraged the Reichsfuehrer to “talk turkey” with the French. While the possibility of Franco-German conversations was being discussed, Rear Admiral Gadow, retired, confirmed widely circulated

1935-08-02.text: GENEVA, Ave, 2 (UP)—Premier Pierre Laval of France told a secret meeting of the League of Nations council tonight that France and Britain had formed a united front to break a deadlock which has developed in their efforts to solve the dispute between Italy and Ethiopia. The council prepared for a night session to approve a compromise on which four nations were believed to be nearing an agreement. Inability of British and Italian delegates to reach an agreement on a compromise plan forced postponement of the council session scheduled for earlier in the day.

GENEVA, Aug. 1. (4) — Italy, France and Great Britain got together tonight on possible ways to keep peace in Africa and only Benito Mussolini’s final approval of the draft plan was needed to get it under way. - The tentative program, which will be submitted to Ethiopia tomorrow, was worked out at two conferences Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy, Premier Laval of France and Anthony Eden of Great Britain held this evening. After the final meeting, Laval told French newspapermen he was still awaiting word from Il Duce, who had been adamant to his earlier telephoned plea to accept peace formulae involving an Italian pledge not to go to war against Ethiopia during peace negotiations. A conference among representatives of Italy, Ethiopia, France and Britain next week, either at Paris or Ventimiglia, Italy, was one recourse reported under discussion. Il Duce had not agreed to that, however. The Lea

Geneva—(/)—Premier Mussolini today failed to accept in its entirety the Italo-Ethiopian settlement formula prepared last night by statesmen of Great Britain, France, and Italy and further telephone conversations with Il Duce appeared necessary. Mussolini’s reply to the suggestion was communicated to Premier Laval of France, one of those who had prepared the formula, by Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy, another who had taken part in its preparation. Despite the fact that Mussolini had balked at accepting the suggestions for a peaceful solution of the conflict with Ethiopia in their entirety, French delegates said they were optimistic, believing the outstanding points would be cleared up rapidly. May Be Public Laval said the League of Nations council definitely would meet today. If the complete accord of all parties, including the Ethiopians, is reached, the session will be public to adopt a f

Addis Ababa, Aug. 2--Sweden is almost certain to lift its arms embargo against Ethiopia, regardless of the attitude of Great Britain and other powers which are trying to avert an Italo-Ethiopian war, it was learned on reliable authority today. Sweden is known to be deeply sympathetic with Ethiopia in its impending hostilities with Italy and is prepared, it was said, to supply Ethiopia’s arms and munitions requirements. A trade treaty signed by the two nations recently was interpreted as giving Sweden a free hand to that end. Sweden, it was understood, will not raise the embargo until the present meeting of the League of Nations council, called at Geneva in an effort to forestall the war, has ended.

LONDON, Ont., (P)—Michael McCardell, who was arrested in Indiana under the name of James Parker, pleaded guilty before Magistrate C. W. Hawkshaw today to a charge of having participated in the kidnapping of John LaBatt, wealthy London brewer, last August. He was remanded to jail for two weeks, pending sentence.

(Copyright, 1935, by the A. P.) Geneva, Aug. 2 — Both Italy and Ethiopia rejected a Franco-British formula today for the settlement of the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. Leaders of the League of Nations, called to an extraordinary session of the council in an effort to prevent war, found they were unable to change the two nations’ attitudes. They cancelled plans for a session of the council in the late afternoon and decided on a cocktail party instead. Hope was expressed that this informal type of meeting might result in some kind of compromise. Premier Mussolini turned down the formula on the grounds there should be no time limit for the projected political negotiations among France, Great Britain, and Italy. The British want them ended some time in September while the assembly and council of the League are in regular session. This would enable the British to demand a League examination of al

Geneva, Aug. 2. — Great Britain and France hope to present to the League of Nations council for formal approval late today a two-part plan of negotiation designed to avert war between Italy and Ethiopia. Anthony Eden of Britain, Pierre Laval of France, and Baron Pompeo Aloisi of Italy agreed on the plan at a hotel room conference last night. Continued on Page ?.

Geneva, Aug. 2 (INS)—Charting a possible pathway to peace in the Italo-Ethiopian dispute, Italy, Great Britain and France today agreed upon a three-power parley to consider the entire East African problem. After 24 hours’ deliberation, Premier Benito Mussolini advised the League of Nations of his acceptance of the major points in a resolution drafted as a desperate effort to avert war. He agreed to the appointment of a fifth member of the League’s conciliation commission, whose task will be to liquidate the various frontier incidents which have led to strained relations between Italy and Ethiopia. Immediately upon receipt of Il Duce’s favorable reply, the British and French delegates here reiterated their willingness to attend a tripartite conference, which is expected to be held in France shortly. Negotiations scheduled for this afternoon are expected to result in complete agreement on

1935-04-09.text: | LONDON, April 9, ()—Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today that Germany demands land, arms and air equality, a navy 35 per cent the size of Great Britain's, proposes a non-aggression instead of mutual assistance pact in Eastern Europe and would be willing to discuss non-interference in Austria if a suitable plan were suggested. This is the first official and complete summary of what he and Captain Anthony Eden, Lord of the Privy Seal, learned on their recent trip to Berlin. Simon declined to outline what the British policy will be at the Stresa conference, but promised the British delegation would not bind the nation to definite commitments until after consultation with Parliament.

LONDON, April 8—Holding firm against biting criticism from the other powers, the British polished up their proposals for a general continental security system, open to all nations, tonight. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, far from robust in health himself, assumed the sick Anthony Eden’s part in British efforts to swing France and Italy around to a cooperative pact providing mutual assistance against an aggressor, but not aimed at Germany for arming in violation of postwar treaties, or at any other country... MacDonald decided to attend the Stresa conference when Eden’s doctor ordered him to bed. Russia Joins Chorus Soviet Russia joined the chorus of criticism with a blast in the press against the dropping of the proposed eastern security pact, and Moscow dispatches indicated the Russians were unwilling to be bound by any decision reached at Stresa not in accord with her views of Europe

The premiers of France, Italy and Great Britain will join in diagnosing the afflictions aggravating European unrest when the Stresa peace clinic opens Thursday. Premier Pierre-Étienne Flandin of France decided today he would lead the French delegation to the consultation of specialists on European relations. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain had announced yesterday he would accompany the British foreign secretary, Sir John Simon... Premier Mussolini will head Italy’s corps of experts in the role of host. Official quarters in London viewed the muddled international situation as gradually becoming clarified. A collective security system within the framework of the League of Nations was widely regarded as the probable remedy for Europe's ailments the Stresa conference will prescribe. Attention was attracted to a statement by Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council and

LONDON, April 9. — Diplomatic quarters today said they were informed that Great Britain has decided to participate actively in an all-inclusive European security system if France and Italy will accept the British proposals to be made Thursday at Stresa, Italy. In addition to growing indications for several weeks past that Great Britain would offer to commit herself actively to participation in a mutual assistance pact for all Europe, came the statement last night by Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council, that the country was willing to do its share in taking steps against any aggressor nation. Diplomatic sources said they understood the cabinet had decided to make a definite offer at Stresa of such active participation as a move to head off any possible anti-German efforts by Italy, because the British are determined that a general peace pact to which Germany...

Europe, with a large part of its population in mental panic over the danger of war, moved definitely today toward a showdown on armaments. Britain prepared to go to the Stresa conference with France and Italy Thursday to make a strenuous effort to bring Germany into a general agreement and block any effort by France and other powers to take strong action against Germany. Britain was understood to have invited Germany to submit new suggestions for a collective security system. The French cabinet met, however, and was understood to have determined on a firm stand for her own security and the curbing of Germany in eastern Europe. It was believed a general European arms conference would be suggested for this summer. Berlin proceeded quietly on its way, waiting for the other powers to show their hands. (By the Associated Press) A slashing northeaster churned the Atlantic into a frenzy Tuesday, battering the Eastern seaboard and imperiling shipping. Far out in the ocean, 200 miles due east of St. John’s, Newfoundland, the British freighter Tower Bridge, the former Badagry, wallowed helplessly, her hold filling. Responding to the stricken vessel’s S.O.S., the freighter S. S. Newfoundland proceeded to her side. The Newfoundland reported that she had sighted the Tower Bridge, which carries a crew of 32, and would “advise further details.” Fears were expressed by the coast guard that an unidentified cabin cruiser with three or four men aboard had sunk during the night off Eaton Neck lighthouse, on Long Island. The cruiser sent out flashlight distress signals Monday night. Three coast guard boats abandoned their search for her Tuesday morning. The steamer Fairfax wirelessed the coast guard s

| New York, April 9.—(UP) The British freighter Newfoundland, speeding to the assistance of the foundering S. S. Badagry, sighted the vessel wallowing in heavy seas at 9:06 A. M., she reported today by wireless. The Badagry was caught in a severe storm which caused wide damage along the Atlantic Coast. | The wind and high winds pounded the coast, damaging resort houses and endangering small vessels at sea. | The Badagry's holds were filling rapidly and she was in dire distress some 400 miles off Newfoundland, previous messages from the freighter advised rescue ships. In addition to the Newfoundland, another freighter, Manchester Producer, and an unidentified American ice patrol boat were in the vicinity. | The Manchester Producer changed her course when the Badagry’s first SOS went out, and the ice patrol boat radioed that she would “Proceed to your assistance at fifteen knots.” Thirty-f

LONDON, April 9. (U.P)—Great Britain has invited Germany to submit new suggestions for a collective security system for Europe, authoritative German sources said today. The report came as Sir John Simon prepared to make a final statement in the House of Commons before he and Ramsay MacDonald, Prime Minister, leave for the Stresa conference which starts Thursday. MacDonald to Go to Stresa MacDonald's decision to reinstate his foreign minister, and the announcement that Premier Pierre-Ettienne Flandin of France would accompany Foreign Minister Laval, assured an allied conference of real leaders. Benito Mussolini of Italy is both premier and foreign minister. It was learned that when Sir John Simon yesterday, in a conference with Dr. Leopold von Hoesch, German ambassador, rejected previous German proposals, he added the request that Germany present new proposals. 1935-10-07.text: Aduwa has fallen, and the flag of Italy flies over the ruins of Adigrat. — This was the Sunday story from the war in Ethiopia. There were “numerous deaths on both sides,” reported Ras Seyoum, commanding Emperor Haile Selassie’s black warriors in the Aduwa-Adigrat area. A report to London spoke of belching Italian machine guns and “terrible slaughter.” The Italians, this report said, claim “more than 2,000 were mowed down before the way to Aduwa was opened.” Thus the military campaign which President Roosevelt has called war and which Italy has described as “police measures”—and which Ethiopia insists is

LONDON, Oct. 7 (P)—Italian planes reconnoitering south of Aduwa ripped an Ethiopian troop column with bombs, hand grenades and machine gun fire, the Exchange Telegraph correspondent on the northern Ethiopian front reported today. The Ethiopian column, retreating from Aduwa, was moving southward along the caravan route toward Makale, which may be the immediate objective of the next phase of the Italian attack. The Italian planes, the correspondent said, encountered the column nine miles from the Italian lines on the edge of Aduwa.

By The Associated Press, Ethiopian situation at a glance: Aduwa—Il Duce’s troops marched into Aduwa after Ethiopian resistance melted away at gates. Rome—Fall of Aduwa officially announced, avenging 39-year-old defeat, citizens and clergy submit, Ethiopian attack at Dobra Finna repulsed. London—Press reports say “terrific slaughter” at Aduwa with machine guns mowing down more than 2,000. Addis Ababa—New mass bombing reported on northern and southern fronts; military strategists called Aduwa “hollow victory;” Selassie flays Il Duce for wanton slaughter of women and children, Geneva—Council committee complete report understood to brand Italy aggressor. Roosevelt embargo stirs Geneva. Paris—Laval reported opposed to immediate stiff sanctions against Italy. Washington—President Roosevelt warns Americans they travel on Italian or Ethiopian vessels at their own risk. Berlin—Reich awaits league
London, Oct. 7. (INS).—Six hundred Abyssinians were killed or wounded in the action before Adowa, Reuter's correspondent with the Italian troops estimated to-day. Many more were taken prisoners.

London, Oct. 6 ()—A withering hail of machine gun bullets from Italian airplanes killed “thousands” of Ethiopians today as the invading forces took Aduwa, the Exchange Telegraph correspondent with the Italian army reported tonight. The dispatch said Italian casualties were light and that the battle, which began at sunrise with the roar of Italian airplanes passing overhead, was fought with the fiercest intensity. As the planes passed over villages in the vicinity, they dropped bombs. Above the detonations, the correspondent reported, could be heard screams of injured and terrified natives.

NEW LONDON, Conn., Oct. 7— The coast guard cutter Agro put in here today and reported it had been rammed by a British rum supply ship, the Ponto, which was badly damaged and is in a sinking condition fifty miles off Montauk Point.

London, Oct. 7—(Monday)—(AP)—A nationwide ballot conducted by the Daily Mail showed today an overwhelming majority against the application of either economic or military sanctions by the League of Nations to attempt to halt the African campaign of Tlah.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 6.—If you believe all you hear, the only man our bold admirals of the grand fleet fear is Cordell Hull, the mild mountaineer from Tennessee. Loquacious gold-braiders parry questions about disarmament, Great Britain’s naval thrust in the Mediterranean and Japan's building program with the explanation that “Mr. Hull has ordered us not to talk.” Some time ago Rear Admiral J. K. Taussig, assistant chief of operations, discussed Japan's naval strategy with almost naive frankness before an audience of newspapermen. He agreed to let them publish his remarks as “background”—that is, without quoting him. The secretary of state flew into a rage—for him—and politely requested Secretary Swanson not to let his men meddle in foreign affairs. There have been two other incidents of the same sort. Though the navy has four friends in the White House—Messrs. Roosevelt, Howe, Early and McIn

1935-02-26.text: ROMFORD, England, Feb. 25 (?) —In a gloomy little coroner's court, British justice drew the last bit of pain and pathos today from the suicide of Elizabeth and Jane Du Bois, who leaped from an airplane to join two men in death. While the grief-stricken father of the girls, Coert Du Bois, United States consul general at Naples, waited with their mother in an adjoining room, a jury brought in a verdict of death “while of unsound mind.” The parents had hoped that the last intimate thoughts of their daughters would be kept from public knowledge but against a consular protest Coroner O.C. E. Lewis revealed those thoughts, written jointly in separate letters to their father and mother, before a jury of eight villagers and half a hundred newspaper men. Letters Tell of Love That the beautiful Jane Du Bois, broken-hearted at the death of Officer John A. C. Forbes in an airplane crash at Messina,

London, Feb. 25. (4) — With creditors hailing him into court, trouble with police regulations threatening, and another creditors’ suit in prospect, James J. Walker, former mayor of New York, announced tonight that his days “of being a good time Charlie were over.” This joyless statement followed an appearance by Walker in chancery court to which he was called to answer to two judgments against him for bills alleged to have been run up by his former wife in New York. The bills mentioned such things as bedroom slippers at $45 a pair. Walker had another big worry on his mind—the annoying British regulation requiring all aliens in England longer than three months to register with the police. The court hearing brought out the fact that the former mayor of Gotham had neglected to register any of his long stays in England during the last two years. Confronted by this added headache, Walker excl

LONDON, Feb. 26—(UP)—A tearful girl dancer today claimed the love of one of the two British aviators for whom Jane and Elizabeth DuBois, daughters of the American consul general at Naples, died in a plunge from a London-Paris airliner. Miss Kathleen Blakely, dark and usually vivacious, said at Watford, a few miles outside London, that she and Flying Officer J. A. C. Forbes were to marry in June. Jane DuBois was in love with Forbes. In a letter read yesterday at the inquest into the death of the two sisters which resulted in a verdict of suicide while of unsound mind, Jane wrote that Forbes was going to break off his engagement to Miss Blakely and marry her. “I cannot believe that the idea Charles (Forbes) would marry one of the DuBois girls existed anywhere except within the sisters’ imagination,” said Miss Blakely in distress. “We were to marry in June. He constantly referred to our pla

London, Feb. 25. Chief Inspector Donaldson of Scotland Yard, who had charge of the famous Brighton mysteries, "trunk crime No. 1" and its sequel "No. 2," tonight took over London's latest dismemberment mystery sensation: the gruesome find of a pair of human legs on a suburban train. The limbs, severed from the body of a man, were discovered by trainmen stuffed under the seat of a coach arriving at Waterloo station from suburban Hounslow. A coach cleaner inspecting a third class compartment found the objects wrapped in bloody newspaper and with an outside covering of heavier brown paper. The legs were almost hairless, and railway police at first could not even identify the sex of the individual to whom they had belonged. Physicians examining the legs estimated their owner had been dead about 12 hours.

London, Feb. 26—Egon Berger-Waldenegg, Austrian foreign minister, said Tuesday he expects Great Britain to request Germany's adherence to the Rome accords on Austrian independence when Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, meets Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler in Berlin. The statesman said he expected Sir John would go to Germany within 10 days. “The chief reason we came to London,” said Berger-Waldenegg, “was to discuss the Rome accords. We have every assurance that Britain considers no other point in the Franco-British proposals for the settlement of European problems of greater importance. He emphatically denied reports that Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg had issued “a warning to Germany to stop the Anschluss talk.”

LONDON (#) — Great Britain has assured Austria, it was learned today on high authority, that she will insist Germany sign the Rome accords guaranteeing Austrian independence as one of the principal conditions to the Reich’s admission to the proposed defensive air pact. Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, was said to have made clear to Kurt Schuschnigg, his Austrian counterpart, that he would not fail to stress this point. Sir John announced yesterday he soon would go to Berlin to undertake the bilateral conversations requested by Reichsfuehrer Hitler. It was considered significant that Sir John pointed out he would discuss all points of the Anglo-French proposals on his visit to Berlin despite indications that Germany desires to conclude the air pact agreement first. The attitude of the British government is that simultaneous agreement must be reached on the proposed system of

London —(#)— Three ships in distress during the last three days reported to the Lands End wireless station Tuesday that they had reached comparative safety as a storm of vast proportions held others on the Atlantic and Mediterranean in the spell of danger. The Italian S. S. Caterina Madre was reported under towage by the S. S. Hoedic. The owners of the Greek S. S. Eftychia Vergotti reported that vessel being towed convoyed toward Brest by a tug. The British S. S. Ottinge arrived Monday night at Brest Roads and was entering port Tuesday morning. The Greek S. S. Adamantios J. Pithis, bound from the Rio Plata to Londonderry, sent a wireless message that she was hove to in a strong gale which had damaged her steering gear. She gave her position as latitude 45.30 north, longitude 11.40 west. The Bay of Biscay, off the coast of France, remained the center of the turbulent tempests which crippl

| TOKYO—(Pp)—Chinese bandits are believed to have murdered Mrs. Ruth Wheatley Frencham, wife of a missionary worker whom they are holding as a hostage, it was learned here today. News of the latest bandit outrage has been suppressed in China and its publication in Shanghai Saturday was forbidden by the authorities. The bandits reportedly captured the town of Ningehao (also known as Ningkiang) near the western border of Shensi Province and carried off the Rev. S. C. Frencham, Melbourne, Australia, and his wife, a native of London. Reports which trickled through the tight censorship corroborated dispatches concerning the outrage said Mrs. Frencham had been slain. The Frenchams were married a year ago in Hanchung, Shensi Province, and on their wedding trip went to Ningchao to open a mission for the China Inland Mission. Shensi Province is several hundred miles west of Anhwei Province, where

1935-04-20.text: London, April 20 (UP)—Five children were killed, 800 persons were made homeless, and 30 houses were destroyed in a fire that for a time threatened to do great damage in the heart of Harbin, Manchukuo, the Exchange Telegraph Harbin correspondent reported today.

Rome, Apr. 19.—Rome’s hundreds of church bells hung in silence today as black-robed priests prostrated themselves before bare altars and led the devout in prayerful commemoration of Christ's death on the cross. Basilicas and churches throughout the eternal city were stripped of ornament, and the sacred images were covered with purple and black drapes for the Good Friday observances. Even the papal throne in the Sistine chapel was divested of its ornaments. In St. Peter's and other churches sermons based on Christ’s reproaches to his crucifiers were delivered. Rome lay like a dead city between noon and 3 p.m.—the hours Christ hung on the cross. In the churches Romans heard the doleful music of the “Stabat Mater,” a hymn dedicated to the Virgin mother as she stood at the foot of the cross. There were sermons on the three hours of Christ's agony—a series of discourses on the seven last word

MOSCOW, (CAP). M. Khripin chief of the Soviet military air force issued an appeal today through the authoritative organ Pravda urging all countries to unite in face of what he declared were German preparations for an aerial, chemical and bacteriological war. “Germany is prepared to use the worst of poison,” he charged. “It is doubtful that she will stop even The danger of a bacteriological attack, the air chief wrote, would be the greatest for countries separated from Germany by water, since there would be less chance of disease spreading to Germany. This observation was generally interpreted as a warning to Great Britain.

Ry The Associated Press BERLIN, April 19.—While Europe tensely awaited Adolf Hitler's reaction to League of Nations condemnation of Germany's rearmament, the Reich tonight made ready to celebrate the realm leader's 46th birthday tomorrow with typical Nazi fervor. An inkling of the course he has decided upon at secret conferences at Munich and in the Bavarian mountains was expected to be given in Minister of Propaganda Paul Joseph Goebbels’ radio address at noon tomorrow. While the fiery little Goebbels ostensibly will devote his ten-minute speech, on “Hitler as the private man” to an elaborate eulogy of the Führer, it was recalled that the propaganda minister has spoken for Hitler before. Observers therefore deemed it likely that Goebbels would hint at the Reich’s course in the face of the Geneva action. A propaganda ministry official said tonight the chancellor would spend his birthday

Rome, April 19 (4?)—Two of the world’s leading fascists, Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy and Vice-Chancellor Ernst von Starhemberg of Austria, talked more than an hour today in Venezia palace and well-informed sources said they discussed the restoration of the Hapsburg dynasty in Austria. Other subjects discussed by the two leaders were said to be the Danubian conference scheduled to take place the latter part of May in Rome and the problem of Austria’s re-armament. Recently there has been noted a trend in Italian sentiment more and more in favor of the restoration of the Hapsburgs to the non-existent throne of Austria as the only permanent means of maintaining Austria’s independence and preventing a union with Germany which would bring the regime of Reichsfuehrer Hitler to Italy's northern border. At the Danubian conference, the nations of Europe will sit in consultation on two of the

BERLIN, April 20.—Adolf Hitler, on his 46th birthday, today sent to fourteen nations represented on the League of Nations council an earnest, temperate protest against the council's denunciation of Germany's violation of the Versailles treaty. He made no threats and he did not bar the way for Germany to return fully to Europe’s councils. The birthday note, delivered to foreign offices in fourteen world capitals in the early afternoon, was accompanied by rumors that Hitler intended to ask Foreign Minister Pierre Laval of France, now the center of European diplomatic efforts to preserve peace, to visit him as his guest. May Return to League. That was no statement that Germany would not, on terms which are regarded as compatible with its honor, return to the league from which it resigned—giving the necessary two years’ notice—in October, 1933. MADRID, April 19.—(4)—Two persons were killed, several wounded, and more than one hundred arrested today during an extremists’ outburst in Zaragoza. The government announced that the outburst had been quickly put down and that the nation was tranquil as the observance of Good Friday proceeded. Beville was enjoying the greatest tourist boom since the overthrow of the monarchy and thousands converged there to view the picturesque Religion processions. Hotel and restaurants were exhausted.

Shanghai, April 20.—(U. P.)—Foreign missionaries fled headlong by air, river and road today, from the menace of the spreading revolt of Chinese rebels in the isolated Szechuan Province. Telegraphic reports from the interior indicated that the rebels virtually were in control of the entire province. They were sweeping the countryside looting as they advanced on Chengtu, the capital. General Li-Hsuing, commanding government troops, advised the foreigners to hasten their flight. Missionary reports showed that there were 52 Americans and 50 foreigners of other nationalities in Szechuan, presumably all on the way to Chingking, where the guns of American gunboats and other foreign warships of the Yangtze River patrol would protect them.

1935-04-14.text: Stresa, Italy—(#)—(Copyright)— Italy, France and England Saturday night closed their history-making conference, asserting they had reached full agreement on ways to save Europe from war. The tri-powered parley was called after Adolf Hitler’s dramatic decision to rearm the Reich which France, in an appeal to the League of Nations, declared perilous to peace. For the first time since the Paris peace conference, the heads of the three great western European powers—Benito Mussolini of Italy, Pierre-Etienne Flandin of France, Ramsay MacDonald of England—met face-to-face to talk over Europe's prospects for peace. Five Results After 18 busy hours at the conference table, these were the authoritatively reported results: 1. A German offer to enter an eastern non-aggressive pact provided she is exempt from any mutual military assistance clause. 2. Decision to call Danubian nations into conference

STRESA, Italy, April 13. UP Europe's faltering footsteps took a definite turn away from the abyss of war tonight. In the most hopeful international conference that has been held on the current crisis, Britain, France and Italy agreed on united action to avert war. They proposed a pact of non-aggression, along lines which Germany's Adolf Hitler has indicated he will accept. France moderated her demand for direct denunciation of Germany by the League of Nations. Britain persuaded Germany to enter an Eastern European pact of non-aggression, as distinguished from a pact or pacts for mutual defense, which Hitler rejected. Italy obtained a conference of the Danube countries to draft a pact of mutual assistance for Central Europe, which satisfies Benito Mussolini. As the conference prepared for its concluding session tomorrow, statesmen of all three countries were jubilant, and apparently in th

It is plainly today that the United States’ reported efforts to deprive her of her Latin-American markets might cost the American cotton grower some of his big market in Japan. A statement the Foreign Office handed to the Japanese press said United States commercial interests were agitating to exclude Japanese products from Central and South America. If Nippon's exports to those markets are restricted, the statement added, “it will affect our purchasing power, especially with reference to United States cotton, and will consequently react unfavorably upon America’s export trade to Japan.” United States cotton sales to Japan average some $100,000,000 annually. They constitute the largest single item in America's agricultural export trade. Sales last year totaled slightly more than all Japan’s exports to the United States, 401,000,000 against 399,000,000 yen (the yen is currently quoted at

MUNICH, Germany, April 13. — (AP) — A meeting of all Nazi department heads in the famed “brown house” here has decided that no quarter henceforth shall be shown the Nazi church opposition, it was disclosed authoritatively today. The heavy hand of the Nazi regime will descend without mercy on the heads of all clergymen and laymen who oppose the regime of Reichsbishop Ludwig Mueller, Hitler-appointed dictator of Protestant churches in Germany. This decision, which is being withheld from the German public for the present, was revealed to The Associated Press by an unimpeachable authority on church affairs. Four Hessian and two Saxon clergymen who have been taken to concentration camps for their activities against Mueller not only will not be released now but their heads have been shaved and they have been put in regular prison garb, it was learned. A few days previously, it was recalled, Dr

WASHINGTON, April 13.—(-)—The creation of a permanent national planning agency to chart the course of a continuing public works program was reported authoritatively today to be envisaged by President Roosevelt in shaping his four billion dollar relief work plan. This disclosure came while the unofficial house democratic steering committee was seeking a conference with the president to ask that members of congress be allowed some say about the projects to be undertaken in their districts. They hoped to see Mr. Roosevelt Monday. Other developments of the day included: Allocation by Harry L. Hopkins, the relief administrator of $113,661,384 for April relief. Georgia was given no funds and Pennsylvania only half a month’s supply, they being among the states which Hopkins has said had not made arrangements to furnish their share of the cost. Bureau of public roads officials said states were r

Washington—(#)—Harry L. Hopkins, the relief administrator, Friday allotted $79,040,959 to 42 states for June relief needs. He also approved grants of $6,051,930 for rural rehabilitation expenses for the next two months. The $85,092,889 came from a $140,000,000 allocation from the $4,000,000,000 work fund. Allotments included: Minnesota, $2,868,744; Wisconsin, $3,132,800.

By The Associated Press Washington, April 13—The grid-iron club tonight celebrated its fiftieth anniversary with caustic satire on the new deal, European diplomacy, and the gold decision. President Roosevelt was its guest of honor and, contrary to precedent, participated personally in one of the skits, that leading directly into his own speech, traditionally, with no reporters present. The fun-poking ranged from a Barnum side show, with cabinet members as the freaks, to a new version of the Pied Piper of Hamlin in which the country was portrayed as plagued by Senators Long, Overton and Schwellenbach, Father Coughlin, Dr. Townsend and Governor Olson. In commemoration of the club’s fiftieth birthday, there was a parade in which the marching groups carried banners running from the “Grover Cleveland Marching (Continued on page 2)

Rockville, Md. Apr. 13. —(U.P)— Five separate investigations were begun today into the death of 14 high school students in the crash of a fast passenger train into a Williamsport bus. The driver, Percy Line, was out on $1,000 bond—provided by the AAA. He was arrested on a manslaughter charge. He will appear at an inquest to be held at 10 a.m. Monday. Almost at the same time the inquest is being held, a mass funeral for 14 senior class students will be held at their homes in Williamsport, Md. 75 miles north of here. Maryland state and Montgomery county police began investigations in an effort to fix the blame. The Interstate Commerce Commission, the railroad and an insurance company conducted separate inquiries. Although the crossing was unprotected and both approaches partially obscured, the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad officials disclaimed

1935-09-03.text: By The Associated Press Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah. Sept. 3—Sir Malcolm Campbell, of England, bettered his own world record for land speed today on the salt beds of Utah with an average of 299.874 miles an hour. Keenly disappointed because he missed by a fraction his goal of 300 miles an hour, Sir Malcolm announced he will make another attempt tomorrow. Sir Malcolm beat his own speed for a measured mile when he sent his Bluebird roaring over the salt beds once in 11.83 seconds, or an average of 304.311 miles an hour. The second run in the opposite direction cut down the average speed. A left tire went flat on the Bluebird, but it came to a stop without accident. Campbell started the run at about 7:11 a.m. and drove into a glaring sun. The thermometer had soared since the cool of early morning.

[BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] GENEVA — Smaller nations are fearful of their own future as the council of the League of Nations prepares to meet tomorrow. LONDON—Belief is growing that Premier Laval of France has secretly guaranteed Mussolini a free hand in East Africa, and is thus lost to Britain's united action plan for peace. ROME—The Italian press demands clarification of the motive behind the “Rickett affair” regarding the granting of oil concessions in Ethiopia to an American corporation. ADDIS ABABA—Emperor Haile Selassie equips some troops with gas masks as others depart from the capital. CIRENCESTER, ENGLAND — Sir Stafford Cripps, socialist statesman, commends the United States for peace efforts, but doubts it could remain free of war.
