This rupture took place on the eve of a vital meeting of the council tomorrow in an effort to avert war in Africa, viewed as a threat to the League and to European peace. Laval told Eden “regretfully” he was unable to sponsor as a co-signer the report Eden will make. The French premier suggested they make parallel reports and this procedure was finally agreed upon. This was interpreted by some of the other delegations as an unfavorable development, indicating both Eden and Laval would maintain liberty of action at the council meeting. There was a difference of opinion upon the probable effect of the decision of the commission in Paris absolving both Ethi

London, Sept. hen incidents tightened in diplomatic quarters today the belief that the League of Nations council session starting tomorrow is doomed to fizzle into a state-saving fiasco similar to the 1932 session on the Lytton commission’s investigation in Manchukuo. The first of these incidents was a growing belief that Premier Laval of France had secretly guaranteed Mussolini “a free hand” in East Africa. The second was the last hour blow dealt by the so-called “Rickett affair” giving Ethiopian oil concessions to an American corporation.

Anthony Eden, of England and Premier Pierre Laval, of France, preparing for a League of Nations council session Wednesday on the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, failed yesterday to patch up their differences over the controversy. With Eden determined to “uphold the League of Nations,” Laval reminded him that France is equally determined to avoid sanctions and declines to concur in Eden’s report on the failure of tri-power peace conversations at Paris. Other developments in the Ethiopian situation were: ADDIS ABABA—Five thousand Ethiopian regular troops left Harrar for a field base and Emperor Haile Selassie directed the first distribution of gas masks to his subjects after rejecting British, French and Italian representations over his concession to American interests. ROME—The Italian press considered the Ethiopian concession final evidence of Italy's duty to turn down any compromise in its disp

Addis Ababa, Sept. 3. — The government announced today that it maintains the right to grant oil and mineral concessions to Francis M. Rickett, British promoter representing an American syndicate. The announcement amounted to defiance of a British warning to withhold the concession pending consultation among France and Italy. The government’s communique charged that Italy, despite the guarantee of Ethiopia’s independence under the treaty of 1906—under which she is protesting the concession—is preparing to violate the treaty openly by resorting to war at the expense of her international obligations.

NEW LONDON, Conn, (AP)—Coast guard patrol boats, called to the aid of the 5,000-ton freighter, Ruth Kellogg, by anxious shore residents, found the vessel not to be in distress today off New London lighthouse. Telephone calls to the base indicated the ship had gone aground near Ocean Beach but officials, after assuring themselves the Ruth Kellogg was safe, said the illusion was created by the deep draft of the boat in a channel close to shore. The craft continued on its way to State Pier here.

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng. Sept. 3. The British liner Neuralia sailed for Malta today with 1,500 troops and 300 sailors and Royal Air Force men. The majority of the troops were anti-aircraft detachments of the Royal Artillery.

1935-02-16.text: MESSINA, Sicily, Feb. 15.—One of the British seaplanes traveling from London to the naval base at Singapore came to grief today on a Sicilian hillside, burning almost beyond recognition the nine persons aboard it. So completely was it destroyed that not until an official investigation late tonight was it correctly identified as the Ace of Diamonds, having been previously reported to be the Singapore. Commander Lang of the Singapore-bound squadron hastened here by train from Naples, whence the plane had started today, to take charge of the wreckage and the bodies of eight officers and men and one civilian. Farmers of the neighborhood said the plane passed through cloud banks and emerged almost in the face of the summit of San Filippo mountain. The pilot swerved the

BERLIN, Feb. 15.--(4)--The German government tonight advised France and England that Germany had “a sincere desire to promote the safeguard of peace” and advised those two nations that the European questions that arose in the recent London conversations will be thoroughly examined. This reply was made by Adolf Hitler’s government to the Franco-British agreement reached two weeks ago and which was made the basis of proposals to Germany. The text of the German reply follows: “Germany is in agreement with the British and French governments in a sincere desire to promote the safeguarding of peace, the maintenance of which is in the interests of Germany's security as well as in the interests of the security of other European states. “The German government welcomes the spirit of trustful discussion between the individual governments which animates the reports from the British and French govern

BERLIN -()— Germany Friday night declared herself ready in principle to use her air forces to preserve the peace of western Europe, inviting Great Britain to inaugurate bilateral discussions to that end. A note couched in broad terms — the reich’s reply to Anglo-French proposals for an inclusive European security agreement — declared this air agreement might be one step toward solution of other problems and promised to examine the question of how to avoid an armament race. Germany agrees with the British and the French governments in desiring sincerely “to promote the safeguarding of peace,” the note said. “The maintenance of which is in the interests of Germany's security as well as in the interests of the security of other European states.” The note specifically avoided mentioning the proposed eastern and Danubian pacts, but a foreign office spokesman said Germany's reply followed the

Messina, Sicily, Feb. 15.—(P)—A British seaplane seeking in vain for an emergency landing field plunged to earth and burned near here today, killing seven British officers and men aboard. Farmers of the neighboring area said the plane, the “Singapore,” passed through cloud banks and emerged almost in the face of the summit of San Filippo mountain. Right Wing Touched Rock. The pilot swerved the ship, but the right wing touched the jutting rock, they said. Nevertheless, the plane wobbled on for about four miles while the pilot evidently sought some place to land. After passing the village of San Filippo, the ship nosed down suddenly and burst into flames as it crashed. Tonight four bodies had been extricated from the ruins, all of them burned beyond recognition. Another body was found 150 feet from the plane. The bodies of Flight Lieut. Henry Longfield Beatty, who was in charge of the plan

LONDON, Feb. 15.—(4)—Douglas Fairbanks Sr. tonight was cooling his ire in the salty breezes of the English Channel as he and Sylvia, Lady Ashley, headed for the Virgin Islands, first port of call on their world yacht cruise. Apparently angry because his carefully laid plans to escape undetected were upset, Fairbanks was the leading player in tempestuous scenes—the station platform where they boarded the boat train was his stage—rivaling any of his screen performances. The actor seemingly was in a fighting mood. Three times he threatened violence, twice offering to punch the nose of anyone approaching and once proposing to swing for the jaw.

Landon, Feb. 15. — Premier Ramsay MacDonald's nationalist government, safely past the laborite threat of a vote of non-confidence, faced a new problem today in the disastrous pepper market speculations. The house rejected the motion of censure for the government's handling of the dole problem by a thumping majority—374 to 68. The pepper gamble, however, was brought up in the debate and seized.

Messina, Sicily, Feb 16 (AP) — The British cruiser Durban was en route here today to take to Malta the bodies of nine British officers and men killed in the crash and burning of the British seaplane “Ace of Diamonds.” Italian authorities have placed a guard of honor over the bodies of the victims of yesterday's crash. The plane, one of a group of four bound for Singapore, struck San Filippo mountain's jagged rocks, after emerging from a cloud bank. The craft nosed down suddenly, struck the earth and burst into flames.

Marseilles, France, Feb. 16 (UP)— Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi embarked today on a flight which they hope will take them across the South Atlantic and beyond Rio De Janeiro to break their world airplane distance flight record of 5,654 miles. Taking turns at the controls, they are piloting their old famous high wing monoplane, Joseph Lebrix, with a payload of 10,000 post cards. Their probable course lies south southwestward across the Mediterranean and Africa and the approximately 1,715 nautical miles of the Atlantic between a point around Dakar, Senegal, to the eastern tip of Brazil, thence down the coast as far as possible. Determined to await the best possible weather conditions, the aviators had been here since mid-January ready to start. They estimated they could fly 6,210 miles without difficulty. That would take them well beyond Rio and they hoped to keep on down the coast toward M

1935-02-03.text: PARIS, Feb. 2.—France was authoritatively reported tonight to have agreed in London to abandon military clauses of the treaty of Versailles and to recognize German rearmament, in return for England’s support of a series of pacts to preserve peace and Berlin's return to the League of Nations. France was said to have England's promise to speed the signing of a Danubian pact to assure Austrian independence, the eastern Locarno pact and a new defensive air treaty. The latter would be signed by Germany, Italy and Belgium, as well as England and France, and would oblige all signatories to come to the instant aid of any nation attacked from the air. Agreement Incomplete A London dispatch on the Anglo-French conference said a complete understanding had not been reached because France has not agreed to all terms under which Germany would be freed from the military clauses of the Versailles treaty

London, Feb 2.—(f)—Agreement by Great Britain and France upon a comprehensive program settling issues causing European tension and relieving Germany from the military restrictions of the Versailles treaty appeared assured tonight. The Anglo-French talks were adjourned shortly before midnight and well-informed French quarters said the conferees were in harmony and that only a few minor points remained to be cleared up tomorrow. A communique is expected after that session. Pierre Laval, French foreign minister, plans to return to Paris Monday. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, in statements to the Associated Press indicated that they also anticipate a complete agreement, “We have not quite finished,” said MacDonald. Simon, asked how the negotiations were progressing, said “oh, very well, but we shall have to sit again Sunday.” Information in Fre

By The Associated Press Stockholm, Feb. 2—Sweden’s most exciting financial scandal since the bizarre Ivaar Kreuger drama was disclosed today with the formal arrest of Baron Nils Stiernstedt, court chamberlain in the special service of Prince Carl, King Gustav's brother. The baron, who previously had been dismissed from his court position, was accused of embezzling 100,000 kronor (approximately $25,000) in an effort to recoup his personal fortunes. Tonight, facing trial on charges preferred by the royal family itself, Baron Stiernstedt was reported on the verge of a nervous breakdown, so that police found it difficult to question him. Stiernstedt is 51 years old. He is charged with appropriating $15,000 in the form of gold acquired in the melting of medals of the seraphim order, which were returned after the death of the recipients, and of embezzling $10,000 from Prince Carl’s estate.

Paris, Feb. 2 ()—French students abandoned their anti-foreign campaign today but they promised to start all over again if they get no “satisfaction” within the month. A proposed mass meeting in Paris to protest “unfair competition” by foreign medical students fizzled out after the 1,000 parading students found their proposed meeting hall “occupied.” To answer the statements published by medical students, whose boycott of classes since Wednesday to protest the asserted “unfair competition,” that 74 percent of the students at the University of Paris are medical students, official figures were issued to show that the proportion is only 21 percent. There are 33 American medical students in Paris and some dozen others in the provinces, the authorities disclosed.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 2 (/P)—The supreme court stepped outside the bounds of precedent today to inform a tense business world that it probably must wait at least another week for the high tribunal's epochal decision on the gold cases. With the administration virtually ready to meet all the eventualities of an adverse verdict, markets ridden with suspense, and all expecting the decision Monday, Chief Justice Hughes summoned the court clerk and dictated: "The chief justice, in order to avoid an unnecessary crowding of the courtroom on Monday, directs the clerk to announce that the court is not ready as yet to announce a decision in the gold clause cases." With this announcement, Monday, Feb. 11, became probably the earliest date upon which the decision, on which the whole Roosevelt monetary program is delicately balanced. (Turn to Page 2, Column 3.)

(Copyright, 1935, by Associated Press.) FLEMINGTON, N. J., Feb. 2 (4, - The grandmother of the murdered Lindbergh baby may be called to the witness stand in the Bruno Richard Hauptmann trial next week to provide a murder night alibi for one of her servants—the dead Violet Sharpe. Mrs. Dwight Morrow, widow of the onetime ambassador to Mexico and Morgan partner, was the employer of the Sharpe woman on March 1, 1932, when the Lindbergh baby was kidnapped. There has been defense testimony that the young Englishwoman—who subsequently committed suicide when police returned to question her—was seen late on the night of the crime, and that she was carrying “a golden-haired baby.” David T. Wilentz, the New Jersey attorney general directing the prosecution of Hauptmann, said tonight that he was undecided as to whether he would ask Mrs. Morrow to face the crowded courtroom as her daughter, Mrs. Ann

WASHINGTON, Feb. 2.—Burly John L. Lewis today thrust the American Federation of Labor and the Roosevelt administration further apart with a bitter assertion that Donald R. Richberg, the president's recovery coordinator, was a “traitor to organized labor.” Lewis, head of the United Mine Workers, held Richberg directly responsible for Mr. Roosevelt's renewal of the automobile code without consulting any federation official. “Mr. Richberg, springing from the loins of organized labor as he did, recommended to the president of the United States the imposition of a code on labor in the automobile industry for continuance of 48 hours a week,” shouted Lewis before a senate judiciary sub-committee. Lewis assailed the “Du Pont family” and General Motors as not entitled to the 48-hour week. He said it was “uneconomical and indefensible.”

WASHINGTON, Feb. 5—A secret conference of Senate appropriations committee Democrats today was marked by such conflict over the administration’s $4,880,000,000 work relief bill that the scheduled meeting of the full committee Monday to report the measure was postponed. Rarely has a meeting of a Senate committee been so carefully guarded as the Democratic parley today. Some of the senators refused even to admit they had attended a meeting. But out of it all came reports of a complete collapse of efforts to reach accord. In one sense the result symbolized the general situation. At the Capitol, as Congress headed into its second month, little has been accomplished despite the huge Democratic majorities in both houses. The Democratic meeting on the relief bill today was held after Republican members of the committee abandoned their plan to act as a group in consideration of the measure. After

1935-04-17.text: GENEVA, April 17—(4)—The League of Nations council today adopted the tri-power resolution condemning Germany for her repudiation of treaty obligations with only Denmark abstaining from voting. The resolution, presented jointly by France, Great Britain and Italy, deplored unilateral abrogation of treaty obligations and requested that the league appoint a committee to consider what measures, economic and financial, may be taken against future repudiators of international commitments. Denmark Doesn't Vote. Dr. Peter Munch, Danish foreign minister, in the discussion which preceded the voting, explained Denmark would not cast its ballot because she feared adoption of the resolution would hinder “the task of reconciliation.” Joseph M. Beck, Polish foreign minister, voted for the tri-power resolution, presumably, league authorities said, under strong persuasion from France. Poland previously ha

Copyright 1935, By Associated Press GENEVA, April 16.——France, Britain and Italy today asked the League of Nations to censure Adolf Hitler for rearming Germany in violation of treaties and punish nations which repudiate — in the future. A resolution the three powers jointly introduced at today's session of the league council asserted Germany had failed “in the duty which lies upon all members of the international community to respect the undertaking they have contracted.” France, in a memorandum accompanying the resolution, declared flatly “the German initiative of March 16 (Hitler's renewal of compulsory military service) must be condemned.” A German government spokesman said at Berlin “you may be sure if this goes through the League of Nations, Germany never will rejoin it.” The tri-power resolution declared Germany's rearmament equivalent to repudiation of the treaty of Versailles and

/ London, April 17.—()-—Seventy-five persons, mostly women and children, were trampled to death in a panic Sunday night among a crowd of alms seekers on Bahrein island, in the Persian Gulf, the India office disclosed last night. The mob assembled when it became known that a Persian merchant had planned to distribute alms to the poor. A clamoring multitude thronged the narrow passageway leading to the inner courtyard of the merchant’s home.

WASHINGTON, April 16, (AP) — Scanning the world’s mounting expenditures for armament, experts today estimated that Japan next year will far outstrip Great Britain, the United States and other great powers in the proportion of her budget to be spent for national defense. It was estimated by the same experts that the Japanese budget figures showed that empire will spend 47 per cent of her total budget for military purposes and that this would make her the leader in such outlays, comparatively speaking for the second consecutive year. Last year compilations available here credited Japan with a 43.7 per cent national defense budget. By comparison with Japan experts calculated the United States will spend about 25 per cent of its ordinary budget for defense in the next fiscal year. Great Britain they said will spend about 16 per cent of a budget amounting to approximately $3,649,000,000, excl

(Copyright, 1935, by Associated Press) LONDON, April 17.—David Lloyd George gave a final polishing to his ‘new deal’ program today in preparation for an interview with the British cabinet tomorrow in which he will try to sell his ideas to the government. Many observers were of the opinion, however, that whatever chance the white-haired Welsh leader had to win adoption of his program has been spoiled by his old political enemy, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer. Rejection Expected Friends of Lloyd George fear that since Chamberlain has finished arranging his finances for the year and presented his budget to the House of Commons, any prospect of the cabinet's accepting the wartime premier’s elaborate public works scheme and the other features of the plan has been precluded. They deplore the fact that the cabinet deferred giving Lloyd George a hearing until after the budget w

(Copyright 1935, United Press.) Geneva, April 17.—The League of Nations Council today approved a resolution rebuking Germany for violating the Versailles treaty and providing for a committee to study the question of imposing penalties on future treaty violators. Denmark abstained, because France, Great Britain and Italy, joint sponsors of the resolution, would not soften the condemnation of Germany for violating the treaty in decreeing compulsory army service and inaugurating a military air force. Those who voted for the resolution were: Argentina, Chile, Mexico, Spain, Turkey, Italy, France, Great Britain, Russia, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Australia, and Portugal. Thus there was a 13 to 0 vote and in the name of the 37 nations belonging to the League, scattered over all the earth’s surface, Germany’s action was formally condemned. Under the resolution, the League council will set up a com

PARIS, April 17. (U.P)—Robert and Marjorie Switz, young American couple, were freed today at the end of France's greatest espionage trial. Confessed leaders in an international espionage gang, they won their freedom under a clause in the penal code which permits leniency for defendants whose confessions implicate others. Both were found guilty at the final hearing today in the 13th Correctional Court, but their 16 months in prison, the judges held, covered the sentences they should serve. It was expected that both would be expelled from the country at once. They had been in prison since Christmas time, 1933, when agents of the French Surete Generale, in a series of raids that startled Paris, arrested the first of the fanciful gang whose spy activities had been watched for months.

(Copyright, 1935, by The Associated Press) - Berlin, April 17—Dazed, ever stunned, by the fact that even Germany’s official friend, Poland, voted in favor of the Geneva resolution of censure; Wilhelmstrasse officials gathered today to determine what official attitude Germany shall adopt. While Germany fully expected the satellites of the three powers that met at Stresa and Russia to support the league resolution, Germany officialdom seemed frankly disappointed by Poland's attitude and intimated surprise that Germany’s old comrade-in-arms, Turkey, and the Latin-American nations led by Argentina have decided to approve the Franco-British-Italian resolution. The evening newspapers, with one exception, denounced Geneva's action. Some of the diplomats on the Wilhelmstrasse regard the unfriendly nature of the resolution as less important, however, than the insistence by the league council upon

The stock exchange supported trans-Atlantic issues. Paris — French financial sources said the supreme court decision would contribute to the stability of all currencies. Berlin—The German press saw the decision as a victory for President Roosevelt. Stockholm—Prof. Gustav Cassel, gold authority, said the decision 'has the greatest moral significance.' Rome — The stock exchange, isolated by government regulation, showed no important changes. Moscow — The Soviet Union showed no interest whatsoever in the supreme court’s findings, the newspapers not even mentioning it. Capetown — Union of South Africa markets firmed and the government is expected to have an $11,000,000 surplus due to gold taxation. Geneva — League of Natio

(Copyright, 1934, by the AP) LONDON. — High diplomatic quarters here stated Monday night that pressure is likely to be brought upon foreign governments to make protests to the United States on the Supreme Court's gold decision. The disappointed holders of American bonds are expected to urge their governments to take this action, it was said.

LONDON, Feb. 19—(UP)—A committee representing British investors in United States gold securities will hold a special meeting next week to decide on possible legal action to force payment in gold, it was announced today. The British investors felt that under the wording of the Supreme Court decision, they could show actual monetary loss and be entitled to court action. This would be because of exchange rates. The London advisory protective committee for American investments, headed by Sir Harry Armstrong, former British consul-general at New York, considered a suit based on the Jay Treaty between England and the United States, drawn in 1794, and including a clause for payment of obligations in gold. Barnett Hollander, counsel for the committee, also cited the post-war treaties of the United States with Germany, Austria and Hungary, in which the United States stipulated payment in gold. “W

(By the Associated Press) London—Holders of United States bonds in foreign countries may ask their governments to seek enforcement of the gold clause, diplomatic sources revealed. Paris—French financial experts indicated they were relieved by the supreme court decision since it indicated to them that the gold bloc countries’ currencies will not be affected. Berlin—Reichsbank officials took cognizance of the ruling in a special meeting. Montreal — The Montreal Stock Exchange reacted with rising prices. Rome—Italy welcomed the ruling with relief, since government and private firms have been paying their dollar debts in devalued American money.

BERLIN— Baroness Benita Von Berg, a society beauty of surpassing charm, and Frau Renate Von Natzmer, another blue-blooded beauty, were beheaded today for spying on behalf of a foreign state. The execution of the two women was carried out at dawn with such secrecy that it was hours before the official veil could be penetrated sufficiently to learn their exact fate. At first, officials said they had been shot by a firing squad. Then the statement was retracted and it was admitted the women had gone to the block, where their heads were chopped off by a silk-hatted executioner with a medieval battle axe. Their necks shaven for death, they were led into the courtyard of Ploetzensee prison and executed before a small, carefully chosen group of witnesses. Other defendants in one of the most fantastic espionage conspiracies in modern times were sentenced to life imprisonment. The latter were Bar

BERLIN, Feb. 18 (4)—Baroness Renate Von Natzmer and Frau Benita Von Falkenhayn were decapitated today as spies, The double execution was announced officially at 2:50 p. m. (8:50 a. m. EST) today. Strict secrecy was maintained until the official announcement was made. The official announcement said Reichsfuehrer Hitler declined to exercise his prerogative of mercy. The two women were beheaded in the courtyard of the prison in which they had been held here. Previous to the announcement of execution, a high official in the ministry of propaganda said that judicial experts ‘were expecting a reply from Munich at any minute.’ Hitler was in Munich.

Dunedin, New Zealand (AP)— Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd and members of his Antarctic expedition returned to civilization in an aura of romance today. After the expedition’s flagship arrived here, Admiral Byrd’s second in command, Dr. Thomas C. Poulter, and Miss Helen Gray, both of Mount Pleasant, Ia., were married. Admiral Byrd gave the bride away. Arrangements for the wedding were completed by wireless. Dr. Poulter first met Miss Gray when he was a member of the faculty of Iowa Wesleyan. She later assisted him in scientific work and during the time Dr. Poulter has been in the Antarctic she has been caring for his three children by a former marriage.

Berlin, Feb. 18 (AP) — Two German women, Baroness Renate Von Natzemer and Fraulein Benita Von Palkenhayn, were killed on the block today as spies. An executioner beheaded them in northwestern Berlin shortly before noon as the German government acted with wartime sternness and in the utmost secrecy to smash espionage of Germany's military secrets. The two women were accomplices of a Polish baron, Col. George Sosnowski, formerly of the Polish army. Sosnowski himself was saved from execution by the intervention of the Polish ambassador, and although the reputed espionage leader escaped with his life, he received a sentence of life imprisonment. Also sentenced to life imprisonment was Fraulein Irena Von Jeyna, a German. The sentences were passed Saturday by the People's Court and the verdict was studied over the weekend by Chancellor Hitler, who is now in Munich.

1935-09-04.text: SALT LAKE CITY, Sept. 4 (®)— Sir Malcolm Campbell and his bluebird racer were poised today for a triumphant return to England with a record—finally computed correctly—of 301.1292 miles an hour on land. A “silly mistake”—the words were Sir Malcolm’s—kept the “human bullet” for hours in the belief he had failed on the Bonneville Salt Flats to achieve his dream of a mile in 12 seconds. The fact he had bettered his previous record of 276.816 miles an hour by more than 23 miles, as originally figured by the timers, brought only a wry face and a declaration he would have to “go through it all again” Thursday. It was far into the night before the officials of the American Automobile Association sent word hurriedly to the intrepid driver, with many apologies, that they had made a mistake. Campbell declared he was “delighted” but that the news was rather in the form of an anticlimax.

| BONNEVILLE SALT FLATS, Utah (UP)—Sir Malcolm Campbell Wednesday prepared to return to his native England after establishing a record of 301.1292 miles per hour in his racing car, the Bluebird, on the salt flats course here. Campbell said he would sail for England from New York on the Majestic September 12. He was undecided whether he would ever race again. “I am delighted and believe the Bonneville track is the best in the world,” he said after being informed he had exceeded 300 miles an hour and attained his long-sought goal. “My Bluebird left an indelible mark on this track, one I am proud of. I do not know whether I shall ever race again, or come here next year, or build a new Bluebird, but I feel the keenest of pleasure in exceeding my goal of 300 miles per hour.” An air of uncertainty was cast over the Briton’s performance by a conflict of corrections in timing. and Great Britain, who have been of somewhat divergent ideas concerning the paths of peace to be taken in the Italo-Ethiopian conflict, were reported today to have attained a common footing. Shortly before the League of Nations council was to meet in private session today at 4 o'clock this afternoon (9 o'clock this morning Iowa time) the British delegates announced that Great Britain and France not only agreed on the text of the report of Sir Anthony Eden, minister for the League of Nations for the Paris parley, but Eden and Premier Laval actually drafted the text and between them decided what course should be taken in this situation, Geneva, Sept. 4 (AP)—France

Saybrook, Conn., Sept. 4. — The 65-foot auxiliary schooner “Edith T.”, out of Boston and carrying a crew of 12, ran aground today off East Lynde Point lighthouse and called for aid from the New London Coast Guard base. The Coast Guard patrol boat 192, a 75-footer, was dispatched here and a 400-foot patrol was made ready to lend assistance if necessary. The “Edith T.” grounded within 35 yards of the light, at the entrance to Saybrook harbor. The Coast Guard base was advised there was “no immediate danger.”

LONDON (#) — Ramsay McDonald, acting Prime Minister, came today from Lossiemouth, Scotland, in the vanguard of cabinet ministers returning to Whitehall to be ready for swift action if warranted by developments at Geneva. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin will return tomorrow to take command of the home front in the Italo-Ethiopian dispute.

Port Said, Sept. 4—Guns of two British warships freshly anchored in the mouth of the Suez Canal frowned from beneath their canvas jackets on four Italian troop ships today, and officers on both sides exchanged grim smiles behind their binoculars. For today, as Geneva decides for peace or war, these troop ships might be the last to pass, and these guns would be among the first to speak should the League of Nations choose to substitute their language for diplomacy.

BONNEVILLE SALT FLATS, Utah, —(#)— Sir Malcolm Campbell, British land speed ace, thundered past an official record of 300 miles an hour in his 6-ton Bluebird on the salt flats of Utah Tuesday, and an official corrective announcement disclosed Tuesday. In one of the most startling reversals in the history of speed racing, the American Automobile Association contest board said Sir Malcolm had actually averaged 301.33 miles per hour instead of the 299.875-mile clip with which he was credited for the 2-way run. Campbell Delighted It brought delight to the 50-year-old “human bullet.” His heart set for years upon a 5-mile-a-minute record, Sir Malcolm curbed his disappointment when told he had failed by a fraction to make it Tuesday, and announced he would take to the 13-mile course again Thursday. With the 300-mile-an-hour record his, however, he called off further runs. “I will leave immediat

Informed circles were convinced that Great Britain’s position had been so weakened by the events of the last few days—including the participation of Francis M. Rick- (Continued on Page Seven.)

1935-10-23.text: The British government, saying it was running risks in its efforts for international peace, proposed today the strengthening of its defensive forces. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, calling the parliamentary elections for November 14, said he would go to the people for support of defensive rearmament. “In the interests of world peace,” Baldwin declared in the House of Commons, “it is essential our defensive services should be stronger than today. “I will not pursue a policy or be responsible for the government of this country if I am not given the power to remedy those deficiencies that have occurred in our defensive services since the war.” The conservative prime minister's declaration came in the midst of peace talk and diplomatic conversations to end Mussolini's invasion in Ethiopia. Previously, Sir Samuel Hoare’s pacific address in the Commons—which left the way clearly open for an e

Fears of a European conflict, precipitated by Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, were allayed generally today. On every hand there was talk of peace. The “behind the scenes” conversations between Paris, London and Rome—seeking a satisfactory solution to end the East African conflict—were progressing. The pacific efforts were given new life by Sir Samuel Hoare’s House of Commons address, in which the British government left the way open for an end to hostilities without imposing military sanctions against Italy. Premier Pierre Laval of France predicted success for his personal peace efforts. Laval sought Mussolini’s minimum terms for ending his invasion of Haile Selassie’s empire. One highly important thing was still emphasized by the British, even with all the peace talk: Any peace must be acceptable both to Haile Selassie and to the League of Nations. London, Oct. 23 (AP)—Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, hard-bitten flier from down under, who has conquered both the Atlantic and Pacific, took off from Croydon airdrome today for a quick three-day flight to Australia. “Smithy” still weak after a “nasty shake-up” from the weekend chill did not aim to break any records, but hoped to demonstrate feasibility of a mail route between London and Sydney. He planned to go by way of Marseilles, Cairo, Baghdad, Singapore, Port Darwin and Melbourne.

Britain continued Tuesday with unabated energy her war against Mussolini's war in Ethiopia. Mussolini accelerated the speed of his fighting machine in Africa and his high command announced the goal was the complete submission of all Ethiopia. England voiced no optimism as regards the chances of achieving peace at this time, but merely clung to the idea with that traditional bulldog tenacity which characterizes the race. There was no gloom in evidence, on the other hand, amongst the heretofore highly successful Roman legions driving through the sands of the Ethiopian desert regions. There was a further lessening of the tension between Britain and Italy, a tension which in recent weeks had developed into a dangerous belligerency, backed by naval guns and troops on both sides. But Italy continued resentfully to regard England as the one mainly responsible for making the former an outlaw amo

Addis Ababa—Emperor Haile Selassie denies Italy used poison gas or dum-dum bullets; says he won't talk peace until soldiers leave the country. London—Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, at opening of parliament makes new peace bid to Premier Mussolini. Rome—Peace parleys are reported under way in Rome, Paris and London. Meanwhile Italy tightens its hold on Ethiopia. With the Italian Army in Northern Ethiopia—Gen. Emilio de Bono, Fascist leader, says his goal is the submission of all Ethiopia. Paris—Premier Laval seeks clarification of Premier Mussolini’s views on peace before submitting them to London.

MARSEILLES, France, Oct. 23.—Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, undertaking a fast flight from England to Australia, arrived here today after a three and a half hour hop from London and took off again in an attempt to reach Baghdad, Iraq, by nightfall. A quick refueling enabled him to hasten his departure. He said he would land at Athens, Greece, if he found he was unable to reach Baghdad by evening.

London, Oct. 22--A new British peace call to Premier Mussolini was sounded in the House of Commons today when Parliament began a three-day debate upon the international situation, preliminary to dissolution and the national elections Nov 14. Striking a definite conciliatory note, Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign secretary, summed up the Italo-Ethiopian situation with assurances that sanctions to be taken against Italy were economic and not military. Still Time, He Pleads He pleaded that there is still time to work out an honorable and acceptable African peace agreement. Hoare’s speech caused vigorous opposition attacks upon government policies, led by Major Clement Richard Attlee, Laborite, and Sir Herbert Samuel, Liberal, which furnished a keynote for the election, expected to be fought out.

ROME, Oct. 23.—(P)—Sir Samuel Hoare’s statement of British foreign policy, excluding military sanctions from Britain's efforts to halt the Italo-Ethiopian conflict, virtually banished from Italy today the dream of a European war. Informed Italian circles believe the British foreign secretary’s address to parliament yesterday lessened further the Anglo-Italian tension already eased by mutual assurances of non-aggressive intentions. A sense of relief spread through Italian quarters after Hoare’s disclaimer of any British intention to employ military measures against Italy. These circles were impressed favorably by his declaration that Britain did not oppose fascism. His admission that a closing of the Suez Canal, Italy’s route to the theater of East African warfare, would mean European war, and his recognition of Italy’s need for expanding lent further encouragement to Italians. Anthony Eden, disclosed to the House of Commons today that, on behalf of the British government, he had offered to cede a strip of British territory to Ethiopia in an effort to end the Italo-Ethiopian dispute. LAKE CHARLES, — La., July 1—(P)—Eight longshoremen were wounded on the docks here early today in a clash of some 600 white and negro workers of two opposing longshoremen’s unions over the right to load the British steamship Queen City. The two forces of about 300 to the side fought with shotguns, pistols and their fists. After the first skirmish each retreated and held their lines while a call went to Governor O. K. Allen for troops. Adjutant General Raymond Fleming was sent to Lake Charles to investigate. The two unions, the International Longshoremen’s Association and the Louisiana Longshoremen’s Association, each claimed they held a contract to load the ship. Arbitrators gained a truce during the night and they believed trouble would be averted. But at dawn, shooting suddenly broke out with each side claiming the other fired the first shot. LAKE CHARLES, La., July 1.—(P) A gunfight broke out on the Lake Charles waterfront this morning when two opposing Longshoremen's unions fought over the privilege of loading the British steamship Queen City. Eight longshoremen were wounded, two critically, in the fight in which pistols and shotguns blazed away in hand-to-hand fighting. Sheriff Henry Reid telegraphed Governor O. K. Allen to call out the militia, and Adjutant Raymond Fleming was ordered from Camp Beauregard to take charge of the situation. The adjutant general was empowered to use the Lake Charles company of militia if necessary.

WIMBLEDON, Eng. July 1— Donald Budge, flaming red-head from Oakland, Calif., sprang the biggest upset of the all-England tennis championships today when he beat Henry Wilfred (Bunny) Austin, England's second ranking player, 3-6, 10-8, 6-4, 7-5 to reach the semi-final round. Using the same terrific backhand with which he had crushed Christian Boussus of France in the fourth round, Budge outlasted Austin in the deuced second set and then took full control of the situation to win and keep America in the running for the title now held by Fred Perry of England. Budge’s victory followed by some hours the unexpected defeat of Sidney Wood of New York, generally rated Perry's most formidable challenger. Wood was beaten by Jack Crawford of Australia, 6-4, 6-3, 6-8, 5-7, 6-1. Budge will play Baron Gottfried Von Cramm of Germany in the semi-finals while Crawford is tackling Perry.

London, July 1—(UP)—Capt. Anthony Eden, secretary for League of Nations affairs, told the House of Commons today that while in Rome he had expressed to Premier Benito Mussolini the British government's "grave concern" over the turn of events between Britain and Abyssinia. "The British government," Eden said, "could not remain indifferent to events which might profoundly affect the League's future. Public opinion in this country feels most strongly on this issue." Italy Rejects Proposal Eden revealed that while in Rome he had suggested to Mussolini Britain's cession to Abyssinia of "a strip of territory in British Somaliland, giving Abyssinia access to the sea." Eden admitted that Mussolini had rejected Britain's offer for settlement of the Abyssinian dispute. In describing the British offer of a territorial concession, he called it "tentative" and said it was intended to facilitate "such

YARMOUTH, N.S., July 1. ()— Hauled off a rocky ledge near Chebogue Point, the 150-foot yacht of Dr. John Brinkley, Del Rio, Texas, was brought into harbor Monday for repairs. The vessel appeared little damaged, and Dr. Brinkley is to continue his cruise along the Atlantic seaboard within a few days.

LONDON, June 30.—"Mystery planes" roared through war-like maneuvers over secret European testing fields today as leading powers engaged in a scramble for air supremacy. Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Russia and others have speeded up their research and expanded aerial programs. They are turning out and testing scores of models of advanced planes of all sorts. Most of these are being kept hidden from public gaze and, the nations hope, from the prying eyes of agents of other countries. Europe often hears the view expressed that the "next war" will be fought in the air. (The navy department in Washington yesterday purchased 60 large patrol planes, whose specifications are closely guarded. It was an $8,507,037 order, one of the department’s largest in peace times.) 1935-06-15.text: LONDON, June 15. (AP)—China has sent notes to the United States and Great Britain regarding Japanese action in Northern China, it was said on reliable authority today. The British government has been continually in touch with the United States and other powers regarding Japan's action, it was learned authoritatively. To the British note at least, it was learned from a trustworthy source, was appended a paragraph which was in effect an appeal not only for consultation but for action by the nations signatory to the nine power Chinese independence treaty. The fact that the appeal assumed the form of an addendum, and was not incorporated in the note, presumably explained an official denial by the Chinese foreign office at Nanking today that China had appealed to the nine power signatories. London, June 14, (4P) An Anglo-German agreement establishing the relative strengths of their navies was almost ready to be signed tonight and observers here hailed it as an important step toward European peace. Gen. Joachim Von Ribbentrop, Adolf Hitler's arms envoy extraordinary, brought back to London Hitler’s affirmative reply to all Britain’s conditions for the agreement. Terms of the pact were quickly decided, Authoritative quarters said it will involve: 1. Germany's pledge to limit her navy to 26 per cent of Britain's underage tonnage. 2. Germany's acceptance of limitation by categories of ships, as well as by total tonnage. But if— 3. A release clause to protect Germany if other powers launch unrestricted construction of smaller warships and submarines.

Wittenberg, Germany —()— The smoke and dust cleared away from the Reinsdorf explosive works Saturday, disclosing a scene of utter devastation. Rescuers, working frantically for two days after a series of tremendous blasts, were able to discover the bodies of only 47 of the 52 persons the Nazi government asserted were missing in the debris of the wrecked plant. While some of the 73 persons injured seriously were still in critical condition, about 100 who suffered minor injuries were allowed to go home. The propaganda ministry announced that about $350,000 marks ($140,000) has been contributed to a relief fund in a nationwide drive. The government arranged for a national mourning ceremony at Reinsdorf June 18 in the presence of Reichsfuehrer Adolph Hitler. Authorities said part of the wrecked factory may be restored as various buildings had been protected from the explosions by huge walls

Wittenberg, Germany, June 14 With the official death toll remaining at 52, rescuers worked in shifts until darkness set in tonight to drag bodies out of the wreckage of the Westfalia-Anhalt munitions factory at Heinsdorf, three miles from here. The ruins still were hot from the explosion and subsequent fire which destroyed a large section of the factory yesterday afternoon when rescuers had accounted for 45 of the announced dead. Officials said that only seven more bodies remained hidden under the debris.

BURBANK, Calif., June 15 (AP) — Wiley Post roared away from the air terminal here today on his fourth attempt to span the continent in a record-setting stratosphere flight to New York City. The noted airman, piloting his famed five-year-old “Winnie Mae,” at altitudes ranging between six and seven miles above the earth's surface, hoped to reach Floyd Bennett Field in New York in seven or eight hours. Post, wearing his “Man from Mars” stratosphere suit, lifted the ship off the ground at 7:25 EST. The take-off was without incident and Post dropped his detachable landing gear about as he neared the end of the runway. He will land the “Winnie Mae” on a special skid forming a part of the plane's belly. Weather reports from the Middle West, particularly in the Chicago region, were not favorable, but Post was determined to make the trip today without further delay. He planned to follow the “Grea

WASHINGTON, June 14—In almost stop-watch time, the “stop-gap” NRA resolution swept through a listless house today by an 11 to 1 majority, and a matter of minutes later was signed by President Roosevelt. The legislation would extend a code-less and bob-tailed remnant of the recovery unit until April 1, 1936. Signs Without Comment Vice President Garner and Speaker Byrns signed the resolution almost immediately after passage by the house. Mr. Roosevelt apparently was waiting with his pen raised, and affixed his signature without comment as soon as it reached the White House. In the house there was some protest from Republicans about “gag” rule—but neither the minority members nor the Democrats used all their allotted 30 minutes of debate before the 336 to 31 roll call adopted the resolution. The extension measure will be sent to the White House, probably tomorrow, after Vice President Garne

Associated Press Staff Writer WASHINGTON, June 14—(AP)—The threat of a soft coal strike Monday all but vanished today with an appeal from President Roosevelt that the miners stay at work, John L. Lewis, president of the United Mine Workers, promised Mr. Roosevelt immediately he would withdraw his strike order if producers would agree to continue present wages and working conditions through June 30. Producers will assemble here tomorrow at 10 a.m. to consider the President’s proposal. Operators here today freely predicted acceptance. Congressional delay in the consideration of the Guffey coal stabilization bill led the President to ask for the strike delay. Later Mr. Roosevelt told newspapermen he was in general accord with that measure and hoped that as a matter of sound policy the strike could be averted until the bill has been considered by Congress. Union Air Terminal, Burbank, Calif., June 15. — Wiley Post, one-eyed Oklahoma flier, began his fifth attempt stratosphere flight to New York at 4:27 a.m. (PST) 7:27 a.m. (EST) today. Dressed in his weird ‘man from Mars’ flying suit, the veteran flier lifted his little cream-colored monoplane, the Winnie Mae, from the ground easily and pointed its snub nose eastward in an effort to rocket through the high altitudes in a record time of eight hours. The plane swept off the ground in an early morning haze and darted into the east without circling the field. The retractable landing gear was dropped about 20 feet off the ground and the ship was speeding on its way, climbing steadily. Many of the spectators at the field missed seeing the ship leave the ground because of the low visibility at the airport. PARIS — British and French experts have drafted a plan for solution of the Italian-Ethiopian war, for submission to the League of Nations and Italy, the foreign office admitted today. Details were refused. The decrees are designed to enable the nation to withstand the economic sanctions being applied by the League of Nations, Prices will be strictly regulated to prevent profiteering, The decrees involved a system somewhat similar to the rationing used dur

GENEVA, Oct. 29—(UP Copyright)—League of Nations leaders believe they may be able to effect peace between Italy and Ethiopia by the new year either through diplomatic negotiations or economic pressure, it was indicated today. It was reported on reliable authority that Great Britain and France are prepared to insist that new penalties, providing for a complete boycott on Italian goods and stoppage of imports of key products to Italy, be made effective by mid-November. Reports from European capitals say that Premier Benito Mussolini is worried both over the effects of penalties imposed and to be imposed and over the difficulties which his armies in East Africa face. Both French and British sources report that Britain and France at last are working closely together on penalties and that emphasis is to be put particularly on the boycott of Italian goods. This, if effective, would reinforce t

LONDON, Oct. 29 ()—Raymond Henry Bousquet, Winnipeg boxer known as Del Fontaine, was hanged today for the murder of Hilda Meeks, while opponents of capital punishment demonstrated outside Wandsworth prison. As Bousquet went to his death, 20 men, employed by Mrs. J. Van Der Elst, walked up and down the street with placards denouncing the death penalty, and a sound truck played hymns. Mrs. Van Der Elst is the leader in a movement which frequently makes such demonstrations. Sir John Simon, home secretary, yesterday rejected an appeal for a reprieve from the National Union of Boxers. Members of the union asserted they knew before Bousquet killed his sweetheart that he behaved abnormally owing to a condition of "punch drunkenness." The prosecution claimed Bousquet killed the girl in a jealous rage. Bousquet was convicted in the Old Bailey last month of murdering Miss Meeks, a 21-year-old wait

BRITAIN imposed its second sanction against Italy today with enforcement of an embargo on credit to the warring Fascist nation. A surprise announcement that Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare, as well as Anthony Eden, would go to Geneva late this week to represent Britain in view of forthcoming "important decisions," led to a belief in some quarters that even further punitive measures soon would be undertaken. British sources expressed hope that the foreign secretary's presence at the League of Nations would lead to more definite Italo-Ethiopian "peace talks" than have been held. Sir Samuel was expected to confine himself to committee work, with possible private meetings with Premier Pierre Laval, a central figure in the European negotiations, and other leading statesmen. Money Market Closed Effective today, the British money market was forbidden to make loans to Italian banks in London.

London, Oct. 28 ()—Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in his first platform speech for the general election November 14, pledged today that Great Britain would not lead the world in an arms race. There is no question of "huge armaments" being ordered by the government, Baldwin said at Wolverhampton. Only the necessary bolstering of the nation’s defenses will be undertaken, he asserted, including the replacement of obsolete warships. At the same time another government leader, Ramsay MacDonald, lord president of the council, urged that "steps should be taken at once to make it possible to arrive at an international economic agreement which would revive international trade." MacDonald, opening his National Labor part of the national government’s campaign here, sought new world enthusiasm for agreement upon trade revival steps. London, Oct. 29 (UP)—An Italian airplane squadron bombed Magalo, 200 miles southeast of Addis Abeba, silenced two anti-aircraft guns, started many fires and spread panic among the Ethiopians, an Exchange Telegraph correspondent with the Italian army reported.

DJIBOUTI — Italy's southern army reported to have established a front more than 400 miles long in southeast Ethiopia. ROME—Northern Italian army advances its position as Fascists observe 13th anniversary of march on Rome. LONDON—Prime Minister Baldwin pledges Britain will not lead in arms race; little hope for peace is seen. ADDIS ABABA—Anti-aircraft guns are mounted as Ethiopia prepares to celebrate Sunday the 39th anniversary of the Italian defeat at Aduwa. ENTISCIO—Italians solidify a new and stronger line. GENEVA—Russia joins nations ready to apply boycott against Italy.

| LONDON, Oct. 29. (AP)—Lady Charles Cavendish, the former Adele Astaire, whose twin sons died Saturday shortly after their birth, “continued to improve satisfactorily” today, a statement issued from her temporary residence said.

1935-01-17.text: GENEVA, Jan. 17.—Germany today agreed in principle to demilitarization of the Saar, as demanded by France and Great Britain. French fears of attack unless the Saar was included specifically in the Rhineland zone caused a dispute which delayed the League of Nations council decision to award the territory to Germany. As a result of the German agreement, the way was believed open for immediate award of the territory to the Reich. As soon as Germany agreed in principle to the demilitarization, France agreed that the Saar should be handed over formally to Germany on March 1, the date suggested. Germany withdrew its demand that the transfer be made by February 15.

FLEMINGTON, N. J., Jan. 16.— Discovery of English and German dictionaries in the Bronx home of Bruno Richard Hauptmann, with words used in the Lindbergh ransom notes heavily underscored, was disclosed tonight by Attorney General David T. Wilentz of New Jersey. Wilentz made the disclosure in answer to a defense question raised at Hauptmann’s murder trial today—why the same man would misspell simple words and correctly spell the more difficult ones in the ransom letters. “Hauptmann is a dictionary student,” Wilentz declared, “and we will prove it.” The state, he added, found two sets of dictionaries in the Bronx house—one German and one English—with words such as “hazardous,” that figured prominently in the ransom notes, heavily underlined.

BOSTON, Jan. 17.—James Roosevelt, eldest son of the President, was reported “very comfortable” today at the New England Baptist hospital, where he is under treatment for colitis. Dr. Sarah Jordan said he would not be operated on and probably would remain at the hospital only a short time.

LONDON, Jan. 17—(AP)—Clarence Guy Gordon Haddon, who was bound over to keep the peace last January after pleading guilty to a charge of blackmailing King George, was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment today for violation of peace bonds. The 43-year-old Haddon claimed to be the king's nephew and was charged with having written letters to the monarch demanding money, asserting he was the legitimate son of the king's late elder brother, the duke of Clarence. Haddon had signed three bonds to keep the peace for three years.

BANGOR, Wales, (A4P).-— ave Lloyd George, white haired veteran of more than a half century in politics, returned to the limelight today with a “new deal” policy for Great Britain. Highlights of his plan, paralleling President Roosevelt's program in the United States, include a national investment and development board, or “brain trust,” a new financial policy, a slum clearance program, and a scheme of land settlement. Some 20 miles away from Little Portmadoc, where the World War premier launched his career as a youth, the “Welsh wizard” will unfold before his constituents tonight details of the sweeping reconstruction.

TOKYO, Jan. 18 — (CNP) — The suggested naval discussions in Washington between Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Japanese delegate to the recent London naval parley, were abandoned today and Koki Hirota, foreign minister, instructed the admiral to come home at once. Instead of leaving London for New York, Admiral Yamamoto is to start at once for Tokyo by way of Siberia.

France over the border, reported today that two communists had been killed at Neuenkirchen and a dozen other anti-Nazis had been beaten at other towns in the Saar Basin Territory. The refugees told tales of horror in stoical voices as the first big rush into France got under way. The scenes along the road leading from the Saar into Sarreguemines were reminiscent of war.

MONTREAL, Que., Jan. 17. — Fumes from a burning motion picture projector in a private residence last night took five lives. Thirteen others were injured. The fire broke out as twenty friends and relatives of Napoleon DeSmarteau met at his home to view a private screening. Suddenly the film in the projector burst into flames, trapping the audience in a small dark hallway. Four children and a 70-year-old woman were asphyxiated by acrid smoke. Nine other guests were injured as they struggled to escape. Four firemen were injured in rescues and in getting the bodies from the burning building.

1935-02-15.text: Berlin, Feb. 15.—(P)—Nazi officialdom sees in the Anglo-French proposals for a western European air pact possible solution of the continent’s gravest problems. This attitude was manifest today as Reichsfuehrer Hitler assured the French and British ambassadors he was ready to discuss the proposed pact. These discussions, official quarters believe, may lead to other agreements of a military and non-aggression character, likely not only to relieve European tension, but also to break down the wall of pacts threatening the Reich’s borders and answer the long-puzzling question of Germany's armament status.

BERLIN, Feb. 14.—Germany tonight told France and England she would be glad to discuss with them an air pact for Western Europe. At the same time, she showed little interest in suggestions emanating from London that she return to the League of Nations, join the French-sponsored Eastern security agreement and adhere to the proposed Central European non-interference pact. The Reich’s note—awaited with intense interest during the week that Adolf Hitler, in virtual seclusion, has been pondering his reply to the Anglo-French proposals—was delivered to Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador, and Andre Francois-Poncet, the French ambassador. The text, it was announced, will not be made public until Saturday, although it had been previously indicated its publication might be expected early this evening. A foreign office spokesman, however, revealed that few lines were devoted to the proposals for Ge

LONDON, Feb. 14. (UP) — A determined labor effort to have the House of Commons censure Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's government for its unemployment relief policies went down to overwhelming defeat late tonight after lengthy and sometimes bitter debate. The vote, coming after charges and counter-charges had been hurled back and forth as MacDonald fought back stoutly at his adversaries, was 374 to 68.

LONDON, Feb. 15. (#)—Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., and Sylvia Lady Ashley sailed from Southampton today on the East Asiatic liner ‘Europa for the Virgin Islands and the start of a world yachting cruise. The American motion picture star was extremely irritated because of the discovery of the plans. The Europa will land the couple at St. Thomas, and afterward they plan to go to Hawaii, Tahiti, and at last to the Orient. In High Spirits In contrast with the actor's chagrin, the golden-haired titled 'ex-chorus girl appeared in high spirits. She smiled gaily and seemed not the slightest perturbed as she kissed her sister goodbye just before the boat train pulled out for Southampton. As they left their residences this morning both Fairbanks and Lady Ashley declined to discuss their plans. The American called a husky British bobby to protect him against inquirers. Later, as the inquirers persisted, F

GENEVA (#) — Hugh Wilson, United States delegate to the world disarmament conference, warned the powers today the people of the world want something done and done quickly to control the manufacture and traffic in war materials. Replying to attacks made on the American draft particularly by England and Italy, Wilson reminded the delegates the Americans merely fashioned their proposals along lines likely to command general support.
ROME, Feb. 15.—(UP)—Seven persons were believed killed today in the crash of a British air force hydroplane near Messina.

SANS ae LARA EN, rev, A AYE Pra authoritative denials were issued today that the Prince of Wales might marry Infanta Maria Christina of Spain, daughter of former King Alfonso. One denial came from the prince’s entourage at Kitzbuehel, Austria, where he is skiing; the other from former Queen Victoria of Spain, who is here. The rumor that the prince and the infanta might marry was the result of a visit of the infanta to Kitzbuehel.

Chicago. —- (AP) -- Charging again that the $100,000 kidnapping of John Factor was a hoax to forestall his extradition to England, Attorney William Scott Stewart prepared to ask the supreme court at Springfield today for a new trial for Roger Touhy, Albert Kator and Gus Schaeffer, now serving 99-year sentences. The state, however, is determined to keep the “terrible Touhys” in prison and Assistant State’s Attorneys Marshall V. Kearney and Wilbert F. Crowley, who obtained the convictions assembled arguments to combat every effort to free the trio.

Since that time, according to the same source, the British government has received no reply from Italy. Ramsay MacDonald became acting prime minister of Great Britain today on the eve of an expected climax to the Anglo-Italian controversy over Ethiopia. (International News Service) BELGRADE, Aug. 7.— Reports published abroad that the English Duke of Kent had been offered the Greek throne during his visit in Yugoslavia were denied here today. The report said Premier Panayoti Tsaldaris of Greece had offered the throne to the young duke during a conference at the castle of Prince Paul, Yugoslavian Regent, near Bled. It was stated officially that Premier Tsaldaris visited Prince Paul at the castle, but missed the duke and his Greek bride, Marina, who were motoring. It was understood the duke and duchess purposely avoided Tsaldaris.

LODON, Aug. 7—(INS)—Revealing that friction between Great Britain and Italy over the Italian-Abyssinian crisis had reached a serious stage, the foreign office disclosed today that Britain has made “strong representations” to Italy against Anti-British attacks appearing in the Italian press. Dispatches from Addis Ababa said today that 3000 gas masks manufactured in Germany had arrived in the Abyssinian capital, in preparation for an expected gas attack from Italian airplanes. Indications that France is accommodating Italy by relieving her of some border defense responsibilities were seen today when no replacements were sent for 42,000 Italian troops which were removed from the French border for service in Africa.

London, Aug. 7 UP)—Minions of flying ants swooped down on London's suburbs today, swarming in gardens and streets. They even held up a tennis tournament, descending on the courts in such a dense cloud that the players were forced to run to shelter. Housewives brushed piles of ants from their doorsteps and worked—often in vain—to keep the ants out of their pantries and kitchens. A. Moore Hogarth, founder of the Institute of Micro-Biology, formerly the College of Pestology, said the invasion was the worst he had known in the area.

BERLIN, Aug. 7 (AP).—An official Nazi announcement proclaimed today that further “measures” would be taken to halt a stream of “undesirable elements,” especially Jews, pouring into Berlin for refuge. The announcement said the measures already have been drawn up by Count Wolf Hendrick von Helldorf, head of the Berlin police, and Julius Lippert, Nazi commissioner for Berlin, to stem the migration from the provinces—“greater than ever before.” No indication was given as to the precise nature of the steps to be taken. Driven from small towns by the Nazi anti-Semitic campaign, the refugees seek protection in the city, saying they have no place else to turn unless they leave the Reich. Despite a warning issued last week, the flow apparently persisted in such proportions that the city officials have decided to act.

Berlin, Aug. 6 (4)—Remnants of the once powerful brown-shirted Storm Troopers, it became apparent tonight, have been chosen to carry on an important part of the Nazi campaign against “saboteurs.” Following parades of brown shirts in several cities, including Berlin, the newspaper Der Angriff announced: “The Storm Troop has jumped into the fight against Jews, political Catholicism and reactionaries,” it printed a picture of a truck full of brown shirts bearing the placard, “We will permit no sabotage against Der Fuehrer's reconstruction.”

(Copyright, 1936, by the Associated Press Port Said, Egypt, Aug. 7.— Approximately 240,000 Italian troops and laborers have passed through the Suez Canal in the six months, en route to East Africa, official figures disclosed today. In a single day recently, nine Italian transports laden with soldiers, airplanes, tanks, and artillery ammunition made the passage from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. Not all Italian transports are bound for East Africa, however. The statistics show that in the last three weeks, six large Italian steamers carrying more than 5,000 Italian soldiers suffering from malaria, dysentery, and typhoid made the passage for Italy. At Alexandria and other ports, Italian officials are chartering all available steamers for use as transports. 1935-06-19.text: (Copyright, 1935, Associated Press) London, June 18.—Great Britain today became virtually boss of Germany's future naval building. In one of the most remarkable agreements on national defense ever concluded between two sovereign nations, the Reich agreed to limit her fighting ships, by total tonnage and approximately by category, to 35 per cent. of Britain's. She agreed further to let Britain set the pace of naval expansion, giving this nation the sole right to decide when the total tonnage of the two fleets shall be raised or lowered. One British Concession An exchange of notes between the two governments officially disclosed the terms of the bi-lateral agreement, reached during two weeks of naval conversations here. Britain made one important concession. She promised to allow Germany to build her submarine fleet—the dread weapon with which she almost won the World War—up to full equali

LONDON, June 19—(UP) Great Britain has arranged for separate naval conferences with France, Italy and Russia, it was learned today. France has accepted the invitation to send a delegation of experts, it was learned, and Italy and Russia are to follow in order. Capt. Anthony Eden, minister for League of Nations affairs, will arrive in Paris Friday in time to lunch with Premier Pierre Laval. It was learned that the primary purpose of his visit will not be to discuss the British-German naval agreement, which led to those in prospect. Though Eden will try to convince France of the necessity for the agreement giving Germany a 35 to 100 naval ratio with Britain, he will principally try to advance the conclusion of an aerial conference embracing Britain, France, Italy, Belgium and Germany. British and German naval delegates met at the admiralty today to discuss such technical problems as buildi

RIS, June 19.—(UP) — France will remain firm in her opposition to the two-power naval pact between Great Britain and Germany, Premier Pierre Laval intimated today in a speech to the foreign affairs commission of the chamber of deputies. Laval said France was disappointed at developments, since there had been seemingly clear indications at the Stresa and Geneva conferences that there would be wide international discussions of important questions in the near future. He indicated France was astonished less at the substance of the Anglo-German pact than at the procedure, by which France was suddenly confronted with an accomplished fact. Pierre Apel, former chairman of the naval commission and former minister, said to the United Press: “The Anglo-German pact is disastrous for France. We must double the pace of our construction. We intend to maintain our position in the face of Germany, which

PARIS, (AP)-- Members of the chamber naval committee said today a majority of that body consider that the British scrapped Washington naval treaty of 1922 when they made their present naval agreement with Germany. This consensus, they stated, was shown at a secret session of the committee. They said the committee agreed with the government's view that “France has a free hand” on the naval question. The committee was understood to foresee a naval armament race as a result of the Anglo-German

LONDON, June 19 (Wednesday) (UM)—A split in the close cooperation among the former allied powers—Britain, France and Italy—was feared today as a result of the new British government granting Germany submarine parity and a 35-100 naval ratio with its own. Both France and Italy dispatched cool notes to the government headed by Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin, registering reservations to the terms of the Anglo-German sea strength understanding. Their attitude failed to deter Britain from rushing to completion her accord with Adolf Hitler and granting the Reich a navy larger than Italy’s and approaching that of France—in further violation of the Treaty of Versailles. The terms, outlined in a “white paper,” include: 1. Germany shall have a navy 35-to-100 with the British, or approximately 400,000 tons, figured on the present British strength. 2. The Reich shall have the right to possess submar
MANSFIELD—(# — Mansfield today surveyed the effects of a near-cloudburst Tuesday. An inch and a half of rain fell in less than an hour.

VANCOUVER, B. C., June 18 (AP)—Bloody street rioting broke out here today when police tried to scatter a crowd of 1000 striking longshoremen and their sympathizers who attempted to march onto the Ballantyne pier. A barrage of tear gas bombs broke among the seething ranks of the marchers, including women, and the fighting soon spread over a wide area. Royal Canadian mounted police broke through the struggling masses to rescue a group of city police who were surrounded by the strikers. Eight policemen and at least nine civilians required hospital treatment for injuries received in the three-hour melee, and scores of other persons received minor hurts or were affected by the tear gas. Ambulances raced to the disorder to pick up the more seriously hurt. At times the police were stopped in their tracks by the fierceness of the assault. Rocks, sticks and other weapons were used by the strikers

(By United Press). Addis Ababa, Abyssinia, June 19.--Throbbing drums in rain-soaked jungles and drilling thousands in Addis Ababa and many villages are preparing Abyssinia for war with Italy in August or September. The entire country is convinced war is inevitable. No one believes the Italo-Abyssinian commission meeting next week at The Hague will settle disputes and the only hope here is that Great Britain and France may influence Italy against its indicated plans. Brisk recruiting in Addis Ababa and Harrar in the last four months have increased the Abyssinian army from 3,000 men to approximately 15,000. The entire populace, from tribes of the interior to official circles of the capital, is wildly excited and grimly determined to repeat the triumph of 1896 when an Abyssinian army annihilated an Italian expedition of 12,000 men. 1935-12-08.text: By The Associated Press London, Dec. 7—Japan announced flatly today she demanded absolute naval parity with the United States and Great Britain. The announcement threw even more gloom about the international conference opening Monday. It was this Japanese demand which caused the breakup of an unsuccessful preliminary conference early this year between the United States, Japan and Great Britain. To enforce their position, the Japanese said no other question can be discussed until their demand is met. Their country is now on the short end of a 5-5-3 ratio with Great Britain and the United States. The Japanese position was conveyed to the British admiralty at a conference which the Oriental delegation asked specially. Japan, the delegates clearly stated, is not prepared to accept any proposals for exchange of a building program unless there is a definite agreement in the question of total t

By The Associated Press Cairo, Egypt, Dec. 7—Police and 1,000 students of Cairo university fought a fierce battle with stones, bird shot and clubs today in Egypt's latest outburst of opposition to British domination. Three British policemen were injured and 60 students were taken to jail. The fighting flared for half an hour at the Giza bridge. Dozens were beaten and knocked down. Police fired bird shot into the legs of the demonstrators and fired guns over their heads in the air before gaining control. The direct cause of the outbreak was a refusal to the students of permission to erect a monument on the campus in honor of classmates killed in a recent anti-British riot. The students had just returned to classes after an enforced holiday.

LIMASSOL, Cyprus, Dec. 7 (UP). —Four British destroyers arrived unexpectedly in Famagusta harbor this morning. They were the Basilisk, Boreas, Boadicea and Bulldog. Cyprus island is one of great importance, 200 miles from the northern entrance of the Suez canal and equi-distant from the now heavily fortified Italian Dodecanese island off the Asia Minor coast. Cyprus is just off the coast of Syria and south of the Asia Minor bulge into the eastern Mediterranean.

Paris, Dec. 7. (AP)—Preliminaries were laid tonight for a Franco-British peace plan to halt the African war and secure a tense Europe. Emerging smiling from a two and one-half hour conference, France's Premier Pierre Laval and Sir Samuel Hoare, foreign minister of Great Britain, announced they would draft a basis for settlement. French officials said the draft would be submitted to Premier Mussolini of Italy and the League of Nations sanctioning committee of 18 as the limit of what France and Britain consider the league can accept. Thus the responsibility for any failure in negotiations would be shifted upon Premier Mussolini. Oil Ban May Be Delayed, An oil embargo undoubtedly will be voted against Italy by a league committee December 12, these officials said, but its application probably will be held in abeyance until after the United States Congress meets in January. London, Dec. 7.— (4) — Funeral services were held in St. George's chapel of Windsor Castle today for Princess Victoria, sister of King George, who died Tuesday at the age of 67. Only members of the Royal family, including King George and Queen Mary, King Haakon and Queen Maud of Norway and King Christian of Denmark, and a few close friends attended.
