(By the Associated Press) The nation’s wheat farmers, on the basis of fragmentary returns from 19 states in Saturday's referendum, showed a trend of more than seven to one in favor of continuing the AAA's wheat regulation program in 1936. Within an hour or two after the polls had closed in the East and Midwest, the early crop of returns showed more than 34,000 voting for continuance, as compared with a little more than 5,000 against. As the first sizeable returns rolled in from the heart of the wheat belt, Kansas farmers were balloting around 11,000 to 1,000 in favor of continuing the AAA plan. In some of the less productive wheat states the percentage in favor was much lower. In Washington, AAA officials watched with particular interest the ballots of the non-signers of AAA contracts. On first returns the non-adherents were voting about two to one for continuation of the program.

HONOLULU, May 25 (2).—Com- pleting the most notable mass naval aircraft operations in history in mid-Pacific, a squadron of 10 fighting planes arrived here tonight from French Frigate Shoals, 500 miles out. The flight required seven hours. An uneventful trip was reported by the fliers, who were commanded by Lieut. Commander R. D. Lyon. The unit returned to the Pearl Harbor base after participating in the great operations that began May 9 with a mass flight from here to Midway Island, 1323 miles out in the Pacific. Thirty other planes, including the famous distance squadron VP-10, returned to Pearl Harbor yesterday and last night, in the van of the entire fleet which moved toward Honolulu to test the feasibility of attempting en masse anchorage in Pearl Harbor. An air review of 225 planes of the fleet over Honolulu climaxed the aerial operations today. The roaring seaplanes sweeping in fr

1935-07-13.text: Aldershot, England, July 13. (AP)—King George, clad in khaki, and mounted on a chestnut charger, took a royal salute from 9,000 massed troops in Rushmoor arena today in a brilliant silver jubilee review before 50,000 spectators. Accompanied by his four sons, also wearing khaki, the monarch rode into the arena and took a salute. Then he joined Queen Mary and watched wave after wave of troops, their swords and medals glistening in the bright sun, march and ride past the royal pavilion. The crowd, cautioned against cheering while the king was astride his charger, thundered its ovation as soon as he dismounted. Foreign observers witnessed a display of the progress Britain has made in preparing for what military experts predict will be the mechanized wars of the future. On display were tanks, created as a single permanent establishment of the army less than a year ago. Before that Britain pos
Southport, Eng, July 13. (— Ellsworth Vines, of Pasadena, Calif, star, defeated Big Bill Tilden, 6-1, 6-8, 4-6, 6-2, 6-2, today to win the British professional tennis tournament.

Paris, July 13. — Police massed in the capital today, in precaution against riots, as 42,000,000 French people began a joyous three-day celebration of the fall of the Bastille. A series of raids for arms on second-hand stores was followed today by an interior ministry announcement that it would deport any foreigner who participated in rival Fascist and left-wing demonstrations tomorrow, the 146th anniversary of the storming of the old, hated royal prison. The air ministry forbade the skies in a 40-mile area about Paris to private airplanes between 6 a.m. and midnight tomorrow. The interior ministry announced that certain preventive measures had been taken. It was widely reported and believed that the measures included preventive arrests of Fascists and leftists all over the city. The United Press indicated in the highest sources that these reports were false. Likewise denied as false was

Vienna, July 13. — Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg, who came into power after the assassination of Engelbert Dollfuss, was injured slightly today in an automobile accident while en route from Vienna to Linz. Schuschnigg’s wife was killed when their automobile smashed head-on into another machine. Their son was injured slightly. The chauffeur was critically hurt and a detective suffered minor injuries. A later official announcement said Schuschnigg was suffering from nervous shock and both he and his son were reported to have been taken to a hospital. His son may undergo an operation this afternoon.

VIENNA, July 13~-Two weeks less than a year after the assassination of his predecessor, Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg narrowly escaped with his life today in an automobile accident which resulted in the death of his wife. The chancellor was seriously injured, but is expected to recover. Little hope is held out for the recovery of his son, Kurt, Jr. Their car crashed into a tree at Ebelsberg near Linz. It was on July 25, 1934, that Schuschnigg's predecessor in office, the late Engelbert Dollfuss, was mortally wounded during an attempted Nazi coup d'état. A little group of Austrian Hitlerites seized the Vienna broadcasting station, sent out a false announcement the government had resigned as a signal for a nationwide uprising, and shot Dollfuss when he refused to bow to their demands. He died a few hours later.

MOSCOW, July 13.—(4)—Russo-American negotiations at Washington have come to a successful conclusion in the form of a Soviet-American trade agreement, it was officially stated here today. Details of the agreement were expected to be made known this afternoon. An exchange of notes between Foreign Minister Maxim Litvinov and the American Ambassador William C. Bullitt today culminated the negotiations. They are understood to provide for a temporary agreement but the granting to the U.S.S.R. of most favored treatment.

PARIS (WP) — Lieut. Col. Alfred Dreyfus, center of the political controversy which stirred France to its depths 87 years ago, died of uremia late Friday. Dreyfus, who had been ill for more than a year, was surrounded by immediate members of his family. Since the World War he divided his time between his quiet villa in Brittany and his Paris flat. He lived a secluded and comfortable old age on a pension awarded after the old verdict against him had been quashed and he was reinstated to rank in the French army. The Dreyfus case whirled France into a fury 37 years ago and sent the then captain to Devil's Island. After his release he was restored to honor. The Dreyfus case scandal stirred France for 12 years. Tempests of emotion over the issue still linger. There remain ardent patriots who believe Dreyfus was not the symbol of persecution he was finally said to have been by the French suprem

ADDIS ABABA, July 12. (UP) — Officials close to Emperor Haile Selassie today said he considers war with Italy inevitable. Their statement caused additional Americans and other foreigners to flee the country. Under American auspices, one Italian, one Greek and six negroes entrained for Djbouti, the French coastal port, from whence they intend to sail for the United States. Military officials said they received reports of increasing Italian preparations to attack from Eritrea in a swift campaign against the fertile oasis of Hadele Gubo, a "paradise on earth," but a key position in the north. Fresh activity was reported also from Italian Somaliland on the south. There were unconfirmed reports of an Italian troop concentration in the Pake Tsana region. Abyssinians, confronted with arms embargoes declared by Britain, Belgium, Denmark and other European nations, said they would pay for smuggle

1935-06-26.text: [MAYVEUOR, JUNE 20 UP] Britain, with Germany’s sweeping promise never again to engage in unrestricted submarine warfare in her possession, Tuesday made ready to discuss naval issues with France, Italy and Russia. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin informed the House of Commons that the three had been invited to send delegations to London, but dodged questions as to whether all the invitations had been accepted. A short time before, Sir Bolton Eyres-Nonsel, first lord of the admiralty, stirred the legislators to cheers with the announcement that the Reich had given her pledge to adhere to the rules and regulations regarding submarine warfare in part four of the Washington treaty, regardless of the attitude of other powers. Part four of the treaty provides that warships, “whether surface vessel or submarine boat,” may not attack merchant vessels “without first having placed her passengers, cre

EDINBURGH, Scotland (AP)—Religious rioting broke out again in Edinburgh Tuesday night when thousands of Protestants attempted to break up an organized procession of the Blessed Sacrament by members of the Roman Catholic community. The procession was in connection with the Eucharistic Congress being held here. Cries of “No Popery” and “Down with the Pope” were hurled at the Catholics. A similar riot Monday in which Police charged some 3,000 Protestants who threw bottles and stones at Catholic women and priests Tuesday resulted in conviction of seven men of creating a breach of the peace.

Anthony Eden of Great Britain talked for an hour “with the greatest frankness” about Ethiopia Tuesday, but British and Italian spokesmen both said afterwards they reached no agreement. An official statement issued after the conference, which wound up the two days’ conversations between the statesmen, merely mentioned the fact that the Ethiopian question had been discussed. Both sides emphasized that the conversation was only an exchange of views, the Italian spokesmen saying Eden made no offers or proposals for settlement of the African issue. No hint was given as to whether Il Duce had softened his stand, previously disclosed as involving: 1—Refusal to accept any partial settlement, such as territorial concessions, 2—Ethiopia’s expulsion from the League of Nations on the grounds that she had violated terms of membership. 3—Establi

London—British efforts to mediate in the threatened war between Italy and Abyssinia have received a severe setback, reliable informants said today, and the threat of hostilities is more serious. Italian Premier Benito Mussolini was said to have intimated to Anthony Eden, British cabinet envoy sent to Rome, that he would reject the offer of British influence to exact important concessions from Abyssinia. Eden was understood to have pleaded vainly that an Italian war in East Africa would hinder full Italian cooperation in European problems, and that a military campaign against a fellow league member would have a devastating moral effect on the world.

ROME, June 26. (U.?)—Authoritative sources intimated today that European powers have agreed to partition among them, in the name of civilization, the Ethiopian Empire whose rulers descend from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Talks between Benito Mussolini and Anthony Eden, British cabinet envoy, and between the foreign office and the French ambassador, it was understood, have resulted in “substantial” concessions to Italy's claim that it has a mission to “civilize” the last really independent nation in Africa. The one possible point of conflict, it was said, was that Britain agreed to the civilizing mission on condition that Italy support its naval agreement with Germany, and that France agreed on condition that Italy oppose it. MUIRFIELD, Scotland. June 26—(7)—Forty-five-year-old MacDonald Smith, registered from Glendale, Cal., made an auspicious start in his old for the British Open golf championship today with a subpar first round of 69 over the Muirfield course. Smith's score placed him one stroke behind the defending champion, Henry Cotton, who shot the layout in 68. Cotton's 68, fashioned from nines of 33 and 35, tied Bobby Jones and Walter Hagen for the second lowest score ever made in the first round of the championship. Hagen had first rounds of 68 in 1926 and 1933 and Jones turned the trick in 1927. The all-time first round low was turned in by Cotton a year ago when he shot Royal St. George's in 67. The defending champion's par-shattering performance gave him a lead of three strokes over his closest pursuer, P. M. Burch, another British pro, who carried nine of 36 and 85 for a 71—one under par. MUIRFIELD, Scotland, June 26.—(?)—In an unprecedented wave of low scoring, Henry Cotton, the defending champion, shot a sub-par 68 today in the first round of the 72-hole British Open golf championship to lead by one stroke at the quarter-way mark. Close on the titleholder's heels were the veteran MacDonald Smith of Glendale, Calif., and a left-handed swinger, Alfred Perry, who turned in 69s, while three players, Ernest Kenyon and Alf Padgham and the amateur Erie Meruvie were bracketted at 70. Four other players broke into the Muirfield course par of 72 with 71s, they were A. J. Lacey, P. M. Branch, P. J. Mahon, and C. A. Whitcombe. Eight players were grouped at par, including Henry Picard of Hershey, Pa., the sensation of the American mid-winter season, and Robert Sweeney, the former New Yorker now living in London.

(®)—Italy announced she has speeded her shipment of troops to East Africa today, and in reply, Emperor Haile Selassie warned the League of Nations if Rome continued its militant preparations he would be forced to call a general mobilization. A communique after a brief session of the Italian cabinet contained friendly gestures toward Great Britain. But Premier Mussolini made it known he is not only continuing his East African campaign, but is accelerating it. After receipt of the communique, Haile Selassie dispatched a message to Geneva protesting against Italy's military preparations and provocative attitude. These included the first call for bids on 25 naval vessels included in the 1935 building program. References of goodwill to Britain in a communique of the Italian cabinet and assurances Rome had no designs against Britain failed to elicit official reaction here. In authoritative quarters the view was expressed that the action in Rome would be wholly or largely ignored, insofar as it dealt with Britain, because of what was called the refusal of Italy to deal with the real issue at stake in the Italo-Ethiopian turmoil. (United Press Staff Correspondent) | ROME, Sept. 28.—The Italian cabinet threatened to-day to leave the League of Nations if penalties are applied against Italy for making war on Ethiopia. The tone of a communique issued after a long meeting of Premier Benito Mussolini with his ministers was one of plain notice to the world that Italy intends to subdue Ethiopia by force of arms. The cabinet declared it nevertheless was determined to keep the war from spreading to Europe, if possible. It made a strong plea for a separate understanding with Great Britain, asserting that Italy has no immediate or remote aims prejudicial to Britain and is ready to negotiate further accords with London dealing with Britain's legitimate interests in East Africa.

ADDIS ABABA.—Emperor Haile Selassie served notice upon Saturday night that if Italy continues her warlike preparations in East Africa he must, in self-defense, order a general mobilization of Ethiopia's warriors. Italy's provocative attitude indicates an offensive is near, the king has told the league. Haile Selassie sent his message after receiving news of the Italian announcement Saturday that the departure of troops for East Africa was being speeded. At the same time, the little ruler expressed confidence the league would support Ethiopia and prevent her from becoming the victim of aggression.

Enroute West with President Roosevelt, Sept. 28: (AP) — President Roosevelt, expressing confidence the new deal’ “principle of farm equality” will live, moved into the western mountain states tonight to study works problems of the area. “Methods and machinery change,” he said in a back platform address at Fremont, Neb., “but principles go and I have faith that, no matter what attempts may be made to tear it down, the principle of farm equality expressed by the agricultural adjustment act will not die.” He apparently was presenting his first issue for 1936. At North Platte, Neb., just at nightfall, Mr. Roosevelt was joined by Senator O’Mahoney of Wyoming; Governor Johnson of Colorado; Senators Costigan and Adams of Colorado; Mayor Stapleton of Denver; Paul Prosser, Colorado attorney general; and John Carroll, Denver attorney. MIAMI, Fla., Sept. 28—Red Cross relief trains speeded evacuation from the treacherous Everglades sections tonight, but the fierce tropical hurricane which had raged toward Miami for 17 hours suddenly veered off and headed up the Atlantic coast, 40 miles off Florida's east coast. The weather bureau said that Miami and cities along the lower Florida east coast, believed earlier to be in the direct path of the storm, would apparently escape the brunt of the hurricane, which had taken 27 lives as it ripped across Cuba and Jamaica. Hurricane warnings all along the Florida coast were ordered taken down and storm warnings hoisted in their places to warn ships in the path of the twister. Lake Area Evacuated Meanwhile, disaster workers at Belle Glade, Fla., notified national Red Cross headquarters that 80 percent of automobile-owning residents of the Lake Okeechobee area already had fled. MEMEL, Sept. 28 (&)—Little Memel was a potential European volcano tonight as it prepared to elect a new diet under the jealous eyes of Nazi Germany and Lithuania. The election is tomorrow. Outwardly the territory was calm and only minor disturbances marred the campaigns. The actual voting was expected to pass off quickly, officials said, and if real trouble occurs it will be when the results are announced several days hence. On the one side of the 88,000 voters, a majority of them German, was an openly displeased Germany and on the other, stubbornly insistent Lithuania. Berlin's leaders, including Reichführer Adolf Hitler, have charged Lithuania with election violations. The pro-German party now has 25 of the 29 seats in the landtag (diet or provincial assembly). LONDON, Oct. 21 (CUP) — Advance guards of more than 800,000 men moving into battle in Southern Ethiopia recoiled from heavy hand-to-hand fighting today and prepared for a major battle described in both Rome and Addis Ababa as only a few days distant. A force of 1,000 Italian Somaliland natives supported by airplanes almost destroyed an Ethiopian unit of the same number yesterday in savage, hand-to-hand fighting, the Exchange Telegraph correspondent with the Italian army said, and pursued the survivors today across the plain. At the same time, two Italian ships passed through Fort Said with 1,000 men wounded on the Somaliland front, indicating guerrilla battles in the Ethiopian interior have been far more savage than official dispatches betray. London, Oct. 20—()—A rescue steamer snatched 22 seamen tonight from the fury of an ocean storm but the Atlantic still held the fate of 87 others. The gale in the last 36 hours claimed two British trawlers and piled up dozens of sails along the shores. Find No Traces. The crew of 22 of the Pendennis, radio messages said, was saved by the Norwegian steamer shortly before the vessel, heavily laden with coal, sank in the North Sea. Two ships, the Oregon and the Visco, which sped to the rescue of the crew of 87 aboard the 735-ton Donaldson freighter Vardulia, reported abandoned about 700 miles northeast of Ireland, wirelessed today they had searched the last given position of the vessel without finding a trace of it. Dorking, England—4uU.r) — Laura La Plante, movie actress, was saved from death today when her doctor carried her in his arms from her blazing home here. Miss La Plante had been ill at her thatched-roof cottage near Boxhill, which had been built in 1933 for former Mayor James J. Walker of New York. She had leased it for six months while the Walkers were in France. Her physician, Dr. C. E. Beare, entered the blazing cottage and carried Miss La Plante to safety through the French windows. He took her to a neighboring home and called the fire brigade. The firemen were unable to save the cottage and its interior was destroyed. They managed to save some furniture. The house, called “The Thatch,” is in Fredley Park. It was believed a spark from a garden bonfire set fire to the thatched roof.

| LONDON, Oct. 21.—Death of the Geneva disarmament conference was feared today with the passing of Arthur Henderson, its president and one of the world’s most untiring workers for peace. Henderson, 72, died at the London Clinic Nursing Home yesterday after a long illness without knowing of Italy's East African aggression, which he had been confident the League of Nations would prevent. He underwent an operation Sept. 23 for gall stones and stomach trouble. When his recovery appeared slow, his physicians ordered that all accounts of the Italo-Ethiopian conflict be kept from him. Peace workers throughout the world mourned Henderson's death. He worked unselfishly and tirelessly in his last years to abolish war. It was only through his diligence and persuasive insistence that the disarmament conference was kept alive, many diplomats believe. Now they fear that the conference will follow its

LONDON, Oct. 21—(UP Copyright)—Hope was expressed in well-informed quarters today that a ten-day breathing spell for troubled Europe may provide the basis for eventual peace between Italy and Ethiopia. Those who at first regarded the lessening of tension between Italy and Great Britain in the Mediterranean as an isolated, if important factor, now believe that fruitful diplomatic negotiations for settlement of the entire crisis may follow. The League of Nations, proceeding with the penalization of Italy for its undeclared war on Ethiopia, is not to take further action until October 31, when it will decide on the date for declaring a complete, immediate boycott of all Italian goods. The Mediterranean, where Great Britain has its gigantic fleet concentrated, and Libya, where Italy has massed three divisions of reinforcements, may prove the key to settlement of the Italian-Ethiopian dispute

GENEVA—(4)— Germany ceased to be a member of the League of Nations at noon today. Just before midday two years ago, the German consul, whose office is adjacent to the league secretariat, walked across the street and deposited the two-year preliminary notice of resignation. Today, just after Germany left the league, the German consul, Dr. W. Krauel, was expected to clarify the character of relations between the Third Reich and Geneva. It was anticipated that Germany would follow the example of the United States and cooperate with the league whenever possible. Dr. Krauel was expected to return by the end of the month to observe the procedure of the 52 nations which will then fix a date for enforcement of economic sanctions against Italy if the war in Ethiopia has not been halted. Addis Ababa, Oct. 21—Emperor Selassie, tearful and in a voice choked with emotion, today bade farewell to 8000 of his crack Imperial guard who departed for Dessye, about halfway between the capital and Makale. After shaking hands warmly with the Belgian officers who trained the Imperial guardsmen, the emperor embraced each of the 40 Ethiopian officers and addressed each with an affectionate persona. They were so affected by the emperor's tears that they wept too. Selassie then shook hands with each of the 8000 men, asking them to defend the empire to the last breath. The Ethiopian government announced that France is camouflaging the railroad between Djibouti and French Somaliland and the Ethiopian frontier for protection from Italian bombs. 1935-08-05.text: LONDON, Aug. 5.—INS—Japan has agreed to supply arms to Abyssinia, and a contract for a huge order has already been placed. This sensational development in the "Holy War" with all the colored races lined up on the side of Ethiopia against Italy, was reported today in an Exchange Telegraph Message from Addis Ababa. The Abyssinian government, according to Exchange, signed a contract Friday for Japan to supply "a very large consignment" of arms and ammunition intended to accelerate the modernization of the Ethiopian army. Arrangements have almost been completed, the dispatch added, for the sending of a Japanese military, commercial mission to Abyssinia. LONDON, Aug. 5.—The Mahatma Gandhi was considered by British circles today to have a great opportunity for a comeback in the new all-India federation. All Indian parties are looking forward eagerly to the information of the federation, being created under authority of the India law recently enacted by parliament, for self-government of that ancient land. Officials expressed doubt, however, that the wiry little ascetic, who retired to the background after struggling along for India’s independence, would re-enter politics. They felt that the Mahatma would press on in his social and economic program for betterment of the masses, but that he would leave political affairs to others. Strong organizing efforts have yet to be made by Britain, to get the new federal system in shape. Repairing of the bonds between Great Britain and France, badly frayed by the former's naval agreement with Germany, was evidenced by Premier Pierre Laval's support of Anthony Eden, British minister for league affairs, climaxed by last night's adoption by the league council of a formula for averting war. LONDON, Aug. 5—(4)—A Reuters (British) news agency dispatch from Paris today said Greek police had suppressed an attempt by 25 Greek soldiers to revolt in the air camp at Athens. The dispatch said one of the soldiers had fired on the police but that 15 of the alleged rebels had been arrested while the other 10 escaped.

BY WAMLMAUE UANNUIsis (Copyright 1935 by United Press) GENEVA, (UP).—Small nations, angry over the compromise effected in the Italian-Ethiopian dispute, intend to force a supreme test of the League of Nations authority if war still threatens next month. So outraged were feelings of representatives of the nations which really make up the league membership that it was indicated today they were ready to envisage the death of the league rather than see it continue to live on its present basis. They called the League council’s compromise two-part negotiatory plan for Italian-Ethiopian peace an evasion, a weak surrender. They denounced it as being not a league plan but a plan dictated by three great powers—Great Britain, France and Italy. Moscow, Aug. 5. (4P)—The Soviet polar plane, which turned back on its first attempt to fly non-stop over the north pole to San Francisco, was reported today to be at an airfield south of Leningrad. A widespread belief prevailed that the ship would take off again within a few days on a second try at the spectacular flight. It landed Saturday night after a defective oil line forced the three fliers to turn back over the southern part of Barents Sea. An official commission was appointed to investigate the source of the trouble. Sigmund Levaneffsky, veteran pilot of the ship, dumped nearly five tons of gasoline before bringing the big craft down to a safe landing.

Rome. Aug 4 - Italy's military program was pushed at the same rapid pace today despite agreement at Geneva upon a formula designed to settle the quarrel with Ethiopia. Political circles examined the result of the meeting of the League council and said it was in no way indicative of the possibility of a peaceful settlement of the problem within the framework of the League. Transport embarked workmen and supplies at Naples with sailings to East Africa scheduled today and tomorrow. Other larger ships are returning from the colonies, and will embark this week with heavy contingents of troops. (W.P)—A revived French-British-Italian conference as a last hope of averting war after the failure of the League of Nations to settle the Ethiopian dispute was mentioned informally today among League delegates. The latest indications received by League circles from Rome suggested that Premier Benito Mussolini's reply to the League's proposals, while making it clear that the compromise is not acceptable in its present form, may be accompanied by a hint that Mussolini would be urged to revive the three power conference which failed in Paris in August. _ Mussolini might hope at such a conference to get better concessions than he could get here. It was indicated in reliable Geneva quarters that if he turns down the present League plan, he will be offered even smaller concessions in Ethiopia.

LONDON, Sept. 19.—(AP)— A dangerous situation in the Mediterranean, where Great Britain and Italy are massing instruments of war, absorbed capitals of the world tonight. Crack ships of both nations, airplanes and troops were moved into strategic points of the sea, some in close proximity. Foreign military observers here, recalling the blowing up of the battleship Maine, called the situation a "powder keg" which any untoward incident could explode. Markets of the world were sharply and variously affected. (In Tokyo and Osaka the exchanges had the highest transactions in history on the strength of the war scare. Wheat soared in Chicago.) Dealings in London and Paris were depressed through nervous selling over the situation. By the Associated Press Securities markets slumped under sporadic waves of nervous selling in principal American and European markets today, as financial centers kept anxious eyes trained on Rome and Geneva. The New York and London stock exchanges were sharply lower, subject to occasional rallies. Some British government bonds in both markets dropped as much as $1 to $1.50 per $100 par value, and prices of Italian issues crumbled more rapidly. Shares in the New York stock exchange declined $1 to $4 under an early selling wave, with some brokers reporting heavy offerings from Europe. Prices stiffened in Wall Street, however, after the close of foreign markets.

GIBRALTAR. (UP)—All three entrances to the Harbor of Great Britain’s mighty base at Gibraltar were closed today with nets. As the booms swung into place, a Spanish air squadron droned overhead, having arrived at Tarifa 15 miles away, across the straits from the British fortress from Seville. After brief maneuvers, it took off again for Seville, but is expected to return to Tarifa soon. The populace of the “Rock” are calmly depending upon its massive shoulders to provide ample defense in case of an attack, of which there is at present no fear. Reports that an obstructive net had been swung into place at the southern entrance to Admiralty harbor were at first doubted by the public, but have been confirmed. The northern entrance is closed in the same way each evening, and remains closed until morning.

(UP) — French sources reported today that Benito Mussolini had approached Great Britain with an offer to cease sending troops to Northern Africa if Britain would forego military penalties in event of an Ethiopian war. A political commentator of the newspaper Echo de Paris, and a leading writer on foreign affairs, asserted that Britain would — refuse the offer.

NEW YORK, Sept. 20, (AP)—Financial circles watched today the reaction of foreign exchange to threats of an Ethiopian war with special attention to the shipment of gold from London. The engagement of $8,200,000 in gold in the British capital in one day—with only about $600,000 worth available on the open market—was reported here. $16,800,000 in a Day Some experts said the already large flow of gold to the United States—$93,000,000 since the first of the year—may rise to unprecedented proportions if Lend-lease's estimated hoard of a billion dollars in the metal begins taking flight. Also reported engaged for shipment here was $7,500,000 in gold from France and $3,100,000 from Holland, making the total for the day $16,800,000. A bull market in wheat came this week on the heels of Italo-Ethiopian developments. Securities markets were depressed on the continent, boosted in the Far East, and h

London, Sept. 20—(?)— Official sources expressed surprise today at a report from Rome that Premier Mussolini had ordered a protest to the League of Nations against the British dispatch of warships to the Mediterranean. These sources said they had not been officially informed of such a protest and that there had not been (Continued on Page Ten) ;

1935-05-27.text: BERLIN, May 26—(AP)—Authoritative sources disclosed today that the German military command plans a highly mobile infantry and artillery which will enable the army to move at 80 miles an hour “over almost anything except woods.” Two motor vehicles for every four infantrymen is the new army's ratio to obtain an unprecedented flexibility and speed. Open automobiles carrying powerful guns will be used over most roads, sturdy trucks with a capacity of 20 men will be employed on congested highways and near the fronts, and tanks or armored cars are planned for front line service. Recall Paris Army Military leaders recall the Paris World War taxi army and technical advances are being scored to make the infantry and artillery into smoothly working complements of the air force. Light field pieces, splendid highways strategically extending to the frontiers, commissariat equipment, motor vehicles, a

Paris, May 26 (AP).— The Flandin government prepared today for a political battle for its goal of a financial dictatorship as the nation’s uneasiness was increased by violence in the provinces. A mob at Neufchatel, raiding a hall where a political meeting was in progress, clashed with gendarmes, leaving several injured in the hall and in the streets. The city of Sens was in turmoil after its newly-elected mayor, Dr. Andre Dupechez, was left for dead in his ditched automobile by political enemies with his membership card in the nationalist veterans’ organization Croix de Feu pinned to his lapel. Col. de La Rocque, leader of the strong organization, issued an order to his followers not to attempt retaliation. Dr. Dupechez was reported out of danger. In Paris, vigorous Premier Pierre-Étienne Flandin, recovered from recent automobile accident injuries, lined up his forces in an attempt to ob

ROME, May 26—(AP)—Diplomatic circles of Rome today regarded Premier Mussolini’s speech to the chamber of deputies as a clear indication of his intention to deal sternly in the Ethiopian situation unless exceptional concessions are made to him. A group of 20,000 subaltern officers and specialists of the class of 1912 prepared to depart for concentration centers as a result of a mobilization order published last night in the official gazette, shortly after Il Duce’s address. The Geneva correspondent of Mussolini’s own newspaper, Popolo D’Italia, spoke today of Italy’s “right to extend her own influence and her own civilizing mission to backward and disorganized countries of the African continent.” Il Duce and his foreign office aides studied reactions from European capitals to his speech, particularly in regard to Ethiopia. Italy’s leader wanted to know how London, Paris and Berlin felt to

Berlin, May 27.—German military plans for creating an army on wheels, capable of speeding to the front and from one sector to another at 80 miles an hour, were disclosed today by an authoritative source. Open automobiles equipped with powerful guns will be employed to rush troops over the new motor highways leading to strategic frontier points. The plans are said to call for a ratio of two motor vehicles for every four infantrymen. Near the front, fast trucks with a capacity of 20 men will provide transportation for the troops while tanks and armored cars will be used to carry them into battle. The belief exists that preparations have been made to make possible the production of thousands of tanks in a comparatively short space of time if the need should arise. Mr. and Mrs. James Turner of Ellob announce the engagement of their daughter Hazel to Glenwood Allen of Kittery. The marriage wi

WASHINGTON, (UP).—The Supreme Court today held the Frazier-Lemke farm mortgage moratorium act invalid as a violation of the federal constitution. The law, passed at the close of the 73rd Congress, provided federal court machinery to scale down farm debts and halt the foreclosure of farm mortgages. Decided on Appeal. The case was decided in an appeal brought by the Louisville Joint Stock Land Bank against William W. Radford, Sr., a Kentucky farm owner. The court’s opinion, by the famed liberal justice, Louis D. Brandeis, held that the law violated the constitution by taking away rights of mortgage holders. ‘It was bad under the Fifth Amendment as a taking without due process,” Brandeis said.

Tacoma, Wash., May 27.—With only 48 hours remaining of the “five days” in which 9-year-old George Weyerhaeuser may be ransomed, his parents today held $200,000 in small bills, and waited for the next move of the kidnapers. The money is ready, the boy's uncle F. R. Titecomb, revealed, and will be paid as soon as the kidnapers arrange a method and a rendezvous. Federal agents and police were doing nothing. “Our first concern,” a spokesman for the department of justice squad said, “is for the safety of the Weyerhaeuser boy. When he is safe at home, we will move into action.” An unsuccessful search for a mysterious tan sedan with California license plates was made all over western Washington by road and by air Sunday. The car was reportedly seen parked near Lowell school, which George attended, several times last week by L. H. Burnett, Tacoma jeweler, and was seen near the school Friday, the

Washington, May 27 (AP).—Recovery act provisions "giving the President the right to proclaim code rules over private industry—a power regarded as the heart of NRA—were held unconstitutional today by the Supreme Court. The Court made this ruling in an opinion delivered by Chief Justice Hughes in the Schechter poultry case from New York, selected by the government to test its power to regulate wages and hours of workers through more than 500 NRA codes of fair competition. The A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corporation, the Schechter Poultry Market, Inc., and four individuals composing those two firms, engaged in the live poultry business in Brooklyn, were indicted for violating the live poultry codes of fair competition and with conspiracy to violate the codes. In the federal district court for eastern New York, the members of the two firms were found guilty on the conspiracy count and given p

Pasadena, Cal., May 26 (/). Search for a desperate band of extortionists who lost one of their number in a running gun battle with Federal “G” men and police last night got under way in this area today. One suspected member of the gang, identified as Jack Williams, 35, lay mumbling in a hospital with two bullets through his neck, two more through his chest, two in his right arm and another in the right hand. Officer Wounded A veteran officer, Perry Archer, also was wounded but apparently not fatally. His shield deflected a gangster’s bullet. The extortionists had been trying to wrest $72,000 from Herbert D. Ivey, bank president and head of the Pasadena Clearing House Association, under threat of death. Ivey was warned by the gang that it had little regard for the lives of its ten members: that he could “get” only one or two of them at the most and in that event would surely be marked for

1935-01-05.text: Mr. Zero, just in from Canada, extended a cold hand to New England Friday and sent the mercury packing off to the cellar. The sharp subzero spell that had cost a dozen or more lives in the Canadian northwest and dropped thermometer readings 56 degrees in Minnesota relented somewhat through the west as the sudden cold wave reached the seaboard. Atop Mt. Washington, N. H., a 130 mile wind whistled, ten inches of snow fell and the mercury dropped 32 below zero. At Boston it was 6 above, and in New York the temperature took a sudden plunge of 20 degrees, hit 13 above and then rose. It was 22 below at Malone, N. Y.

SAN FRANCISCO, Jan. 5 (A.)—Contact with two missing ships was sought today while a lashing Pacific storm swept inland. The British tanker La Crescencia with 35 men aboard and unreported for two weeks and the steam schooner Dan F. Hanlon, manned by a crew of 25, were the vessels hunted along the sea lanes.

A Canadian cold wave which sent temperatures toppling as it swept across the northern part of the United States was abating today. Fair and warmer in the Midwest, the east and in the New England states was the weather man’s prediction, welcomed especially in the northeastern states and upper New York state, where the mercury sank far below zero on Friday. It was 32 below zero atop Mt. Washington, New Hampshire, and 22 below at Malone, N. Y. The northern plains states, however, were due for another cold snap, the weather forecasters said by this afternoon or tonight. Meanwhile, western Canada took stock of the suffering and death caused by the cold. Seven fishermen, however, escaped. They were marooned for nearly 24 hours on ice floes in Lake Simcoe, Ontario. Three of them were picked up by an airplane. The other four made their way ashore when the lake froze over. A near-cloudburst fell

HONOLULU, Jan. 5.—The British tanker La Crescenta was reported long overdue today on a voyage from San Luis Obispo, Cal., to Kobe, Japan. She was expected in Kobe last month. The S.S. President Coolidge requested all vessels in the mid-Pacific to keep a sharp lookout for the tanker, which carries a crew of 35 men. Built in the United Kingdom in 1923, the tanker is listed as a 5880-ton vessel, 400 feet long, with a beam of 53 feet and a draught of 32 feet. She left the California Coast November 22.

: Ottawa, Jan. 4. (P)—A Canadian new deal paralleling President Roosevelt's in important essentials was promised Canada’s voters tonight as Premier R. B. Bennett, in his second campaign address, outlined proposals for economic and social reform. “There must be an end,” he said, “to the reckless exploitation of human resources and the trafficking in the health and happiness of Canadian citizens. “There must be an end to the idea that a workman should be held to his labors throughout the daylight hours. There should be a uniform minimum wage and a uniform maximum working week.” Asserting the present economic system has broken down and needs radical alterations if it is to be saved, the premier listed these needed reforms: 1—Contributory employment insurance. 2—A remodeled old age pension scheme. 3—Health, sickness and accident insurance. 4—Amended income tax laws to correct inequality of w

(Copyright, 1935, By Associated Press) ROME — A cordial kiss on both cheeks was Benito Mussolini's greeting to Pierre Laval tonight as the French statesman arrived to start conversations expected to end old Franco-Italian animosities. Thousands massed about the railroad station cheered as Il Duce gave Laval the fascist salute, clasped his hand strongly and kissed his cheeks. The warmth of the welcome to the first French foreign minister to visit Rome since the World War augured well, observers believe for | ‘See Mussolini Page 8)

ROME, Jan. 5 — Premier Mussolini and Pierre Laval, foreign minister of France, plunged today into the negotiations they hope will promote friendship between their countries and bring assurance of peace to Europe. Laval arrived at the Palazzo Venezia accompanied by Ambassador Charles de Chambrun and received the salute of a Fascist guard drawn up before the building. Mussolini greeted the French emissary and escorted him to his office, where Laval sat beside a desk piled high with maps and documents bearing on Italo-French relations. A tentative draft of the agreement the statesmen expect to approve had been prepared, and it was known that several important points remained to be discussed. As Laval and Il Duce began their conversations, expected to continue into Monday afternoon, three experts who accompanied Laval on his mission here went into conference.

ATHENS, Jan. ..—The newspaper Acropolis reported today that King Zog of Albania, fearing an advance by rebels, had sent his sisters abroad and had secluded himself in Dyrahio Palace, ready to flee abroad by airplane if necessary. “Wild terrorism

1935-06-30.text: TOKIO, June 29 (4)—Floods that devastated rich western Japan were subsiding tonight, leaving 71 known dead and damage estimated at 40,000,000 yen (about $11,600,000) in their wake, but heavy rainfall resumed tonight. The storms and floods, the worst in the last half century, struck at the industrious heart of the empire, ravaging such thriving and populous regions as those about Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe. With communications shattered, it was believed the toll of death and damage would be increased with fuller reports. Fears of new floods were voiced, and officials in Osaka warned residents to be prepared for further rises of flood waters. Thousands throughout the stricken area were left homeless, with preliminary surveys of the affected area indicating at least 150,000 houses and buildings were inundated. It was the second major disaster suffered by the industrial area in less than 10 month

|. PARIS (4) — A pistol duel early Saturday between Pierre Chiappe, president of the Paris Municipal Council, and Pierre Godin, his predecessor, left Godin slightly wounded in the thigh. Tonight the two men were still angry at each other. They met secretly at dawn on the estate of Mme. Coty, widow of the millionaire perfumer, in the Bois de Boulogne. They set off 25 paces. Seconds gave the word. Both fired—and missed. At the second exchange, Godin fired, again missing. Chiappe took more time. His bullet struck Godin in the thigh. Godin fell. They left the field unreconciled.

WASTERNANCE LOIN, TD COIN Pe wide open by internal insurgency over President Roosevelt's demanded “death sentence” for utility holding companies, the democratic house adjourned a bitter session on the verge of a vote that will test administration strength Monday. The big test will come on a teller vote on an amendment to substitute the senate approved provision to outlaw utility holding companies in seven years for the house interstate commerce provision, leaving their fate to the securities exchange commission. It will be offered by Representative Fischer (D., Iowa), of the interstate committee. A record vote on the amendment will be impossible at this stage, but administration men are preparing to check the democrats as they file through the counters. White house pressure may be used on the dissenters. To bring the issue to an early showdown, the house agreed to sidetrack all other bus

GENIN VILJUR, N. Y., June 9.—An adolescent boy who plays the violin in the church choir confessed to New York state's Scotland Yard tonight that he mistreated and killed the 9-year-old daughter of his pastor. He is Alfred S. Volckmann, the son of well-to-do parents, and the announcement of his confession was made by Lieut. Garry Sager and Sergeant J. Walter Wheeler, of the Yard. Breaks Under Grilling The 19-year-old lad broke tonight after 12 hours’ questioning, the lieutenant said, admitting he lured Helen Glenn into his home and attacked her. He then took the unconscious child to a secluded road a mile and a half out of town, the detectives said. There he covered her face with the dress she had donned to receive a prize at school commencement exercises for perfect attendance, according to the confession. He admitted he drove into her body a butcher knife, said Lieutenant Sager. Lynchin

Washington, June 29.— (#) — Direct pressure was exerted on chieftains of congress today by President Roosevelt to rush through his wealth-tax program unchanged, with the apparently vain hope of adjourning August 1. This date was mentioned by Senator Harrison (D. Miss.), after the finance committee chairman conferred with the chief executive. The emphasis on speed was repeated by Senator Pittman (D., Nev.), who also talked with Mr. Roosevelt. Pressure Renewed The program projected in White House discussions as congress reached the year's half-way mark involved an administration determination to squelch any attempt to expand or contract the wealth taxes specifically asked by Mr. Roosevelt. It contemplated, too, renewed pressure behind all the bulky administration legislative program. Out of the talks came an announcement by Harrison that the finance committee would open tax hearings next w

MERIDIAN, Miss., June 29.—()— Weathering tempest and overcoming fire, Al and Fred Key, the long distance Meridian fliers, today winged their way past 600 hours of sustained endurance flight. The recognized official world record was passed Thursday afternoon at 3:13:30 p.m. (CST) on their 23rd day of continuous flight over and around the Meridian airport and a new world record was set an hour later. But a new world record did not satisfy the intrepid fliers, and the brothers flew on in their attempt to surpass the 647-hour flight of Dale Jackson and Forest O’Brine which was not officially recognized because of an improper barograph. Fight Off Fire; Al and Fred entered their 600th hour of flight at 12:31 p.m. today after they had run safely through a night storm and had fought off a morning fire in the plane’s battery. Today just after a refueling contact the plane's battery burst into fla

Chicago, June 29 (4)—A series of temporary orders restraining collection of nearly $2,000,000 in processing taxes tonight initiated a new sector in the battle of big millers, textile and packing concerns to overturn the AAA. Temporary injunctions issued by Federal Judge Joseph W. Molyneaux at Minneapolis at the request of five large milling firms and one paper concern prevented collection of nearly $1,590,000 and set the site for one of the leading assaults on the statute for that jurisdiction. The federal revenue collector for Oklahoma was likewise temporarily restrained against collecting wheat processing taxes on petition of three milling and elevator firms at Oklahoma City. The Minneapolis actions brought by Gold Medal Foods, Inc., a subsidiary of General Mills, Inc.; International Milling Company; Russell-Miller Milling; King Midas Milling Company; Pillsbury Flour Mills Company, and

NEW YORK, June 29. (1)—The New York Times says in a special dispatch from Washington that former President Hoover will formally announce late this summer that he is not a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination. His intentions were revealed, the dispatch explains, to several Republican senators who had been on the point of asking him for a public statement of his position.

1935-12-25.text: BETHLEHEM, Dec. 25. () Electric Star of Bethlehem, blazing suddenly out of the darkness in the age-old Church of the Nativity, early today betokened the advent of Christmas Day to thousands of pilgrims assembled in the Holy Land from many countries. Red-capped Arabs, uniformed British officers and soldiers, numerous Americans and Europeans, native peasants in their huge white crusader voifs—a polyglot throng of many creeds but a single faith—witnessed the symbolic climax to a day and night of religious rites. The star, signifying the heavenly light that guided the three wise men of the east to Bethlehem nearly 2,000 years ago, flamed forth above the church altar, directly over the site where the Christ child was born in a manger. Fervid "Hallelujahs!" burst from the vast congregation. Then slowly, in groups of fifty, the pilgrims filed into the dark little grotto, illuminated by flickeri

NEW YORK, Dec. 25 (4)—Christmas came to 3-year-old Jon Lindbergh today in mid-Atlantic. The freighter American Importer, bearing the light-haired boy and his parents, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, to England to escape kidnap threats, neared the halfway point of its ten-day crossing. But the United States Line saw to it that the holiday would not be a cheerless one for the ship's three passengers. A Christmas tree, three large stockings before a fireplace, and a big turkey dinner were on the program. Reaction among New York officials of crime conditions which reputedly caused the Lindberghs to leave this country brought acceptance by Herbert A. O'Brien of a city magistrate’s post offered by the mayor. O'Brien, who twice had refused the position, said he was impelled to accept it finally because of his indignation over threats to the Lindbergh family. He decided it was his duty, h

Moscow, Dec. 24. (AP)—Soviet Russia, looking both to the Pacific and the Baltic, bluntly let Japan and Germany know today that she has quadrupled her submarine and destroyer fleets in the last four years. An announcement in the government newspaper Izvestia said the coast-guard fleet has been increased by 1100 percent since 1931. Said Izvestia: “Soviet Russia is always the bearer of the standards of peace, but it will answer threats of invasion with an increase of armed forces. “The enemy who dares attack the Soviet Union from the Baltic or the Pacific will feel the force of our submarine and surface fleets as well as their quick mobility. “It will quickly be seen that Rear Admiral Rozdestvensky (who commanded the Russian fleet destroyed in the Russo-Japanese war at the battle of Tsushima) is now in command. Follows Conference Significantly, the statement came after a conference here bet

GROSS HERINGEN, Germany, Dec. 24 (#)——Twenty persons were killed and 80 injured Tuesday night when an express train rammed a local. Thirty were seriously injured in the crash, which occurred at the station while a holiday crowd pushed aboard the local.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 25---(AP)— Tang Yu-Jen, vice minister of railways and former vice minister of foreign affairs of China, was assassinated tonight by gunmen as he stepped from his automobile into a home in the French concession here. Tang was the right hand man of Gen. Wang Ching-Wei, and a strong member of the pro-Japanese clique in the Chinese government. Tang's chauffeur, who witnessed the shooting, said two men in Chinese dress approached his master as he stepped out of the car, shoved revolvers against his body, and fired seven times. The victim slumped to the ground, instantly dead. The assassins escaped on foot.

War shadows clouded the Christmas of the old world, for it prepared to observe the anniversary of Christ's birth in its most critical period since the World War. The day found two Christian nations at war in Africa. Most European powers were rearming as rapidly as possible while eyeing their neighbors with suspicion. There was a lull, apparently, in the bloodshed in Ethiopia, but sentries did not relax their vigilance. Few Christmas Trees Italian soldiers, perhaps a bit homesick, were thousands of miles from their homeland amid the strange surroundings of the near-tropics. There were few Christmas trees and no foreign toys for Italian children—sanctions and the “buy at home” program barred these. Pope Pius sorrowfully noted the failure of peace. NEW YORK, Dec. 24—(AP)— Cut off from the rest of the world, the Lindbergh family found at sea tonight the traditional peace of Christmas-tide in the snug smoking room of the SS. American Importer. While professing to have had no word from the vessel, Basil Harris, vice president of the United States Lines, said that Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh undoubtedly would hang their young son's Christmas stocking at the fireplace in the smoking room. It is a real fireplace, he said, and a yule log probably glowed in the hearth as the young couple decorated the Christmas tree they took along and laid young Jon's toys about. Jon Three Years Old Jon, born after the death of his kidnapped brother, is three years old—just the age when youngsters begin to be impressed by the vision of a ruddy-faced old gentleman coming down the fireplace chimney and stuffing their stockings with toys. By midnight,

Roosevelt was free from the anxiety with which war and threats of war tinged its observance in some other parts of Christendom. Heavy Yuletide business was reflected in the full cargo of the stockings Santa filled throughout the land. Hymns Chanted. The weather man contributed his share by insuring a "white" holiday over most of the northern states. But as "Glory to God in the Highest" was chanted in Bethlehem’s ancient ceremonials, the prayers of thousands of pilgrims beseeched the "Peace on Earth" of which Christmas message sings. And in Rome, Pope Pius sadly told the cardinals bringing him the felicitations of the season that this anniversary of the nativity was darkened by melancholy, menacing clouds and human bloodshed. Italy Determined. In the eternal city of Christianity the spirit of the day was everywhere curtailed by evidence of Italy's determination to carry on its East Africa

1935-10-06.text: - LONDON, Oct. 6 (Sunday) (UP) — The Italian forces driving on Aduwa are within three miles of the city and expect to occupy it by noon, the Sunday dispatch correspondent reported today. The city had been re-bombed by Italian airplanes, the dispatch said. It was estimated that 63 inhabitants were killed. Some bombs were dropped on the governor’s palace. The dispatch said the Ethiopians returned the bombardment with lively rifle, machine-gun and anti-aircraft gunfire.

(By The Associated Press) GENEVA, Oct. 5—The council of the League of Nations appointed a ‘strategy’ board of six to handle the Italo-Ethiopian warfare tonight but failed to take immediate action upon a solemn Ethiopian appeal to ‘stop the massacre of innocent populations.’ Ethiopia Absolved A report submitted to the council by its committee of 13 absolved Ethiopia of blame for the African fighting. A member said it inferred Italy was “clearly in the wrong.” Failure of the council to act immediately upon Ethiopia’s plea for adoption of military, naval and air sanctions against Italy brought forth later private expressions of reproach from even the most ardent advocates of the league. League circles heard one of the first actions of the committee of six was to ask the league secretariat to draw up a statement based on the assumption Italy has committed unprovoked aggression. ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 5.—(4)—Fierce fighting raged today on the northern front, near Adigrat, where Ethiopian warriors engaged in hand-to-hand combat with the Italian troops, fighting with bayonets and daggers against enemy forces that used planes overhead. The number of casualties was not learned. There was further fighting reported on the southern Ogaden front, facing Italian Somaliland, with 2000 Ethiopians dead. On the northern front the Ethiopian lines are stretched over a fertile plain en route to Askum, 22 miles south of the Eritrean border. Throughout the day, since the beginning of hostilities, the native women have been rushing to the battle lines with great black jugs of water and tej (a liquor) on their shoulders. They also bore sacks of corn to the fighters. Unofficial reports reached the capital that Aduwa had been occupied by an unopposed Italian army, the Ethiopians having wi

PARIS, Oct. 5. -- The Havas News agency reported from Addis Ababa tonight that 40 women and 32 children were killed in the recent air bombardment of Aduwa by Italian planes. A clash between 400 Ethiopians and 1,000 Italians between Aduwa and Aksum, it announced further, resulted in the killing of 45 Ethiopians and 25 Italians, with 65 Italians, including some officers, taken prisoners.

GENEVA, Oct. 5—(UP)—The League of Nations Council took the first step today towards designating Italy as the aggressor in the Ethiopian dispute, thus preparing the way for speedy application of international penalties. Italy's resignation from the League was expected to result if any but the mildest sanction or penalties are imposed. The result of today’s deliberations follow: 1. The Council's committee of 13, comprising all members except Italy, published its report on the disputes, holding Ethiopia guiltless of aggression, and by implication censuring Italy. The report made only one recommendation—that hostilities cease pending a settlement. 2. The Council decided to vote formally on the report Monday. Its adoption is considered certain, since the membership of the committee of 13 and of the Council is identical. Penalties Expected 3. The Council approved the appointment of a committee

(Copyright, 1935, The Associated Press); SMARA, ERITREA, Oct. 5 (P)—Two powerful columns of Ethiopian regular troops advanced to a new position late this afternoon in the vicinity of Aduwa as Italian military sources announced the imminence of a major battle. Italian officers said they believed the occupation of Aduwa would be “only a matter of hours.” Shortly before the arrival of reconnaissance planes, Count Galeazzo Ciano, air squadron commander and son-in-law of Premier Mussolini, had announced Aduwa would fall about 3 or 4 o’clock in the afternoon. Italian aviators, however, returned to report the Ethiopian columns only 20 or 30 miles from the Italian front line. The Ethiopian regulars were declared to be “extremely strong,” although Italian officers declined to estimate their number after reading the aviator’s reports. Italian troops under General Maravigna were at the gates of Adu

WRIGLEY FIELD, CHICAGO, Oct. 5.—(7)—Alvin (General) Crowder, a baseball veteran who served with the United States army in Siberia, capitalized his experience with wintry weather today to pitch the Detroit Tigers to their third straight victory and within one game of their long-sought goal, the world championship. The 34-year-old North Carolina right-hander turned back the youthful Chicago Cubs, most of whom were in knee breeches when the “General” was carrying a musket on Asiatic duty and whipped them, 2 to 1, with a brilliantly-executed five-hit performance. The old warhorse, in achieving his first world series triumph in three starting attempts, not only gave a masterful exhibition, marred only by the home run ball he served to Gabby Hartnett in the second inning, but figured in the scoring of both Detroit runs to make it a glorious day for this captain of the “old guard.” Crowder sing

WASHINGTON, Oct. 5.— (#) Frankly recognizing a “state of war” between Italy and Ethiopia, President Roosevelt today declared an immediate embargo on American shipments of “arms, munitions and implements of war” to either nation. Acting under provisions of the new neutrality act in an effort to assure the United States shall not become involved in the conflict, the president confined this embargo to implements and munitions actually used in warfare. These included airplanes, airplane engines and parts, rifles, guns, ammunition, poison gas, war ships and their equipment. Hereafter, any American who violates the embargo may be punished by a $10,000 fine, five years imprisonment, or both. If the president chooses he may later expand the proscribed list to include such things as cotton, copper and other raw materials. 1935-10-12.text: London, Oct. 11. —Utterly unconfirmed reports that the famed village of Aduwa had been recaptured by Ethiopians in a bloody, night-long battle, came out of Africa tonight. They shared front pages over the world with news that the League of Nations had decided to help Ethiopia get the arms she needs while barring them from Italy. The Italian general staff threw 110,000 men into a slow and steady march toward the heart of Ethiopia, said delayed dispatches from the southern front. In the south, some unverified reports said, there were Ethiopian successes, the warriors of the Negus, allegedly taking Walwal and nearby Wardair. It was at Walwal that a boundary clash last December started the explosive Italo-Ethiopian conflict. In their first step toward applying sanctions, half a hundred nations at Geneva composing the league's coordination committee, voted to lift the existing embargo as to E

Washington, Oct. 12 ()—Government authorities said today that the British monopoly of the best radio circuit between Europe and the United States which prevented broadcasting in America of a speech by Baron Pompeo Alcisi, Italian delegate to the League of Nations, would soon be broken. A contract was recently signed between the American Telephone & Telegraph company and the French government, officials said, for 28 similar circuits direct from Paris to the United States. The federal communications commission issued a license to the A. T. & T. for the new circuit only this week. It will not, however, become operative until a new station is erected near Paris to connect with the telephone company station at Lawrenceville, N. J. The contract between the A. T. & T. and the French government was negotiated upon the urging of the communications commission and the state, war and navy department

Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, Oct. 11.—(AP)—The British government acted speedily today to pave the way for more drastic sanctions as the League of Nations took the first punitive action against Italy. Anticipating developments requiring the possible approval of parliament, the government announced that body would reconvene Oct. 22 instead of Oct. 29. It was officially explained the action was taken because of requirements for the public interest. All authoritative quarters readily agreed, however, it was because of the Italo-Ethiopian war and presaged an ever-increasing British determination to penalize a covenant breaker. These sources said presumably a British embargo upon munitions shipments to Ethiopia was lifted automatically when the League committee recommended that all members take such a step. Hereafter, it was said, Ethiopia may buy anything she wants from British mun

MOSCOW. CP, Fifty persons were killed and 300 injured in an earthquake at Tovildolinsky, in the district of Tadjekistan, near the border of Afghanistan, Oct. 8, reports received Friday night disclosed. First reports of the disaster reached Moscow late Friday night, all telephone and telegraph communications having been down previously. The first message said the population was without doctors or medicines and appealed for immediate help. Bridges across the Khangan river were destroyed and the property damage was reported heavy. Doctors, with medical and food supplies, were being rushed in from surrounding districts. Other physicians and supplies will leave Moscow by airplane as soon as the weather permits.

GENEVA. (F. A determined League of Nations’ committee began to apply the screws to belligerent Italy by slapping a general arms embargo upon that nation and by removing all restrictions for a flow of arms and ammunition to Ethiopia. This co-ordination committee of half a hundred nations also appointed a sub-committee to study the possibility of a financial boycott against the fascist kingdom. A resolution adopted by the powerful group recommended that any league state restricting the shipment of arms to Ethiopia should immediately lift such an embargo. Thus the league will aid Emperor Haile Selassie to arm his poorly equipped warriors, but will hinder Premier Mussolini from replenishing his munitions needs from foreign markets. Haile Selassie has repeatedly protested against an arms embargo upon his country, pointing out that Ethiopia has no munitions factories, while Italy has several.

(Copyright, 1935, by the Associated Press.) Addis Ababa, Oct. 12.—Emperor Haile Selassie granted the Italian minister, Luigi Vinci-Gigliucci, a time extension of twenty hours today within which to leave the country after the minister had barricaded himself in the legation in defiance of the ruler's orders to quit the capital immediately. The King of Kings extended his ultimatum from 11 a.m. today to 7 a.m. tomorrow, but announced that if the Italian minister failed to leave then, he would be expelled. His military attache had barricaded himself in the Italian legation with the minister. Ethiopian government officials said the Italian minister was deliberately trying to create an incident by compelling Ethiopian troops to invade his legation and drag him out. They said they feared that such action would give Premier Mussolini a pretext for saying Italian sovereignty had been violated. Emp

Athens, Oct. 11 (4)—Greece’s new royalist government issued a proclamation to the people today calling former King George, for 12 years in exile, “the father and protector of all Greeks.” The statement was signed by General George Kondylis, “The Little Corporal,” and minister of war who seized the reins of the government in a sudden coup d’etat yesterday which dealt a death blow to the republic. (In London former King George smilingly went his way. His equerry said “his majesty has no plans for an immediate return which can be published. We are very busy, that is all I can say.”) Athens newspapers issued special editions this afternoon asserting George would return to Greece the first week in November and already has his baggage packed. The Greek minister to Great Britain, the newspapers asserted, called upon the former monarch to congratulate him. In his message Kondylis made a warm bid

Rome, Oct. 11 (#)—Premier Mussolini plans to alter the commercial map of Europe if League of Nations’ powers interfere too much with his changes in the map of Africa, it was learned tonight from an authoritative source. His army will go ahead with the war in Africa, officials said, but in the meantime Italy at home will fight an economic battle. Countries that refuse to sell Italy goods in the application of sanctions, they claimed, “will cut off their noses to spite their faces.” Italy will remember her friends and her enemies, the officials said, and will buy where she is a welcome customer. At the same time a source close to the government asserted Italy would remain a member of the League unless military sanctions are adopted. This source, however, said the League was too much under British domination and was being used as a “tool” of Britain's hostility to Italy. Italy last year bro

1935-05-19.text: (UP)—T. E. Shaw (Lawrence of Arabia) was slowly sinking early today, and his end was believed near. It was feared that the glamorous hero of the World War was about to die, victim of an accident in which he swerved his speeding motorcycle on a country road near Woel to avoid striking a lad on a bicycle, and sustained critical injuries. Shortly after midnight, Dr. C. P. Allen, of the staff of the Bovington Military Camp here, and several nurses began a stern fight to check the patient’s sinking condition. They described his condition as “most doubtful.” Bulletins issued during the evening were increasingly pessimistic. Congestion in a lung and the chest complicated the condition of his fractured skull and lacerated brain. Shaw had been unconscious since the accident on Monday and had to be artificially fed in his comatose condition. A witness said Shaw came around a turn in the road, side

OBCOW, May 18—The world's largest land plane, the Maxim Gorky, collided with an escorting plane today, broke in mid-air and crashed to the ground, bringing death to 28 persons in the worst disaster ever to befall a passenger plane. The wreckage of the two airships and the broken bodies of the victims fell over the village of Socol, on the outskirts of Moscow, crushing at least one house, but reports that several villagers died under the debris failed to find confirmation. Watches With Horror "The Gorky dived crazily and I watched with horror while it went to pieces in the air," said one eyewitness. One house was hit by a wing weighted down by four motors, and it tore the roof and the whole side off the building. The bodies of the victims, some of them women and children, were strewn about with the wreckage, many dismembered. Blame for the tragedy was fixed by Soviet officials on the pilo

Munich, Germany, May 18, (7)— Police curbed Catholic Charity Day drastically today, seizing all contributions collected after previously forbidding further rattling of money boxes in the streets. Many of the collectors for Catholic charities were arrested, and priests were molested as Nazis staged anti-Catholic demonstrations. All collectors were summoned to police stations where their tin cans were confiscated. The action followed numerous minor clashes in which uniformed storm troopers were conspicuous. Aroused members of the Catholic clergy filed a protest with the ministry of the interior.

MOSCOW, May 18 — Struck in midair by a small pursuit plane, the Maxim Gorki, world’s largest airplane, plunged to destruction today, bringing death to 48 persons. The magnificent airliner, pride of all Soviet Russia, disintegrated high above ground, and its wreckage, together with the bodies of crew and passengers, was scattered over a 2000-foot radius. Of the victims, eight were women and six were children, members of the families of workers who were being taken on a flying holiday as a reward for faithful service. Eleven of the 48 were members of the crew. The pilot of the plane that crashed into the vitals of the air monster also was a victim. Directly Blamed The accident, according to the government, was the direct fault of the aviator in the smaller plane, who had been instructed specifically not to perform any stunts near the liner. In defiance of these instructions, it was declare

Paris, May 20. — A jury's choice of a German girl as "Miss France" in a beauty contest nearly resulted in a riot among the audience Saturday. A committee picked Elizabeth Fitz, 22-year-old Saarlander, who took French nationality after the recent plebiscite. The decision was greeted with cat calls. Order was restored with difficulty. After the spectators had been pacified, the winner announced she would not accept the title because of the reaction of the audience, so the jury awarded the crown to a 16-year-old Parisian, Giselle Preville.

By The Associated Press WASHINGTON, May 18.—While President Roosevelt completed in seclusion a sternly worded bonus veto, a check of senate votes today disclosed that his rejection of the inflationary $2,200,000,000 Patman bonus bill almost certainly would be upheld. FD Needs 33 Votes A virtually complete survey failed to show a single change in the 35 votes registered or announced against the inflationary bill when it passed the senate early last week despite the intense anti-veto campaign conducted by its friends. Should 33 vote with the president the veto would be upheld. On the other hand, several senators who voted for the bill originally appeared to be wavering in view of the president's dramatic show of determination to kill the bill. The executive's intention to appear personally to present his veto, a hitherto unprecedented action, was held by administration leaders to have alre

DALLAS, May 18.—Raging winds and flood waters killed at least eight persons and probably fatally injured many others in a devastating, estimated million dollar outburst in Texas today. Four persons were killed as a series of twisters swept through north, central and east Texas. Wind-whipped structures lay in wreckage; railroad and highway bridges sagged in swollen streams; rampaging waters entered towns and crops and cattle were destroyed. Twisters struck viciously at Weches, Weldon, Cadmor and Belott in Houston county; Teague, Hearne and the small communities of Oakwood and Turlington, both near Palestine; Gilmer and Timpson. Dead were J. P. Phillips, 69 killed near Timpson; Mrs. J. P. Phillips, 57; George Crenshaw, 70, killed at Weches and an unidentified negro, killed at Weldon. Hundreds of homes were destroyed and business houses were wrecked. Unofficial estimates of the widespread d

WASHINGTON, May 18.—House and Senate Democratic chiefs engaged today in some additional underground defy-hurling which seriously threatened the very life of NRA. Word was sent to the House that there would be dangerous delay in the Senate if any major changes were made in the Clark resolution extending NRA only 10 months and stripping control over intrastate business. Retort Sent Back And promptly the retort went back that the Senate should let the House do its own legislating. One of the messengers was S.Q. Clery Williams, former NRA chief. He conferred with Chairman Harrison of the Senate Finance Committee and Chairman Doughton of the House Ways and Means Committee. But since the situation was actually endangering chances of getting a bill through before NRA dies June 16, the disputants generally declined to let their names be used.
